Flood victims wait four years for repairs to homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
21:41:50 UTC
06:41:50 KST

Tradie shortages leave flood-hit residents waiting almost four years for repairs
In short:
Homes affected by the River Murray flood event in 2022 are still waiting for repairs.
Nationally, there is a 141,000-person skilled workers shortage, according to Master Builders Australia.
What's next?
The SA and federal governments have committed funding to help cover the travel expenses of rural or regional apprentices travelling long distances to keep them on the job.
For almost four years, Jamie Bruce has been sleeping on a fold-out couch.
Their family home at Morgan was inundated by floodwater during South Australia's third-largest River Murray flood in 2022, just 10 months after moving in.
It destroyed the lower level of the home, washing away Jamie's bedroom and identity.
"I was just starting to decorate the walls and get things to a state where the space was me," they said.
Jamie Bruce is still sleeping on a fold-out couch waiting for the house repairs to be finished. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
"Then I watched my little dragons that were on the wall slowly disappear under the water."
Loading...
Floodwaters peaked at 186 gigalitres a day, leaving only concrete and wooden cladding behind in Jamie's bedroom.
"It looks like Armageddon in here,"
The family's staircase is being held up by two wooden panels. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
Tradie and insurance 'nightmare'
Jamie's mum, Kay Bruce, describes the first 12 months following the flood as "a nightmare".
The family spent five of those months living out of a friend's large tin shed.
"Thinking about [that time] now still brings tears to my eyes," Ms Bruce said.
Frustrated by the delay for their insurer to send out a tradie, the family took a payout so they could source their own workers.
"[I had] so many phone calls where they would never come back to me," she said.
Kay Bruce says the situation has taken a mental and physical toll on her family. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
"I've got a spreadsheet, and it shows just name after name after name."
Despite trying to project-manage the rebuild, after three years Ms Bruce was still yet to have a tradesperson follow through and do the job.
"I can't understand when people make arrangements to come and do work or make quotes and then just don't turn up, don't phone you, don't text you," she said.
"I feel like we are just treading water and are in limbo … we just want to get back to some resemblance of how things were."
Her husband, Rob Bruce, said that while the process had been exhausting for the whole family, it came with a level of guilt.
"We have friends that lost their entire place and they're still in the caravan park whilst their houses are being built," Mr Bruce said.
"We'd feel bad knowing that our place was all done and they're still in the caravan park waiting."
With the cost of materials to build a home spiking in recent years, Mr Bruce said the family felt trepidation about the future.
"It worries me that it's going to be a hit for us [to rebuild]," he said.
Material costs through the roof
The cost to build a new home in South Australia has risen by almost 40 per cent since 2021, according to the Insurance Council of Australia.
It is something social policy, climate and international engagement manager Alix Pearce says is a growing national issue.
"The average cost to build a home has increased 30 per cent nationally over the last five years, which considerably outstrips inflation at 24 per cent,"
"We're seeing this [rise] in materials and labour costs, too; for example, roof tiles have gone up 77 per cent over the last five years."
Alix Pearce says governments need to increase investment in resilience to build stronger homes. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)
Ms Pearce said state and federal governments needed to do more to uplift their investment in housing resilience and address tradie shortages across the country.
"The cost of extreme weather is rising considerably … last year disasters drove $4 billion worth of insured losses,"
"We need to see increased investment in trades and construction, particularly in those high-risk areas in Australia."
Building up the workforce
There is currently a 141,000-person skilled workers shortage nationally, according to Master Builders Australia.
In South Australia, about 20,000 workers are required over the next five years to meet major project and housing demand, according to a state government spokesperson.
The spokesperson said it has committed $11 million over the next two years, alongside the federal government, to help the travel expenses of rural or regional apprentices travelling long distances to keep them on the job.
Master Builders Australia projects a worker shortage of 935,600 by 2035. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
"The new measure will support an additional 400 regional apprentices and trainees to undertake their training," the statement said.
It also said it was building three new technical colleges, including in Murray Bridge, and a new TAFE Trades Workshop in Mount Barker, which aims to support 1,200 additional construction trade apprentices.
Andrew Johnson says council reserves and infrastructure are still being rebuilt and revegetated following the flood event. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
Mid Murray Council chief executive Andrew Johnson said any commitment is welcome as his regional community continues to recover from the 2022-23 flood while experiencing trade shortages.
"We have a number of open spaces and reserves along the river that still need to be rehabilitated [post-flood] and still need irrigation systems put back in," he said.
The 2022-23 floodwater line is still visible from the Morgan wharf. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
Federal Minister for Trade and Tourism, Senator Don Farrell, said the Albanese government announced steps to introduce new Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements that are "simpler and fairer for all Australians" back in June.
"The independent Colvin review made it clear that our current arrangements have not kept pace with the changing nature of disasters," he said.
"We are currently consulting with the states, territories and councils on our proposed new Disaster Recovery Funding Framework.”
Mental and physical recovery
While grateful to be back living in their family home, the Bruce family said their life by the river was filled with complex and conflicting feelings.
They said a completed home would help give them some closure.
Kay, Jamie and Rob Bruce say they have made it through the situation together. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)
"I'm grateful for where we are, it's paradise really," Kay Bruce said.
"But I'm probably not as happy as I used to be, not as cheerful, not as satisfied with life.
"If you promise to come and help, please do it, please follow through."

Leo on a larger tour of France
Leo is on a whirlwind four-day visit to France. Local Church leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church's standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
The pope told an estimated 150,000 people gathered for a Mass in a field near the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes earlier on Sunday that the Church must have the courage to face its past.
"In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze," the first US pope said.
Véronique Garnier, one of the survivors in the meeting with the pope, said she had found the Mass, in which Leo referred to abuse without directly apologizing for it, troubling and wondered why she had attended.
But she said she was encouraged by her meeting with Leo.
"I do indeed believe there is hope – hope that there can be change and truly listening to us at a deep level, rather than just superficially with beautiful words that are never followed by any real action," she said.
Leo also spoke about the abuse scandals in a closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sunday, according to a Vatican-provided text.
The pope thanked the bishops for the "courageous measures" he said they had taken to confront the scandals and urged them to buttress their safeguarding efforts and "continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
Leo has drawn large crowds on his visit to France. Around 800,000 people came for an outdoor Mass on the Champs-Élysées with the pope in Paris on Saturday. He has also again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence.
'Cannot ignore this issue,' Leo says
Leo has previously apologized directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church's credibility across the world. On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops there that they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.
Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for the French bishops, said the pope's desire to have the meeting "shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns."
The pope's itinerary in France included six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains that attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.
The site is also connected to a scandal that has dogged the Vatican in recent years. The shrine's facade has a series of mosaics by Rev. Marko Rupnik, a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse.
Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations. Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the pope on Thursday, sharply criticizing an ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.
The mosaics, stories tall, have been covered for the pope's visit with large, muted yellow tarps. Arriving for the Mass on Sunday, Leo was driven in his open-top popemobile near the facade of the shrine and the covered mosaics.
The pope, who on Friday sharply reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illnesses, again mentioned the Church's pro-life stance in Lourdes.
Meeting with volunteers who help sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in the shrine's waters, Leo urged them to remember the "profound meaning" of healthcare work.
"That is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person," the pope said. "Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death!"

The US-China relationship has stabilised but on Beijing’s terms
Managed rivalry is not peace; it is a rules-based pause with China largely writing the rules. The test is whether the US can live with it
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Wenran Jiang, the founding director of the China Institute and Mactaggart Research Chair Emeritus at the University of Alberta, is an adviser at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy. 
For all the solemnity of the B-2 flyover with four F‑22 Raptors and a silent South Lawn drill, the real business of US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was narrower than the choreography. The Chinese readout reiterated the concept that should frame the relationship’s next phase: constructive strategic stability – cooperation as the primary track, competition kept within bounds, differences managed, conflict avoided.
Stripped of banquet rhetoric, the Washington leg of the 2026 Xi-Trump cycle cements a managed rivalry on Beijing’s terms: China sets the boundaries while Washington – constrained by rare earth dependence, market jitters and a crowded election calendar – accepts stabilisation over confrontation.
Trump called it a “great meeting” and revived the “friendship” trope; Xi was more doctrinal. Having previously raised the Thucydides Trap and asked if their countries could transcend a rising power-vs-hegemon collision, he announced last Thursday: “The Thucydides Trap can be overcome.” Competition, he said, “should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses”; it should be “healthy”, “kept within bounds”.

Dmitri Shostakovich at 120: How the icon drew on Bach, jazz, and cinema to create his own musical language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
21:06:00 UTC
06:06:00 KST

Dmitri Shostakovich at 120: How the icon drew on Bach, jazz, and cinema to create his own musical language
Dmitri Shostakovich was born on September 25, 1906. Probably the most famous Soviet composer, he was forced to collaborate with the state even as he suffered under its campaign against “formalism.” For many, his life embodies the plight of an intellectual in the arts and humanities under totalitarian rule. But Shostakovich’s creative life was about far more than his fraught relationship with the authorities. At Meduza’s request, music critic Stepan Furin explores how the composer drew on classical music, jazz, and film.
In his book “Stolen Time,” Dutch composer Louis Andriessen playfully divided his fellow composers into “hedgehogs” and “foxes.” A hedgehog is prickly and nearsighted. He develops one fundamental approach that shapes how he sees the world and music. A fox keeps looking around until he darts off in an unpredictable direction.
In this playful dichotomy, on the 120th anniversary of his birth, Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich is unmistakably a “fox.” People who knew him remembered a nervous man who fidgeted constantly, his hands always moving. American conductor Robert Craft wrote:
Shostakovich’s face is the most expressive and intelligent we have seen in the Soviet Union. He is the shyest and most nervous person I have ever met. He smokes incessantly, wrinkles his nose, and keeps adjusting his glasses. He has a habit of peering intently at someone, then looking away guiltily when caught. You can read his thoughts in those frightened, very intelligent eyes, and find no hint of treachery.
His nervousness did not affect his piano playing: onstage, Shostakovich was a confident, composed virtuoso. His foxlike cunning runs through countless stories about him — some funny and ironic, others grotesque, with undercurrents of terror and hopelessness. In a twentieth-century world where “today there’s a fire, tomorrow football, and the day after that — who ate whom,” it is hard to imagine how a great artist under constant state scrutiny could have survived any other way.
More than anything, Shostakovich’s foxlike nature shaped his music. He borrowed from everyone and everything, whether it was the elevated style of the preludes and fugues in “The Well-Tempered Clavier,” the abstruse twelve-tone structures in Arnold Schoenberg’s pieces, or the popular dance rhythms of jazz. He thought nothing of putting a tune he had heard on the street into a symphony, or a Broadway hit into a piano concerto. A good fox can make use of anything.
Like any self-respecting musician, Shostakovich’s tastes ranged widely across periods and styles. He held Gustav Mahler in high regard, drew inspiration from Modest Mussorgsky and Benjamin Britten, and revered Bach, whose every prelude and fugue, he maintained, could be “played at any tempo, with any dynamic shading.”
Shostakovich himself wrote in nearly every musical genre, from symphonies to film scores. He changed quickly and radically: within a couple of years, he could move from sprawling, decadent modernism to classical rigor, from large orchestral works to small chamber pieces, from thunder, clatter, and postmodernist quotation to quiet, brevity, and musical gestures of utmost restraint. He reshaped every borrowed musical idea and technique, keeping his sound unique no matter how much he took from others.
No single article could do justice to the Leningrad school’s brightest star. So we’ll look briefly at several areas of music whose conventions Shostakovich made his own.
Film
“I am now devoting myself to cinema worship. Yesterday, something rather interesting happened at the movie theater. They were showing a nature film, ‘Marsh and Water Birds of Sweden.’ I sat down to accompany it. I got carried away and started imitating birds like a man possessed,” the 19-year-old Shostakovich wrote to his friend, the pianist and composer Lev Oborin.
During his lean student years, he earned extra money playing piano for silent films, and he did it with flair. Audiences booed, thinking the pianist was drunk or out of his mind. The orchestra musicians shook his hand, though, and Shostakovich himself was delighted. Cuts between contrasting scenes, sudden shifts in mood, and the emotional counterpoint between sight and sound — as when pointedly proper or banal music accompanies vulgarity and cruelty — all eventually became part of his musical language.
Shostakovich also wrote a great deal of music for films, including Grigory Kozintsev’s avant-garde “Novy Vavilon” (“The New Babylon,” 1929), Sergei Yutkevich’s “Zlatye gory” (“Golden Mountains,” 1931), Sergei Gerasimov’s monumental Stalinist film “Molodaya gvardiya” (“The Young Guard,” 1948), and Kozintsev’s later Shakespeare films “Hamlet” (1964) and “King Lear” (1971).
Since the composer’s death, his music has continued to appear in other directors’ films. Leos Carax uses “String Quartet No. 3” in “The Lovers on the Bridge” (1991). The familiar “Waltz No. 2” plays over the opening credits of Stanley Kubrick’s “Eyes Wide Shut” (1999). The Largo from “String Quartet No. 8” accompanies the cold detachment of Yorgos Lanthimos’s “The Lobster” (2015).
Jazz
Always eager to hear something new, Shostakovich was bound to take an interest in jazz — especially since Soviet party ideologues couldn’t stand it, and he never missed a chance to annoy them. According to the article “Muddle Instead of Music,” the young Shostakovich had borrowed the “nervous, convulsive, spasmodic music” of his opera “Ledi Makbet Mtsenskogo uyezda” (“Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk District”) from jazz. But he also drew on jazz for far less bloodthirsty works.
Shostakovich wrote “Tahiti Trot” in 1927 in 45 minutes — to win a bet, according to conductor Nikolai Malko. It is an orchestral arrangement of Vincent Youmans’s famous jazz standard “Tea for Two”, which legends including Oscar Peterson and Thelonious Monk also recorded. Shostakovich later wrote suites for jazz orchestra (1934) and variety orchestra (1938) featuring similar waltzes. Yet for many listeners, these are his most recognizable melodies.
Neither “Piano Concerto No. 1” (1933) nor the ballet “Svetly ruchey” (“The Bright Stream”) carried a formal jazz label — and Soviet party ideology ruled it out. Could stalwart Soviet collective farmers possibly dance to capitalist jazz, or model Soviet pianists play it? Apparently they could: the infectious, off-kilter rhythms, prominent brass, and abrupt juxtapositions of contrasting passages all owe something to the jazz craze of the “Roaring Twenties.”
The works labeled “jazz” are relatively light, with a hint of sardonic eccentricity, and orchestras often play them as encores. Their only real ties to jazz are their lightness, danceable rhythms, and use of the saxophone — all striking in Shostakovich’s brooding, sardonic sound world. Deeper jazz structures and ideas also entered his musical language, heavily modified, and surface from time to time in all sorts of works.
The symphony
The twentieth-century symphony poses one small problem: nobody knows what it is. Obvious criteria, such as four contrasting movements in a prescribed structure or a fixed orchestral lineup, don’t hold up. It can seem as though every major composer pulls a random piece for a random group of performers from a desk drawer full of manuscripts and stamps “Symphony” on it.
Shostakovich wrote all kinds of symphonies. Traditional ones, like the First and Fifth; modernist, Mahler-length ones, like the Fourth; ones with a chorus and soloists, like the Thirteenth. Even among such varied works, “Symphony No. 14,” completed in 1969, stands out. Its instrumentation: a chamber orchestra of strings and percussion, plus soprano and bass soloists. Its structure: eleven movements set to poems by four writers — Federico García Lorca, Guillaume Apollinaire, Wilhelm Küchelbecker, and Rainer Maria Rilke.
In form, the Fourteenth recalls vocal song cycles: Modest Mussorgsky’s “Pesni i plyaski smerti” (“Songs and Dances of Death”), which Shostakovich loved and orchestrated in 1962, though he regretted how quickly it ended; Franz Schubert’s “Winterreise”; and Gustav Mahler’s “Des Knaben Wunderhorn.” Death is one of the forces shaping the symphony. It appears in different guises in every movement, except perhaps the ninth, “O Delvig, Delvig!” (“Oh, Delvig, Delvig!”), set to Küchelbecker’s words.
What makes it a symphony, then? Its development, the way the work takes shape. The music is not assembled from random pieces in random order. Shostakovich gives it an intricate structure of recurring motifs, sounds and familiar musical ideas. He presents them in different lights and from different angles, gradually weaving them together and developing them. There is the frozen time of the slow movements, where the music stirs slowly and almost inaudibly before suddenly exploding. The void between answering phrases from the voice and strings. And the angry, desperate, macabre grotesquerie that emerges whenever dance rhythms take shape in the orchestra.
In a letter to one of his closest friends, Isaak Glikman, Shostakovich wrote: “Sasha Chorny’s death struck me. He was fighting a fire, and then, just like that, he died. A beautiful death.” Shostakovich himself came to be associated with fighting fires through his work with the conservatory’s firefighting crew during the siege of Leningrad. Around the world, people recognize the 1942 cover of “Time” showing the profile of a frail man in a gleaming helmet and large glasses against a backdrop of bombed-out ruins in flames.
The task of the mad, doomed Romantic hero of the nineteenth century was to stoke the fires of struggles for freedom, fleeting national unity, and a new world order. The poetic voice of the 20th century, having witnessed the Battle of the Somme, the gates of Auschwitz, the ashes of Hiroshima, the abyss of the Gulag and the ruined fourth reactor of the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, desperately tried to put those fires out — mostly without success. Shostakovich’s music today, on his 120th birthday, will not stop wars, is unlikely to raise anyone’s fighting spirit, and certainly will not bring a rush of happiness. It will lead us down the narrow paths of a labyrinth with infinitely many dimensions, into emptiness — the only place where we can avoid losing ourselves. And that, you must admit, is worth a great deal.

UK police arrest five men amid bomb alert outside US air base
The UK authorities have apprehended five men on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack outside RAF Fairford, a British air base that also hosts US warplanes involved in strikes on Iran.
According to a statement by Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone on Sunday, police received “a call relating to three suspicious vehicles travelling towards RAF Fairford.” The local media later described the vehicles as three white vans.
Officers arriving at the scene subsequently arrested five individuals near the village of Whelford “on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act,” with Counter Terror Police investigating what officials characterized as a “major incident.”
The BBC published an unverified photo purportedly showing the arrested suspects sitting half-naked on the ground with their hands behind their backs and faces blurred.
A British Army bomb disposal unit was deployed to the scene to examine the vehicles, with approximately 85 households evacuated as a precaution, Ocone told reporters. Several British media outlets have carried what appears to be helicopter footage depicting a specialized wheeled robot operating near the vans.
Local residents who have nowhere else to stay have been provided temporary shelter inside a leisure center.
Commenting on the incident in a post on X, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged “people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.”
Later on Sunday, Gloucestershire Constabulary’s Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth gave an update, saying that the authorities believe the “matter to be contained.” However, she declined to reveal whether the police were looking for any more suspects.
She also clarified that local residents would be unable to return to their homes tonight.
Meanwhile, Sky News claimed that while there are “no conclusions yet,” the police are looking into Iran’s potential involvement in the suspected bomb plot, among several other lines of inquiry, with Reuters carrying a similar report.
The US Air Force has operated out of RAF Fairford for decades, with heavy bombers stationed there, including those used in strikes on Iran.
Back in July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps issued a statement warning the UK specifically that “any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces.”
Commenting on Sunday’s incident, a US military spokesperson told local media that the Pentagon was “working closely with our UK counterparts to monitor this situation.”
US President Donald Trump, for his part, told reporters that the suspects “were looking to do big damage to our fort.”
“We had them under investigation… We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he claimed, adding that “working with Britain – it was an amazing job.”

Assistant Foreign Affairs and Trade Minister Matt Thistlethwaite says Australia’s budget position remains "relatively strong" compared to other countries.
He told News24 the war in the Middle East had put pressure on global economies, but said Australia was faring well.
"We've got one of the lowest budget deficits to GDP anywhere in the world, our debt to GDP ratio is one of the lowest in the OECD, and our expenditure to GDP is very low by international comparisons," he said.

NEW DELHI, September 27. /TASS/. The United States will seek to contain India as the country grows stronger and emerges as a global power, Russian Ambassador to India Denis Alipov said.
"This year, at the Raisina Dialogue, a senior US official publicly said that the United States would never allow India to become the next China - a competitor [to the US]. It sounded like a Freudian slip," he said at the NDTV Defence Summit.

Flag carrier Air Algerie will resume flights from Algiers to Doha, Qatar, after a suspension of nearly seven months, Algeria’s state news agency APS reported Sunday, citing the airline.
The first flight is scheduled to depart at 12.55 am Tuesday, local Algeria time.
The route will initially operate three times a week, on Sundays, Tuesdays, and Fridays, expanding to daily flights starting on Oct. 25, at the same departure time, APS reported.
Air Algerie suspended flights to and from Doha in late February amid deteriorating security conditions in the Middle East following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and sites elsewhere in the region, disrupting air travel across the Middle East.

Malaysian history is already Malay-centric. Why do some Malays think their history is suppressed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Despite controversy, Malaysian scholars’ nativist views draw support
- Malaysian history is viewed by some Malay nativists as suppressed or misrepresented, with figures like Solehah Yaacob promoting alternative histories linking Malays to ancient achievements and Islamic origins.
- This nativist view arises from Malay socio-political anxieties, despite Malays being the majority with constitutional privileges, reflecting fears over economic competition and historical marginalisation.
- Scholars warn that such unsubstantiated alternative histories, popularised through seminars and books, risk distorting Malaysia's complex multicultural past and oversimplifying historical narratives.
AI generated
KUALA LUMPUR – From claiming that Malays could fly to arguing that they taught the Romans how to build ships, Malaysian linguistics professor Solehah Yaacob has become the butt of international ridicule and a source of embarrassment at home.
Although she was fired by the International Islamic University Malaysia in April, she still has plenty of supporters who believe that Malay achievements have been suppressed, misrepresented or hidden in mainstream history.
New videos continue to be uploaded daily on Solehah’s social media accounts, followed by more than 500,000 people across Facebook and TikTok, drawing supportive comments from viewers.
“Professor Solehah is not only smart, but also sincere in spreading the truth, and bravely uncovering the dirty work of colonisers,” Facebook user Muhammad Muadzam wrote.
Support for Solehah’s work extends beyond the internet.
Her multi-day Lost Malay History and Civilisation seminar is in its fifth iteration since the inaugural series was held in Kuala Lumpur in November 2025, signalling sustained demand for such content.
ST contacted Solehah for comment, but she did not respond by press time.
Malay socio-political and economic anxieties
Sociologist Aziff Azuddin from Iman Research told The Straits Times: “My reading is that the multicultural landscape of Malaysia, as well as Malay socio-political and economic anxieties, is why nativists, right-wingers – and people like Solehah – have such a purchase among some sections of the Malay community.”
Nativism is the belief that a country should primarily reflect and protect the interests and identity of those regarded as its original inhabitants, often at the expense of groups seen as later arrivals.
Support for nativist views reflects a persistent sense of historical marginalisation among some Malay Muslims, say sociologists, even as Malaysia’s mainstream history is itself often criticised for privileging Malay-Muslim narratives over the country’s pre-Islamic past.
Malays make up more than 60 per cent of Malaysia’s 34 million people and enjoy constitutionally protected privileges, but perceptions of Chinese economic strength have long fuelled unease among some over their own position.
Scholars who challenge mainstream Malaysian history
Aside from Solehah, there are others like historian Azmi Arifin from Universiti Sains Malaysia.
He has been vocal on social media in challenging mainstream accounts of Malaysian history, arguing that they rely excessively on biased British Orientalist sources.
Azmi, who has more than 28,000 followers on TikTok, argues that Malaysian history inherited terms such as “feudal” and “absolute monarchy”, which he says do not fully reflect the political and cultural realities of traditional Malay government.
“When we use concepts from Europe, we are indirectly and automatically making a Eurocentric comparison,” he said in a podcast in August.
He cited how Malay anti-colonial figures like Mat Kilau, a Pahang chieftain who led an uprising against the British, were labelled as “rebels”, noting that this reflected a British perspective.
For some Malay nativists, the country’s multi-ethnic character has diluted Malay historical primacy and obscured the place of Malays at the centre of the national story.
This is despite Malaysian schools placing heavy emphasis on the 15th-century Melaka Sultanate as the golden age of Malay political power and the starting point for the story of modern Malaysia.
Aziff, who recently published an article titled “Why Malaysians cannot agree on their own history”, said each ethnic group has a stake in where the country’s history begins.
“The non-Malays are disinclined to accept a pre-British administrative history because that’s not where ‘Malaysian history’ began for them,” he argued, adding that doing so also means “surrendering to the Malay nativist agenda”.
Malay nativists like Solehah have turned further into the past to reinforce the claim that Malays possess a historical primacy that gives them a special claim over the country in the present.
In a video published on Sept 6, she dismissed the Malays’ Hindu-Buddhist past as “mere propaganda”.
“It is a systematic propaganda from the 1800s,” she claimed, perpetrated by Western figures including Stamford Raffles.
“The so-called (Hindu-Buddha) relics found are put there recently.”
Her other lectures, shared widely on YouTube, also blend Malay history with Islam, with claims such as that Abraham was Malay and that Moses travelled to Gunung Jerai in Kedah, while drawing links between the Malay world and Khadijah, the wife of Prophet Muhammad.
Historian Eddin Khoo said the close identification of Malayness with Islam has made the region’s pre-Islamic past uncomfortable for some nativists, despite abundant evidence of Hindu and Buddhist influence in ancient Kedah.
“Solehah is a fantasist, but people want to believe that about themselves,” Khoo told ST. “To them, everything must trace back to their puritanical idea of Islam; otherwise, it is illegitimate.”
He describes this as “essentialist history”, in which communities look to the past for evidence of their own superiority.
Khoo said there is an irony in seeking a culturally pure Malay past when historical Malay societies were deeply cosmopolitan, shaped by centuries of interaction with India, China, the Middle East and Europe.
Evidence of this can be found in the records of Portuguese chronicler Tome Pires who said that 84 languages were spoken in Melaka in the 1500s.
“Malays today are struggling to come to terms with their own historical ‘worldliness’,” Khoo argued. “Nowadays, foreign influences are sometimes treated as a threat rather than enriching Malay civilisation.”
Alternative history books
While fantastical histories have long circulated on the fringes, the involvement of credentialled academics can give such claims legitimacy.
Nor is it just about one or two academics with unorthodox views.
Novelist and Malay sociologist Faizal Musa from Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia pointed to the wide acceptance of alternative history books, which popularise the idea of hidden and esoteric historical facts.
The appetite for such books is reflected in the reach of publishers such as The Patriots, whose official Shopee store has more than 52,000 followers and whose books on history, geopolitics and civilisation have recorded thousands of sales on the platform.
Its catalogue includes titles such as Jangan Selewengkan Sejarah Melayu (Don’t Distort Malay History), which has spawned a sequel and an updated edition, as well as Ilmu Alam Melayu: Mistik, Manuskrip & Mitologi (Knowledge Of The Malay World: Mysticism, Manuscripts & Mythology), which explores subjects including supposedly lost Malay manuscripts.
For those who believe in hidden facts, the absence of a claim from textbooks or conventional scholarship can itself become evidence that the “true” history has been deliberately hidden.
“Simple explanations are often seen as more appealing and credible than complex ones, particularly when they appear capable of being tested or disproved,” Faizal told ST.
The persistence of such beliefs, the scholars said, reflects how debates over history are often driven as much by contemporary anxieties over identity and status as by disagreements over the past itself.
Faizal said the phenomenon was neither uniquely Malay nor Malaysian, citing similar ethno-religious currents in India and the United States.
“It’s a global issue in understanding history.”
Khoo, however, warned that the continued propagation of this unsubstantiated alternative history chisels away at the intricacies of a community’s collective history.
“Myth has an important role in not just Malay, but also Asian history; however, this is not even myth – it is fantasy,” he said.

US-China summit delivers 'modest but practical' outcomes: Citi
The big US investment bank Citi says the just concluded US-China summit delivered "modest but practical" outcomes.
Those outcomes included a two-month trade "truce" extension, a $US30 billion Board of Trade tariff reduction, a new AI dialogue and an agreement for further meetings at APEC in Shenzhen (Nov 18–19) and the G20 in Miami (Dec 14–15).
Citi's chief China economist, Xiangrong Yu, said the meeting delivered on optics with the prospect of further meetings this year "would see an unprecedented four Trump-Xi meetings, helping lower near-term risk of any breakdown in relations".
"The renewed stability commitment would perhaps ease risks such as new restrictions on Chinese AI infrastructure products and open-weight models as well as large-scale US arms sales to Taiwan within this year," Yu said.
The two sides agreed to communicate on AI incidents.
"With the coordination mechanisms in place, neither Washington nor Beijing appears inclined to slow AI development — rather, the dialogue offers a channel to address mutual concerns without resorting to more confrontational measures such as expanded export controls," Yu wrote in a research note over the weekend.
He said the summit didn't produce major economic outcomes beyond the two-month extension of the trade "truce."
"We are not concerned by the short extension window, as it can be pushed further at the next Trump-Xi meeting around APEC or the G20—and a broader deal is not out of the question."
Both sides confirmed $US30 billion in goods under the Board of Trade for reciprocal tariff cuts.
The White House fact sheet detailed US export categories—agricultural goods, fish & seafood, logs & wood products, cosmetics, and medical devices—alongside Chinese export categories including small appliances, toys, holiday decorations, and children's car seats.
Separately, the fact sheet flagged China's coal imports of 10mn tons in 2027-28.
"Following the summit, we see a lower chance of a breakdown in US-China relations within the year, averting the kind of tariff-driven volatility that markets experienced last year," Yu added.
US, China agree to tariff cuts, AI dialogue
The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $US30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.
The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said.
"The two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.
The three-day summit between Xi and President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
The two sides also agreed to set up a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.
On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to hold a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.
Reuters
This week: RBA rates decision, inflation and home prices
Australia:
Tue: RBA rates decision, Household Spending Indicator (Aug)
Wed: CPI (Aug), Dwelling approvals (Aug), Private sector credit (Aug)
Thu: Home prices (Sep), Trade balance (Aug), Job vacancies (Q3), RBA Financial Stability Review
International:
Mon: CN — Industrial profits (Aug)
Tue: US — Home prices (Jul)
Wed: CN — NBS & Rating Dog PMIs
US — PCE inflation (Aug), GDP (Q2), Trade balance (Aug)
Thu: EU — Unemployment (Aug)
US — ISM manufacturing (Sep)
Fri: EU — CPI (Sep)
US — Nonfarm payrolls, unemployment (Sep), Factory orders (Sep)
It's a busy week in the economic diary, although the RBA rates decision (Tuesday) will tend to overshadow everything locally.
A full 25 bps rate hike has been priced in by the market. Most market economists — and the big four retail banks — agree.
Certainly, a barrage of RBA-speak in recent weeks has pointed to a hike, and anything else would be a major surprise.
The Minutes of the August meeting stated that Board members thought it may be appropriate to tighten policy "pre-emptively" if risks to the inflation forecast were judged to be "significantly skewed to the upside". As Societe Generale pointed out in a note over the weekend, this is now playing out.
"RBA staff also argued a 'pre-emptive approach' to tightening is needed when the economy is subject to capacity constraints and adverse supply shocks, and this is currently the case." Societe Generale said.
September CPI inflation is released the day after (Wednesday).
While there has been much furrowing of brows and cliched hectoring of the RBA about putting the cart-before-the-horse, it doesn't really matter.
Inflation is very unlikely to suddenly disappear, nor is the RBA boardroom suddenly going resemble a cooing dovecote. The hawkish sentiment is aimed at getting ahead of the problem, rather than reacting to it.
If anything, the threat is inflation will come in even hotter than the RBA hoped for — with the consensus forecast showing trimmed mean inflation at 3.6%, and headline inflation lifting from 3.5% to perhaps 4%.
We'll get important updates on the housing market.
Building approvals (Wednesday) are always volatile. They fell marginally in July, and the consensus, without great conviction, is they will fall again.
Cotality publishes its September Home Value Index on Wednesday.
Depending on your view of things, home prices are expected to fall again nationally/housing affordability is expected to improve.
Australia's trade surplus has been narrowing in recent months, but an increase in iron ore and coal shipments and prices may well see the surplus widen again beyond $2 billion in August. Once again, volatile gold exports make tipping it accurately a mug's game.
Overseas, the main interest will be US PCE inflation and jobs data.
The Fed's preferred measure of inflation, Personal Consumption Expenditure (Wed) is likely to have taken another step up to 0.4% month-on-month in August, mainly thanks to higher fuel prices. It gained 0.2% in July.
Nonfarm payrolls (Friday) are likely to show around 80-thousand new jobs were created in the US in September, which would be in line with the recent trend. Unemployment is likely t hold at 4.1%.

However, the ASX, ahead of this week's likely RBA rate rise, remained under pressure, clocking the fourth successive losing week, down 0.8%.
Futures trading on the ASX shows the bleeding may have been cauterised, at least briefly, but the pulse is weak.
A gain of just 0.03%, or 3 points, was priced in when trading closed on Saturday morning.
Wall Street's gain was driven by an almost 4% jump in Microsoft shares after announcing its AI tool Copilot had new capabilities.
Chipmaker Qualcom gained 4% as well, while Akamai Technologies rallied 3.2% after an $US11.6 billion cloud services deal with AI leader Anthropic.
The deal, another one of those circular trades in vogue in the AI sector, includes a warrant that could give Anthropic up to 5% of Akamai.
"That's a positive from the standpoint that people are still investing, deals are still being done," Globalt Investments portfolio manager Thomas Martin, said without much enthusiasm.
"It's another circular deal, so OK … but Akamai stock is up."
Meta Platforms dipped 3.3% after the social media company's stock soared about 13% this week amid a strong reception to its Muse AI agent, which analysts say could benefit tech infrastructure stocks, while challenging banks, online shopping platforms and other consumer businesses.
Interestingly, the big earnings upgrades among the AI titans now sees the S&P 500 trading at its lowest level (19 times expected earnings) since 2023.
NAB's head of FX Strategy Ray Attrill said lower oil prices on Friday, on ongoing hopes for a phased deal that would see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lift its blockade of Iranian ports, supported stocks and brought Treasuries off Friday morning's new cycle highs.
"In equity markets the S&P500 and NASDAQ both gained 0.5% Friday for weekly gains of 1.2% and 2.1% respectively, eye opening in the context of the rise in bond yields but perhaps less so in as much as the US economy, and the outlook for corporate profits, is showing no ill-effects from the rise in yields to date."
Key global oil benchmarks Brent crude and WTI crude future both fell around $US2 a barrel. However, Brent crude futures are still trading well above $US100/barrel.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note hit a fresh 19-year high and was last up 3.4 basis points at 5.196%.
"In bond markets, (there was) a little relief Friday from the intense mid-week sell off in Treasuries — and bond globally — aided by the small pull back in oil prices. 2 and 5 year Treasury yields finished Friday down 6.5bps on the day for weekly gains of 11.5 and 14bps, respectively," Mr. Attrill said.
Traders see a 66% chance of the Federal Reserve increasing interest rates by at least 25 basis points in October, up from around 50% earlier this week, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed.
However, the Greenback still dipped on Friday with the Aussie dollar making a marginal gain to remain above 70 US cents.

Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
20:49:34 UTC
05:49:34 KST

Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
Key developments on Sept. 26-27:
- Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine, with Odesa Oblast targeted in 'mass strike'
- Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
- Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
- Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
- Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
At least 14 people were killed and 57 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as Odesa Oblast in particular came under mass attack, local authorities said on Sept. 26-27.
In southern Odesa Oblast, Russia launched "a mass strike," damaging a residential building, a medical facility, a hotel, a shop and a grain storage facility, local governor Oleh Kiper said. One person was killed while two others were injured, he added.
Overall, overnight on Sept. 27, Russian forces launched 170 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 147 drones, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at eight locations, the Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27 that residential buildings, energy infrastructure, and other civilian infrastructure were attacked in Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv oblasts overnight.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, four people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region, local authorities said. Over the past day, Russia carried out 989 attacks on 59 settlements of the region.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the northeastern city of Sumy, a Russian glide bomb attack hit a residential area, killing two people and injuring 28 others, including four children, regional authorities said.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured six others over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Sept. 26 and Sept. 27.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing two people and injuring three others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kyiv, Russian drones injured five people over the past day, damaging residential buildings and warehouses, local authorities reported.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day damaged 23 facilities, injuring two people, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured one person, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. He added that, as a result of the attacks, a high-rise apartment building, nine houses, a shop, and vehicles were damaged.
In Poltava Oblast, power lines have been damaged following the crash of a Russian drone, local governor Vitalii Diakivnych said. Around 500 customers were temporarily left without power while power company staff worked to restore the electricity supply, he added.
Zelensky said that over the past week, Russian forces launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types.

Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
Russia launched another drone attack on Kyiv on the night of Sept. 26-27, marking the third consecutive day of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
"Just today, and only in Kyiv, Russian kamikaze drones 'defeated' two kindergartens and two schools, a residential building, a car repair shop, several warehouses, and communication facilities," Zelensky said. "Everywhere in the world, such a choice of targets would be called one word: terrorism."
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 27 that a pre-trial investigation was launched into the commission of a war crime by the Russian military, which resulted in the death of a man.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at 5:17 p.m. local time that a drone struck a nine-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv.
Klitschko also said at 4:09 p.m. local time that an administrative building in the Holosiivskyi district was hit, according to preliminary reports.
In the morning of Sept. 27, Russia struck a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, Klitschko said at 9:26 a.m. local time. At least three people, a woman and two 16-year-old children, were injured in the area.
Air defense units were operating over the city, Klitschko said in an evening update. Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground also heard air defenses operating in the city.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, a Russian drone struck an uninhabited residential building at around 10 p.m. local time on Sept. 26, according to Klitschko.
A fire at the building was later brought under control, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
In the Solomianskyi district, a drone fell in an open area overnight. The resulting blast wave damaged a five-story residential building, breaking windows and damaging its facade, Klitschko said.
A fire also broke out at a warehouse in the district after the site was struck by a Russian drone, he added. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that a car service center was on fire as a result of the attack.
A woman was injured in the attack and handed over to medics, and a man was killed, the State Emergency Service said.
Zelensky said that on the morning of Sept. 27, Russian forces struck a data center in Kyiv twice.
Ukraine's largest mobile operator Kyivstar said that its headquarters was damaged during the drone attack on Sept. 27, as reported by the Ukrainian media outlet Suspilne.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In Vyshneve, five cars were damaged, and a fire broke out after a drone struck the area. In Brovary, the attack caused fires in a warehouse and an office building, according to Tkachenko.
The latest attack follows a series of Russian drone strikes on Kyiv that began overnight on Sept. 24.
Russian drones continued targeting Kyiv during the day on Sept. 26, with further damage and casualties reported. By the evening, Ukrainian officials said five people had been injured in attacks on the capital during the day.
In recent months, Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones, placing additional strain on Ukraine's air defenses.
One of Russia's newer jet-powered drone models, the Geran-5, can reportedly reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), has an estimated range of up to 950 kilometers (590 miles), and can fly at altitudes of up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).
Ukraine is developing interceptor drones aimed at countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some systems having undergone successful tests, according to Ukrainian officials. The government has not announced plans for mass production.

Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
Ukrainian forces have killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops over the past week while making gains in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast, Zelensky said on Sept. 27.
"The occupiers continue to be eliminated, and the designated objectives are being achieved," Zelensky wrote on X, citing a report by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces have video evidence confirming every Russian loss included in the weekly figure. Russia does not routinely disclose its military losses, and the figures could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15 that Russian forces have lost more than 300,000 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026. After the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, Russian losses exceeded 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Zelensky said the past week's results were achieved as part of Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman sector and another active defense operation involving Ukraine's Air Assault Forces.
Zelensky added that the heaviest fighting has been taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Lyman sectors, while Ukrainian forces are also carrying out operations in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Sumy oblasts.
He did not provide further details on the territorial gains.
Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
On Sept. 20, the 3rd Corps said it liberated a further 40 square kilometers (15.4 square miles) of territory in Donetsk Oblast and retook several villages during the ongoing offensive.

Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
Ukrainian forces have delivered around four tons of food to residents of the occupied front-line town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, distributing supplies to 100 locations across the city with the help of drones, the Kherson Oblast Military Administration head said on Sept. 27.
The operation was carried out in cooperation with several Ukrainian military and law enforcement units, according to Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Residents of Oleshky have reported that the town is running critically low on food due to a lack of supplies, while only a small number of residents have managed to evacuate.
The drone delivery is part of an effort that has been supplying food to Oleshky residents by drone since March 2026, according to the governor.
A local resident who left Oleshky in April told the Kyiv Independent that drones had previously delivered food.
"(Drones) dropped the packages in several places. (The packages) contained a little bit of medicine and food. I don't know whose drone it was, but I reckon it was Ukraine that dropped them for us," the resident said.
Prokudin said Russian forces have attempted to disrupt the deliveries, including by shooting down the drones carrying food. He also accused Russian forces of confiscating or reselling humanitarian supplies and detaining residents who receive aid.
"The occupiers are detaining residents of Oleshky for receiving humanitarian aid parcels, throwing them 'into the cellar', beating them brutally and resorting to violence," Prokudin said.
Volunteers who used to organize the evacuation from Oleshky raised concerns about such deliveries in local Telegram groups, saying they feared this might lead to checks from the Russian side and a "nightmare for people".
The last successful food delivery to the city by vehicles was on May 26. Further attempts to supply the city on June 2 and Sept. 1 were disrupted by Russian drone attacks that killed two and injured others.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, less than 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the regional center of Kherson. The town has been under Russian occupation since Feb. 24, 2022.
Oleshky's population has fallen from around 24,000 to approximately 2,000 as of spring 2026, according to the Foreign Ministry.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
Tolokonnikov said Russia shields its positions from Ukrainian strikes through the continued presence of civilians.
"Oleshky and its people are necessary for Russian troops so that Ukrainian troops cannot actively attack them in these settlements," he said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips. Now, they said, the high risk made evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
On Sept. 25, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, raised concerns about the worsening humanitarian situation in Oleshky. O'Flaherty said civilians, including children, were struggling to access adequate food, medicine, medical care, clean water, and electricity, warning that some could face a serious risk to their lives.
O'Flaherty said international humanitarian law requires occupying authorities to ensure civilians have access to food and medical supplies and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
"The hardship and suffering of people caught along the frontlines of the war and in occupied territories demand international attention and action," O'Flaherty said.
read also
Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 26, citing Ukrainian military intelligence.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents showing the volumes of weapons Russia is preparing to produce next year and the funding allocated for them.
In recent months, Russia has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones in attacks on Ukrainian cities. In some attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
"Next year, just for the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Russia plans to spend $12 billion on this one category of weapons," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is scaling up production of interceptor drones to counter Russia's increasingly widespread use of jet-powered drones. Several interceptor prototypes are already being tested in combat, he said, with some identified as potential primary means of defense against the weapons.
"We are scaling up production and components. There will be a response," Zelensky said.
The remarks come as Russia has intensified its attacks against Ukraine in recent days, despite renewed international efforts to secure a ceasefire. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an end to the war during his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, while Zelensky said following their meeting that Ukraine was ready to accept a ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure if Russia agreed to the same terms.
Zelensky said Russia's planned spending on attack drones shows that Moscow is not preparing to halt the war "at least for now."
He also said Ukraine's partners need to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and strengthen joint efforts to defend against drones.
Ukraine currently intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to Zelensky. More than 2,730 jet-powered Shaheds were launched against Ukraine in September, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine aims to raise the interception rate to the level achieved against conventional Shahed drones, which he said is above 90%.
Ukraine has already signed 11 drone deals, according to Zelensky. The 11th, with Finland, was signed this week in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Ukraine is preparing a 12th agreement, which it expects to sign with another country in the coming weeks.
"For Ukraine, this means more production capacity, more funding, and more technological advantages," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also said Russia is conducting a campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers, infrastructure, and communications. He said the goal is to leave Ukrainians without internet access, communications, and digital services.
Earlier, Russia's attacks on Kyiv on Sept. 26 caused internet outages across the capital and disrupted access to some online services.

Israel gives Dutch envoys in Ramallah 7 days to return diplomatic documents over ban on West Bank settlement goods
Unknown

Rania Abushamala
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Israel has given Dutch diplomats working in the West Bank city of Ramallah seven days to return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documents, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said Sunday, in response to a Dutch ban on trade in goods from Israeli settlements.
Sa’ar said the Dutch Embassy in Israel was informed of the decision on Sunday evening.
After the deadline, the diplomatic privileges and immunities Israel grants the diplomats will expire, he wrote on US social media company X.
“If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests with the Palestinians, it may do so from Palestinian Authority territory,” Sa’ar said.
He linked the decision to a Dutch order that took effect last week banning the import, purchase, and sale of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The Dutch government says its measure, effective Sept. 22, covers goods from settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and also prohibits services facilitating such trade.
The foreign minister said Israel had removed a Dutch delegation from an international support center for Gaza in Kiryat Gat last month following other Dutch government measures against Israel.
The Dutch ban on importing, purchasing, or selling goods from Israeli settlements took effect on Sept. 22.
Israeli media previously reported that some products made in settlements in the occupied West Bank had been presented as originating within Israel’s pre-1967 borders to circumvent similar European bans.
There was no immediate comment from Dutch authorities on Israel’s decision.
The Dutch measure followed an announcement on Sept. 14 by 12 countries – France, Britain, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden – that they intend to impose trade restrictions on Israeli settlements.
They also called on Israel to immediately halt settlement expansion and occupier violence.
Israel’s current government says that since taking office in late 2022, it has approved 104 new settlements, while 160 agricultural settlement outposts have been established in the West Bank.
The UN has repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, warning that they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.

forget doomscrolling: meadow shrinks the smartphone down to only the most essential apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
20:35:04 UTC
05:35:04 KST

Meadow is a unique phone made for the times you decide you would rather leave your smartphone behind. The device is only three inches square, with a touchscreen taking up most of its face and a deliberately short menu of things it can do. Calls and texts are there. So are maps and Uber. Spotify and Apple Music cover music, while tickets can be pulled up at the door to a concert or event.
It looks almost like somebody cropped a smartphone down to its useful corner. The proportions are chunky and a little odd, especially beside the long black rectangles we have grown used to carrying. Meadow runs on Android, though there is no open app store waiting to fill the screen back up again. The software comes with a fixed group of services chosen around getting somewhere, meeting someone, listening to something, then heading home.
images courtesy Meadow
the camera makes you wait
The camera is where Meadow gets more interesting. There is a rear lens and a tiny mirror beside it for framing a selfie, while the usual front-facing camera disappears altogether. You can still take photos and video, but they are sent away to sync later instead of appearing instantly for review on the screen.
It changes a familiar little gesture. Take the picture, put the phone away. There is no immediate zooming in, deleting, retaking or passing the screen around for approval. Meadow still gives you the photograph. It simply separates taking it from looking at it.
the small device works independently from a user’s primary smartphone
a second phone comes with a second number
Meadow has its own cellular connection and phone number, so it works independently from the smartphone sitting back at home. Service runs on T-Mobile in the US, with plans beginning at $15 per month. That makes the whole setup more involved than switching on a stripped-back mode on an iPhone, though the physical separation is also the point. The distracting device is somewhere else.
The first larger batch has now begun reaching preorder customers. Meadow enters a growing category of phones built around doing fewer things, but its design feels especially literal: take the pieces of a smartphone that help you move through a city and put them into a much smaller object. Meanwhile, everything else can wait.

‘Atrocious’ crime: Cuban official decries possibility of US military action

2026-09-27

‘Atrocious’ crime: Cuban official decries possibility of US military action
Cuba’s deputy foreign minister slams US sanctions, labelling them ‘equivalent to genocide’.
A senior official in Cuba has warned that any prospective United States military action taken against the island nation would constitute a serious international crime, and has rejected claims made by US President Donald Trump that Cuba is a failed state.
On Sunday, Carlos Fernandez de Cossio, the country’s deputy foreign minister, told the US cable television channel C-SPAN’s flagship programme, Washington Journal, that it would be an “atrocious international crime for the US to use military force against Cuba, which is a peaceful neighbouring country”.
His comments come after Trump said during his Tuesday speech at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) that “freedom will be coming” to the island. His remarks prompted the Cuban delegation to exit the assembly hall. On Saturday, Trump brought up military action, telling reporters, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
Fernandez de Cossio said that coercing nations who do not “submit” by disrupting their commercial shipments, attempting to handicap a population through starvation, depriving it of stable healthcare and withholding fuel, as the US has “done for nine months now”, is “equivalent to a genocide”.
The US has maintained a foreign policy of maximum economic pressure against Cuba for more than 60 years. The Trump administration has previously said that it wants a shake-up in Cuba’s government. Earlier this year, the administration enforced an additional oil and fuel blockade against the island, which has crippled the nation’s infrastructure, causing widespread fuel scarcity and rolling power outages. Government officials in Cuba cited systemic difficulties in securing food supplies and other basic necessities for the country of more than 10 million.
Fernandez de Cossio said Havana must ready its citizens for the prospect of US military aggression, adding that while Cuba recognises it might stand alone, it will still exercise its legitimate right to self-defence.
He explained that bilateral diplomatic channels with the US remain open but have yielded minimal results due to the economic stranglehold of ongoing sanctions, adding that Havana remains willing to engage with Washington in a “respectful manner” only if discussions accommodate mutual dignity, benefit both populations, and respect state sovereignty.
Several countries condemned the US’s continued economic sanctions and blockade of Cuba during the UNGA earlier this week.

EU is drawing up membership action plans for most promising candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
20:33:01 UTC
05:33:01 KST

EU is drawing up membership action plans for most promising candidates
For the first time, Brussels is considering setting target dates for Montenegro, Ukraine, Moldova and Albania to complete key stages of accession talks.
Edi Rama, Gitanas Nausėda, Ursula von der Leyen and Yulia Svyrydenko participate in a conference in Gdańsk, Poland on June 25, 2026. | Woitek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU is developing proposals that would see the four countries closest to joining the bloc given a clear, step-by-step path toward membership — while the others languish behind.
Targeted “roadmaps” are being considered for Montenegro, Ukraine, Moldova and Albania, two senior European Commission officials working on the draft proposals told POLITICO, as part of efforts to speed up the decades-long process. They were granted anonymity to speak about the sensitive plans.
The four countries are seen as frontrunners to join the EU, but still face slow progress and unclear timelines as to when they might formally be admitted. While Brussels has long backed their membership bids, the roadmaps mark the first time they will be given assurances that if they continue with essential reforms, they will be admitted — and offered indicative timelines for the completion of negotiations.
Advertisement
The roadmaps will make clearer exactly what’s expected of each candidate country, one of the officials said, as well as create obligations for current members, which need to give their blessing for the process to go ahead. The plans also set rough dates for when groups of reforms, known as negotiating “clusters,” will be formally completed — major milestones on the path to membership.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged targeted support for the candidate countries “that have made most progress” during her State of the Union speech earlier in September.
However, other candidate countries at an earlier stage in the process, like Kosovo, North Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be offered the roadmaps at this stage, the officials confirmed. Nor would Georgia, Turkey or Serbia, which have seen their applications grind to a halt over concerns about democratic and judicial backsliding.
A spokesperson for the Commission confirmed that the new roadmaps “will provide a pathway toward the conclusion of the accession negotiations. They will set out a clear priority list: timelines and deliverables to help the most advanced candidates complete the necessary reforms.”
‘Geopolitical imperative’
EU leaders are increasingly looking to other pro-trade democracies, particularly in their neighborhood, amid tensions with partners like the U.S., hostile practices from China and threats from Russia. Officials are concerned that joining the EU takes too long, exposing would-be new members to disillusionment or pressure from rivals not to pursue membership.
The move comes as the EU’s “pre-enlargement” policies undergo a separate overhaul. Candidate countries need to be offered a better path toward “gradual integration” into the bloc, officials believe, one that would use economic benefits and access to joint projects to reward them for progress. That policy review, led by von der Leyen’s close adviser Alexandre Adam, is to be presented to top officials Oct. 6; it is designed to keep them on the path toward the EU while their applications unfold.
Advertisement
“Enlargement … remains a geopolitical imperative. Accession, however, takes time,” reads a draft version of the pre-enlargement review text seen by POLITICO. “Candidate countries must complete a rigorous, merit-based process and deliver far-reaching and lasting reforms. That time should be put to full strategic use to both prepare the Union for larger membership and deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest.”
As part of that review, von der Leyen and Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos will propose changes to the bloc’s internal workings to ensure safeguards are in place to prevent new joiners from disrupting key policies or reneging on their commitments. The revisions could include emergency clauses and transition periods before certain membership rights are fully granted.
“The policy reviews show that the Union can accommodate a larger membership through targeted adaptations, largely within the existing Treaty framework,” the draft reads, arguing that the EU’s fundamental laws don’t need to change to assuage concerns about enlargement.
Capitals are cautious about admitting new members, some of which have had only a few decades of democratic governance, following Hungary’s backsliding on rule-of-law principles under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and its use of veto powers to block key policies like sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine. The support of current members must be unanimous for candidate countries to move through the process of joining the EU.
National leaders will weigh in on how, and how fast, new members can be brought in during a two-day summit in Brussels from Oct. 15; in turn, the Commission will ask them for political support to pick up the pace. The European Council will hold “a strategic discussion on enlargement and internal reforms,” a draft agenda shows.
Kos told POLITICO earlier this month that she hopes the changes being proposed, and the talks with leaders, will make for an “autumn of enlargement” after years of slower progress.
Von der Leyen travels to the Western Balkans this week for talks with leaders in Montenegro, Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo. She will skip Bosnia and Herzegovina, however, as well as Serbia, both of which are in the midst of national elections.

Europe faces a struggle with Asia for liquefied natural gas amid record-low inventories
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
23:30:36 EEST
05:30:36 KST

Europe faces a struggle with Asia for liquefied natural gas amid record-low inventories
Kyiv • UNN
EU gas storage levels have fallen to a record low of 67% ahead of winter. The cold season could push LNG prices to $40 per million BTU.
Europe is entering the winter season with record-low gas storage levels for this time of year, meaning it will have to compete more actively with Asian countries for liquefied natural gas supplies in the coming months. In the event of a cold winter, this competition could lead to another price spike, the Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
Gas reserves in EU storage facilities currently stand at around 67% of their capacity—the lowest level for this time of year. By comparison, the European target calls for storage facilities to be filled to approximately 80% by December.
The situation is being exacerbated by disruptions to LNG supplies from the Middle East. Due to transportation problems through the Strait of Hormuz, the global market has received tens of millions of tonnes less liquefied gas from Qatar and the UAE this year.
Europe will have to compete for American gas
According to market participants’ estimates, in the event of a cold winter, simultaneous growth in demand in Europe and Asia could trigger a scramble for available LNG cargoes, primarily from the United States.
Asian spot prices for liquefied gas have already nearly tripled this year compared with pre-war levels and approached $30 per million British thermal units. Experts warn that under an unfavorable scenario, they could rise to approximately $40 in winter.
Europe is particularly vulnerable because of the small amount of spare gas available on the global market. If winter is cold in both Europe and Asia at the same time, buyers from both regions will be forced to raise their bids for the same American LNG cargoes.
At the same time, a warm winter could significantly ease pressure on the market. However, even under such a scenario, analysts expect gas prices to remain elevated due to low storage levels and supply problems from the Middle East.
