Another catch in Hormuz
IRGC captures second US spy sub in Hormuz, exposing the limits of Washington’s undersea warfare
TEHRAN — In another humiliating blow to the US automated naval warfare doctrine, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy has intercepted and captured a state-of-the-art American autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz, further cementing Iran’s control over the world’s most vital energy chokepoint.
The Sunday operation marks the second time in less than a month that an advanced Pentagon spy submersible has fallen intact into the hands of Iranian naval and intelligence units. Crucially, the vessel was neither neutralized nor destroyed; it was methodically tracked, electronically commandeered, and seized as operational war booty—delivering an invaluable intelligence bonanza straight to Iranian military labs.
In an official statement, the IRGC Navy confirmed the captured asset as a REMUS 600, a premier autonomous unmanned submersible manufactured for sensitive expeditionary warfare. The platform is currently in the custody of IRGC technical specialists to decode its onboard encrypted mission computers and extract critical mission logs.
“IRGC Navy forces intercepted an advanced underwater drone belonging to the terrorist US military, which was conducting clandestine espionage operations in the Strait of Hormuz, through a synchronized, multi-layered operation combining tactical intelligence and advanced electronic warfare,” the IRGC said in a statement.
Underscoring Iran’s uncompromising posture, the statement firmly warned: “The IRGC Navy declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to hostile entities, and we will take decisive, relentless action against any unauthorized passage or hostile regional movements.”
Developed by American defense contractors, the REMUS 600 is a modular, high-endurance autonomous system tailored for deep-water intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), seabed mapping, naval mine detection and classification, and clandestine environmental data collection.
Engineered to operate at depths reaching 600 meters (roughly 2,000 feet), the vessel relies on sophisticated inertial navigation systems (INS), Doppler Velocity Logs (DVL), acoustic transponders, and GPS fixes upon surfacing. These systems allow the platform to execute complex, long-range missions fully autonomously, devoid of real-time tethering or manual operator intervention. Armed with cutting-edge side-scan imaging sonars, environmental sensors, and multi-channel data-logging architectures, the platform represents the backbone of US clandestine littoral reconnaissance.
The strategic windfall goes far beyond the captured physical hull. The recovery of intact mission hard drives, pre-programmed transit corridors, high-resolution acoustic seabed imaging, search patterns, and firmware configurations provides Iranian specialists with an unfiltered, forensic blueprint of how the US Navy conducts undersea reconnaissance within Iranian territorial and adjacent waters. The treasure trove of data will allow Iranian countermeasures to systematically anticipate and neutralize future hostile uncrewed deployments.
From Dive-LD to REMUS 600
Sunday’s operation directly parallels the IRGC’s historic seizure on September 8 of another flagship American autonomous system: the Dive-LD. Manufactured by California-based defense tech firm Anduril Industries and delivered to the US Navy’s Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group 1 in 2025, the 2.7-tonne, 5.8-meter Dive-LD was heralded by Washington as the pinnacle of deep-sea endurance, capable of reaching depths of 6,000 meters.
That capture—achieved through an audacious electronic warfare strike that pierced the vehicle’s encrypted command links and brought it safely ashore—unraveled the Pentagon’s narrative of invisible undersea superiority. When US Central Command scrambled an MQ-9 Reaper drone in a desperate bid to locate the stranded asset, Iranian air defense batteries promptly blasted the multi-million-dollar surveillance aircraft out of the sky.
Washington’s frantic attempts to downplay the September 8 capture by alleging mechanical failure or framing the platform as “attritable” were thoroughly ridiculed by regional observers.
The subsequent capture of the REMUS 600 confirms a definitive pattern: far from experiencing accidental drift, the US military’s most secretive autonomous systems are being methodically hunted down and netted by Iranian forces.
The latest capture comes amid the US-Israeli war against Iran launched on February 28, underscoring Tehran’s continued ability to counter advanced US surveillance systems.
Facing formidable Iranian Anti-Access/Area-Denial (A2/AD) envelopes that preclude manned US capital ships from operating safely in the Persian Gulf without catastrophic risk, the Pentagon wagered its strategic deterrence on an uncrewed, three-tiered hybrid architecture spanning aerial drones (UAVs), robotic surface vessels (USVs), and subsurface craft (UUVs). With the consecutive, intact seizures of the Dive-LD and the REMUS 600, alongside the regular downing of high-altitude spy aircraft, Iran has systematically shredded all three layers of Washington’s unmanned warfare concept.
An unbreakable maritime bastion
The capture of the REMUS 600 offers resounding proof that the Islamic Republic’s electronic and asymmetric warfare capabilities have outpaced the Pentagon’s technological hubris. By pulling the veil off Washington’s most secretive undersea assets twice in four weeks, the IRGC Navy has sent an unmistakable signal across the Persian Gulf and beyond: the strategic waters of the Strait of Hormuz belong entirely to regional nations, and every covert imperialist footprint beneath the surface will be severed and seized.
As Washington grapples with the fallout of its failed regional adventurism and dwindling asymmetric options, Iran’s indigenous defense apparatus continues to turn the enemy’s prized hardware into its own intellectual property. The Strait of Hormuz is no longer a permissive playground for American covert aggression, but a fortified bastion where imperial arrogance sinks and Iranian technological mastery reigns supreme.

Ukraine's 1st Medical Battalion reveals that over 50% of evacuation missions using Maul ground robot are successful
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's 1st Medical Battalion reveals that over 50% of evacuation missions using Maul ground robot are successful
Over half of the missions carried out by soldiers from the 1st Separate Medical Battalion (MedBat) using the Ukrainian Maul unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) have been successful. On average, one ground robot saves the lives of nearly two soldiers.
Source: a report by the 1st Separate Medical Battalion
Details: According to the unit, the Maul UGV was first used in combat conditions in January 2025, and by October 2025, the ground robot had carried out its first successful evacuation of a wounded soldier.
As of late September 2026, soldiers from the 1st Separate MedBat have carried out "hundreds of missions" using the Maul, 51.9% of which were successful. The unit explained that operations are considered successful when a wounded soldier is transferred to subsequent stages of evacuation.
Quote: "On average, during its lifespan, one Maul evacuates 1.92 wounded soldiers. However, practice shows that a Maul can survive anywhere from 20 minutes to 12 successful missions. Factors affecting mission outcomes include preparation time, situational awareness, coordination with adjacent units, weather conditions and enemy activity in the sector. In the vast majority of missions, time of day was not a decisive factor."
Details: Meanwhile, an unsuccessful mission does not necessarily mean the death of a soldier on the frontline. In more than half of incomplete operations, the reason was the vehicle returning without a casualty. The remainder involved the loss of the vehicle prior to loading.
Quote: "Unfortunately, in 4.6% of all missions, the UGV was destroyed with the casualty on board."
Details: To increase mission success rates, the 1st MedBat prioritises operations based on information regarding the circumstances and severity of wounds, as well as logistical threats and capabilities. The technical condition of the UGV is also checked before operations, and more than 10 military personnel are involved in executing each mission.
Quote: "An important component of the mission team is the rapid response group, which we call the 'lively group' – these are service members involved in delivering the Maul to the launch point, inspecting its technical condition and performing maintenance. After a mission is completed, they also retrieve the vehicle, sanitise it and inspect it for damage."
For reference: The Maul UGV is an ATV-based ground robotic system equipped with a special armoured capsule for transporting a wounded person. It features an internal combustion engine, suspension, an armoured capsule and electronic warfare equipment.
The robot's average speed during evacuations is 30-40 km/h, and the maximum distance covered by the Maul during a single mission is 110 km.
Background:
- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Come Back Alive Foundation announced the launch of the RoboBro project to purchase ground evacuation robotic systems. The project's goal is to save at least 1,000 Ukrainian soldiers' lives using UGVs. Ukrainian ground robots, including the Maul, will be purchased as part of the project.
- Ukrainska Pravda has described how the 1st Medical Battalion uses UGVs for evacuations in this article: Two wounded Ukrainian soldiers rescued from right under Russians' noses: the heroic exploits of the Maul robot and the 1st Medical Battalion

Israel quietly lifts block on Syrian airport night flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:00:35 UTC
02:00:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel quietly lifts block on Syrian airport night flights
Syria's two main international airports can now operate night flights after Israel reportedly lifted a months-long block on the activation of new navigation systems in Damascus and Aleppo.
The Syrian General Authority for Civil Aviation and Air Transport announced that it had completed calibration and flight testing of modern navigation equipment at Damascus and Aleppo international airports.
The systems will allow the airports to operate around the clock, including at night and during fog, poor visibility and difficult weather conditions, according to Syria's official SANA news agency.
However, the equipment had reportedly been installed and ready for more than six months, with Syria unable to activate it because Israel had objected to the flights required to calibrate the systems.
Regional officials and diplomats told Middle East Eye that Israel had previously threatened to shoot down the specialist aircraft used to carry out the tests.
The apparent lifting of the Israeli objection represents a significant development for Syria's efforts to rebuild its battered civil aviation sector and restore international connections following years of war and sanctions.
The new equipment includes an Instrument Landing System with Distance Measuring Equipment (ILS/DME), which helps aircraft safely approach and land in darkness or poor visibility, and a DVOR/DME system used by aircraft to establish their direction and distance from an airport.
Syria's civil aviation authority said the upgrades would increase the number of flights the airports could accommodate and help open new routes connecting the country with regional and international destinations.
17 Syrian, Arab and international airlines currently operate from Damascus International Airport, while 14 use Aleppo, according to the authority.
Why did Israel oppose the airport upgrades?
According to Middle East Eye, the problem centred not on the navigation equipment itself but on the flights necessary to calibrate it.
Specialist aircraft normally have to fly repeated patterns around an airport to test navigation signals and ensure the systems are accurate before they can be used by passenger aircraft.
The original calibration process reportedly required the aircraft to operate within a radius of around 50 kilometres from Damascus airport, which brought it closer to areas considered sensitive by Israel.
Officials said a technical compromise was eventually developed reducing the calibration area to a radius of around 25 kilometres.
Syrian authorities informed Israel of the revised flight plans but received no response, according to the report. The calibration flights subsequently went ahead without Israeli intervention.
SANA reported on 17 September that testing had begun at Damascus airport using a specialised calibration aircraft, with work expected to take around four days before the aircraft moved to Aleppo.
The civil aviation authority confirmed a week later that testing at both airports had been successfully completed and the systems had entered service.
The development comes as Syria attempts to restore regional and international air links following the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Syrian airports were repeatedly targeted by Israeli air strikes under Assad, with Israel saying it was attempting to disrupt Iranian weapons transfers to Hezbollah and other Iran-aligned groups.
Israel has continued carrying out strikes inside Syria under the country's new authorities and has expanded its military presence in southern Syria, while demanding the demilitarisation of areas close to its border.
At the same time, Damascus and Israel have held indirect and direct talks aimed at establishing new security arrangements between the two countries.
The apparent decision not to intervene against the calibration flights could therefore mark a small but tangible easing of Israeli restrictions on Syria's civilian infrastructure, although neither side has publicly announced an agreement covering the airports.

How neutral should Switzerland be? Voters deliver decisive verdict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:59:05 UTC
01:59:05 KST

Supporters of the proposal, led by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP), argued that Switzerland had moved too close to the European Union and NATO, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Swiss voters overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to strengthen the country's neutrality in a referendum on Sunday, with around 70% voting against the measure.
According to final results published by the Swiss government, the proposal was rejected in all 26 Swiss cantons.
The initiative would have restricted Switzerland's ability to impose sanctions on other countries, allowing such measures only if they had been approved by the United Nations.
That would have limited Switzerland's ability to adopt sanctions against Russia, which holds veto power as one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
Supporters of the proposal, led by the far right Swiss People's Party (SVP), argued that Switzerland had moved too close to the European Union and NATO, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"This result is not a vote against neutrality," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said at a press conference on Sunday as the referendum results were announced.
"Switzerland was neutral yesterday, it will be neutral today and it will remain neutral," he stressed.
A costly campaign ends in defeat
The initiative was championed by Christoph Blocher, the 85-year-old billionaire and influential figure within the SVP, with campaign posters promoting the so-called "neutrality initiative" carried the slogan "No to war".
Its defeat had been widely anticipated. According to Swiss media reports, the foreign ministry in Bern had privately forecast the outcome several weeks before the vote.
Despite the expected result, Blocher invested heavily in the campaign.
According to Swiss newspaper Berner Zeitung, he spent 3.8 million Swiss francs on the initiative, reportedly the largest amount ever contributed by a single individual to a Swiss referendum campaign.
The result prompted criticism from political opponents.
"The initiative would have set neutrality in stone and would no longer have allowed an adequate response to a given situation," argued said Susanne Vincenz-Stauffacher, a member of the Swiss National Council, referring to Russia's war against Ukraine.
She warned that defining neutrality in such rigid terms could prevent Switzerland from imposing sanctions on an aggressor.
"At the end of the day you are not neutral but on the aggressor's side," she said.
"Blocher has completely lost his way here," said Marianne Binder, a Centre Party member of the Council of States representing Aargau.
What does neutrality mean for Switzerland?
Switzerland has maintained a longstanding policy of neutrality and is not a member of any military alliance.
However, the interpretation of that neutrality has been the subject of political debate for years, particularly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The Swiss government currently advocates a policy of "cooperative neutrality", under which the country remains militarily non-aligned while retaining the ability to impose sanctions when it considers them necessary to uphold international law.
Swiss Defence Minister Martin Pfister has also called for closer cooperation with NATO.
The rejected initiative sought to enshrine "perpetual and armed neutrality" in the Swiss constitution. It would also have restricted military cooperation with NATO to situations involving an imminent military attack.
While Swiss voters rejected the proposed restrictions, support for neutrality itself remains widespread.
According to the latest survey cited in the debate, 82% of respondents continue to support Switzerland's neutrality.
The referendum was part of Sunday's nationwide round of votes on national and local issues.
Under Switzerland's system of direct democracy, citizens typically vote four times a year on proposed legislation, constitutional amendments and other policy questions.

Russia strikes data centers, logistics sites in Ukraine – MOD

In Kiev Region, the Russian military hit a large warehouse belonging to the Zammler Group, the ministry said. The strikes also targeted a data center in Kiev belonging to the Vodafone Ukraine mobile operator. The ministry described the major provider as one of “the largest companies providing mobile communication and high-speed internet services” to the Ukrainian military. Later in the day, the Russian military also hit data centers of the internet provider Omega Telecom and the mobile and internet operator Kievstar. Recently, the Russian military turned its attention to Ukrainian data centers, with multiple internet and mobile providers reporting damage and connectivity issues due to strikes.
Two warehouses used to store attack drones were hit in Nikolayev Region, another stockpile, used to keep interceptor UAVs, was attacked in Odessa, according to the ministry. Earlier in the day, Ukrainian drone maker Pegasus Arms announced a halt to its operations, claiming its manufacturing site was heavily damaged in Russian strikes earlier this week. The company had halted operations late last year due to Russian strikes, yet resumed them later on after moving production to another location.
The Danube River port town of Kiliya was extensively targeted during the latest round of the Russian strikes. According to the ministry, port infrastructure sites, a naval base, a border guard site, and four warehouses used to stash military equipment were hit. On top of that, the military hit two dry cargo vessels off Odessa, said to be used to carry military equipment and dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military.
Both Kiev and Moscow have ramped up long-range strikes in recent weeks after Ukraine launched its attempted “pressure campaign” during the summer. Russia has retaliated in force, greatly expanding the range of targets it strikes across the country, with the campaign virtually paralyzing Ukrainian shipping through ports in the Black Sea, as well as causing severe disruptions in logistics elsewhere.

World Insights: Polish-Ukrainian solidarity frays amid growing differences
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:52:38 CST
01:52:38 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A knife attack by a Ukrainian national at a monastery in southeastern Poland has brought renewed attention to the ever more complicated relationship between the two neighbors.
A 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen reportedly killed a priest and injured four other people at a Benedictine monastery in Jaroslaw on Thursday. A court on Saturday ordered him held in pretrial detention for three months, and the motive for the attack remained unclear.
The incident has quickly stirred political reactions in Poland. Members and supporters of National Movement, a Polish right-wing nationalist party, gathered outside the monastery, while some politicians called for tighter controls on migrants, including Ukrainians.
Poland remains a major supporter of Ukraine and a key logistical hub for assistance, but the strong solidarity with Ukraine forged in the early days of the Russia-Ukraine conflict is giving way to the harder politics of a long-term relationship, as migration, competing economic interests and historical grievances return to the fore.
FROM SOLIDARITY TO FATIGUE
When the Russia-Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, Poland became a major destination for Ukrainians fleeing the fighting. The country introduced special measures giving eligible Ukrainians access to employment, public healthcare and social benefits.
Public support was overwhelming. According to Poland's Public Opinion Research Center (CBOS), 94 percent of respondents supported accepting Ukrainian refugees from conflict-affected areas in early 2022.
Four years on, however, what began as temporary refuge has evolved into a longer-term challenge of migration and integration, adding to friction between Poles and Ukrainians. According to Eurostat, more than 953,000 people displaced from Ukraine remained under temporary protection in Poland at the end of July, the second-largest number in the European Union (EU) after Germany.
Public attitudes have shifted markedly. A CBOS survey released in July showed that 52 percent of respondents opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees, the first time since the agency began tracking the issue that opponents outnumbered supporters.
The change in public attitudes has been accompanied by signs of growing hostility toward Ukrainians. Polish police received 180 reports of suspected hate crimes targeting Ukrainian citizens in the first half of 2026, up more than 30 percent from the same period a year earlier, according to police data.
POLITICAL FRICTIONS GROW
Political tensions have also grown as Ukraine-related issues become increasingly intertwined with domestic politics in Poland and historical disputes resurface between the two countries.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed legislation extending assistance measures for Ukrainian citizens, arguing that the country's 800-zloty (210 U.S. dollars) monthly child benefit should be available only to Ukrainians who work in Poland.
The employment requirement took effect in February, as Poland began scaling back some of the special arrangements for Ukrainians. Special access to public healthcare was largely phased out in March, and state-funded collective accommodation was restricted mainly to specified vulnerable groups.
Historical disputes have further fueled friction between the two countries, particularly over the Volhynia massacres during World War II and the legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
In late May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the UPA. Nawrocki responded by revoking the Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest state decoration, which was awarded to Zelensky in 2023, calling the Ukrainian move "outrageous, incomprehensible and deeply disappointing." Zelensky returned the decoration the following day.
Polish geopolitical analyst Malwina Talik noted that although the two presidents' decisions had triggered a deep diplomatic crisis, both moves enjoyed broad support in their respective countries. She said the dispute was rooted in divergent historical memories of the UPA in Poland and Ukraine, making it particularly difficult to resolve.
DIVERGING INTERESTS
A study published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace said security remains the area where Polish and Ukrainian strategic interests are most closely aligned, but appears to be the "lowest common denominator" in their relationship rather than the foundation for a comprehensive partnership.
Differences have emerged even over security. Edwin Bendyk, president of Poland's Stefan Batory Foundation, has highlighted a growing asymmetry between the two countries: while the conflict remains an existential issue for Ukrainians, Poles are primarily concerned with avoiding direct confrontation.
The Carnegie study, citing interviews with Polish officials, said some viewed Ukraine as a buffer state rather than a full-fledged ally integrated with Europe. It also pointed to Warsaw's cautious approach to the Coalition of the Willing, with Poland ruling out sending troops to Ukraine.
Economic relations reveal another limit to the partnership. Disputes over Ukrainian agricultural exports led Poland to restrict some imports and sparked border protests, while tensions persist over increasing Ukrainian grain transit through Poland. The Carnegie study said the issue had grown from an economic concern into an electoral issue before "spiraling into a serious bilateral crisis."
The stakes extend beyond bilateral relations, with tensions between Poland and Ukraine carrying potential implications for Ukraine's accession to the EU, according to Talik. ■

Feature: From ancient trees to new saplings, Egypt's green push takes root
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:52:30 CST
01:52:30 KST

A large old tree is seen in the middle of a road in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 27, 2026. On a street near the gate of Cairo Tower in Egypt's capital city, a large old tree rises from the middle of the roadway, with its thick, aged branches stretching above passing cars. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
by Mahmoud Fouly
CAIRO, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- On a street near the gate of Cairo Tower in Egypt's capital city, a large old tree rises from the middle of the roadway, with its thick, aged branches stretching above passing cars.
The tree quickly caught the eye of Hazem Ismail, a senior high school student visiting the landmark. He stopped to snap a selfie with it.
"What struck me was that it stands in the middle of the street and has not been removed," he said, adding its old branches particularly drew his attention.
Scenes of ancient trees flourishing alongside modern urban life have become increasingly common in Egypt as tree preservation and planting receive growing public and official attention.
Earlier this month, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi directed authorities to expand green spaces nationwide, while Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly ordered governorates to speed up tree planting along major roads.
The Ministry of Local Development and Environment later tightened controls on cutting or uprooting trees and pushed ahead with the presidential initiative to plant 100 million trees.
Alongside the new greening drive, efforts are underway to preserve trees that have stood for decades, and in some cases centuries.
Mohamed Abu Saada, head of Egypt's National Organization for Urban Harmony, said his group is building a "national archive" of rare and long-lived trees as part of its work to document the country's natural heritage.
More than 2,000 rare and long-lived trees have been recorded in Cairo, Giza and Aswan, with work now underway in the Nile Delta city of El Qanater El Khayreya, according to Abu Saada.
The idea came after he saw people abroad celebrating and preserving a 60-year-old olive tree, he added. "I thought that Egypt is even more deserving of caring for its trees, especially since we have trees that are more than 200 years old."
Teams are using geographic information system technology to log the trees' locations and conditions, feeding the data into the organization's "Memory of the City" mobile app so users can discover rare and historic trees nearby.
The project has covered palaces and gardens so far, with plans to create tree trails where visitors can explore rare and long-lived trees and the stories behind them, Abu Saada added.
While one initiative looks to the past to safeguard Egypt's living heritage, another has spent the past decade planting new roots for the future.
Shagrha, an environmental initiative launched in April 2016, has planted over 750,000 fruit and timber trees across 22 of Egypt's 27 governorates, involving over 250,000 volunteers, founder and CEO Omar El-Deeb said.
"Sustainability is our goal. It is not about taking a picture and that is it," El-Deeb said, adding the initiative works with local authorities, schools, hospitals and other institutions to select locations where trees can receive continued care.
Egypt's presidential "100 Million Trees" initiative, launched in 2022, aims to expand green spaces nationwide and improve air quality.
Mona Kamal, an Egyptian environmental expert and former head of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency, said tree-planting efforts should be measured not simply by how many trees are planted, but by whether they survive and are maintained long-term.
"Planting new trees is worthwhile, but the important thing is that the goal should not be publicity. It should be environmentally sustainable," Kamal told Xinhua.
The expert stressed that protecting mature trees is especially vital in Egypt's desert climate, where growing new ones demands scarce water.
"If you have a 200-year-old tree and it is healthy, that is heritage, and you should preserve it," she added. ■

Letter from Mideast: Chinese robotaxis help drive Dubai's smart mobility future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:51:55 CST
01:51:55 KST

by Xinhua writer Xia Xiao
DUBAI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- On a sweltering summer afternoon, a black Apollo Go robotaxi eased to the curb along Dubai's Jumeirah coastline. I unlocked the door with my smartphone. There was no driver, no steering wheel, and no doubt that artificial intelligence was in control.
The car glided smoothly through roundabouts and dense seaside traffic, stopping at red lights, yielding to pedestrians, and changing lanes without fuss. In most cities, such a ride would still be a novelty. Here in Dubai, it is becoming everyday reality.
And this reality, which once belonged to science fiction, is being brought to life by Chinese technology.
As Gulf countries, including the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia and Qatar, invest heavily in artificial intelligence and smart-city projects, Chinese autonomous-driving companies are emerging as some of the region's most active technology partners.
Dubai, which aims to make 25 percent of all transportation trips smart and driverless by 2030, has become one of the first overseas markets where Chinese robotaxi companies are putting autonomous-driving technology into commercial service.
Apollo Go, Baidu's autonomous ride-hailing platform, began commercial operations in Dubai in March. WeRide has deployed more than 200 autonomous taxis across the Middle East and says the region has already become profitable. Pony.ai, meanwhile, plans to launch commercial robotaxi services in Dubai later this year.
Together, these Chinese companies illustrate how Gulf countries are embracing Chinese technology to advance their ambitions for smarter, better-connected cities.
"The UAE offers one of the world's most supportive environments for autonomous driving," Chen Qiang, Baidu's general manager for intelligent driving business development in the UAE, told me. "Modern infrastructure, efficient regulation and strong demand for smart mobility allow companies to move more quickly from testing to commercial operation."
According to Chen, as the UAE provides a favorable business environment for Chinese tech companies, Chinese autonomous-driving firms have also been adapting their technologies and service models to local conditions, including optimizing their systems for the UAE's climate, roads, and regulatory requirements.
Wang Ludi, head of global communications at Pony.ai, said growing consumer acceptance of intelligent vehicles in the UAE had created favorable conditions for Chinese autonomous-driving technologies to expand at scale.
Wang added that Chinese automotive and technology brands had also gained broader recognition in the local market. "For autonomous mobility, the key question is whether the technology can deliver a safe, reliable and convenient service," he said.
The growing presence of Chinese autonomous-driving companies reflects a broader shift in China-Gulf cooperation, with partnerships expanding beyond traditional energy ties into emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics, cloud computing, and intelligent transportation.
Mattar Al Tayer, director general and chairman of the Board of Executive Directors of Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority, described China as a global leader in transport infrastructure, digital technologies and artificial intelligence. Dubai, he said, was strengthening long-term partnerships with leading Chinese companies to bring advanced technologies and operational expertise to future transport projects.
Speaking with local experts and scholars has reinforced my view that Chinese technology companies are uniquely positioned to support the Gulf countries' economic diversification.
Their commercially proven solutions are readily applicable to large-scale smart-city projects, while the region's digital transformation provides an ideal testing ground for Chinese firms to further develop and internationalize their technologies.
These days, I'm growing accustomed to riding in autonomous taxis. Yet each time I step into one, I find myself reflecting on what has brought this once-futuristic journey within reach: not technology alone, but the spirit of cooperation behind it and a shared determination to harness innovation to improve people's lives. ■

Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:50:35 UTC
01:50:35 KST

Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
TEHRAN — Iran has warned the United States against any intervention in the Strait of Hormuz, while stressing that its Armed Forces have developed new military technologies and capabilities to respond to any potential aggression.
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesman for Iran’s Armed Forces, issued the warning on Saturday night, saying that any U.S. attempt to interfere in the strategic waterway would face an Iranian response.
“If the United States intervenes in the Strait of Hormuz, it will get slapped,” Shekarchi said, using a colloquial expression to underline the consequences Washington would face in the event of direct intervention.
He also said that the United States had “no way out other than leaving West Asia,” arguing that the sooner American forces withdrew from the region, the lower the losses they would suffer.
Shekarchi described the Islamic Republic as a “global power” and said Iran would not allow the United States to return to its former position in a “new world order.”
Iran’s military doctrine and new technologies
The senior military spokesman said Iran’s Armed Forces had sought to strengthen their combat capabilities and incorporate advanced technologies since the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, also known as the “imposed war.”
He cited the beginning of Iran’s indigenous missile production during the conflict with the former Ba’athist regime in Iraq as a tangible example of the country’s efforts to develop defense capabilities under wartime conditions.
According to Shekarchi, one of the most significant changes in Iran’s military doctrine following the Islamic Revolution was the shift from conventional warfare toward asymmetric warfare.
He said conventional military methods could be vulnerable when confronting an adversary equipped with costly and technologically sophisticated heavy weapons.
“Asymmetric warfare means standing up to the enemy’s expensive heavy weapons and achieving victory with lower costs and simpler but more effective and practical defense equipment,” Shekarchi said.
’A surprise in store for the enemy’
Shekarchi said Iran’s adversaries had miscalculated the country’s resilience and defensive capabilities.
He argued that if the enemy had properly assessed Iran’s capabilities, it would not have chosen to attack the country.
The general also emphasized information security as a key principle within the Armed Forces, saying that safeguarding military information was essential to preserving the element of surprise.
He said Iran possessed unique elements of national power and pointed to the participation of the Iranian people both on the streets and on the battlefield as a fundamental factor in the country’s ability to withstand attacks.
Referring to recent threats against Iran, Shekarchi said the Armed Forces would employ newly developed military technologies in responding to any future aggression.
“The powerful Iranian Armed Forces are many times stronger than they were at the outset of the second and third imposed wars,” he said, describing the current condition of the Armed Forces as “very good.”
He said Iran’s missile and drone capabilities had become more advanced and powerful and warned that Tehran had capabilities that had not necessarily been publicly disclosed.
“This time we have a surprise in store for the enemy,” Shekarchi said, adding that Iran would respond to any potential aggression with new military technologies.
Hormuz at the center of the dispute
Shekarchi also reiterated Iran’s position on the Strait of Hormuz, saying that the strategic waterway was under Iranian management.
“Management of the Strait of Hormuz is in Iran’s hands,” he said. “Any ship that wants to pass outside the Iranian route will not have security.”
The comments come as control and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz have emerged as a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington.
In recent indirect negotiations in New York, Iranian officials presented conditions under which Tehran said it could facilitate the reopening of the waterway and the resumption of nuclear talks. According to Axios, U.S. negotiators told their Iranian counterparts that Iran did not control the strait and therefore could not impose conditions concerning it.

Earlier, Gor and lieutenant general Vikrant Suresh Deshpande, general officer commanding, 10 Corps, observed a joint firing demonstration by Indian and US Army personnel at the Mahajan Field Firing Range as part of Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, showcasing the depth and complexity of bilateral training between the two forces.
The demonstration showcased the Pinaka multi-barrel rocket launcher, M777 ultra-light howitzer and Dhanush artillery system, alongside AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, L70 air-defence guns and Swathi weapon-locating radars.For its part, the US Army deployed HIMARS and M-LIDS systems, bringing together a wide range of artillery, aviation, air-defence and surveillance capabilities in a challenging field setting.The first edition of Tarang Shakti was held in 2024, with defence minister Rajnath Singh describing it at the time as a step towards deepening cooperation, coordination and trust among partner nations.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to meet Trump with AI safety concern rising
SAN FANCISCO - Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei is set to have dinner with President Donald Trump on the night of Sept 27, according to people familiar with the matter, with the meeting bringing together two men at opposite ends of the artificial intelligence safety debate.
Their dinner would mark the first private sit-down between Amodei and Trump after months of rocky relations between the Anthropic chief and the administration.
Tensions erupted during a bitter contract dispute with the Pentagon early in 2026 and deepened when the Commerce Department briefly imposed export controls on Anthropic’s breakthrough Mythos model in June.
It’s unclear what the two men will discuss, and the people confirmed the meeting on condition of anonymity to describe confidential planning. Axios reported earlier on the dinner. Spokespeople for Anthropic and the White House didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
The meeting is set to take place against a backdrop of growing global anxiety over AI safety following a series of high-profile security breaches carried out by cutting-edge models, including disclosures by OpenAI last week that its models had hacked an Australian government website earlier in 2026. Those episodes have fuelled calls for new AI standards from US lawmakers and many across the tech industry.
Amodei and Trump have staked out starkly different positions about the threats posed by AI.
The Anthropic chief brought the safety debate to the mainstream with an essay on Sept 12 warning of AI’s existential risks and urging more regulation of the technology.
He also promised to slow development of the most advanced models, a pledge that was embraced by his rivals, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk.
Trump, on the other hand, has belittled those doomsday fears as “a hoax” and rejected calls for more international coordination on AI as “a globalist conspiracy.”
Following Amodei’s essay, Trump launched a string of social media posts opposing any slowdown in AI development – one of which named the Anthropic chief directly – a disagreement that significantly raises the stakes of the Sept 27 dinner.
Signalling the friction between Anthropic and the administration, Amodei was one of the few high-profile Silicon Valley CEOs to miss Sept 24’s state dinner at the White House to fete the visiting Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Those in attendance included Altman and Musk, as well as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company’s chips have helped power the AI industry’s growth.
The dinner between Amodei and Trump is also set to take place days before Trump welcomes Musk and Huang back to Washington for an event to herald the launch of a new AI-powered government website.
Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, who has served as a point person for the company in negotiations with the Pentagon and Commerce Department, is also among the executives set to attend the Sept 29 ribbon-cutting.
Also on Sept 29, Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to host a separate gathering of AI CEOs. In recent weeks, US lawmakers have increasingly expressed their concerns about the safety of AI models and unveiled measures that include required testing of new systems and more disclosure about risks.
The groundswell for more safety guardrails has faced pushback from Trump and his top aides, who have insisted that they would oppose any moves that would slow development of AI.
Trump has made the technology central to his economic agenda and insisted that the US maintain its lead over China. In lieu of new rules, the president and his advisers have said that companies should be held individually responsible for the tech they release. BLOOMBERG

Two years after Nasrallah's death, Hezbollah faces a new Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:49:18 UTC
01:49:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Two years after Nasrallah’s killing, Hezbollah faces a changed Lebanon
Hezbollah supporters gathered near Hassan Nasrallah’s tomb in Beirut’s southern suburbs on Sunday to mark two years since Israel killed the group’s longtime leader. Many carried the group’s yellow flags, a show of loyalty after two wars that have weakened Hezbollah and left parts of its stronghold in ruins.
Nasrallah was killed on 27 September 2024 in an Israeli strike on Haret Hreik, in Dahiyeh. Israel said it had targeted Hezbollah’s central headquarters beneath residential buildings. The explosions brought down several apartment buildings; Nasrallah’s body was recovered from the rubble two days later.
The site of the strike remains devastated two years on. The building where Nasrallah was sheltering and others beside it have yet to be rebuilt, while surrounding residential blocks still bear visible damage. Posters of the former leader mark the place where he was killed.
Across Dahiyeh, his face remains a familiar sight on walls, roadside posters and billboards, including along the road to Beirut’s international airport. Some displays also show Iran’s late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on Tehran last February.
Nasrallah led Hezbollah for more than three decades, becoming its most recognisable voice and a powerful figure in Lebanese politics. To supporters, he embodied resistance to Israel. The United States sanctioned him, while Hezbollah’s armed wing was placed on the European Union’s terrorism list.
His killing was part of a devastating September 2024 for the Iran-backed group. On 17 September, pagers used by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon; booby-trapped walkie-talkies detonated the next day. Together, the attacks killed 39 people and wounded more than 3,400, including civilians.
An Israeli strike killed Ibrahim Aqil, a senior commander associated with Hezbollah’s elite Radwan force, on 20 September. Hashem Safieddine, widely seen as Nasrallah’s successor, was killed in an Israeli strike the following month.
A movement under pressure
Sunday’s gathering showed that Hezbollah retains a committed base. But the loss of senior leaders was followed by damage to its military capabilities, disruption to its supply routes and a second major confrontation with Israel this year.
The group faces a changed regional landscape following developments in Syria and Iran, as well as growing pressure at home over the cost of renewed war.
That pressure has sharpened since Hezbollah launched rockets towards Israel on 2 March in support of Iran, triggering another devastating Israeli offensive which has killed more than 4,300 people. Despite a ceasefire announced in June, Israeli attacks and occupation of parts of southern Lebanon remain a daily reality. The group has not launched a new full-scale response.
Lebanon’s president and government, meanwhile, are pressing ahead with the principle that weapons should be held by the state alone.
A framework signed by Lebanon and Israel in Washington on 26 June sets out a phased process under which the Lebanese army would extend state authority, non-state armed groups would be disarmed and Israeli forces would withdraw from Lebanese territory. Hezbollah opposes disarmament, leaving the question of its weapons at the centre of Lebanon’s political debate.
Destruction still visible
A walk through Dahiyeh offers a reminder that reconstruction has not kept pace with destruction. Small excavators can be seen clearing rubble and working around damaged buildings, but the scale of the task extends well beyond individual sites. Repeated Israeli strikes have made lasting repairs harder.
A UN-backed assessment published in June put direct building damage across Beirut and Mount Lebanon at more than $365 million. It found 146 buildings completely destroyed and another 264 partially damaged, and estimated that the destruction had generated nearly 649,000 cubic metres of debris.
Damage was concentrated in several areas of Beirut’s southern suburbs, including Haret Hreik, Hadath, Chiyah, Burj el-Barajneh and Laylaki.
Funding is also another obstacle. Lebanon’s reconstruction needs far exceed the sums its cash-strapped state has allocated, while analysts say major international support is unlikely to arrive on the scale seen after the 2006 war without progress on Hezbollah’s disarmament.
Existing reconstruction funding is directed in part towards rubble removal and public infrastructure rather than compensation for every family whose home was destroyed

AI boom fuels ‘k-shaped’ divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:45:06 UTC
01:45:06 KST

While Taiwan is benefiting from a global artificial intelligence (AI) boom, many traditional industries have seen little of the benefit, widening the country’s “K-shaped” economic divide, an economist said.
A “K-shaped” economy is one in which some sectors expand rapidly while others struggle, head of the commerce development and strategy research division at the Commerce Development Research Institute Ju Haw (朱浩) said in an interview.
In Taiwan’s case, high-tech and AI-related industries have continued to grow while traditional industries have come under increasing pressure, he said.
Photo: EPA
AI development has created crowding-out effects, as large high-tech firms generating strong profits are better able to attract investment, skilled workers and energy resources, including renewable energy, Ju said,
Traditional industries, by contrast, face high barriers to transformation because they lack resources such as capital and manpower, he said.
As capital continues to flow into AI-related industries, the gap between the technology and non-technology sectors has widened, exacerbating the country’s “K-shaped” economic development, Ju said.
Taiwan has an unusual economic landscape in which AI development continues to boost GDP growth, while the headline growth rate masks uneven wealth distribution because the benefits of AI are not reaching the broader business community and the general public, he said.
Citing strong export performance, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics forecast last month that Taiwan’s GDP would grow 11.05 percent this year, following an 8.76 percent increase last year.
Data compiled by the Taiwan Stock Exchange and the Taipei Exchange, which operate Taiwan’s main board and over-the-counter market respectively, showed that average annual pay at listed semiconductor firms was NT$2.58 million (US$81,000) last year, compared with NT$543,000 in the tourism sector, almost five times more.
FDC International Hotels Corp (雲品國際) president David Ding (丁原偉) said rising labor and food costs have led many hospitality firms to target higher-end customers, while others have been forced out of the market because of labor shortages and shrinking profit margins.
Shane Global Holding Inc (商億) chairman Jay Shane (謝智通) said this year has been a difficult year for the global furniture industry, as investment has continued to flow into AI-related industries and the booming stock market.
Furniture suppliers have faced pressure from US tariff policies, inflation and weakening demand, he said.
However, Eslite Spectrum Corp (誠品生活) distribution division head Lin Chia-hsien (林家賢) said AI development has helped boost consumption, allowing the retail industry to share in some of the benefits.
Visits to Eslite stores have increased by about 10 percent from a year earlier so far this year, Lin said.
In response to the difficulties facing traditional industries, Ju said they do not need to transform themselves into technology companies but should use AI applications to create higher-value products and services.
For example, a screw supplier should not simply sell screws but combine manufacturing capabilities, software and services to transform itself from a basic product supplier into a higher-value solutions provider, he said.
The government should allow traditional-industry companies to rent or share AI infrastructure, lowering the barriers to AI adoption for small and medium-sized enterprises seeking to upgrade production, he added.

Earlier on Thursday, New York Fed President John Williams said he and his colleagues “still have a lot of work to do” in dealing with lingering inflation risks. Several other officials have aired similar comments, in line with the signal given last week when policymakers voted

Guermantes Lailari On Taiwan: Taiwan’s Sweet Potato Roots of Defiance: Shattering China’s Post-Invasion Blueprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:45:05 UTC
01:45:05 KST

If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets.
Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.”
To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook executed through seven lines of action:
Peacetime Shaping: Beijing sets psychological conditions for surrender before invading by mapping littoral approaches, modifying commercial ferries for armor deployment, and weaponizing “Cognitive Defeatism” (wangguo lun, 亡國論) to brand resistance as futile.
Legal Formalism: The People’s Republic of China (PRC) weaponizes local laws using security decrees to reclassify civic defiance as criminal subversion.
Identity Erasure: The PRC imposes state narratives to systematically erase and rewrite local heritage, mirroring its cultural erasure campaigns in Tibet and Xinjiang (East Turkestan).
Structural Surveillance: The PRC embeds surveillance via tracking matrices, facial surveillance, and biometric databases.
Manipulating Freedom: The PRC manipulates economic freedoms to keep populations unsteady.
Institutional Co-optation: The PRC hijacks bureaucracies to force local civil services to execute occupation directives.
Generational Patience: The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) treats time as a strategic asset, absorbing decades of international sanctions to normalize its territorial control permanently.
To counter this psychological framing, Taiwan’s mindset must shift toward po f? chen zh?u (破釜沉舟) — breaking cooking pots and sinking boats — signaling an unyielding determination to resist.
THE PARAMILITARY ENFORCEMENT MACHINE
The PRC does not rely on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) for post-invasion governance. Post-combat, the architecture pivots to specialized constabulary forces led by the People’s Armed Police (PAP). Trained in counter-riot operations and urban suppression, the PAP isolates communities, executes political purges, and enforces population control.
THE BLIND SPOTS IN THE RESISTANCE EQUATION
The IWC report distinguishes two broad seizure scenarios with different post-seizure dynamics:
Scenario A: Capitulation Under Coercion. Physical infrastructure remains intact under maritime blockades, but digital and civic campaigns of disobedience ensue.
Scenario B: Compellence Through Invasion. Kinetic military conquest shatters the country and triggers a prolonged, armed guerrilla campaign. This scenario forces planners to decouple total kinetic war from ongoing gray-zone escalation.
In classical Chinese military thought, Sun Tzu emphasizes shi (勢) — the strategic configuration of power and momentum. Beijing attempts to manipulate this shi through a psychological inversion of the “Empty Fort Strategy” (k?ngcheng ji, 空城計), weaponizing gray-zone maneuvers and Cognitive Defeatism to project an illusion of absolute mastery, tricking Taiwan into psychological surrender. Countering this requires injecting three alternative, high-probability scenarios into the equation to disrupt China’s calculated configuration.
Scenario C: The Decapitation and “Puppet State” Infiltration. The IWC report assumes institutional co-optation occurs after infrastructure collapse. However, the PRC “playbook” involves leveraging fifth columnists to compromise defenses alongside cyberwarfare and electronic warfare attacks. These actions paralyze communications to allow PRC special forces to eliminate Taiwan’s command structure.
Beijing then installs a pre-vetted puppet administration, which issues an “invitation” to the PAP and PLA to restore public order during a “domestic crisis.” This maneuver exploits political polarization and discredits ROC legitimacy. This collaborationist setup, mirroring the historical WWII Vichy France model, avoids the trauma of an amphibious invasion, deflates global sympathy, and complicates foreign intervention. Resistance networks would face a civil-bureaucratic entity in which local officials and police — coerced by the puppet government — execute Beijing’s directives under local legal authority.
Scenario D: The “Salami-Slicing” and Partial Seizure Limbo. International law binds Penghu (the Pescadores) to Taiwan under the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki, the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco, and the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) — meaning a strike there could trigger a direct military response from Taipei and Washington. To bypass these treaty tripwires, Beijing is highly likely to target outposts outside this diplomatic framework by annexing Kinmen or Matsu or capturing Dongsha (東沙群島) or Itu Aba (太平島) in the South China Sea. Since the critical February 2024 Kinmen speedboat incident, the China Coast Guard has already been utilizing “Legal Formalism” via regular incursions. Severing these remote outposts allows the PRC to evaluate occupation and surveillance matrices on captive territory while trapping Formosa in a suffocating economic limbo designed to drive capital flight and demoralize the population.
Scenario E: The “Failed State” Chaos and Fractional Survival. The IWC report overlooks how a stalled invasion could deteriorate into ‘Failed State’ chaos or a scorched-earth stalemate. If the PLA shatters central infrastructure but fails to secure Taiwan’s rugged terrain, the island fractures into autonomous resistance zones cut off from essential resources. Neighborhood civil defense forces must fight occupying patrols and fend off starvation to show Beijing it will inherit a multi-generational resource drain rather than a submissive province. This decentralized survival tactically validates the uniquely Taiwanese proverb: “sweet potatoes are not afraid of rotting in the soil; they only ask that their branches and leaves be passed down from generation to generation.” Mirroring the island’s shape and the plant’s hardy biology, an unyielding local identity ensures decentralized survival even under total devastation.
THE INSULAR BOTTLENECK
Geography affects Taiwan’s deeply entrenched civic identity. Unlike Ukraine, which has overland supply routes, a maritime blockade could sever the continuous flow of weapons, food, energy, and medical supplies into Taiwan. There are no porous land borders to supply an ongoing insurgency. This fundamental isolation is compounded by an acute physical bottleneck: Taiwan’s dependence on a limited network of undersea fiber-optic cables risks an instantaneous, total communications blackout.
Taiwan’s vulnerability to blockade means that a resistance movement might not be organized effectively once a kinetic conflict begins. The Resistance Operating Concept (ROC) emphasizes that a viable resistance architecture cannot be an ad-hoc civilian undertaking during an invasion; it must be legally established, structured, and driven by the sovereign central government during peacetime. This pre-emptive, state-directed strategy embodies the timeless strategic principle of j? ?n s? w?i (居安思危) — prepare for danger in times of peace. This hard lesson was forged under Nazi occupation during World War II and decades of Soviet Communist occupation of Eastern Europe. The architecture, clandestine command loops, and resource networks should be legally and structurally hardcoded into the civil fabric by the state before a crisis erupts. Domestic self-sufficiency is a baseline survival necessity.
THE PEACETIME MANDATE
The IWC report delivers an urgent mandate for Taipei and Washington. Grounding these alternative scenarios in international relations theory uncovers a profound application of Deterrence by Denial. While traditional deterrence emphasizes punishment, structuralizing whole-of-society resistance shifts the cost-benefit matrix before a missile flies, denying Beijing confidence by turning conquest into a multi-generational asymmetric trap.
Crucially, this architecture relies on a multi-layered application of Assurance Theory. Externally, Washington must assure Taipei of its conventional commitment so that post-invasion planning is never misread as beachhead abandonment. Internally, institutionalizing a resistance operating concept assures Taiwan’s population by providing the structured agency to survive extreme conditions and maintain democratic sovereignty. Simultaneously, this domestic readiness delivers reciprocal assurance to Washington, signaling a firm “will to fight” that minimizes the domestic political risk for US intervention.
This framework addresses a severe regulatory blind spot within Taiwan’s All-out Defense Mobilization Agency (ADMA): the core statute, the All-out Defense Mobilization Readiness Act (全民防衛動員準備法), permits only full mobilization, completely lacking statutory mechanics for partial mobilization during a creeping gray-zone crisis. This statutory gap leaves the nation vulnerable to pre-war paralysis.
Therefore, President William Lai’s (賴清德) “Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience” focus must explicitly expand into a comprehensive “Whole-of-Society Resistance” architecture, channeling the historic ethos of sweet potato resilience through horizontal defense networks. While resilience merely absorbs a crisis to bounce back, resistance actively denies the adversary its political objectives. This requires adopting lessons from the Baltic “Forest Brothers” — the underground partisan movements in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania that fought Soviet communist annexation for a decade. While they ultimately struggled without secure maritime lifelines or peacetime state structures, the Lai administration can avoid this fate by hardcoding clandestine mechanisms now, under a functioning democracy.
In alignment with the Resistance Operating Concept doctrine, this entire architecture must be mandated during peacetime but designed for decentralized execution to survive a decapitation strike. The state must legally vest local municipal districts and civil defense units with autonomous communication loops, staged supplies, and explicit continuity-of-governance protocols to instantly bypass a treasonous puppet administration. Given Taiwan’s acute vulnerability to maritime blockades — particularly its limited, days-long reserve of liquefied natural gas — food and medical stockpiles, water-purification capacity, and off-grid emergency energy must be structurally embedded into every local township and apartment block.
True deterrence lies in forcing CCP planners to realize that subduing Taiwan means confronting an island where every city block and mountain village is engineered by the state to function as a bastion of defiance. Taiwan’s ultimate contribution to deterrence is the unyielding psychological infrastructure of a populace that flatly refuses to be ruled by the CCP, turning any occupation into a multi-generational trap the CCP cannot survive.

Chiayi Science Park signaling Phase III development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:45:05 UTC
01:45:05 KST

The National Science and Technology Council has issued a formal notice to solicit public feedback on further expansion in Phase II of the Chiayi Science Park (嘉義科學園區), which local industries have viewed as the starting point for the park’s Phase III development.
The Chiayi Science Park is in the county’s Taibao City (太保). Its development would connect with other Southern Taiwan Science Park (南部科學園區) branches in Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County, as well as the Central Taiwan Science Park (中部科學園區) and Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區) to form the world’s most comprehensive artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor industry corridor, the council said earlier.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) intends to increase its investment by building five additional advanced packaging plants at the Chiayi Science Park, the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister newspaper) reported yesterday, citing sources in the semiconductor supply chain.
Photo: Lin Yi-chang, Taipei Times
If realized, TSMC’s total advanced packaging plants at the park would reach 10, making it the world’s largest and most technologically advanced packaging hub, the report said.
TSMC has two advanced packaging facilities in Phase I of the park. The company started mass production at Phase I in June and has installed equipment at Phase II, the report said.
In Phase II, TSMC plans to build three packaging plants, with Phase III already under construction. The company’s goal is to complete construction of all three facilities in Phase II by 2031, the report said.
As for the Phase III site, which is estimated at 198.65 hectares and primarily leased from Taiwan Sugar Corp (台糖), the council said the development would focus on technologies related to AI, heterogeneous packaging, silicon photonics, high-speed broadband networks, quantum technology and net zero emissions.
It would undergo a one-month public comment period to gather opinions from local communities and various sectors. Following that, a feasibility assessment and planning would be conducted and submitted to the Executive Yuan for approval before entering urban planning and environmental impact assessments, the council said.
The robust demand for TSMC’s chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging technology from Nvidia Corp, Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Apple Inc is the primary driver behind TSMC’s continued capacity expansion at the Chiayi Science Park, the report said, citing industry observers.
The Phase III investment would help transform the county into a global production hub for advanced semiconductor packaging, it said.
In July, TSMC raised its capital expenditure forecast to US$60 billion to US$64 billion for this year, up from a range of US$52 billion to US$56 billion announced in April.
In addition to the company’s investments in the US, Japan and Germany, TSMC operates 19 advanced wafer fabs and chip packaging plants in Taiwan and is building 13 additional fabs and packaging facilities in Hsinchu City, Taichung, Chiayi County, Tainan and Kaohsiung, according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
Further investment is planned as TSMC seeks to maintain its lead over global competitors in advanced process development, the ministry said.

Vietnam cannot beat China with the lights out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:45:01 UTC
01:45:01 KST

The world’s attempts to reduce its reliance on China’s juggernaut manufacturing sector depend to an outsized extent on just one country: Vietnam. The nation’s efforts to meet those expectations, in turn, might come down to the fate of a handful of mothballed wind farms. With energy costs soaring, the government is warning of blackouts looming as soon as next year. A fix is long overdue.
Vietnam might be a victim of its own success. More than perhaps any other country, it has been a beneficiary of the tariffs and diversification that have attempted to restrain China’s trade since the first administration of US President Donald Trump. The manufacturing sector is one of the fastest-growing on the planet. Exports are equivalent to almost all of GDP, and the economy grew 8 percent last year.
Keeping that industrial machine going requires phenomenal amounts of electricity. That is where the problems start. Grid demand is increasing at about 10 percent a year, but supply growth has stalled after a renewable-power boom ran out of control at about the time of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The war in Iran has made the situation worse: Liquefied natural gas, once seen as the backbone of Vietnam’s future grid, no longer looks like the affordable or reliable fuel it was once presented as being. Even coal is being considered as a way to relieve chronic shortages.
There is only one fix that is up to the scale of the problem, and it is the one that Vietnam has been avoiding: Ending the pricing squabbles with state-owned utility Vietnam Electricity Corp (EVN) that have kept gigawatts of clean energy switched off for much of the past five years.
It seems extraordinary in a country where blackouts in 2023 shut down factories and wiped 0.3 percent from GDP, but Vietnam is sitting on significant numbers of stalled but largely finished renewable generation projects.
Two wind farms amid the tea and coffee plantations of the Central Highlands are emblematic: Originally scheduled to be completed in 2021, they gathered dust in regulatory limbo for years before receiving licenses in January, allowing them to finally start operating.
They are far from alone. An EVN database lists 85 wind and solar projects totaling 4.7 gigawatts (GW) that have been caught up in similar shenanigans, with just 1.6GW delivering power. The remainder would, in theory, be sufficient for millions of homes. Not all of those are completed, but at least 0.5GW of the total appears to be tested and ready for grid operation.
The backlog is not entirely EVN’s fault. Driven by overly generous guaranteed revenues, Vietnam’s renewable power boom from 2019 to 2021 resembled a gold rush in every sense. Developers raced to stake out contracts, cutting corners and leaving permits, land-use rights and grid connections to be sorted out later.
The pricing disputes that have dragged on ever since represent the utility’s attempt to regularize the chaotic aftermath, without overpaying for electricity that can now be bought more cheaply.
When considered in the context of Vietnam’s surging power needs, however, this haggling has been penny-wise and pound-foolish. In attempting to rewrite agreed contracts with generators, the government has made the country look like a risky place for private capital.
Hanoi wants to roughly triple the size of its grid over the next five years and would require US$136 billion to pay for it — far beyond what the state can afford on its own. Renewables are the only power source capable of being built at the required rate, but the fate of Vietnam’s Just Energy Transition Partnership, a UN-brokered energy transition framework, shows how much it is at the mercy of private capital.
After four years, just three of 50 planned projects have received investment, representing about 7 percent of the US$11 billion needed.
EVN can afford to be magnanimous. It has eliminated cumulative losses after several dicey years. Paying 10 percent over the odds for a gigawatt of legacy projects would be a bargain if restoring investor confidence shaved even a few basis points from the cost of financing the extra 150GW or so Hanoi wants to install by 2030.
A quick but dirty resolution that gets the most viable ones connected, while avoiding giveaways to outright rule-breakers, would be far better than allowing the current purgatory to drag on.
That does not mean teaching developers that Vietnam is a pushover. The bargain for the next generation of projects should be the opposite: Hanoi would not rewrite contracts after investors have spent their money, and developers cannot expect deadlines and permits to be negotiable.
With the government attempting to finalize a trade deal with the Trump administration, Vietnam is in a prime position to be one of the biggest beneficiaries as the world decouples from China. However, if it cannot generate the electrons needed to power its production lines, multinationals are likely to conclude that other countries — or even China itself — represent better bets.
Vietnam’s chaotic first renewables boom has proved the country can increase its electricity generation at a prodigious rate. The long hangover that followed has demonstrated it is going to need to tempt private capital back in the door if it is ever to repeat the trick.

EDITORIAL: Free lunch policy needs an overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:45:00 UTC
01:45:00 KST

Soon after school started this month, a series of suspected food poisoning incidents involving school lunches were reported in Taipei, once again stirring concerns among students and parents about the quality and safety of free meals.
Eighty-seven students from Chengyuan High School’s junior-high division reported diarrhea and other food poisoning symptoms after eating school lunches on Sept. 7, and some received emergency medical treatment that evening.
The Taipei Department of Health said it received a report the following day and sent inspectors to investigate and collect samples. It also ordered that the lunch service be suspended. Five hygiene deficiencies were found during the on-site inspection.
Test results released by the department on Sept. 18 confirmed that Staphylococcal enterotoxin B — a toxin known for causing severe food poisoning — was found.
In the same week, the Affiliated Dali High School of the University of Taipei reported that more than 10 students experienced gastrointestinal discomfort after eating school lunches on Sept. 10. Those meals were provided by the same caterer as the Chengyuan incident.
The case is still being investigated.
The health department on Sept. 14 said it also sent inspectors to Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls’ High School after three students felt sick shortly after eating fishcake tempura from the school’s cafeteria. One of the students was later diagnosed with peritonitis and hospitalized, but whether it was the result of food poisoning was not determined.
A city councilor on Wednesday last week said some Taipei Municipal Jinhua Junior High School students reportedly vomited and had diarrhea after eating school lunches on Sept. 4.
The city’s education department denied it was a food poisoning incident, saying that only three students felt ill and they all had different symptoms, adding that samples had been disposed of and could not be tested.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) in January announced that the city would provide free school lunches to all elementary and junior-high schools starting this month, prompting several other local governments to follow the policy.
When he made the announcement, parent groups expressed concerns that uniform pricing would lead to parents being unable to decide what is on the menu, and that without subsidies for lunches that meet the government’s “Three Labels and One QR Code” (3L1Q) standards, lunch providers might start using cheaper ingredients with poorer quality and less supervision.
However, they probably did not expect so many suspected food poisoning incidents the same month the program began. Some parents are beginning to question the program and wonder if the phrase “there is no such thing as a free [school] lunch” holds true.
The city government has terminated several contracts of the caterer responsible for the Chengyuan High School incident and fined it NT$180,000. The school was also ordered to set up a single point of contact to help affected students and faculty apply for compensation.
However, some city councilors and parents are asking the city government to explain how the food became contaminated and how it plans to prevent similar incidents. Others also requested the creation of transparent and uniform standards in handling school lunch food poisoning incidents, from service suspension to sampling and testing, as well as criteria for resuming service.
Local media had reported that public health specialists urged the city’s education department not to prematurely rule out food poisoning before completing comprehensive investigations, saying that such cases are highly time-sensitive and sample collection should not be delayed. They also called for standardized early warning mechanisms and the establishment of investigation procedures and tools.
Some people have proposed allowing parents associations at schools to decide if they want to pay out of pocket to “upgrade” the quality of their lunches and choose caterers they trust, as city government funding limits flexibility.

Ministry warns of rising nearsightedness in kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:59 UTC
01:44:59 KST

Last academic year, 45.13 percent of elementary-school students, or one in every 2.2 students, were nearsighted, Ministry of Education data showed.
The ministry made the comment amid growing concerns over the impact of digital learning tools on children’s eyesight, saying that almost every classroom is equipped with a digital display and nearly every student with a tablet.
The numbers in Kaohsiung were higher than the national average, with 45.91 percent of elementary-school students nearsighted, compared with 45.2 percent two years ago and 45.34 the year before that, the Kaohsiung Education Bureau said.
Photo courtesy of the Kaohsiung Education Bureau
The rate had declined slightly each year before the COVID-19 pandemic, but rose again as students switched to online learning, said Yen Min-su (顏敏夙), director of the bureau’s physical education and healthcare division.
Preventive efforts should prioritize younger students, as children who are not nearsighted by the middle of elementary school are less likely to develop it later in life, Yen said.
As myopia is hereditary, the bureau is seeking central government subsidies to cover one annual registration fee for parents who take their children to ophthalmology clinics for dilating eye drops, she said.
The bureau said it is promoting eye-health education, vision screening and healthy use of digital devices.
Students should rest their eyes for 10 minutes for every 30 minutes of screen time and spend two hours outside every day, the bureau said, encouraging students to go outside during class breaks.
The bureau said it is intensifying digital device management on campuses by requiring schools to establish guidelines for device use, set up application procedures and limit screen time to help students develop healthy digital habits.
Protecting children’s vision requires parents, schools and medical professionals to work together, the bureau said, adding that prevention, early detection, follow ups and corrective measures are needed to help children properly care for their eyes in the digital age.
One mother surnamed Hsu (許) said she kept her child from using digital devices too early, but with tablets and digital lessons at school, they are no longer avoidable.
Her child, who is going into fourth grade, has vision of 0.9 in both eyes and the family’s strategy is to limit the child’s daily screen time, Hsu said.
Japan has the world’s most comprehensive strategy for protecting children’s vision, ophthalmologist Hung Chi-ting (洪啟庭) said, adding that 36.8 percent of elementary-school students in Tokyo are nearsighted.
In addition to annual school health checkups, Japan screens three-year-old children for vision problems so they can be detected and treated early, Hung said.
Children should limit screen time and follow the 20-20-20 rule: After 20 minutes of close-up work, look at something at least 20 feet (6 meters) away for at least 20 seconds, he said.
Kids should spend two hours outdoors every day, or at least 14 hours a week, and undergo their first comprehensive vision examination at age three or four, followed by regular checkups every six months, he added.
Changes in a child’s habits, such as moving closer to the TV or screen, squinting to see distant objects, frequent eye rubbing or blinking, headaches and difficulty concentrating, could be signs of myopia, Hung said, encouraging parents to have their child’s eyes checked if they notice these signs.
