====================================================================================================

The AI folks do not seem to understand intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:58 UTC
01:44:58 KST

Just three years after OpenAI said its models were good at grade-school math, the company announced they had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours, something that had stumped humanity’s greatest mathematical minds since the 1930s. Project that trend forward and you see why OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman thinks artificial intelligence (AI) will cure all diseases — and why people are afraid that a rogue AI might harm humanity.
Santa Fe Institute scientists Melanie Mitchell and David Krakauer described AI’s mantra as “scale is all you need.” What that means is the bigger the training sets and the more compute you have, the better AI becomes.
Altman’s vision of AI’s exponential growth curve, and the related hopes and fears, are similarly driven by an unspoken assumption that intelligence is all you need. If you are smart enough, you can cure cancer — or destroy the world — but that is not how power and intelligence work.
Illustration: Yusha
Anthropic PBC says Claude, its AI model, already writes more than 80 percent of the code its engineers merge. Push that to 100 percent and AI would be building its own successors. It could keep racing ahead until finally it understood everything and could control everything.
That is the fear and, for some, the hope. AI could create what Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei calls “a country of geniuses in a datacenter.”
The US ran that experiment at Los Alamos. It put legendary physicists such as Niels Bohr, Richard Feynman and Robert Oppenheimer to work building the atomic bomb. However, Alex Wellerstein, a historian of science and nuclear weapons at the Stevens Institute of Technology, calculated that Los Alamos accounted for just 4 percent of the Manhattan Project’s almost US$2 billion cost. Eighty percent of the budget went to plants in Tennessee and Washington that produced uranium and plutonium.
In his 1945 Congressional testimony, Oppenheimer said that without scientists there would have been no bomb, but “if there had been only scientists, there also would be no atomic bomb.”
AI has changed coding, mathematics and weather forecasting. They all have a vast pool of available training data, rapid feedback, and clear right and wrong answers. These keep models moored to reality, not spiraling off to disaster as the result of compounding small errors.
Constant corrections are why we remember the Wright brothers. The best-funded attempt at flight in 1903 was made by Samuel Langley, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, who had US$50,000 in government funds and an engine four times as powerful as the one in the hands of the Wrights. Langley designed a plane that was inherently stable, but his brilliant design plunged into the Potomac River because the models he built did not scale.
The Wright brothers were bicycle mechanics. They did not have his resources, but they knew that bikes were unstable machines kept upright by constant corrections from the rider. They used that insight, plus wind tunnel tests of as many as 200 wing shapes, to beat their better-funded rival.
Intelligence needs input. The faster and clearer the input, the more powerful intelligence becomes. Math, coding and weather forecasting? Check. Financial markets qualify, too. Hedge fund Two Sigma Investments boasts that its computing power would rank among the world’s top five supercomputer sites, and that is not an accident.
Writing fails the tests, hence the deluge of AI slop on LinkedIn. So does curing cancer, because it requires experiments on living systems that take years to respond. Intelligence might improve your hit rate, but it cannot get you around that limit.
Intelligence gets used first in the places with the fastest and clearest feedback. What is left are the problems where it is worth less. That is why its power is unlikely to keep climbing. The more you know, the harder it becomes to learn even more. We ran that experiment in theoretical physics.
In the early days after the quantum mechanics revolution, progress leapt forward. Over time, despite better instruments and tools, foundational breakthroughs got harder. In a 1975 lecture, Nobel Prize-winning physicist Paul Dirac said: “It was very easy in those days for any second-rate physicist to do first-rate work. There has not been such a glorious time since then. It is very difficult now for a first-rate physicist to do second-rate work.”
Research-heavy industries show the same pattern. In semiconductors, Stanford University economist Nicholas Bloom and three coauthors found that doubling chip density takes more than 18 times as many researchers as in the early 1970s. Even Tom Davidson and Tom Houlden of the research group Forethought, whose model gives about 60 percent odds that fully automated AI research would compress three years of progress into one, assume the returns fall as software approaches its limits.
So, when Amodei predicts that powerful AI could compress 50 to 100 years of biological progress into five to 10, and that reductions of 95 percent or more in cancer deaths and new cases seem possible, skepticism is appropriate. The key question, one AI leader wrote, is how much progress each additional increment of intelligence buys, and which other inputs become the constraint when intelligence is plentiful.
That leader was Amodei himself, in his 2024 essay “Machines of Loving Grace.” In the same essay, he wrote that today’s particle physicists have no shortage of theories, but lack the accelerator data to choose between them, and it is not clear superintelligence would change that.
Other Anthropic researchers said that Amdahl’s Law dictates that speeding up one part of a process tends to move bottlenecks, not eliminate them. They even forecast that this would apply to a world dominated by self-improving AI.
That is why we all need to take a breath before plunging into the utopian and apocalyptic forecasts about AI, and to watch the bottlenecks instead. An advantage in thinking is not an army, a power grid or a supply chain, and it cannot build them overnight. Doing that would take more time and investment than the roughly US$760 billion in capital spending Google parent Alphabet Inc, Amazon.com Inc, Meta Platforms Inc and Microsoft Corp alone expect this year.
Altman’s curve is real in mathematics. Maybe not far beyond it. Transforming coding is important. It is not the first sign of a cybernetic god.
Gautam Mukunda writes about corporate management and innovation. He teaches leadership at the Yale School of Management and is the author of Indispensable: When Leaders Really Matter. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

UK: five arrested for on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:56 UTC
01:44:56 KST

Breadcrumb
UK police arrest five on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act' near air base
British counter-terrorism police were Sunday probing "a major" incident near a base used by the US air force after arresting five men on suspicion of "preparing a terrorist act", police said.
Armed officers detained the group in the early hours after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base", London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.
A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.
Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.
Incident 'contained'
"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.
Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400 metre (1,300 feet) cordon had been put in place.
Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.
Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out".
Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in Liverpool he had been in contact with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and the UK was "working closely with our American friends".
Asked if there was any Iranian involvement, he said it would be "irresponsible to speculate".
Gloucestershire police said earlier it had declared a "major incident" with several men arrested "on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act".
Villagers evacuated
Residents from Whelford were evacuated to a nearby leisure centre.
"My understanding is that the whole village was evacuated in the early hours of this morning," district councillor Tristan Wilkinson told AFP.
"Most people got in their cars, so when the police knocked on the doors and told them to go, most people were able to kind of drive away."
They were now waiting to see if the cordon would be relaxed later Sunday, as many were worried about pets which had to be left behind. "I'm hoping that the police will actually reduce the cordon quite quickly," Wilkinson said.
Villager Julian Tudsbery said it was his fellow villager who had alerted police first after they "phoned the airbase police who didn't answer the phone. It just rang out so she dialled 999".
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

‘Time’ cover focuses on China threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:54 UTC
01:44:54 KST

Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Pacific Command, is featured on the cover of Time magazine’s Oct. 12 issue, alongside an interview published online on Thursday in which he outlined a “deterrence by denial” strategy aimed at countering a potential Chinese attack on Taiwan.
In the interview, Paparo detailed his approach to defense, describing deterrence by denial as central to preventing a conflict in the Taiwan Strait.
The goal of the strategy is to convince China that “where America’s direct vital interests are involved, there’s a high probability of denying your aggression,” the magazine quoted him as saying.
Photo: Screen grab from Time’s X account
Should diplomacy fail, Paparo has proposed using large numbers of low-cost, mass-produced precision drones alongside conventional high-tech missile firepower to create what he calls a “Hellscape” — a battlefield environment designed to prevent or significantly delay a Chinese amphibious landing on Taiwan.
Paparo commands the oldest and largest US geographic combatant command, which covers about half the globe. It has about 400,000 military and civilian personnel, while the Pacific Fleet has about 200 warships, five carrier strike groups and more than 1,000 aircraft.
US dominance in the Pacific is facing its most serious challenge since World War II, with Paparo’s primary mission being to deter China from taking military action against Taiwan, Time said.
Referencing Chinese strategist Sun Zi’s (孫子) The Art of War (孫子兵法), Paparo said that “winning without fighting is the acme of skill.”
“Mission success for me is not to fight and win a war; it’s to provide a deterrent capability so that we never go to war in the first place,” he said.
The key to deterrence by denial is demonstrating credible military capabilities and the will to use them while protecting critical military secrets, he said.
However, with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy now 12 times larger than it was 25 years ago, the US military must still prepare for combat in case deterrence fails, Paparo said.
If a conflict erupts in the Taiwan Strait, the US military could institute the “Hellscape” strategy to prevent China from launching an amphibious invasion of Taiwan or, at a minimum, significantly delay the operation, he said.
“We need not gain air or maritime superiority of a space; we need only deny its use to aggressors,” he said.
A 2023 war game conducted by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies found that although US forces could repel a Chinese invasion of Taiwan in most scenarios, the effort would include the loss of two aircraft carriers, dozens of warships and hundreds of aircraft — losses that would rank among the heaviest suffered by the US military since World War II, Time said.
The war game did not account for the depletion of US missile stocks resulting from military operations in the Middle East at the time.
Despite the severity of the challenges, Paparo said he was confident in the US’ ability to prevail.
The focus is not to prove that the US military can win a war, but to maximize the margin of victory while minimizing the costs of war in terms of lives, military capabilities, money and time, he said.
The goal is to “drive that bill down to zero,” he added.

Tourism Administration issues diving guidelines for better water activity safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:54 UTC
01:44:54 KST

The Tourism Administration has issued new guidelines for diving activities, following a series of diving-related accidents over the past few years.
Earlier this month, a diving student experienced hypoxia, lost consciousness and died after a training dive at a bat cave in New Taipei City’s Rueifang District (瑞芳) when sea conditions worsened.
On Sunday last week, six divers were trapped by high waves off Longdong (龍洞) in New Taipei City’s Gongliao District (貢寮). They were rescued by the Coast Guard Administration and no injuries were reported.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
To improve safety and provide a clearer regulatory framework for operators, the Tourism Administration published guidelines covering snorkeling, scuba diving and freediving.
The guidelines define snorkeling as diving activities involving a mask, fins or snorkel; scuba diving as diving with a mask, fins, snorkel and breathing apparatus; and freediving as diving without breathing equipment.
The guidelines outline the legal framework governing water recreation activities, clarify the responsibilities of the authorities, and define diving activities and equipment requirements, the administration said.
They also provide guidance on dive leaders and dive buddies, and address safety and risk management, it added.
Under the guidelines, people scuba diving or freediving must hold a qualification certificate issued by domestic or international diving organizations.
People who engage in such water activities should meet internationally recognized training standards, including age and health requirements, basic swimming ability, marine safety awareness, and appropriate supervision and companion arrangements, the guidelines state.
Scuba divers should be equipped with a complete breathing system, including a regulator, buoyancy compensation device and air tank, while freediving gear includes a snorkel, mask, wetsuit and surface identification devices, they say.
Contravening the Act for the Development of Tourism (發展觀光條例), such as engaging in water recreation activities in prohibited areas, are punishable by a maximum fine of NT$50,000, while commercial operators may face fines of up to NT$200,000, the guidelines state.
Other violations involving facilities, personnel or certification requirements would be handled under the regulations of the responsible authorities.
Taiwan Freediving Development Association secretary general Wu Ping-yu (吳秉宥) said the guidelines are an important first step in clarifying responsibilities and obligations.
While the guidelines primarily aim to help the public and operators understand regulations, few follow new rules, he said.
The Tourism Administration could produce simplified guides or use other methods to improve public awareness of the new standards, he added.
The Tourism Administration said the guidelines are advisory in nature and can serve as a reference for local governments, national park administrations and national scenic area administrations responsible for managing water recreation activities.
Government agencies, site managers, diving organizations and divers can also use the guidelines as a reference for site management, professional practices and improving safety standards, the administration said.

South Korea’s excess tax revenue might exceed 50 trillion won (US$36.9 billion) this year, according to a Yonhap News report, reflecting factors including a stronger-than-expected semiconductor cycle.
That could push the size of the Future Response Fund, a government tool that channels excess tax revenue into strategic investments and fiscal reserves, to above 200 trillion won, according to Yonhap’s calculations.
South Korean Ministry of Economy and Finance is expected to publish the figure in its revised 2026 national tax revenue estimate due later this month, according to the report.
Photo: Bloomberg
The revenue windfall would give the government more room to increase spending without a corresponding rise in borrowing.
Under the 2027 budget proposal, much of the semiconductor-driven windfall is set to flow toward helping finance artificial intelligence (AI), chips and youth support while limiting bond issuance and building a fiscal buffer.
The finance ministry said in a statement on Sunday no decision has been finalized on the revised estimate of this year’s national tax revenue.
The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to 3 percent last month, its second consecutive hike, as stronger-than-expected growth and persistent underlying inflation prompted policymakers to act pre-emptively.
The central bank also upgraded its GDP growth forecast to 3.3 percent from 2.6 percent for this year, citing robust exports and investment driven by the global AI build-out.
The strength of the chip cycle has boosted corporate earnings and investment in South Korea, though policymakers are still waiting to see how much those gains boost household consumption and ripple through the rest of the domestic economy.

Four more Taiwanese are missing or have been detained in China: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

Four more Taiwanese have gone missing or been detained or had their freedom of movement restricted in China compared with the previous week, with the total reaching 449 since Jan. 1, 2024, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said in a weekly report on Saturday.
Of the 449 cases, 168 people have been reported missing, up from 165 from the previous week, and 39 have been detained for questioning, unchanged from the previous week, the council said.
Another 242 people are suspected of having their freedom of movement restricted in China, up by one, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Mainland Affairs Council’s Facebook page
With the new Chinese entry and exit regulation that took effect on Sept. 15, five groups should exercise caution when traveling to China, the MAC said.
First, people in the semiconductor and technology industries, should be aware of risks arising from the overlap of technical, commercial and national security regulations, it said.
Second, Taiwanese businesspeople and senior corporate executives could become entangled in investigations, judicial proceedings or exit bans stemming from commercial disputes, patent issues or contractual conflicts, it said.
Third, civil servants and people traveling to participate in cross-strait exchanges, whether traveling on official business or privately, should ensure they are in compliance with regulations governing travel to China.
Fourth, people engaging in religious exchanges, including attending religious gatherings or delivering sermons, should be aware of local regulations concerning religion and national security, it said.
Fifth, people who have publicly expressed their views on politics, human rights or other issues through social media, overseas events or related organizations should be mindful of uncertainties in the application and enforcement of local laws, the council said.
The US Department of State on Sept. 4 updated its Level 2 travel advisory for China, urging US citizens to “exercise increased caution” in China due to “the arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention,” the MAC said.
The travel advisory highlighted five categories of US citizens who could be targeted by Chinese authorities: US citizens of Chinese heritage or origin; anyone involved in business disputes or who has ties to US corporate entities involved in business disputes in China; anyone with a current or prior affiliation with US law enforcement, military or intelligence agencies; anyone traveling on US government-funded programs; and people with current or former connections to the US government.
“Expansive national security, counterespionage and data security laws grant Chinese officials broad discretion to detain or interrogate foreign nationals,” the department said.
That places US citizens at risk for conducting even routine business, research or expression in the public domain, it said.
Local authorities have detained and charged US citizens involved in civil business disputes with criminal offenses under the laws, it added.

Trump-Xi meeting: Official rejects Xi’s WWII claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:47 UTC
01:44:47 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) had no standing to discuss US-China relations in World War II (WWII), as the People’s Republic of China did not exist at that time, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said yesterday.
Taipei would ensure that Washington has a clear understanding that it was the Republic of China (ROC), not the People’s Republic of China (PRC), that was a steadfast ally of the US in WWII, Shen said.
Shen was referring to a White House fact sheet released on Friday about Xi’s meeting with US President Donald Trump in Washington.
Photo: CNA
It said that “the two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war.”
“Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II. Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country and that legendary Flying Tigers group,” Trump said on Thursday in his opening remarks at a state dinner for Xi, referring to the First American Volunteer Group, nicknamed the “Flying Tigers,” who formed in 1941 to help oppose Japan’s invasion of China.
Xi in his remarks said that the “Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people.”
Shen said Xi had no standing to talk about the US-China alliance in WWII, adding that then-Chinese Communist Party leader Mao Zedong (毛澤東) later described the party’s role during the war as 70 percent developing [its forces], 20 percent dealing with circumstances and 10 percent fighting the Japanese.
Moreover, the PRC had not yet been established, making it absurd to claim that the “China” in the US-China alliance was the PRC, he said.
Xi has been repeatedly promoting a narrative that frames WWII history from a perspective led by the PRC, Shen said.
The Republic of China Air Force has a long history of cooperation with the US Air Force, he said, adding that Taiwan would use the appropriate channels to ensure that the US has a clear understanding that the ROC was a steadfast US ally during World War II.
Whether in terms of geopolitics or economic and trade ties, Taiwan is also the US’ most reliable ally, he said.
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) said he thinks Trump’s references to WWII and the Flying Tigers were intended to highlight that “the US has always helped China.”
However, Beijing specializes in “cherry-picking from history” and distorting historical events, he said.
China could continue to emphasize that narrative and claim that Washington recognizes that it was the PRC that worked with the US to resist Japanese militarism in WWII.
Soochow University associate political science professor Chen Fang-yu (陳方隅) said that Taiwan needs to address how the ROC is portrayed in the WWII narrative.
Taiwan finds itself compelled to defend the ROC’s status before 1945, but it is unclear whether doing so could conflict with the Democratic Progressive Party government’s broader narrative about Taiwan’s history and identity, he said.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in a speech in July last year said that Taiwan’s national identity was established through democratization in the 1990s, Chen Fang-Yu said.
However, the government has not clearly articulated the relationship between the ROC and Taiwan before 1949, or prior to 1945, he said.
Taiwan should carefully consider what the relationship between the ROC and Taiwan was before 1949 and how to safeguard the status of the ROC as it existed then, he added.

THSR sees record number of riders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:46 UTC
01:44:46 KST

The Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR) carried a record 348,000 passengers on Thursday, the day before the Mid-Autumn Festival long weekend and 315,000 riders on Friday, the operator said.
The four-day holiday began on Friday and ends today, which is Teachers’ Day in Taiwan.
The high number of passengers led to overcrowding on some trains, with people with non-reserved seat tickets spilling into reserved-seat and business-class cars, prompting complaints on social media.
Photo: CNA
One person who identified themselves as a business-class passenger wrote on Threads that they had chosen business class tickets to avoid being disturbed, adding that regulations prohibit non-reserved seat ticket holders from entering business-class cars.
People with non-reserved seat tickets who stand in business-class cars should pay the fare difference, they said.
A business-class ticket from Nangang (南港) in Taipei to Zuoying (左營) in Kaohsiung costs NT$2,500, while a non-reserved seat ticket costs NT$1,480, the THSR’s Web site shows.
Passengers with non-reserved seat tickets who stand in higher-priced cars will be charged the fare difference and might face a penalty equivalent to 50 percent of the difference, the Web site says.
The operator expected another wave of heavy traffic yesterday and today as travelers return home.
They recommended people to return earlier if possible, and advised people with non-reserved seat tickets to check the non-reserved seat wait time on its Web site and to travel during periods with a green indicator to avoid peak hour-crowds.

More digital safeguards for children are needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:45 UTC
01:44:45 KST

Meta Platforms Inc last month reached a multibillion-dollar settlement with 52 attorneys general of US states and territories agreeing to impose daily usage limits and lockout periods for young users.
The settlement has bolstered the argument that social media addiction among children is not simply due to poor self-discipline, but also a result of mechanisms engineered by tech giants to increase engagement with their platforms.
From major US state litigation and settlements to New Zealand’s proposed minimum-age requirement for social media use, advanced democracies are treating the risks created by algorithmic recommendation systems and platform design as a systemic problem.
As a nation at the heart of the advanced technology supply chain, Taiwan must keep pace with its democratic peers in establishing regulations to protect children online.
As a teacher, I can see that the social media crisis among young people is eroding the foundations of Taiwanese democracy. Children’s brains are being hijacked by the dopamine rush of short-form content. They are losing not just the ability to concentrate in class, but also the capacity for sustained reading and logical reasoning.
Taiwan is on the front line of countering foreign cognitive warfare and disinformation. If children and adolescents lose the foundation for critical thinking and become trapped in fragmented information echo chambers, it would create a serious vulnerability in Taiwan’s democratic defenses.
Faced with the aggressive expansion of multinational social media companies, Taiwan must show determination in defending its digital sovereignty.
Such platforms enjoy enormous user bases and advertising revenue in Taiwan, all while externalizing the psychological harm and educational costs they create.
The government cannot stop at soft educational campaigns. It must establish robust digital governance mechanisms. It should require that social media platforms implement age verification systems and greater algorithmic transparency, and hold the companies liable for the safety of their young users in Taiwan.
Taiwanese institutions must also protect educators. Looking at global education trends, countries in Europe and Asia have introduced legislation restricting or banning mobile phones in primary and secondary schools. Meanwhile, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Teaching and Learning International Survey showed that Taiwanese teachers spend an excessive amount of time maintaining classroom order.
The Ministry of Education should develop guidelines for phone-free schools. This would give educators a clear legal basis for managing students’ devices, and ensure that teachers are no longer left alone to confront addictive technologies developed with billions of dollars in corporate investment.
Ultimately, protecting children’s attention skills means safeguarding Taiwanese civil society.
The Executive Yuan should coordinate across government agencies to build a national digital defense strategy through forward-looking legislation. We must reject the continued colonization of Taiwanese children’s minds by commercial mechanisms of capitalism.
Only with effective regulations can we help young Taiwanese develop the resilience and strength of character needed to sustain the country’s democratic future.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.

Trump-Xi meeting: ‘Anti-China card’ has lost impact: KMT lawmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:41 UTC
01:44:41 KST

Last week’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has rendered ineffective an “anti-China card” that Washington and Taipei could play together, Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said.
Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan (彭麗媛), on Friday concluded their three-day state visit to the US, during which Xi and Trump held their second face-to-face meeting this year, following a summit in Beijing in May.
Taiwan remains China’s top concern, with Xi telling Trump that he hoped Washington would oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the Taiwan issue with caution, while the US Department of State said its policy toward Taiwan has not changed, Lee said.
Photo: Reuters
Washington understands that the Taiwan issue is a “core interest” for China, and that the “Taiwan card” remains an important bargaining chip for Trump, she said.
The State Department statement provided a lifeline for the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) domestic messaging, but the scale of the second Trump-Xi meeting also stripped away the effectiveness of the “anti-China card,” she added.
Lee was referring to comments by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍), who in a radio interview broadcast on Sept. 15 said the Chinese Communist Party was seeking to portray a situation of “US-China joint management of Taiwan.”
In reality, Taiwan and the US maintain close communication and are partners, Lin said, adding: “We should be managing China.”
The US and China have maintained their longstanding positions, but Taiwan’s role in that relationship can only be determined based on developments in US arms sales to Taiwan, the level of official exchanges between Taipei and Washington, and whether transit diplomacy resumes, Lee said.
Taiwan’s core interests lie in trade and economic ties, security and international space, she said.
The DPP should take a more pragmatic approach by focusing on securing preferential treatment on chip tariffs, ensuring the smooth approval and delivery of US arms sales, and regaining the nation’s presence on the international stage, she said.
While during Trump’s first term, the US imposed tariffs and technology sanctions against China as part of a broader policy of strategic competition, the two meetings this year confirmed a shift toward a “constructively stable strategic relationship,” with Washington moving toward “transactional bargaining and relationship management based on realism,” Lee said.
For Trump, “America First” remains a core principle, but rather than relying on containment, deterrence and comprehensive decoupling, he increasingly seeks to use a combination of “carrots and sticks” to secure economic returns or strategic concessions for the US, she said.
Trump favors government-to-government negotiations where he can leverage his personal influence, with his meeting with Xi establishing a “G2” framework for global decisionmaking, she said.
While the artificial intelligence (AI) race and efforts to contain each other would continue, the agreement to launch official AI dialogue mechanisms to establish crisis notification systems and hotlines is important, she said.

Anime actor fights TikTok over AI voice cloning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:37 UTC
01:44:37 KST

A high-profile Japanese anime voice actor has taken TikTok to court over videos he says feature an artificial intelligence (AI) clone of his “lustrous” baritone, with a verdict due on Wednesday.
AI imitation is a growing concern among performers worldwide, and the threat has roiled Japan’s storied animation industry, whose voice actors are sometimes worshipped as much as their characters by fans.
The lawsuit filed by Kenjiro Tsuda, known for his starring roles in mega-franchises including Jujutsu Kaisen and Yu-Gi-Oh!, is believed to be the country’s first seeking to defend a person’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies.
Photo: AFP
Tsuda is demanding that TikTok remove a slew of videos narrated by a distinctively “deep” and “lustrous” voice that the 55-year-old said can only be his.
However, the platform argues it is a “generic male voice” whose perceived similarity to Tsuda’s is subjective at best, court records showed.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship” to hone talent, Japan Actors Union executive director Yuko Sasaki said.
“It’s something we spend lots of time and money perfecting,” said Sasaki, a fellow voice actor, adding that “we support Tsuda wholeheartedly.”
The court should “acknowledge that ownership of a voice is a fundamental right,” she said.
An anonymous account, whose picture resembled a Jujutsu Kaisen character dubbed by Tsuda, posted the videos in question.
They combined images and seemingly AI-generated speech about urban legends, occult phenomena and conspiracy theories.
The account at one point boasted more than 200,000 subscribers and would have brought in upward of ￥500,000 (US$3,179) in monthly revenue, the legal complaint argued.
The account, whose posts mostly lacked original substance, “only gained popularity, because its dubious, sordid content was narrated by the attractive voice of a popular actor,” Tsuda’s legal team said, according to the court records.
That infringes Tsuda’s so-called publicity rights — the ability to control and profit from the use of aspects of one’s identity, his attorneys said.
Although the account itself is no longer viewable on the platform, the Tokyo District Court will rule on whether TikTok was responsible for deleting the posts.
Parallel to the lawsuit, Sasaki and other Japanese voice actors have launched a campaign, called “No More,” against using generative AI to mimic performers without permission.
“Our industry can be crushed” if a court win for TikTok triggers “unbridled” AI voice cloning on social media, actor Bin Shimada said.
That could cause younger actors to “lose hope,” said Shimada, who is part of the campaign group.
It is also fast becoming a global issue.
“In many countries copyright and data protection laws are not being adequately adapted” to protect performers from AI clones, the International Federation of Actors said last year.
ChatGPT maker OpenAI was forced to apologize in 2024 to star Scarlett Johansson over a synthetic voice that sounded like her, released after she declined to work with OpenAI on the project.
While no law explicitly enshrines a person’s voice in Japan, the Japanese Ministry of Justice published legally non-binding guidelines last month clarifying its protection under existing rights.
As “the symbol of one’s personality” voice is subject to “publicity rights” and “rights to prevent unauthorized use of one’s portrait and likeness,” the ministry said.
However, it remains to be seen whether and how the guidelines will influence Wednesday’s court decision on Tsuda’s case.
TikTok has questioned the actor’s “national fame,” rejecting his accusations that the account was free-riding on a well-known brand in a contravention of Japan’s unfair competition prevention laws.
As a platform, all it did was “host a forum where users could post creative and ingenious content within the scope of free speech,” it told the court.
It is “very unlikely” that Tsuda’s voice would be outright denied publicity rights, said Tatsuhiro Ueno, a professor of intellectual property studies at Waseda University.
Given the actor’s Jujutsu Kaisen role as a stoic, elite sorcerer that made his voice “highly recognizable in Europe,” Ueno believes the verdict “will garner a lot of international interest.”
Veteran voice actor Michihiro Ikemizu, 83, also expressed solidarity with Tsuda — but said that AI, however sophisticated it gets, would never outperform human actors.
“You need to constantly feel and adapt while performing your role. That’s something AI can never do,” Ikemizu said. “That’s our only weapon.”

Irish soccer team split on genocide boycott

Unknown Publisher

01:44:32 KST

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has found itself divided ahead of their two Nations League clashes with Israel, with the players disagreeing over whether to boycott the first game today and goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrawing from the squad.
After hours of fraught meetings among the players and occasionally involving coaches and officials, FAI chief executive officer David Courell said at a news conference that had been delayed by several hours that a “significant majority” of the squad had agreed to play the game in Hungary, but it was far from a unanimous decision.
The handful of Irish journalists present questioned Courell and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson, asking how it came to be that such heated discussions were still taking place a day before the game.
Photo: AFP
“Obviously, this affects all of them — nobody is comfortable at the moment, but it’s about limiting the damage both personally and also for Irish football. We need to find some solution on it,” Hallgrimsson said. “There’s nothing that we can do, there’s no action that we can do that everybody will agree to, so we need to find the solution and that will limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and for the Association, the future of football in Ireland.”
Ireland is one of Europe’s most vocal critics of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and Irish fans and politicians had called on the team to boycott the Nations League B, Group 3 games, but the nation’s governing body said it would go ahead with the games.
The decision to play is at odds with a motion passed by the FAI’s members last November calling on Israel to be banned from European competition due to a number of breaches of UEFA regulations.
The game in Hungary is Israel’s home game in the Nations League group, and no Irish fans are to be present. Security concerns mean that the game which should have taken place in Dublin on October 4 has been moved to the Serbian town of Backa Topola, where it would be played behind closed doors.
BOYCOTT CAMPAIGN
Led by Irish fans and political and sporting figures, there has been a strong campaign to boycott the games and the announcement that the players had voted to play against Israel was met with an immediate backlash against the governing body.
“There is widespread public revulsion in Ireland at the prospect of our national team lining up against an Israeli side as its government carries out a genocide in Gaza and facilitates ethnic cleansing in the West Bank,” said Irish parliamentarian Daniel Ennis, a former League of Ireland soccer player with Bohemian FC, Shelbourne FC and Bray Wanderers, said in a statement. “But it is not the players’ failure — it is a failure of the Irish Government, the FAI and UEFA to do the right thing.”
Israel has denied committing genocide and said on Saturday that soccer and politics should be kept apart.
The group Irish Sport for Palestine was scathing about the decision to play.
“Today is a colossal failure by the FAI. They have further exposed their lack of leadership and total incompetency,” the group said in a statement.
At the press conference, Courell said that a number of protest measures would be taken, such as an absence of handshakes between the players and no exchange of the customary pennant before the game.
He said the Irish players would wear black armbands in honor of all the victims of the conflict while donating their match fees to charity.

Notes from Central Taiwan: The environmental cost of  a war over Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

Off the coast of Taichung lies the well known Gaomei Wetlands (高美濕地), a popular nature preserve. On weekends, especially in the evenings, the site’s walkways are crowded with sunset watchers, its mudflats filled with people wading and taking pictures of the local wildlife. Birds, amphibious fish, crabs and other organisms flourish.
A few hundred meters to the south Berth number 8 of the Port of Taichung juts inland, surrounded by chemical plants, cement factories, chemical storage sites, warehouses and wind turbines. This infrastructure, critical to the running of a major industrial economy, will be targeted in wartime. Though they do not know it, the nearby creatures of Gaomei and elsewhere are going to be among the first casualties of strikes by the People’s Republic of China (PRC).
CHEMICAL DISASTER
Photo: Michael Turton
Observers often comment on Taiwan’s power plants and its nuclear plants, but chemical and physical disasters will also result from PRC strikes on chemical plants and storage sites. These strikes will almost certainly have catastrophic effects on nearby wildlife. The PRC need not deliberately target wildlife, near misses and accidents will take a terrible toll, as will the diversion of resources from environmental care-taking to warfighting. The same thing will happen as Taiwan attacks PRC ports and near-shore facilities with its own missiles. A cross-strait war will be an environmental disaster.
Many have written on a cross-strait war and occupation. Few have considered the environment and clean-up. History shows it will be long. The aftermath of the US’ failed adventure in Vietnam left Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam covered in mines and bombs, still killing after all these years.
Russia’s invasions of Chechnya have left 30 percent of that nation unable to “meet environmental conditions for life,” according to research by the Central Asia-Caucasus Institute & Silk Road Studies Program. Soils become laden with toxic metals after war, the layers underneath the surface compacted by explosions, altering water flows and reshaping local ecologies. Some areas of France still cannot be farmed, the legacy of two invasions by Germany.
Occupation is expensive, and the population of Taiwan likely to be restive. Anyone out there think the PRC is going to be sparing occupation funds for expensive remediation of the nation’s soils after impregnating them with every kind of poison during a bombardment and invasion?
Industrial waste handling has been remiss, to say the least. One common method is to pave over a fishpond after filling it with waste, then build a pre-fabricated steel building on top. In other areas wastes are simply piled up and ignored. Illegal waste sites are still a chronic problem. Many of these sites are going to take damage in a bombardment. No one knows what is inside them.
Toxic chemicals, already a problem for the nation’s water tables, are going to dramatically worsen. Not only will domestic chemical production and storage facilities be hit, but missile and rocket fuels, chemical explosives and toxic metals from munitions (almost all munitions contain large quantities of lead) will contaminate the water table as well. Rocket fuels often contain sulfur, which forms sulfuric acid in the presence of water, burning the land. PRC planners may well consider water facilities such as reservoirs fair game for missile attacks, further poisoning the water supply. The coastal regions of the PRC, alive with industry, will suffer in the same way, as Russia is under the growing bombardment by Ukraine.
Photo: Reuters
FIRE HAZARDS
In Ukraine, forest fires created by the war are a problem. Nor can firefighters access them when they occur along the front lines or in areas planted with land mines or swept by hostile drones. Consider how many small fires set by locals clearing graves for Tombsweeping Day blossom into conflagrations requiring local fire departments to respond. PRC munitions will set hundreds of such fires on hillsides, in fields or in forests, which will burn out of control as firemen will be assigned to even more urgent fires at buildings and factories. Many of these fires generate toxic wastes and dust. Are Taiwan’s firefighters equipped to deal with them?
Taiwan’s petrochemical plants will not escape bombardment, since they produce war materials (the PRC will likely systematically destroy firms that compete with PRC companies). Under normal operating circumstances fires are a hazard (11 fire incidents in Taiwan’s petrochemical plants since 2009). In war it will be much worse, and the resulting toxic pollution vast. Taiwan’s chemical firms, which also produce war materials and compete with PRC firms, will be struck as well. The infamous industrial chemical disaster at Bhopal resulted in thousands of deaths and many more injuries, in part because local hospitals were ill-equipped to deal with chemical poisoning. Taiwan may not suffer injuries on that scale, but it will suffer large-scale injuries as chemical clouds, released by combat damage, expand over nearby built-up areas, especially in the north. Can local hospitals handle mass chemical casualties?
That waste won’t disappear when the war is over. Both the PRC and Taiwan will be stuck with enormous clean-up bills, degraded and useless urban and farm land and long-term medical bills for large numbers of people. The atmosphere and water will be polluted for months afterwards. Oil will leak from the bunkers of ships sunk in the sea around the island.
The horrors will not be confined to the west coast. Hualien will be under constant missile and drone attacks, and east coast ports will be targeted. The nation’s most important cement plant, the Asia Cement Corp (亞洲水泥) plant near Sincheng (新城) in Hualien, will be a major target. Pristine natural areas, archaeological sites, orchards and farms, would be impacted. Yet skilled workers to carry out clean up and remediation during wartime are few and far between on the east coast.
EVACUATIONS
One aspect of defense preparedness is going to be practicing for evacuations and remedial measures in the wake of all this destruction. Much attention has been given to military drills, perhaps in part to instill confidence in the public. What Taiwan needs is a far broader set of drills, along with investment in equipment and personnel development.
For example, precinct captains and neighborhood chiefs will need training in simple procedures like getting everyone in their neighborhood evacuated, and in handing orders and information up and down the chain of command. Individual Taiwanese will need to practice evacuating as well. These systems for evacuations, established with a conventional bombing in mind, will break down when the war begins if local residents do not practice.
A drone hit a cooling tower at the Kursk nuclear power plant in Russia last week. Barakah Nuclear Power Plant in the United Arab Emirates was attacked by three drones in May. One got through the defenses. Taiwan is moving to restart at least one of its nuclear power plants. It will almost certainly be a target in a PRC bombardment.
Is anyone prepared for a radiological disaster?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.

EU floats energy demand curbs in price crisis letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:28 UTC
01:44:28 KST

The EU warned its member states about a potential energy price crisis driven by the Middle East conflict, asking them to consider measures to cut demand and to continue filling gas storage ahead of winter.
In a letter to energy ministers in the 27-nation bloc, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said the region’s dependence on imported fossil fuels exposed it turmoil in energy markets and called on national governments to urgently prepare for the heating season.
“We are facing a price crisis linking to a supply crisis,” Jorgensen wrote in the letter.
Photo: EPA
Europe is heavily dependent on imported oil and gas. Foreign suppliers cover about 80 percent of the bloc’s gas needs, leaving it highly exposed to surging global energy prices caused by the Iran war’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, normally a transit route for 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas.
European gas prices have more than doubled since the start of the US-led war on Iran in late February, reaching their highest level since late 2022 earlier this month. Rising costs have been elevated to the top of the EU’s political agenda, with companies across the bloc blaming them for undermining Europe’s competitiveness. Governments have come under pressure to do more to support voters squeezed by ballooning bills.
Gas stockpiling has been particularly difficult this year because the Middle East conflict has driven up near-term prices relative to winter contracts, making summer supply injections economically less viable. The region’s facilities are just over 70 percent full, compared with a seasonal norm of 86 percent for this time of year, data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed.
EU rules allow for a 10 percentage point deviation from the goal of filling facilities to 90 percent ahead of the heating season. A further five percentage point flexibility can be used in the event of unfavorable market conditions.
“Making use of the flexibility provided by the Gas Storage Regulation and reducing the filling target to 80 percent can help alleviate immediate pressure on prices and refilling costs,” Jorgensen said. “However, and where relevant, I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can sustain injections or reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary.”
Such measures could include limiting temperatures in public buildings, preventing outdoor heating and switching off unnecessary public lighting, he said.

Fu wins Taiwan’s first Asian Games high jump title in 60 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:27 UTC
01:44:27 KST

Taiwan’s Fu Chao-hsuan (傅兆玄) won gold in the men’s high jump at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Sunday, becoming the first Taiwanese man in 60 years to win an Asian Games athletics title.
The 23-year-old high jumper cleared 2.25 meters in the final, matching his season best and securing Taiwan’s third gold medal at the Asian Games.
The victory marked Taiwan’s first medal in the men’s high jump at the Asian Games since Liao Hsueh-sung (廖學松) won bronze in 1990.
Photo: Chen Chih-chu, Taipei Times
It was also Taiwan’s first Asian Games gold medal in a men’s athletics event since Wu Ah-min (吳阿民) won the decathlon in 1966.
Separately, starter Lin Yu-min (林昱珉) yesterday pitched eight scoreless innings as Taiwan beat China 5-1 to secure the bronze medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
The victory at Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Baseball Stadium was Taiwan’s 10th consecutive win over China in Asian Games baseball, and their fourth bronze medal in the sport at the Asian Games since it was officially added at the 1994 Games in Hiroshima, Japan.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan won gold in 2006 and four silver medals, including at the most recent Games in Hangzhou, China, in 2023. They also won in a demonstration tournament at the 1990 Asian Games in Beijing.
Lin, a left-hander in the Arizona Diamondbacks’ farm system, struck out 10 Chinese batters, while allowing just one hit and one walk over eight dominant innings.
Taiwan led 2-0 through the first six innings, with Yang Po-hsiang (陽柏翔) hitting a timely two-run triple in the second. China kept Taiwan’s bats quiet from the third through sixth innings, stranding five runners.
Taiwan broke through in the seventh inning, when Chen Min-shih (陳敏賜) hit a two-run double to extend their lead to 4-0. Kao Yu-wei (高育瑋) followed with another RBI double to give Taiwan a comfortable 5-0 lead.
However, in the top of the ninth inning, Chinese catcher Luan Chenchen (欒臣臣) hit an RBI single off Taiwan reliever Wang Cheng-hao (王政浩), denying Taiwan a shutout.
Taiwan finished with 13 hits, while China had three.
Last night in the final, South Korea defeated Japan 3-1.
South Korea have won a record seven gold medals in baseball at the Asian Games, followed by Taiwan and Japan with one each.
During the Taiwan-Japan baseball super round the previous day, signs posted at the stadium entrance prohibited the display of Republic of China (Taiwan) flags and Japan’s Rising Sun flags.
The ban followed an incident on Friday during Taiwan’s game against China, when a staffer demanded a spectator put away a cloth that read “Taiwan,” saying the competition bans political messages.
Saturday’s ban drew backlash from Taiwanese fans, with significant criticism also surfacing on Japanese social media.

Young Asian Game athletes raise concerns about age

The Asian Games has crowned teenage champions before, but this edition has witnessed stunning successes by child prodigies, including Yuki Kurihara standing atop the podium aged just 11.
The Japanese primary school student beat opponents three times his age on the way to a historic gold in e-sports in Nagoya.
He is Japan’s youngest Asian Games winner in history and almost certainly the youngest the Games have ever seen.
Photo: AP
Kurihara did not even react after taking home the gold in Saturday’s final in Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of colored blobs by lining them up and popping them.
The boy, who does not turn 12 until June and wants to be a train driver when he grows up, later explained that he felt “embarrassed.”
Kurihara’s face was splashed across national newspapers yesterday.
There is no publicly available official list of the youngest medallists ever at the Games, which first ran in 1951.
But the introduction of events intended to attract younger viewers has resulted in some eye-catching displays by children.
In skateboarding, Taiwan’s 12-year-old Ku Yong-yan took home silver on Friday in the “men’s” park final.
The winner, Japan’s Izuru Nagahara, was a relative old-timer at 15.
Nagahara had anaesthetic injections in his knee to dull the pain from injury before his winning run.
Also skateboarding was Mazel Paris of the Philippines, who was just nine when she competed at the previous Asian Games.
Asked what has changed since Hangzhou in 2023, the 12-year-old replied: “I got taller for sure.”
This week is going to see another teenage phenomenon enter the fray with India’s 15-year-old cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
ABUSE CONCERNS
The presence of young children competing on the international stage against adults and under expectations to win for their country comes with concerns.
Kanae Doi, Japan director at Human Rights Watch, said ahead of the Games that “moments of triumph do not come easily. They are built on years of disciplined training, often beginning in childhood”.
“At its best, that journey should provide children with the joy of play and competition, along with opportunities for physical, mental and personal growth,” she wrote in the Japan Times. “Many young athletes instead encounter physical, verbal and even sexual abuse in the very environments meant to help them develop.”
She said that in Games host Japan, children “frequently experience abuse in sports training within Japanese schools, federations and elite sports programs”.
In 2024, the International Olympic Committee released its consensus statement on youth athletes at the Olympic Games.
It said that 50 percent of common mental health conditions first emerge before 18.
Adolescent athletes are more susceptible to certain injuries, it said.
Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi became the youngest medallist in world championships history last year with bronze aged 12.
Now teenaged and expected to make a splash at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, Yu is one of the faces of the Nagoya Games with three golds, all in record times.
But when it came to facing reporters after races, she looked all of her 13 years. “Interviews are way harder than the race,” she said.
UNDER PRESSURE
Each sport has its own rules on minimum age.
For World Aquatics, the minimum age for major international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for younger swimmers if, such as Yu, they are fast enough.
Yu has spoken about struggling to balance her swimming with school work.
Yu’s teammate Zhang Yufei, 28, a multiple Olympic gold medallist and world champion, said the youngster’s stunning displays were no longer a shock.
However, she cautioned: “I hope she can withstand that pressure.”

The teenager, ranked 18th in the world and regarded as a rising star back home, had been due to face China on Tuesday. Taiwan to build more anti-ship missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:25 UTC
01:44:25 KST

The Ministry of National Defense has prepared a NT$22 billion (US$692.3 million) program to acquire about 200 improved Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles from next year to 2035, a source said.
Commenting on condition of anonymity, a high-ranking defense official said the ministry’s plan for enhanced-capability Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III missiles would be funded as part of the regular defense budget.
The 200 missiles would be added on top of the 1,400 missiles being funded via the Sea-Air Combat Power Improvement Plan, they said.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The program is not about padding missile numbers, but expanding the capability to defeat electronic countermeasures and sink the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy’s (PLAN) Type 052D and Type 055 destroyers, he said.
The improved Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III missiles feature advanced microchips that use signal filtering technology to cut through electronic interference to achieve first-shot kills, the official said.
The massive ammunition consumption observed in the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine demonstrated that Taiwanese military must improve magazine depth to sustain combat operations in a conflict, he said.
Military planners expect to fight a large number of PLAN warships, each of which would take two to four missiles to sink, he said.
High missile expenditure rates mean warships would exhaust their missile loads in one volley and need to re-arm, the official said, adding that losses of ships and missiles to the enemy must also be considered.
Taiwan would need to prepare about 1,600 missiles to meet operational requirements, the official said.
Continuing missile production would increase the resilience of the defense industry, as keeping assembly lines open would prove essential should the nation be involved in a prolonged conflict, they said.
More missile orders would also ensure indigenous missile assembly lines and manufacturing capacity remain in use, which would prove essential should the nation ever need to fight a prolonged conflict, the official said.
The navy’s strategy is to counter PLAN fleets with surface combatants and coastal defense batteries deployed in Taiwan proper and the nation’s outlying islands.
The warships and land-based batteries’ arsenal would be comprised of US-made subsonic Harpoon missiles and the indigenous subsonic Hsiung Feng II and supersonic Hsiung III missiles, forming a “low-high” mix to overwhelm enemy defenses.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:22 UTC
01:44:22 KST

1. 政府呼籲全國民眾共同對抗新冠病毒的擴散。
ˇ The government called the whole nation to combat the spread of COVID-19.
χ The government called all the nation to combat COVID-19 from spreading.
Photo: AdobeStock 照片：AdobeStock
註︰「全國」一般用 the whole country/nation，「全民族」用 the whole nation/people，「全城」用 the whole town；不用 all the country, all the nation, all the town（或 city, village 等）。
防止病情擴散，英文習慣說 prevent the spread of 疾病，台灣常誤寫成 to prevent 疾病 from spreading。因此防止新冠擴散，英文是 to prevent the spread of COVID-19、to combat the spread of COVID-19。若搜尋Google，限制網域為美國，則搜尋不到：No results found for “to combat COVID-19 from spreading” site:us.
2. 他是有錢人。
ˇ He is a rich man.
ˇ He is rich.
χ He is a rich.
註︰rich 是形容詞，the rich ＝ rich people，必須用定冠詞，不可以說 a rich。屬於同類性質的有：the poor, the strong, the weak, the unemployed, the wounded, the oppressed 等。
3. 他太老了，不能做太多的工作。
ˇ He is too old to do much work.
χ He is too aged to do much work.
註︰aged 常用作修飾性形容詞，如 an aged man，讀 [?ed??d]；或在名詞之後，如 He is a man aged seventy.，讀 [ed?d]。它不同於old，不能作補語形容詞用。
4. 這張桌子是木頭做的。
ˇ This table is made of wood.
ˇ This is a wooden table.
χ This table is wooden.
註︰wooden 只能用作修飾性形容詞，如 a wooden leg, a wooden box，不可以用作補語形容詞。
5. 那人喝得爛醉。
ˇ The man was dead drunk.
χ The man was dead drunken.
註︰drunken 通常作修飾性形容詞用，很少作補語形容詞用；而 drunk 只作補語形容詞用。例如：a drunken fellow, to get drunk, to be very drunk。
Exercises
A. 這張椅子是木頭做的。
This chair is __________ .
1. wooden 2. made of wood
3. produced by wood 4. done by wood
B. 一個醉漢躺在街上。
A __________ fellow lay in the street.
1. drunken 2. drunkard 3. drunk 4. drinker
Answers: A. 2 B. 1

Thousands of protesters on Saturday wore red and carried symbolic coffins during a demonstration in Mexico City, demanding answers about the 43 trainee teachers who went missing 12 years ago.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, who regularly meets with the disappeared people’s families, is expected to present a report today on the latest progress in the case, following an exhaustive review of the evidence by the attorney general’s office.
“Because they were taken alive, we want them back alive,” one banner slogan read.
Photo: Reuters
The protest was led by parents of the 43 teacher trainees from Ayotzinapa, who led the procession to the capital’s main square, where the government palace is located.
Others counted to 43 several times to honor each of the trainees from the rural teachers’ college who disappeared on Sept. 26, 2014.
“Another year of strain, of exhaustion, of hopelessness,” said Estanislao Mendoza, one of the parents of the 43.
“We want to know, whether it’s good or bad, alive or dead, but to know the truth, to know where they are,” he said. “Twelve years of suffering, of lies.”
The students were traveling from Guerrero state to a protest in Mexico City. Local police stopped them in the town of Iguala, where six died in an hours-long street clash and 43 later went missing.
Prosecutors initially said the officers delivered the 43 teacher trainees to drug cartel hitmen, who killed them, incinerated their bodies and dumped the remains in a river.
However, independent human rights experts have rejected the government’s conclusion, and the unsolved case remains a stain on Mexico’s reputation.
A former governor was arrested last month, on accusations of deleting the security videos of the scene of the crime in Iguala. The former state attorney general was also arrested in 2022.
More than 134,000 people are listed as disappeared in Mexico.
“It’s necessary to support a struggle against the indifference of a government that refuses to accept that there is a disappearance crisis,” said 69-year-old Atanacio Pina, whose missing son was later found dead.

Madrid housing protest camp grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:20 UTC
01:44:20 KST

A protest camp in Madrid yesterday grew to include dozens of tents after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home triggered outrage over gaps in tenant protections.
Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher on Wednesday after police broke down her door have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due next year.
Thousands of people on Saturday marched through the streets of Madrid rattling keys and blowing whistles to call for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult.
Photo: Reuters
“You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner on display at the rally.
Spanish government authorities put the turnout at about 25,000, while the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organized the protest, said more than 300,000 had taken part.
After the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp at Puerta del Sol square in the city center, the union said in a statement, urging people to gather there.
“It’s time to change the rules of the game,” said protester Maria Juarez, a 47-year-old psychologist. “People aren’t going to leave until something changes once and for all.”
Police looked on as about a dozen tents were set up in the square in front of the headquarters of the Madrid regional government, surrounded by thousands of protesters.
By the early hours of yesterday, El Pais reported that the number of tents had grown to about 150, with hundreds of people planning to spend the night.
News agency EFE put the number at about 100 tents.
Abascal was forced to leave the apartment where she had lived for 70 years after a real-estate firm acquired the property and raised the rent by 275 percent to 2,650 euros (US$3,019), the union said.
Now a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis, she had urged Spaniards to join the protest in a video message posted online just hours before it got under way.
“I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction.
“I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added in the video posted by the tenants’ union.
Protester Enrique Ortega de Miguel, a 38-year-old graphic designer who lives with his mother, said the housing market in Spain was “impossible.”
“It is a struggle to find a place you can afford, then you live in fear of being forced out,” he said at the march on Saturday.
Maricarmen Arnedo, a 76-year-old pensioner, said that while older people were being forced out of their homes, “young people can’t move out of their parents’ homes.”
“We want house prices and rents to come down, because I’m fed up with washing the underpants of my 53-year-old son,” she added.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, a socialist, has faced regular protests across Spain over housing since Abascal’s eviction.
The Spanish government is expected to approve a package of measures dubbed the “Maricarmen decree” at its next Cabinet meeting, which would include the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions.
However, it is unclear whether the package will be approved by parliament, where Sanchez’s government lacks a majority.
While a similar bill was defeated earlier this year, Abascal’s case has increased pressure on political parties to act.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country of about 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Spain has little public housing, while rents have been driven up by increased demand, including from tourism and population growth linked to immigration, analysts say.

Pope Leo urges Church to face failings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

Pope Leo XIV yesterday urged the Catholic Church to admit its own failings and heal “deep wounds” inflicted within its ranks, hours before he was set to meet victims of child abuse by priests in France.
Leo, addressing crowds stretching out over a large field near the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, said the Church must have the courage to face its past, but did not directly reference abuse scandals in France that sparked nationwide shock.
“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within [the Church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told an estimated 150,000 people gathered in the field on a sunlit day.
Photo: AFP
Leo is on a whirlwind three-city, four-day visit to France, where he has again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence. He on Saturday drew about 800,000 people for an outdoor Mass on the Champs-Elysees in Paris.
Local Church leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church’s standing after a 2021 report found that about 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
In an earlier, closed-door meeting with French bishops yesterday, Leo did directly refer to “the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy,” a Vatican-provided text showed.
The pope thanked the bishops for the “courageous measures” he said they had taken to confront the scandals and urged them to buttress their safeguarding efforts and “continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance.”
Leo has previously apologized directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church’s credibility across the world. On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops there that they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.
The pope was due to have a closed-door meeting with seven French victims of abuse by clergy later yesterday. Some survivors said they were doubtful the encounter would result in quick changes by the Church.
“I am quite skeptical that the pope will solve the issue, at least not immediately,” said Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, copresident of an association for survivors in western France.
“Things are moving very slowly,” she said. “It isn’t going to happen overnight.”
Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for the French bishops, said the pope’s desire to have the meeting “shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns.”
The pope’s itinerary in France includes six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains that attracts about 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.
The site is also connected to a scandal that has dogged the Vatican in the past years. The shrine’s facade has a series of mosaics by Reverend Marko Rupnik, a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse.
Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations. Five of his alleged victims on Thursday wrote an open letter to the pope, sharply criticizing an ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.
The mosaics, stories tall, have been covered for the pope’s visit with large, muted yellow tarps. Arriving for the Mass yesterday, Leo was driven in his open-top popemobile near the facade of the shrine and the covered mosaics.
The pope, who on Friday sharply reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illnesses, again mentioned the Church’s pro-life stance in Lourdes.
He said the shrine’s welcome for sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in its waters stood opposed to “current trends that seek to redefine the value of human life in illness.”

Trump-Xi meeting: Xi made little progress in summit: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

The second meeting this year between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) ended with little progress, as Beijing’s attempt to pressure Washington to reduce arms sales to Taiwan failed to gain traction, a national security official said yesterday.
Beijing had hoped to use the summit to frame US-China ties as a stable and constructive relationship between equal powers, while deflecting attention from its economic slowdown, excess production capacity and authoritarian expansion, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
While the US rolled out the red carpet for Xi, Washington focused on its own political values and challenged Beijing’s narrative, they said.
Photo: AP
US-Taiwan ties are based on US national interests, shared democratic values and Taiwan’s key role in the global high-tech supply chain, which Washington cannot simply set aside in dealing with Beijing, they said.
With China unable to make concrete gains such as lower tariffs or lifting high-tech restrictions, it might turn to propaganda, using images of Xi receiving the red-carpet welcome to promote narratives that China is rising as the West declines and that the US has abandoned Taiwan, the official said.
If Taiwan wavers between authoritarianism and democracy under pressure from pro-Beijing forces, it could lose international trust and its strategic advantages, they said.
Taiwan needs to strengthen its “silicon shield,” maintain its leading position in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and advanced manufacturing, and accelerate technological and industrial development, turning its economic strengths into a central part of its national defense, they said.
Taiwan should deepen its alliances and asymmetric defense capabilities by bolstering cooperation with the EU and other democracies in the Indo-Pacific region on supply-chain security, cybersecurity, civil defense and geopolitical strategy, the official said.
It should continue to build its defense capabilities and pursue greater self-reliance, ensuring that any regime seeking to change the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait would face unacceptable costs, they added.
Taiwan should also maintain a steady approach to cross-strait relations by not provoking the other side, while playing an active role in promoting regional peace, they said.
In his remarks, Trump highlighted US-China cooperation during World War II, cited the US founding documents to emphasize liberal democracy as the “true approach” and invoked Sparta’s final victory to take aim at Xi’s Thucydides Trap narrative, they said.
Washington’s references to World War II cooperation underscored that the history being invoked was not one the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had experienced firsthand, as it was the Republic of China at that time, they added.
That challenged Beijing’s claims that “the East is rising and the West is declining” — a political narrative introduced by Xi in January 2021 — as well as the CCP’s legitimacy as China’s representative, the official said.
On trade and economic issues, Washington kept diplomatic gestures separate from its strategic interests, making no concessions on tariffs or AI controls, they said.
US-China relations have entered a new normal of frequent communication and intense competition, they said.
While the two sides use dialogue to prevent immediate conflict, competition over high-tech restrictions, supply-chain restructuring and geopolitical influence is likely to intensify, the official said.
The government would continue to provide timely and transparent information to help people understand relations between major powers, they said, adding that Taiwan’s future depends on its own strength and democratic values.
