China sends two giant pandas to US’ Zoo Atlanta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:15 UTC
01:44:15 KST

China yesterday sent two giant pandas to the US, Chinese state media said, after a Washington summit that was heavy on symbolism and light on major breakthroughs.
The pandas’ transfer had already been agreed, but the departure was announced on Thursday during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) visit to Washington.
The black-and-white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a “panda diplomacy” program to foster foreign ties.
Photo: Xinhua via AP
Ping Ping (平平) and Fu Shuang (福雙) departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight at about 3am yesterday, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots have been prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their 15-hour flight, Chinese state-run media the Global Times reported.
The Boeing 777 operated by FedEx was the top-tracked aircraft on aviation information platform FlightRadar24 as it neared Alaska, about halfway into its journey.
The pandas were headed to a zoo in Atlanta, Georgia, where they will be spending the next 10 years.
A farewell ceremony was held for the pair before their departure by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Experienced keepers were dispatched by the US side to accompany the duo on their flight, the Global Times reported.
In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers.
It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate very similar to Chengdu.
Zoo Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China for a quarter of a century starting in 1999, but it has not had any since 2024.
Both the expected arrivals were born in 2020. Ping Ping, a male, is now six years old, while Fu Shuang, a female, is to turn six next month.
Pandas in captivity typically live for about 30 years.
The furry creatures have been sent across the globe for decades as soft-power ambassadors of Beijing’s diplomatic goodwill.
In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following then-US president Richard Nixon’s historic visit to the communist nation.
Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of an attack on Taiwan.

Coast guard takes action to protect local sea turtles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:15 UTC
01:44:15 KST

Coast guard personnel conducted an enforcement action and rescue operation to protect sea turtles on a beach on Siaoliouciou (小琉球) and in the seas off Pingtung County, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said last week.
The CGA said its Patrol Area Office 7 on Monday last week received a report that a foreign national was touching a sea turtle near the Beauty Cave (美人洞).
The beaches of Siaoliouciou Island are breeding grounds for close to 200 sea turtles, and disturbing them is an offense under the Wild Life Conservation Act (野生動物保育法), it said, adding that it carries a sentence of up to one year in prison and a fine between NT$60,000 and NT$300,000.
Photo courtesy of the Dapeng Bay National Scenic Area Administration
A patrol dispatched to the area shortly before 6pm found a woman from Germany and her companion, who were drinking beer, the agency said.
The woman apologized profusely and said she was unaware that touching the turtles was a crime, it said.
The person who reported the woman had taken pictures of her touching the animals, which was forwarded to CGA personnel, it said, adding that the case has been transferred to the Penghu District Prosecutors’ Office.
Photo courtesy of the CGA
The Council of Ocean Affairs, the Tourism Administration and the Pingtung County Government have worked for years on a public education campaign telling visitors not to harass the turtles, the CGA said.
The number of people touching turtles had been very low until this year, when incidents rose again, it said.
People who see others bothering turtles should call 118 to summon the coast guard, it added.
Separately, the CGA Maritime Parol Directorate General on Tuesday last week freed a small green sea turtle entangled in a fishing net 0.3 nautical miles off Pingtung’s Singhai Fishing Harbor (興海漁港), the CGA said.
Patrol boat PP-10052 of Flotilla 14 found the tangled young sea turtle during a routine patrol and immediately freed it from the net, it said.
Personnel aboard the boat checked the turtle for injuries and found none, and released the animal back into the sea, it said.
Debris at sea, including discarded fishing nets, vessel propellers and trash, poses a significant danger to marine life, as sea animals could be trapped in flotsam or become sick after eating undigestible materials, the CGA said.
The CGA called on the public to protect the environment by not dumping waste into the sea.

DPP’s Puma Shen sparks discussion on coffee napping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:15 UTC
01:44:15 KST

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) comment that he relied on “coffee napping” to stay alert during his campaign has sparked discussion about the practice’s health effects.
On Sept. 21, Shen told reporters that he has been getting only three hours of sleep per day and that he drinks coffee before napping for short periods to keep himself energized.
Drinking coffee before napping can provide a short-term energy boost, Chinese-language SET News cited family medicine doctor Neil Lee (李思賢) as saying.
Photo: Reuters
Caffeine takes effect about 20 to 25 minutes after consumption, which means a fatigued person can sleep briefly and wake up just in time to be reinvigorated by the substance, he said.
The practice, dubbed “coffee napping,” has been popular in the West for quite some time, but its effectiveness comes with caveats, he added.
Sleep is divided into three stages: N1 and N2 are shallow sleep and N3 is deep sleep, SET News reported.
Interrupting N3 sleep increases drowsiness and fatigue, so a person taking a nap after coffee should sleep for 20 minutes or less to prevent waking up at that stage, it reported.
Although brief rest can bring about a temporary feeling of well-being, it cannot substitute for real sleep or make up for long-term exhaustion, Lee was cited as saying.
“People feeling tired after long periods of exhausting work or a night of poor-quality sleep should rest for a full sleep cycle of 90 minutes, a luxury most office workers sadly cannot afford,” he said. “Nevertheless, even a quick afternoon nap can restore short-term memory and relieve exhaustion.”
The Ministry of Health and Welfare recommends that adults limit their daily caffeine intake to no more than 300mg.

China’s consumer stocks face lost decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

In the shadow of Beijing’s single-minded focus on artificial intelligence (AI), China’s consumer stocks are trapped in a lost decade.
The industry is showing a stark contrast with the high-flying tech sector. MSCI China’s consumer goods sub-indices plunged roughly 18 percent over the past six months to near 10-year lows, while the AI-heavy technology gauge surged to more than double its 2016 level. During the latest earnings season, consumer staples firms in the MSCI gauge missed profit expectations by nearly 50 percent.
The malaise reflects China’s lopsided economy, where Beijing’s drive for tech supremacy has fueled an export boom and funneled capital into AI firms with limited spillover to domestic demand. Last month’s retail sales crept up just 0.4 percent, and there are few signs that investor pessimism toward the sector will ease after the Golden Week holiday — a crucial period for travel and spending.
Photo: Reuters
“Data this summer has disproved that there is any recovery in spending, and affirms that it still is a one-way bet on exports,” Shanghai Jade Stone Investment Management Co (上海謙璞投資管理) fund manager Chen Shi (陳實) said. “From a market perspective, that has created a crowding-out effect. Investors have become increasingly concentrated in AI beneficiaries, while sectors such as consumption have been sold indiscriminately.”
The sour mood marks a dramatic reversal from the pre-COVID-19 pandemic years, when the rise of China’s middle class was celebrated as one of the world’s most compelling growth stories.
That optimism has all but evaporated as a protracted property slump, sluggish income growth and a crisis of consumer confidence have made the sector a losing bet. A drip feed of policy support over the years to revive housing sales — a key pillar for spending — has fallen short. The latest data showed property prices extending their slide.
Authorities could rebuild consumer confidence through measures from stabilizing asset prices to creating stronger wage growth prospects and raising minimum income, Chen said, adding that any meaningful improvement will likely be be gradual.
Weak consumer demand emerged as a recurring theme during the latest earnings season. Shede Spirits Co (捨得酒業) described the sector as being in a “deep adjustment,” while department store operator Nanjing Central Emporium (南京中央商場) flagged softer visitor traffic and lower spending. Top liquor maker Kweichow Moutai Co’s (貴州茅台) first-half net profit dropped.
Earnings for consumer staples firms in the MSCI China gauge fell 47 percent short of expectations in the latest season, while those producing discretionary goods missed by nearly 10 percent, data compiled by Bloomberg showed. In contrast, industrial and tech companies delivered upside surprises.
The sector’s woes are unfolding against a global backdrop in which investors have shunned consumer shares for beneficiaries of the AI investment boom, Bank of America head of Asia-Pacific equity strategy Winnie Wu (吳馨怡) said. For China, domestic policy headwinds including tighter tax rule enforcements also create a heavier financial burden for both households and businesses, she said.
To be sure, depressed valuations and light positioning might rekindle interest in consumer shares if market volatility returns, as was briefly seen during July’s global tech rout. Still, Beijing’s reluctance to use aggressive stimulus to encourage more consumer spending will likely weigh on the sector for now.
“China’s consumer stocks lack a compelling catalyst amid a protracted economic slowdown,” said Shen Meng (沈萌), director at Beijing-based investment bank Chanson & Co (香頌資本). “In the long term, I see stronger growth opportunities in technology, while consumer shares will likely remain caught between weak fundamentals and capital flowing elsewhere.”

Labour conference begins with mass arrests of pro-Palestine Action protesters
UK police arrested protesters holding placards in support of the banned direct action group Palestine Action on Sunday, with organisers telling The New Arab the government should focus on holding the Israeli government to account rather than targeting protesters.

Almost 230 people took part in a silent vigil, taking place outside the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, holding signs reading, “I OPPOSE GENOCIDE. I SUPPORT PALESTINE ACTION”, calling on Andy Burnham to de-proscribe Palestine Action, which was listed as a terrorist organisation in 2025.
At least 20 people, including a 94-year-old woman, were arrested as hundreds continue to hold the vigil, organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ).
“Scenes of elderly people being hauled away by the police and arrested for terrorism, for quietly protesting against genocide and the repression of those who resist it, have become almost normal in Britain,” a spokesperson for Defend Our Juries told The New Arab.

When Burnham became prime minister last July, rights groups and activists called on him to remove Palestine Action’s terrorist designation.
“If the British Government were serious about ending its complicity in genocide, it would be sanctioning the government of Israel and Elbit Systems, not silencing and jailing those who oppose their crimes.”
The arrests come after Massive Attack’s Robert Del Naja was arrested after taking part in a similar vigil on Saturday by the DOJ.
At the same time, to mark the start of the conference, dozens of top scholars from the United States, including Norman Finkelstein, Judith Butler and Rashid Khalidi, wrote to Burnham to urge him to lift the ban.
Following the group’s designation, hundreds of protesters, many of whom are elderly, have been arrested under terrorism offences for supporting a proscribed group.
Palestine Action was proscribed in June 2025 after a group of protesters broke into the UK’s largest air base and vandalised two planes.
The designation drew outcry from activists and officials, who said the ban targets freedom of speech and the right to protest.

UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:39:41 UTC
01:39:41 KST

An air base in England where American bombers used to strike Iran are based was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27.
Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after being stopped close to RAF Fairford, police said, and explosive ordnance disposal technicians were dispatched to the scene. RAF Fairford is a British base currently hosting a dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which have been stationed there for around seven months for strikes on Iran.
President Donald Trump said the suspects were “looking to do big damage” to the U.S. at RAF Fairford and called the arrests “fantastic” before boarding Air Force One on Sept. 27.
“We had them under view for a long time and we got them,” Trump added. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”
The base has been under increased security for days, which included the placement of vehicles around the perimeter, people familiar with the matter said. The threat level at the base was raised before the suspects were arrested. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures, citing operational security.
Explosive ordnance teams from the British Army were called in to inspect the scene, and helicopter video footage aired by multiple U.K. news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting three white vans near the base fence, with B-1Bs parked on base nearby.
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.
Police said they were called by a local after receiving a report about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is located in Gloucestershire in southwest England.
“At around 12:45 a.m. today … police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be traveling towards the air base,” the Metropolitan Police, which investigates terrorism cases in the U.K., said in a Sept. 27 statement.
The U.K. government is still investigating the incident, counterterrorism officials said.
“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”
RAF Fairford does not have permanent U.S. Air Force aircraft assigned there, but it has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”
Roadblocks, large machinery, and armed police have been seen around the base. Eighty-five homes in the nearby village of Whelford were evacuated.
“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”
The B-1Bs at Fairford were heavily used during Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale air campaign against Iran in the spring, when the base housed some two dozen bombers including B-52 Stratofortresses.
Since a shaky ceasefire in April, most of the B-1Bs have remained while the U.S. carried out occasional strikes, including at least one involving a B-1 from Fairford. The bombers have regularly conducted training sorties out of the U.K.
The U.K. government gave permission for the base to be used in strikes on Iran in March under former Prime Minister Kier Starmer, for what the U.K. considers collective self-defense strikes. Burnham reaffirmed that decision in July, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned the U.K. government that it considered Fairford a legitimate target for attack. The U.K. government said in July it was prepared to use the British armed forces to defend the base.
The U.S. Air Force said it would continue to cooperate with the U.K. government to ensure the safety of its bases in Britain. Another U.K. base with U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath is also used as a stopover location for fighters heading to the Middle East from the U.S.
“The safety and security of our Airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities.”

Satellite Imagery: Strike Damaged Five Workshops at Plant Involved in Kh-101 and Oreshnik Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:34:27 UTC
01:34:27 KST

Satellite imagery shows damage to the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant (AOMZ), which is involved in the production of Kh-101, Kh-35U, and Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, as well as Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
The Absolutely Reliable Source Telegram channel published the satellite imagery.
Judging by the imagery, six buildings were hit. According to the channel, they house five production workshops.
Workshop 022, a foundry comprising two buildings, was hit. A fire and significant damage were recorded at the site.
Workshop 024, the machining workshop, also sustained significant damage, with part of its roof collapsing.
In addition, workshop 008, which produces optics; workshop 009, an assembly workshop; and workshop 010, an electroplating workshop, were damaged.
The Ukrainian Navy and the SSU’s Special Operations Center Alpha launched the strike on the night of September 26.
The attack involved Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles as well as RUTA, Palianytsia, and Bars jet-powered drones.
The Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant joint-stock company is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and is one of its key optoelectronic production facilities.
The plant produces, among other things, radar and infrared seekers for guided missiles, thermal imaging devices, and electronic systems for precision-guided artillery.
The plant also supplies components for anti-tank weapons production, weapon stabilization systems for armored vehicles, navigation and laser equipment for aircraft and UAVs, and electronic warfare systems.
The enterprise also manufactures optomechanical and optoelectronic products and equipment for Russia’s aerospace industry.
Following a document leak, researchers found that AOMZ is involved in producing Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, short-range R-74 and long-range R-37M air-to-air missiles, Kh-101 and Kh-35U cruise missiles, Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
Open-source information also indicates that the enterprise is involved in producing KAB-250, KAB-500, and KAB-1500 guided aerial bombs and the Kh-38ML short-range air-to-surface missile.

Changing UK benefits for young people a ‘moral crusade’, says minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:33:17 UTC
01:33:17 KST

Labour MPs have a moral responsibility to accept significant changes to the welfare system to help get more young people into work, the work and pensions secretary has said.
In a sign he is looking to overhaul the welfare state, Pat McFadden said it was time for Labour to “renew” the system first created by the Clement Attlee government and given a new deal by New Labour.
The cabinet minister said there would be “decisions to make and responsibilities to take” after two reviews of the system are published this autumn – on young people by Alan Milburn, and on a key disability benefit by the Timms panel.
He said Labour must decide “how we have a new system focused on opportunity, how we move from asking what are you entitled to, to asking how do we change your life … It falls to us, the party which did so much to create it, the party that holds it dear, to embrace the change needed.”
His speech is a sign that the government is preparing the ground again for changes to the welfare system after Keir Starmer’s government was forced to U-turn last year on a £5bn-a-year programme of disability benefit cuts in the face of a Labour backbench rebellion. The revolt was fuelled by outrage that the plans would push hundreds of thousands of disabled people into poverty.
Andy Burnham, Starmer’s replacement as prime minister, has said he will not shy away from changing the system in a “Labour way” that helps people back into work, rather than putting a figure on trying to save money on the overall bill.
However, many charities supporting disabled people are nervous about the prospect of an overhauled system, after so many cuts in the past.
After the Timms and Milburn reviews conclude, the government is expected to design a new system and assessment process for disability benefits that is likely to require new legislation. It will also focus particularly on how to support younger people into jobs and training, building on the current “jobs guarantee” that funds employment placements for under-25s for six months, with disabled young people given fast-track access.
Officials have been looking to see whether elements of other countries’ benefit systems can be borrowed, such as the Netherlands, where youth hubs tackle unemployment, and Denmark, which restricts access to the country’s “disability pension” for the under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they permanently have no ability to work.
A million young people are now out of work, employment and training in the UK, and there has been a sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic. This has prompted a political debate about the sustainability of working-age disability benefits spending, which is forecast to rise from £14bn in 2019 to £34bn in 2030.
Some types of claim have particularly surged among young people. About 205,000 16- to 24-year-olds received the personal independence payment (Pip) for disabilities linked to ADHD or autism in April this year, a more than threefold increase since 2019, at a cost in 2025-26 of £1.36bn. The average Pip claim for this cohort was £8,800 a year.
McFadden said both the financial cost and the human cost of the system were “too high”.
The interim findings of the Timms review found that Pip was unfit for purpose and too often left vulnerable claimants feeling dehumanised and degraded.
The benefit, which helps with the extra costs of disability, is non-means tested and not related to employment status. A panel is consulting on measures to overhaul the system, with input from disability organisations.
Milburn’s interim report, published in May, made it clear young people diagnosed with lifelong complex needs who are never able to work must be protected by the benefit system. But it also hinted that young people with less severe conditions, who could be supported to work, may see reductions in benefits.
In his speech, McFadden said it was a “moral crusade” to stop so many young people being trapped on disability benefits instead of being helped into work, saying: “A young person who signs on for sickness benefits when they are 20 is now more likely to reach the age of 30 and still be on them than to have held down a steady job in a single year in between.”
He added: “And a young person left out of work is far more likely to die before their time than the friends they sat beside in school … this is shameful. We should not accept it. We have to change it.”

Pope Leo XIV urges French Church to continue fight against sexual abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:33:00 UTC
01:33:00 KST

Speaking in Lourdes on Sunday morning, the Pope addressed the issue of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church, a closely watched aspect of his visit.
Pope Leo XIV called on the Catholic Church to acknowledge its failings and confront sexual abuse as he celebrated an open-air Mass in Lourdes on Sunday, the latest stop on his visit to France.
After drawing nearly 800,000 people in Paris on Saturday, the pontiff was greeted by further crowds in Lourdes, where around 150,000 people attended Sunday's Mass.
In his homily, Leo urged the Church to take responsibility for wrongdoing within its ranks.
"The Church must have the courage to be the first to undergo this conversion. To heal the deep wounds, the acts of infidelity and the painful deviations committed in its midst, we must stand humbly under the Lord's purifying gaze," he said.
"Acknowledging our own faults is essential to our spiritual progress," he added.
Pope meets French bishops amid scrutiny over abuse
Earlier on Sunday, Leo met privately with France's bishops, praising their efforts to address sexual abuse while urging them to remain vigilant.
"In recent years, you have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse against minors committed by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context," he told them, according to remarks published by the Vatican.
"You have taken courageous measures to respond, through listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness, reparation and a firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."
The Pope urged the bishops to continue their efforts while also supporting members of the clergy.
"It is important to continue along this path while maintaining the greatest vigilance. At the same time, your clergy needs to be supported and encouraged; I know it is the focus of your fatherly concern," he said.
Survivors question selection process for papal meeting
The Pope was also scheduled to meet seven survivors of clerical sexual abuse on Sunday, including one person who was abused as an adult.
However, the meeting has drawn criticism from some survivors, who questioned how participants were selected.
In an open letter published by French newspaper Libération on the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors called on him to acknowledge the Church's responsibility and criticised the decision to allow Church officials to select those attending the meeting rather than leaving the process to survivors' organisations.
"The Church must relinquish its position as both judge and party to the proceedings," they wrote.
Monsignor Pierre-Antoine Bozo, spokesperson for the French bishops' conference, said two of the seven participants had been proposed by survivors' organisations.
He explained that the Pope had deliberately chosen a small group to allow for a more personal discussion.
"When it comes to listening to them, you can't have 50 people in front of you," Bozo said.
"So I think that's really what the pope chose: to listen so that we can act and respond more effectively."
France's Catholic Church confronts its abuse legacy
The French Catholic Church has faced intense scrutiny over its handling of sexual abuse.
An independent investigation published in 2021 estimated that approximately 330,000 children had been sexually abused over a 70-year period by priests, other Church workers and people associated with Catholic institutions.
The report identified around 3,000 alleged perpetrators among priests and Church workers.
Despite criticism of the report's methodology and conclusions, French bishops established an independent compensation system for survivors.
To date, the system has recommended that the Church pay more than €20 million in compensation.

The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:30:09 UTC
01:30:09 KST

This month, a cross-party parliamentary committee said Thames Water should be placed in temporary state control and that any takeover by its creditors should be halted. The MPs were right. The “special administration” regime keeps the taps running while shareholders are wiped out, creditors take a haircut and the firm’s £19bn of debt is restructured. But it must not then be handed back to private hands. After Thames Water has failed its 16 million customers, polluted rivers, paid out billions to shareholders and repeatedly demanded higher bills, a City-friendly reprieve would only reward the outrageous behaviour that the regulatory system is meant to deter. Ministers ought to seize the opportunity to nationalise Thames Water.
In July, Andy Burnham agreed. On the campaign trail in Makerfield, he told reporters that “there’s a very strong case for public ownership [for Thames Water] to sort out its problems”. Having entered parliament and become prime minister, Mr Burnham is instead looking at letting elected mayors “oversee” private water companies. There is nothing wrong with more democratic scrutiny. However, oversight without ownership and proper control seems like a sleight of hand. Voices from different wings of the party recognise this. Mr Burnham can’t kick the decision down the road for ever.
In less than two weeks, water privatisation will be on the ballot in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when voters elect an MP to succeed Sir Keir Starmer. A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the London constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes. When asked by the Camden New Journal when the mains were last inspected, maintained or replaced, Thames Water gave “no answers”. If Labour cannot take a failing private monopoly that ruins lives into public ownership, voters may ask themselves who will?
Polls suggest comfortable majorities of Britons believe water companies should be run in the public sector. Under Sir Keir, Labour’s review of the water sector ruled out nationalisation. Some claim that new models of corporate governance could “subordinate” profits to the common good. But it’s hard to see how a failed regulatory regime will be fixed by more regulation. History has been turned on its head when British Rail is cited as proof that nationalisation is wrong. The state-owned rail firm had productive staff working in an ageing railway starved of investment. By 2011, privatised rail cost 20%-30% more. Sound familiar? Mr Burnham called water “an industry where the shareholders never lose and the bill payers never win”. Deeds, not just words, are needed.
England and Wales are outliers: 90% of the globe keeps water in public hands because others understand that a natural monopoly in water offers no competition to raise standards and leaves households as captive customers for financiers eyeing easy profits. Nationalisation comes with a price tag. But, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies acknowledges, assessing the true cost to the state requires valuing the whole deal and future cashflows, not just looking at metrics that exclude most of what is being acquired. An efficient nationalised water industry should mean cheaper bills. Currently, Ofwat allows industry’s backers to recoup £22bn over five years. A Greenwich University study calculates that nationalisation could save households up to £160 a year by accessing low-cost state financing. The upshot of public ownership is that it puts an asset on the nation’s books, whereas privatisation puts the cost on customers’ bills.

Why is Israel taking an increasingly hard line on the Golan Heights?
During the UN General Assembly last week, the issue of the Golan Heights, Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967, returned to the forefront of the political arena. 
In a speech at the UNGA last Tuesday, Sharaa said that the Golan would remain Syrian land and that Israel’s 1981 annexation was null and void. 
He also reiterated Damascus’s commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement with Israel and called on Israel to withdraw from territory it seized beyond the Golan Heights after the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who addressed the UN on Thursday despite being  wanted by the ICC for war crimes, replied with a claim that “Jews have been present in the Golan Heights since the time of Moses” while telling Sharaa to read the Bible.
Israeli officials have adopted an increasingly hard line regarding both the Golan and the areas of southern Syria it occupied since 2024.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz threatened on Wednesday to seize and permanently retain more Syrian territory.
"If our forces or the territory of the State of Israel is attacked from Syria, we will have no choice but to act and respond. Any area we seize this time will remain ours forever, in accordance with the laws of war," Katz said.
Israel’s UN ambassador Danny Danon, likewise wrote in a post on X following al-Sharaa’s speech, that the Golan Heights “will always remain part of Israel.”
Struggle over legitimacy
In his address to the UN General Assembly, President Al-Sharaa said that Israel had carried out around 500 air and artillery strikes and more than 1,200 incursions in Syria since late 2024. He also mentioned the detention of around 300 Syrians.
He called for an Israeli withdrawal to the pre-2024 lines and affirmed Syria’s commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
On his trip to the US, the Syrian president also jokingly suggested that US President Donald Trump give New Jersey to Israel instead of the Golan Heights. Trump recognised Israeli “sovereignty” over the occupied territory during his first term as US president in 2019.
Khaled Khalil, a Syrian expert on Syrian-Israeli relations told The New Arab that Sharaa’s insistence that the Golan is Syrian land and his criticism of Israeli strikes in Syria had prompted Israel to treat the issue as part of a broader struggle over legitimacy and the political narrative.
Khalil linked this to the international pressure and criticism facing Israel, including from some of its allies.
Another Syrian political analyst, Ghazi Dahman, told The New Arab that Israel’s domestic politics and upcoming elections on October 27 were behind the bellicose Israeli statements.
He said that political one-upmanship regarding security usually precedes Israeli elections, but also suggested that Israeli statements might be an attempt to head off American pressure aimed at resuming Syrian-Israeli negotiations over new security arrangements.
The real history
Netanyahu brought ancient history into the Golan issue when he claimed in his UN speech that Jews had been present in the Golan for thousands of years, referring to the Bible.
However, the history of the Golan is more complex than presence of a single group. Different civilizations and peoples successively inhabited the plateau, including the Arameans, Assyrians, Nabataeans, and Ghassanids, among others.
Settlement in the Golan dates back to very ancient times. The region was home to multiple languages and cultures, including Canaanite, Aramaic and Arabic. 
As for the account concerning the Prophet Moses, different religious texts, including the Torah, indicate that Moses did not ultimately enter Palestine. He died in the Sinai Desert during the years of wandering, while the Israelites entered Palestine later under the leadership of Joshua, by crossing the Jordan River.
Consequently, using the story of Moses to establish Jewish presence in the Golan appears to be simply a political maneuvre on Netanyahu’s part.
In 1967, the Golan Heights contained around 150,000 Syrian residents. The vast majority – around 130,000 – were displaced after the war. 
Some Syrian residents still remain in several predominantly Druze villages, notably Majdal Shams, Mas’ade, Buq’ata, and Ghajar. 
With the exception of the United States and recently Colombia, no country recognises Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, with the UN considering it occupied Syrian territory.

The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.
Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.
“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”
Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.
Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.
In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.”
Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.
Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.
“Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.
“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.
Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.
“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”
Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.
“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”
Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.
“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

Karnataka flags drug landing cost-MRP gap at hospitals of up to 52.6 times; seeks Centre's intervention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:25:47 UTC
01:25:47 KST

Concerns have been raised over critical-care medicines, oncology medicine, high-value injectables, implants and surgical supplies, besides diagnostic-linked consumables and disposable devices.
BENGALURU: Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration commissioner K Srinivas has sought urgent regulatory intervention over the pricing of medicines, medical devices and consumables supplied to hospitals at discounted institutional prices but billed to in-patients at the printed maximum retail price (MRP) or close to it.In some cases the difference between the landing cost and MRP is as high as 52 times. In a letter to the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) and the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Srinivas has flagged critical-care medicines, oncology medicine, high-value injectables, implants and surgical supplies, besides diagnostic-linked consumables and disposable devices. The letter says the practice “may be especially harmful” in these categories.Tens of examples have been enclosed with the letter, showing substantial differences between the reported landing cost and MRP of several products.Some with massive margins are: Gufipol, manufactured by Criticare, has a landing cost of Rs 86 and an MRP of Rs 4,528, a difference of 5,165.1%, or 52.6 times the landing cost. Guficycline-50 injection, manufactured by GUFI, has a landing cost of Rs 160 and an MRP of Rs 7,110, a 4,343.7% difference or 44.4 times the landing cost.
Terlitis has a landing cost of Rs 118 against an MRP of Rs 4,416, a 3,642.4% difference or 37.4 times.Among the cancer drugs listed, Taxocare 120 mg from Intas has a landing cost of Rs 1,000 and an MRP of Rs 21,617.6, a 2,061.8% difference or 21.6 times. Romy 250 mcg injection, also from Intas, has a landing cost of Rs 1,650 and an MRP of Rs 4,109, a 149% difference or 2.5 times.The commissioner said a recurring pattern had been reported in hospital procurement and billing: a manufacturer or importer supplies an item to a hospital at a very low institutional price, while the pack carries a substantially higher retail MRP. The hospital then supplies it to an in-patient and charges the MRP or a nominal discount on it despite the lower acquisition price.“The patient, who is generally unable to obtain an immediate substitute during admission, bears the entire benefit of the manufacturer-hospital discount being retained within the supply chain,” the letter says.Srinivas described the issue as an “information-asymmetry and captive-patient problem”, saying patients generally do not know the institutional acquisition cost and do not have an effective choice at the point of use.The letter argues that MRP-only regulation is insufficient. “MRP operates as a ceiling on retail sale to a consumer, but it does not by itself ensure that the MRP is a fair patient-facing price in an institutional setting,” it says.It proposes mandatory disclosure of institutional transaction prices, a patient-facing price ceiling linked to acquisition cost, anti-evasion provisions, MRP rationalisation and an enforceable reporting and penalty framework.
Under the proposed system, the patient-facing price would be the lowest of the applicable statutory ceiling or notified retail price, the printed MRP, and the net institutional acquisition cost plus a prescribed maximum service margin and applicable taxes.The letter also proposes disclosure on hospital bills of the product details, MRP, net institutional acquisition cost, permitted service margin, taxes and final amount charged. It seeks quarterly electronic reporting, risk-based audits, a grievance channel and refunds with interest where overcharging is established.Srinivas has also sought an expert working group and amendments to the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, and asked that the matter be treated as “urgent” with a reasoned action taken report communicated.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

IndiGo A321 suffers tail strike during go around at Bangalore; plane lands safely in second attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:25:15 UTC
01:25:15 KST

(Representative Image): IndiGo spokesperson said 6E 6542 “experienced an ‘abnormal runway contact’ while landing during gusty weather at Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru. All customers and crew are safe and have disembarked safely.
NEW DELHI: In yet another instance of an IndiGo Airbus A321 tail strike, an aircraft (VT-NHP) operating a Guwahati-Bengaluru flight on Sunday suffered the same while going around at its destination. The flight (6E 6542) aborted landing on the first approach at the destination. During ascent, it suffered a tail strike. The aircraft landed safely on the second attempt. The DGCA is probing this latest tail strike.IndiGo spokesperson said 6E 6542 “experienced an ‘abnormal runway contact’ while landing during gusty weather at Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru. All customers and crew are safe and have disembarked safely. In line with standard operating procedures, all relevant authorities were informed, and the aircraft is undergoing maintenance checks. It will resume operations after securing necessary clearances. As always, the safety of our customers and crew is our top priority.”The DGCA has raised this issue with IndiGo, and the airline has told it that the focus on pilot training for this particular area has been enhanced.
About a year back, they used to happen mostly during landings. Now they are seen more during go-arounds. Airbus itself says, “There is also a higher risk of tail strike when a go-around is required near the ground.”UK’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau says the “rate of tail strike incidents per aircraft landing for the A321 is four times greater than that for the A320, probably as a result of the smaller margin from the normal flare attitude. Damage to the structural integrity of the fuselage should not pose a significant flight risk to the aircraft provided the tail strike is detected during or after landing.”An Airbus publication on safety says: “Performing a go-around near the ground is a very dynamic phase with a risk of tail strike. If a go-around is initiated, the (required) manoeuvre must be completed. Between Jan 2022 and Sept 2024, 49 tail strike events were reported to Airbus, with five (10%) during takeoff, 23 (47%) during landing and 21 (43%) during a go-around near the ground.”
Tail strikes are a global phenomenon. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Safety Report, tail strikes were the most frequent type of incident in 2024 and in 2025, although fatality risk remains low. IATA data shows tail strikes were the most frequent non-fatal incidents globally at nine, followed by landing gear issues at seven and runway excursion at six.“The ATR 72 and Boeing 737NG (-800/-900ER) were most frequently involved, accounting for 46% of events. Most tail strikes occurred during landing (69% when including rejected landings). Asia Pacific recorded the highest number of events, with the US, India, and Brazil among the most affected countries,” says the IATA Annual Safety Report - 2025.

Most of UK’s essential food supply grown in drought-risk areas, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:24:27 UTC
01:24:27 KST

The vast majority of the UK’s essential foods, including cereals, potatoes, sugar and oil, are grown in areas of England rated as having a moderate to very high risk of drought.
A very high proportion – 81% – of England’s fresh produce is concentrated in parts of the country that are already experiencing water stress, according to the analysis by the nature-focused investment fund Rebalance Earth.
Three-quarters of England’s wheat (77%), barley (75%) and oilseed rape (74%) grow in parts of the country rated as being at a moderate to very high drought risk, along with 70% of sugar beet and 67% of potatoes, it found.
It said about a quarter of the country’s staple crops were grown in areas facing an acute risk of drought, including 30% of wheat and barley, 28% of oilseed rape, 27% of fresh produce and 21% of potatoes.
“Drought builds slowly and quietly, and rarely gets the same attention as flooding, but its impact runs right through the economy: lower yields, strained supply chains and higher prices in all of our shopping baskets,” said Kirsty Wilman, the fund’s chief operating and financial officer.
Some of England’s traditionally most productive agricultural areas – such as East Anglia, long known as the country’s breadbasket, and Kent, often described as the garden of England – are among those facing the greatest pressure from drought and have seen prolonged periods of dry weather in recent years.
The yield from this year’s cereals harvest in England and Wales was described as disappointing in the final 2026 harvest report from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), with volumes of wheat, spring barley and oats below historical averages across the UK.
Crop yields are also significantly lower than normal on the Elveden estate in Suffolk, which is owned by the Guinness family and includes 9,000 hectares (22,000 acres) of farmed land.
“For three years out of five we have been in drought conditions,” said Andrew Blenkiron, who manages the farms on the estate in Breckland, an area on the Suffolk-Norfolk border known for its sandy soil. One of England’s largest commercial farms, they grow cereals including wheat and barley and root crops including onions and potatoes.
“Water for food is key for us to function as a business and make sure we produce 100,000 tonnes of food here on an annual basis,” he added.
Despite the challenges, Blenkiron believes the UK needs to better use its water resources to continue growing staple foods in productive areas. “If we didn’t grow on this land that is totally suitable for it, we would just import more and let other people deplete their natural resources.”

IDF enacts closure, heavy restrictions on Palestinian movement in West Bank during Sukkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:15:00 UTC
01:15:00 KST

The IDF has enacted a closure preventing virtually all Palestinians from entering Jewish areas of the West Bank for the remainder of hol hamoed Sukkot through October 4.
Such a closure often occurs during extended periods of Jewish holidays, which are a potential powder keg for Palestinian terror. But it was especially noteworthy only days after the IDF brought in its 98th Division (consisting of commandos and paratroopers) to assist with West Bank security following three successive terror incidents last week.
The US Embassy in Jerusalem issued a statement warning that "there is no regular entry into Israel" from the West Bank during the coming week "except for strictly medical and humanitarian reasons."
It added, "Jerusalem ID holders can still commute and travel freely. However, Arbel permit holders cannot cross checkpoints even by the shuttle. Exceptions can be considered only for medical and humanitarian reasons."
Defense Minister Israel Katz issued a statement on Sunday taking credit for the closure, though the IDF recommended it and it is standard practice around this time of year.
IDF is prepared for potential terror threats
Last week, the IDF reinforced its deployment across the West Bank amid concerns over a new potential terror wave during the intermediate Sukkot holiday days when hundreds of thousands of Israelis are expected to visit nature sites, prayer sites, and public events throughout the area.
A senior IDF official said that though there was no specific intelligence about such a terror wave, given the number of recent terror incidents, experience has taught the military to be extra prepared for copycat attackers inspired by previous recent terror attacks.
IDF Central Command and Israel Police's Judea and Samaria District are both deployed at their highest levels of readiness and volume to account for the much greater number of Israelis who may need protection.
In addition to ordering the 98th Division headquarters staff into the West Bank, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir ordered the Israel Air Force to shorten response times and prepare even more than during standard periods to respond to rapidly developing incidents.
Zamir also decided to place responsibility for the Judea and Etzion Regional Brigade sectors, with an emphasis on the fault line between Israeli and Palestinians areas near Jerusalem, under the authority of the 98th Division.
A senior IDF official said the decision was intended to reduce the burden on the Judea and Samaria Division headquarters' staff amid concerns over a potential new wave of terrorism.
More than double the normal number of battalions stationed in the West Bank
The last time so many IDF battalions were deployed to the West Bank was nearly 25 years ago, when the number of battalions exceeded 40. About 24 battalions are currently operating in the area, up from a peacetime average of around 11.
While the number of battalions has jumped and injecting the 98th Division is an aggressive move, Zamir so far has only sent the the division's command staff, not all of their troops.
It is presumed that if a new terror wave took off in the West Bank, having the command staff already in place would facilitate quickly deploying the 98th Division troops as well, to jump to the high 20s in terms of battalions.
Already last month, the IDF Central Command brought the Golani Brigade and Paratroopers Brigade through the West Bank to stabilize the security situation when Jewish terror against Palestinians spiked, and some IDF reservists did not push back on it sufficiently.
IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) sources have warned over an extended period that, in addition to Palestinian terror levels that occur even in peacetime, Palestinian terror could explode due to the Israeli police's failure, and sometimes the IDF's weak responses, to preventing Jewish extremist violence against Palestinians.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s capital in the fifth year of its invasion with Ukraine charging that Moscow is deliberately hitting civilian targets as the country braces for another tough winter.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi announced Russian strikes hit a children’s centre in the northern city of Sumy, killing three people including a 16-year-old girl.
Zelensky said three people were killed in night-time strikes on the southern Zaporizhzhia region and a Russian drone strike had killed one man in Kyiv.
The authorities in the Odesa region said a “massive strike” on the south of the Black Sea region had killed one more person.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said a woman and two 16-year-olds had also been wounded and hospitalised in the capital.
“The enemy continues to relentlessly attack the Kyiv region with strike drones,” the city’s administration said.
“Sixteen sites have been damaged,” including 12 private houses in Kyiv’s outskirts, as well as a warehouse and production facility, it added.
Russian strikes in the Odesa region damaged housing, a shop, a hotel, a medical building and a warehouse storing grain, said regional head Oleg Kiper.
Targeting ‘civilian infrastructure’
“This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles,” Zelensky posted on social media.
The strikes had targeted housing “and other civilian infrastructure” in various parts of the country, he added.
“If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of “shahed” terror would not be happening,” Zelensky said in later comments.
In Moscow, Russia’s defence ministry said it bombed a Kyivstar data centre in Kyiv and another belonging to the Omega Telecom company, claiming that the firms were providing services to the Ukrainian army.
It also released an image of a drone bearing the ironic message “Digital Detox”, confirming that the strikes were aimed at disrupting internet access in Ukraine.
On Sept 26, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told the UN General Assembly his country intended to continue its military campaign “to the end”.
Russia denies that it aims at civilian targets.
The defence ministry also said that Russian forces had seized the border village of Khrypuny in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, where Russia controls pockets of land.
Russia does not claim the Kharkiv region as its own – unlike the Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson region.
Throughout the war, however, it has attacked the region and seized land there.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to produce a breakthrough and the UN has highlighted the growing civilian toll as the two sides become more entrenched. AFP

The Zionist consensus behind Israel’s anti-Arab election bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:09:58 UTC
01:09:58 KST

Breadcrumb
The Zionist consensus behind Israel’s anti-Arab election bans
If we do not believe in the justice of our cause, the legitimacy of our demands and our right to express them, then there is no life for us in this country, our country.
For the past three or four decades, Israeli right-wing parties have made a habit, at every election, of submitting petitions to disqualify Arab parties or Arab MPs and prevent them from standing for parliament.
One of the many peculiarities of Israeli 'democracy' is that political parties are entrusted with deciding whether rival parties should be allowed to contest elections at all.
It has become a recurring populist ritual, one that people have grown accustomed to, just as they have grown accustomed to so many other abnormalities that have become normalised in Israeli society. They should not be.
Each time, the victims of their fellow parliamentarians turn to the Supreme Court in search of redress. This plays out within the familiar Israeli tension between right-wing party populism and a Supreme Court that, by comparison, presents itself as the last bastion of Israeli liberalism. In previous elections, the court has indeed overturned attempts to bar Balad from standing.
But in truth, it is a bastion of Israeli liberalism only beneath a Zionist ceiling, one that has been dropping steadily.
In recent years, that ceiling has fallen below much of what was achieved in the 1990s in the fields of civil rights, freedom of expression and other liberal gains. This has taken place amid Israel’s continuing drift to the right, the growing convergence between Zionism and religious Zionism, the denial of Palestinian rights and the normalisation of occupation violence as something society can simply live with.
The changing composition of the Supreme Court reflects this shift too. It has moved steadily rightwards, to the point where the court now has a right-wing majority.
Much changed after 7 October and Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. So too did the Zionist conditions placed on freedom of expression and civil rights, even if we limit the discussion to what is happening within the 1948 borders. Palestinian citizens have faced a wider crackdown on expression and dissent since 7 October, including arrests, disciplinary action and punishment over political speech.
The nature of the debate inside the Central Elections Committee has also changed, if “debate” is still the right word for it.
This time, there was a full Zionist consensus in favour of disqualifying MP Sami Abu Shehadeh, going beyond the usual Zionist majority that supports banning Arab parties.
More unusually still, the committee chairman, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, voted in favour of the disqualification.
The case rests on a single article Abu Shehadeh wrote on 7 October itself and which was published the following day in The New Arab, before the full nature of the operation had become clear. This is despite the fact that, throughout the three years since, he has repeatedly expressed positions that contradict what is being attributed to him on the basis of that article.
Dangerous precedents
We are therefore facing two dangerous precedents.
The first is the consensus inside the committee, including the vote of its chairman, a Supreme Court justice, in favour of disqualification.
The second is the disqualification of a candidate not because of a consistent political position or a sustained course of action, but because of a single article.
What seems clear is that, in the first election of the post-7 October era, an Arab sacrifice is required as the price for allowing Arab parties to participate at all.
Someone must be placed on the altar of the racist Zionist consensus that has hardened since 7 October.
There is no other convincing explanation for disqualifying Abu Shehadeh and barring him from the election. The current proceedings have targeted not only Abu Shehadeh but Palestinian parties and candidates more broadly.
They would prefer to disqualify Balad as well because of its advocacy of a state of all its citizens. But they have not found a legal pretext for doing so, and cannot easily do so while the party is contesting the election within a Joint List rather than independently.
One has to make a real effort to remain composed when remembering that the petition was submitted by Itamar Ben-Gvir, a man known not only to Palestinians but to the Israeli courts themselves for racist, violent and extremist conduct, and who has criminal convictions. His record includes a conviction for racist incitement and support for a terrorist organisation.
Yet the chairman of the committee, a Supreme Court justice, found more common ground with Ben-Gvir than with Sami Abu Shehadeh, the Balad and Joint List candidate, a democrat who believes in human values, the rights of peoples and equality between Arabs and Jews.
Then came the familiar chorus in the Israeli media.
Journalists known for their hostility towards Balad, precisely because it is in many respects more democratic and more liberal than they are, rushed to join in. Many remain trapped in their obsession with Dr Azmi Bishara without having read a single word of his books or articles, not even the political writings that should be accessible to them.
His writings over the past three years have repeatedly affirmed the legitimacy of resisting occupation, while placing two clear limits on that resistance.
The first is moral. Resistance does not have the right to cross certain ethical lines, and he has consistently rejected targeting or harming civilians.
The second is strategic. Resistance cannot be allowed to damage the cause of the people it is supposed to serve. Bishara has continued to develop his thinking on resistance, political strategy and the future of the Palestinian struggle in his writing on the Palestinian national project after the Gaza genocide.
Zionist-only elections
The current effort to restrict electoral participation according to the boundaries of a wartime Zionist consensus should surprise no one.
This is a state and a society in which no genuine protest movement emerged against the genocidal war being waged on the Palestinian people, no serious protest emerged over the killing of more than 20,000 children, and no meaningful movement arose against settler violence carried out under the protection and with the support of the Israeli army in the West Bank and Gaza. Recent cases have documented settlers acting while Israeli forces blocked Palestinians and activists from intervening.
The populist hysteria inside the Elections Committee, its decisions and the chorus of incitement surrounding them are therefore not surprising to Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Nor is the chorus in the media, or the panic of those among us who have become frightened of their own shadow. We have seen three years of blood-soaked hysteria. The pressure has extended beyond electoral politics into universities, where Palestinian students have faced disciplinary proceedings over expressions of Palestinian identity and opposition to the war.
What is more remarkable is that some frightened figures on the margins of the Zionist left are now whispering that Sami Abu Shehadeh should withdraw his candidacy before the Supreme Court considers the disqualification.
They say he should not challenge the decision, even though a decision by the Elections Committee to disqualify a candidate is automatically referred to the court for approval or rejection, whether or not the candidate himself files an appeal.
They also suggest that Balad and Abu Shehadeh should avoid the Supreme Court altogether, lest a legal precedent be created.
Their assumption is that the court will inevitably uphold the disqualification and thereby establish a precedent for barring a candidate from elections on the basis of a single article.
Supreme Injustice
The injustice, in other words, may go ahead. What matters to some is that “Israeli liberalism” should not be stained by having its name attached to it.
As though Israeli liberalism had not already been stained by the killing of Gaza’s children, the legitimisation of the dispossession of the West Bank, and the abuse of its people.
Imagine a qualified person applying for a job at an institution and being told: do not apply, because you will be rejected for being Arab, and then the institution will look racist.
That is essentially what Balad, Abu Shehadeh and their supporters are being told.
Do not force the court to issue a ruling that reveals it to be more Zionist than liberal.
Do not force it to appear to be on Ben-Gvir’s side.
But is the victim of injustice expected to remain silent and abandon a legitimate legal case merely to spare the court the embarrassment of endorsing injustice?
Is that the responsibility of the person seeking justice, or of those who choose to deny it?
Withdrawing Abu Shehadeh’s candidacy under these circumstances would mean three things.
First, it would amount to recognising the legitimacy, or at least the validity, of the disqualification.
Second, it would mean abandoning legal arguments that are both available and sufficient, arguments that any just court ought to accept. Anyone who opposes the disqualification should begin from that premise.
Third, it would help conceal the racist face of the current Zionist consensus.
If the answer is that the decision has already been made and that it is fundamentally political, then so be it.
Legal argument does not replace principled political argument over the occupation, freedom of expression, citizenship, the limits of political participation, or Ben-Gvir and what he represents.
But neither, from the standpoint of law or justice, should the legal argument be abandoned.
Let the court make a political decision if that is what it chooses to do. It should then bear responsibility for that decision.
The burden should not be shifted onto those challenging the injustice.
Balad should put forward its understanding of liberal democracy against the chauvinistic, nationalist-religious Zionist understanding now being imposed on it.
It should defend its vision of a state of all its citizens, the very position that has earned it so much Zionist hostility and has frightened even those who are afraid to articulate their own rights.
Whatever the court ultimately decides, Balad and Sami Abu Shehadeh have already said they will call on Arab citizens to increase voter turnout in the election. The renewed Joint List entered the election campaign pledging to confront racism and supremacy.
If they were politically colour-blind, they would hardly be doing so.
If we do not believe in the justice of our cause, the legitimacy of our demands and our right to express them, then there is no life for us in this country, our country.

5 arrested near British air base used by US over alleged bomb plot

The base “serves as the preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe for USAF Global Strike Command,” according to the Air Force.

Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:02:17 BST
01:02:17 KST

Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
- Published
Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.
More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.
The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.
Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.
Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.
"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.
This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.
Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.
Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.
Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Iran is ready to negotiate with the US but “fully prepared” to respond to renewed military attacks, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday, as he outlined a seven-day proposal under which Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
“We are ready for diplomacy. We are ready for war at the same time,” Araghchi told NBC’s Meet the Press.
Araghchi said Iran had heard President Donald Trump reject the proposal but was “still waiting for an official response through the mediators.”
He said Tehran would reopen the strait if Washington first took steps Iran has sought, including ending the war, releasing frozen Iranian assets, removing the blockade and allowing Iran to sell its oil.
“Our proposal is very clear. We are ready to open the strait if certain things are done by the US,” he said.
Araghchi said he believed the US could take the required steps within four or five days. Under the proposed sequence, Iran would reopen the strait on day six and the two sides would resume negotiations on a final agreement on day seven.
Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint, following US-Israeli attacks in February and a maritime blockade on the country.
Distrust
The Iranian minister expressed deep distrust of negotiations with the Trump administration, accusing Washington of attacking Iran during talks in both 2025 and 2026, and violating a subsequent agreement shortly after it was signed.
“There is always hope for diplomacy,” he said. “But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn’t miss any chance for peace.”
Asked whether he trusted Trump, Araghchi replied: “We trust ourselves.”
Araghchi disputed that Iran had violated the June memorandum of understanding with the US first, saying if Washington believed Tehran had done so, it could have invoked a dispute-settlement provision in their interim deal instead of bombing Iran.
Asked about the prospect of further US strikes, Araghchi said Iran had learned from earlier fighting and changed its military tactics.
“We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed,” he said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even it comes to a doomsday war. But at the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy.”
He said the decision between renewed military action and negotiations was up to Trump.
On Iran’s nuclear program, Araghchi maintained that enrichment was for “peaceful” purposes, including medical uses, and said Iran had offered to negotiate over its 60%-enriched material.
“We decided to put everything nuclear for the later stages and go for confidence building in this stage,” he said, explaining why the issue was not part of the initial seven-day proposal.
He argued that questions about Iran’s nuclear program should be settled through negotiations rather than military action.
Asked about why Iran’s supreme leader had not appeared publicly on video since taking power in March, Araghchi cited security concerns, saying there were indications he faced threats from the US.
“We receive his comments and orders and opinions,” Araghchi said.
He rejected suggestions of competing centers of power in Iran, saying the Foreign Ministry coordinated with the government, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Supreme National Security Council and parliament.

Nor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outages
