Netanyahu battles October 7 warnings revelations with defiant UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:41:26 UTC
00:41:26 KST

With Israel’s election approaching, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is battling new revelations of alleged warnings about Hamas’ 7 October attack and countered the political storm with a fiery UN speech directed at his voters and the world.
The political storm engulfing Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu over reports of additional foreign warnings about Hamas’ 7 October attack expanded on Saturday and Sunday when more revelations surfaced amid the looming Israeli elections, with the Israeli premier countering with a fiery and defiant speech about Israel’s defence at the UN.
The New York Times on Saturday confirmed a previous Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed secretly warned Netanyahu of the Hamas’ 7 October attack and that Israel’s premier did not pass on the warning to his security officials.
Also on Saturday, the US news magazine The Atlantic reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel secretly visited Israel 11 days before 7 October attack to warn of a significant Hamas attack.
And on Sunday, former Israeli Defence minister Yoav Gallant told the Israeli Army Radio that Israel received a message from Hamas through Israeli internal national security agency Shin Bet channels weeks before the 7 October attack, in which the then Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar warned that he would "shake the prisons".
The revelations come at a time when Israel’s election campaign is in full swing for the vote next month and Netanyahu’s handling of the 7 October attack is a key issue in the campaign. The revelations also coincide with the prime minister's fiery speech at the UN General Assembly, widely considered asa message to the voters in Israel.
Israel’s opposition leaders have launched a series of scathing attacks on Netanyahu, calling for an investigation into the warnings that Israel’s prime minister allegedly received in the run-up to the attacks and whether he ignored them.
The prime minister’s office (PMO) repeatedly denied the media reports calling them false.
Haaretz previously reported that 10 days before the attack, the UAE president allegedly warned Netanyahu in a 45-minute-call that the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major attack against Israel. The Haaretz report claimed Netanyahu "reacted with relative calm" and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
At the time, Netanyahu's office called the report "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader. "The press reports are false. No warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October," the PMO said in a statement.
Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over alleged warnings before 7 October
But on Saturday, the New York Times published its own extensive investigation citing multiple officials matching the Haaretz revelations, alleging that Netanyahu was warned by the Emirati president before the Hamas attack and that the warning was not shared with Israel security chiefs.
In parallel with the New York Times report, the Atlantic published its own investigation alleging that on 26 September 2023, Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel made a secret 67-minute visit to Israel to warn of a possible Hamas attack, but the warning did not include specific details.
The Atlantic report said Kamel urged Israel to reduce tensions in the Gaza Strip and that it was not clear whom he met during his 1-hour long stay in Israel.
According to The Atlantic, officials from seven countries told its journalists that such a short personal visit from Egypt’s intelligence chief himself should have been noticed by Israel’s political and security leadership and that Egyptian warnings allegedly continued until two days before the attack, but still without further specifics.
Just days after the 7 October attack, the PMO said that Netanyahu "has not spoken or met with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the establishment of the government, neither directly nor indirectly". Then on Saturday, the same office repeated that the report in The Atlantic "was denied at the time and is being recycled to manipulate the Israeli public," the Jerusalem Post reported on Sunday.
"On October 11, 2023, Egypt officially denied that it had warned Israel of the October 7 attack," the PMO said, adding that "in the months preceding 7 October, prime minister Netanyahu neither met nor spoke with Abbas Kamel, then head of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service. No Israeli intelligence official conveyed such a warning to the prime minister".
The US media reports were followed on Sunday by new revelations from former Israeli Defence minister Yoav Gallant who said that the Hamas leader at the time of the 7 October, Yahya Sinwar, warned Israel before the attacks that he would "shake the prisons".
In an interview with Israeli Army Radio, Galant said that Sinwar allegedly sent his message to Israel’s Shin Bet security agency through a former senior Fatah official during secret negotiations for a prisoner exchange deal before the Hamas attack.
Gallant also alleged that Netanyahu did not include him and senior security officials in sensitive conversations with the United Staes during the war.
"During the war, I learned many times about important conversations Netanyahu held with the Americans on the most sensitive issues, such as hostages and ammunition, only after the Americans called me and tried to verify what had been said in those conversations," Gallant told the Israeli Army Radio, adding that "their trust in the prime minister was low".
When asked about the foreign warnings’ allegations, Gallant said he was not informed of them during his time as defence minister.
"I first heard about these warnings from media reports," he said, adding that "assuming these things are true, such a warning that a prime minister receives from the leader of a country is not a political asset; it is a fundamental failure in the overall assessment of the situation".
Netanyahu attacks critics at UN as Israeli election looms
Israelis are due to head to the polls on 27 October for a national election to determine the 120-seat Knesset (parliament).
Despite a growing onslaught by the opposition, Netanyahu has so far rejected multiple calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the 7 October attack following other accusations of his handling of the crisis.
As the Israeli election campaign is in full swing, Netanyahu used his speech at the United Nations General Assembly last Thursday to reaffirm his hardline stance on Israel’s protection to voters at home, but also as a series of messages to the world.
"You know any other country the size of New Jersey capable of fighting a seven front war? And for three years? They all ganged up on us to wipe us off the face of the Earth," Israel’s prime minister said in his speech outlining his doctrine against Israel’s enemies, but also its critics.
But as he walked to the podium to begin his speech, dozens of delegations walked out of the General Assembly hall in protest at Israel’s policies, but many others stayed, including the United States, Germany, France, Italy, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, Japan, India and others, prompting Netanyahu to say: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t yet left this hall, please do so now."
"Now, you want to hear the ultimate irony? Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," Netanyahu reacted to the departures.
He then engaged in a series of fiery attacks on countries and leaders that he perceives as enemies of Israel or of himself.
On Iran, he predicted that "this evil regime will fall" because “the power of the people will overcome the people in power!” as the "murderous regime will be toppled by its lies, by its corruption, by its cruelty".
To showcase the danger of Iranian missiles, he explained to the assembly that a one-ton ballistic missile "would obliterate the entire compound," and that "two such missiles would obliterate the UN".
He mocked Hezbollah by taking out a pager and saying "you remember the beepers? Remember these things? Remember them? Well, I can tell you this, Hezbollah certainly remembers them."
He singled out "people" in the United Kingdom and France when talking about accusations of "colonialism" againt Israel, saying "who accuses us? Among them, people in the United Kingdom and France. But for the love of God, they are the ones who invented the term! Their colonies stretched across the entire planet. Colonialism? Leave us alone!"
He again accused Qatar repeatedly, saying that Qatar had spent millions to "brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America and hate the West," culminating with "this is the same Qatar that hosts the Hamas butchers of October 7th."
He also accused several countries, including Qatar and Turkey, of spending billions to spread lies in the media against Israel.
Qatar rejected the accusations saying that "this continuing rhetoric against Qatar is nothing more than an attempt to divert attention from the atrocities committed by his government in the occupied Palestinian territories and their grave humanitarian consequences".
But his strongest words went against President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan whom he accused of being "a tyrant who also hosts Hamas terror leaders," who "illegally occupies Northern Cyprus, an EU member," who "as a NATO member, regularly violates Greece’s borders," "who wants to take over Syria" and, most of all, who "calls for Israel's destruction and he says he will be the ruler of Jerusalem".
"No, sir, you won’t. It is our city," Israel’s prime minister said.
While Netanyahu maintained that accusing Israel of "genocide" is the "biggest lie of the century," Turkish president Erdoğan declared in his own UNGA speech that "we face a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with humanity, mercy or conscience can turn a blind eye," describing Gaza as "the most inhumane, most shameful concentration camp of our time".

Ukraine Now Neutralizes 55% of Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:40:57 UTC
00:40:57 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Now Neutralizes 55% of Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine is currently neutralizing about 55% of the jet-powered Shahed-type drones launched by Russia, with more than 1,500 such UAVs shot down or suppressed since the beginning of September.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in his evening address on September 26, Russia launched more than 2,730 jet-powered Shahed drones during September. More than 1,500 were intercepted or electronically suppressed, putting Ukraine’s current neutralization rate at approximately 55%.
The rate remains below Ukraine’s interception performance against conventional Shahed-type drones, which Zelenskyy said now exceeds 90%. He said Ukraine aims to bring protection against the newer jet-powered variants to a comparable level.
Ukraine has already developed several effective prototype interceptors designed specifically to counter the faster drones, Zelenskyy said. Some are already being used by Ukrainian units under combat conditions, while several systems have been selected as potential primary tools for defending against the threat.
Ukraine is now working to expand production of those interceptors and the components required to manufacture them at scale, according to the president.
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian military intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents detailing Moscow’s weapons-production plans for 2027, including planned volumes and financing.
According to the documents cited by Zelenskyy, Russia intends to spend about $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions alone.
The growing use of jet-powered Shahed variants has added another layer to Russia’s long-range drone campaign against Ukraine. Unlike conventional propeller-driven Shaheds, the newer systems travel at higher speeds, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses to detect and intercept them.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is developing dedicated countermeasures for the systems identified in Russia’s production plans, with interceptor drones expected to play a larger role in defending Ukrainian airspace as production expands.

The message states that the relevant formations may be needed in 90–120 days. At the same time, the document contains no evidence that military units have already received deployment orders. The information made public also does not confirm that a decision has been made to conduct an operation.
It should be noted that Cuba is not mentioned directly in the text of the request. Several U.S. officials, speaking to CBS on condition of anonymity, described its connection to military planning regarding the island.
What forces could be involved
Subordinate commands were asked to provide information on the availability of six types of formations. Responses to the request were due by September 25.
It is currently known that a significant part of the request concerns logistical support. In particular, it refers to an expeditionary sustainment command, which coordinates theater-level supply and transportation. The request also covers engineering units, a medical brigade, an advanced surgical unit, and a military police brigade. Medical forces could provide emergency operations and care for the wounded near the locations of deployed troops, while military police could perform security and detainee-related duties. However, the specific role of these forces in a possible operation has not been disclosed.
A SOUTHCOM representative, for his part, declined to discuss potential troop movements and the timing of their involvement, citing operational security. The command explained that it continuously coordinates with other components of the armed forces to assess potential needs within its area of responsibility.
Options for action regarding Cuba had been considered previously
In May, U.S. intelligence agencies assessed Havana’s possible response to U.S. military action. In July, military planners considered various scenarios, including a large-scale airborne operation involving the 101st Airborne Division. It was also reported that the U.S. military had surveyed the waters and seabed around Cuba.
In addition, aviation units had previously been placed on heightened readiness for a potential deployment that ultimately did not take place. Officials emphasized that working through scenarios did not mean the president or the Pentagon had decided to launch an operation.
Trump expects an agreement with Havana
Against the backdrop of reports about military planning, Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on September 26 that he expects an agreement between the United States and Cuba.
I don’t think we’ll need the military
Trump also said he wanted to help Cuba and open it up to Americans. At the same time, no specific agreement was reported to have been concluded.
How Cuba responded
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez, speaking at the United Nations General Assembly on September 26, said that Havana hoped to avoid U.S. military intervention. At the same time, he emphasized that, in the event of an attack, the country would exercise its right to self-defense. According to Rodríguez, the use of force would result in the deaths of Cubans and U.S. service members, as well as widespread destruction.
The head of Cuba’s Foreign Ministry confirmed a readiness to negotiate with Washington to resolve bilateral differences and to establish trade relations with U.S. companies. He emphasized that dialogue must be based on respect, sovereign equality, and compliance with international law, without interference in internal affairs and without preconditions.
Context
On September 17, the United States announced sanctions against four state-owned enterprises in Cuba’s nickel industry, four military enterprises, and three military officials. The restrictions apply, in particular, to entities linked to weapons research and development. On September 22, during an address to the UN General Assembly, Trump called Cuba a failed state and predicted the fall of communist rule on the island. The Cuban delegation left the hall during his speech.

France denies joining war on Houthis, says support for Saudi Arabia 'defensive'
French military support being given to Saudi Arabia to help it confront attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis is "strictly defensive", French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Sunday.
His comment, made on state television network France 2, follows President Emmanuel Macron's announcement Thursday of French troops, radar units and "defence systems" being sent to Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has come under repeated missile and drone attacks from the Houthis, after Yemen's war reignited in July after a years-long truce, adding another front to the Middle East war.
The attacks have targeted Saudi oil installations and the key oil terminal of Yanbu. Saudi Arabia is militarily backing Yemen's government forces against the Houthis.
The Houthis are seeking to impose a blockade on Saudi energy exports, which were shifted to the Red Sea after Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz choked transits in the Gulf.
Asked whether France's aid meant that Paris had become a partner in Saudi Arabia's war against the Houthis, Barrot said: "Absolutely not... This is strictly defensive."
He added that "since the start of the (US-Israeli) war against Iran, we have deployed military assets to protect our allies, our partners".
"Does that mean at any time we can be considered co-belligerents? Never."
Barrot said the scale of the French deployment to Saudi Arabia would depend on what Riyadh requested, as well as "our own capacities and how the situation develops".

Tense standoff over loyalist march in Portadown as protesters block route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:33:57 UTC
00:33:57 KST

Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parade in Northern Ireland after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on a historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years.
The loyalist Drumcree parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness”.
It led to a weekend of intense legal wrangling which concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision.
In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution.
The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear.
Among the protesters was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.”
She added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”
Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”.
She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea?
“No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community.”
The local Democratic Unionist party (DUP) MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest.
“It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.”
Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said: “We now have lawmakers acting as law breakers,” and he accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”.
The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so. He said the nationalist protest was unlawful and called on politicians to “calm things down”.
Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before … inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.”
The tense standoff also drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”.
The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”.
He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”.
The Drumcree parade on the Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history.
On Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm, and that it should be held in silence.
The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.
That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning.
The final, time-limited sitting, which began at 20 minutes past midnight on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.
Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

For Libya, the Hormuz crisis can be a trap or an opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:29:19 UTC
00:29:19 KST

For Libya, the Hormuz crisis can be a trap or an opportunity
Libyan hydrocarbons are increasingly sought after. To take full advantage, the country needs a new economic strategy.
Amid the worsening global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, European countries, desperate for alternative energy supplies, trade routes and partnerships, have looked across the Mediterranean for solutions.
As a result, governments across North Africa have started to reassess their strategic value. Algeria is in an especially strong position as an established gas supplier, while Egypt can offer infrastructure, refining capacity and access through the Suez Canal.
Libya has also seen its strategic value increase. It has around 48 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, the largest in Africa, and produces 1.5 million barrels of oil per day. It also has substantial natural gas reserves.
Its oil reaches international markets through the Mediterranean, while the Greenstream gas pipeline connects its Mellitah complex directly to Europe.
Libya cannot replace the Gulf in terms of oil and gas exports, but it can become a major player in diversification efforts not just in Europe but elsewhere in the world. The challenge the country faces is how to take full advantage amid structural constraints and insecurity.
Energy insecurity at home
Libya is simultaneously a major energy exporter and an energy-insecure state. Although the country possesses vast oil and gas resources, Libyans experience regular electricity blackouts due to an inefficient domestic energy system.
More than 70 percent of Libyan gas production is consumed domestically, mostly for electricity generation. Production has struggled to meet both domestic needs and export commitments. Gas exports consequently fell year on year from around 200 billion cubic feet in 2019 to 35 billion in 2025, the lowest export levels in 22 years.
At the same time, the country is flaring at least 200 billion cubic feet of gas annually due to underdeveloped infrastructure. Gas that could generate electricity, support industry or increase exports is instead being wasted.
The International Monetary Fund has estimated Libya’s total energy subsidy burden at around $17bn, equivalent to roughly 35 percent of GDP – one of the largest in the world.
Much of these funds go into subsidising imported refined fuels, as domestic refining capacity is largely underdeveloped and cannot meet demand.
The domestic energy situation is compounded by political fragmentation, institutional disputes and periodic disruptions to production due to conflict.
Increasing exports without addressing these problems risks improving energy security abroad while neglecting it at home, and that is a recipe for more instability in an already fragile nation.
Opportunity or trap?
The global energy crisis triggered by the Iran war is surely a major opportunity for Libya to increase its revenues from hydrocarbons. But it also carries a risk.
As I pointed out during the 5th meeting of the Mediterranean Energy Experts Circle earlier this month, greater demand for Libyan oil and gas could reinforce the economic model the country has struggled to escape from for decades: producing hydrocarbons, exporting them, distributing the revenues and postponing structural reform.
This model does not allow Libya to capture the full economic potential of its resource wealth. It keeps the Libyan state stuck in the all too familiar “resource curse”, which promotes economic stagnation and inefficiency.
That is why when taking advantage of heightened demand for energy, it is crucial that Libya uses the proceeds to transform its energy system.
That means capturing flared gas, modernising electricity generation and transmission, expanding domestic refining where economically viable, reforming subsidies, investing seriously in renewable energy and participating in sustainable regional energy cooperation.
Libya’s National Sustainable Energy Strategy aims to have 22 percent of electricity generation from renewable sources by 2035, an ambitious target that requires major positive shifts in security and governance conditions. Increased revenue flows can help jump-start the process.
Another important consideration is how the country should approach heightened foreign interest. Libya’s first major oil and gas licensing round since 2007 was concluded in February, with the US’s Chevron, Italy’s Eni, QatarEnergy, Spain’s Repsol, Hungary’s MOL, Nigeria’s Aiteo, and Türkiye’s TPAO securing new licences.
Commercial and geopolitical interests are rarely completely separate in energy. For Libya, this creates bargaining power—if managed coherently by the Libyans. Rather than becoming an arena in which external actors compete for individual assets and relationships, Libya could use diversified partnerships to attract investment and technology while reducing dependence on any single partner.
From energy exporter to Mediterranean energy hub
The transformation Libya seeks should not be confined to its borders. Its strategic objective should be to become an integral player in a Mediterranean energy hub by expanding cooperation with neighbouring states and leveraging existing production capacities and infrastructure.
To Libya’s east, Egypt has a large electricity system and significant refining and processing capacity. To its west, Tunisia provides access towards the wider Maghreb and increasingly towards European markets. Libya sits between them with enormous hydrocarbon resources, considerable solar potential and existing energy connections with both neighbours.
Important steps have already been taken to deepen regional energy integration. In January, Egypt and Libya signed an energy cooperation agreement covering exploration and the development of crude-oil refining. The two countries are also discussing the construction of an 800km pipeline connecting Tobruk to Alexandria. The project is worth $1bn and would carry Libyan crude directly to Egyptian refineries.
Libya and Tunisia are also expanding cooperation. Earlier this month, the Libyan-Tunisian company Joint Oil opened an international licensing round covering around 3,000 square kilometres of shared offshore acreage and development of the cross-border Zarat oil and gas discovery. Formal awards are expected by the end of April 2027.
The risk here is that expanded cooperation could develop into dependence. How to avoid that is the lesson Libya can learn from the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country still needs sufficient domestic electricity, refining and production capacity to protect itself. Regional integration should add alternatives rather than create new vulnerabilities: more markets, more electricity connections, more processing options and more export routes.
The objective should therefore be specialisation, connectivity and redundancy all achieved in the right sequence depending on needs and conditions.
A moment for strategic redesign
The Iran war has given Libya something potentially more valuable than temporarily higher hydrocarbon prices: renewed strategic relevance. But greater strategic relevance does not automatically make the country a more reliable energy partner.
Converting the former into the latter requires a radically different approach not just to the domestic oil and gas industry, but also to overall economic development and regional geopolitics.
Libya must use this moment to pursue strategic redesign: to increase production while recovering wasted gas, improve electricity infrastructure, develop refining and renewables, strengthen regional connections and cooperation, and use competition among international partners to attract investment.
Libya already has the resources and the geography to become an even bigger player in the energy market. The question is whether it can build the rest.

Bill Gates says global AI framework ‘more difficult’ to create than Cold War nuclear limitations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:24:39 UTC
00:24:39 KST

Efe Özkan
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Microsoft co-founder and billionaire Bill Gates warned on Sunday that getting countries to agree to a global framework on artificial intelligence could be “more difficult” than Cold War-era negotiations to limit nuclear weapons.
“This is more difficult than that was,” Gates told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” during a wide-ranging discussion on AI.
Gates also addressed US President Donald Trump’s stance against regulating AI, with Trump rejecting calls for the federal government to impose guardrails for companies building AI models.
The tech pioneer argued that regulating AI companies with monitoring systems would not hamper the US in any race with China to develop superior technology.
“What he said is fine, but I think after he hears from me and other people, including that this does not handicap us in whatever he thinks the nation-state race is, that, you know, we will come to a consensus,” he said.
The billionaire later highlighted other times the US led the world in coming up with broad agreements to protect humanity since World War II, with its friends and allies, citing the global challenges of “aviation safety, ozone layer, nuclear weapons, a lot of things where we played the fair actor, not aggrandizing whatever our unique strengths were.”
He added: “And AI is one we’re going to have to go back to this:, ‘Hey, humanity is all in this together’.”
The debate comes in the wake of recent incidents of AI agents going beyond what many experts thought possible, spurring industry insiders to issue warnings and call for stricter regulation of the sector.

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Destroy Training Base of Russian GROM Kaskad Drone Brigade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:21:48 UTC
00:21:48 KST

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) have destroyed the training base of the Russian GROM Kaskad unmanned aviation brigade, which launches Geran-type strike drones, including jet-powered versions, against Ukraine.
The Exilenova+ community published satellite imagery.
Satellite imagery suggests the base was located on the grounds of the Viktoria boarding house in the village of Bilosarayska Kosa on the coast of the Sea of Azov, near Mariupol.
The attack took place on the night of September 15-16, 2026. According to reports, at least 15 explosions were heard at the site. Satellite imagery shows that four buildings containing hotel rooms were completely destroyed.
The GROM Kaskad Separate Unmanned Aviation Brigade is the first unmanned aviation formation within Russia’s Aerospace Forces. It was formed in October 2023 from the Kaskad BARS volunteer detachment, which had operated since 2022.
The brigade has at least two reconnaissance and strike battalions equipped with ZALA/Lancet, Orlan-30, SuperCam, and FPV drones, as well as one specialized reconnaissance battalion that is also involved in directing ballistic missile strikes.
In August 2025, the first reports emerged that the brigade had received Shahed-type strike UAVs. At the time, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence established that GROM Kaskad’s commander was Lt. Col. Ruslan Negrub.
According to intelligence estimates, the brigade also includes Russian officials and lawmakers who sign short-term contracts and receive combat veteran status.
Reports claim that the brigade has launch teams for various types of UAVs at the Tsimbulova droneport, as well as at the Donetsk and Hvardiiske airfields.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence established that on July 26, 2026, Combat Group No. 3 of the brigade launched a Geran-4 jet-powered drone at an ATB supermarket in Chernihiv. Two people were killed, and 25 others were wounded in the strike.
In late September, Ukrainian drones hit bunkers and hangars at the Tsimbulova droneport in the Oryol region. Some drones penetrated the bunkers. Several hits involving detonations and damage to hangars were also recorded, while fragments of destroyed UAVs were found at a launch preparation site.
The Tsimbulova droneport is a large Russian military complex near the village of the same name in the Oryol region, designed to store and launch strike UAVs. Satellite imagery shows numerous launch positions, shelters, and other infrastructure, including facilities for Geran-4 jet-powered drones and Geran-5 small cruise missiles.

Opinion | How to Put Time Back on the Clock in Iran

15:18:00 UTC

Opinion | How to Put Time Back on the Clock in Iran

====================================================================================================

Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:17:23 UTC
00:17:23 KST

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would call an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear there would be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win.
There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had been hanging around the fringes of the conference as he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.
Fast forward a year and Burnham is in No 10, Reform UK’s lead in the polls has disappeared, and Labour is looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets.
No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as he kicked off conference with the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream.
“You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura. Somehow biting her lip and refraining from adding that it is early days and we’ll see how much you’ve aged by this time next year. Andy smiled. He was, he said. Not because he had the job he had always coveted. But because now he had a chance to make a difference. To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. You’re going to hear a lot of the H-word in the next four days. It’s plastered over every wall of the conference centre.
And Burnham speaks as if he genuinely means it. He has the easy-going charm and self-confidence of a man who is comfortable in his own skin. He reaches parts that other politicians don’t get near. Nige has the same quality. Only, where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.
All of which is a much in demand – if not essential – skill for a politician. One that gives you a fighting chance of success. People feel both heard and seen by him. It’s almost uncanny. Burnham talks of being a different sort of politician, when the reality he is the archetypal career politician. You’d imagine he had spent years doing what he calls a real job as a hospital porter, but he’s been a politician almost all his adult life. Few understand the Westminster system better than him, he also suggests. You can’t escape the irony. Keir Starmer actually had a long and successful career outside politics, but he is the one who always sounded like the career politician. Speaking in soundbites and half truths. You’ve either got it or you haven’t.
The message Burnham really wanted to get across on Sunday morning was that social care was the hill he would die on. Other politicians had said they would tackle the issue but had recoiled when they realised how difficult it was. “I will grasp the nettle,” he said, opening his eyes still wider, hoping that viewers would fall into them. He would create a national care system that incorporated the NHS and social care. Old people were either paying through the nose for their own care, falling through the cracks or ending up bed blocking in hospitals. It was unsustainable and undignified.
How this would be paid for would be laid out in due course. It would be what Labour would campaign on in 2029. But make no mistake, people were already paying for it. Here he was preaching to the converted. My sisters and I had to sell my mother’s house to pay for her care during the last seven years of her life as she suffered from Alzheimer’s. We didn’t mind so much, but my mother would have been gutted had she been aware. It had mattered to her that she could leave her house to the three of us. Paying a little extra in tax to make sure that other people – possibly even you – don’t have to burn through their assets seems the kind of thing any fair-minded society would do.
Burnham ended by saying he very much hoped to work cross-party on all this. It was too important not to. This aspiration lasted all of five minutes. Because that’s how long it took the ever ridiculous Chris Philp – Kuenssberg’s next guest – to start going on about a “death and dementia tax”. Like clockwork. The Philpster becomes more and more a parody of himself. The Tory party’s very own Alan B’Stard. Venal, self-serving and not very bright. A man whose answer to everything is to cut the welfare bill still further, seemingly unaware his leader has already spent the cuts her party has proposed.
It’s as if Philp regards getting dementia as a personal failing, just as he sees being on benefits as morally deficient. If you get dementia then you deserve to pay for your own care. Now is not a good time to be one of Chris’s relatives. If you find yourself in need of care then you’re very much on your own. There’s no way the Philpster is missing out on his inheritance.

He won both Rejinagar and Nowda in the 2026 assembly elections but retained Nowda, leaving Rejinagar vacant.The BJP has fielded Sakharav Sarkar, while the TMC has nominated Rabiul Alam Chowdhury. Rebel TMC leader Ritabrata Banerjee's faction has fielded Safiuzzaman Sheikh. The Congress candidate is Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi and the CPM has nominated Syed Asad Ali. Kabir's AJUP has fielded his son, Ghulam Nabi Azad.
Rejinagar is a significant constituency in Murshidabad, which has a large Muslim population. Kabir's AJUP won the seat in the 2026 assembly elections, when he defeated BJP candidate Bapan Ghosh by a substantial margin.Kabir and Suvendu have also clashed repeatedly over political activities in the area. Kabir has previously warned against Suvendu's political activities in his constituency, while the chief minister has responded to his attacks.The latest remarks have taken their confrontation beyond political disagreements, with Kabir's references to the deaths of political leaders drawing a strong response from the BJP.The Rejinagar and Nandigram bypolls are scheduled for October 6, with counting set for October 9. The contests are being closely watched amid political realignments following the 2026 assembly elections.

AI giants probing tens of thousands of security incidents – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:13:47 UTC
00:13:47 KST

AI giants probing tens of thousands of security incidents – Axios
Global AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, along with security researchers, are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took actions that outside experts consider problematic, Axios reported on Saturday, citing unnamed sources.
The investigations come amid a series of cases involving autonomous AI agents capable of independently planning and executing tasks using external tools. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have all disclosed instances of their models accessing real-world systems during testing, including coordinated cyberattacks on government resources.
The incidents under investigation include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping ‘sandboxes’, hijacking websites, self-prompting, and attempting to evade monitors, sources told Axios. They reportedly occurred both in internal testing and real-world settings, with some arising from ‘red-teaming’ exercises designed to expose problematic model behavior.
Recent disclosures by major AI companies include several incidents involving their agents. On Friday, OpenAI said its agents posted 53 images uploaded by ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites and accessed publicly available information on US government websites. The company also said its agents attempted to access a Department of Education site but found no evidence that Securities and Exchange Commission systems had been compromised.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier this week that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the government health portal in June. On Saturday, The Guardian reported that Australia’s Senate invited OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to appear before an inquiry into AI and data centers.
The incidents follow OpenAI’s disclosure in July that models used in a cybersecurity evaluation escaped their sandbox, accessed the internet, and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure by exploiting vulnerabilities in the open-source machine-learning platform. Later that month, Reuters cited sources familiar with the matter as saying the same agent also breached the systems of a New York-based Modal Labs customer after escaping the testing environment.
In August, Axios cited OpenAI research and independent experts as saying that around 1,200 agents coordinated in an attack on Hugging Face. The agents reportedly appeared to know they were exceeding the test’s scope but continued without alerting human operators.
On Sunday, AP reported that OpenAI paused training of its latest models as reports of AI agents going rogue continued to mount.
Anthropic has also disclosed incidents involving Claude models, including four cases in which they gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. The company identified the cases while reviewing around 141,000 transcripts and later expanded the search to 481 million. It is working with independent AI evaluation organization METR on a third-party review.
Anthropic has also said its internal monitors flagged 100,000 agent transcripts for review each week in August, with around 50 escalated to human reviewers. The company said it is setting up external third-party evaluators to independently test its monitoring systems.

Jordanian Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Saleh Al-Kharabsheh speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Amman, Jordan, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Mohammad Abu Ghosh/Xinhua)
AMMAN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Jordan regards China as an important partner in its efforts to modernize the energy sector, given China's advanced expertise and broad technical and industrial capabilities in renewable energy, energy storage and smart grids, Jordanian Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Saleh Al-Kharabsheh has said.
Al-Kharabsheh, who accompanied Jordan's King Abdullah II during his visit to China in August, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that the visit provided an opportunity to see China's advances in technology, innovation and the energy sector, particularly in renewable energy, energy storage, smart grids and mining.
In the energy sector, the signing of a memorandum of understanding with China's National Energy Administration was an important step towards moving bilateral relations from general cooperation to more practical prospects, he said.
The memorandum covers opportunities for cooperation in national electricity grid modernization, energy storage, renewable energy, green hydrogen and green ammonia, as well as an integrated system of clean energy-related industries and services.
Al-Kharabsheh said the cooperation complements Jordanian-Chinese efforts on environmental protection and climate change, and is in line with the two countries' shared goal of building more sustainable, resource-efficient economies and reducing emissions.
He noted Jordan's new energy strategy focuses on developing and modernizing the energy sector, increasing the share of renewable energy, upgrading the electricity grid with battery storage technologies and artificial intelligence.
Cooperation with China can help attract high-quality investment to Jordan, develop new projects, create jobs and strengthen energy and mining industries and services, thereby increasing local added value and enhancing the competitiveness of the Jordanian economy, he added.
Al-Kharabsheh praised the contribution of Chinese companies to expanding Jordan's domestic energy supply, saying that cooperation with Chinese firms allows Jordan to draw on China's experience in developing smarter and more flexible power grids capable of efficiently meeting the growing demand for renewable electricity.
Chinese expertise and technology can also help improve energy efficiency, reduce losses, with positive effects on sectors including water, industry and transportation, he said.
"Jordanian-Chinese energy cooperation is not limited to meeting the Kingdom's energy needs. It can also be a driver of economic development, a platform for developing emerging industries, and an opportunity to strengthen Jordan's role as a regional hub for green energy and related services and technologies," he said.
Looking ahead, Al-Kharabsheh said Jordan sees significant opportunities for successful partnerships with Chinese companies and looks forward to expanding cooperation into broader areas, including technology, innovation and knowledge transfer, thereby helping to build local value chains.
The minister said the partnership between the two countries could serve as a model based on investment, technology transfer, capacity building and shared value creation, helping to advance the aspirations of both countries and lay a foundation for further development in Jordan-China relations. ■

NAIROBI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A senior United Nations official has called for pooled resources to address the deepening crisis in the Horn of Africa and the impending threat of El Nino.
Rein Paulsen, director of the Office of Emergencies and Resilience at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, said on Friday that while regional governments have prepared response plans, a severe funding shortfall threatens implementation.
"Plans are in place, and actions are already being taken, but we need more financing and support to deliver," Paulsen told journalists in Kenya's capital of Nairobi following a fact-finding mission to Sudan.
Of the 193 million U.S. dollars sought for FAO's Sudan emergency and resilience portfolio under its 2026-2028 Emergency Response Plan, only 44.1 million dollars has been received, Paulsen said.
Paulsen urged stakeholders not to view El Nino in isolation, but rather alongside ongoing conflicts and rising food prices across the region.
To help mitigate risks, he said that FAO and the World Food Program launched a joint anticipatory action plan on June 18 covering 22 priority countries in Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
He said the El Nino anticipatory action appeal seeks 202 million dollars to protect 8.8 million vulnerable people across 22 high-risk countries from extreme weather driven by El Nino.
"It is always more expensive to respond to a crisis than to mitigate its impact in advance," Paulsen emphasized, calling on governments, humanitarian agencies, and development partners to prioritize monitoring and early action.
He added that FAO is actively supporting Sudanese farmers by introducing drought-resistant seed varieties tailored to locally suitable climate zones, expanding irrigation to reduce dependence on rain-fed agriculture, launching nationwide livestock vaccination campaigns, and securing livestock feed and water supplies in building long-term resilience.
The World Meteorological Organization said in its latest update that El Nino is expected to strengthen to a very strong event, peaking towards the end of 2026, with a nearly 100 percent likelihood of persisting through February 2027. ■

Fresh shipment on Chancay-Shanghai route gets faster clearance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
23:07:47 CST
00:07:47 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Shanghai Customs on Sunday said a 12.2-tonne shipment of fresh blueberry imports became the first cargo covered by China-Peru bilateral regulatory mutual recognition on the Chancay-Shanghai maritime route.
The mutual recognition applies to supervision of cold-treatment probes for imported fruits. Cold treatment is a globally recognized phytosanitary measure. It uses sustained low temperatures to kill potential quarantine pests on fresh produce.
Under this mutual recognition framework, China and Peru accept each other's verification results for cold-treatment temperature probes fitted to Peruvian fruit consignments. The arrangement streamlines on-site checks after cargo arrives in China. It speeds up customs clearance and helps maintain berry freshness during long ocean voyages.
Launched in late 2024, the Chancay-Shanghai route slashed sea transit time between the two nations from 35-40 days to 23 days, cutting logistics costs by more than 20 percent.
Shanghai Port now handles more than 70 percent of China's fruit imports from Peru.
Under the bilateral protocol, Peruvian blueberries must undergo cold treatment for 15 to 22 days before arriving in China. Valid temperature probes must be placed at specified spots inside containers to ensure proper cold-treatment performance.
Shanghai Customs estimates that the new mutual-recognition deal will sharply shorten inspection time for imported cold-chain fresh fruits and reduce traders' overall expenses across clearance, logistics and warehousing.
In the first eight months of this year, the Chancay-Shanghai route recorded 170 voyages. These trips carried 141,000 tonnes of imports and exports worth 4.04 billion yuan (about 602 million U.S. dollars). Cargo volume rose 13.7 percent year on year, while cargo value jumped 33.3 percent. ■

Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:05:21 UTC
00:05:21 KST

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have required Switzerland to curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.
All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).
Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amid increasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.
Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’s decision to mirror EU sanctions against Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the UN.
The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2m francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign.
Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.
The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy”, leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate with Nato.
Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.
Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve, leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.
She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.
Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.
The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

====================================================================================================

There is no ethnic cleansing in Israel and the West Bank - this is why - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:02:57 UTC
00:02:57 KST

A recurring accusation promoted by the Palestinian Authority is that Israel has pursued a policy of “ethnic cleansing” and/or “genocide” against Palestinians and Israeli Arabs since 1948.
What was once largely a PA libel is now echoed by anti-Israel voices worldwide. At the UN General Assembly this week, UN Secretary-General António Guterres accused Israel of actions that he said risked “ethnic cleansing.”
In the film world, anti-Israel activists are similarly linking the film NAZA to what they describe as Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza.
However, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics recently published a chart showing the combined Palestinian and Israeli Arab population growth since 1914 within Israel, or what the PA calls “historic Palestine.”
The PA’s chart highlights the utter failure of Israel’s "ethnic cleansing policy."
From 1948 to 1967, the years that Jordan illegally occupied Judea and Samaria (aka the West Bank), the Arab population dropped 4.2 percent, from 1.42 million to 1.36m. That period of Jordanian rule is the only period on the chart since 1914 when the Arab population dropped.
Under Israeli rule of Judea and Samaria since the 1967 Six Day War, which brought the entire Arab population under Israeli administration, the Arab population started to skyrocket. Over the next 60 years, according to the PA, the Arab population grew from 1.36m. to 7.41m. today, a staggering 445% rise.
Evidence of ‘ethnic cleansing’: None
The PA’s statistical data demonstrates an “epic failure” of Israel’s “ethnic cleansing policy.”
The population growth experienced by Arabs living under Israel since 1967 isn’t just noteworthy – it’s unique. By comparison, Germany’s population grew from 78m. to 84m. from 1967 to 2026, a rise of 7.7%. Britain rose from 55.7m. to 69.6m., a 25% increase.
Even when comparing the growth to neighboring Arab states, the Arab population’s growth under Israel has been monumental. The population of Lebanon rose from 2.2m. to 5.8m. – a 164% rise. 
Syria’s population grew from 6.3m. to 24m., a 281% increase. No other Arab population grew 445% as did the Palestinians and Israeli Arabs under Israel.
There are many reasons for Israel’s “failed ethnic cleansing policy.” First, Israel imposed major changes in healthcare, including training Palestinian doctors to follow the standards of Israel’s healthcare system.
As a result, infant mortality dropped in Judea and Samaria from 152/1000 births before Israeli rule to 29/1000 under Israel by 1996.
Life expectancy for the Arabs of Judea and Samaria before Israeli rule was 48 years, while under Israel’s “ethnic cleansing,” it rose to 72 years by 1996, according to the UN.
Israel also introduced modern agricultural techniques to the Arab residents of the West Bank, like drip irrigation and other advanced Israeli farming methods. As a result, harvest yields surged, and Arabs in Judea and Samaria experienced an economic boom as early as the 1970s.
By any benchmark, Israel’s treatment of Israeli Arabs has been the worst ethnic cleansing failure. The Israeli Arab population has grown from 150,000 in 1948 to 2.15m. today – a 1,333% increase.
Israel’s Christian population is 5.4 times larger as well, as it grew from 35,000 to almost 190,000, a 443% growth, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics.
So, if Israel has a policy of ethnic cleansing, as claimed by the PA, it has been an utter failure. If Israel wants to persist in its so-called ethnic cleansing policy, it will have to look for new and better ways.
Fortunately, Israel does not have to reinvent the wheel. There are examples of highly successful ethnic cleansing by the Palestinians that Israel can learn from.
During the period between 1990 and 2005, when Israel handed the Gaza Strip to the Palestinian Authority in stages, until before Hamas’s Gaza war in 2023, estimates are that the Christian population dropped from approximately 3,000 to 1,000 – a 66% drop.
Looking at Bethlehem’s Christians, the PA had a similarly successful “ethnic cleansing.” Under Israeli rule, Christians in Bethlehem and the surrounding area made up 50% of the population. Since Israel handed Bethlehem over to the PA in 1994, the number of Christians has dropped to less than 10% of Bethlehem’s population.
Israel must now learn from its neighbor. If Israel ever wants to get its “ethnic cleansing policies” in order, it should stop everything that it’s been doing since 1967, which has caused exponential Arab growth.
Instead, Israel should echo the model used by the PA to “ethnically cleanse” Christians in Bethlehem since 1994, which caused them to drop to 10% of the population.
Now that’s ethnic cleansing.
The writer is the director of Palestinian Media Watch.

Iran is prepared for renewed fighting with the United States but remains open to diplomacy, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday after U.S. President Donald Trump publicly rejected Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” Araghchi said Iran had not yet received an official response through mediators despite Trump’s announcement that he had turned down the proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” Araghchi said when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Trump could seek to resume bombing after the U.S. midterm elections. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”
Iran presented the proposal this week through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Under the plan, Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore normal maritime traffic through the critical global oil route within seven days, alongside a return to negotiations with Washington. Recent reporting has also described the proposal as tied to conditions similar to those contained in the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding reached in June. CNN Transcripts
Trump said Saturday that he had rejected the proposal. “I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly.”
Araghchi, however, told moderator Kristen Welker that Trump’s rejection had not yet been formally communicated to Tehran through the countries mediating between the two sides.
The Iranian foreign minister said Tehran remained prepared to reopen the strait as part of a broader agreement ending the conflict. In return, he said, “we want our monies, our assets, which are illegally frozen, to be released. We want to be able to sell our oil.”
Araghchi described those conditions as “not new,” saying Washington had previously committed to them under the memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June. The arrangement collapsed within days after the sides exchanged fresh strikes.
“If you ask us, there is no reason why we should go back to diplomacy,” Araghchi said. “But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn’t miss any chance for peace.”
He also dismissed suggestions that Tehran’s calculations were being shaped by the approaching U.S. midterm elections.
“We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections,” he said. “We care about our national interests.”
Before Araghchi’s appearance, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz also spoke to “Meet the Press,” saying Washington rejected Tehran’s proposal for “a number of reasons.” Waltz is serving as the U.S. ambassador to the UN.
“I think this was a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable, to ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions, and access to billions in assets,” Waltz said.
Waltz also questioned “who’s calling the shots in Iran right now,” and accused Tehran of violating the previous memorandum of understanding by attacking international shipping.
“I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago,” Waltz said. “What I can tell you is the president will leave all options on the table to ensure the world is safe from Iran holding the world hostage with a nuclear weapon.”
Asked what kind of agreement Trump would be prepared to accept, Waltz declined to lay out terms.
“I’m not going to negotiate for the president.”
“This is about keeping the next generation safe from Iran threatening the world with a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump earlier this week said he was still weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran or reach an agreement, while publicly linking the timing of a possible deal to the November midterm elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
The confrontation with Iran has become an increasingly prominent issue in U.S. politics ahead of the November vote. Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly last week to defend his approach toward Iran and again said his administration would not allow Tehran to obtain a nuclear weapon.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim that the vehicle is a REMUS 600 and has been handed over to Iranian military experts "to retrieve its data," but the US military denies the claim. Top Iranian army commander says "the war is not over" and that it is now in "a critical and decisive stage".
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy claims to have intercepted a US underwater vehicle during a reconnaissance mission in the Strait of Hormuz, but the US military denied the Iranian claim shortly after.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it had seized the vessel following a "coordinated intelligence and electronic warfare operation". They further claim that the vehicle is a REMUS 600 and has been handed over to Iranian military experts "to retrieve its data".
According to Iranian media, REMUS 600 autonomous underwater vehicles are used by the US Navy and several NATO member states. They are relatively lightweight, modular systems compared with larger ocean-going submersibles.
Equipped with various sensors, cameras and advanced sonar systems, the vehicles are primarily designed for surveillance, seabed mapping, mine countermeasures and underwater inspections and can operate at depths of up to 600 metres.
The US CENTCOM, which coordinates US military operations in the Middle East, denied the Iranian claims shortly after. In a statement to Al Jazeera, CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the US has “positive control of all of our operational drone assets."
It is the second time in recent days that Tehran has claimed to have seized US underwater equipment.
On Tuesday, the IRGC announced that it had intercepted another autonomous underwater vehicle, identified as a Dive-LD manufactured by US defence company Anduril, near the entrance to the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. Washington has yet to publicly respond to that claim.
IRGC claims Strait of Hormuz is still closed
In the final part of its statement, the IRGC Navy reiterated Tehran's claim that "the Strait of Hormuz is closed", warning that its forces would confront any unauthorised passage or military activity in the waterway.
Also on Sunday, the commander in chief of Iran's army, Major General Amir Hatami, reaffirmed Iran's control and sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, saying that the waterway “is the strait of our honour, and we will not allow the enemies of the country to use this great logistical bottleneck.”
He also called on the Gulf countries once again to push US forces out of the region claiming that "security in the region will not happen except with the removal of the United States and the Zionist regime – and this is not far away.”
Hatami also said “the war is not over; we have won, but we must consolidate this victory, and the aggressor enemy, which has suffered severe blows, must still be ready to receive severe blows from the dear Iranian soldiers."
But US President Donald Trump told the US media on Sunday that oil prices will decrease “as soon as Iran gives up, as soon as the war is over, which will be soon”.

Israel cannot call itself a democracy while excluding Arabs from political power - opinion

As a child, I learned in synagogue that Israel is the “Holy Land.” Last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar all Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, from running in the upcoming elections.
I found myself asking: What makes a land holy if the people who share it are not treated as equals?
Israel has spent decades proudly calling itself the only democracy in the Middle East. Attempting to exclude the political representatives of Arab citizens, who make up roughly a fifth of Israeli society, is dangerous and fundamentally undemocratic.
The attorney-general’s office opposed disqualifying the Joint List and Ra’am because the evidence did not meet the legal threshold. The leaders of these parties have repeatedly condemned Hamas’ war crimes committed on October 7.
We need to bridge the divide
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has made tremendous strides toward bridging the gap between Jewish and Arab society in Israel. Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former senior Israeli Police commander, is running second on Ra’am’s list. Demanding full equality and opposing military occupation should not place anyone outside legitimate political life. Arab citizens have the same right as Jewish citizens to elect representatives who express their convictions and aspirations. When political legitimacy depends on ethnic or national identity, political inequality reflects a society’s deep-rooted racism.
This matters especially now because the debate over Arab participation extends well beyond the Central Elections Committee. It concerns who will help shape Israel’s future and whether Israelis and Palestinians will be able to live in peace and security.
For Israelis and Palestinians to end the cycle of killing, fear, and revenge, Arab citizens of Israel and their political leaders can help build trust and serve as bridges between Jewish Israeli society and Palestinian society.

Learning to share power inside Israel builds the trust and habits of cooperation needed for reconciliation beyond its borders. Ra’am and the Joint List must be free to run in the upcoming elections. Jewish-Arab partnership must be a foundation of the next government.
The day will come when asking whether an Israeli government can include Arab parties will sound as strange as asking whether the president of the United States can be Black. Our responsibility is to help bring that day closer.
Jews and Arabs did not choose the national identities into which we were born; however, we can choose to live in the Holy Land as equals.

EU Commission calls on countries to cut energy demands as costs surge
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen asked ministers to introduce new measures “in the context of constrained global supply.”
The European Commission has told capitals to reduce demand for gas and electricity in a bid to tame prices amid a global energy crunch.
"In the context of constrained global supply and high price volatility, demand reduction can be an effective tool to contain prices," EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen wrote in a letter to EU ministers, dated Sept. 25 and seen by POLITICO.
In the letter, Jørgensen invites ministers to take measures to reduce demand for gas and electricity "for as long as necessary." He argues that while the situation is "challenging", there are "currently no immediate risks to security of supply."
Advertisement
Gas storage levels in Europe are currently at historic lows as the war in Iran disrupts global gas flows, which could set up the continent for an expensive winter.
Storage levels currently sit at 68% of capacity, which is well below the 71% measured at the same period in 2021 — just before the start of a historic energy crisis in the wake of Covid-19 and the start of the war in Ukraine.
The EU has a baseline target to have gas storage filled to 90% by the start of November, but some flexibility was granted on this in March, allowing countries to aim for 80% this year to avoid panic buying and alleviate costs.
Measures taken by EU countries to regulate prices should be "well-targeted" and "temporary", Jørgensen's letter reads, to avoid a surge in demand.
