Serbia's politicians return to TV debates ahead of parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:58:18 UTC
23:58:18 KST

A month before the early parliamentary elections, Serbia's high ranking politicians from the ruling and opposition parties engaged in a debate on the N1 channel after a prolonged boycott between the anti-government station and officials. The ownership change provided a new opportunity for dialogue.
For the first time in nearly a decade, a Serbian media hosted a televised election debate with opposing politicians which drew significant public attention ahead of the 25 October parliamentary vote, in Serbia's highly polarised media and tense society landscape. Equally for the first time, a top official from the ruling Serbian Progressive Party appeared on N1 television in a live election debate.
Ana Brnabic, Speaker of the outgoing parliament and a former prime minister, as well as top figure in Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic's political camp, faced the top candidate of the opposition Student List - Students win political platform and Dean of the Arts University in Belgrade, Mirjana Nikolic.
The two contenders agreed to appear together live, but not without hesitations, and engaged in a fiery one-on-one debate, confronting their views on education, the chosen theme of the debate, before descending into the wider Serbian society turmoil and political conflict.
The N1 televised debate was the most watched programme during its time slot, with a rating of over 48 points, and the most followed television show of the past month.
The N1 host invited them to present their programmes, but the contenders went into trading accusations of violence, mismanagement and intolerance which matched the heated national political discourse as the country is gearing up for early elections called after months of demonstrations and protests which led to violent incidents.
Triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station in November 2024 which killed 16 people, the protests were started by students who blocked state universities for a prolonged period of time before spreading across the country. The protesters blamed the tragedy on corruption and mismanagement. Eventually, the ad-hoc student movement registered their political list for the elections and are now seen by part of the public and by most pollsters as the main challengers to president Vucic’s rule.
The political tension was obvious even before the TV debate started, with Brnabic declaring that Nikolic would not even shake her hand when they met in the studio.
“You are constantly offending me, starting from your refusal to shake my hand. I consider that to be a basic human gesture. Generals are at war with each other and still shake hands,” Brnabic said.
She asked her contender if “is that your decent Serbia?,” to which Nikolic fired back saying “decent Serbia is yet to come.”
The intense buzz around the debate
The debate sparked surprise and stirred significant interest in Serbia as government officials have largely avoided the N1 channel throughout multiple election cycles, claiming negative bias, a qualification N1 rejected.
At the same time, not many expected such a programme to happen at all as real debates by political opponents are rare in Serbia, with the media openly supporting one political camp or the other and thus rarely inviting politicians or activists across the partisan lines. In turn, politicians rarely agree to take part in programmes at channels they deem to be hostile and combative.
Therefore, the debate surprised Serbia and, moreover, that it was hosted by N1 television whose editorial policy has so far been seen as consistently and openly anti-Vucic. Viewers have not seen government or ruling party officials on N1 since at least 2017.
Ana Brnabic, who is in third position on Vucic's United Serbia electoral list, said she has not been on N1 since 2017, stating that “in previous election campaigns N1 would not even allow us to have paid promo clips (in their programme), that is how objective you were."
"I wasn’t thrilled about coming now either, remembering how your television tried to dehumanise my friend and my president. You criminalised him. I could hear in your programme that he was the product of a viper’s nest,” Brnabic said.
She then explained why she eventually accepted the N1 debate invitation, saying “I came because Aleksandar Vucic insisted. You changed your owner and the man said let’s give them a chance, let the people see how unbiased you are.”
Brnabic referred to N1 television recently changing its ownership. Alpac Capital, a Portuguese private equity and venture capital investment firm, which also owns Euronews, acquired the ownership of the channel as part of a wider regional media acquisition. Alpac promised the media's business transformation and no direct influence on the editorial decisions other than the request for a professional, unbiased, objective and fair reporting.
Viewers and politicians alike therefore watched the debate as a test and as one of many to come in the month leading to the elections as the channel said it would organise further thematic debates in the run-up to voting day.
The representative of the opposition in the debate, Mirjana Nikolic, said she was also skeptical about the odds that the debate could happen when "the invitation came through regular channels, straight from the media."
Nikolic said she wondered whether the debate was indeed an opportunity and "whether it was the right moment to take part in this debate," explaining that she did not know "whether their (the channel) concept would allow for the other side to come."
"I was fearful because recently it became unpleasant to talk to someone who comes from the position of power," Nikolic went further, adding that "Ms. Brnabic has the advantage of having all the information at her disposal. Also, our recent meeting at the parliamentary committee for education was full of shouting, stomping and humiliating opponents, so there’s a danger in that.”
Heated exchanges between the two contenders
After a botched handshake attempt at the start of the debate, the contenders engaged in a series of heated exchanges, multiple accusations and both sides claiming they were offended. They sifted through the incidents of recent months, including the beaten students and the disruptions across Serbia.
Brnabic criticised the students protests, the university blockades and the Students List political platform, while Nikolic argued that voters deserved to hear and the proposals of the other electoral lists for education and the country's youth.
Ana Brnabic hailed the government's achievements on education, saying that the education budget has been increased more than threefold since 2012, from 140 billion dinars (over 1 billion Euros) to 425 billion (3.6 billion Euros). She added that the percentage of children going to pre-school increased from 48 to 64% and that four science and technology parks were built alongside investments in digitalisation.
“Teacher’s salary went up from 391 euro in 2012 to 1,030 euro by December 2026. That is 2.6 times higher. University professors earned 77,000 dinars (655 Euros) in 2012 and by the end of this year they will earn 191,000 dinars (1,600 Euros). That is 2.5 times increase. This is what we did for their dignity and their living standard, to thank them for all they did,” said Brnabic.
Nikolic countered that figures are not for television and that they can be misleading as it is uncertain that the teachers, despite the increases, can buy what they could in 2012.
“We want dignity, professionalism and safety. In the complex of ideas we stand for, free education in the absolute frontrunner. We stand for free education, not as a populist phrase “free school books”, but for truly free education in all its aspects,” said Nikolic.
She ended by telling Brnabic that she "failed the exam".
The debate ignited Serbian social media, with many commenting its novelty, the nature of the debate and its takeaways as well as the performances and the punches by the two contenders, with both camps declaring victory. Some doubted it as an intermittent democratic exercise or its concrete conclusions, while others said that the N1 debate could now signal an improvement in Serbia's polarised media landscape and its culture of dialogue.
Disclaimer: Euronews is owned by Alpac Capital, the same investment firm mentioned in this article as the new owner of N1 television.

Swiss voters overwhelmingly reject initiative to enshrine stricter neutrality rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:57:36 UTC
23:57:36 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Swiss voters on Sunday roundly rejected an initiative seeking to enshrine stricter neutrality rules in the country's Constitution, according to official results.
 
Official results showed 70.15% voting against the "Safeguard Swiss neutrality" initiative, while just 29.85% backed it.
 
Results broken down by the country’s cantons – which played a role in the overall vote – mirrored the rejection, as "no" votes led in all 26 of Switzerland's cantons.
 
To pass, the initiative had to secure a majority of both voters nationwide and Swiss cantons.
 
The rejection reached over 70% in cantons such as the capital Bern and Zurich, as well as Basel Landschaft, Jura, Lucerne, Solothurn, Vaud, Neuchatel, and Zug, while results were closer in some, such as Ticino, where the opposition stood at 51.75%
 
Voter turnout for the referendum was at 47.06%.
 
 
 
- Neutrality yesterday, today, and tomorrow: Foreign minister
 
Evaluating the outcome of the neutrality vote, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis welcomed the nation retaining its maneuvering room, particularly amid an increasingly uncertain global geopolitical landscape.
 
"Swiss women and men have chosen a neutrality that has proven its worth," he said on US social media platform X. "Switzerland maintains its maneuvering room to protect its security, its independence, and its prosperity."
 
At a later press briefing, he said that the result was "not a vote against neutrality," adding that Switzerland "was neutral yesterday, is neutral today, and will remain neutral in the future."
 
"The world is unpredictable. Every war, every crisis, every threat is different," Cassis said, arguing that Switzerland must retain the ability to assess each situation individually.
 
He pointed to Bern's 2022 decision to largely adopt EU sanctions against Russia following the start of the war on Ukraine, saying the government can continue deciding case by case whether economic sanctions serve Switzerland's interests.
 
"Being neutral does not mean being indifferent. Nor does it mean standing aside," he added, stressing Switzerland's role in facilitating dialogue between states in conflict.
 
 
 
- Food initiative also rejected by voters
 
The initiative sought to enshrine "perpetual and armed" neutrality in the Constitution and restrict Switzerland from cooperating with military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, except for UN sanctions and measures.
 
The Federal Council and parliament opposed the initiative, arguing that it would restrict Switzerland's maneuvering room in protecting its security, independence, and prosperity.
 
Supporters argued that constitutional safeguards were needed to protect the country's neutrality from external pressure and preserve its credibility as a mediator and provider of good offices.
 
Voters also decisively rejected a food initiative, with 72.52% voting against and 27.48% in favor.
 
The initiative sought to strengthen sustainable domestic production, promote more plant-based foods, and protect clean drinking water.
 
Addressing the rejection of the food initiative, Swiss President Guy Parmelin told the same press briefing that Switzerland must ensure its food security "in an increasingly uncertain international context."
 
He said the rejection "does not mean that nothing needs to change," stressing that the country's agri-food system must continue evolving to strengthen its resilience, protect natural resources, and prepare for future crises.

Ukraine hits five workshops at a Russian military plant in Rostov Oblast – OSINT
At least five workshops have been damaged following an attack by the Ukrainian defence forces on the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant military facility in the Rostov Oblast in Russia.
Source: Absolutely Reliable Source OSINT project on Telegram
Details: Damaged buildings at the plant are used at various stages of production for components supplied to Russian weaponry. In particular, strikes were recorded at foundry workshop No. 022, which consists of two buildings.
Quote: "The lower building (the main one for the foundry workshop) experienced burning and significant damage in both its right section and its eastern side. The upper building was also affected, but only a portion of the roof and wall was torn down."
At workshop No. 008, which handles optics manufacturing, analysts recorded two strikes on the southwestern side along with a crumbling façade.
At least three strikes were registered at assembly workshop No. 009, with another hit recorded at electroplating workshop No. 010.
According to information from the Absolutely Reliable Source project, two more strikes were recorded at the machining workshop, one of which caused a roof collapse. In the images published by the analysts, it is located on the right.
Quote: "To its left is the frame-stamping workshop, next to which lies debris – a wall hit is likely there as well."
Details: Ukrainian defence forces attacked the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant on the night of 25-26 September. The strike was carried out by units of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Navy using Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles, as well as Ruta, Palianytsia and Bars jet-powered drone missiles. Military officials previously reported damage to optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly section, an electroplating workshop and a printed circuit board manufacturing workshop.
For reference: The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of the Russian Tactical Missiles Corporation. The company manufactures electronic systems for high-precision artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, radar homing heads for tactical guided missiles, on-board thermal imaging and thermal imaging equipment, as well as optical-mechanical and optoelectronic products, according to the "War&Sanctions" website by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
The plant in Rostov Oblast is currently under sanctions imposed by the US, Canada, Switzerland, the EU, New Zealand, Japan and Ukraine.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that on 25 September, Ukraine's defence forces struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.
- Ukrainian forces also damaged five launch units for Shahed drones near Tsimbulova in Russia's Oryol Oblast.

But when you see all the destruction in just one active website, it really broke my heart," Abed told The New Arab. "I couldn't even bear continuing looking at that because seeing the place where I grew up, seeing the place where I was born, lined in ruins in that way was absolutely heart shattering."
Google Maps has been updated to show Zionist-holocausted Gaza. This is part of Rafah. pic.twitter.com/Ys7KQNsu5w
— Ali Abunimah (@AliAbunimah) September 26, 2026
The imagery around Al-Shifa Hospital, once Gaza’s largest medical complex, shows extensive destruction at and around the site. Israeli forces withdrew from the hospital on 1 April 2024 after a two-week siege. A World Health Organization mission that reached it days later described an "empty shell" and reported extensive damage to its emergency, surgical and maternity buildings.
"What I was most struck by is that every place that I used to visit before the genocide was a mountain of rubble, and heaps of rubble are everywhere", Abed said, referring to the paths he followed on Google Maps.
Along the coast, tightly packed rows of makeshift shelters form another striking feature of the satellite views. Some encampments stretch across broad areas of land, showing how displacement has altered the landscape as well as the lives of those forced from their homes.
google maps' satellite view now shows Gaza post carpet bombing https://t.co/fxfahLMjbH pic.twitter.com/6N3Urg0AAJ
— Zavain Dar (@zavaindar) September 26, 2026
A UN report published on 24 September estimated that around 1.9 million people in Gaza had been displaced, many repeatedly, and that more than 60 percent of the population had lost their homes. The Palestine Shelter Cluster said earlier this month that around two-thirds of households were living in tents or makeshift shelters.
The damage visible on the map reflects the scale recorded by UN assessments. UN Trade and Development estimated on 24 September that Gaza needs $71.5 billion for recovery and reconstruction, and said 92 percent of its economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed since October 2023. An assessment released in April by the UN and European Union, conducted with the World Bank, recorded more than 371,888 housing units damaged or destroyed.
"People right now can see the destruction themselves - they don't even need to go to Gaza, they can see what happened to Gaza which is obvipously genocide," Abed told The New Arab. "It doesn't need scholars, it doesn't need anyone to justify this as a genocide because you can see it from the Google Maps."
Israel’s war has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since October 2023, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Users sharing the images have said Google Maps has recently updated its satellite view of Gaza. The New Arab has not independently established when the images were recently captured or added to the platform, or which areas may have changed in a recent update. The New Arab has contacted Google for comment.
Google has itself faced accusations of complicity in Israel’s genocide through the provision of cloud and artificial intelligence technology.
In a June 2025 report, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese named Google’s parent company Alphabet, as well as Amazon, in connection with Project Nimbus, a $1.2 billion cloud contract with Israel. Her report argued that technology firms providing such infrastructure were part of an economy sustaining Israel’s occupation and assault on Gaza.

Sunken Russian Military Tug Kapitan Ushakov Raised in St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:40 UTC
23:47:40 KST

More than a year after it sank, the Russian military tug Kapitan Ushakov, designed for Arctic operations, has been raised in St. Petersburg.
Navy Of Russia, a Russian specialized media outlet, reported this.
According to it, the vessel is expected to be sent to the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant for a major overhaul, including replacement of the propulsion system, reconstruction of the hull and refurbishment of life-support systems.
However, given the vessel’s prolonged submersion and the need to replace all cabling, electronics and machinery and carry out a major hull overhaul, it may not return to service because of the cost of repairs.
Project 23470 sea tugs are designed to tow vessels, floating objects, and structures in seas and oceans, with no restrictions on their operating area.
Key specifications:
The tugs can operate in ice conditions under the Arc4 ice class. They are also designed for search-and-rescue operations, firefighting, and other tasks.
The Project 23470 sea tug Kapitan Ushakov was launched in 2022 at the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant and transferred to St. Petersburg in autumn 2023 for completion at a berth of the Baltic Shipyard. The tug was being prepared for operations along the Northern Sea Route.
On the evening of August 8, 2025, the vessel began to list. Workers spent the night trying to stop the list, but on the morning of August 9, the tug listed to starboard and partially sank. According to Russian investigators, water entered the auxiliary machinery compartment.
In August, the port administration gave three months to remove the sunken tug from the Neva. The vessel was not raised within that deadline.
According to PortNews, work was delayed in November 2025 because of financial problems at the owner, the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant. Active preparations to raise the vessel began only in May 2026, about nine months after the accident.
On June 24, contractor Baltspecflot told Kommersant that it had reinforced the shoreline and begun pulling the tug out using towing equipment. As of the morning of June 25, the hull had already been partially raised, but the vessel was still listing heavily.
The vessel was reported to have been fully raised on July 18. However, photos published at the time showed the vessel still listing to one side. It was then planned to inspect the vessel over two weeks to one month. The plant was to coordinate further action with the customer, the Russian Defense Ministry.

Swiss voters reject tighter neutrality rules that would have curbed NATO cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:33 UTC
23:47:33 KST

Swiss voters on Sunday firmly rejected a proposal to adopt a more restrictive form of neutrality that would have blocked their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
More than two-thirds voted against a proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, according to the latest referendum projections by state broadcaster SRF.
Having failed to win the required support of the majority of Switzerland's cantonal constituencies, the initiative has effectively been rejected.
While Swiss neutrality has been internationally recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815, how the government implements it is not spelled out.
The right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) has said that Switzerland's traditional position has been eroded after Bern imposed sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
The campaign had funded posters across the country urging people to vote "No war, yes to neutrality," featuring white peace doves, ahead of the vote.
Swiss government, most parties oppose proposal
Apart from the SVP, most parties and the Swiss government oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national security and prevent Switzerland from training with NATO.
The Green Party and the smaller Evangelical People's Party (EVP) expressed relief over Sunday's projections.
"Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on," said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green Party.
The SVP meanwhile accepted the defeat and said it currently had no plans for further action.
"I'm of course not pleased with the result," said SVP lawmaker Lukas Reimann, adding that the commitment to Swiss neutrality expressed by all sides during the campaign was encouraging.
"It is absolutely clear that neutrality belongs to Switzerland and is part of Switzerland's identity," he said. "Going forward, we will judge the opponents of the initiative by that commitment."
If the government or opponents of the initiative were to stray from neutrality, for example by adopting tougher sanctions, the party would need to become active again, Reimann said.
'Swiss voters like neutrality'
Fabio Wasserfallen, a professor of European politics at the University of Bern, said before the vote: "Swiss voters like neutrality, but they approve of how the government is implementing it at present."
"They are also generally in favor of the sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, and don't want that to change."
The campaign wanted the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defense alliance unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
It says Swiss neutrality has served the country well in the past, keeping it out of both world wars, and also helps Bern offer its 'good offices' to help negotiate peace between warring parties.
"Switzerland has not had a war for 200 years because it is permanently armed and neutral," Christoph Blocher, the billionaire businessman and backer of the SVP, said ahead of the vote.
"But neutrality has been followed less and less in recent years," he told Reuters, with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions.

Christa Pike set to be first Tennessee woman executed in 200 years, lawyers ask Gov. Lee for mercy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:32 UTC
23:47:32 KST

Christa Pike is set to be the first woman executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years for her involvement in the murder of a 19-year-old in 1995.
Her lawyers and loved ones, however, say that if she committed the same crime today, she would not be on death row.
If her execution goes through, she will be the first woman since 1819 to be put to death in Tennessee.
Notably, only 17 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, whereas 1,663 men have been put to death under the death penalty, the BBC reported.
The murder case of Colleen Slemmer
Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed Colleen Slemmer, whom the pair met at a job camp for troubled teenagers.
Slemmer’s body was found on the University of Tennessee’s Agricultural campus in Knoxville with a pentagram carved into her chest and her head bludgeoned.
Court records showed that Pike and Shipp, along with their friend, Shadolla Peterson, lured Slemmer to a remote part of the campus before torturing her and beating her to death.
Pike reportedly took a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Pike was sentenced to death for the murder, but Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was given a life sentence without the possibility of parole.
Pike has a history of childhood sexual abuse and neglect that her lawyers claim were not considered in the initial sentencing, the BBC reported on Saturday.
"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," Sandra Babcock, a lawyer who worked on Pike’s defense and an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, told the BBC.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."
Christa Pike's childhood sexual assaults, abuse
Since the sentencing, Pike’s defense uncovered proof that she was sexually and physically abused by her mother’s boyfriends and husbands throughout her teenage years. In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr. Diana McCoy, who was hired by Pike’s team, found that Pike was raped when she was 11 and 17 by two of them. She was also repeatedly raped by her grandmother’s boyfriend when she was a toddler.
Her aunt testified in court that her mother routinely let her crawl through filthy, dog-feces-littered floors. Court documents showed that Pike attempted suicide when she was 12 years old.
She was later diagnosed with manic depression, also known as bipolar disorder, in 2021.
Pike’s lawyer during the trial did not call McCoy to testify or call any of the witnesses she recommended, the BBC reported. Her findings about Pike’s background came to light over 10 years later during a review of her case. A new team of lawyers argued that Pike received ineffective assistance of counsel, which the judge denied.
“If someone would have stepped in at age 5, if someone would have stepped in at age 7, if someone would have stepped in at age 11, if anyone would have done anything to help me, to get me psychological help or anything, maybe something would have been different,” Pike said in a recent documentary about her case, Dead Woman Walking: Pike Vs Tennessee.
She also said in the documentary that she regretted her actions and felt remorse.
“I’ve always felt bad for her mother, that I took someone’s child, someone’s sister, someone’s friend away,” Pike said in the documentary. “I feel remarkably remorseful for what I did.”
Still, her victim’s mother, May Martinez, says she thinks that Pike should suffer for her actions.
"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she told Knoxville station WBIR in 2021.
"I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did. My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.
"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."
She told the BBC that she stands by the statements.
Her attorneys are now asking Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life without parole, and have sought relief from the state’s Supreme Court as well as the federal court.
On Tuesday, the Tennessee Supreme Court rejected Pike’s lawyers' challenge that lethal injection would be considered cruel and unusual punishment for Pike, who has thrombocytosis, a bone marrow disorder characterized by an overproduction of blood platelets. Medical experts on the case argued that her condition would cause her to essentially drown in her own blood during her execution, Nashville’s WTVF reported.
Teen killer Christa Pike to be executed on Wednesday
Because of her trauma, Pike has requested an all-female team for her execution. She said that being held down by a team of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state has not guaranteed her request, but said that a team of female guards will transfer her to the prison where she will be executed.
On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
"If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke,” Babcock told the BBC.
“It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable,” Babcock said.

An Ohio hospital is being sued by the US government for firing a surgeon for “being Jewish,” according a lawsuit filed last week.
The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a lawsuit against Mercy Health in Youngstown, claiming a violation of federal law by subjecting a Jewish orthopedic surgeon to unfavorable terms and conditions of employment and “firing him because of his religion and race, shortly after the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel.”
The surgeon – named in other media as Dr. Ian Walton – had a successful practice with Mercy for many years and performed well, “including exceeding Mercy’s productivity goals”, the lawsuit claimed.
However, Mercy reportedly subjected Walton to antisemitic remarks throughout his employment and ultimately fired him in November 2023, advising him that he was “being terminated for a reason other than work performance.”
“After years of antisemitic harassment, shortly after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the charging party faced a barrage of comments in the workplace blaming ‘the Jews’ for the attack,” said EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas.
EEOC attempted to reach a settlement before filing the lawsuit
Lucas also said Walton was excluded from scheduled meetings and had his surgery time blocks reduced. Shortly thereafter, his contract was terminated.
“The EEOC will not hesitate to bring litigation to protect Jewish workers from unlawful discrimination and ensure they do not face adverse action simply because they are Jewish. Antisemitism has no place in the American workplace,” Lucas added.
This alleged conduct violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on religion and race. The EEOC filed suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Ohio after first attempting to reach a pre-litigation settlement through its administrative conciliation process.
Walton’s Jewish identity was not a secret at his workplace. The lawsuit said that he had family photographs in his office depicting relatives wearing kippot and prayer shawls.

Israeli passengers stopped, searched at Dutch airport as West Bank import crackdown begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:20 UTC
23:47:20 KST

The Netherlands has begun enforcing its strict crackdown on the import of goods from Israeli settlements, with passengers reporting thorough bag checks at Schiphol Airport.
As of September 22, 2026, the Netherlands officially enacted the sanction decision on settlements in the West Bank, the Golan Heights, and east Jerusalem.
The ban extends to all imported goods, including travelers' personal luggage and souvenirs. Those found to have adjusted origin labels will also be penalized.
The prohibition additionally applies to goods that are only partially made or produced in the settlements (i.e. if one ingredient is from the area, even if the product was predominantly made in, say, Tel Aviv).
The date of purchase of the product has no bearing on the penalty, meaning the law is effectively backdated to all purchases prior to its implementation.
Penalty for violating sanctions could result in six-year imprisonment
Under the new law, intentional violation or circumvention of the rules is punishable by up to six years' imprisonment or a significant fine.
Unintentional violations can carry a prison sentence of up to one year.
According to conservative news site Nieuwsrecht, the day after the ban came into effect, travelers arriving at Schiphol from Tel Aviv walked past customs through the “Nothing to declare” lane when a customs officer asked: “Are you coming from Tel Aviv? Yes? Everyone from Israel, come over here!”
Nieuwsrecht said all El Al passengers were made to put their luggage through a screening machine.
The news site later learned that a unit of the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee has been assigned to carry out additional checks on passengers arriving on flights from Israel at the national airport to determine whether they are carrying wine, dates, olives, or other products brought from East Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Golan.
Posters listing prohibited items have now also been distributed.
Nieuwsrecht called it a "witch hunt."
Customs in the Netherlands did not respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment by the time of publication.

Ben-Gurion Airport parking lots full as holiday travel surge leaves passengers seeking alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:05 UTC
23:47:05 KST

Passengers planning to fly in the coming days and leave their vehicles at Ben-Gurion Airport will need to find another solution, as all airport parking lots are currently full, the Israel Airports Authority said on Sunday.
According to the authority, the number of passengers increased significantly during the High Holy Days, resulting in all airport parking facilities reaching full capacity with no available spaces. The authority asked travelers and their companions not to arrive in private vehicles and instead use public transportation. The situation will continue until further notice, IAA noted.
Parking shortage returns during peak travel periods
This is not the first time the airport’s parking lots have reached capacity. In August, on a day when around 101,000 passengers passed through Ben-Gurion Airport, the authority announced that the "Kerem" and "Pardes" parking lots were completely full and directed passengers to other lots.
That situation occurred during the peak of the summer travel season, while the current shortage comes during the peak holiday period, meaning both were times when heavy traffic was expected in advance. Despite this, passengers traveling to the airport cannot reserve a parking space in advance.
The long-term parking lot does not offer advance reservations, and vehicles can only enter if space is available. Travelers leaving home do not know whether they will find parking until they arrive at the airport.
The alternative suggested by the authority, public transportation, is also limited. The train is the fastest way to reach the airport, but its schedule changes during holidays. During Rosh Hashanah, for example, trains operated between Herzliya and Jerusalem and did not reach Ben-Gurion Airport. On weekends and holidays, train service does not operate at all.
Public transportation options remain limited
The Airports Authority said last year that exceptional congestion at the airport was mainly caused by traffic jams and the lack of train service on weekends. When trains are not operating, passengers are largely left with Egged’s 485 bus line, which runs 24 hours a day between Tel Aviv’s Central Bus Station and Ben-Gurion Airport, including on Saturdays. The line serves only one area.
Taxis have also failed to solve the problem. Passengers who landed at Ben-Gurion Airport in recent days reported long taxi lines, confrontations between travelers and drivers, and a severe shortage of available cabs. Drivers said that many prefer to work within the city rather than travel to the airport because fares and regulations have, in their view, made airport trips financially unattractive.
As a result, the authority is asking passengers to avoid private vehicles at precisely the time when alternative transportation options are most limited. Anyone who still needs to reach the airport in the coming days should check train schedules in advance and leave home with significantly more time than usual.

New Vivaldi tactic: Ukraine’s ground robots, each carrying two Bullspike grenade launchers, attack Russian positions and then detonate inside their shelters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:43:15 UTC
23:43:15 KST

Ukraine has employed a new tactic during its major Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk Oblast. During the 3rd Army Corps' offensive, fighters from the world's first experimental unit of unmanned ground-strike vehicles, "NC13", have upgraded their kamikaze ground drones with grenade launchers.
Vivaldi is the counteroffensive the corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast. Over its first two "seasons," the 3rd Army Corps and attached units have retaken more than 125 square kilometers, half of it de-occupied outright, and inflicted more than 3,000 casualties on Russian forces.
Through this offensive operation, the 3rd Army Corps, commanded by Brigadier General Andrii Biletsky, disrupted Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014.
From intensive training to the world-first operations
The NC13 unit has been through Bakhmut, Avdiivka, and other of the toughest sections of the front.
Among its achievements: the world's first robotic assault carried out without infantry involvement, resulting in the capture of two Russian soldiers, a sabotage operation in the enemy's rear — blowing up a crossing and disrupting an offensive — using UGVs alone, and Ukraine's first fully robotic defense of a position for 45 days without involving infantry.
"No one in the history of warfare has used this kind of tactic before," the soldiers commented on the offensive.
The defenders say that a lack of combat experience is no barrier to joining the unit. Every recruit goes through an intensive training course led by experienced instructors.
Grenade launchers were developed based on the Soviet RPG-22
During the operation, UGVs equipped with two Bullspike grenade launchers attacked Russian positions, then detonated directly inside their shelters. The occupiers believed they were being attacked by an entire assault group. In reality, they were being torn apart by robots from the 3rd Assault Corps.
"Yes, the UGVs carry out three tasks at once: they strike, they exert psychological pressure, and they clear the position. And most importantly, this happens without risk to our infantry," the force says.
The Bullspike grenade launchers were developed based on the Soviet RPG-22 anti-tank grenade launcher, which was previously manufactured under license by a Bulgarian defense company.
According to data from the manufacturer's website, the Bullspike RPG has a maximum aimed firing range of 350 meters, a direct-fire range of 150 meters, and armor penetration of 400 mm, Militarnyi reports.
The total weight of the launch unit, together with the 72.5 mm PG-22 grenade, is 3.4 kg. The length of the launcher is 780 mm.
The manufacturer states that the Bullspike-AT round is designed to destroy tanks, self-propelled artillery, and other armored vehicles, as well as to target enemy personnel located in bunkers, field fortifications, and urban-type brick fortifications.
The robots were controlled by operators from a safe shelter dozens of kilometers from the line of contact.
Earlier, for the first time in the world's history, the 3rd Army Corps dropped ground robots behind Russian lines from the air. The soldiers behind the mission say their heavy drones delivered kamikaze unmanned ground vehicles more than 10 kilometers into the Russian rear during the "second season" of Operation Vivaldi, letting Ukrainian troops flank them and clear another 40 square kilometers.

Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27

23:36:44 KST

Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
There are fears that fighting between the US and Iran will renew, after President Trump rejected a deal for the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran, Iran – Hours after US President Donald Trump rejected a diplomatic solution put forward by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, explosions were heard in the waterway, according to Iranian media.
Reports of blasts near southern Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz suggested that multiple antiship missiles and drones were fired at vessels transiting the waterway against Tehran’s wishes.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
- list 2 of 4Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Yemen government forces widen attacks against Houthis: What we know
- list 4 of 4‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
While Iranian authorities did not confirm any attacks in the Strait of Hormuz that day, shipping continues to be attacked in the waters, including an Indian cargo ship last week, which killed a sailor.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) maintains that the strait is closed to any ship that does not coordinate with Iranian authorities. On Sunday afternoon, it released video of what it said was a second US underwater drone seized this month.
Tehran has issued instructions to shipping companies transiting the Strait of Hormuz to use a temporary route approved by Iranian authorities and pay relevant fees. But it has also said the strait will not fully reopen until the US blockade on Iranian ports ends.
Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority announced on Saturday that it would blacklist any shipping charterer company which orders crews to use routes it considers to be unauthorised.
It also published what it described as an apology from an unnamed shipowner blaming commercial pressure from its charterer for trying to pass through the strait.
Washington still insists that its warships are successfully guiding oil tankers out of the strait via a different route. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News on Sunday that the “running average” of crude oil in transit was nearly 13 million barrels per day.
A September 19 operational update by US Central Command claimed that its forces had helped move more than one billion barrels of crude out of the Gulf over roughly two months.
The US military also says its forces have redirected 122 commercial vessels to enforce the naval blockade of Iran’s ports, halting all Iranian crude exports.
Tehran has claimed that the US is providing false information regarding Strait of Hormuz traffic to project control over the key waterway. Shipping has been severely disrupted since the US and Israel started their war on Iran on February 28.
Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, said Iran’s strategy of launching maritime attacks has spread the economic costs of the conflict beyond its borders.
While Iran has suffered economically from war damages, the US naval blockade and sanctions, it would be a mistake “to assume that reaching that threshold produces submission”.
“The next Iranian move is therefore likely to be an attempt to increase the pain experienced by the Gulf rather than simply absorb further American pressure,” Krieg said.
“That could mean more aggressive vessel interdictions in Hormuz, attacks on energy infrastructure, greater Houthi pressure around Bab al-Mandeb and pressure from Iranian-aligned groups against alternative Saudi export routes. We are already seeing how pressure on Hormuz, the Red Sea and Saudi infrastructure can interact.”
More escalation on the way
At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Iran projected a message of defiance while also proposing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if its seven conditions were met.
They included lifting the blockade on Iran, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to attacks on all fronts, including Israel’s assault on Lebanon. The demands mostly amounted to a return to the June memorandum of understanding between the US and Israel.
Tehran has added that reopening the strait must be undertaken through a bilateral arrangement already finalised with Oman, the only other country with territorial waters in Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump told reporters he rejected the offer, but Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday they were adamant about the conditions and would await an official response through mediators, such as Pakistan, Qatar and Oman.
Abolfazl Shekarchi, chief spokesman of the Iranian armed forces, warned that if the US further intervenes in the Strait of Hormuz, “it will get slapped”.
“The Americans have no way out other than withdrawing from the West Asia region. The sooner they leave, the fewer losses they will incur and the region will certainly become safe after that,” he said.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said conditions were deteriorating so badly for the US that it might launch another “military aggression” on Iran.
Krieg said that as the US moves to isolate Iran via sanctions, Tehran, unable to respond with mutual financial measures against Washington, will be forced to rely on continued coercion in the Strait of Hormuz.
“The most likely level remains controlled attrition rather than an immediate return to the massive air campaign of the opening months,” Krieg said.
“Over the coming weeks, I would expect further attacks or attempted attacks on tankers, US-enabled shipping and regional infrastructure, followed by limited US strikes against IRGC maritime assets, coastal missile positions, drones or vessels involved in those operations. That tit-for-tat cycle has already re-emerged around Hormuz.”

‘Russia’s attempt to exert influence did not go down well’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:35:51 UTC
23:35:51 KST

‘Russia’s attempt to exert influence did not go down well’
Swiss voters have rejected the neutrality initiative, but what of neutrality do they want? Urs Bieri from the gfs.bern research group explains what can – and cannot – be gleaned from the September 27 result.
SWI swissinfo.ch: Urs Bieri, Switzerland has clearly voted against a stricter version of neutrality. But what kind of neutrality is it for?
Urs Bieri: That’s the question. The population is obviously in favour of a neutrality that gives the government room for manoeuvre and allows it to take decisions on a case-by-case basis. It has clearly come out in favour of this view of neutrality – a situational view.
But the question was also whether there is a problem that would justify an alternative conception of neutrality. And here, the population’s answer on Sunday was no.
SWI: There are already many interpretations of what Sunday’s result means. Was it a vote against Russia?
U.B.: This is indeed a context for these discussions. And Russia also tried to exert influence on this vote. That was not appreciated – particularly by people who lived through the Cold War, and who thus developed a friend-or-foe mindset.
SWI: Can we conclude from this that the Swiss population has clear sympathies for Ukraine?
U.B.: It’s difficult to draw that conclusion, but sympathies evidently lie more on this side than on the other.
SWI: What about the idea that this was a vote in favour of a more activist neutrality policy?
U.B.: I wouldn’t go that far either. The result supports the position of the government, which has concluded that sanctions against Russia are right tool. That was the basis of this discussion; the population made its decision through this lens.
SWI: The Swiss People’s Party and parts of the pacifist movement backed the initiative, but above all Christoph Blocher with a great deal of money. How do you interpret that?
U.B.: Indeed, Christoph Blocher made the largest recorded donation by a private individual since such figures have been openly available. Apparently, for him it wasn’t just about winning a majority, but about driving a discussion that is important to him and that he wanted to lead. Looking at the result, he didn’t ultimately succeed. This suggests he was led by his heart rather than his head in this case.
SWI: Did the initiative at least manage to unite People’s Party’s supporters behind it?
U.B.: That’s something that needs to be looked at. The People’s Party’s potential [among voters] is currently one to two percentage points higher than the 29% who voted yes on Sunday. As said, our surveys showed the older generation was particularly irritated by Russia’s meddling and voted no – this included those from the People’s Party camp. And overall, the party was visibly isolated, and did not succeed in winning votes beyond its own circles.
More
Swiss democracy in the crosshairs of Russian propaganda
SWI: The debate about Swiss foreign policy is not over. With an upcoming referendum on the arms export law, discussions are set to continue. What signals can politicians take from this vote?
U.B.: The next big test is indeed coming in November. It’s certainly not a disadvantage for the war materiel reform if the population wants flexible neutrality. Looking at Russia and Ukraine, you could also assume that certain arms deliveries will be questioned less than in the past. But I wouldn’t simply transfer today’s decision to the next vote. Citizens will make a different – a new – decision in November.
SWI: How do you interpret the clear defeat for the food security initiative?
U.B.: This initiative is interesting because it at least addressed a problem. The population clearly acknowledges climate issues and think climate protection is necessary. The same applies when it comes to environment issues.
SWI: But backing for the initiative dropped sharply over the campaign, despite an extremely hot and dry summer. Why did its backers not manage to make more of the population’s concerns?
U.B.: Ultimately this is down to the fact that, towards the end of the campaign, its weaknesses were judged more harshly. People’s questions about it stem from everyday experience: can I still eat meat, and if so, how much?
But questions also came up at a more structural level: is it even possible to achieve a self-sufficiency rate for food production of 70%, and within ten years? All of this led to this very clear no.
SWI: This initiative was run without any support from political parties or in parliament. Has there ever been an initiative which was successful in such a situation?
U.B.: Yes, the 2013 fat cat initiative, which aimed to curb excessive bonus payments. It is possible to have a broad impact even under such conditions. The initiator of the food initiative, Franziska Herren, already proved this with her drinking water initiative in 2021. That time, she managed to get 40% of votes; this time it’s less than 30%. This shows that the message didn’t come across to the population as well this time around.
SWI: With two clearly rejected initiatives today, Swiss voters have once again roundly backed the government and parliament. Is the government greatly trusted at the moment?
U.B.: Trust in the government is at rather medium-high levels – nowhere near as high as five or ten years ago. Nevertheless, it shows that parliament and the government are indeed backing policies which are in line with what the population expects.
Edited by Samuel Jaberg; adapted from German, sub-edited by Domhnall O’Sullivan

Geologists found traces of mountains as tall as the Himalayas beneath the Antarctic ice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:32:53 EEST
23:32:53 KST

Geologists found traces of mountains as tall as the Himalayas beneath the Antarctic ice
Kyiv • UNN
Zircons point to ancient mountains that formed during the formation of Gondwana. Their erosion may have enriched the oceans and supported the development of life.
Scientists have found geological evidence that large mountain systems similar to the Himalayas existed in Antarctica during the formation of Gondwana. Their erosion may have contributed to enriching the oceans with nutrients and promoting the development of animal life. This is reported in a study published in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, U.N.N. reports.
Details
The authors of the study, Bei Chen and Ian Campbell, examined detrital zircons—minerals whose composition and age help reconstruct the geological history of rocks. The scientists concluded that the roots of ancient mountains formed during the assembly of Gondwana are preserved beneath the Antarctic ice sheet. According to their calculations, during the Cambrian interval studied, approximately 46% of the zircons in the weighted global database came from Antarctica. Among grains associated with formation under high pressure, this share was 55%. These figures characterize the mineral database studied, not the area of the ancient mountains.
Marine sediments near Antarctica’s coast help scientists study the continent’s geology hidden beneath the ice. Glaciers erode rocks and carry their fragments into the ocean, where the material can be obtained by drilling the seafloor.
In a related paper published in Communications Earth & Environment, Chen, Campbell, and Richard A. K. Arkulus analyzed the ages and trace-element contents of 1,712 zircon grains. The oxygen and hafnium isotope compositions were also examined for some of the samples. The predominant age group of the minerals was 650–450 million years. The researchers link it to tectonic processes during the era of Gondwana’s formation. The authors estimate that the studied material originated from glacial drainage areas covering approximately 90% of Antarctica’s territory.
How ancient mountains could have influenced the development of life
The hypothesis linking large-scale mountain building with the development of complex life is based on the consequences of erosion. The erosion of mountains supplied the oceans with nutrients, particularly phosphorus and iron, which supported biological productivity. According to the authors’ interpretation in the new study, increased photosynthesis and the subsequent burial of organic carbon contributed to the accumulation of oxygen. This may have created favorable conditions for the development of animals and the Cambrian explosion—a period of rapid growth in their diversity.
Context
In 2022, researchers from the Australian National University had already described ancient “supermountains” that may have reached the height of the Himalayas and extended for up to 8,000 kilometers. One of the stages of this mountain-building process that they identified occurred 650–500 million years ago.
We should note
Somewhat earlier, it became known that scientists had identified a rare dinosaur fossil from Antarctica that had been kept in a drawer for decades.

====================================================================================================

65 Years of Hotel Ukraine: From Kyiv’s Lost Skyscraper to a Wartime Landmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Hotel Ukraine is one of Kyiv’s most recognizable high-rise buildings. Opened in 1961 in the heart of the capital, it was built as part of the postwar reconstruction of Khreshchatyk and the city center.
On Sept. 28, the landmark will mark its 65th anniversary.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But the story of the building begins long before 1961 – with another Kyiv skyscraper that did not survive the war.
Before Hotel Ukraine stood here, the site was occupied by the Ginzburg Building, an 11-story early 20th-century landmark built by Kyiv businessman and developer Lev Ginzburg. Completed in 1912, it was one of the tallest buildings in Kyiv and among the early high-rises in Eastern Europe.
Instytutska Street, with L. Ginzburg’s 12-story skyscraper, 1930s. (Photo via the Hotel Ukraine.)
The building housed apartments and shops, while Ginzburg’s own residence stood at the rear of the property.
It was destroyed in September 1941, when central Kyiv was devastated during World War II.
After the war, Soviet authorities sought to create a new architectural landmark on the site and reshape Kyiv’s skyline.
A series of proposals followed. The project was eventually developed by a team led by architect Anatolii Dobrovolskyi, with architects including Abraham Miletskyi, Borys Pryimak, Vadym Sozanskyi, and Anatolii Kosenko.
Budanov Announces Major POW Exchange With Russia as Early as Next Week
Collage via Kyiv Post
The original concept was considerably more ambitious than the building Kyiv knows today.
Inspired in part by the monumental high-rises being built in Soviet cities, the hotel was initially planned as a much taller structure, with a tower and spire. The final design was scaled back, however, and the building was completed at 14 stories.
Construction took place from 1958-61, taking advantage of Kyiv’s distinctive hills and terrain.
Hotel Ukraine officially opened on Sept. 28, 1961, under the name Hotel Moscow.
Collage via Kyiv Post
For decades, the hotel was one of Kyiv’s principal places for visiting politicians, diplomats, artists, athletes, and other international guests. Its location overlooking Independence Square made it part of the visual identity of the capital.
In 2001, on the 10th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence, the hotel was renamed Hotel Ukraine.
Today, the four-star property has more than 360 rooms, including conference and event facilities in the center of Kyiv.
Photo: Hotel Ukraine.
Another layer of the building’s history lies underground.
The hotel retains a Cold War-era shelter built in 1961. Designed as a protected space, it includes areas for people to stay during an emergency and reflects the security concerns of the Soviet era.
More than six decades later, the shelter has acquired a very different relevance.
In 2024, Hotel Ukraine became one of the major state assets offered for sale as part of Ukraine’s large-scale privatization program.
At the Sept. 18 auction, the hotel was sold for Hr.2.5 billion ($56 million) to ARS Capital.
In the early hours of May 24, 2026, Russia’s massive missile attack on Kyiv once again brought war into the history of Hotel Ukraine.
The blast wave damaged the building, breaking dozens of windows and balcony units, affecting parts of the façade, interiors, and rooms. Temporary wooden panels replaced some of the shattered windows.
Later, Ukrainian teenagers decorated some of the panels with traditional Petrykivka paintings, turning traces of wartime damage into temporary public artwork.
Photo: Hotel Ukraine.
The hotel continues to operate as Kyiv itself does – under the conditions of a full-scale war.
Hotel Ukraine was conceived as a symbol of postwar reconstruction. It survived the Soviet era, the transition to independence, privatization, and now Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Its history began on the site of a skyscraper destroyed by war.
Today, the building stands again in a city at war – damaged, awaiting transformation, but still part of Kyiv’s skyline.
Hotel Ukraine has changed its name, ownership, and political era. What has remained is its place in the city and its ability to reflect Kyiv’s history as it is being written.

Self-determination over religious freedom: Zurich sends strong signal on assisted dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:28:47 UTC
23:28:47 KST

Self-determination over religious freedom: Zurich sends strong signal on assisted dying
Voters in canton Zurich have made it obligatory for care homes and hospitals to offer assisted suicide. This presents faith-based institutions with a dilemma and sends a signal far beyond the boundaries of the canton.
In Switzerland, voters do not vote against the right to assisted suicide and the trend continues. In the canton of Zurich, a two-thirds majority approved a legislative amendment this Sunday that obliges care homes and hospitals to provide right-to-die organisations with access to their residents and patients – even if this violates the core values of these institutions.
The proposal affects nearly 30 private Christian care homes in the canton that reject this practice. They must now open their doors to Exit, Dignitas, and other assisted suicide organisations, or relocate their operations to another canton that does not yet have such regulations.
The law also brings changes for doctors, as hospitals in the canton of Zurich are now required to allow assisted-dying representatives as well. Critics had warned in vain of a conflict between palliative care and assisted suicide in hospital settings. Among them was the Zurich cantonal government, which had opposed the proposal for that reason.
What lies ahead for Christian care homes
What does this legislative change mean for the affected facilities? Markus Schaaf, director of the Christian care center Zentrum Rämismühle in Zell and a leading voice among the proposal’s opponents, does not consider relocation a realistic immediate scenario.
He assumes that most affected institutions will attempt to adapt to the new legal reality and continue to uphold their own principles and values as far as possible.
One point is particularly important to him: “The law obliges an institution to tolerate assisted suicide carried out by third parties. It does not oblige us to offer suicide assistance ourselves or to involve staff members in it.” Proponents of the law had also consistently highlighted this distinction, which applies equally to hospitals.
Schaaf states that his institution will continue to do everything possible to ensure that people in difficult life situations receive comprehensive care, human compassion, palliative support, and—if desired—pastoral care. Only the legal situation has changed, he says: “Not, however, our fundamental stance on life, dying, and accompanying people at the end of life.”
What Zurich hospitals now face
Zurich hospitals must also establish operational rules for handling assisted suicide, something only a few facilities have done so far. This involves questions such as how attention is drawn to the option of assisted suicide within the hospital or how external assisted suicide organisations can be integrated into hospital routines.
Health Director Natalie Rickli told the media on Sunday afternoon that she does not expect a high volume of cases. Assisted suicide had only been used rarely, even in hospitals where it was already permitted. Furthermore, she expressed trust in the common sense of patients and their relatives to exercise their right prudently.
For care homes, too, not much will change. The majority of the slightly more than 200 care homes in Zurich had already granted entry to right-to-die organisations. In the remaining, mostly Christian facilities, Rickli noted that most residents would likely choose not to make use of this option in the future either.
Provided no appeal is lodged, she anticipated the law coming into force next spring.
The deeper significance of the vote result
With this vote, the population of Zurich has prioritised the fundamental right to a self-determined death over the free exercise of religion and the economic freedom of care homes.
Opponents had aligned along these two value systems, including the Federal Democratic Union and Evangelical Party whose voters is largely drawn from free church circles and who view assisted suicide critically—as well as the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, which advocates for minimal state regulation.
The economically and socially liberal Radical Liberal Party allowed a conscience vote on this matter, where individual and institutional freedoms clashed. All other parties, from the left-green spectrum to the centre, voted in favour of the law—including the Centre Party, which emerged from the Christian Democratic Party. This serves as a sign of how open even the base of the Swiss national churches is toward assisted suicide.
Legally, the precedence of self-determination is already protected. The Federal Supreme Court ruled on this 10 years ago following an appeal against a legislative revision in the canton of Neuchâtel. It concluded at the time that requiring care homes to tolerate assisted suicide did infringe upon their freedom of thought and conscience, but that this infringement was not severe and was outweighed by the right to self-determination.
With Zurich’s decision, the path is clear for right-to-die organisations to demand the same rules in additional cantons or nationwide. Exit and Dignitas, the two major right-to-die organisations, had initiated the legislative revision in Zurich through a popular initiative.
Room for discussion in the pioneer country of assisted suicide
Switzerland, internationally known as a pioneer in assisted dying, is moving closer toward advanced countries that have partially overtaken it in handling end-of-life care.
One such example is Canada, where assisted dying in hospitals has been taking place for a decade. There, however—unlike the future model in Zurich—it is fully integrated into hospital operations and carried out by medical staff, a practice that continues to face criticism in Canada.
For Switzerland, Zurich’s decision marks the first new development in a long time. The rules governing assisted suicide, which have remained unchanged since the enactment of the first Swiss Criminal Code in 1942, remain progressive in many respects. For instance, they permit assisted suicide for individuals without a terminal illness, provided the desire to die and decision-making capacity are present, and the individual acts independently. However, every effort to update these rules through specific legislation has so far failed.
A discussion facing Switzerland in the future concerns assisted dying in cases of dementia. Countries like the Netherlands allow dementia patients to document their wish to die in advance, with the lethal injection subsequently administered by medical personnel.
In Switzerland, by contrast, active direct euthanasia remains a punishable offence. The act of suicide must be carried out by the individual, and assisted dying requires the person seeking death to possess decision-making capacity.
This puts pressure on patients diagnosed with dementia who wish to end their lives on their own terms to act quickly. They have to confront the difficult question of how long they can afford to wait. Now Switzerland as a whole faces the same question regarding regulation.

Iranian runner Zahra Zarei aims to compete at Olympics
TEHRAN - Iranian national team female athlete Zahra Zarei says her goal is to compete at the Olympics.
She won a silver medal in the 400 meters at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday.
"I feel really good and happy right now. I am proud to have won this medal for my country, and I will try to improve my performance in future," Zarei said.
Speaking about her plans for the future and competing at the Olympics, she said: "I have set my goal on being at the Olympics from now on, and I will try to get better day by day and to earn my place at the Olympics."
Zarei also commented on her rival Bahrain’s Salwa Naser, who snatched the gold medal.
"She is originally of African descent, and this has made competition somewhat harder for Asian runners. She is a world champion, and Bahrain has granted this athlete citizenship. As we saw here, most Bahraini runners are of African descent."
"I dedicate my medal to the people of my country, and I hope this medal has made them happy,” the 400-meter silver medalist concluded.

Russia hits Ukraine's largest mobile provider, strikes data centres
KYIV, Sept 27 - Russia hit the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile service provider on Sunday, the company told local media, as Moscow continued a bombardment of Ukrainian data centres and communications infrastructure.
Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties.
Russia's defence ministry also said on Sunday it hit a data centre belonging to Vodafone Ukraine, the country's second-largest cell network provider.
Vodafone Ukraine did not respond to a request for comment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia struck a data centre in Kyiv twice on Sunday morning, wounding two children and an adult.
Moscow has also hit data centres belonging to Ukrainian internet providers over the past week, causing service outages to about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraine's digital ministry.
"Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centres, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives," Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on Wednesday. REUTERS

Swiss voters crush neutrality initiative that would have ended sanctions against Russia—70% say No
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:27:06 UTC
23:27:06 KST

Swiss voters overwhelmingly rejected a neutrality initiative that would have banned Switzerland from adopting sanctions against warring states and blocked cooperation with NATO, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported. The measure failed by 70.2% to 29.8%, with zero cantons voting in favor.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has expanded beyond the battlefield into a campaign of sabotage, political influence, and pressure on European institutions. Every European country that has adopted sanctions or cooperated militarily with Ukraine faces some variant of the same push—to weaken the sanctions regime and fracture the coalition. Russia expressed sympathy for the initiative—which backfired. Opponents warned the measure would benefit Moscow.
What the initiative would have done
The initiative, formally titled "Safeguard Swiss Neutrality," sought to enshrine neutrality as "permanent, armed, and comprehensive," bar cooperation with military alliances unless Switzerland was under direct attack, and ban economic sanctions against warring states—with only UN-mandated measures exempted.
Switzerland currently adopts sanctions autonomously and has largely followed EU sanctions against Russia since the full-scale invasion in 2022. The Swiss government's own explanatory materials stated the initiative would affect sanctions against Russia, SRF reported.
Blocher's Russian connection
Former Federal Council member Christoph Blocher, 85, launched the initiative in autumn 2022—six months into the full-scale war and the same year his daughter Magdalena Martullo-Blocher, who controls Ems-Chemie, decided the two Russian plants would stay. He led the campaign through the organization Pro Schweiz.
Ems-Chemie produces plastics, adhesives, sealants, and technical fibers. Two subsidiaries, operating under the Eftec brand, continued working in Russia after the full-scale invasion, Swiss magazine Republik reported earlier this month. Company and government documents contain strong indications that Eftec products may have been purchased by KamAZ, UAZ, GAZ, and AvtoVAZ—sanctioned companies tied to military vehicle production and financial support for Russian soldiers deploying to Ukraine. Ems-Chemie denies supplying them.
The Federal Council and Parliament both recommended rejection. In the National Council, 124 members voted against and 65 in favor. In the Council of States, the vote was 29 to 10 against.
Politico: Fico is first in line for Orbán’s disruptor crown — but Brussels has four more leaders to worry about
Drones over Swiss military bases
Unidentified drones were spotted over Swiss military installations this year. In about 20% of sightings over military sites, authorities cannot identify who is responsible, army chief Benedikt Roos said earlier this month. Asked whether Switzerland is a target for Moscow, he said yes—the country holds critical infrastructure vital to Europe that anyone seeking to destabilize the continent could target.
Across Europe, pro-Russian forces continue to push back against sanctions. Germany's far-right AfD won 43.8% in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September—its strongest result ever, though every other party refuses coalition. In France, Marine Le Pen leads first-round polling for the 2027 presidential election at 36%. Slovakia's Robert Fico earlier demanded the EU lift Russian energy sanctions.
Russia has combined kinetic and political pressure across Europe—drone incursions into NATO airspace, arson at defense-linked sites, and sabotage of critical infrastructure—alongside support for political forces that oppose sanctions and military cooperation with Ukraine. Switzerland's own intelligence service assessed earlier this year that Russia is waging a long war against the West and escalating it.

Somali pirates escape with suspected police help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:24:22 UTC
23:24:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates escape with suspected police help
Around 30 suspected pirates, arrested during the rescue of a hijacked oil tanker, escaped while being taken to jail, with suspicions emerging that police might have assisted their getaway, four security sources told AFP on Sunday.
There has been a resurgence in Somali piracy since April, with at least 15 attacks this year, the highest since 2013, according to the UN's International Maritime Organisation.
An oil tanker, Sibu 1, also known as Seamull, was rescued after being intercepted by maritime police on Friday, with 41 suspected pirates arrested and taken to the port town of Garacad.
It was seen as a victory for authorities in the semi-autonomous state of Puntland, who have been criticised for failing to act against the pirates, believed to benefit from protection by the local community.
What came next is likely to trigger further criticism, as 28 of the pirates were able to escape as they were being transferred by road from Garacad to the state capital of Garowe on Friday night.
The four local security sources interviewed by AFP said the decision to transport the suspects at night was unusual.
Then, along the route, the truck they were in experienced a burst tyre and the suspects found the door was unlocked, allowing them to flee, the sources said.
Police recaptured only 13 of the group, including one who was fatally wounded by gunfire.
"In Puntland, we don't move (suspects) at night across multiple provinces. Then later on the trip, the pirates ran from the vehicle because the lock on the door was missing. I don't need to say anything else. It's obvious," said one source.
Another source said the suspects' hands and feet had been tied during their initial arrest, but the ties were removed before they were transported.
The brother of one of the suspects confirmed to AFP that he had escaped and was "safe".
"There had to be insiders within the armed security detail," one of the four sources said.
"The dirty (police) who were involved in the escape are no better than the pirates on the run," another added.
Somalia is ranked last on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, tied with South Sudan.
The Seamull tanker is sanctioned by the United States as part of Iran's "shadow fleet", accused of secretly exporting Iranian oil. It was seized by pirates off the coast of Yemen on August 20 and brought to Somali waters.
