From 39th to 10th, India breaks into WorldSkills top league
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:23:07 UTC
23:23:07 KST

India’s rise has been steady. From 39th in London in 2011, it improved to 33rd in Leipzig in 2013, 29th in São Paulo in 2015 and 19th in Abu Dhabi in 2017.
SHANGHAI: Fifteen years ago, India stood 39th in a global competition that tests whether young people can actually make, repair, design, build and deliver to international occupational standards. On Sunday, it broke into the top 10 for the first time. More telling than the jump itself was where the results came from — bakery and dental prosthetics to digital design, logistics and retail — signalling a skills base widening beyond India’s traditional trades.India finished 10th at WorldSkills Shanghai 2026 with six silver medals and 20 Medals for Excellence, improving from its 13th-place finish at Lyon in 2024, where it had won four bronze medals and 12 Medals for Excellence. China topped the Shanghai standings, followed by Korea and Chinese Taipei.India’s six silvers came through Smriti Nambiar in Bakery, Mohammed Salam in Dental Prosthetics, Kovid Ajay Gangrade in Digital Interactive Media Design, Parth Vohra in Industrial Design Technology, Mehrunissa Begum in Logistics and Freight Forwarding and Saniya Joshi in Retail Sales. Nambiar was also named India’s Best of the Nation competitor.
Three of the silvers — Dental Prosthetics, Digital Interactive Media Design and Retail Sales — came in categories India entered for the first time, making the performance significant beyond the medal count. India debuted in 11 disciplines in Shanghai, including unmanned aerial systems, intelligent security technology, software testing, aircraft maintenance and optoelectronic technology.Another 20 Medals for Excellence came across a wide spread of occupations, including mechatronics, autonomous mobile robotics, Industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, robot systems integration, automobile technology, chemical laboratory technology, jewellery, fashion technology and health and social care. The medallions are awarded to competitors who demonstrate a high level of professional proficiency against WorldSkills standards.India’s rise has been steady. From 39th in London in 2011, it improved to 33rd in Leipzig in 2013, 29th in São Paulo in 2015 and 19th in Abu Dhabi in 2017. Kazan 2019 brought a breakthrough to 13th and India’s first WorldSkills gold. After again finishing 13th at Lyon, Shanghai has now taken India into the top 10.The scale of India’s participation has expanded too. Its largest-ever contingent of 70 competitors took part across 63 skills, spanning advanced manufacturing, engineering, digital technologies, creative industries and specialised services.Congratulating the team, minister of state for skill development and entrepreneurship Jayant Chaudhary said: “Team India’s remarkable performance at WorldSkills Shanghai 2026, with 6 Silver Medals and 20 Medallions for Excellence, marks a significant leap in our global skills journey. Surpassing our previous performance, our young competitors have demonstrated the growing strength and competitiveness of India’s skilled talent. I congratulate every competitor, expert, trainer and industry partner who contributed to this achievement. Beyond the medals, what makes us proud is the confidence, determination and excellence with which our youth represented India on the world stage. Their success reinforces our commitment to building a future-ready skilling ecosystem and giving every young Indian the opportunity to compete with the best in the world.”Manisha Sensarma, official delegate, WorldSkills India and senior economic adviser in the ministry, said the value of the competition extended beyond medals. “WorldSkills is as much about learning as it is about competing. Shanghai has given our competitors and experts invaluable exposure to evolving global occupational standards, new technologies and international best practices. Our focus now is to translate these learnings into stronger training methodologies, improved assessment standards and deeper industry engagement, so that the benefits of this experience extend well beyond the competition to India’s larger skilling ecosystem.
”That may be the larger significance of India’s 10th-place finish. Shanghai shows that its best young trainees can increasingly compete across a much wider spectrum of occupations. The next test is whether the standards, training practices and industry exposure behind that performance can be translated into improvements across the country’s broader skilling ecosystem.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

U.K. Police Investigate Suspected Terror Plot Near Base Used by U.S. Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:19:05 UTC
23:19:05 KST

British counterterrorism police are leading an investigation after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing a terrorist act near an air base used by U.S. forces.
Police received a report at around 12:45 a.m. Sunday about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. Armed officers responded and arrested the men in nearby Whelford.
Fairford is used as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has hosted U.S. B-52 and B-1 bombers during the Iran war, according to ABC News. American forces have used Fairford to carry out strikes against Iranian missile sites, the Associated Press reported.
In a press conference Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that about 85 households in the area were advised to evacuate early Sunday morning as a precaution.
"A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles, while the Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit examine them,” Ocone said. A statement from police earlier Sunday said that they believe the situation is “contained.”
Aerial footage from Sky News shows a bomb disposal robot moving between three white vans at the site, with the rear doors of two vehicles open.
Ocone added that the men remain in custody and will be questioned by police.
The base is home to both the 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron, and serves as the “preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe,” according to the U.S. Air Force.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Air Force for comment on the incident.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed the post in July, called the incident “deeply concerning” on X.
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he wrote. “The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.”
When asked by reporters about the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump called them “fantastic.”
“They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” Trump said of the suspects, “and working with the British worked out great.”
Trump also said the suspects had been under surveillance before their arrests. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
British police have not confirmed that RAF Fairford was the intended target of the suspected attacks. The Associated Press reported that investigators were considering a possible connection to Iran, but no such link has been confirmed.

Asian Games | Roundup: China's shuttlers reach semifinals

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's Wang Zhiyi and Chen Yufei advanced to the women's singles semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, while both of China's mixed doubles pairs also secured semifinal berths.
World No. 2 Wang eased past Chinese Taipei's Lin Hsiang-Ti 21-7, 21-12 in the quarterfinals, while Chen came from a game down to beat India's Pusarla V. Sindhu 11-21, 21-18, 21-10.
"Winning the team title gave me a big boost in confidence going into the individual event," Wang said. She added that her goal was to challenge for the individual title but that she would focus on preparing for each match and fighting for every point.
Chen said the match was "more intense and closely contested" than the scoreline suggested. After dropping the opening game, she said she kept telling herself to hold on and fight for every point rather than give up.
South Korea's An Se-young, the women's singles champion at the Hangzhou Asian Games and Paris Olympics, also reached the semifinals with a 21-8, 21-9 win over Thailand's Ratchanok Intanon.
In mixed doubles, Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin opened China's quarterfinal campaign with a 2-0 victory over South Korea's Kim Jae-hyun and Jang Ha-jeong, while Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping beat India's Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto 2-1.
China's men's doubles pair Liang Weikeng and Wang Chang defeated Malaysia's Nur Izzuddin and Goh Sze Fei 2-0 to reach the semifinals, while women's doubles pair Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning beat Chinese Taipei's Hsieh Pei-shan and Hung En-Tzu 2-0 to advance to the last four.
The individual semifinals will be held Monday. ■

Asian Games | Wang Manyu beats Sun Yingsha to win table tennis women's singles gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
22:18:25 CST
23:18:25 KST

Gold medalist Wang Manyu (2nd L) of China, silver medalist Sun Yingsha (1st L) of China, bronze medalists Harimoto Miwa (2nd R) of Japan and Hayata Hina of Japan pose during the awarding ceremony for the women's singles of table tennis at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Cheong Kam Ka)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Wang Manyu beat compatriot Sun Yingsha 4-2 in an all-Chinese final to win the table tennis women's singles gold at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, while China's Huang Youzheng and Lin Shidong defeated Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto and Hiroto Shinozuka 4-2 to claim the men's doubles title.
In a meeting between the world's top two women's singles players, Wang took two closely contested opening games 11-8, 11-9. Sun responded by winning the third 13-11, but Wang rallied from four points down to take the fourth 11-9 and move within one game of the title.
Sun stayed in contention with an 11-4 win in the fifth before Wang closed out the match by taking a hard-fought sixth game 15-13.
Wang captured her second Asian Games women's singles gold, eight years after winning it in Jakarta in 2018. Japan's Hina Hayata and Miwa Harimoto took bronze.
"My mindset is different this time. Eight years ago, I was still in the role of a challenger," Wang said. "The pressure was greater this time. But I think Sun and I were both able to get the job done."
In the men's doubles final, Huang and Lin faced Harimoto and Shinozuka, who had earlier rallied past Chinese pair Wen Ruibo and Xiang Peng in the semifinals.
The pairs were level at 2-2 after four games before Huang and Lin took the fifth 11-5. A string of errors from the Japanese pair helped the Chinese duo dominate the sixth 11-1 to seal a 4-2 victory.
"We both went into the match with the belief that we had to win. Even when we were trailing early on, we didn't give up. We fought for every game and were prepared to battle it out over all seven games," Lin said.
"Our teammates' loss to them in the morning also gave us a reminder. We just focused more on our own match," he added.
It was Lin's second gold medal of the Asian Games after his mixed doubles triumph with Kuai Man on Saturday. He will face Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju in the men's singles semifinal on Monday.
Japan's Sora Matsushima and Shunsuke Togami and China's Wen and Xiang took bronze.
Monday is the final day of table tennis competition at these Games, with gold medals to be decided in the women's doubles and men's singles. ■

Asian Games | Day 8: Boonson equals Asian 200m record, Shavkatov provisionally suspended
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
22:18:17 CST
23:18:17 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Puripol Boonson stormed to men's 200m gold in 19.88 seconds to equal the Asian record at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, while Uzbekistan's MMA bronze medalist Nodirbek Shavkatov was provisionally suspended after testing positive for meldonium.
Shavkatov, 23, who won bronze in the men's modern MMA 71kg event, became the first medalist and third athlete at these Games to return a positive doping test. No decision has been announced on the status of his medal.
On the track, Boonson completed an Asian Games sprint double, winning the men's 200m in 19.88 to equal the Asian record set by China's Xie Zhenye in 2019. China's Huang Youwen took silver in 20.45, while Japan's Soshi Mizukubo was third in 20.56.
The 20-year-old Thai had broken the Games record with 20.10 in Saturday's semifinal before shaving another 0.22 seconds off the mark despite a slight headwind. He won the 100m on Friday in a Games-record 9.90.
"It's not that different - just more adrenaline and more excitement, and I was more eager to win the gold," Boonson said of his mindset at the Games. "I'm going to aim for more golds and more records. I can't say how fast it's going to be, but there will be more records and faster times."
China's 17-year-old Chen Yujie, winner of the women's 100m, took silver in the 200m in 22.93, 0.15 seconds behind Singapore's Shanti Pereira, who won in 22.78. India's Harita Bhadra was third in 23.20.
Asian record holder Yan Ziyi of China won the women's javelin with a Games-record 70.46 meters on her opening attempt, while compatriot Huang Yingying took the women's long jump gold with a leap of 6.55 meters.
China's Chen Yuanjiang won the men's 110m hurdles in 13.15, while Wu Yanni took bronze in the women's 100m hurdles in 13.12 behind Japan's Mako Fukube.
Japan's Hayato Katsuki won the men's marathon race walk on home soil, while Kazakhstan's Yasmina Toxanbayeva took the women's title.
China claimed two more table tennis golds. Huang Youzheng and Lin Shidong beat Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto and Hiroto Shinozuka 4-2 in the men's doubles final, while Wang Manyu defeated compatriot and Paris Olympic silver medalist Sun Yingsha 4-2 to win the women's singles title.
China also swept the day's synchronized diving titles. Chen Yiwen and Chen Jia won the women's 3-meter springboard synchro, while Yang Hao and Lian Junjie claimed the men's 10-meter platform synchro title.
In artistic swimming, China's Lin Yanjun and Xu Huiyan won the duet title after the free routine, ahead of Japan's Moe Higa and Tomoka Sato.
BMX freestyle park made its Asian Games debut, with China's Sun Sibei recovering from a warm-up crash and a disappointing first run to win with 93.80 points on her second attempt. Japan's Miharu Ozawa took silver with 91.20, while China's Sun Jiaqi claimed bronze with 90.20.
China also struck gold in women's street skateboarding as 15-year-old Zhu Yuanling climbed from fifth in qualifying to win with 166.57 points. Japan's Yumeka Oda earned silver with 161.96, while China's defending champion Cui Chenxi took bronze. World No. 1 Ibuki Matsumoto of Japan finished fifth.
"I'd been practicing that trick in my second run for a long time, and it's one I can usually land, so I didn't feel like I needed to be that nervous," Zhu said. "It's amazing. I still feel a bit dazed. Actually I didn't expect to win gold."
China took the top two places in the men's trampoline super final, with Yan Langyu winning gold with 65.09 points and Wang Zisai taking silver with 63.83.
Weightlifting produced three world records as Song Kuk Hyang of the DPR Korea won the women's 69kg title. Song set a snatch world record of 121kg before lifting a world-record 152kg in the clean and jerk for a world-record total of 273kg.
China took the women's 77kg gold with lifts of 118kg in the snatch and 140kg in the clean and jerk for a 258kg total.
In fencing, Kirill Prokhodov helped Kazakhstan claim its first gold of the competition with a dramatic 43-42 comeback victory over South Korea in the men's epee team final. South Korea won the women's sabre team title after beating host Japan 45-31.
After eight days of competition, China leads the medal table with 119 gold, 48 silver and 38 bronze medals. Japan is second with 37 gold, 61 silver and 58 bronze, while South Korea is third with 20 gold, 23 silver and 39 bronze. ■

Int'l Exchange | American teacher's 12 years in China inspire enduring friendship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
22:17:47 CST
23:17:47 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival, 73-year-old American teacher Gail Chou spoke with Xinhua via video link about the years she spent living and teaching in China. Reflecting on people in China and the United States, she said they share many similarities -- they are both friendly, kind, warmhearted, and always willing to help others.
Twenty-two years ago, Chou came to Luoyang No. 2 Foreign Language School through the U.S.-China Teacher Exchange Program to teach for one year. When that year ended, she volunteered to stay, spending twelve years of her life teaching in China.
For Chou, it was never simply a job. What she saw was "a group of children eager to see the world."
Chou summed up her approaches to teaching in three principles. "No one cares how much you know until they know how much you care," she said. "The second is to give my heart to children, and the third one is that love is always the answer."
Before each new semester, she would spend weeks writing words of encouragement on cards. On the first day of school, she waited at the school entrance to greet students with the cards and "welcome candy," a tradition she kept for years.
Over her 12 years in China, Chou wrote more than 50,000 such cards for students. Many of her former students have still kept them today.
To bring English lessons closer to everyday life, she constantly experimented with new ways of teaching. When introducing western food culture, she used local Luoyang flatbread as a pizza base, adding tomato sauce and cheese to make "pizza" with her students.
For a lesson on Hawaiian culture, she guided students to turn green trash bags into grass skirts and use colored paper, drinking straws and yarn to make leis before learning a Hawaiian-style dance.
Basketball became another way for Chou to connect with her students. She started a basketball tournament named after herself and helped organize more than 3,000 games, using the court to teach sportsmanship and teamwork. The tournament has still been held at the school today.
In June 2016, after 12 years of teaching in China, Chou prepared to return to the United States. At a farewell gathering, Bai Fan, principal of Luoyang No. 2 Foreign Language School, presented her with two keys, one gold and one silver. "One opens the school gate, and the other opens the door to home. You are always welcome to come home."
"China has long been another home to me," Chou said during a visit to the Chinese Embassy in the United States at the embassy's invitation during this year's Dragon Boat Festival.
Ronald Sakolsky, another American teacher, also came to Luoyang through a teachers' exchange program. After learning about efforts to combat desertification in China, he helped raise funds to support Yin Yuzhen's tree-planting efforts in Inner Mongolia. Twenty-seven years later, Sakolsky returned to China and traveled to Inner Mongolia, where he revisited the forest he helped fund years ago and planted a tree of friendship with Yin together. He also returned to the school in Luoyang, where he once taught, to meet with teachers and students.
From friendships formed in classrooms to bonds that have endured for decades, the stories of Gail Chou and Ronald Sakolsky reflect the lasting connections between ordinary Chinese and Americans.
Correspondents: Wu Jingdan, Sun Ruibo, Li Jianan
Video editor: Lin Yu
Photo credit to Luoyang No. 2 Foreign Language School■

Most Companies Supplying Molniya Drones Remain Outside Western Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:16:22 UTC
23:16:22 KST

Most companies that supply components for Russian Molniya-series drones are not under Western sanctions. The manufacturer itself is currently not subject to U.S. or U.K. sanctions.
The Kyiv Independent reported this, citing a study by the Ukrainian think tank Center for Defense Reforms.
According to the media, Molniya has become one of the most widely used Russian strike UAVs. Its low cost, relatively simple production, and reported effectiveness have contributed to its widespread use.
In June alone, the Defense Forces shot down about 30,000 Russian Molniya drones. Depending on the modification, the UAVs are used for reconnaissance, air defense, strikes, or to carry FPV drones into the combat area.
The manufacturer, Atlant-Aero, is under sanctions imposed by the EU, Canada, and Ukraine, but is currently not subject to sanctions in the United Kingdom or United States. According to the study, Prominvest JSC, which controls Atlant-Aero, is not under sanctions in any jurisdiction.
Another 10 Russian companies that supply critical components and services for Molniya drone production are also not subject to Western sanctions.
Atlant-Aero’s ultimate beneficial owner, Viktor Grigoryev, and the company’s four other co-owners are also not under Western sanctions.
The study also identified 11 Chinese companies not under sanctions that supply critical components for Molniya drone production. They include Shenzhen Xingkai Technology Company, which supplies equipment for mesh networks. This allows Russian drones to fly deeper into Ukrainian territory. On its website, the company openly states that the technology has military applications.
Ukraine has repeatedly launched drone and missile strikes against Molniya production facilities in Taganrog. In particular, a drone attack on the night of September 12 destroyed three production and storage buildings, while in April, Neptune missiles hit two production halls and completely destroyed another workshop at the plant.

Collateral damage: How Cognac is paying the price for Europe’s trade wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:16:04 UTC
23:16:04 KST

French Cognac producers are battling falling sales as trade disputes with China and the US squeeze the export-dependent industry and leave growers seeking EU support.
As the Cognac harvest draws to a close in southwestern France, winegrowers already know they face another difficult year.
Cognac makers are struggling. The 300-year-old amber brandy is only produced around the Charente River, but it has been caught in the trade wars between the EU and China, as well as by tensions with its top export market, the US.
For months, producers have watched largely powerless as access to both markets has been squeezed.
The industry has a historic connection to the EU. Jean Monnet, the French statesman regarded as one of the EU's founding fathers, came from a Cognac-producing family and worked in the family business.
Today, however, the sector is in disarray as sales plummet. Cognac is overwhelmingly dependent on foreign markets, with 98% of production exported outside the EU.
“Collateral damage” from trade wars
Ironically, this year's drought has helped bring supply closer to falling demand.
“We thought the harvest was going to be promising, but in the end the drought took its toll,” Matthieu Augier, a winegrower in Gondeville, told Euronews. “Compared with a typical year, we’re looking at a 30 to 40% reduction in the harvest in economic terms. You could say in a way that nature helps regulate our surpluses.”
Since 2023, Cognac sales have fallen from 230 million to 140 million bottles. The four main trading houses – Rémy Martin, Hennessy, Martell and Courvoisier – had to slash their orders from winegrowers in the region after clients cancelled contracts.
First, it was because of the trade war with China, the second-largest market after the US, which represents around 25% of Cognac’s exports.
“We have been collateral damage in the trade war which started in 2023 between Brussels and Beijing over Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), a symbolic product for the EU market,” Raphaël Delpech, Director of the National Interprofessional Cognac Bureau (BNIC), told Euronews.
France was among the strongest supporters of EU action against Chinese EVs over concerns that state subsidies were giving Chinese manufacturers an unfair advantage over European carmakers.
Beijing retaliated by targeting European brandy. In 2024, it imposed provisional duties of up to 34.8%, just days after the EU imposed tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs.
China later confirmed its measures but exempted major Cognac producers that agreed to sell above undisclosed minimum prices. By then, however, the damage had been done, according to the industry.
“Once the Chinese government singled us out and associated us with an anti-Chinese European and French policy, consumers started to distance themselves,” Delpech added. “The distributors stopped buying our bottles and stopped putting our products on their shelves.”
Then came another blow, this time from the US, which accounts for around half of Cognac exports.
During Donald Trump's first administration, the US had already imposed tariffs on French Cognac as part of the long-running Boeing-Airbus trade dispute. The duties were later suspended under President Joe Biden.
But in April 2025, Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on US trading partners. In July, the EU and US reached a deal at Turnberry, Scotland, setting a 15% tariff on most European exports to the US, including Cognac.
Turnberry talks stall
The European wine and spirits industry has since lobbied hard for carve-outs from the 15% tariff.
But uncertainty continues to weigh on the US market, where inflation has also pushed up prices. Trump has repeatedly threatened much higher tariffs on French wines and spirits as part of wider political disputes.
“It created an extremely anxiety-inducing environment for all our importers in the US, who, just as in China, eventually came to the conclusion that it was better to bet on something safer than Cognac,” Delpech said.
After EU lawmakers agreed in July 2026 to remove the bloc's remaining tariffs on US goods covered by the Turnberry agreement, Washington agreed to reopen discussions on possible exemptions from the 15% tariff. So far, however, there has been little sign of progress for Cognac.
“I get the impression that not much is moving forward,” French MEP Eric Sargiacomo (S&D), deputy chair of the European Parliament’s intergroup on wines and spirits, told Euronews. “The only ones who have managed to make clear progress on this issue are the British.”
The UK secured the removal of US tariffs on whisky in May, while Irish whiskey received similar treatment in mid-September. French Cognac, however, remains subject to the tariff.
“For us, the recovery will only come through the US market. That’s obvious. China will come eventually, but it will be more complicated,” Delpech said.
The sector has written to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and held talks with the Commission's trade and agriculture departments.
“Everybody knows us in Brussels,” Delpech said.
French President Emmanuel Macron also visited the region several times, and promised winegrowers they would be entitled to compensation. So far, however, none has arrived.
Cognac, 'a textbook case for Europe'
Delpech argues that the Cognac crisis raises a broader question about how the EU protects sectors hurt by retaliation against European trade measures.
“The European policy cannot be strong if it does not protect the industries that bear the brunt of these trade-offs,” he added. “So, when it is deliberately decided that in order to protect the EU automotive industry, Cognac will suffer by losing markets and being subject to sanctions from China, there needs to be a solidarity mechanism.”
To adapt to lower demand, the industry has launched two vine-grubbing schemes backed by financial support.
The first offers growers support to remove vines permanently, but take-up has been limited. Applications cover just 560 hectares out of the 96,000 hectares within the Cognac appellation.
“A vineyard is a means of production,” Augier said. “When you plant a vineyard, you’re planting it for at least 40 to 50 years. It’s a form of heritage.” The winegrower, who is only 40 years old, might instead choose the second type of vine-grubbing offered for some of its vines, which is temporary: he will not be able to replant them for five years, but he will keep his vineyard.
The slump is weighing on the wider regional economy. Cognac supports around 70,000 direct and indirect jobs in France. Alongside some 260 trading houses that age and sell the spirit, the industry sustains barrel and cask makers, still manufacturers, transport companies and agricultural contractors.
“Cognac is a textbook case for Europe,” Sargiacomo said. “I understand why other agricultural sectors are now questioning Europe’s ability to come to their aid if they were to face difficulties as a result of free-trade agreements, anti-dumping measures, or tariffs imposed from outside.”

planted roof connects concrete casa cieno by TAC to oaxacan coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:15:10 UTC
23:15:10 KST

Casa Cieno’s diagonal volume wraps a pool in green courtyards
Located in Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca, Casa Cieno by TAC Taller Alberto Calleja is organized around enclosed courtyards, framed views, and a central pool. Instead of facing directly toward the sea, the house turns inward, using vegetation and controlled openings to establish a relationship with its surroundings.
The house occupies a 1,500 sqm plot in the El Vigía sector. Its main volume is rotated diagonally in relation to the property boundaries, creating green patios along its perimeter that act as a vegetated buffer between the residence and neighboring properties. The resulting rectangular volume is organized around a central courtyard, with the pool serving as the main spatial and visual anchor.
all images by Cesar Belio
Concrete, wood, and water connect Casa Cieno to the landscape
The design team at TAC Taller Alberto Calleja organizes the program around the central water element, separating the social and private areas. Paths that cross the pool lead to the two bedrooms, while the courtyard connects the different spaces and creates a transition between them. A circular opening in the roof slab frames the sky above the pool, bringing natural light into the interior and making the passage of time visible throughout the day.
The material palette combines exposed concrete and wood, selected in response to the climatic conditions of the Oaxacan coast and intended to age with the site. Above, a green roof extends the living space while restoring part of the vegetation occupied by the building. The rooftop also opens views toward the sea and the Oaxacan mountains, while contributing to the house’s natural climate control.

Why Norwegians are buying more Chinese EVs despite growing scepticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:14:45 UTC
23:14:45 KST

Electric cars account for more than 95% of new car registrations in Norway, the highest share in the world. About one in four new EVs registered there are from fully or partly Chinese-owned brands.
Chinese car brands are taking an increasingly large market share in Norway, even as their electric vehicles are being met with growing scepticism in the country, which leads the world in EV adoption.
According to a new survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, conducted from 31 March to 3 May among nearly 15,000 EV owners in Norway, nearly one-third (31%) of Norwegian electric car drivers said they would avoid buying a Chinese brand for political reasons, compared with 23% a year earlier.
“New cars are, in practice, computers on wheels,” the association’s secretary general, Christina Bu, said in a statement.
“As data security and privacy receive more attention, it is only natural that more consumers become concerned about where the cars come from and how the data is handled,” she added.
A few years ago, Norwegian security researchers discovered that a car made by the Chinese maker NIO was transmitting data to China.
Other tests carried out on a bus from China’s Yutong revealed that the manufacturer had access to the vehicle’s control system and could, in theory, stop it or render it unusable remotely.
Sales of Chinese brands such as BYD, NIO and Dongfeng, and brands owned by Chinese companies like Volvo and Polestar, have nonetheless grown significantly in Norway, accounting for about 25% of new EV registrations in the first half of the year.
Back in 2019, they were virtually non-existent.
“This suggests that consumers weigh several factors against one another when they are buying a car,” Bu said.
“For some, factors such as price and technology are decisive, while others are influenced by moral dilemmas and uncertainty about data sharing and security issues,” she said.
Chinese-owned brands gain ground in Norway
In just a few years, Chinese-owned brands have gone from a negligible share of Norway’s new EV market to becoming its second-largest group by origin, according to an earlier report by the association.
The report suggested they could overtake European brands as soon as 2027 if current trends continue. It also said Norway could become one of the first European markets where Chinese EV makers gain a dominant position.
Gaining ground in Norway matters because the country leads the world in EV adoption. Electric cars accounted for 97.8% of new car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Norwegian Road Federation (OFV).
Norway remains far ahead of the EU, where electric cars accounted for 21.7% of new registrations between January and August, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).
Chinese brands are gaining ground in the wider EU, too. Registrations across five groups with Chinese brands listed by ACEA rose by about 71% in August from a year earlier. Their combined share of the overall new car market climbed from 6.6% to 10.8%. This means that roughly one in nine new cars registered in the EU came from these groups. The figure includes brands with European roots, such as Volvo Cars, which is owned by the Geely Group.
In the EU, among the fastest-growing manufacturers were Leapmotor (up 211%), Chery (201%), BYD (129%) and Geely Group (24%). Registrations of cars made by US carmaker Tesla grew by 53%.
Tesla resistance falls
Political resistance to Tesla has fallen in Norway, too. According to the survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, the share of respondents who said they would avoid Tesla for political reasons dropped to 24% from 43% last year. Musk’s political involvement and support for far-right leaders have drawn opposition to the brand.
“Last year, Elon Musk’s political involvement was highly visible and, unsurprisingly, provoked strong reactions,” Bu said.
“This year, there has been less attention on this, and that may have led to fewer people saying they would not have chosen Tesla,” she added.
Tesla remains Norway’s best-selling new car brand, with a 17.5% share of registrations so far this year, according to OFV data through 24 September.

Pakistan, Afghanistan trade accusations as both claim killing dozens of militants

2026-09-27
14:14:11 UTC
23:14:11 KST

Aamir Latif  I
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Pakistan and Afghanistan on Sunday claimed to have killed dozens of militants, while accusing each other of supporting "terrorist" activities.
Islamabad said its forces killed 71 militants "backed and sponsored" by Afghanistan and India in security operations across southwestern Balochistan province over the past 96 hours.
Weapons, ammunition and explosives were also recovered during the operations, Pakistan Army said in a statement.
Kabul and New Delhi have so far not responded to Islamabad's accusation.
Afghanistan, for its part, said on Sunday its forces killed 28 militants and wounded 32 in the eastern province of Nuristan after alleged ISIS (Daesh) operatives crossed from Pakistan.
Kabul's Defense Ministry accused "Pakistani militias" of supporting the slain militants, adding that most of them were security personnel of the former Afghan government.
Pakistan, however, rejected the claim as "frivolous, baseless and devoid of any truth."
"Pakistan categorically rejects the fabricated claims of involvement by its security forces or intelligence agencies in any internal clashes in Nuristan or elsewhere in Afghanistan, including allegations of recruiting or training former Afghan security personnel or facilitating Daesh or any other terrorist group operating in Afghanistan," the Information Ministry said in a statement.
Pakistan, which has seen a series of militant attacks on its soil in recent years, accuses India and Afghanistan of patronizing militant groups.
India and Afghanistan reject the accusations.

27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
A member of British trip-hop group Massive Attack was arrested in Liverpool while taking part in a protest against the UK outlawing the group Palestine Action and calling for an end to British arms supplies to Israel, according to protest organizers
Robert Del Naja was arrested Saturday under anti-terror laws after holding a sign reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

The demonstration took place ahead of the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool and was attended by supporters of Palestine Action and campaigners opposing the UK government’s policy toward Israel and Gaza.

Ukrainian exporters should check foreign buyers before granting deferred payment — Dun & Bradstreet
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:12:34 EEST
23:12:34 KST

The expansion of Ukrainian companies into foreign markets increases the importance of conducting preliminary checks on potential buyers and distributors. The risks are particularly high when working with a new counterparty on deferred payment terms, Dun & Bradstreet analysts note.
One of the tools for such checks is Dun & Bradstreet’s (D&B) international business information databases, which make it possible to identify a company, verify its registration data, ownership structure, financial indicators, operating history and associated risks.
When entering a new market, Ukrainian companies often focus primarily on finding a buyer and agreeing on commercial terms, while checking the buyer’s solvency remains a secondary task.
“Receiving an order does not yet mean receiving the money. For an exporter, a situation is particularly dangerous when the first large shipment is made to a new partner with deferred payment. Before signing such a contract, it is necessary to understand whether the company actually exists, how long it has been operating, what its financial indicators are, who its owner is and how high the credit risk associated with this counterparty is,” said Maksym Urakin, Director of Development and Marketing at Interfax-Ukraine, Head of the D&B-Interfax-Ukraine business unit, PhD in Economics.
Dun & Bradstreet has a global database containing information on hundreds of millions of companies. A unique nine-digit D-U-N-S Number is used to identify businesses, making it possible to distinguish between legal entities with similar names and link companies within corporate groups.
For a Ukrainian exporter, such a check is particularly relevant when working with companies that are offering a large contract for the first time, requesting a significant payment deferral or acting as intermediaries between the manufacturer and the end buyer.
Depending on the country and the availability of information, a D&B business report may contain registration details, information about executives and owners, financial statements, information on corporate relationships, credit ratings and other indicators used for risk assessment.
“The cost of a check is almost always incomparable with the potential loss from a single unpaid export shipment. International business information should be viewed not as an additional reference, but as one of the elements of the decision-making procedure regarding the credit limit, the amount of prepayment and the terms of the contract,” Maksym Urakin believes.
At the same time, negative information about a potential partner does not necessarily mean that the transaction should be rejected. It may serve as a basis for changing its terms — increasing the prepayment, reducing the size of the first shipment, using a bank guarantee, trade credit insurance or shortening the deferred payment period.
Dun & Bradstreet is an international provider of business data and analytical solutions whose history began in 1841. The company provides tools for business identification, counterparty verification, assessment of credit and commercial risks, compliance, supply chain management and work with corporate data.
The official representative of Dun & Bradstreet in Ukraine is the Interfax-Ukraine news agency. The specialized D&B-Interfax-Ukraine unit helps Ukrainian companies work with international business data, verify foreign partners and obtain a D-U-N-S Number.
Questions can be submitted through the specialized D&B resource — dnb.ua, by email at [email protected] or by phone at +38 (044) 270-65-74.

Iran captures another US spy drone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has captured a US autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz, the second such incident reported this month.
According to an IRGC Navy statement carried by Iranian media, the military UROV was conducting espionage in the strategic waterway.
The IRGC identified the vessel as a Remus 600, an advanced autonomous underwater vehicle used by the US Navy for mine detection, surveillance, and reconnaissance. It released footage of the vehicle being lifted from the water and said specialists are now working to recover its data.
The IRGC also warned that the Strait of Hormuz remains “closed,” saying it will continue confronting what it described as “dangerous movements and unauthorized” vessel activity. The US has not yet commented on the incident.

Iran has captured a second US unmanned underwater vehicle intact in the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/XP343uFzoU
The claim follows a series of drone incidents in the Strait of Hormuz this month.
In early September, Iran said it had seized a US underwater drone, with IRGC footage appearing to show an Anduril-built Dive-LD. The Pentagon acknowledged losing the submersible but said it was an older, damaged model carrying no sensitive data or classified equipment. Days later, the IRGC said it had destroyed a US Saildrone Explorer near the entrance to the strait, releasing footage of the craft burning in the water. In mid-September, the US military said it had thwarted an IRGC attempt to seize another Saildrone, striking two Iranian boats allegedly involved.
The incidents come amid an escalating maritime standoff between Washington and Tehran. The US has destroyed several Iranian oil tankers after accusing the IRGC of firing ballistic missiles at US warships. Iran, meanwhile, has targeted US vessels and commercial tankers it accused of violating restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this week, reports claimed that Washington had increased military activity around the waterway, with reconnaissance aircraft spotted near Iranian territory and additional fighter jets reportedly deployed to the region.
Meanwhile, this week’s diplomatic efforts to break the Iran-US deadlock appear to have failed. At the UN General Assembly, Iran presented what Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a “concrete seven-day plan,” offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks if Washington lifted its naval blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets, and observed a ceasefire, including an end to Israel’s operations in Lebanon. US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal as “unacceptable.”
“I reject their proposal,” he told reporters outside the White House on Saturday, claiming Tehran wants a deal “because they’re losing so badly.” At the UN gathering, he also said he faced a “big decision” over whether to “annihilate” Iran if negotiations failed.
Iran’s top army commander, Major General Amir Hatami, on Sunday argued that the “war is not over,” insisting Tehran had won the initial phase of the conflict but now needs to “consolidate its victory.”

Would you read a book if it was printed like a newspaper?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:09:45 UTC
23:09:45 KST

Would you read a book if it was printed like a newspaper?
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Typically, book formats are pretty standard. Hardback, paperback, e-book. But in the 1970s, a Dutch publisher tried a new configuration for novels: the newspaper.
Theo Knippenberg attributes his publishing career to his mother, who had for years nagged him to find a respectable trade.
“Totally by accident, I became a publisher,” Knippenberg told DutchNews.
The now 80-year-old stumbled on his success at an arts festival in Utrecht in the late 1960s. He sold a series of tiny books, bound together with an elastic band, by Dutch writers.
Knippenberg expalined that he ran into author Harry Mulisch at a road crossing and convinced the writer of The Discovery of Heaven to let him publish an excerpt of an essay. Once Mulisch was on board, Knippenberg used it as leverage to convince other famous Dutch writers, such as Jan Wolkers, to contribute.
A voracious reader, Knippenberg found books unaffordable during his student years. He took the proceeds from the mini book sales and invested them into publishing equipment – not a traditional printing press but one built to print newspapers.
Thinner newsprint was cheaper to produce and therefore cheaper to sell. Together with his wife, Patty Voorsmit, Knippenberg launched Bulkboek.
The first edition, published in 1970, was Schroot by Belgian writer Jef Geeraerts. It follows a former colonel in the Belgian military who is struggling to adapt to life in the Congo.
Over the following 26 years, Bulkboek would publish 250 novels in the newspaper format.
Readers could sign up for an annual series of 10 issues, which cost 1.50 guilders apiece, equivalent to around €4 today. At its peak, the company had over 100,000 subscribers.
The editions were aimed at secondary students and included interviews, critical essays and explanatory texts to help readers understand the work.
The works were selected based on published availability and “my own tastes,” Knippenberg said.
He knew nothing about how publishing worked and had to learn how to create the text sheets, include illustrations and run the books off. He describes his early set-up as “so primitive.”
The initial print runs were all books from Dutch or Flemish authors but by the late 1970s, Knippenberg began branching out. “I got ambitious,” he says. Leo Tolstoy, Pablo Neruda and Iris Murdoch were a few of the authors whose works found their way into the Bulkboek format.
The publisher also moved beyond the Netherlands into Belgium, Germany and France, and began to publish books in languages other than Dutch.
In the early 1990s, the economics of publishing had changed, as cheap paperbacks came onto the market.
Last year, Bulkboek was taken over by educational publisher BruutTAAL, but Knippenberg continues to be involved with some aspects of the company. The new endeavour is working on a series of publications of short stories.
“Students have much shorter attention spans these days,” he says, explaining why short fiction is a better way to draw in young readers.
The publication format continues. On second-hand book websites, Bulkboeks are still available for sale. Leo Tolstoy’s Boyhood, Cees Nooteboom’s Half the World and Willem Frederik Hermans’s The Signet Ring can all be found, many for two or three euros. Less than you would have paid when they were first published by Bulkboek.

Yemen’s health system could collapse in some areas, minister warns
Yemen’s healthcare system may not be able to support the population as war strains resources, minister tells Al Jazeera.
Some areas in Yemen could suffer from a complete loss of health services if a decline in funding continues, Yemen’s Minister of Public Health and Population Qasim Buhaibeh has told Al Jazeera.
He said that the health sector may not be able to absorb additional waves of displacement from the ongoing war while a lack of resources has forced the closure of health facilities and caused shortages of medicines, supplies and fuel.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Yemen’s government offers amnesty to Houthi defectors
- list 2 of 3Djibouti urges world to help as Yemen war drives refugee influx
- list 3 of 3Yemen government forces widen attacks against Houthis: What we know
Buhaibeh added that emergency services, maternal and child healthcare, vaccination and nutrition services, as well as dialysis and cancer treatment, are all particularly threatened by the decline in funding.
He noted that health data updated through June 2026 indicates that 19.3 million people in Yemen require health assistance, while funding for the response has reached only 17 percent of the required amount.
Buhaibeh said that the proportion of health facilities operating at full capacity has likely dropped to less than 50 percent. The World Health Organization had cited 60 percent.
The minister cited figures indicating that 134,550 people have been displaced by the war between June and September 22, with most of them being in Taiz, Lahij and Aden. He said the influx of displaced people has placed additional pressure on health facilities that were already struggling with limited resources.
Buhaibeh said the reporting of health data from Houthi-controlled areas has been suspended for nearly a year, preventing authorities from forming a complete nationwide picture of the epidemiological situation.
Additionally, Buhaibeh warned that displacement, malnutrition and low vaccination coverage are coinciding with outbreaks of cholera, measles and polio.
He noted that more than 27,000 confirmed measles cases were recorded in 2025 and that around half of Yemen’s children under the age of five suffer from chronic malnutrition.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has found that nearly 130,000 people, or 30,000 households, have been displaced across seven governorates in Yemen since fighting escalated between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Yemeni government coalition forces in early September.

UK prime minister proposes free social care for all in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:07:11 UTC
23:07:11 KST

Aysu Biçer
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants to introduce free social care for everyone in England, putting the proposal before voters at the next general election as part of a major reform of the country’s care system.
In an interview with BBC on Sunday, he said he envisaged a system based on the principles of the National Health Service (NHS), in which “everyone contributes, everyone is covered.”
He did not rule out tax rises to fund the reforms, acknowledging that such measures could be “difficult or unpopular” with some voters.
Burnham is expected to set out his vision for social care on Tuesday.
The proposal would mark a significant change to the way adult social care is funded in England. Unlike the NHS, which is generally free at the point of use, social care is means-tested.
He noted the current system placed a “huge cost” on individuals and families. “I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work,” he said.
“There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don’t think it’s right that people in England don’t get the same and it’s not something we’re going to rush,” he added.
Burnham also linked social care reform to pressure on the NHS, arguing that a lack of available care contributes to delays in discharging patients from hospitals.
He said there was a “huge number” of people in hospitals across England who could not return home because the necessary social care was unavailable.
Asked whether everyone would have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham said: “It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS.”
He has yet to set out how the proposed system would be funded or whether it would require higher taxes.

Three in four UK GPs ‘too busy to talk to their patients in depth’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:03:56 UTC
23:03:56 KST

A friendly chat with your GP about your life, health and happiness was once a key part of the UK’s family doctor service.
But most GPs no longer have time to have pastoral conversations, because they are too busy dealing with the country’s rising tide of illness, research reveals.
Three out of four family doctors are now too time-pressed to talk to patients in depth about how they might stop smoking, lose weight or get more sleep, the Royal College of GPs has found.
Intense demands and 10-minute appointment slots mean they also miss opportunities to discuss taking more exercise or review their medications to see if they still need to be on them.
The time to explore patients’ circumstances more fully and offer healthy living advice has been squeezed out of family doctors’ busy schedules, the head of the college said.
An RCGP survey of 2,316 GPs across the UK found that 75% had too little time to offer preventative healthcare, such as offering lifestyle advice and giving advice on vaccinations. The results have raised concern about the government’s drive for the NHS – especially GPs – to do more to prevent people getting ill in the first place. One health expert called them alarming.
The college’s president, Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, who is a GP in east London, said: “General practice is dealing with enormous demand, so in a busy consultation we inevitably have to prioritise the problems that most need our attention that day.
“We will always act on symptoms or findings that need investigation or treatment. What can be squeezed out is the time to step back and look more holistically at how we can help that patient stay well in the long term.
“That might mean having a proper conversation with someone who smokes. We will of course advise patients about stopping smoking. But in a busy consultation there may not be enough time to explore in depth whether they want to stop, what has made it difficult in the past, what concerns they have and what support or treatment might work best for them.
“It is often the depth of those conversations, rather than simply identifying a risk and giving brief advice, that requires time.”
GPs already deliver important preventative care every day, she said. But “the reality is that when you’re working in a busy surgery, with a long list of patients to be seen, there isn’t always enough time in consultations to go beyond the issue a patient has come in for that day”.
The chief executive of the King’s Fund health thinktank, Sarah Woolnough, said: “With life expectancy in the UK among the lowest of most comparable countries, these findings are alarming as many GPs say they are too overwhelmed to carry out these important interventions, and may be missing conditions that could be treated earlier.
“GPs are often frustrated that the increasing demands for appointments mean they don’t have time to provide the holistic care they were trained for.”
The RCGP makes clear in its report that the NHS needs to employ more GPs and ensure they have more time with patients in order to fulfil the prevention ambition.
The findings raise questions about ministers’ plan to make the NHS in England move “from sickness to prevention” in how it operates – one of the three “big shifts” outlined in the government’s 10-year health plan last year.
“Talk around shifting from sickness to prevention is meaningless if we cannot get these basics right first,” Woolnough said.
“If the government is serious on prevention, then more action is needed to support and enable GPs to consistently catch conditions and ill-health early, keeping people healthier for longer, and reducing pressures on wider NHS services down the line.”
A separate representative survey of 2,000 UK voters which the pollsters Censuswide undertook for the RCGP showed that 64% of the public trust family doctors to offer advice on healthy living. That was more than trust the NHS website (51%), pharmacists (38%), family and friends (22%), AI chatbots (7%) and social media influencers (5%).
The Department of Health and Social Care did not comment directly on the RCGP’s findings, but a spokesperson said: “GPs play a vital role in our National Health Service, which is exactly why we’ve placed them at the heart of our 10-year health plan and our shift to community and neighbourhood health services.
Noting an investment of £1.7bn into general practice and the recruitment of 2,000 additonal GPs, they said: “We know there is more to do and we will continue to work with the Royal College of General Practitioners and other partners as we rebuild and modernise the NHS.
“We are already making progress, with record numbers of appointments being delivered, and 77% of patients now saying they have a good local GP service.”

Israel’s Smotrich calls for ‘war’ in West Bank: Rhetoric or real threat?

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for a full-scale war in the occupied West Bank, urging the military to use the tactics employed in Gaza, which has been devastated by the ongoing genocide.
Smotrich, known for his inflammatory, racist and dehumanising language against Palestinians, also called for the annexation of southern Lebanon and Gaza’s territories under Israeli control.

The minister told Ynet News in an interview published on Sunday that Israel should “go to war” in the occupied territory and repeat what it “did in Gaza”. They “reveal the truth of the Israeli plans aimed at implementing attempts at annexation and displacement”, the ministry said in a statement, adding that it would undermine the possibility of establishing an independent Palestinian state.
The threats are a translation of the policies pursued by the Israeli government “of killing, displacement, settlement, and land confiscation and an attempt to impose a new reality by force on the occupied Palestinian land”, it also said.
The ministry urged the international community to take action against Israel’s “aggression”.

He has previously called on Israel to annex more than 80 percent of the West Bank. Smotrich along with Netanyahu has publicly opposed the so-called two-state solution. Settlement expansion is the biggest hurdle in the realisation of a sovereign and independent Palestinian state living side by side with Israel.

That followed June’s announcement of 2,162 new Jewish homes in a new illegal settlement near Jerusalem.
In campaigning for next month’s election, he has promised yet more expansions of Israeli settlements in the territory.

In May, Smotrich said the International Criminal Court (ICC) had requested a warrant for his arrest. The ICC’s accusations centre on the minister’s forced displacement orders for Palestinians, his support for moving Israeli settlers into occupied territory and his claim it may be “justified and moral” to starve Palestinians in Gaza.
Last September, before the “ceasefire” in Gaza, Smotrich said there was a “business plan” to turn the Strip into a “real estate bonanza”, stating that he had been discussing with the Trump administration how to share the proceeds.
In March, he also threatened to turn the southern suburbs of Lebanon’s capital into another Gaza Strip.
Are Smotrich’s calls just rhetoric ahead of elections or real threats?
Smotrich’s words should not be dismissed as mere election rhetoric, warned Bishara.

“And any response by Palestinians is met with even more ferocious force,” said Zonszein.
Smotrich is not just gearing up for next month’s election – he has a calculated vision of wanting to continue his expansionist policies, she said.
“It’s the government’s vision, and it’s what they’ve been doing, and this is what they will continue to do as long as they’re in power.”

“We are exactly a month from the election … If this is the tone … and this is what’s presented to the voters and if someone like him on the basis of this ideology will be elected again, he might find it as [an] endorsement of this kind of attitude,” Mekelberg told Al Jazeera.

Britain and Russia have been to war before. Ask the British fleet how that went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:03:38 UTC
23:03:38 KST

Britain and Russia have been to war before. Ask the British fleet how that went
On June 14, 1854, the allied Anglo-French fleet dropped anchor off Krasnaya Gorka, a village 20 km from Kronstadt and around 50 km from St. Petersburg. Dozens of screw-propelled frigates and steam and sail-powered ships – carrying 3,500 guns and over 30,000 sailors – formed an armada the likes of which had not been seen since the Battle of Trafalgar. They stood by, ready to attack the capital of the Russian Empire.
The press boasted that before setting sail, British Admiral Charles Napier reportedly promised to have breakfast in Kronstadt and dinner in St. Petersburg. Riding a wave of anti-Russian sentiment, the British public hoped to see the Union Jack on the spire of the Russian Admiralty.
The plans of the British were not destined to come to fruition, however. Why did the formidable Anglo-French squadron back down in the face of Russian military-technical power? Why did Britain demonstratively refuse to fight against Russia? And how is the legacy of this 19th-century war being utilized by militaries across the globe today? RT explores this little-known chapter of the Crimean War.
The unknown front of the Crimean War
The war of 1853-1856 – fought between Russia on one side and a coalition of Great Britain, France, Sardinia, and the Ottoman Empire on the other – is known as the Crimean War. Although the main events unfolded in Crimea, the war actually raged across a number of theaters: the Danube, the Caucasus Mountains, the icy waters of the White and Barents seas, distant Chukotka, and the Baltic.
The objective of the anti-Russian coalition was articulated with utmost clarity and candor by then-British Prime Minister John Palmerston, who demanded that Russia be stripped of its growing naval power. Achieving this required capturing and destroying Russian naval fortresses on all fronts, as well as annihilating the Russian military and merchant fleets.
In the Baltic, the British targeted Kronstadt – the naval fortress guarding St. Petersburg. The plan was to seize this maritime gateway to the Russian Empire and subsequently force Russia to capitulate by bombarding the capital. Other targets in the campaign included the Sveaborg sea fortress, which defended Helsingfors (Helsinki), as well as smaller fortresses in Finland and on the islands in the Baltic Sea.
The British were not merely interested in Russia’s surrender. Following their planned victory, they wanted to strip Russia of Crimea and the Caucasus and hand them over to Türkiye. They also planned to cede Moldavia and Wallachia to Austria; transfer parts of the Baltic region to Prussia; return Finland and the Aland Islands to Sweden; and re-establish an independent Poland on the territories of the Kingdom of Poland and Little Russia. In short, Britain aimed to inflict a devastating geopolitical defeat on Russia – one comparable to the events of 1917 and 1991.
These geopolitical ambitions should come as no surprise; the coalition comprising Britain, France, Sardinia, and the Ottoman Empire was, in itself, a formidable force. Moreover, Prussia and Austria – Russia’s recent allies from the Holy Alliance – each kept over 100,000 troops stationed near the border. While formally maintaining neutrality, they were in fact waiting for an opportune moment to share in the spoils should Russia suffer defeat.
One might blame imperial diplomacy for Russia’s lack of allies in the war; yet in other situations, it had no problem forging alliances with European powers. The crux of the matter was that, in the period immediately preceding the Crimean War, the Russian Empire’s power reached its zenith.
In the early 19th century, Russia stood as the undisputed leader of the anti-Napoleonic coalition and the Holy Alliance formed in the wake of the Napoleonic Wars. Furthermore, in 1849, shortly before the Crimean War, Russian troops suppressed the Hungarian uprising, effectively saving the Habsburg dynasty in Vienna. Russia was confidently emerging as a continental hegemon. This development deeply alarmed other European powers, prompting them to unite and join forces to crush – or at least weaken – Russia.
The war also had an ideological dimension. A dispute between Orthodox Christians and Catholics over the right to administer Christian holy sites in Jerusalem and Bethlehem rapidly escalated into a demand by the Archbishop of Paris Marie-Dominique-Auguste Sibour, to “put an end to the Orthodox heresy of the Russian people.”
‘Progressive West’ vs. ‘Backward Russia’
The Crimean War is frequently portrayed as a confrontation between ‘backward Tsarist Russia’ and the ‘progressive West’. From a strictly technical standpoint, the armed forces of Great Britain and France were indeed superior to the Russian Army of that era. They were already armed with rifled muskets having an effective range of 250-300 meters, compared to the 100-120 meter range of the smoothbore muskets with which the Russian forces were mostly equipped. Moreover, the British and French navies already had a significant number of steamships and screw-propelled frigates, whereas Russia’s transition to these new types of vessels proceeded more slowly.
Does this justify the claim that the Russian Army was weak and the Russian Empire backward? If so, we find that the losses suffered by the ‘weak and backward’ Russia in the war were actually lower than those of its progressive allies. Moreover, in Crimea, where the main battles took place, elite Anglo-French units were opposed by standard regular units of the Russian Army.
The true reason for Russia’s difficulties in the war was that the Russian Army was compelled to achieve several things at once: confront allied forces in the Crimea, maintain large and better-trained forces to counter the potential threats posed by Austria and Prussia, and keep its Imperial Guard Corps stationed near St. Petersburg to defend it from Anglo-French attacks. The allies, by contrast, could choose their points of attack and concentrate substantial forces.
St. Petersburg, as the capital of the Russian Empire, was naturally a tempting target for the allies. As British propagandist Friedrich Engels wrote in 1854, “The more sanguine portion of the British public expect shortly to hear of Kronstadt bombarded, the approaches to St. Petersburg forced, and who knows? perhaps even the Union Jack hoisted on the glittering spire of the Russian Admiralty.”
To this end, Britain assembled the largest fleet seen since the Napoleonic Wars, placing it under the command of Vice Admiral Charles Napier – a seasoned naval commander who received his ‘baptism of fire’ in the Napoleonic wars. Counting French forces, this armada comprised 11 steam-powered and 15 sailing ships of the line, along with 32 steam frigates and 7 sailing frigates; the fleet mounted over 3,500 guns and carried a combined crew and marine force of over 30,000 men.
The Russian Baltic Fleet was inevitably inferior to the allied Anglo-French forces in both the number of men and technical equipment. When Napier’s squadron approached the entrance to the Gulf of Finland on April 19, the Russian ships prudently avoided combat, withdrawing under the protection of the guns and forts of Kronstadt and Sveaborg.
It seemed that the Anglo-French fleet would ultimately break the resistance of Kronstadt’s defenders and proceed to bombard St. Petersburg. Yet, on approaching the fortress, Admiral Napier encountered a surprise prepared by Russian engineers.
‘I could do nothing with my powerful fleet’
“Kronstadt is the decisive point for any naval attack against Russia in the Baltic. Take Kronstadt, and St. Petersburg is at your feet, the Russian Navy exists no longer, and Russia is reduced to what she was before Peter the Great,” Engels wrote before Napier’s armada set sail. And he had ample reason to think so.
Established by Russia’s first emperor, Peter I, Kronstadt was a maritime fortress featuring a formidable system of forts, batteries, and fortifications that shielded the Russian Empire’s capital from the sea. The straight-line distance from Kronstadt to the center of St. Petersburg is around 30 km. The Russian command clearly understood the strategic importance of the fortress and had prepared in advance to repel Anglo-French attacks.
Before the war, Emperor Nicholas I personally inspected the Kronstadt fortifications, and they were further secured. Consequently, in spring 1854, the Anglo-French fleet was confronted by granite fortifications arranged in multiple lines, engineered to deliver artillery crossfire, and armed with over 700 cannons.
Despite these advantages, however, this was a classic fortification strategy. While Kronstadt’s forts were formidable, the Anglo-French squadron had superior artillery firepower, making the outcome of the confrontation by no means obvious. Recognizing this, Russian engineers went a step further and undertook an unprecedented feat.
Russian engineers established the world’s first naval minefield to protect Kronstadt. In total, more than 1,500 of these “infernal machines” guarded the fortress from the sea. They were developed by academician Boris Jacobi – who created galvanic mines (detonated from shore via wire) – and Immanuel Nobel, founder of the famous industrial dynasty, who developed contact mines. Placed at a depth of 3.5 meters, the five-row mine lines (and later, 13-row mine lines) were a technological marvel of the time and proved impassable for enemy ships. (Now would be a fitting moment to recall stories about the ‘technologically backward Russian Empire’.)
Napier was initially unaware of the mines. It was only upon approaching Kronstadt at close range on June 14, 1854 that the British admiral was able to gauge the scale and strength of the Russian defenses. As Napier said, “I could do nothing with my powerful fleet, since any attack on Kronstadt or Sveaborg would have meant certain death.” After spending several weeks in the waters near Kronstadt and realizing that there would be no breakfast, not to mention dinner in St. Petersburg, Napier was forced to turn back. The fleet also left Sveaborg.
However, returning to England without any victory was not an option. While Napier had managed to constrain elite units of the Russian Army near the capital and disrupted trade in the Baltic, the ambitions of British command spread far beyond that. They needed at least a semblance of military success to return home with.
Doomed fortresses
Realizing the futility of the attempts to capture Kronstadt, the British fleet decided to plunder coastal villages. However, this hardly justified the enormous resources the British had expended. Thus, the allies resolved to direct their full might against Bomarsund – an isolated, unfinished fortress on the Aland Islands.
The Aland Islands hold a critically strategic position in this part of the Baltic Sea, being just 22 km from Finland and 38 km from Sweden. Russia seized these islands during its war with Sweden in 1808-1809. At the time, in the midst of a very cold winter, General Bagration’s troops traversed the frozen waters of the Baltic Sea basin, moving from Finland to the Alands and then to Sweden, less than 100 km from Stockholm.
Understanding the strategic importance of the islands, Russia began constructing the Bomarsund fortress. Yet by the outbreak of the Crimean War, it was only partially complete and had only a quarter of the planned towers and weapons. The garrison comprised just 1,600 soldiers; their ammunition was extremely limited. Once a forward outpost of the Russian Empire, Bomarsund now found itself completely cut off as Napier’s fleet appeared in the Baltic.
The massive Anglo-French fleet approached the doomed fortress. Bombardment lasted several weeks before the Anglo-French coalition landed 11,000 troops, supported by dozens of heavy siege cannons. The Russian forces found themselves in a hopeless situation: Their artillery was far inferior to the long-range guns of the Anglo-French ships, and the invading force outnumbered the defenders six to one.
Despite these odds, the garrison fought fiercely. After another fortnight of intense fighting, on August 16, 1854, the Anglo-French troops finally breached the outer defense line of the fortress. By that point, the garrison had spent nearly all the ammunition, leaving Commander Yakov Bodisko with no choice but to surrender.
The British acknowledged the heroism of the defenders, and Bodisko was allowed to retain his sword while in captivity. Upon his return from imprisonment, a military tribunal deemed his actions at Bomarsund justified and commendable.
The garrison of another Russian fortress, Gangut (now the Finnish city of Hanko), did not wait for a similar fate to befall it, and blew up its own fortifications on imperial orders. Nevertheless, the success of the Anglo-French forces in the Baltic was mostly limited to these minor incidents. As British media noted, “English guns did not speak in the Baltic Sea. They whispered in Bomarsund, but the whole of Europe waited for them to resonate in Kronstadt and Sveaborg. One could not have dealt a heavier blow to Britain’s naval honor.”
Second attempt
British accounts of the Baltic campaign assess Napier’s actions in a rather flattering way, implying that though he didn’t secure any significant victories, his forces managed to tie down the Russian fleet and prevented reinforcements from reaching Crimea.
This theory is fundamentally flawed, since during wartime, Russia would have defended its capital no matter what. It’s hard to imagine the Baltic fleet abandoning St. Petersburg and making its way through the English Channel and Gibraltar, navigating hostile waters controlled by England and France, on the way to the Black Sea. Thus, the first year of the Crimean War in the Baltic was clearly a success for Russia: It distracted the Anglo-French fleet, which expended great resources without achieving significant military success.
The winter of 1854-1855 proved particularly harsh, particularly in the primary theater of war, Crimea; the allied forces got bogged down near Sevastopol. The military challenges and the inefficient use of resources, including during the Baltic campaign, were so severe that Aberdeen’s ministry was forced to resign. By the 1855 campaign, the allies urgently needed to turn their fortunes around.
For operations in the Baltic Sea that year, they again assembled a massive fleet of 67 ships. Just like the previous year, they set their sights on Kronstadt, hoping to lure out the Russian fleet stationed there. However, they only stumbled on underwater mines. Four British steamers became the first victims of these mines, leading the Anglo-French command to realize that capturing Kronstadt was out of the question.
Following this, light Anglo-French vessels began raiding the Finnish coast and plundering local fishermen. Meanwhile, the main forces of the allies aimed to capture Sveaborg – the second most significant Russian stronghold in the region, which defended Helsingfors.
In August, the Anglo-French squadron approached Sveaborg with plans to destroy the fortress and incinerate the strategically vital Russian shipyards. However, after a 45-hour bombardment and firing over 20,000 shells at the fortress, they failed to inflict any substantial damage on it. Russian military engineers had set up impressive defensive positions.
With no other options, the British and French had no choice but to leave the Baltic Sea by autumn 1855. This effectively marked the end of the Crimean War in the Baltic.
Lessons learned
Beyond the disastrous military operations, Britain also faced diplomatic setbacks in the Baltic.
After occupying the Aland Islands, Admiral Napier suggested that Sweden take them over. Following the resignation of Aberdeen’s ministry, the new British prime minister, Palmerston, spent all of 1855 actively working to draw Sweden and Norway – then united by a personal union – into the war against Russia. Britain frightened them with tales of ‘Russian imperialism’ while simultaneously hinting at the potential return of territories lost in previous wars with Russia.
In Sweden, revanchist sentiments were strong but pragmatism ultimately prevailed. The country declined to occupy the Aland Islands and did not sign a defensive alliance with Britain until the end of 1855. This was a disappointing outcome for London, which intended to open a second front against Russia.
Sweden’s pragmatic approach is understandable: Having suffered major defeats in past wars with Russia and lost the Baltics and Finland, it recognized the futility of engaging in another war with the Russian Empire on Britain’s behalf.
With its advanced military technology and strategic decisions in the Baltic, 19th-century Russia effectively anticipated the military strategy of the 21st century called ‘anti-access/area denial’. While the Anglo-French fleet formally surpassed the Baltic Fleet of the Russian Empire, it was paralyzed by Russia’s impregnable fortifications and minefields.
Today, various countries are implementing similar strategies. China has developed hypersonic anti-ship missiles known as ‘carrier killers’ to counter the US Navy, effectively closing off the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea in the event of war. Another example is Iran. While it clearly pales in military strength compared to the US, its missiles and drones enable it to control the Strait of Hormuz, making any US naval operation in the region costly.
However, the most significant lessons from this conflict were undoubtedly learned by Russia. Although the Baltic campaign was successful for Russia and the powerful Anglo-French fleet didn’t achieve much, the war in general ended unsuccessfully for the empire. It exposed numerous areas of governance that required serious improvement. As a result of the Crimean War, Russia undertook crucial reforms in military affairs, finance, economics, law, and public life. This ushered in a new and more prosperous era.
