Study reveals which values actually stop voters from supporting antidemocratic politicians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:00:29 UTC
23:00:29 KST

New research suggests that an individual’s personal commitment to the institutions of liberal democracy can act as a buffer against voting for politicians who threaten democratic rules. The findings indicate that while political party loyalty heavily influences voter choices, a deep-seated support for democratic principles helps people resist candidates who might otherwise erode democratic norms. The study was published in Public Opinion Quarterly.
Democratic backsliding is an ongoing concern in many modern nations. This process occurs when elected officials gradually dismantle democratic institutions, such as free elections, independent courts, and a free press. A major factor driving this decline is the willingness of ordinary citizens to vote for candidates who violate democratic rules.
Past studies show that voters generally dislike antidemocratic behavior in theory. Yet they often end up supporting politicians who break democratic rules if those politicians belong to their preferred political party or share their policy views. This creates a tension between a voter’s abstract democratic values and their practical political loyalties.
The research was led by Christopher Claassen, a professor of political behavior at the School of Social and Political Sciences at the University of Glasgow. The study aimed to understand whether specific aspects of a country’s political culture might help prevent this trend.
“A growing body of research shows that voters frequently support politicians who threaten democratic institutions, particularly when those politicians belong to their preferred party or agree with them on important issues,” Claassen told PsyPost. “But we know much less about whether people’s underlying attitudes toward democracy help them resist those pressures.”
“I wanted to connect that recent work on democratic backsliding with the much older political-culture literature, which argues that citizens’ orientations toward democracy can help sustain democratic government,” he explained.
To test this, the researcher analyzed data from 5,951 participants across three democracies currently facing backsliding pressures. The sample included 1,983 people in the United States, 1,967 in Poland, and 2,001 in South Korea. The participants took part in a candidate-choice experiment, which is a type of survey design that simulates an election. Participants were shown pairs of hypothetical political candidates and asked to choose who they would vote for, completing twelve different matchups in total.
The candidates varied randomly in age, gender, occupational background, political party, and policy positions on taxes and gender equality. The central feature of the experiment was that each matchup pitted one prodemocratic candidate against one antidemocratic candidate. The antidemocratic candidates proposed actions like cutting polling stations in opposition areas, ignoring court rulings, or prosecuting journalists. The prodemocratic candidates took the opposite stances, promising to respect these institutions.
Before the simulated elections, the survey measured six dimensions of political culture for each participant. These included preferences for democracy over autocracy, support for liberal democratic institutions, and trust in political institutions. The survey also measured political tolerance, which is the willingness to allow political opponents to have civil rights. Finally, the survey assessed emancipative values, which prioritize individual autonomy and equality, alongside authoritarian values, which prioritize obedience and conformity.
Across the three countries, support for liberal democracy was the most consistent predictor of a willingness to vote for the prodemocratic candidate. This specific measure captures a person’s backing of core institutions like free speech, equal voting rights, and the rule of law. People who scored high on this measure were consistently less likely to reward candidates who threatened these democratic pillars.
“One broader implication is that democratic culture is not a single thing – its multidimensional,” Claassen noted. “I examined several kinds of orientations that political scientists have linked to democracy, and they behaved quite differently.”
“Support for liberal-democratic institutions was the most consistent predictor of pro-democratic choice, which suggests that the particular democratic commitments citizens hold may matter more than simply possessing a generally ‘democratic’ political culture,” he added.
The author looked closely at difficult scenarios known as cross-pressured choices. These are situations where a voter must choose between a prodemocratic candidate from an opposing party and an antidemocratic candidate from their own party. Even in these demanding situations, support for liberal democracy made a noticeable difference. It helped voters resist the temptation to blindly support their own political side.
Specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in a person’s support for liberal democracy was associated with a 2 to 12 percentage point increase in the probability of choosing the prodemocratic candidate across party lines. This shift depended on the specific country and the statistical model used. While this increase might seem modest, it represents a meaningful shift in competitive elections.
“The effects are meaningful but not enormous,” the researcher said. “That can matter in a close election, but the results also show how powerful partisan loyalties remain.”
Other aspects of political culture showed mixed or weak associations. For instance, having a general preference for democracy over autocracy and holding emancipative values sometimes predicted prodemocratic choices. However, these factors did not predict voting choices consistently across all countries and policy scenarios. Interestingly, trust in political institutions showed almost no relationship with resisting antidemocratic candidates.
“Two findings surprised me,” Claassen explained. “First, political trust had virtually no consistent relationship with choosing the pro-democratic candidate, despite a long tradition of treating trust in institutions as important for democracy. Trust may matter for democracy in other ways, but our results suggest that it does not necessarily make people more willing to defend democratic institutions at the ballot box.”
Claassen was also struck by the weak results for authoritarian values. “There is an obvious theoretical connection between authoritarian values and authoritarian political systems – they even share the same name – but those values were not strong predictors of candidate choice in my study,” he noted. “It may be that these underlying social values are simply too distant from concrete decisions about electoral choices.”
The statistical models controlled for various factors to isolate the role of political culture. These controls included age, gender, education, income, and geographic region. The models also accounted for political interest, preferred party, and the participants’ actual positions on redistribution and gender equality.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The voting choices were made in a simulated survey environment rather than a real election. In actual elections, voters face intense campaign messaging and social pressures that might alter how they weigh democratic violations against party loyalty. The hypothetical nature of the survey means we cannot be certain these exact percentage shifts would appear at a real ballot box.
The findings are also observational regarding political culture. Because a person’s values and beliefs cannot be randomly assigned in an experiment, the results show an association rather than a direct cause-and-effect relationship. We can see that strong democratic beliefs predict certain voting patterns, but we cannot isolate those beliefs from other lifelong personal traits that might influence a voter’s decisions.
“The candidate attributes were experimentally randomized, but respondents’ democratic orientations were measured rather than manipulated,” Claassen noted, reinforcing that the relationship should be understood as an association rather than a causal effect.
Finally, the pull of partisanship remains incredibly strong. In the Polish and South Korean samples, the predicted support for prodemocratic candidates from an opposing party often remained below 50 percent, even among citizens with high democratic commitments. This suggests that while strong democratic values help people resist backsliding, they do not always create a majority willing to cross party lines to punish bad actors.
“I would avoid interpreting the findings as showing that strong democratic attitudes will necessarily defeat anti-democratic politicians,” Claassen cautioned.
“The main takeaway is that what ordinary citizens think about democracy does matter,” the researcher summarized. “People who more strongly support liberal-democratic institutions were more likely to choose the pro-democratic candidate, including in situations where their partisan identity or ideological position pulled them in the opposite direction.”
“So democratic resilience is not something entirely outside citizens’ hands,” he added. “At the same time, public support is only one part of the story: what political leaders, parties, and institutions do matters enormously for whether democracy survives.”
Looking ahead, the researcher plans to refine how these attitudes are studied. “One next step is to develop more fine-grained measures of democratic orientations,” Claassen noted. “Most research focuses either on support for democratic institutions or democracy itself, and I think there is room to measure underlying democratic values more carefully and systematically.”
“I’m also interested in why people sometimes bring their democratic attitudes to bear on a voting decision and sometimes do not,” he said. “In particular, I’m looking at factors such as attitude importance and accessibility: whether democracy is something people care deeply about and whether those considerations are readily available in their minds when they actually make a political choice.”
The study, “Voting for Democracy? Testing Political-Cultural Constraints on Democratic Backsliding,” was authored by Christopher Claassen.

Britain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:00:06 UTC
23:00:06 KST

The “complex and unsettling” story of what Britain knew during the Holocaust is being explored amid plans to create a new permanent national memorial.
An exhibition highlighting how news of the atrocity reached Britain much earlier than is commonly understood will tour the country after being viewed privately by MPs at Portcullis House on the parliamentary estate at Westminster in September.
The research draws upon newspaper reporting, broadcasts, academic scholarship, witness testimony and government archives. The exhibition is a sample of a more extensive, permanent exhibition for the national Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which is planned for a site in London.
Martin Winstone, the senior historical adviser to the Holocaust Educational Trust, said: “There’s a feeling today that Britain really only found out about the Holocaust at the end of the war. But in 1942, the year in which most victims of the Holocaust were murdered, you couldn’t really escape this information in Britain. It was in every newspaper. It was on the BBC.
“The Manchester Guardian was the newspaper that reported most extensively on the Holocaust, taking a crusading position that there was more the British government and allied governments could be doing.”
For years, the Manchester Guardian, which was banned from Germany in 1933 for highlighting Adolf Hitler’s antisemitism, called for immigration restrictions to be lifted for Jews, lobbied for pressure to be applied to neutral nations to open their borders to refugees and for special rescue measures, realising that “the Nazis were aiming at the complete elimination of an entire group of people”.
Much of the information about the Holocaust, including the locations of death camps, was smuggled out of Poland – where the murders were “happening in plain sight” – by couriers to the London-based Polish government-in-exile.
Winstone said: “It was a challenging situation. There were lots of things the government had to deal with. And for much of that war, Britain was on the defensive.
“On one level, the government’s response was always, ‘we’ll win the war, that’s how we stop this’; while critics said, ‘there’ll be nobody left to save, if that’s what you’re waiting for’.”
During the second world war, the government commissioned reports on antisemitism in Britain, with agents opening people’s mail and recording conversations overheard in air raid shelters to gauge public opinion.
In what Winstone described as a “complex and unsettling story”, Ministry of Information bulletins revealed that while there was mass public sympathy for Jews in occupied Europe, it contended with anti-migration and antisemitic sentiment.
Winstone added: “Nearly everybody in Britain was disgusted about these mass murders, but at the same time you start getting more antisemitic discourse about Jews in Britain – that Jews were running the black market, avoiding military service and spreading panic.
“Even before the mass murder began, during the 1930s, there was a significant body of opinion which felt Britain should not be admitting refugees.”
Winstone said UK immigration laws in the 1930s were highly restrictive, in part because of antisemitism earlier in the 20th century. But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938, Britain relaxed restrictions to some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas. The Manchester Guardian reported how Jewish communities and Quakers in the city set up organisations to support refugees.
British women – from MP Eleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said.
A 2021 survey by Claims Conference found 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941.
UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial.
The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed.
The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The Holocaust Memorial Act 2026 received royal assent this year, granting legal clearance and government funding for the project.

Leaked Files Reveal Struck Russian Plant Was Feeding Kh-101, R-37M and Oreshnik Missile Programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:56:14 UTC
22:56:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Leaked Files Reveal Struck Russian Plant Was Feeding Kh-101, R-37M and Oreshnik Missile Programs
A Russian optical plant struck on September 26 was involved in the production chains of at least seven Russian missile programs, including the Kh-101 cruise missile, R-37M long-range air-to-air missile, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile, newly published internal documents indicate.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Dallas Analytics on September 26, records obtained from the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, or AOMZ, show that the facility’s role extended well beyond its publicly known production of tank sights, rangefinders, and thermal imaging equipment.
The documents include internal correspondence, state contract records, and industrial cooperation schedules covering the period from April 2023 through March 2025. They involve AOMZ, Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation, the Michurinsk Plant Progress, and the Kurganpribor design bureau.
Dallas Analytics said the correspondence also shows direct oversight of production by Russian Defense Ministry military representatives stationed at enterprises participating in the state defense order system.
One document dated September 9, 2024, refers to seven state contracts connected to AOMZ’s 2025 production program. Five of those contracts were signed in 2022.
An attached two-page production schedule contains 71 component entries, identifying suppliers, required quantities, installation rates, and funding. The component budget for the 2025 program totaled 583.6 million rubles, with 497.6 million rubles already paid in advances, according to the documents.
The records also provide details on components used in several Russian cruise missiles.
For the Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile, Dallas Analytics identified AOMZ as the producer of two major assemblies: the Otblesk navigation lidar and a flight automation unit responsible for controlling missile systems and flight surfaces.
The Kh-101 is carried by Russian Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers and has been extensively used in strikes against Ukraine. The same records connect AOMZ to flight automation systems for the Kh-35U and Kh-59/Kh-69 missile families.
Dallas Analytics also identified 44 component suppliers in the plant’s documentation, including Russian manufacturers of capacitors, resistors, semiconductors, connectors, relays, and optoelectronic equipment.
Among them is TRV-Engineering, the procurement arm of the Tactical Missiles Corporation holding. The company is listed as supplying microcircuits for the Kh-101 navigation system. Dallas Analytics has previously identified TRV-Engineering as an intermediary involved in obtaining foreign electronic components.
Separate correspondence reviewed by Dallas Analytics names AOMZ as an assembler and supplier of components for the system designated 760K (L), described in the documents as a modification of the R-74 family of air-to-air missiles developed by Russia’s Vympel design bureau.
The R-74 family forms part of the weapons package developed for Russia’s Su-57 fighter aircraft. The documents also place AOMZ within the production chain for components used in the guidance system of the Oreshnik, Russia’s nuclear-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile.
Another document, dated March 4, 2025, details plans to increase production of components for the R-37M long-range air-to-air missile from 2026.
According to Dallas Analytics, Tactical Missiles Corporation informed AOMZ that the Russian Aerospace Forces were seeking higher delivery volumes and gave the plant three days to determine whether it could meet the requirement.
The requested annual production included 500 units each of several switching, power supply, battery activation, wiring, and circuit-board assemblies, together with 1,000 missile housings.
Based on the quantities listed in the correspondence, Dallas Analytics assessed that the request corresponded to components for as many as 500 R-37M missiles annually.
The R-37M is a long-range air-to-air missile with a reported engagement range of roughly 300 kilometers and is used by Russian aircraft against targets at extended distances.
The investigation also links AOMZ to the production of seeker components for the Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, which is designed to target radar systems.
AOMZ has been subject to international restrictions for several years. The plant was added to the US Entity List in April 2022 as a facility associated with Tactical Missiles Corporation and has also faced sanctions from the European Union, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand, and Ukraine.
Dallas Analytics argues that the documentation shows how Russian missile production continues to rely on broader networks of suppliers and procurement intermediaries despite restrictions placed directly on final manufacturers.
The group assessed that a prolonged disruption at AOMZ could affect production of navigation and flight-control systems for the Kh-101 and other cruise missiles, electrical assemblies for the R-37M, and components used in anti-radiation weapons.
However, Dallas Analytics noted that disruption at one production site would more likely delay output than permanently eliminate Russia’s ability to manufacture the systems, particularly if alternative supply chains and component procurement networks remain operational.
Earlier, in July 2025, Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov region. Russian authorities said air defenses had repelled the attack, while eyewitness footage showed drones approaching the facility followed by explosions and smoke.

Why Ireland's match against Israel will be like no other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:55:47 UTC
22:55:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Ireland's football match against Israel will be like no other
Ireland will face Israel in the UEFA Nations League on Sunday after an extraordinary four-hour meeting in which players voted on whether to boycott the controversial fixture over Israel's genocidal war in Gaza.
The match in Debrecen, Hungary, was thrown into doubt on Saturday after goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad, saying that he believed it would be "wrong to participate" in the two upcoming games against Israel.
His decision prompted hours of discussions between players, coaches and Football Association of Ireland (FAI) officials, delaying both training and a scheduled press conference.
FAI chief executive David Courell later said a "significant majority" of players had voted to fulfil the fixture, although he declined to disclose the result. Irish media reported that some players opposed playing, with The Irish Times reporting that one teammate confronted Bazunu directly during the heated discussions.
Bazunu later said his decision was "not in opposition to the Israeli people or the Jewish community", but in opposition to the killing of civilians.
"There are few times when you get a chance in life to stand for something bigger and I strongly believe that this is one of them," he said.
Midfielder Jason Knight had already become the first Ireland player to publicly question the fixture following Thursday's defeat to Kosovo, saying he did not believe the game against Israel should go ahead.
Despite ultimately deciding to play, the Irish squad will stage a series of protests around Sunday's match.
Players will wear black armbands in recognition of those killed in the conflict, while the team will not participate in elements of the usual pre-match ceremony, including the traditional handshake with their Israeli counterparts. Players and the FAI will also make a charitable donation from match fees and revenues.
Israel's football association responded to the vote by declaring that "football has won", while Israeli players said they would still offer to shake hands with the Irish team.
Mounting pressure
Pressure on Ireland to boycott the matches has intensified for months, despite the FAI itself having formally called on UEFA to suspend Israel from European football.
The association nevertheless says refusing to fulfil the fixtures could result in forfeiting six points, possible relegation from the Nations League and further disciplinary measures, with consequences for Ireland's international ranking and qualification prospects.
The controversy escalated further this month when Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
The Israeli FA accused Hallgrimsson of displaying "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy", prompting Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin to intervene, describing its response as "unacceptable" and call for the remarks to be withdrawn.
Hallgrimsson subsequently acknowledged that using such strong language had drawn attention away from football, saying it had been "not clever" from a leadership perspective, but stressed on Saturday that taking the field did not mean players supported or accepted what was happening in Gaza.
"Nobody is comfortable playing this game for so many reasons," he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris has also opposed a boycott, arguing that Ireland rather than Israel would suffer the sporting consequences and urging that pressure not be placed on individual players. Opposition parties including Sinn Fein however have called for Ireland not to play.
Even Irish broadcaster RTE has distanced itself from treating the fixtures normally. While contractually obliged to show them, it will have no studio presentation or punditry, will use international-feed commentary and has taken no advertising or sponsorship around the broadcasts.
Sunday's match is nominally a home game for Israel but will take place in Debrecen because Israel is unable to host UEFA fixtures.
The return fixture on 4 October will be equally unusual. Ireland has moved its own "home" game from Dublin to Backa Topola in Serbia, where it will be played behind closed doors.
Ireland supporters have not been allocated tickets for Sunday's match, meaning that when the two teams finally take the field, almost nothing surrounding the fixture will resemble an ordinary international football match.

Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:53:39 UTC
22:53:39 KST

Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- UF Health
- Summary:
- A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.
- Share:
A widely used supplement for joint pain has been linked to a potentially concerning outcome in people with early cognitive problems.
Researchers at the University of Florida found that glucosamine use was associated with a greater likelihood that mild cognitive impairment would progress to dementia. Mild cognitive impairment, often shortened to MCI, describes measurable problems with memory or thinking that are greater than expected with normal aging but do not necessarily interfere substantially with everyday life.
The findings come from a large retrospective analysis of patient health records, supported by experiments involving human brain tissue and mouse models of Alzheimer's disease. The results remain preliminary and will need to be tested in a human clinical trial, but the researchers say they add to growing evidence that disrupted metabolism may play an important role in neurodegeneration.
The study was published in Nature Metabolism.
A Popular Supplement Comes Under Scrutiny
"In the United States, there are about 7 million people living with Alzheimer's and millions more with related dementias such as Lewy body or frontotemporal dementia," said senior author Ramon Sun, Ph.D., director of the Center for Advanced Spatial Biomolecule Research and associate director for innovation of UF's McKnight Brain Institute. "A lot of these people actively take an over-the-counter supplement that could be making their disease progression worse."
Glucosamine is widely sold without a prescription and is especially popular among older adults who take it for joint discomfort and joint health. Because of how commonly it is used, the researchers wanted to know whether it might influence Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, known as ADRD.
Working with Yi Guo, Ph.D., and Jiang Bian, Ph.D., the team used artificial intelligence to analyze deidentified UF Health records collected from 2012 to 2024.
The researchers focused on patients diagnosed with either ADRD or mild cognitive impairment, or MCI. In both groups, 8% of patients reported using glucosamine. That included 1,896 people with ADRD and 2,750 people with MCI.
Glucosamine Linked to Dementia Progression
After accounting for age, sex and demographics, the researchers found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood that mild cognitive impairment would progress to dementia.
Among people who already had ADRD, glucosamine use was also associated with a 25% higher mortality risk, meaning a greater likelihood of death during a defined period of time.
The researchers did not observe that mortality association in the MCI group. That difference suggests glucosamine may have a stronger effect once dementia is already established.
Importantly, the health record findings do not show that glucosamine itself causes dementia to progress. Observational studies can reveal associations, but other differences between people who take a supplement and those who do not may contribute to the results.
"The electronic health record data are very provocative," said Matt Gentry, Ph.D., chair of UF's Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and a study co-author. "While it's an association and not proof of causality, it does raise an important clinical question that now deserves much more attention."
A Metabolic Pathway May Help Explain the Link
The researchers also uncovered evidence of a biological mechanism that could help explain the association.
Their work points to a metabolic pathway involving the attachment of sugar structures to proteins. This process is a normal and important part of cell biology, but the researchers found signs that it becomes excessively active in Alzheimer's disease.
Sun said that abnormal activity in this pathway could eventually become a target for new treatments.
"Our results suggest that altered metabolism is a significant contributor to Alzheimer's progression and, in addition, addressing the metabolic defect could be an important complement to approaches focused on Alzheimer's plaques and tangles," Sun said.
Plaques and tangles are two of the best known features of Alzheimer's disease. Plaques are abnormal deposits of a protein called amyloid beta that accumulate between brain cells, while tangles are twisted forms of the tau protein that develop inside neurons. Much Alzheimer's research has traditionally focused on these abnormalities, but scientists are increasingly studying additional processes that may contribute to the disease.
Mapping Thousands of Molecules in the Brain
A spatial technology developed in Sun's laboratory helped researchers examine the metabolic changes in much greater detail.
"This technology allows us to examine thousands and thousands of molecules created when the body breaks down food or drugs and to uncover intricate pathways that otherwise would stay hidden," Sun said.
The team then focused specifically on glucosamine. Glucosamine is a naturally occurring, sugar-related molecule that can cross the blood-brain barrier, the protective boundary that tightly controls which substances can move from the bloodstream into brain tissue.
Once inside the brain, glucosamine can enter biochemical pathways that construct complex sugar structures and attach them to proteins. Commercial glucosamine supplements can be produced from materials including shellfish shells or corn.
According to the researchers, the effects of glucosamine may depend heavily on the biological environment in which it is acting. A healthy brain and a brain affected by Alzheimer's may therefore respond differently to the same molecule.
The Alzheimer's brain appeared to be particularly vulnerable to this metabolic pathway.
Mouse Experiments Point to a Possible Mechanism
To explore the mechanism more closely, the scientists studied genetically modified mice.
Glucosamine significantly increased the attachment of sugar residues to proteins inside cells. At the same time, glucosamine-treated mice developed worse deficits in "social memory" -- or memory of recognition -- compared with the other animals.
When the researchers used a chemical treatment to suppress the sugar attachment process, memory performance improved.
That experiment suggested that excessive sugar tagging could play a direct role in the memory problems seen in the animals rather than simply occurring alongside them.
Human Alzheimer's Brain Tissue Shows the Same Pattern
The researchers next examined human brain tissue with Stefan Prokop, M.D.
Brain specimens from people with Alzheimer's disease, provided by the UF Neuromedicine Brain and Tissue Bank, showed significantly more sugar attachment than tissue from normal controls.
Combined with the mouse experiments and health record analysis, the findings suggest that abnormal metabolism may be more than a secondary consequence of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers reported that it could instead contribute to the disease process itself.
"Proteins are the cell's molecular machines, and many of them need sugar tags added in just the right way to fold correctly, travel to the right place and do their jobs," Gentry said. "What we found in Alzheimer's is that this sugar-tagging system appears to be overactive. The Alzheimer's brain is adding too many of these sugar structures, and this seems to contribute to the disease rather than protect against it."
The results raise a potentially important question about glucosamine use among people with cognitive impairment or dementia, but they do not yet establish that people should stop taking the supplement. A controlled human clinical trial will be needed to determine whether glucosamine directly accelerates Alzheimer's progression and, if so, which patients may be most vulnerable.

No: 184, 27 September 2026, Regarding the Visit of H.E. Hakan Fidan, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, to the United Arab Emirates

European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
September 27, 2026
In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.
But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.
Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:
Vienna: The city is the landlord
The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions.
The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.
Basel: Public land, private buildings
The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.
The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.
Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes
It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035
Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.
Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers
The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.
The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.
Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing
It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.
In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).
The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.

U.S. Navy Tests Blackbeard Hypersonic Missile on F/A-18F Super Hornet

Unknown Publisher

22:41:15 KST

The U.S. Navy has begun flight testing the Blackbeard hypersonic missile on an F/A-18F Super Hornet fighter.
The Naval Air Systems Command released a video showing the testing of the new missile on X.
Two missiles were mounted on the aircraft during the test flight, allowing the Navy to assess the missile’s integration with the aircraft.
The released footage shows the aircraft flying with the missiles mounted on its weapon stations but does not show them being launched.
U.S. company Castelion is developing Blackbeard under the Multi-Mission Affordable Capacity Effector (MACE) program.
The U.S. Navy describes it as a long-range hypersonic strike missile designed to engage land and maritime targets. It is intended for deployment from carrier-based fighters, including the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet.
One of the program’s features is its focus on mass production and a relatively low unit cost.
The U.S. Navy plans to acquire a significant number of Blackbeard missiles to increase the carrier air wing’s weapons capacity and expand the long-range strike assets aircraft can employ against defended targets.
According to Navy plans, a single F/A-18E/F will be able to carry up to four of the missiles.
In U.S. Navy budget documents, MACE is listed as a separate procurement program.
Plans for fiscal years 2028-2031 call for the acquisition of more than 4,000 missiles, indicating that the program is intended for full-scale production.
Militarny previously reported that U.S. startup Castelion, founded by former SpaceX employees, had demonstrated its low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missile.

Gaza's destroyed sewage plants spread pollution amid devastation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:40:41 UTC
22:40:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Contaminated water in Gaza: Destroyed sewage plants deepen humanitarian crisis and spread pollution beyond the Strip
For families in Gaza, finding drinking water has become a daily struggle, and even paying for a container does not guarantee that what they bring home is safe.
In al-Mawasi in Khan Younis, 45-year-old Omar Abu Salah lives with his four children in a worn-out tent, in a camp with other displaced residents, surrounded by pools of wastewater.
His family buys water from trucks supplied by desalination plants, but Abu Salah told The New Arab that there is no reliable way to verify its quality or how it was stored and transported.
"We have to buy water because we have no other choice," he said, explaining that the cost has become a heavy burden on a family already struggling to afford basic necessities.
"We need it for drinking, cooking and washing. We cannot simply stop buying it," he added.
In al-Zawaida in central Gaza, 36-year-old Saniya Abu Steita faces a similar struggle with her three children.
She told TNA that her children frequently suffer from gastrointestinal problems, forcing her to seek treatment at mobile clinics.
Regularly buying bottled water is beyond the family's means, while other available sources may pose contamination risks.
"Before the war, my children did not suffer like this so often," she said.
Their experiences reflect a much wider crisis that has developed during nearly three years of genocidal Israeli war. Gaza's water and sanitation infrastructure has suffered extensive destruction, while mass displacement has placed unprecedented pressure on systems that were already severely strained before October 2023.
The result is a cycle in which residents struggle to obtain clean water while untreated sewage accumulates around homes and displacement sites, contaminating land, groundwater and the sea.
A water and sanitation system in ruins
Since Israel's war on Gaza began in October 2023, wells, desalination plants, water networks, sewage systems and pumping stations have sustained extensive damage.
According to Doctors Without Borders (MSF), Israeli bombardment has destroyed or damaged around 90 percent of Gaza's water and sanitation infrastructure.
Even before the war, Gaza's water system was under severe strain. Around 80 percent of its water supply came from the coastal aquifer, but decades of over-extraction, combined with seawater intrusion and sewage contamination, had already rendered much of the groundwater unsuitable for human consumption, MSF said.
"More than 210 of Gaza's 320 wells have been destroyed, while around 80 percent of desalination plants have been damaged, leaving only one central desalination plant operating," environmental expert Saeed Al-Aklouk told TNA.
The widespread use of cesspits has further intensified the problem. Al-Aklouk estimates that around 320,000 cesspits are discharging untreated wastewater into the ground, threatening further contamination of the aquifer.
UNICEF reported in May 2026 that 82 percent of Gaza households faced water insecurity, while up to 70 percent could not access the minimum six litres per person daily minimum for drinking and cooking. Desalination output also fell from 20,000 to 16,000 cubic metres per day due to shortages of essential supplies.
"Overall daily water production fell from approximately 300,000 cubic metres before the war to less than 120,000 cubic metres in February 2026," Munzer Salem, director general of the Gaza Water Authority, told TNA.
The sanitation system has also largely collapsed. OCHA reported in September that all six wastewater treatment plants were out of service and around 70 percent of sewage pumping stations had stopped operating, resulting in more than 150,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage being discharged into the environment daily.
The 2026 Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment estimated damage to Gaza's water, sanitation and hygiene sector at around US$1.7 billion, with 88 percent of above-ground assets and 76 percent of underground networks damaged.
Gaza municipal spokesperson Hosni Muhanna told TNA that around 220,000 meters of sewage networks were destroyed during the war, along with eight pumping stations.
Municipal crews have managed to temporarily restart some facilities, he says, but operations remain constrained by shortages of electricity, fuel, batteries and maintenance materials.
From Gaza's sewage to the Mediterranean
The destruction of Gaza's sewage system has created another problem: even where wastewater can be pumped away, there is often nowhere to treat it.
Omer Shtayyeh, deputy executive director of the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU), told TNA that Gaza's pre-war sewage system consisted of around 74 pumping stations connected to nearly 2,000 kilometers of sewage networks, lines and manholes, as well as five central treatment plants.
"Around 80 percent of the system has sustained partial or total damage," he said.
All five treatment plants are currently out of service, according to Shtayyeh, while emergency rehabilitation work is underway at the Sheik Ajlin plant. Under current conditions, restoring the facility could take six to seven months.
"Out of 28 pumping stations, 18 are currently operating in accessible areas, while crews are working to repair another ten," he explained.
But restoring pumping capacity alone cannot solve the problem because wastewater still needs to be treated before discharge.
Shtayyeh noted that untreated sewage is currently discharged through around ten main outlets along Gaza's coastline, with daily volumes estimated at between 40,000 and 45,000 cubic meters.
The consequences can extend beyond the areas where the sewage is discharged. Marine currents move along the coastline, carrying pollutants away from their original source and potentially towards Israel.
A September 2026 report by The Guardian said several Israeli Mediterranean desalination plants experienced disruptions after an unusual microalgae bloom clogged filters at five of the country's six major desalination facilities.
Scientists cited by the newspaper said the destruction of wastewater infrastructure in Gaza and the resulting discharge of untreated sewage into the sea could be among the factors contributing to conditions that fuel such blooms.
Israeli environmental organisation Zalul has warned that "pollutants do not recognise political borders", pointing to nitrogen and phosphorus in untreated sewage as nutrients that can encourage the growth of microalgae and cyanobacteria.
Jack Gilron, professor emeritus and a water desalination expert at Ben-Gurion University's Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research, said that untreated sewage discharged from Gaza increases the risk to desalination infrastructure along the southern Mediterranean coast.
For Gaza's residents, however, the consequences remain most immediate at the household level.
Families are forced to choose between spending scarce money on water of uncertain quality and relying on sources that may expose them to contamination.
Around them, sewage collects in streets, displacement sites and damaged drainage basins, while the infrastructure needed to contain and treat it remains largely out of service.
The destruction has created interconnected crises: declining water production, damaged distribution networks, groundwater contamination, inadequate sanitation and the discharge of untreated wastewater into the sea.
Temporary repairs to individual wells or pumping stations may restore limited services, but they cannot rebuild a system in which most infrastructure has been damaged and treatment capacity has collapsed, according to Shtayyeh.

Zurich will extend assisted suicide to private care homes and hospitals
Unknown

Zurich will extend assisted suicide to private care homes and hospitals
The canton of Zurich is set to become the first German-speaking Swiss canton to extend access to assisted suicide to all care homes – both public and private – as well as to hospitals and rehabilitation clinics. On Sunday, voters overwhelmingly approved a legislative amendment to this effect.
A strong majority of 68.11% of voters backed a counter-proposal requiring private care homes, hospitals and rehabilitation clinics to allow assisted suicide on their premises. The government had opposed the proposal.
In the canton of Zurich, only care homes with a municipal service mandate have been required to allow assisted suicide since 2023. The approved counter-proposal takes up the idea of universal access sought by a popular initiative, which has since been withdrawn. However, it excludes psychiatric clinics and prisons.
More
Self-determination over religious freedom: Zurich sends strong signal on assisted dying
Zurich thus aligns itself with the French cantons of Vaud, Neuchâtel, Geneva and Valais in the area of hospitals. Its legislation goes even further by including private care homes.

Spain PM vows action as housing protest sparked by Madrid eviction grows

Spain PM vows action as housing protest sparked by Madrid eviction grows
- A protest camp in Madrid's Puerta del Sol emerged after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, highlighting Spain's severe housing affordability crisis.
- Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged swift government action and proposed a housing law with rental protections, but faces parliamentary challenges.
- The crisis reflects a national shortage of 700,000 homes, soaring rents, and public frustration, intensifying ahead of the 2027 general election.
AI generated
MADRID – A growing protest camp in the heart of Madrid over unaffordable housing pushed Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Sept 27 to pledge swift government action.
Hundreds of protesters on the weekend set up tents in the capital’s busy Puerta del Sol public square to press their demands.
The movement was triggered by a police eviction on Sept 23 of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong Madrid apartment.
The woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was carried out on a stretcher after the police broke down her door, in a scene that caused widespread outrage.
Her plight tapped into long-simmering resentment in Spain’s major cities over spiralling costs to rent or buy homes.
Tens of thousands of protesters took to Madrid’s streets on Sept 26, rattling keys and blowing whistles.
The authorities said 25,000 people took part, while the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organised the protest, said over 300,000 turned out.
Many then set up their tent camp in Puerta del Sol, vowing to stay until housing access is improved, or the government falls.
“We’ll stay as long as necessary. Even as we mobilise the pressure keeps mounting, and we’re already at our limits,” one 28-year-old protester, who gave his first name as Sergio, said in front of his tent.
The housing problem in Spain has become a burning issue ahead of a general election due for 2027.
Sanchez, in a political rally organised on Sept 27 by his Socialist Party, addressed the evicted woman, saying: “Maricarmen, I have a message for you. The government is working all out to present the law on housing.”
He urged other political parties to back the Bill, which is expected to contain measures such as the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions.
But Sanchez’s party lacks a majority in Spain’s Parliament, where it is unclear whether the package would be approved. A similar Bill was defeated earlier in 2026.
‘Can’t take any more’
The Madrid Tenants’ Union urged on X for city residents to join the Puerta del Sol protest.
“We can’t take any more. Either the rental system falls, or the government falls,” it said.
Abascal was forced to leave the apartment where she had lived for 70 years after a real estate firm acquired the property and raised the rent by 275 per cent to €2,650 (S$3,858), according to the union.
Now a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis, she urged Spaniards to join the protest on Sept 26 in a video message posted online just hours before it got under way.
“I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction.
“I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added in the video, posted by the tenants’ union.
Many who took part in the street demonstration said that the rental market had become impossible. A Madrid real-estate site, Idealista, estimates that rent has nearly doubled in the past decade.
“It is a struggle to find a place you can afford, then you live in fear of being forced out,” demonstrator Enrique Ortega de Miguel, a 38-year-old graphic designer who lives with his mother, told AFP.
Puerta del Sol – a busy hub intensively used by commuters and tourists – has been the venue for past protests. In 2011, young demonstrators railing against poor economic conditions and corruption occupied it for three weeks.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country of around 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Spain has little public housing, while rents have been driven up by increased demand, including from tourism and population growth linked to immigration, analysts say. AFP

‘Unrestricted Permission to Kill’: Inside Kherson’s Drone War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:37:00 UTC
22:37:00 KST

Deep inside Kherson’s red zone, a staircase leads below ground.
Here, as in many parts of the city, spaces beneath the surface provide protection for people and essential infrastructure. Inside the bunker, the way leads through long corridors under fluorescent light, turning left, then right, then around another corner. Each passage gives way to another, stretching the walk into what feels like an endless underground maze.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Above ground, Kherson remains terrorized by Russian drones as the war grinds into autumn. In a city often dubbed a “human safari,” civilians have been pursued while walking, cycling and driving through the city. Human Rights Watch has documented attacks in which drone footage showed that operators could see the civilian nature of their targets and struck anyway.
September brought further attacks on the ordinary movements of civilian life.
On Sept. 4, a Russian drone struck a bus in the city’s Tsentralnyi district, killing a 47-year-old man; a 76-year-old woman died of her injuries the following day. On Sept. 13, a drone hit an ambulance carrying a patient in Korabelnyi district, injuring its driver and a paramedic and leaving the vehicle burned out. Three days later, explosives dropped from a drone killed a 68-year-old man in the open, according to local authorities and prosecutors.
In the room at the end of the underground passage sit Oleh and Mykola, known by their respective call signs “Hades” and “Cousin.” The two National Guard soldiers serve in a mobile fire group whose task is to intercept and destroy Russian drones.
EU Unveils €710M Aid Package for Displaced People in Ukraine, Middle East, Africa
Hades, the chief sergeant of an artillery company, has served since 2014, including in Ukraine’s Anti-Terrorist Operation (ATO) – Kyiv’s official designation for Russia’s initial 2014 invasion using proxy militants. He transferred to the air-defense unit about two years ago. Cousin, a junior sergeant commanding a machine-gun squad, joined the regiment’s anti-aircraft missile and artillery battery in May 2024, around the time it was established.
Kyiv Post met the two members of the National Guard’s 34th Kherson Regiment to discuss the changing drone threat, the difficulties of defending the city and the personal demands of confronting weapons that can kill within seconds.
Kyiv Post: What kinds of aerial threats do you encounter most frequently?
Cousin: The principal threats in Kherson and the surrounding region are [first-person view] FPV drones, along with the large number of Molniya drones now being deployed.
The Molniya is a Russian design that uses an anti-tank mine as its explosive payload. Its destructive effect is considerable. It is among the Russian weapons causing the greatest destruction in this region.
How does the intensity of drone attacks fluctuate?
Hades: The intensity rises and falls rather than following a consistent trajectory. One week there may be fewer incursions; the following week can be a nightmare, when ordinary civilians cannot even venture outside.
The situation keeps changing. I cannot give you a definitive assessment that the overall threat is either increasing or diminishing.
Have you noticed changes in the way Russian forces deploy their drones?
Hades: The changes are unmistakable if you compare the situation with two years ago. Drone technology has developed considerably. New variants have emerged, including fiber-optic FPVs, and the enemy’s pilots are accumulating experience.
They continually refine their equipment and improve its performance. Their capabilities are developing rapidly, and they are constantly adapting their tactics.
What is the hardest part of your work, personally?
Cousin: One of the greatest difficulties is anticipating the enemy’s approach. There is no fixed method, no single playbook that they consistently follow. Their tactics vary from day to day. They approach at different speeds and use different types of drones.
Sometimes they deploy a swarm; sometimes they bring drones in succession, in a kind of carousel. Once they identify a target, they make every effort to destroy it. They do not hold back on the drones they expend. They also use reconnaissance drones to direct artillery fire. Once a target has been located, they try to eliminate it completely.
Hades: I would add that the hardest part is overcoming your own fear before going out on a mission. You have to understand that a drone is approaching and that your responsibility is to destroy it. Simply opening fire is not enough. You have to bring it down so that it cannot continue toward another target.
To put it bluntly, not everyone has the balls to run out and confront a drone that could kill them in two seconds. Not everyone is capable of doing that. Overcoming that instinctive fear is a very significant part of the job.
Looking back over the past year, what has changed most in the drone threat around Kherson?
Cousin: The number of drones has increased. The enemy also has drones equipped with machine vision. Once a drone with that capability has acquired its target, electronic jamming or even severing the fiber-optic cable does not necessarily prevent it from continuing the attack. It will still attempt to strike the target it has locked onto.
Those are the kinds of challenges we are confronting now.
Editor’s note: Machine vision uses software to interpret camera images. When combined with onboard automatic flight control, it can allow a drone to continue toward an already acquired target after losing contact with its pilot: The camera and onboard computer keep tracking the target and guiding the aircraft. This capability is distinct from the fiber-optic connection itself and is not present on every FPV drone.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Behind the drone attacks
The mobile fire group confronts the threat once it reaches the skies over Kherson. For the regiment’s intelligence chief, whose call sign “The Great” refers to Kyiv’s Prince Volodymyr the Great from the 10th-11th century, reducing that threat also requires action against Russian crews, training centers and supply routes. Kyiv Post met him at the same underground location.
How would you describe the current security situation in your area of responsibility?
The Great: The security situation remains difficult, particularly because the enemy’s conduct forces us to devote considerable effort to protecting civilians and evacuating them from the red zone – the areas under fire.
They do not allow us to establish safe evacuation corridors, whether to bring civilians out, evacuate the wounded, including those with serious injuries, or even recover the dead. In our area of responsibility, military casualties are considerably lower than civilian casualties. That tells you something about the adversary we are facing.
They have also shifted toward a greater reliance on FPV drones because their artillery is being successfully knocked out. The artillery systems they are using have a shorter reach than the FPVs, and deploying those systems exposes them to greater risk than operating drones. A drone is an exceptionally dangerous weapon because of the precision with which it can strike.
How does the situation around Kherson today compare with a year ago?
The Great: It has deteriorated. The enemy’s ability to monitor the city and strike critical and civilian infrastructure has increased.
They have brought in the 50th Unmanned Systems Brigade specifically for this sector. In effect, its personnel train here as drone operators before being sent to more demanding sectors of the front.
I want to emphasize that this is a presidential brigade, directly subordinate to the supreme commander of the Russian Armed Forces, Vladimir Putin. In my view, the way they conduct this war reflects the decisions and instructions of the Russian president.
Their commanders give them what amounts to unrestricted permission to kill: Whatever you see, you strike.
Do you see a clear strategy behind the Russian attacks on Kherson?
The Great: There is no strategy that would fundamentally change the military situation here. If there is a strategy, it is to intimidate the civilian population and reduce the number of people remaining in Kherson, which would make it easier for them to strike military personnel and military facilities.
But that does not give them the means to alter the strategic situation. At present, they lack the capability to force a crossing of the river or carry out an operation on that scale.
Are Russian forces primarily trying to destroy infrastructure, disrupt logistics or terrorize civilians?
The Great: These are interconnected measures. They form part of the same effort to terrorize the population. Striking critical infrastructure and civilian infrastructure is part of that.
They also attack medical facilities and deliberately strike people they can clearly identify as civilians.
Do you expect the drone threat to continue increasing? Civilians here repeatedly say that there were fewer drones a year or two ago. What could reverse that trend?
The Great: I think the situation will continue to deteriorate unless specific measures are taken against the enemy’s drone crews and their logistics. We have to prevent them from bringing in drones, personnel, ammunition and the fuel needed to transport those supplies.
Our military and political leadership needs to concentrate on addressing the source of the problem: The crews themselves and the centers where they are trained and prepared for operations. That is how we can change the situation and ease the pressure on Kherson and other cities exposed to enemy drones.
The same principle applies across different types of unmanned aircraft, from short-range FPVs and drones dropping munitions to Shaheds and other long-range systems.
Would you say that artillery, tank and mortar fire are being used to destroy Kherson, while drones are being used to terrorize its civilian population?
The Great: Yes. Absolutely. To terrorize our civilians.
So the main objective here is not to capture more territory?
The Great: I think the objective here is less about territorial conquest than about applying pressure to force negotiations. The purpose is to foster public discontent and force our government to the negotiating table on terms dictated by the Russian Federation.
Russia no longer has the capacity to seize territory as it did in previous years. Its offensive capabilities have fallen almost to zero. We can all see how it is struggling to advance in difficult sectors of the front, including in the Donetsk region.
They now set themselves the objective of taking all the territory of the so-called Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics by the end of 2026. Previously, the deadline was the end of 2025; before that, it was the end of 2024. Year after year, they also say they will capture Kherson. But they do not have the capability to do so.
Looking ahead to the coming months, what concerns you most, and what gives you confidence?
The Great: My greatest concern is an increase in civilian casualties, alongside the risk that attacks could cut off supplies to our units and prevent food and humanitarian assistance from reaching civilians.
What gives me confidence is that we know how to counter the enemy and are continually learning and refining the way we operate. We work closely with the other units in our sector, and that cooperation produces tangible results, including periods of reduced enemy activity.
Ukraine has increased pressure on Russian military infrastructure and supply routes connected to Crimea. Have those operations had an effect in the Kherson sector, and have Russian tactics changed as a result?
The Great: Yes, the situation has changed. Disruption to the routes supplying provisions, fuel and lubricants has had a substantial effect on the enemy’s tactics.
Previously, they could travel by vehicle to within 5 to 6 kilometers [3 to 3.7 miles] of the line of contact, dismount and cover the remaining distance to their forward positions on foot. Now, because of shortages of fuel and lubricants, they may have to walk 24 to 30 kilometers [15 to 18.6 miles] simply to reach their positions. I am not exaggerating those distances.
Food supplies have also been affected. Enemy food depots in Crimea have been destroyed. We know that their units are experiencing difficulties obtaining provisions and that personnel are not getting enough to eat. That undermines morale and reduces their physical capacity to move, make short dashes and take up positions.
They are adapting by minimizing vehicle use and trying to reduce personnel losses through concealed movement. I cannot discuss how they intend to conceal those movements. We are aware of what they are considering, but, in our assessment, their thinking and their actions are flawed.
                                                                                                                                                                         
What would you say to people still living in Kherson’s red zone? Can you offer reassurance that things will improve soon, or would you urge them to leave?
The Great: Please leave the red zone. We cannot save everyone, and it is very difficult to promise that everything will be all right.
I do not know whether I will survive today – whether I will make it home or back to our headquarters.

Are you in pain?  In some cases, exercising may be as good as painkillers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:35:13 UTC
22:35:13 KST

From pilates to tai chi, even modest amounts of exercise can relieve pain as effectively as common pain medicines, opening the door to holistic therapeutic approaches, according to a new study.
Whether you often suffer from migraines, period cramps or chronic pain, exercise could help ease the symptoms in a similar way to common painkillers.
Across a wide range of conditions, exercise can significantly reduce acute and chronic pain, a new study by Adelaide University has found after analysing 157 systematic reviews encompassing 2,736 randomised controlled trials and over 220,000 participants.
“At a time when we’re looking for safe and effective ways to manage pain beyond medication, these findings provide strong evidence for making exercise a more routine part of pain care,” said Carol Maher, senior researcher at Adelaide University.
The researchers examined how the type, intensity and duration of exercise influenced pain relief.
Overall, exercise reduced pain by around 1.1 points on a zero-to-10 scale – a reduction roughly 60% larger than the average relief reported for common medications in separate chronic pain trials.
Low-intensity exercise produced greater pain relief than moderate-to-vigorous activity and shorter programs, of around 12 weeks, showed larger effects than longer ones.
“Importantly, we found that more exercise wasn’t necessarily better. In fact, shorter-duration and lower-intensity programs showed greater reductions in pain, suggesting people may not need to exercise harder or for longer to experience meaningful benefits,” said lead researcher Ben Singh.
Programmes under 120 minutes per week were more effective than higher weekly-duration ones that can feel unattainable for people living with chronic pain, the researchers wrote.
“When we exercise, our body releases chemicals including endorphins and serotonin that can help reduce how strongly we feel pain and increase our pain tolerance,” said Singh, adding that exercising helps calm inflammation and change the way the brain responds to pain, while also improving mood.
Despite these findings, the study noted that exercise remains underused as a treatment for pain: it is not yet routine practice and is rarely prescribed with the same precision as medication.
“Instead, people experiencing pain may be told to ‘stay active’, rather than being given a specific, evidence-based exercise program that considers what type of exercise to do, how hard to work and for how long,” added Singh.
Healthcare providers need definitive guidance, not just whether exercise helps, but which exercises work for which patients, and how to prescribe them effectively, the authors added.
Yet, they warn that exercise should not be considered a universal solution or expected to eliminate pain, as its effects depend on individual factors such as the condition causing the pain, a person's level of fitness, and adherence to the programme.

Why Iran's new push for a deal to end the war appears to be stalling - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:35:02 UTC
22:35:02 KST

The perception is that Iran may be slowly losing the attrition blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran gambled on the idea that it could cut off shipping and hoped it would roil global markets. It wanted leverage that would pressure the US to end the war and the blockade. But the US has called Iran’s bluff for the most part.
The question is now why Iran has begun to talk up a seven-day relaxation of the blockade. That ceasefire plan has been floated for more than a week.
Tehran likely believed it could make this happen at the UN General Assembly. What happened, however, is that the US showed little interest. At least, most reports describe this cold shoulder as the US rejecting Iran’s push for a seven-day interim agreement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly said on Saturday that Tehran had yet to receive a formal response from Washington. While Iran had given a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the US has rejected this, Rudaw Media Network, a news channel in the autonomous Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq, reported.
Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi’s “remarks came hours after [US President Donald] Trump told Rudaw at the White House that he had ‘rejected’ Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days,” the report said.
Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting on Saturday quoted Araghchi as saying to journalists in New York: “We saw the first reaction from the US president, but nothing has yet been conveyed to us by the mediators.”
Rudaw Media Network quoted an Iranian diplomat as saying: “Reopening the Strait of Hormuz depends on these conditions being met; and we will make decisions based on a definitive response from the mediators.”
“Iran’s conditions for reopening the strategic waterway include the release of its frozen assets, an end to the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, and the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iran,” the report said.
As such, it’s not clear whether the Trump administration would be willing to be seen as conceding to Iran. The US has invested a lot in this war since February. It will want something to show for it.
One of the main goals is preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. The focus of the war, however, has not actually been on the nuclear program.
This leaves a perplexing question, since Iran has shifted most of the talks to the Strait of Hormuz issue. Tehran has thus leveraged its proximity to the strategic waterway to make it the main issue of discussion.
“The Iranian initiative comes after Washington and Tehran resumed diplomatic contacts in New York this week on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly,” Rudaw Media Network reported. “Araghchi and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff held talks on Tuesday through Qatari mediators.”
The US is now waiting out Iran. The Trump administration appears to think time is on its side, and that it can wait until the midterms.
Even if it does go back into some kind of memorandum of understanding with Iran, or a deal, it will want something to show for six months of conflict, and that is the key.
So far, Tehran is not handing the US a “win.” Iran is talking about kicking the can down the road and doing more interim deals. It tried this in the summer as well.
Tehran also appears to be binding the hands of its negotiators so that it can’t get a deal anyway. The US no longer trusts this kind of Persian bazaar of negotiations.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before... or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly… with no chance of survival and no hope?”
Iran thinks it is winning
As long as the US believes the attrition is slowly going in its direction, there is no incentive to engage in another short-term deal in which Iran benefits. Tehran will need to come up with something more than its “seven days” concept, and it might have to adjust its demands for US concessions.
Iran thinks it is winning. The US also thinks it is winning. When both sides think they are winning, it is harder to get to an agreement.
Where Trump has excelled in the past is giving both sides the appearance of a win. The challenge today is that both sides believe time is on their side.
