Beach cleanup removes 257 kg of trash from Penghu islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A three-day beach cleanup on the remote islands of Dongji and Xiji in Penghu's Southern Four Islands National Park collected 257 kilograms of marine debris during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday weekend.
The Marine National Park Administration worked with the Taiwan Kayak Association to organize the cleanup, bringing together about 15 volunteers with professional water-safety training to remove debris deposited along the islands' shorelines by ocean currents and winds, per LTN.
Volunteers used kayaks to reach beaches and coastal areas that are difficult to access by conventional vessels. After collecting the debris, they transported it by kayak to a waiting motorized vessel, which carried the waste back to Penghu for sorting and disposal.
The operation was particularly challenging on Xiji, an uninhabited island surrounded in places by steep coastal terrain and basalt formations. Volunteers had to carry the collected waste from the shoreline and coordinate transfers between the kayaks and support vessel.
The kayak association said the volunteers prepared equipment and supplies in advance and were trained to operate in open water, allowing them to safely navigate the difficult conditions while minimizing the cleanup's environmental impact. Although the amount of debris was greater than expected, volunteers said the difference was visible after the waste was removed, with sections of coastline regaining a more natural appearance, per LTN.
Organizers said the cleanup demonstrated how recreational water activities could be combined with marine conservation and environmental education. They said cooperation with professional groups such as the kayak association allowed volunteers to reach coastal areas that are difficult for larger vessels to access.
The administration has previously conducted large-scale cleanups in the area. During another three-day cleanup last year, volunteers removed 868.5 kilograms of debris from two northern coastal zones on Dongji. Fishing gear, expanded polystyrene, and other non-recyclable waste accounted for 65% of the debris.
The Marine National Park Administration has developed a long-term coastal cleanup strategy for the park and divides the Dongji and Xiji coastlines into 14 cleanup zones covering a combined 7.27 kilometers. It has used different techniques, including boats, kayaks, and rope-access operations, depending on the coastal terrain.
The administration urged visitors to the Southern Four Islands to reduce waste, avoid leaving trash on the islands, and take their garbage with them when they leave, noting that waste removal from remote islands is considerably more difficult than on Taiwan's main island.

====================================================================================================

People with higher autistic traits tend to avoid positive relationship-maintenance tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

A recent study suggests that people in the general population who possess higher levels of autistic-like traits tend to avoid positive, affectionate behaviors to maintain their romantic relationships. The research, published in Evolutionary Psychology, indicates that these traits influence relationship dynamics largely through a person’s attachment style rather than broad evolutionary reproductive strategies.
The research was led by Andrzej Łukasik, a PhD with habilitation and head of the Department of Psychology at the University of Rzeszow’s Collegium Medicum in Poland, who aimed to explore how subtle personality traits shape romantic behavior from an evolutionary perspective. The central focus of the study is autistic-like traits, which refer to patterns of social functioning, communication difficulties, and rigid thinking. “Autistic-like traits (ALTs) are personality, social, and cognitive characteristics associated with autism that can also occur, to varying degrees, in the general population,” Łukasik told PsyPost. “They are not considered a disorder.”
To understand how these traits impact relationships, the scientists looked at mate retention tactics. These are behaviors people use to keep a partner and prevent them from leaving. Mate retention is generally divided into what Łukasik described as “benefit-provisioning tactics, such as showing affection, giving compliments or gifts, and offering support, and cost-inflicting tactics, such as inducing jealousy, engaging in controlling behavior, or making threats.” The authors suspected that the way a person tries to keep a partner depends heavily on their attachment style.
Attachment styles describe how people form emotional bonds, generally falling into secure, anxious, or avoidant categories. “People with anxious attachment usually have a strong need for closeness and may react strongly to distance or uncertainty,” Łukasik explained. “In contrast, people with avoidant attachment may feel uncomfortable with emotional closeness and place greater value on independence.” In fact, a 2016 study found that insecure attachment predicts how frequently people use various mate retention behaviors, and a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicated that anxious attachment is linked to both positive and negative mate retention strategies.
The researchers also framed their study around life history theory, an evolutionary concept describing how individuals allocate their limited time and energy. In this framework, people adopt varying reproductive strategies. A fast strategy involves high mating effort, characterized by seeking multiple partners and short-term relationships. A slow strategy involves high parental effort, prioritizing stable, long-term investments in a single partner and offspring.
Previous evolutionary theories proposed that autistic-like traits might be an adaptation linked to a slow reproductive strategy. However, because these traits are also associated with insecure attachment, which typically aligns with a fast strategy, the authors designed this study to test how all these factors connect. “Research by Marco Del Giudice and colleagues (2010) has suggested that ALTs may be associated with a slow reproductive strategy,” Łukasik noted. “However, higher levels of ALTs are also linked to insecure attachment styles (avoidant and anxious), which have more often been associated with characteristics of a fast strategy.”
Therefore, the researchers examined whether ALTs might actually predict a fast strategy and whether attachment style moderates that relationship. To map out these connections, the scientists recruited 796 Polish adults. The participants were 52 percent female and had an average age of 36.4 years. Every participant had been in a romantic relationship for at least three months.
The researchers administered a series of established questionnaires. They used the Autism-Spectrum Quotient to measure the degree of autistic-like traits, the Experiences in Close Relationships scale to assess anxious and avoidant attachment, and the Mate Retention Inventory to evaluate the frequency of benefit-provisioning and cost-inflicting behaviors. They also used brief scales to measure mating effort and parental effort. The team then used a statistical technique called structural equation modeling to analyze the complex web of relationships between all these variables at once.
The results suggest that autistic-like traits are notable predictors of insecure attachment. Participants who scored higher on autistic-like traits reported higher levels of both anxious and avoidant attachment styles. This indicates that people with more of these traits often worry about their partners leaving while simultaneously struggling with emotional closeness.
When looking at mate retention, the researchers found that individuals with higher autistic-like traits were less likely to engage in benefit-provisioning tactics. They tended to avoid showering their partners with affection or gifts as a way to maintain the relationship. The initial statistical models suggested that these individuals were also less likely to use cost-inflicting tactics. However, when the scientists controlled for the participants’ ages, they found a positive link between autistic-like traits and cost-inflicting tactics.
Age acted as a masking variable because older individuals naturally tend to use fewer negative tactics. Once age was factored out, the data suggested that people with higher autistic-like traits might actually use cost-inflicting tactics slightly more often.
In terms of evolutionary strategies, autistic-like traits proved to be weak predictors of life history outcomes. “The results did not support the hypothesis that ALTs predict a fast rather than a slow reproductive strategy,” Łukasik said. “ALTs were only weakly related to reproductive strategies.” Instead, attachment styles acted as a bridge between the variables.
Anxious attachment was linked to higher mating effort and lower parental effort, and it predicted the use of both positive and negative mate retention tactics. Avoidant attachment was similarly linked to higher mating effort and lower parental effort, but it predicted a lower use of benefit-provisioning tactics. “Individuals with an anxious attachment style tend to use a mixed partner-retention strategy involving both attraction and distancing, probably due to an overperception of the risk of infidelity,” Łukasik pointed out. “In contrast, individuals with an avoidant attachment style tend to use benefit-provisioning tactics less often, possibly because such tactics allow them to avoid closeness with their partner and maintain distance from their partner.”
Age played a broad role across the entire study. The scientists found that as participants got older, their levels of attachment anxiety decreased. Older participants also reported lower mating effort, higher parental effort, and a decreased use of both types of mate retention tactics. This aligns with the idea that as people age and relationships stabilize, they shift their energy away from securing a mate and toward investing in their existing family.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on cross-sectional data, meaning the researchers measured all variables at a single point in time. This design makes it impossible to determine the true direction of the effects, and one cannot assume that autistic-like traits cause specific attachment styles or relationship behaviors. In addition, the participants self-reported their behaviors, which can introduce bias if people alter their answers to appear more socially acceptable.
The researchers also note that the Autism-Spectrum Quotient might measure elements of social anxiety or general interpersonal difficulty rather than pure autistic traits. This overlap could skew the interpretation of the results. The weak link between autistic-like traits and reproductive strategies also suggests that broad evolutionary models like life history theory might not fully capture the nuances of modern human relationships, pointing to a need for different measurement approaches in future studies.
Ultimately, the findings offer insight into the practical challenges some people face in romance. “These findings may help explain relationship difficulties experienced by individuals with higher levels of autistic-like traits,” Łukasik concluded. “Benefit-provisioning tactics are generally associated with greater relationship satisfaction, whereas cost-inflicting tactics are linked to lower satisfaction and may contribute to difficulties in developing and maintaining stable close relationships.”
The study, “Autistic-Like Traits in Members of the General Population and Mate Retention Tactics: The Mediation of Attachment Styles and Reproductive Strategies,” was authored by Andrzej Łukasik and Agnieszka Łaba-Hornecka.

Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing.
“All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.
“Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.”
Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.
Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second.
He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.
A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn.
Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)
Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.
“President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.”
Civility in politics
Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.
In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”.
Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”.
A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard.
These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.
Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.
“The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.
“Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.”
In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.
Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”.
Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.”
Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.
Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.
Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.”
A rhetorical maneuver
While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.
“The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.”
Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language.
“There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.
“It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.”
Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”.
The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.
“I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.”
But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.”
In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.
“We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.
“Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

How to make cornbread – recipe | Felicity Cloake's masterclass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Like banana bread, a rather less ancient North American creation, cornbread isn’t a loaf in the conventional sense. Though it’s perfect for soaking up chilli, brothy bean soups and the like, it’s actually substantial enough to be the main event, rather than something you might reach for to mop the plate after it. (It’s also gluten-free, should that be a consideration.)
Prep 10 min
Soak 2 hr
 Cook 25 min
 Serves 6
200g coarse cornmeal, or polenta, preferably stoneground
240ml buttermilk (see step 3)
2 tbsp bacon grease, or butter or oil
½ tsp salt
  2 eggs, beaten
1 tsp baking powder
  ¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda
  2 tsp soft light brown sugar (optional)
1 A note on the cornmeal
The best, most flavourful cornmeal is stoneground but, depending on where you’re based, it may not be that easy to find, so you may have to compromise on the stoneground element of things. Coarse cornmeal is often found in the world food sections of larger supermarkets, usually from Caribbean brands, but if you do see stoneground polenta, grab that.
2 Toast the cornmeal
Either way, you can enhance the flavour of your cornmeal by toasting it before use. Put a large, dry frying pan on a medium-high flame and, when it’s hot, add the cornmeal and toast, shaking constantly so it doesn’t catch and burn, until fragrant but not browned; this should take only a couple of minutes.
3 Soak half the cornmeal
Tip half the cornmeal into a large bowl and add the buttermilk (if you can’t find buttermilk, use the same amount of milk instead, and add a teaspoonful of lemon juice or vinegar in step 6). Leave to soak for at least a couple of hours, if possible (though you can use it immediately), or overnight if you’re making this for breakfast.
4 Get everything else ready
Once you’re ready to cook, get all the ingredients ready, because, once the bicarb meets the buttermilk in step 6, it’ll get straight to work. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. For a really crisp base, you’ll need a roughly 20cm ovenproof frying pan, though you could use a (not loose-bottomed) cake or tart tin, greased with hot fat in step 7.
5 A note on the fat
If you eat pork, cornbread is particularly delicious cooked in bacon fat, so it’s worth saving drippings or even wiping a piece of fat from a rasher of bacon around the warm pan to grease it before adding another fat. Put the drippings, butter or oil in the pan and heat until sizzling and, in the case of butter, browning.
6 Finish the batter
Meanwhile, stir the remaining toasted cornmeal into the bowl of buttermilk-soaked cornmeal, then mix in the salt, beaten eggs, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and sugar (that last is sure to horrify those from the American South, but, according to Serious Eats, corn used for milling is traditionally ripened for longer, which makes it sweeter and more flavourful, so unless you have some really good cornmeal, a pinch of sugar will help replicate that).
7 Add the fat
Stir the hot fat into the batter bowl, then turn up the heat under the pan. Pour in the batter – it should sizzle as it hits the pan (or quickly grease a tin and pour the batter in there instead) – level it out, then bake for about 20-25 minutes, until golden and firm. Serve warm. Cornbread reheats well in a moderate oven; it’s good to freeze, too.
8 Or flavour with chilli and cheese …
This is a very adaptable recipe. Try stirring 70g grated cheddar or red leicester cheese and two-thirds of a chopped jalapeño chilli into the batter in step 7, then sprinkle 10g more cheese on top, plus the rest of the chilli, before baking (you can also use another variety of mild chilli or jarred pickled jalapeños, if you prefer).
9 … or bacon, beans or veg
Other good things to include: cooked drained beans, crumbled fried bacon, chunks of feta, cured chorizo, drained tinned corn, chopped chives, spring onions or caramelised onions, cooked peppers – if it goes with corn, it’ll probably work here. I especially like to serve mine with room-temperature butter whipped with hot honey (two to four teaspoons per 100g butter).

Where the road became a destination: Iran’s historical caravanserais
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:59:03 UTC
20:59:03 KST

Where the road became a destination: Iran’s historical caravanserais
TEHRAN - For centuries, crossing Iran was as much a test of endurance as it was a journey of discovery. Merchants moved goods between distant markets, pilgrims traveled toward sacred places, and ordinary travelers followed routes across deserts, mountains and plains. Between these long stretches of road stood caravanserais, places where a journey could pause, animals could be rested, goods could be protected and strangers could share food, stories and news.
Today, many of these historical roadside inns offer a different kind of journey. They are destinations in their own right, allowing visitors to step into the infrastructure of travel that shaped Iran long before motorways, railways and airports.
The importance of these buildings was formally recognized in 2023, when UNESCO inscribed The Persian Caravanserai on the World Heritage List. The serial property comprises 54 caravanserais selected from the country’s much larger network of centuries-old examples.
Together, they represent far more than individual buildings: they form a testimony of the roads, trade, pilgrimage, architecture and human encounters that connected different parts of the Iranian soil and the wider region.
For travelers today, this network offers an unusual way of experiencing the ancient country. Rather than visiting heritage only in the form of palaces, mosques or ancient cities, visitors can follow the roads between them and discover the places where earlier generations stopped along the way.
Glimpses of an architecture that was shaped by the road
Though, there are many differences and similarities between those caravanserais countrywide, there is no single architectural formula for an Iranian caravanserai.
Their designs evolved according to geography, climate, available building materials, security requirements and the character of the routes on which they stood. The UN cultural body describes the 54 selected caravanserais as demonstrating a wide range of architectural styles and adaptations to different climatic conditions across thousands of kilometers.
Yet many share a recognizable shape and design. A traveler approaching a caravanserai would often first encounter a substantial entrance, sometimes marked by a monumental portal. Beyond it was a central courtyard around which rooms and service spaces were arranged. The courtyard provided an organized space for people, animals and goods, while the surrounding rooms offered shelter.
The design was practical but rarely devoid of architectural ambition. Brickwork, vaults, domes, arches, geometric patterns and carefully proportioned courtyards could transform what was essentially roadside infrastructure into an impressive architectural ensemble.
In desert areas, thick walls and enclosed courtyards helped moderate the harsh climate. Elsewhere, local materials and construction traditions produced different forms. The result is a remarkable architectural map of Iran: buildings responding to the same basic human need while reflecting very different landscapes.
UNESCO’s documentation notes that the location and setting of each caravanserai were decisive in shaping its design, particularly in relation to climate, water availability and defensive requirements.
This is one reason that visiting a caravanserai can be more revealing than looking at photographs of one. Sometimes, the relationship between building and landscape becomes part of the experience.
A caravanserai in a desert does not tell the same story as one near a mountain pass or a historic urban center. The surrounding terrain, the distance from other settlements and the availability of water help explain why the building was constructed where it stands.
More than roadside inns
The word “caravanserai” can easily create an image of merchants stopping overnight with their camels. That picture is not wrong, but it is incomplete.
These places were part of a much larger social and economic system. They provided shelter, food and water for caravans, pilgrims and other travelers. They also facilitated the movement of goods and information between regions.
A caravanserai could therefore function as a small temporary community.
Merchants from different regions might meet there. Pilgrims could rest beside traders. People speaking different languages and following different religious traditions could spend a night under the same roof. News traveled with the caravans, as did commercial information, cultural practices and technical knowledge.
UNESCO considers this interaction central to the property’s significance. It says caravanserais served as meeting places for people from different ethnicities, languages and religions and contributed over centuries to the exchange of human values, ideas and knowledge.
Seen from this perspective, the caravanserai was not simply a building beside a road. It was part of the road itself.
The road carried people and commodities, while the caravanserai provided the physical infrastructure that made long-distance movement possible.
Iran’s caravanserai tradition is closely associated with the country’s position between major cultural and commercial regions. Routes crossing the Iranian plateau linked Mesopotamia, Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Persian Gulf and the Indian subcontinent, while pilgrimage routes connected important religious centers.
The World Heritage property reflects a tradition that developed over a very long period. UNESCO traces the evolution represented by the selected caravanserais from the Achaemenid period through the Qajar period, with examples reflecting different historical stages and architectural traditions.
The buildings therefore should not be viewed as belonging to one dynasty or one architectural period.
The network reflects successive generations of travelers and builders. Iranian caravanserais were constructed, modified and used over centuries as routes changed and economic and political circumstances evolved.
The UNESCO nomination documentation identifies historical continuity from the Sasanian and early Islamic periods through the Buyid, Ziyarid, Seljuk, Ilkhanid, Timurid, Safavid and Qajar eras, while also considering the continuation of historic routes and the evolution of architectural forms.
That continuity gives the caravanserais an unusual place in Iran’s heritage landscape. A palace can reveal how a ruler lived; a fortress can show how a territory was defended; a mosque can reflect religious and artistic traditions. A caravanserai, by contrast, reveals something about movement, how people travelled, where they stopped and how distant communities remained connected.
From ancient shelter to modern travel experience
For modern visitors, the appeal of a caravanserai lies partly in its ability to change the rhythm of travel.
Iran’s major tourist attractions are often concentrated in well-known cities: Isfahan, Shiraz, Yazd, Kashan and Tehran.
But, caravanserais encourage a different itinerary. They invite travelers to leave the main urban centers and follow historical roads into smaller towns, villages, agricultural areas, deserts and mountain landscapes.
A visit can begin with the architecture. The entrance may frame the courtyard like a stage. Arched rooms reveal the practical organization of the building. Brick vaults and domes demonstrate how builders created large covered spaces without modern construction technology.
But the landscape outside can be equally important.
Standing inside a caravanserai in a remote setting, a visitor can begin to understand the scale of earlier journeys. A road that now takes hours by car could once have required days of travel. The presence of a caravanserai was therefore not incidental. It marked a point at which travelers could find water, shelter and a degree of security.
Perhaps the most evocative space in many caravanserais is the courtyard.
Today it may appear quiet, with visitors photographing arches and brick walls. Historically, however, it would have been a place of constant activity.
Animals were brought in after a day’s journey. Goods were unloaded. Travelers looked for rooms. Food was prepared. Conversations continued between people who might never have met anywhere else.
Rooms around the courtyard could accommodate travelers, while spaces for animals, storage and other services supported the practical needs of caravans. The arrangement allowed the building to function as a compact and controlled environment along a difficult route.
So, such a combination of hospitality, logistics and security was fundamental to the success of long-distance travel before modern transport.
A new chapter for old roads
The UNESCO inscription also creates an opportunity to rethink how Iran’s caravanserais are presented to international visitors.
They can be experienced as architectural monuments, but they can also serve as gateways to wider cultural landscapes. A caravanserai visit can be combined with local food, handicrafts, rural tourism, desert excursions, archaeological sites or visits to historic towns.
Some have already undergone restoration and adaptive reuse. UNESCO has highlighted the need for sustainable approaches that allow modern commercial and hospitality functions while protecting their historical and architectural values.
This balance will be important.
A caravanserai that becomes a hotel, restaurant or cultural center can acquire a new economic life. But excessive alteration could weaken precisely the qualities that make the building valuable. Conservation therefore has to remain at the center of any tourism strategy.
The challenge is not simply to make old buildings usable. It is to allow them to remain legible as historic places.
UNESCO’s management framework recognizes this issue. The World Heritage Centre notes that the component sites have individual restoration plans and that local communities are involved in the management of caravanserais located in or near settlements.
For a traveler, perhaps the most rewarding way to experience Iran’s caravanserais is not to regard them as isolated stops.
They make more sense when encountered as part of a journey.
A route through Iran can become a journey through layers of history: ancient roads, old bazaars, water systems, villages and cities, with caravanserais marking the points where travelers once rested. The buildings provide physical evidence of a world in which distance shaped everyday life and hospitality was an essential part of travel.
The modern visitor, of course, arrives by car, bus or other contemporary transport. Roads are faster, navigation is digital and a night’s accommodation can be booked from thousands of kilometers away.
Yet inside a centuries-old caravanserai, the basic idea remains familiar.
A traveler arrives after a journey. A door opens. There is shelter, a place to rest and a courtyard around which the building gathers its life.
Such a continuity is perhaps the greatest attraction of Iran’s caravanserais.

Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
September 27, 2026
Voters in Switzerland look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.
According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.
Although Swiss neutrality has been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.
The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.
What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve
The group said its aims were for:
- Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"
- Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense
- Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties
- Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked
- The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them
Swiss sentiment on neutrality
According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.
Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).
"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."
Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'
Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.
"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.
In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.
Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.
According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.
The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

Labour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it go | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:57:37 UTC
20:57:37 KST

As I wrote last week, whatever its current troubles, Reform UK has hardly disappeared. Meanwhile, those black-clad quasi-paramilitaries may well be another augury of a frightening immediate future. One more English settlement – the town of Barnham, in Norfolk – is seemingly poised to stage a pretend independence referendum in protest at plans to locally accommodate asylum seekers. Oh, and our new Labour prime minister has just held cordial talks with a US president who has not only brought a modern de facto fascism to his homeland, but wants to export it to Europe.
But hold all those cheerful thoughts for a moment, and let us have a look at the Labour party as it gathers in Liverpool. The slogan plastered all over its conference is “Hope Again” – which, unlike last year’s dreadful “Renew Britain”, suggests that a few people at the top might have belatedly learned the basics of pithy political storytelling.
The influence of the two slogans that are accepted modern classics – “Take back control” and “Make America Great Again” – is obvious. In Labour’s case, “again” not only implies how badly Starmer’s reign went, but looks back to a better past and implies that something comparable is eminently possible. You might take it as a reference to the best aspects of the New Labour period, Harold Wilson in his pomp or the magical glories of the Attlee years.
The slogan also echoes some of the pronouncements made by Andy Burnham when he became leader, about the positive response of the voters of Makerfield to “the promised return of the Labour they once knew”. And it has to be said: those words and the conference tagline tap into his party’s ingrained nostalgia, and the idea that with enough effort, Labour might return to winning a commanding share of the vote, as it did back in the days when footballers chain-smoked and bowler hats were still a common sight (in 1951, although it lost to the Tories, Labour won a record 48.8%, and Wilson came very close to the same figure in 1966).
Numbers aside, Labour still largely believes that by rights it should monopolise the progressive half of politics. The Tories have the same idea about the right of the spectrum, which has recently fed into a seductive notion held by both “main” parties and many pundits: that with Zack Polanski’s PR slip-ups and the trouble that has engulfed Nigel Farage, we may be witnessing the rebirth of comfy, cosy, simple two-party politics.
What utter rot that is. The UK’s passage into a multiparty system is deeply rooted in a society and economy whose complexity can no longer be smothered by our ludicrous voting system. Look at what has happened where the electoral machinery is different. Labour recently lost control of Wales to Plaid Cymru, attracting a mere 11% of the vote. The SNP’s dominance in Scotland may have weakened, but it is more than intact. Meanwhile, even with first past the post still creakingly in place, whole swathes of what used to be considered middle England – particularly in the home counties – have switched from the Tories to the Lib Dems.
At the time of writing, the latest YouGov poll puts Labour on 23% (if that’s accurate, the “Burnham bounce” looks more like a modest bunny-hop), the Tories level with Reform at 21%, and the Greens and Lib Dems on 14% and 12% respectively. The same polling group has also done a multi-level regression and post-stratification – or MRP – that offers a picture of the House of Commons that would be elected if a contest were held today. It forecasts a hung parliament, with Labour dropping to 241 seats, and facing the inevitability of cross-party cooperation. Here, clearly, is further evidence of a fragmented model of politics that will endure for the foreseeable future. And in Liverpool, mostly at fringe meetings, it will be talked about, but not nearly enough.
Before he became leader, Burnham seemed to be the only senior Labour politician positively responding to these shifts. He has repeatedly backed proportional representation (which he insists he still supports), and said that embracing it would pave the way “for agreement with other parties on wider reforms”. With that, he said, would come “a more honest and collaborative way of doing politics”, a phrase that chimes with his promises of a lot less “finger-pointing” and “point-scoring”. Aside from his talks with the Tories and Lib Dems about social care, what this might look like is unclear; all we know is that Burnham’s drive for English devolution will definitely mean ceding power to other parties, and probably substantially change politics at a national level.
And so to the really important bit. Eleven days after the start of Labour conference comes the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Publicly at least, Labour seems to be running a content-lite campaign, though it has attacked the Greens’ alleged fiscal impossibilism and sent members a communique framing the contest as a chance to “get our revenge” for Green triumphs in May’s local elections. The Green leader and candidate, Polanski, is aggressively accusing Labour of a miserable lack of solidarity with Palestine, while an ally also charged Burnham’s party with choosing its contender – the former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali – on the basis of opportunistic “identity politics”. It all looks like politics as usual – and as the far right gains more and more traction here and abroad, what is happening in this corner of London should make us feel very nervous about the next UK general election.
The left-leaning cross-party pressure group Compass is about to convene the first meeting of a “council for the progressive majority”, which will bring together leading figures from each of the UK’s progressive parties – including Plaid and the SNP – to firm up how they might collectively defeat Reform. To quote from a recent Compass statement: “There is a progressive majority in this country … yet our outdated political system divides us … splitting the vote and clearing a path for extremist voices to win with little public backing.” This is the kind of urgent warning that will become very vivid in the buildup to the next election, amid campaigning – whatever the efforts of Burnham’s new National Centre For Information Defence – festooned with lies, deepfakes and worse.
A lot of us remain unsure of the exact solutions to a split left taking on a confident, tech-savvy and possibly united right. Electoral pacts tend to look like stitch-ups; parties agreeing to limit their campaigning in certain marginal seats can work much better. Whatever, millions of us – including, it seems, the new PM – increasingly feel that a cultural change is overdue, not least to stop the most basic civilisational values buckling before our eyes.
Talking of which, it’s grimly ironic that the man still benefiting most from the fractured politics of the 21st century is Farage, a self-styled throwback permanently surrounded by a cloud of Rothmans smoke. Here, then, is a question for everyone gathered by the old Liverpudlian docks: how can he be comprehensively beaten, possibly when he may end up healing divisions on the right by striking a deal (pre- or post-election) with the Tories, and even Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain? By ludicrously insisting that people must vote Labour whatever their political circumstances? Or somehow cooperating with other parties to ensure his defeat? Those parties also need to change, of course. But the age of monopolistic Labour hegemony is over. Let it go. We need to fight today’s most important battles together, so the prospect of hope might actually start to feel real. Again.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:55:50 UTC
20:55:50 KST

1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
Ancient Australian fossils suggest oxygen helped fuel the rise of complex life more than 1.5 billion years ago.
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.
- Share:
Stored in an open-air warehouse in tropical Darwin, Australia, are dozens of trays containing cylindrical cores of rock. They are from drill holes bored hundreds of metres below the surface by mineral exploration companies decades ago.
Some of these cores at the Northern Territory Geological Survey are mudstone – a type of sedimentary rock formed from hardened seafloor mud. The companies that drilled these cores were largely unaware that within these mudstones were fossils of microscopic organisms buried on the seafloor of an ancient inland sea that covered much of northern Australia over 1.5 billion years ago.
As our new study, published in Nature, shows, these fossils are crucial for addressing a longstanding puzzle about the major evolutionary leap that led to all complex life on Earth: the origin of eukaryotes.
Small but complex
All life on Earth can be placed into one of two types which are fundamentally different at the cellular level.
Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have simple cellular organization and are mostly single celled. Eukaryotes – including all animals, plants, algae and fungi – are very different. They have much more complicated cells featuring a nucleus and other specialized structures such as organelles which perform specific jobs.
The eukaryotic revolution transformed the planet. It led to the rise of animals and, eventually, to us. Based on observations from the genes of living organisms, it is now widely agreed that the last common ancestor of all living eukaryotes resulted from the symbiotic union of (at least) two prokaryotic microbes: an archaeon and a bacterium.
The first evidence for eukaryotic life comes in the form of these fossils of single-celled organisms. They show a level of cellular complexity not seen among prokaryotes, but common in eukaryotes.
Eukaryote fossils can be found around the world in rocks dating back at least 1.5 billion years. The fossils of the Northern Territory, the oldest of which date back to 1.75 billion years ago, are the oldest currently known eukaryote fossils globally.
But the ancient world in which early eukaryotes evolved remains shrouded in mystery. And so many fundamental aspects regarding their nature are unknown.
Oxygen – friend or foe?
Many types of bacteria can live and grow in places without oxygen. But nearly all eukaryotes alive today use oxygen for their survival. That’s because aerobic respiration – breaking down food using oxygen – provides the vast amounts of energy that complex life demands.
But the idea that oxygen has always been beneficial for all eukaryotes has come under fire in recent years. This follows the surprising discoveries of enigmatic eukaryotes that can thrive in conditions without oxygen.
There is also mounting evidence from the geological record that when eukaryotes were first evolving, oxygen was likely much scarcer. This means oxygen-free marine habitats would have been the norm. Collectively, these observations have called into question the assumption eukaryotes have depended on oxygen since their inception.
Genetic studies of living microbes belonging to groups considered closest to the ancestors of the first eukaryote can offer key insights into eukaryote ancestry. But only the fossil record can tell us about long-extinct lineages. And only geology can offer a window into the kind of world these organisms lived in.
More than 12,000 fossils
For our new study, we crushed up samples of the mudstone cores stored in Darwin, then dissolved them. We identified more than 12,000 fossils by analysing the organic residue left behind by this dissolution under a microscope.
We also studied the mudstones the fossils were preserved in to better understand what the environment was like when the sediments were deposited. This offered insight about the habitats in which these eukaryotes lived. And by analysing the chemistry of these mudstones, we could determine whether oxygen was present in the ancient seawater.
Our results show that eukaryote fossils were found in environments ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea. But they were present only in samples deposited in oxygenated settings. Samples from oxygen-free environments contained only simple, prokaryotic forms.
This suggests that even the oldest known eukaryotes that lived on Earth 1.7 to 1.4 billion years ago were dependent on oxygen. These data lend support to a long-held hypothesis that oxygen played a key role in driving the evolution of early eukaryotes.
Resolving the drivers and context of the major evolutionary leap represented by early eukaryotes is one of the major outstanding questions in the life sciences. Ongoing studies of these enigmatic, ancient microfossils will no doubt tell us more about our own origins – and our place in the cosmos.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Maxwell Lechte and Leigh Anne Riedman. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maxwell A. Lechte, Leigh Anne Riedman, Susannah M. Porter, Galen P. Halverson, Margaret Whelan. Early fossil eukaryotes were benthic aerobes. Nature, 2026; 655 (8123): 670 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10533-4

Kosovo arrests nine Serbs on suspicion of war crimes over missing intellectuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:54:05 UTC
20:54:05 KST

Kosovo police have arrested nine Serbs in the northern town of Zubin Potok on suspicion of war crimes linked to the disappearance of ethnic Albanian intellectuals during the 1998–1999 war.
Police and the Special Prosecutor’s Office said in a joint statement on Sunday that the operation, codenamed “Dossier 23”, was related to the case of the missing intellectuals. No further details were disclosed, including the identities of those arrested.
The arrests follow the excavation in July and August of two newly discovered mass graves in the Serb-majority Zubin Potok area, where the remains of at least 23 people were found.
The remains are believed to include members of the so-called “Group of Intellectuals”: Albanians from Mitrovica, including doctors, professors and human rights activists, who disappeared in April 1999.
Three sets of remains have been identified as belonging to members of the group, authorities confirmed earlier this month.
The police operation was part of a months-long war crimes investigation in the Zubin Potok area following the discovery of the mass graves. Three other suspects from the area had previously been arrested as part of the investigation.
‘The aim was to put additional pressure’
Serbia’s government office for Kosovo condemned the operation, saying “nine Serbs were arrested under the pretext of alleged involvement in a war crime”.
“The aim was to put additional pressure on Zubin Potok, drive out and intimidate the remaining Serbian population,” the statement added.
The 1998–1999 war between independence-seeking ethnic Albanian guerrillas and Serbian forces killed around 13,000 people and left around 4,000 missing.
Decades of efforts to locate mass graves have recovered the remains of thousands, but around 1,600 people remain missing.
Efforts to locate those who disappeared during the conflict have been slow, with relations between Belgrade, which does not recognise Kosovo’s independence, and Pristina remaining strained.

DOE steps up efforts to restore Persian yellow deer population
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) is carrying out research, conservation, and breeding programs aimed at restoring the population of Persian yellow deer in designated natural habitats and wildlife breeding centers across the country.
Conservation efforts to recover the threatened species are being pursued through two complementary approaches: in-situ conservation in its natural habitats and ex-situ conservation in managed settings, IRNA quoted Mohammad Nosrati, an official with the DOE, as saying.
To conserve the animal in its natural habitat, the feasibility study for the reintroduction of Persian fallow deer in chosen habitats in Fars and Yazd provinces is placed on the agenda to be conducted.
As part of the plan to reinforce the number of Persian yellow deer and enhance its restoration, DOE has allocated funding for monitoring and assessing the population of the species introduced into Ilam, Khuzestan, Fars and Yazd provinces. The effort aims to study the population dynamics, identify threats, evaluate habitat desirability, and assess the conservation status of the species, he added.
Referring to the conservation measures being conducted outside the natural habitat, Nosrati said the DOE is organizing fallow deer breeding centers at different sites such as Azadi, Arsanjan, Miankotal, Dasht-e Naz, Rashkan, Bagh-e Shadi, Mahour Dasht-Yafteh, Karun Agro-Industry, and Fandoqlu, where population management, the translocation of Persian deer to natural habitats, and the assessment of the species’ genetic purity are put on the agenda.
According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, the Iranian yellow deer is categorized as an endangered species.
Almost half a century ago, it was thought that the yellow deer species was extinct in the world. However, about 50 years ago, four yellow deer were observed in Dez and Karkheh forests, the primary habitats of the Persian yellow deer. They were released in different regions of Iran for better reproduction.
Thanks to the effective implementation of the conservation program, the number of Persian yellow deer has risen from 5 in the Iranian year 1398 (2019 – 2020), to 19 this year.
Genetic map for endangered species being developed
The DOE is developing a genetic map of endangered wildlife species to increase their chance of survival, create a breeding plan, manage their population, and address the risks facing them in their natural habitats.
Effective conservation of endangered species is almost unattainable without a precise understanding of population genetics. To this end, genetic and molecular studies of key wildlife species in the country have been put on the agenda, ensuring that management decisions are based on accurate scientific data, IRNA quoted the head of the National Museum of Natural History and Genetic Resources, Leila Ezzeddinlou, as saying.
Preserving genetic diversity within and between populations, preventing declines in effective population size, avoiding inbreeding and genetic erosion, conserving genes adapted to diverse environmental conditions, and providing genetic resources for species restoration, propagation, and introduction or reintroduction programs are among primary objectives of these studies, she added.
Referring to three research agreements signed between the DOE, the College of Agricultural and Natural Resources of the University of Tehran, and Gorgan University, the official said that as part of the cooperation, a project is underway to investigate the genomic diversity and phylogeny of Levant viper and Latifi’s viper populations, employing conservation and therapeutic approaches based on genomic markers.
Moreover, the development of genetic profiles and maps for the Asiatic cheetahs, black bear, and Persian yellow deer, as keystone and threatened species, has kicked off.
The other part of the agreements focuses on the assessment of genetic variation, inbreeding, and kinship relationships within the Persian zebra population, which is being conducted in collaboration with Yazd’s provincial DOE department. The initiative plays a key role in managing small populations and preventing the loss of genetic biodiversity, she highlighted.
From accelerated extinction to successful revival of species
Despite worrisome facts about the speed at which species are disappearing, there has been good news of endangered species making a comeback, highlighting the role of conservation efforts in preventing extinction and helping vulnerable wildlife recover.
According to the latest report by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, about 154 vertebrate animal species, and around 25 percent of plant species in the country are at risk of extinction, with 117 species being classified as critically endangered in the national list. Persian zebra, Asiatic cheetah, black bear, great bustard, and yellow deer are among animals that are in danger of extinction.
Among extinct animals, the Hyrcanian tiger and Persian lion are the two feline species that have disappeared forever in the country. Fortunately, Persian zebra and Persian yellow deer are examples of successful conservation efforts where scientific measures and local community participation have resulted in the species’ recovery, doe.ir quoted Hamid Zohrabi, an official with the DOE, as saying.
Referring to successful recovery stories of species in Iran, Zohrabi noted that for years, it was thought that the yellow deer species was extinct in the world. However, about 65 years ago, some yellow deer were observed in Dez and Karkheh forests, the primary habitats of the Persian yellow deer.
Their conservation program commenced immediately by breeding them in captivity and transferring them to natural habitats for better reproduction, Zohrabi noted.
The birth of the first Persian yellow deer in the current Iranian year, which started on March 21, in Karkheh National Park, southwestern Khuzestan province, has raised hopes for the revival of this unique animal species.
The Persian zebra is a subspecies of onager, which is critically in danger of extinction. With the birth of a foal in Yazd province, the current population of Persian zebra is estimated to be more than 50, indicating improved habitat conditions and effective conservation management of the endangered animal.
The conservation efforts include a field program that encompasses strengthening natural infrastructure and promoting environmental sustainability, such as monitoring water resources.
According to DOE, the total number of Asiatic cheetahs in the country’s protected areas amounts to 27, with five other cheetahs living in breeding sites, and six in captivity.
In September 2025, the DOE resumed the implementation of the national project to protect Asiatic cheetahs after a six-year hiatus.
Expounding on the DOE's achievements and measures, the official said that for each endangered species, a specific action plan has been developed, and a specialized committee, in collaboration with universities and scientific organizations, is working to protect and restore species based on scientific data and studies.
There are over 337 protected areas under the supervision of the DOE; the country has 13 biosphere reserves and 226 wetlands nationwide, out of which 26 are inscribed on the Ramsar List as wetlands of international importance.
The country has so far prepared plans for the preservation of 25 endangered species, such as the Persian cheetah, zebra, Asiatic black bear, yellow deer, lesser white-fronted geese, white-headed duck, Persian salamander, blind cave fish, and luristanica Sorbus (a rare plant species that is native to Iran). The DOE is preparing thirteen more plans.
MT/MG

Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27

Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
September 27, 2026
Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.
The shrine, located near the Spanish border, is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.
On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.
"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."
Later, the pope also said it was "impossible to regard causing death as something normal."
"What is legal is not necessarily moral," he added, in what could be seen as a reference to France's euthanasia and assisted suicide law which came into effect last month.
"We must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said the 71-year-old pontiff.
Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone
The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.
A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.
While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.
"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."
But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.
"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."
Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops
Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."
He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."
"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

What a Palestinian university’s Sbarro exhibit revealed about Second Intifada extremism - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:49:03 UTC
20:49:03 KST

A quarter century ago, Al-Najah University in Nablus hosted an exhibition that celebrated a suicide bombing in Jerusalem that had murdered 16 people.
The bombing took place on August 9, 2001. Soon after, the exhibit was created at the university. The exhibit showcases how massacres and bombings were celebrated by mainstream Palestinian institutions.
The memory of this disturbing exhibit was brought to our attention by an account on the social media platform X/Twitter. The account is called “2001 Live (@25YearsAgoLive),” and it posts news from 25 years ago, as if it is happening in real time. The account has gained a large number of followers because it is chronicling in real time the lead-up and aftermath of the September 11 attacks in the US.
The account has also brought back the story of the Sbarro bombing exhibit. 2001 Live noted the university in the “West Bank sets up an exhibition celebrating the August 9 [2001] bombing of a Sbarro restaurant in Israel, in which 16 civilians were killed.” It added that “the Palestinian Authority makes the effort to build a mock Sbarro storefront and include props of mutilated body parts, to trumpet the perceived success of Palestinian resistance against Israel. Visitors are required to walk over Israeli and American flags to enter and leave the exhibition.”
It’s worth looking back at this exhibit and the 2001 bombing to draw lessons regarding the conflict. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency at the time noted that in late September the exhibit had been closed. “The closure of a Palestinian university exhibit re-enacting a terrorist attack on Israel is being seen by observers as ‘too little, too late,’” the JTA noted.
“Palestinian Authority president Yasser Arafat bowed to pressure Tuesday to order the closure of the Al-Najah University exhibit, which celebrates the August suicide bombing at the Sbarro Pizzeria in Jerusalem, which claimed the lives of 15 people.”
Palestinian Authority was pressured into banning mass murder exhibit
Note how this is presented. Arafat is said to have “bowed to pressure.” Instead of banning an exhibit at a university that was celebrating mass murder, the Palestinian Authority had to wait to be pressured.
This shows the support this kind of incitement to mass murder had at the time. “The exhibit was altered but was not shut down completely on Tuesday.”
Let’s recall how the exhibit was described. “In one room of the exhibition, students dressed as suicide bombers, clasping a Quran in one hand and a gun in the other, conduct what is intended to be their final interview before setting out on their suicide mission,” JTA noted.
“Another student, dressed in a military uniform and face mask, is featured setting a supposed bomb. This scene takes place at a replica of a restaurant with the word “kosher” written in Hebrew above the door.
Sbarro was a popular kosher restaurant frequented by religious Jews.” JTA noted that “Arafat’s delayed response was condemned by Rabbi Marvin Hier, head of the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Center, as ‘outrageously too little, too late.’”
The Associated Press also did a video on the exhibit, which is still online. The video shows how the exhibit was set up. It has a placard to make it look like the entrance to the Sbarro restaurant.
BBC claims Arafat was 'disturbed' by suicide bombing exhibit
Students step on US and Israeli flags to enter. Inside, there is fake blood and destruction, as well as mock pieces of people, as if it were the restaurant. Photos show the actual carnage. Photos of the terrorist who carried out the bombing are shown, celebrating his action. Other parts of the exhibit justify the attack by showing Palestinian victims of the Second Intifada.
How did the BBC report on the exhibit? “Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat has closed down an art exhibit which featured a recreation of the scene of a suicide bombing,” the report said on September 26, 2001. “The exhibition, at Al-Najah University in the West Bank town of Nablus, was organized to mark the first anniversary of the Palestinian intifada.”
The report claimed that a source from Arafat’s circle noted that “the president [Arafat] was gravely disturbed and offended by the images in the exhibit.” The BBC claimed that the exhibit “divided” those who saw it. “A university branch of the militant Palestinian group Hamas built the exhibit, which recreates the scene of last month’s attack on Sbarro Pizza house in Jerusalem. A suicide bomber – Izz al-Din Shuheil al-Masri – blew himself and 15 other people up during a busy lunchtime at the restaurant.”
The report quoted someone it said was named Alas Hmeidan, head of Islamist students at the university: “We don’t like blood, but this is a way to retaliate against the massacres committed by Israel. We want to show them we can hit back.” At the time, the BBC noted that then “former Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu showed pictures of the restaurant exhibit. He said that Mr. Arafat is not stopping terror attacks against Israel.”
The Sbarro bombing was one of the worst and most tragic massacres of the Second Intifada. One of those involved in the bombing was Ahlam Tamimi.
Tamimi was convicted in Israel for her role. She was then released in the 2011 deal with Hamas, and she lives in Jordan.
The US Rewards for Justice program noted that there is a $5 million reward for information on her. “On August 9, 2001, Tamimi transported a bomb and a Hamas suicide bomber to a crowded Jerusalem Sbarro pizzeria, where the bomber detonated the explosives. The blast killed 15 people, including seven children.
Americans Judith Shoshana Greenbaum, a pregnant 31-year-old school teacher, and 15-year-old Malka Chana Roth were among those killed. More than 120 others were injured, including four Americans. Hamas claimed responsibility for the bombing,” Rewards for Justice noted.
Jewish American organization urges US to extradite Sbarro bombing accomplice
On the 25th anniversary of the attack, the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations wrote an open letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “Five days before the 25th anniversary of the August 9, 2001, bombing of the Sbarro restaurant in Jerusalem, the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations sent the following letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, urging the United States to demand that Jordan immediately extradite Ahlam Aref Ahmad al-Tamimi.”
The story of the Nablus exhibit is important to recall because it illustrates how mainstream Palestinian institutions, such as universities, normalized massacres such as suicide bombings. It’s difficult to remember now, because so many worse massacres and wars have taken place, but during the Second Intifada there was a lot of focus on suicide bombers. In the West, they were often depicted as desperate young men driven to this act, sometimes promised paradise as a reward.
The film Paradise Now, for instance, was produced to tell the story of two men preparing to carry out a suicide attack. It won a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film and received an Academy Award nomination.
This was part of the normalization of this kind of attack. The fact that it was normal at a major Palestinian university to celebrate blowing up a pizzeria full of civilians, and that students walked through an exhibit showing bloody body parts, is emblematic of the intifada and the foundations of extremism that led to the October 7 massacre, more than two decades later.

Over 1,100 Jews visited the Temple Mount in Jerusalem to pray on the first day of hol hamoed Sukkot, the Israeli non-profit Beyadenu – Returning to the Temple Mount announced in a social media post.
Visitors to the Temple Mount are limited to 90-100 people per group, Beyadenu explained in a separate post, adding that police removed five visitors from the site after they recited the blessing of the Four Species and said the Kaddish prayer.
Among the hundreds of visitors was MK Yitzhak Kreuzer (Otzma Yehudit), who visited the Temple Mount with his family.
At the same time, Jerusalem District and Border police are preparing to receive and protect the thousands of visitors expected to arrive at the Temple Mount, Western Wall, and the Old City during the rest of the Sukkot holiday, including during the Birkat Kohanim (the Priestly Blessing) ceremony set to take place on Monday and Thursday.
Under the longstanding status quo, Jews and Christians are permitted to visit the Temple Mount but are generally prohibited from praying there, while Muslims are permitted to worship.
Jewish men permitted to pray on Temple Mount with prayer books for first time
In mid-August, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told The Jerusalem Post that Jewish men were permitted to bring prayer books onto the Temple Mount after right-wing journalist Arnon Segal shared a photo of Jewish men praying and reading from prayer books, claiming the photo was taken on the Temple Mount.
“Still no blanket permit, but an initial experiment aimed at ensuring the Middle East doesn’t lose its mind over this,” Segal claimed in his post. “History.”
“The Israel Police operates on the Temple Mount in accordance with the directives of the political echelon, the established rules governing the site, and operational assessments, with the aim of safeguarding public safety, security, and public order,” Israel Police said in response to the Post’s request for comment at the time.
