Explora I: A luxury cruise between Italy and the French Riviera - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:48:55 UTC
20:48:55 KST

At the beginning of September, just before Rosh Hashanah, I was lucky enough to join a press cruise aboard Explora I, the first ship launched by Explora Journeys, the luxury cruise brand of the MSC Group.
This was the first cruise of my life. In a few words, my conclusion is simple: This is an experience everyone should try at least once in their life.
I spent three days and two nights aboard Explora I, beginning in Civitavecchia, near Rome, and sailing to Porto Santo Stefano before continuing to Monaco. On our final day, the journey took us through Monte Carlo and the French Riviera, including Èze and Saint-Paul-de-Vence, before ending in Nice for the flight back to Israel.
Explora Journeys describes its ships as mega-yachts, and it did not take long to understand why.
A small city on the water
Explora I entered service in 2023 and accommodates a maximum of 900 guests in 461 ocean-facing suites, all with private terraces. This time, the cruise was almost full, with around 850 guests on board.
The ship has four pools - three outdoor and one indoor with a retractable glass roof - along with whirlpools, more than 700 sq.m. of wellness facilities, a gym and fitness spaces, six main restaurants, 12 bars and lounges, a casino, culinary school, art gallery, and luxury boutiques including Rolex and Cartier.
In the evening, there is live entertainment and music around the ship, while a DJ plays as the sun goes down and the ship pulls away from shore.
The best thing is that you could spend several days aboard without really running out of places to discover.
But what stood out almost immediately was not the size of the ship or even the facilities. It was the service.
With up to 900 guests and 640 crew members, Explora I has a guest-to-crew ratio of around 1.41:1. And you feel it. Almost everywhere you go, someone is there to help, answer a question, offer a drink, or simply greet you. It’s pretty unusual, so it takes some time to get used to.
Sunrise might be the best part
Life aboard the ship continues for most of the day and well into the night. The pools and spa are open throughout the day, while restaurants, bars, shops, the casino, and entertainment venues keep the ship alive in the evenings.
But surprisingly, my favorite time aboard Explora I was early morning.
During our trip, the ship generally spent the daytime anchored near its destination, allowing passengers to go ashore, while much of the sailing took place in the evening and overnight.
That meant waking up somewhere new.
I started getting up at around 6 a.m. just to watch the sunrise from my terrace. With nothing but the sea outside, it was worth losing a little sleep.
At 7:15 a.m., I went to a hatha yoga class in a studio overlooking the water. The class had already been fully booked, but the instructor managed to fit one more mat along the side of the room just for me, which I really appreciated.
After yoga, while most passengers were still sleeping or having breakfast, I headed straight to one of the pools.
For about half an hour, I had it completely to myself.
Floating alone in a silent pool while looking out at an apparently endless Mediterranean became one of the simplest but most memorable parts of the trip. There is something almost meditative about being surrounded by water while watching even more water beyond the edge of the ship.
Eating your way through the Mediterranean
Food, unsurprisingly, is a significant part of the experience.
My favorite everyday option was Emporium Marketplace, the ship’s all-day dining venue. It has the freedom of a buffet but with many dishes prepared to order.
At breakfast, the selection included omelets, pancakes, smoked fish, pastries, fruit, vegetables, and smoothies. Later in the day, there was everything from sushi to pizza, burgers, and pasta, with several dishes prepared individually on request.
It was also probably the easiest restaurant for a group: Everyone could choose something completely different and still meet at the same table.
For something sweet, there was Crema Café, where ice cream, crêpes, pancakes, and waffles provided plenty of reasons to stop by throughout the day.
Dinner was a different experience.
Explora I has six main restaurants and nine dining experiences overall, ranging from the pan-Asian Sakura to the Mediterranean-inspired Med Yacht Club and European steakhouse Marble & Co. Grill.
On the first evening, I tried Sakura; on the second, Marble & Co. Grill. Both were considerably more elaborate, with multi-course menus and extensive wine selections. Marble & Co. also gave me what may have been my favorite combination of the trip: excellent red wine and warm, cheesy bread.
Spa, swim, repeat
As someone who loves spas, I made very enthusiastic use of the wellness area.
Any free hour I could find usually ended with me either in a pool or back at the spa. And with more than 700 sq.m. of indoor and outdoor wellness facilities, there was plenty to explore.
There is a Finnish sauna, steam room, salt cave, hydrotherapy pool, heated marble loungers, and treatment rooms. I also had what became one of the highlights of the trip - an excellent massage on our second day.
For those whose idea of wellness involves slightly more movement than mine, the fitness facilities cover more than 270 sq.m., with Technogym equipment, fitness and Pilates studios, an outdoor fitness area overlooking the sea, and different classes throughout the day.
There is also a 360-degree outdoor running track circling the ship - an interesting fact: four laps around the track equal a 1-km run.
A penthouse I barely used
My home for the trip was an Ocean Penthouse on Deck 9, designed for two people but occupied, rather happily, only by me.
Explora I is an all-suite ship, and even its smallest suites start at 35 sq.m. Ocean Penthouses range from 43 to 68 sq.m., with separate living and working areas.
Mine had separate sleeping and living areas, a walk-in wardrobe, bathroom, and, most importantly, a private terrace overlooking the sea.
It may also have been one of the most comprehensively equipped hotel rooms I have ever stayed in.
There was a Dyson hairdryer, binoculars, fitness equipment, a coffee machine, room-service menus, and a daily schedule of activities. Fruit and chocolates were waiting on the table alongside a bottle of Moët & Chandon, while the minibar was stocked with wine, beer, champagne, and non-alcoholic drinks.
The minibar is included in the fare, as is 24-hour room service - meaning that, in theory, you could stay in the suite for most of the cruise and be perfectly content.
Perfect for introverts. But I did exactly the opposite.
Knowing I had only a few days aboard, I spent as little time in the room as possible, determined to see practically every corner of the ship.
Life beyond the ship
On our second morning, we arrived in Porto Santo Stefano, a small Italian port town on the Tuscan coast. After breakfast, we went ashore and walked through the town and along the waterfront. It was a nice walk, and it was really convenient to be able to take a tender between the yacht and the town throughout the day.
Later that day, we met the ship’s captain, Francesco Russo, a 39-year-old Italian from Sorrento with around 20 years of experience at sea.
Russo spends roughly half the year at sea and half on land with his family. He told us that commanding a ship is ultimately less about the machinery than the people: A captain has to earn the crew’s trust, motivate them, and make them want to follow him.
Life at sea, he said, requires commitment because it is more of a lifestyle than simply a job. His description of Explora I was considerably more poetic.
The ship, he said, is a “nice lady,” and steering her is a little like dancing with a woman.
From Monaco to the French Riviera
By the following morning, we had arrived in Monaco.
After one final early swim overlooking the principality, it was time to leave Explora I.
Our last day began with a walk through Monaco and Monte Carlo before we continued on to France and the medieval hilltop village of Èze.
There, at a perfume factory, we took part in a fragrance-making workshop, mixing different notes to create our own personal perfumes to take home.
From Èze, we continued to Saint-Paul-de-Vence for lunch. During lunch, I tried a fantastic lavender crème brûlée made by a French chef - which deserves a mention of its own.
Rain began falling as we wandered through the narrow streets of the village afterward, eventually leading us, somewhat unexpectedly, to the grave of Marc Chagall.
Finally, we drove to Nice airport for our journey back home.
Celebrating life at sea
One thing stayed with me after leaving the ship.
On our final evening aboard, I looked around and realized I could not remember the last time I had seen so many people dressed up simply to enjoy an evening.
Women wore dresses and heels; men wore shirts and jackets. People drank cocktails, listened to live music, danced beneath the evening sky, and moved between restaurants and bars.
And that was essentially what everyone aboard had been doing for days.
They ate. They drank. They went to the spa. They swam. They dressed for dinner. They listened to concerts, shopped, danced, sat in whirlpools, and watched the Mediterranean pass by.
They were celebrating life.
That, perhaps, is the appeal of this kind of cruise.
For a few days, you do not have to think about where to eat, how to get from one destination to another, what to do in the evening, or even where you will wake up tomorrow. You unpack once, and the world moves around you.
If your idea of a vacation is being able to travel across Europe while swimming, drinking cocktails, eating excellent food, and having practically everything taken care of, Explora I makes a compelling case for seeing it all from the sea.
How much does it cost?
Explora Journeys cruises start at around $3,500-$5,500 per person for the itineraries provided, depending on the destination and sailing. For example, a seven-night Mediterranean cruise aboard Explora I in June 2027 starts at $4,200 per person for an Ocean Suite and $5,790 for an Ocean Penthouse.
The fare includes most dining, premium alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, the suite minibar, 24-hour room service, Wi-Fi, gratuities, thermal spa access, and onboard fitness and wellness programs.
The biggest problem comes afterward.
You eventually have to go home and remember how ordinary life works again after this once-in-a-lifetime experience. I have no solution for that yet, other than planning my next cruise.

20:48:47 KST

Houses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers across England and Wales.
The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain.
Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilience conference on Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent.
As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF).
“This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said. “Tragically, we’ve lost the battle in north Somerset, but we need to change the framework as a matter of urgency, so this ruling doesn’t result in planners and developers across the country making similar speculative housing applications.”
Charles Banner KC, who represented Persimmon Homes at the court case brought by the local council, agreed the decision was of national significance. His chambers, Keating Chambers, said the result was “hugely important”. “This decision will be of immense interest to the planning and development sector,” it added.
Persimmon Homes won permission despite failing the “sequential test”, which is designed to be the ultimate barrier for floodplain development UK planning policy, after the inspector found 12 alternative sites at less risk of flooding.
They also overcame heavy opposition from politicians, local and regional tiers of authority and locals – many of whom fear houses surrounding the site will be at increased risk of flooding.
Munt said the high court judgment “flies in the face of everything insurers, lenders, Flood Re – a joint UK government and insurance industry initiative that makes the flood cover part of household insurance policies affordable – the Environment Agency and Defra are trying to do on a national policy level”.
The Environment Agency objected to the development on flood risk grounds. But the high court agreed that even though the sequential test had failed, the inspector was entitled to consider the development’s wider benefits and whether it could be made safe for its lifetime when weighing the application.
Annemieke Waite, North Somerset council’s cabinet member for planning and environment, accused Persimmon of exploiting a legal loophole.
“We’re not being nimbys, we accept we need to build these homes,” she said. “But we don’t accept the establishment of a highly controversial legal precedent whereby vital local environmental protections can be overridden to build on floodplains across England and Wales.”
Local people living around the site are distraught. With just a few hours’ notice, 51 residents converged at the site earlier this week to meet the Guardian’s photographer, many leaving work early to be there – and one coming straight from a hospital bed.
“We represent everyone living in areas at risk of flooding in England and Wales,” said Sue Gardiner, whose living room window opens out over the site. “This ruling massively increases the likelihood of developers building up near you, without having to answer for your increased flood risk.”
Gazing over the fields, Gardiner broke down. “I’m petrified,” she said. “Persimmon claims we’re not at any significant greater risk of flood, but no one else agrees: we’ve been refused by three major house insurers on the grounds of increased flood risk on the back of these plans.
“Without insurance, our home – the home we worked hard throughout our lives to pay for so we could leave it to our children – could become unmortgageable, and then unsellable,” she said. “Thanks to Persimmon, our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard for us – and a worthless inheritance for our children.”
Richard Croucher, whose home also abuts the site, agreed. “The value of our home was supposed to fund our care when we get old,” he said. “Now we’ve got nothing for when we’re old and in need: that’s terrifying.”
Persimmon Homes said: “Our proposals to deliver much-needed new homes in Yatton were subject to detailed scrutiny at a public planning inquiry before being approved by an independent planning inspector.
“Flood risk was considered in detail through the planning process, including at the public inquiry by the inspector, before planning permission was granted.”

Thirteen Turkish naval ships paraded through the Istanbul Strait on Sunday as Türkiye marked the 488th anniversary of the Battle of Preveza and Navy Day.
The procession organised by the Defence Ministry included TCG Istanbul, the country’s first domestically built frigate.
As the Turkish frigate passed the Barbaros Monument on the Besiktas waterfront, sailors aboard the frigate saluted the nearby tomb of Barbaros Hayreddin Pasha, the Ottoman admiral who led the fleet to the historic victory against the Holy League.
"On the anniversary of the victory, we commemorate Grand Admiral Barbaros Hayrettin Pasha, our glorious ancestors, our Commander-in-Chief Gazi Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, and all our martyrs and veterans with mercy, gratitude, and respect," the Turkish Defence Ministry said on X.
The procession included a range of TCG naval vessels, accompanied by two submarines.
Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the 1538 victory continued to inspire Türkiye’s efforts to achieve energy independence at sea. In a post on X marking the anniversary, he said Ankara would keep working towards “full energy independence” using its own ships, engineers and equipment.
The Battle of Preveza followed a series of Ottoman naval gains in the Mediterranean that prompted several European powers, including Venice, Spain and the Papal States, to assemble a fleet under Genoese admiral Andrea Doria.
Barbaros Hayreddin Pasha’s fleet of 122 ships defeated the allied European fleet of 262 ships, more than twice its size, according to data cited by AA.
The Ottoman victory is widely regarded by historians as a turning point that consolidated the empire’s naval power in the Mediterranean.

From the Cold War to post-Assad: 80 years of Syria-Turkey ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:46:31 UTC
20:46:31 KST

Breadcrumb
From Cold War rivalry to post-Assad cordiality: 80 years of Turkey-Syria relations
In another sign of how swiftly relations have improved, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will soon visit Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on 14 September after a two-day visit.
This year marks the 80th anniversary of the two neighbours establishing diplomatic relations in 1946, the same year Syria became independent.
A brief look at the history of Turkey-Syria relations suggests that the present moment may mark the closest the two countries have ever been.
Disquieting developments
Syria and Lebanon were under French mandate from the collapse of the Ottoman Empire until the aftermath of the Second World War, when both countries became independent. Turkey immediately established diplomatic relations. At the time, it was viewed as “a Turkish step towards a closer union with the Arab world”.
From those early years of relations, the two neighbours joined rival alliances and forged close ties with the two superpowers. Turkey joined the NATO alliance in 1952. After Turkey concluded a mutual defence treaty with Iraq, then under the pro-Western monarchy, Syria in 1955 recalled its envoy to Turkey for consultations.
Tensions reached an unprecedented high point in 1957 when regional fears spread of a communist takeover in Damascus following the appointment of leftist officers to the Syrian Army in August. Ankara deployed thousands of troops along its border. Damascus charged that Turkey massed its troops in a “manner which presages imminent attack”.
The crisis reached a breaking point by that October, with Damascus additionally charging that Turkish soldiers fired at Syrian border residents and Turkish warplanes flew over Syrian territory.
It even risked drawing in the superpowers, with the US warning the Soviet Union that it would honour its commitments to Turkey’s defence and Moscow declaring it would “inevitably” intervene if Turkey went to war. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wasn’t so subtle when he remarked that “if war breaks out, we are near Turkey and you are not”.
The crisis showed signs of thaw and ultimately ended that month. In early October 1957, Syria’s new minister to Turkey clarified that Syria only feared an attack by Israel, adding: “I hope Turkish-Syrian relations become better for both of our countries have close ties in language, history and custom.”
Khrushchev seized the opportunity presented by Turkey’s National Day on 29 October to “unexpectedly” show up at the Turkish Embassy in Moscow and toast “peace,” crediting Soviet diplomacy with “cooling off” Turkey.
Syria entered into a brief political union with Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, then known as the United Arab Republic, in 1958. In January of that year, Turkey again warned its southern neighbour of communist infiltration, arguing that such danger “has introduced in our region disquieting developments”.
Damascus seceded from the UAR in 1961 following a coup. Nasser broke off diplomatic relations with Turkey for recognising the new provisional government in Damascus on the day it was formed, citing a “hostile attitude” toward the UAR.
Any hopes for warmer relations between Ankara and Damascus were short-lived. The 1963 coup brought the Ba’ath Party to power, and Syria entered a closer, lasting relationship with Moscow, which became its leading arms supplier for the rest of the Cold War.
Still, the neighbours avoided another crisis like 1957 until the end of the century.
Insurgency, territorial disputes, and water-sharing
The rule of the Assads in Syria began in 1970 when Hafez al-Assad seized power in yet another coup, invariably justifying his family’s long and brutal reign by citing the endless coups that preceded them.
Assad’s first decade in power coincided with Turkey beginning its damming of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, both of which originate in Turkey and flow downstream to Syria and Iraq. Ankara’s move would create recurring tensions in the relationship over the decades to come.
Another dispute Assad would raise was over Turkey’s Hatay Province. During the French Mandate over Syria, it was known as the Sanjak of Alexandretta. France supported its transfer to Turkish sovereignty in 1939, hoping to convince Ankara to join the Allies against Nazi Germany. It didn’t work. Alexandretta became Hatay.
The Hatay and water-sharing disputes persisted for years. Assad would host the Kurdistan Workers’ Party group, well-known by its Kurdish PKK acronym, and its leader Abdullah Öcalan for years after it launched its armed rebellion against Turkey in 1984. While the two sides signed a border security agreement in 1985, relations between them were strained in this period by Syria’s support of the PKK and the Armenian Secret Army for the Liberation of Armenia.
In 1989, two Syrian MiG-21 fighter jets flew 12 miles into Turkish airspace and shot down a civilian Turkish plane, killing all five people aboard. Syria offered condolences and ordered an inquiry.
By 1990, Turkey’s massive Ataturk Dam on the Euphrates neared completion, again raising objections downstream, with Syria fearing it could lose 40 percent of water it could hitherto rely upon.
Turkey’s state minister said his country had “no international obligations” to provide other countries with water but added that Ankara would do its “best not to harm our neighbours”.
In 1992, Turkey promised to honour past water-sharing agreements. Turkish Foreign Minister Hikmet Cetin said Ankara would respect a 1987 pact on water-sharing under which Turkey would allow at least 500 cubic meters of Euphrates water a second into Syria. The two signed an accord committing to reach a “final solution” on Euphrates water allocation by the end of 1993.
From brink to thaw
Exactly forty-one years after the end of the 1957 crisis, 10,000 Turkish troops amassed along the Turkish-Syrian border in October 1998. Turkey’s military threatened “economic, political and military sanctions” on Damascus. Ankara finally had enough of Syria providing its PKK arch-enemy sanctuary.
“I am not only warning Syria, I am warning the world – this cannot continue,” declared Turkish President Suleyman Demirel. In addition to expelling the PKK, Turkey demanded that Syria drop territorial claims to Hatay.
The crisis lasted less than a month. On 20 October, they signed the Adana Agreement, under which Syria would end its support of the PKK. Damascus expelled Ocalan, who Turkey captured the following year, and restricted the group’s activities on its soil.
Hafez Al-Assad passed away in 2000. Under his son and successor Bashar, Turkey-Syria relations experienced a notable thaw.
Bashar Al-Assad became the first Syrian head of state to visit Turkey in 2004, declaring that his visit coincided “with a period when Syrian-Turkish relations are reaching a peak”.
The following year, Turkish President Ahmet Necdet Sezer visited Syria for two days. In April 2008, Erdogan flew to Damascus, where he discussed the possibility of direct Syria-Israel talks with Assad. The following August, they would meet again when Assad visited the Turkish resort of Bodrum, where he was also vacationing that month.
In 2009, Turkey and Syria reached a deal allowing their citizens to travel to each other’s countries without visas. As Turkey-Israel relations sharply deteriorated following the deadly May 2010 Israeli raid on the Mavi Marmara flotilla, Turkey-Syria ties briefly blossomed as tens of thousands of Syrians visited Turkey’s southeastern Gaziantep monthly.
In a far cry from the 1957 and 1998 crises, Turkey and Syria even held joint military exercises along their shared border in 2009 and 2010.
Little could anyone at the time know that the lowest point in relations was just around the corner.
Lowest point
Assad would ultimately initiate the worst of the regional crackdowns that followed the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, killing and torturing what were initially peaceful civil demonstrators.
Turkey sought to preserve relations and urge restraint. By August, Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu went to Damascus to deliver Erdogan’s message that Ankara had “run out of patience” with the Assad regime’s unrelenting violence, which at that point had killed more than 2,000 people. Assad remained unmoved.
The war grew increasingly violent with larger numbers of Syrian refugees pouring over the border into Turkey. The Syrian refugee population peaked at up to 3.7 million over the next decade, more than any other country hosting refugees from that bloody conflict, which eventually left more than 500,000 dead.
Turkey closed its embassy in Damascus in March 2012, hosted the anti-Assad opposition, and banned all Syrian flights from its airspace. Aleppo University even withdrew an honorary doctorate in international relations it had awarded Erdogan in 2009. In December 2015, both states cancelled their 2009 visa agreement.
Syria shot down a Turkish RF-4E reconnaissance jet after it briefly violated its airspace on 22 June 2012, killing both crew members.
Turkey would later intervene directly in Syria in August 2016 with its cross-border Euphrates Shield operation that targeted both the Islamic State and the Kurdish YPG. Ankara avoided fighting Assad’s forces, who were ferociously bombarding east Aleppo with Russian support at the time.
Instead, Turkey remained largely focused on combating the Kurdish forces in a series of cross-border incursions that followed in 2018 and 2019. At the same time, it established an on-the-ground military presence in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province, where the Islamist armed opposition Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) had come to control and govern.
The deadliest clash ever between Turkey and Syria occurred in Idlib in early 2020. After an airstrike killed at least 33 Turkish soldiers, Turkey launched Operation Spring Shield, devastating Assad’s forces with heavy air, artillery, and drone strikes.
New leader, new thaw
After the deadly February 2023 earthquake, which affected both sides of the Turkey-Syria border, regional states offered the Assad regime a second chance in return for reforms and ending the Captagon drug trade. Syria was readmitted into the Arab League but made little tangible effort to implement any reforms or even basic policy changes.
By June 2024, Erdogan offered to restore diplomatic relations for the first time in over a decade. In reference to the 2008 vacation, the Turkish leader said, “In the same way that we kept our relations with Syria alive in the past - we had these meetings with Mr Assad that included family meetings – we cannot say that it will not happen again”.
It did not. Not under Assad anyway. In his final days, the Syrian leader was detached from any semblance of reality, reportedly spending a lot of his time playing Candy Crush on his phone.
By December, a victorious HTS burst out of Idlib, swiftly captured Aleppo and marched on Damascus. Assad fled into exile in Moscow. HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa has succeeded Assad as interim president, ending a half-century of that family’s rule.
Sharaa quickly forged close relations with Turkey, making his first visit in February 2025. Turkey reopened its embassy in Damascus mere days after the transitional government seized power, and Turkish Airlines resumed flights to Damascus for the first time in 13 years.
Turkey even seems poised to replace Moscow’s traditional role as Syria’s main military client. However, Sharaa has shown signs that he wants to diversify Syria’s relations to avoid over-reliance on any one country.
The new leadership in Damascus has heralded a new era in Turkey-Syria relations, which may prove much more resilient and long-lasting than past thaws.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.

Thailand's Puripol Boonson seals sprint gold double, equals Asian 200m record at Asian Games

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Puripol Boonson completed an Asian Games sprint double on Sunday, winning the men's 200 meters in 19.88 seconds to equal the Asian record set by China's Xie Zhenye in 2019. China's Huang Youwen took silver in 20.45, with Japan's Soshi Mizukubo third in 20.56.
The 20-year-old had broken the Games record with 20.10 in Saturday's semifinals, then cut another 0.22 seconds from that time despite a slight headwind. He won the 100m on Friday in a Games-record 9.90 seconds. ■

Assefa, Adola seal Ethiopian double at Berlin Marathon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27

Participants compete during the Berlin Marathon 2026 in Berlin, capital of Germany, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haofu)
BERLIN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Tigst Assefa and Guye Adola secured an Ethiopian double at the 52nd Berlin Marathon on Sunday, with Assefa winning the women's race in a course-record 2 hours, 11 minutes, 4 seconds after her world-record bid unraveled in the closing stages.
The 29-year-old had targeted Ruth Chepngetich's world record of 2:09:56, set by the Kenyan in Chicago in 2024, and remained on pace to challenge the mark until late in the race.
Supported by several pacemakers, Assefa quickly pulled clear of her rivals and built a commanding advantage. Although she started more cautiously than Chepngetich had during her record run, the Ethiopian maintained a strong pace through the second half and was still inside world-record pace at the 40-kilometer mark.
Her challenge ended shortly before the finish as physical problems forced her to slow sharply. Assefa nevertheless crossed the line in 2:11:04, lowering the Berlin course record and recording the third-fastest women's marathon time in history.
It was her third victory in the German capital following wins in 2022 and 2023. Her 2:11:53 performance in Berlin in 2023 was a world record before Chepngetich lowered the mark in Chicago the following year.
Ethiopia swept the women's podium, with Bedatu Hirpa finishing second in 2:16:53 and Dera Dida taking third in 2:16:55.
Adola completed Ethiopia's double by winning the men's race in a personal-best 2:02:50. The 35-year-old, the oldest athlete in the men's elite field, claimed his second Berlin Marathon title after previously winning in 2021.
Fellow Ethiopian Gemechu Dida Diriba finished second in 2:03:19, while Tanzania's Gabriel Gerald Geay was third in 2:03:59.
Haftom Welday was the fastest German man, finishing in 2:08:25. In the women's race, Esther Pfeiffer abandoned her attempt to challenge the German record before the 15-kilometer mark.
A total of 56,187 runners registered for the 42.195-kilometer race. The elite field started in temperatures of around 13 degrees Celsius and near-ideal running conditions. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Skills on display, employment changes in motion at WorldSkills Shanghai
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:41:55 CST
20:41:55 KST

* The seven new skills making their debut at the WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai offer clues to where economic demand is heading, reflecting growth in areas ranging from the digital economy and smart manufacturing to service consumption.
* Artificial intelligence is reshaping what happens inside jobs, expanding what workers are expected to do and changing the division of labor between humans and technology.
* China is updating vocational programs, expanding skills training and strengthening links between schools and industry to keep talent supply in step with rapidly evolving industry demand.
by Xinhua writers Ding Yinghua and Zhou Rui
SHANGHAI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A drone assembled from scores of parts navigated its way around obstacles. A mobile robot, after programming and fine-tuning by a competitor, identified and grasped objects. In a mock store, meanwhile, another competitor arranged merchandise, served customers, and switched between in-store sales and livestreaming.
Over four days at the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, scenes involving 64 skills told a broader story of economic transformation: new technologies and shifting market needs are creating fresh demand, job roles are being reshaped, and the skills economies need are evolving with them.
With all competition events completed, the global skills gathering is set to conclude with a closing ceremony on Sunday. This year's edition brought together 1,385 competitors from 68 countries and regions, while seven skills made their debuts, including unmanned aerial systems, software testing and retail.
Francis Hourant, president of WorldSkills International, said trades today are not exactly the same as they were in the 1960s, adding that the competition adjusts its portfolio to stay connected with "the reality of the industry."
NEW DEMAND TAKING SHAPE
The seven newcomers in Shanghai offer some of the clearest clues to where economic demand is moving.
In the unmanned aerial systems arena, competitors began with around 200 separate components. They had to assemble and calibrate a drone, write the code and prepare it for autonomous flight. Once airborne, this drone was expected to scan an unfamiliar environment, map obstacles and plan its own route -- with no human intervention during the flight.
Beyond the competition, similar technologies are already finding their way into everyday life. In Shenzhen in south China, drones deliver takeout to smart pickup lockers, while in southwest China's Chengdu, urban logistics drones carry goods along regular low-altitude routes, and over rice fields in northeast China, agricultural drones have become part of routine farm work.
Retail presented a different scene at the Shanghai event, but still reflected the same trend. Across different modules, competitors had to take on multiple roles: arranging merchandise, pitching products to customers, hosting livestreams and handling unexpected complaints.
"We are not training simply a top salesperson, but an all-round retail expert," said Chen Ying, head of the expert group at the Shanghai training base for this skill.
Such a combination of skills reflects a consumer market increasingly extending beyond goods toward services and experiences. In the first eight months of 2026, China's service retail sales rose 4.9 percent year on year, outpacing the 1-percent growth in goods retail sales, as demand expanded in areas including tourism, culture, sports and leisure.
"Where industries develop, new occupations emerge, and WorldSkills sets up skills accordingly," said Zhang Rui, deputy director of the WorldSkills Competition China (Tianjin) Research Center.
Among the seven new skills, software testing and digital interactive media design reflect the rise of the digital economy, while unmanned aerial systems and rail vehicle technology are among the skills tied to smart manufacturing and advanced equipment, Zhang explained.
AI REWRITING THE JOB
If changing demand helps explain why new occupations are emerging, artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping what happens inside a job.
In the web technologies competition, contestants are no longer assessed simply on their ability to write code. They must analyze user needs, decide what functions a business scenario requires, complete front- and back-end development, and deliver a finished product.
Wu Yingxiang, a technical expert and coach for the Chinese team in WorldSkills web technologies, said AI is making code generation much faster, thus expanding what programmers are expected to do. "Every programmer may now become a project manager and a product manager," he said.
At another hall, contestants in the digital interactive media design competition moved from product planning to image processing, video production and interaction design during more than 20 hours of competition across four days.
Notably, even as AI begins to take over some basic work in the industry, the training remains highly demanding. Zhou Jiaxiang, a member of China's national training squad for this skill, described a six-hour video-production module in which contestants may have to adjust dozens or even hundreds of parameters and fine-tune transition effects frame by frame.
Data show that demand for AI-related skills has risen rapidly in China. Newly posted campus-recruitment positions in AI surged 47.3 percent year on year in the first five months of 2026, according to data from the talent research arm of Maimai, a Chinese networking and recruitment platform.
For Hourant, this shift points to a changing division of labor rather than an either/or choice between humans and AI. "It is not AI in the end," he said, adding that the future lies in combining human skills with AI.
BUILDING SKILLS FOR TOMORROW
The skills on display in Shanghai point to a challenge, namely whether the supply of skilled workers can keep pace with industries that are evolving faster than before.
Official data reveal that China has more than 220 million skilled workers, including over 72 million highly skilled workers. Yet gaps remain in fast-growing sectors. According to the Ministry of Education, China faced a shortage of more than 10 million highly skilled workers in areas related to the digital economy and intelligent manufacturing in 2025, making the expansion of skilled talent a top priority.
The country has been stepping up efforts to reduce this shortfall. The ministry added 27 programs to the country's vocational education catalog in July, covering fields like the digital economy, AI, the low-altitude economy and advanced equipment, with new offerings related to humanoid robots, to better match talent supply with emerging and future industries.
Over 5.5 million instances of subsidized vocational skills training were provided in the first half of 2026, with programs focusing on areas such as AI, advanced manufacturing, new-energy vehicles and the low-altitude economy, the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security noted.
Shanghai Information Technology College, for example, has added four programs tailored to the city's AI industry and brought real production scenarios, technical standards and company projects into the teaching environment.
Elsewhere, schools are strengthening links with industry to keep training in step with swiftly changing industry needs. At Jiangxi Software Vocational and Technical University in east China, the campus is integrated with an industrial park, with nearly 100 companies involved in tailored training. Enterprise engineers teach classes, while real commercial projects are brought onto campus.
"Vocational education cannot be run behind closed doors," said Vice Principal of Shanghai Information Technology College Sun Pengtao. "Programs have to be updated along with industry."
(Video reporters: Ding Ting and Zhou Rui; Video editors: Hong Liang and Zhu Cong) ■

Feature: CPEC-driven connectivity gives fresh impetus to Pakistan's tourism, local businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:41:46 CST
20:41:46 KST

by Misbah Saba Malik
ISLAMABAD, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Haidar Baig's father once ran a small gift shop in Shigar district of Pakistan's northern Gilgit-Baltistan region, earning most of his income during the peak tourism season in June and July. In recent years, however, the growing influx of domestic tourists, facilitated by improved road connectivity under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), has transformed the family business.
Seeing the steady rise in visitors, Baig decided after graduating from college to expand his father's business rather than seek a job elsewhere. Today, the family runs a much larger gift shop, "The Baig's Treasure," in the heart of Shigar.
"Due to improved road connectivity, travel has become cheaper, and people from even southern Sindh province now frequently visit the northern areas. Initially, only wealthy people who could afford air travel could come, but now CPEC is gradually changing that equation. Because of better roads, a large number of middle-income families also visit and spend time in the mountain areas," Baig told Xinhua.
Baig is not alone. Across the region, improved road connectivity has helped local businesses expand as more tourists travel to previously remote destinations.
"CPEC has played a great role in promoting domestic tourism in Pakistan. Access to areas that were previously considered remote and far-flung has improved with the development of a vast road network connecting the southern, eastern and northern parts of the country," Aftab Ur Rehman Rana, managing director of the Pakistan Tourism Development Corporation (PTDC), told Xinhua.
According to Pakistan's Ministry of Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, the 392-km Sukkur-Multan Motorway has made road travel between Punjab and Sindh shorter and more convenient, while the 120-km Havelian-Thakot section of the Karakoram Highway (KKH) has improved connectivity toward the scenic northern areas.
As more tourists arrive, businesses ranging from hotels and restaurants to transport services, handicrafts and retail shops are benefiting from the expanding tourism economy.
Talking to Xinhua, Muhammad Ali, a tourist who took a road trip from the country's southern port city of Karachi to Gilgit with his family last month, said that a friend had recommended the trip after improved roads shortened travel time.
"We wanted to explore the northern areas as a family, but the long journey and high cost of air travel had discouraged us in the past. With improved roads, traveling by car has become more affordable and flexible," Ali told Xinhua.
He said the journey itself had become part of the experience, allowing his family to stop at different places along the route and spend money at local restaurants and shops.
Multan district in the country's eastern Punjab province offers another glimpse into how improved connectivity is reshaping Pakistan's tourism and hospitality landscape.
Once primarily known as a historic and commercial center of southern Punjab, the district has increasingly emerged as an important stop for business travelers moving between different parts of the country.
Talking to Xinhua, Farhan Hussain, a tour operator in Multan, said improved road links have made it easier for businessmen, investors and other travelers to reach the city, bringing a steady stream of visitors who need places to stay, eat and conduct meetings.
"The change brought by CPEC is clearly visible in Multan's hospitality sector, where many new hotels and restaurants have emerged to cater to growing demand. Unlike the northern areas, Multan is neither primarily a leisure destination nor a major tourist hub. Nevertheless, the number of travelers visiting the city has increased rapidly, particularly for business and shopping," he added.
For local entrepreneurs, the growing flow of visitors means a larger customer base and new opportunities to expand businesses that once relied largely on local customers.
"Multan's handicrafts, traditional dresses and jewelry are unique in their design and quality. In the past, the city was mainly visited by wholesale dealers, who purchased these products and took them to other parts of the country. With better road connectivity, however, we are now seeing a growing influx of end consumers who come directly to the city and throng its markets for shopping," Hussain said.
From the winding roads of Gilgit-Baltistan to the growing hotel sector of Multan, improved connectivity under CPEC is bringing people, businesses and markets closer together, helping tourism become an increasingly important source of income and entrepreneurship for communities across Pakistan. ■

====================================================================================================

The secret Cold War history of Tetris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:41:36 UTC
20:41:36 KST

Earlier this month, the Trump administration released a politically charged clone of Tetris called Build the Wall. The Tetris Company (TTC), which owns the rights to the iconic video game, swiftly responded with a thinly veiled legal threat, writing on X: “We take copyright infringement very seriously.” Four days later, the White House took down the game without explanation.
Whether TTC’s post prompted the removal is unknown. But the episode points to a broader and more dubious claim advanced by the company: that it holds exclusive rights to what it misleadingly refers to as “Tetris” pieces — and, more broadly, to any electronic puzzle that involves falling shapes. The claim relies on a flawed ruling rendered in 2012 in Tetris Holding, LLC v. Xio Interactive, Inc., a case in which a federal judge decreed that geometric forms made of four equal-sized squares, each joined together with at least one other square along an edge, were copyrighted and belonged to Russian engineer Alexei Pajitnov and game designer and entrepreneur Henk Rogers, collectively organized as TTC.
The problem: Pajitnov did not design these puzzle pieces, known as tetrominoes, and despite TTC’s relentless public-relations campaign to the contrary, they are not unique to Tetris. In fact, famed Caltech mathematician Solomon Golomb first described them in 1953 during a talk at the Harvard Mathematics Club, and they were later popularized in Scientific American.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But TTC’s false claim to originality is only one aspect of the game’s dark and bizarre history.
Rewind to 1993. First Lady Hillary Clinton is pictured aboard an Air Force plane, absorbed in her Game Boy, playing Tetris. The black-and-white White House photograph doesn’t show the cartridge clearly enough to make out the details, but Clinton’s Staff Secretary, Robert Russo, confirmed to me that she was indeed playing the game.
The irony was great. The United States was boasting that it had just won the Cold War. A major instrument of that victory had been the spread of Western culture throughout the Eastern bloc through films, television, popular music, and other media. Yet the video game that had made it aboard the First Lady’s plane, and into a vast number of U.S. and Western-European households, was not an American product, but a Soviet one. What’s more, it had been designed and coded in a state artificial-intelligence research lab tightly controlled by the KGB, the dreaded secret police of the Russian dictatorship, at a time when U.S. President Ronald Reagan referred to the Soviet Union as the “evil empire.” The story of the commercial success of Tetris is the poster child for two systems radically opposed in history, culture, economics, and politics. In fact, it arises out of this opposition.
Ironically, Tetris’s success began because the totalitarian Soviet regime did not recognize what we take for granted in the West: the freedom to publish. After Pajitnov adapted Golomb’s geometric discoveries for the nascent digital world, he had no choice but to distribute his game as a samizdat, a self-published underground cultural good passed on the sly—except that rather than being mimeographed on paper like its illustrious sibling, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s “The Gulag Archipelago,” Pajitnov’s samizdat got passed around on floppy disks.
The game rapidly made its way through the Eastern bloc before reaching Hungary, where British software entrepreneur Robert Stein recognized its commercial potential. From there, its licensing history became notoriously tangled. Rights to various versions passed, under sometimes competing claims, through the Robert Maxwell group, Atari, Sega, and finally to Nintendo, which packaged Tetris as the Game Boy’s “killer app.” By then, the USSR had taken control of the game through its technology export agency, ELORG, run by a stern bureaucrat, Nikolai Belikov. The micro-computers, Nintendo, and coin-op versions sold in the West filled the Communist Party’s coffers handsomely.
And then, the Berlin Wall collapsed. The floodgates of capitalism—and, in Russia’s case, mayhem—opened. At the game of perestroika (Gorbachev) and privatization (Yeltsin), the rule of law and Russia lost. Out of the resulting confusion emerged two competing claims to ownership of Tetris: one advanced by Patjinov and the other by Nikolai Belikov.
Despite the fact that the USSR generally did not recognize private property, or the copyrightability of software for that matter, or the fact that he had designed the game on his work time using his work computer, Pajitnov, who by then had moved to the U.S., cast himself as the victim and claimed that the game’s copyright had been his all along. The appeal to pity was powerful and should not have survived reasonable legal scrutiny, but thanks to a few sympathetic judges, it did.
Meanwhile, the nomenklatura man in charge of exporting the game on behalf of the USSR pulled a rather bold trick: He created a corporation in Delaware, also conveniently named ELORG, and, as head of Soviet ELORG, assigned the Tetris rights to that American shell. This was most likely done through a backroom deal with Yeltsin’s people and the KGB, although specific details have not been documented.
What has been documented is that in exchange, Belikov owed Soviet generals and colonels, now organized as a mafia entangled with the nascent Russian state, 50 percent of the Tetris proceeds. In grand oligarch fashion, Belikov then crossed the Russians and hid the proceeds through a flurry of shell corporations and accounts in the U.S., Africa, the Grand Cayman Islands, and the Bahamas. Lest this sound too much like a spy movie to be true, years of litigation produced Belikov’s own testimony, along with detailed charts of the opaque setup.
After the Soviet Union collapsed, Belikov and Patjinov—who by then had teamed up with Nintendo’s fixer Henk Rogers — sued each other over the rights to the game in federal court in New York. Pajitnov had very little going for him. The USSR did not recognize software copyright, or any private property for that matter other than for household pots and pans. Further, he developed the game on his work computer during work hours, which under U.S. legal principles would make it his employer’s property.
Belikov, for his part, claimed that ELORG, a Soviet state agency, had miraculously morphed into the Delaware company he had formed, and that he therefore owned the rights. When the new Russian state, entangled in its own domestic mess, failed to react, Pajitnov, Rogers, and Belikov settled. The pair of friends would get the rights, while the bureaucrat received $15 million, which he quickly made disappear from his homeland’s sight through an elaborate web of offshore corporate shells and a Panamanian passport he bought for $200,000 for the occasion.
Pajitnov and Rogers also proceeded to erase anything that would come in the way of Pajitnov’s miraculous claim of original exclusive ownership. That included a young Soviet programmer named Vadim Gerasimov. In 1985, Gerasimov worked closely with Pajitnov to develop the game and single-handedly designed and coded the MS-DOS port (the original game had been coded by Pajitnov on an arcane Russian minicomputer, the Electronika 60). Although Pajitnov had originally credited Gerasimov for his work (including in an under-oath testimony in U.S. court), he later testified (also under oath) that he was the sole author. Rogers played his part in supporting his friend and changed the credits on the console port he developed for the Nintendo Famicom to erase any mention of Gerasimov. The before-and-after screenshots of the credits are telling.
By the mid-1990s, Pajitnov and Rogers seemed to have a firm grip on the Tetris intellectual property. But the World Wide Web changed the picture. The Web enabled a flurry of Tetris derivatives to flourish and be widely distributed as freeware. TTC would have none of it and aggressively unleashed its army of lawyers after what were often teenage amateur creators. It was ironic, since the early success of Tetris happened by virtue of it being distributed as freeware. TTC didn’t hesitate to overreach, going after any game that had falling shapes, such as Alphatris, which involves single-square blocks featuring letters. In these post-perestroika days, a symbol of the socialist republic had become a symbol of capitalist copywrongs.
TTC went one step further, falsely claiming in a court filing that the “seven Tetrimino playing pieces made up of four equally sized square [sic] joined at their sides,” and “the visual delineation of individual blocks that comprise each Tetrimino piece and the display of their borders” are “original and distinctive” and “were designed in the 1980s by Alexey Pajitnov.” As we saw, however, the tetrominoes are elementary geometric forms that Golomb had identified and described in the 1950s. And although U.S. copyright law does not protect geometric forms, the Xio court fell for TTC’s bait and effectively extended copyright protection to the tetrominoes themselves. Which is doubly flawed because if such shapes were copyrightable, then Golomb would be the copyright holder, and Pajitnov should have been found to be infringing!
Tetris is a story of contrasts. Contrasts between two systems: the oppressive Soviet communist dictatorship and the Western free-market capitalist economy, and the story of what happens when the two meet. Contrasts between the official corporate story and a more nuanced reality, which shows a darker side to the Tetris story: a pattern of internally contradictory statements by Pajitnov; blatant misstatements of facts, some of which were made under oath; a systematic erasure by TTC of important facts and characters; and the monopolization through copyright law of geometrical forms and mathematical concepts that should have remained in the public domain.
But Tetris is also a story of ambiguities caused by the murkiness of changing times in the East — first with Mikhail Gorbachev’s perestroika and then amid the rise of oligarchs under Boris Yeltsin, from which Belikov benefited handsomely before fleeing and disappearing with his Tetris millions. In sum, Tetris is a story of tumultuous times.

ATLANTA, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A chartered FedEx cargo plane carrying a pair of Chinese giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, landed in Atlanta in the southeastern United States on Sunday morning.
The two giant pandas are expected to stay at Zoo Atlanta for 10 years, according to an agreement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association.
Chinese veterinarians and caretakers have arrived in Atlanta in advance to prepare for the pandas' arrival and support their life in quarantine, training and adjustment to the new environment, Xinhua learnt.
Gina Ferrie, vice president of collections and conservation, Zoo Atlanta, said on Thursday that they were "very excited" to be able to have giant pandas return to Zoo Atlanta "after a long two years."
"We've been preparing for Ping Ping and Fu Shuang's arrival. We have added many enhancements to their habitat, including new day rooms that have much more room and very top-of-the-line zoological lighting and floors and other conditions to give them the best welfare," Ferrie told Xinhua.
Ping Ping, the male one born on March 17, 2020, and Fu Shuang, the female one born on Oct. 18, 2020, departed for Zoo Atlanta from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in southwest China's Sichuan Province. ■

Voters in canton Vaud says ‘yes’ to a significant tax cut
On Sunday, voters in the Swiss canton of Vaud approved a 12% reduction in cantonal income and wealth tax. A slight majority of 53.1% voters were in favour.
The initiative, launched by business associations, has thus prevailed against opposition from left-wing parties and trade unions. The result also marks a defeat for the cantonal government, which had spoken out against the initiative.
The initiative will reduce cantonal income and wealth tax by 12% from the 2027 tax year onwards. Its supporters aim to make Vaud more attractive from a tax perspective compared with other cantons and to ease the tax burden on the middle class.

Swiss voters reject bid to enshrine stricter neutrality by big margin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

Swiss voters reject tighter neutrality rules that would have curbed NATO cooperation
- Swiss voters rejected a proposal to enshrine stricter neutrality in the constitution, allowing the government to maintain flexible interpretation and sanctions against Russia.
- The initiative aimed to make neutrality "eternal and armed", ban military alliances, and block non-UN sanctions, but received only about 31% support.
- The vote preserves current policy favouring sanctions on Russia and pragmatic neutrality, reflecting public approval of government actions despite opposition from the Swiss People’s Party.
AI generated
ZURICH – Swiss voters on Sept 27 firmly rejected a proposal to adopt a more restrictive form of neutrality that would have blocked their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
All cantons and about 70 per cent of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed.
“This result is not a vote against neutrality. Switzerland was neutral yesterday, it is neutral today, and it will remain neutral in the future,” Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said at a press conference following the outcome.
While Swiss neutrality has been internationally recognised since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815, how the government implements it is not spelled out.
The right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP) has said that Switzerland’s traditional position has been eroded after Bern imposed sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
The campaign had funded posters across the country urging people to vote “No war, yes to neutrality”, featuring white peace doves, ahead of the vote.
Cassis said the rejection allows Switzerland to continue deciding on economic sanctions on a case-by-case basis and to cooperate with partners when doing so strengthens the country’s security, which, he stressed, also depends on the security of its neighbours and the European continent.
Swiss government, most parties oppose the proposal
Apart from the SVP, most parties and the Swiss government opposed the proposal. The Green Party, the Social Democrats (SP), the Centre Party and the FDP all expressed relief over the outcome on Sept 27.
“Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green Party.
An FDP statement said the decision was important for an armed, neutral Switzerland that retains the ability to act.
The SVP meanwhile accepted the defeat and said it currently had no plans for further action.
“I’m of course not pleased with the result,” said SVP lawmaker Lukas Reimann, adding that the commitment to Swiss neutrality expressed by all sides during the campaign was encouraging.
“It is absolutely clear that neutrality belongs to Switzerland and is part of Switzerland’s identity,” he said. “Going forward, we will judge the opponents of the initiative by that commitment.”
If the government or opponents of the initiative were to stray from neutrality, for example by adopting tougher sanctions, the party would need to become active again, Reimann said.
‘Swiss voters like neutrality’
Fabio Wasserfallen, a professor of European politics at the University of Bern, said before the vote: “Swiss voters like neutrality, but they approve of how the government is implementing it at present.”
“They are also generally in favour of the sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, and don’t want that to change.”
The campaign wanted the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defence alliance unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
It is the second SVP-backed initiative voters have rejected in 2026.
In June, they turned down a proposal to cap Switzerland’s population at 10 million. Under the country’s system of direct democracy, voters can be called to the polls up to four times a year.
In a separate ballot on Sept 27, voters also rejected a plan to produce more food locally. The proposal, which would have indirectly reduced domestic meat production, received just 24 per cent support. BLOOMBERG, REUTERS

Northern Ireland march set for first time since Good Friday Agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:38:42 UTC
20:38:42 KST

Protesters block Northern Ireland march being held for first time since Good Friday Agreement
Tensions ran high in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was blocked from making its way through the town of Portadown by thousands of protesters.
The demonstrators, many wearing balaclavas, congregated on a street in the town, where many favor unification with the Republic of Ireland. They came after an early-hours decision from the High Court in Belfast to give the parade the go-ahead.
Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald and First Minister Michelle O'Neill are among the protesters blocking the road, according to BBC News. O'Neill urged the crowd to stay until at least midnight.
Gavin Robinson, the leader of the loyalist Democratic Unionist Party, has accused O'Neill and her party of breaking the law and "giving two fingers to the police, the courts and the rule of law," according to the BBC.
It's the first time in nearly 30 years that the Orange Order parade has been allowed to go down the Garvaghy Road, which had been a notorious flashpoint between the communities in the years before the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 largely ended the bloodshed in Northern Ireland. During the so-called Troubles, some 3,600 people were killed while some 50,000 were wounded.
Ending the Troubles meant balancing competing identities in Northern Ireland, which remained in the United Kingdom when the rest of Ireland won independence a century ago. Irish nationalists in the north — most of them Catholic — seek union with the Republic of Ireland, while largely Protestant unionists want to stay part of the U.K.
Both sides appeared to be adhering to calls from across the political spectrum, including from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, to avoid stoking tensions further.
"I am hoping we will bring all of today's events to a sensible and peaceful conclusion," said Jon Boutcher, the head of the Police Service of Northern Ireland.
Boutcher said there had been many "sensible voices" calling for calm which he thought had been "listened to by all parties."
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, who represents Sinn Féin, the party historically linked to the Irish Republican Army, faced criticism for attending the unlicensed protest on the Garvaghy Road to support the local community.
"She's the head of an executive and she is prepared to wilfully disregard the ruling of our courts, the determination by the statutory body charged with determining parades in Northern Ireland," said Gavin Robinson, who is the leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, the largest pro-U.K. party in Northern Ireland.
O'Neill, whose government is made up of a cross-section of Northern Ireland parties as part of the power-sharing agreement within the Good Friday Agreement, defended her actions, saying "the progress of the last 28 years have been brought into question by the actions of the Orange Order and those within political unionism that want to drag us backwards."
For days, there had been uncertainty about whether the parade, which celebrates Northern Ireland's Protestant heritage and links with the U.K., was given the final go-ahead at a court hearing concluded at 2:15 a.m. Sunday, a move that prompted the protesters to take to the street.
The Orange Order is named after William of Orange, a Protestant prince of Holland who defeated the Catholic King James to take over the British throne in the 17th century.

'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
12:38:03 BST
20:38:03 KST

Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes
- Published
Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".
The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.
The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.
The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.
"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.
Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.
The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement.
"It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.
The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.
Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.
On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.
During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".
The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church".
"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.
The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.
But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.
Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.
The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.
Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.
A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain.
Later on Sunday, the Pope met staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, and took part in a torchlight procession.
It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025.
Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots.

EU Unveils €710M Aid Package for Displaced People in Ukraine, Middle East, Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:37:01 UTC
20:37:01 KST

The EU will provide €52 million ($59 million) to help Ukraine prepare for winter as part of an almost €710 million ($809 million) aid package, with most of the remaining funds to be allocated to displaced people in Sub-Saharan Africa and crisis relief elsewhere.
President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen unveiled the package during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Saturday, Sept. 26, as the high-level week of the summit was wrapping up.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a statement from the Commission’s humanitarian aid department, the funding for Ukraine will cover humanitarian assistance and emergency preparedness, including winterization, shelter, essential services and energy-related support ahead of the cold season.
“With today’s package, we will support displaced communities across Africa – as well as the communities welcoming them,” von der Leyen said.
“We are also boosting emergency aid for those affected by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine,” she continued, pointing to conflict, extreme weather and the rising cost of living as the main forces upending lives around the world.
The pledge was made as part of the 2026 campaign run by international advocacy group Global Citizen, according to von der Leyen’s statement on X.
Most of the funding allocated to Africa
The largest share of the funding, roughly €380 million (approximately $433
Budanov Announces Major POW Exchange With Russia as Early as Next Week
million), will be allocated to Sub-Saharan Africa this year in an aim to protect vulnerable migrants, help people who choose to return home rebuild their lives, and improve how countries in the region manage migration and forced displacement.
Out of that sum, approximately €240 million ($273 million) will be provided to the EU’s Migration Protection, Return and Reintegration program for the region, according to the EC.
The remaining €140 million ($159 million) covers projects such as migration management and support for displaced people and host communities in eastern Mauritania, as well as services for refugees in Kenya, where the refugee crisis has dragged on for years.
Part of the funding will go toward job training tied to employment opportunities.
Brussels is also setting aside another €10 million ($11 million) to back peace efforts in Africa’s Great Lakes region and promote social cohesion.
The money is intended to link local mediation led by women, young people and civil society groups with national and international peace talks.
Another €7.5 million ($8.5 million) will be deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fight its Ebola outbreak and build up its health surveillance and emergency response over the long term, including through the work of the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development and the Institution Buisson Bernard (IBB).
Emergency aid for the Middle East
Ukraine’s €52 million (roughly $59 million) is part of around €252 million ($287 million) drawn from the EU’s Emergency Aid Reserve, which still needs approval from the bloc’s budgetary authority, according to the EC.
Lebanon and Palestine will be allocated €103 million ($117 million) due to continued hostilities and mass displacement, which have put heavy strain on essential services and overall daily life.
The remaining €97 million ($111 million) is earmarked for Sub-Saharan Africa, where conflict, hunger, malnutrition and climate shocks are deepening humanitarian needs.
The funding includes Ebola response in Congo and neighboring countries.
New health investments
Alongside the aid package, the EC announced three new health investments under its Global Gateway strategy during the UNGA.
They include an EU guarantee to draw private investment into health and nutrition businesses in Sub-Saharan Africa, a European Investment Bank loan backed by the EU to expand vaccine and biological medicine production in Colombia, and €60 million ($69 million) to strengthen primary health care in Ethiopia.
With the new pledge, the Commission has allocated more than €2.53 billion ($2.89 billion) in humanitarian aid since the start of the year, pending budget approval.
Ukraine continues preparing for winter
Meanwhile, Ukraine is racing to secure additional funding and air defense support from its partners before its fifth year of war.
On Friday, EU member states agreed to release €6.6 billion ($7.5 billion) from the European Peace Facility (EPF), a fund Hungary had kept blocked since 2023 under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
During his trip to New York for the UNGA this week, President Volodymyr Zelensky met with US President Donald Trump, aiming to continue a diplomatic push that gained momentum when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited both Moscow and Kyiv in early September.
Kyiv is also working to secure urgently needed Patriot interceptors – one of the very few systems capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles.
According to Zelensky, Trump has promised that Washington will grant Ukraine a license to produce Patriots domestically.
The US president initially announced the license transfer in July but later backtracked on the commitment by saying Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology.
Earlier this month, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Ukraine was working to secure about 1,000 Patriot missiles with allies’ support and an EU loan, though most are expected to arrive over several years.

The disruption to air travel followed a September 8 warning by the U.S. Treasury Department that airports providing services to 27 Iranian airlines could face secondary sanctions. Iraqi authorities subsequently ordered aviation officials at airports in Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah and Kirkuk to suspend flights operated by Iranian carriers.
The suspension has stranded thousands of passengers, including religious pilgrims, students and people traveling to Iraq for medical treatment.
The Iranian minister said thousands of Iraqi students would continue their studies at Iranian universities during the new academic year. He also referred to the allocation of 200 scholarships for Iraqi students as part of efforts to further strengthen academic exchanges between the two countries.
Iran has attracted students from 101 countries despite existing challenges, Saeed Habiba, head of the Organization of Student Affairs, said in October 2025.
He said the scientific capabilities of Iranian universities and their positive record in international cooperation constitute a valuable opportunity that should be leveraged to turn the presence of international students into a national discourse and a basis for strategic planning.
According to Habiba, foreign students studying in Iran mainly come from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan.
