EU tells countries to curb energy demand as gas prices face winter squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:33:43 UTC
20:33:43 KST

Although the EU is not facing immediate gas shortages, Energy Commissioner Jørgensen warned capitals that soaring prices driven by rising global demand could lead to shortages as winter approaches, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen urged EU governments to continue curbing energy demand to reduce gas and electricity consumption amid "exceptionally low" storage levels, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
"I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can sustain injections or reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," reads the letter, noting that the situation "has not improved" since Jørgensen's first warning in March.
The warning comes as EU gas storage is around 70% full, roughly 12 percentage points below the same point last year, according to the latest figures from the trade association Gas Infrastructure Europe. Continued disruption in the Middle East and fierce competition from Asia for liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes are pushing prices up, threatening a supply crisis.
The Dutch TTF, the European benchmark for natural gas prices, is trading at around €72 per MWh, up €40MWh since the United States and Israel bombed Iran on 28 February. Analysts are warning of potential spikes above €100/MWh during peak winter if LNG export volumes from the Gulf fail to grow or if Norwegian maintenance prolongs export constraints.
The EU's top energy leader said that using less electricity at peak times can mean burning less gas in power plants, easing pressure on both gas supplies and power prices. Households and businesses are already sensitive to energy bills, while governments are under pressure to cushion consumers from another price shock.
The Commission points specifically to measures that were used during the 2022 energy crisis, including reducing electricity consumption during peak hours, encouraging consumers to shift demand through smart meters and retail tariffs, limiting temperatures in public buildings, restricting outdoor heating and switching off unnecessary public lighting at night.
However, Jørgensen stops short of imposing mandatory measures.
"Voluntary and well-planned demand reduction measures proved useful during the 2022 energy crisis, and we can draw on the lessons from that experience in the current situation," the letter reads.
Nonetheless, the EU's energy top leader also points ministers towards their national emergency plans, which contain more serious tools that could be activated if conditions deteriorate — including interruptible gas contracts and switching power plants from gas to other fuels.
No storage rush, though
Jørgensen also encouraged capitals to use the flexibility in EU gas-storage rules to avoid panic buying and consider an 80% filling target, rather than pushing aggressively towards the 90% goal.
Normally, filling storage is about security since more gas underground means a bigger buffer when winter demand rises. But buying large quantities of gas when global markets are already tight can itself push prices higher.
The Commission has argued that reaching 80% can be sufficient for winter security under current conditions, while allowing countries to spread purchases over a longer period and avoid a late-season scramble for gas.
The Danish Commissioner suggested the EU is entering the winter with a more resilient energy system than it had before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but not a comfortable one.
"Although EU gas storage is exceptionally low and the situation remains challenging, there are currently no immediate risks to security of supply," reads the letter.
From price to supply
Despite the reassurances, Brussels is no longer talking only about protecting consumers from high prices. It is asking EU governments to manage demand because consumption itself is becoming part of the supply problem.
"As we discussed in the Energy Union Task Force, we are facing a price crisis linking to a supply crisis," reads the letter.
For now, Brussels remains careful to distinguish between a deteriorating price situation and an immediate physical shortage, saying there is currently no immediate risk to security of supply.
The EU may have enough gas to get through the winter, but securing it could come at a much higher price, especially if global LNG markets remain tight and European countries have to compete with buyers.

Disqualifying Ra'am from Israeli elections: It’s good for Zionism, bad for democracy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:32:37 UTC
20:32:37 KST

I support the decision to disqualify Ra’am from the upcoming election. I also believe that disqualifying a political party and denying citizens the ability to vote for it is bad for democracy.
Those statements are uncomfortable together, but they are not contradictory. They expose one of the hardest questions buried inside Israel’s definition of itself as both Jewish and democratic: What happens when democratic participation collides with the preservation of the Jewish national character of the state?
My answer is that Israel should not sacrifice its Jewish character on the altar of democracy. But anyone making that argument should also be honest enough to admit that defending a democracy can sometimes require measures that carry a democratic price.
On Wednesday, the Central Elections Committee voted 18-5 to disqualify Ra’am from participating in the October 27 election. Likud, Otzma Yehudit, and the Choosing Life Forum submitted the petitions against Ra’am, and together invoked the grounds in Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset.
The attorney-general’s office opposed the disqualification, saying the evidence did not satisfy the stringent legal standard required to exclude the list. Because this is the disqualification of an entire candidate list rather than an individual candidate, it does not automatically require Supreme Court confirmation.
Ra’am and its representatives can appeal the decision, and such an appeal is expected.
The distinction matters because the case against Ra’am should be made from what can actually be established, not from slogans. Ra’am is the political wing of the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement, an organization whose ideological roots were influenced by the Muslim Brotherhood.
The movement’s 2018 charter described Zionism as a racist and occupying project, supported a Palestinian right of return, and rejected identification with Zionism. Those are not marginal disagreements over taxation, borders, or social policy. They go directly to the ideological legitimacy of the movement that created the Jewish state.
At the same time, intellectual honesty requires acknowledging what has changed. Mansour Abbas publicly declared in 2021 that Israel “was born a Jewish state” and would remain one.
Ra’am subsequently participated in an Israeli governing coalition and today presents itself as a pragmatic vehicle for advancing the interests of Arab citizens within the Israeli political system. The attorney-general’s representative specifically cited Abbas’s recognition of Israel’s Jewish character when arguing against disqualification.
That evolution matters. I do not believe it settles the question.
There are also serious institutional questions surrounding the broader movement.
In May, the Lod District Court ordered the dissolution of the Association for Humanitarian Actions, a nonprofit associated with Ra’am and the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement, after a Justice Ministry investigation found reason to believe the organization had transferred funds to or cooperated with organizations outside Israel designated as terrorist organizations.
The court cited serious and continuing problems, including joint activity with a declared terrorist organization.
Here is where precision becomes essential. That ruling was against the nonprofit. It was not a judicial finding that Ra’am itself financed Hamas, and the attorney-general’s office has said the evidence presented in the election petitions did not sufficiently connect the party to support for armed struggle or allow the conduct attributed to charitable organizations to be imputed to Ra’am.
I still support the disqualification.
I support it not because the words “Islamist” or “anti-Zionist” should automatically remove someone from Israeli politics. They should not.
Section 7A itself does not prohibit a party merely for offending Zionists. It prohibits a list or candidate whose purposes or actions negate Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, incite racism, or support armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
For me, the cumulative picture matters: Ra’am’s institutional origins, the Southern Islamic Movement’s ideological charter, its rejection of Zionism, the continuing controversy surrounding organizations in its wider ecosystem, and the fundamental question of whether pragmatic participation has genuinely replaced the movement’s earlier ideological commitments or merely learned to operate alongside them.
The attorney-general reaches a different legal conclusion about whether that evidence satisfies Section 7A. The Supreme Court may ultimately reach the same conclusion. That is precisely what judicial review is for.
But Zionism is entitled to have red lines.
Where does Israel draw the line?
A Jewish state is not simply a country in which a majority of the population happens to be Jewish. Israel exists because the Jewish people reclaimed the right to national self-determination after centuries in which their survival depended upon the decisions of others.
If Israel loses that purpose, it does not simply become a different version of Israel. It ceases to fulfill the purpose for which Zionism created it.
Yet this is where my own argument becomes uncomfortable, because democracy is not foreign to Zionism either.
Zionism was democratic before it was sovereign. Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, bringing together roughly 200 delegates from 17 countries and establishing the institutions of a movement seeking Jewish national restoration decades before the state’s establishment.
The World Zionist Organization today explicitly defines Zionism as adhering to principles of justice, equality, and democracy, while its Jerusalem Program describes strengthening Israel as Jewish, Zionist, and democratic as a foundation of the movement.
Jabotinsky understood the same duality. Few Zionist leaders were more uncompromising about Jewish sovereignty, Jewish military power, and the necessity of a Jewish majority. Yet the Knesset’s account of his political thought notes that the constitution he envisioned would guarantee equal civil rights and cultural autonomy for the Arab minority.
Strength did not require inequality. Jewish sovereignty did not require Arab civic inferiority.
The Declaration of Independence carried that same tension into the founding of Israel itself. It asserted Jewish national independence while committing the state to equality of social and political rights and calling upon its Arab inhabitants to participate in building the country based on full and equal citizenship and representation.
That is why I call this decision good for Zionism and bad for democracy.
Removing a political party from an election is an extraordinary act. It limits the choices available to citizens. It places enormous power in the hands of institutions deciding which political ideas fall beyond legitimate participation.
Israel’s history demonstrates why courts have traditionally demanded exceptionally strong evidence before allowing that power to be exercised. Previous Central Elections Committee disqualifications of Arab lists and individual candidates have repeatedly been overturned by the Supreme Court.
That democratic danger should not be dismissed merely because I support the outcome this time. A weapon one welcomes when it is pointed at an ideological opponent remains a weapon when political power changes hands.
But democracy is not the only value a democratic Jewish state is obligated to preserve. Democracy describes the system through which citizens exercise political power. Zionism explains why there is a sovereign Jewish state in which that democracy exists.
Neither should casually consume the other.
Ra’am therefore presents a test far larger than Mansour Abbas.
The question is not simply whether Arab citizens deserve political equality. They do. It is not whether Arab parties may disagree profoundly with Jewish governments. Of course they may. Nor should opposition to Zionism, standing alone, become a convenient excuse for removing millions of citizens from meaningful political participation.
The harder question is where Israel draws the line between opposition to the policies of a Jewish state and opposition to the continued national character of the Jewish state itself.
Reasonable people, and reasonable Zionists, can disagree over whether the evidence against Ra’am has crossed the demanding legal threshold established by Section 7A. The attorney-general believes it has not. Those who petitioned for disqualification believe it has. The courts will have their say.
My position remains that the Jewish state is entitled to defend the foundational purpose of its existence, even when doing so exacts a democratic cost.
That cost should trouble us.
It should not paralyze us.
Israel was founded on the audacious proposition that Jewish sovereignty and democratic equality could occupy the same state. Nearly eight decades later, that remains the challenge.
Defending democracy cannot require Israel to surrender what makes it Jewish. Defending Zionism cannot permit Israel to forget what makes it free.
The writer is the founder and CEO of The Israel Innovation Fund (TIIF) and author of the forthcoming book, What is Zionism: Why Never Again Is Not Enough!

‘Science-based approach essential to address environmental hazards’
TEHRAN – Environmental health plays a key role in preventing hazards and safeguarding public health; addressing environmental health challenges requires scientific, evidence-based decision-making, enhanced intersectoral collaborations, and benefiting from the country’s scientific capabilities, Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi has stated.
Today, environmental health constitutes a fundamental component of the healthcare system and a critical investment for the country’s future, the health ministry website quoted Zafarqandi as saying.
The official made the remarks on the occasion of the World Environmental Health Day, which is observed on September 26 every year.
Maintaining the safety of water and food, managing waste and air quality, improving hygiene in public spaces, addressing climate change-related hazards, and monitoring workplace health risks and environmental pollution all play a decisive role in shaping and developing healthy, safe, and sustainable communities, Zafarqandi added.
Air pollution, water stress, sand and dust storms, climate change, urban and medical waste management, contamination of water and soil resources, and the consequences of rapid urbanization are among the challenges faced by the country, he noted.
The health ministry, with the help of environmental health experts, is trying to develop monitoring and surveillance systems, improve water and food safety, strengthen specialized laboratories, utilize modern technologies, increase preparedness to address environmental hazards, and implement preventive programs, Zafarqandi said.
The official went on to say that expanding public education and improving health literacy are among other main policies of the health ministry, as protecting environmental health is almost impossible without informed participation of the public, and cooperation of other executive bodies like municipalities, industries, scientific centers, media, and non-governmental organizations.
For sure, a healthier and more sustainable future relies on boosting the synergy among science, social responsibility, and public participation in the conservation of the environment and environmental health, the official further noted.
World Environmental Day aims to raise awareness about environmental health issues and promote actions to improve and protect the environment for the wellbeing of all living creatures.
This year’s theme, ‘Standing with Science to Protect Communities’, directly aligns with the World Health Organization’s science-based decision-making narrative and highlights the role of environmental health professionals as applied public health scientists translating research into policy, regulation and community protection.
The key messages of the day include: Environmental health practice is evidence-based public health action; Science protects communities from environmental risks; Environmental health professionals are the bridge between science and implementation.
National document on health, climate change strategy being developed
The Health Ministry is developing a national document on health and climate change to mitigate the impacts of climate change on public health and to develop a climate-resilient health system.
So far, a draft of the document has been provided and revised by experts and professors from medical universities in an expert working group on reducing environmental threats to health, IRNA reported.
The document aims to strengthen inter-sectoral cooperation to protect public health, prevent and reduce adverse impacts of climate change, and promote health system resilience in the face of natural hazards.
Climate resilience of health systems is the touchstone of their ability to anticipate, prevent, respond to, cope with, and recover from adverse conditions and climate-related tensions.
The document comprises five goals, 24 strategies, and 106 action plans, establishing a framework for coordinated planning and implementation by various agencies to address health-related consequences of climate change.
The document will be submitted to the supreme council for health and food security to be approved.

A 15-ship naval parade was held in Istanbul’s Bosphorus on Sept. 27 to mark the 488th anniversary of the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Preveza, also hailed as Turkish Naval Forces Day.

The vessels passed off Barbaros Monument in Istanbul’s Beşiktaş district and rendered a ceremonial salute.
Personnel aboard the ships also saluted the tomb of Barbaros Hayreddin Pasha, the Ottoman admiral who commanded the fleet to victory at Preveza in 1538.
Large crowds gathered along the waterfront to watch the event and take photographs.
The Battle of Preveza, fought on Sept. 27, 1538, is regarded as a landmark naval victory for the Ottoman fleet under the command of Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha and as a decisive moment in establishing Ottoman naval supremacy in the Mediterranean.
The anniversary of the victory is commemorated annually as Turkish Naval Forces Day.
Speaking at a reception for Naval Forces Commander Adm. Ercüment Tatlıoğlu and accompanying personnel on the occasion of the 488th anniversary of the victory and Naval Forces Day, Defense Minister Yaşar Güler said the Turkish Navy’s current capabilities reflected not only a powerful fleet but also the country’s national determination, engineering expertise and years of sacrifice.
Güler said Türkiye developed domestically designed and produced warships, submarines, frigates, unmanned naval vessels and advanced technological systems with the capabilities provided by the country’s defense industry, further strengthening the Navy’s operational capacity.
The Turkish Navy wraps up a large-scale military exercise on Sept. 25 involving 100 naval vessels, 50 aircraft and 14,000 personnel across the Black Sea, Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.
The exercise, dubbed “Denizkurdu-I” (Sea Wolf-I), involved frigates, corvettes, fast attack craft and other naval assets. Units conducted operational readiness training and live-fire exercises across a maritime area stretching from the Black Sea through the Marmara and Aegean seas to the eastern Mediterranean.

Ethiopia’s army chief has accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting a new alliance of armed groups trying to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, saying the groups could not succeed unless they were “pushed, supported and supplied” from abroad.
Field Marshal Birhanu Jula also accused Eritrea of acting as a link between foreign backers and armed groups inside Ethiopia. He made the comments in an interview with the Ethiopian army’s media outlet.

The accusation comes as fighting has resumed in northern Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces have seized airports and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions.

Nile dam dispute adds to tensions with Egypt
Birhanu’s accusation against Egypt follows a new exchange between Cairo and Addis Ababa over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, or GERD, on the Blue Nile.
Egyptian Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam said last week that Ethiopian politicians needed to understand that building a dam on a shared river was “not like laying a carpet in their homes”.
He rejected Ethiopia’s argument that decisions about the dam fall solely under its national sovereignty.
Ethiopia’s Water and Energy Ministry responded two days later, saying Sewilam’s remarks reflected a “crude colonial mentality”. It accused Cairo of acting as though its approval was required before countries farther up the Nile could use the river’s water.
Egypt and Sudan want a legally binding agreement covering how the dam is operated, particularly during long periods of drought, as well as the sharing of information about water releases.
Ethiopia says the dam is essential for producing electricity and supporting the country’s development. It maintains that it will not cause significant harm to Egypt or Sudan.
Egypt relies on the Nile for more than 90% of its freshwater. Ethiopia formally inaugurated the GERD in September 2025 without reaching a binding agreement with the two countries.
Relations with Sudan and Eritrea have also worsened
Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan rose in May after Sudan accused Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates of involvement in drone attacks on Khartoum airport.
Sudan said the drones had taken off from Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. Ethiopia rejected the accusation as baseless and accused Sudan of supporting Tigrayan fighters. Neither side’s accusation has been independently verified.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army against Tigrayan forces during the 2020–2022 war. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara later deteriorated following the peace agreement that ended the conflict.
Ethiopia’s government now accuses Eritrea of supporting members of the new armed alliance. Eritrea has repeatedly denied the allegation.

Best Party Speakers (2026): JBL, Sony, Marshall, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

The best party speakers are introducing the idea of raving anywhere to a whole new generation who may have missed the classic block-party boom box of the 1980s. These new speakers look like compact PA systems, and often sound just as loud, with bold and brash looks and bass-heavy profiles. They’re honestly a huge amount of fun.
The rising popularity of party speakers coincides with a broader shift toward entertaining at home rather than in bars and nightclubs, particularly among younger consumers. A July 2026 Harris Poll found that 68 percent of US Gen Z adults say going out is just too expensive, while Attest found that 64 percent now drink primarily at home, up from 42 percent a year earlier.
Where people socialize may be changing, but the need for good atmosphere certainly isn’t. Traditional Bluetooth speakers are convenient and sound great, but they struggle to bring the party. Party speakers, with their serious volume, portability, and LED lights, don’t have that problem.
For more audio guidance, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Turntables, and Best Computer Speakers.
What Is a Party Speaker?
Party speakers are large, high-output Bluetooth speakers designed for social gatherings, sitting somewhere between a conventional wireless speaker and a portable PA. Current battery-powered models range from around 100 to 800 watts of power, with most offering between 12 to 25 hours of battery life, if not more. Expect large drivers, bass-boost modes, LED lighting, handles, wheels, and even replaceable batteries to keep the party going. Microphone and instrument inputs, karaoke controls, and the ability to link multiple speakers are also common, as are partner apps that give you the chance to play DJ, curate the lighting, and alter the sound.
How I Test Party Speakers
I’ve tested party speakers indoors and out, and at background, party, and ear-bleeding volumes. Sound quality is still important, but it’s party time, so bass, vocal clarity, and minimal distortion are key, as is how well the sound can travel (especially outdoors). Karaoke testing was dutifully undertaken by a gaggle of excitable but discerning tweenagers.
As well as playing rave classics at top volume (sorry, neighbors), I’ve analyzed the various EQ and control apps, AI features, digital signal processing (DSP) modes, and the speaker's ability to pair with DJ equipment, separate sources, and musical instruments.
What Should I Look for in a Party Speaker?
Power: Party speakers range from boxes one person can comfortably carry to 60-pound-plus towers on wheels. Power varies, but I’ve tested designs from 100 to 800-plus watts. As a general rule, the more watts it can output, the louder it will be, but clever DSP means brands like JBL and Sony can often make more noise with less watts than you might think.
Battery life: Your needs will again depend on how you party, but between 12 to 25 hours is common. Remember, though, high volume and lighting can cut that number down. Soundboks, for example, quotes 40 hours at mid volume but only six to eight hours at maximum, depending on the speaker.
Connectivity: As well as Bluetooth for wireless convenience, 3.5-mm or other line inputs are useful for DJ controllers, mixers, and sources beyond your phone, while some models add RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections. Outdoor users should look for an IP rating. Replaceable batteries, wheels, sturdy handles, and physical controls become considerably more important once a speaker leaves the living room.
Can I Use a Party Speaker With DJ Decks?
Yes, provided it has a suitable wired input. DJ controllers and mixers typically have a line-out option, commonly through RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections, although a 3.5-mm aux input can also work with the right cable.
If you are mixing, use a cable where possible, as Bluetooth introduces enough latency between moving a control and hearing the result to make accurate cueing and beat-matching difficult. Some specialist DJ systems like the Aiaiai Unit-4 Wireless+ Studio Monitors use proprietary low-latency wireless connections to get around this, but ordinary Bluetooth isn’t designed for the job.
What About Karaoke?
There’s plenty of crossover between party speakers and karaoke machines, but they’re not always the same thing. Some party speakers include one or two microphone inputs, while better-equipped models add wireless mics, separate vocal volume, echo or reverb, ample controls, and even vocal removal. The $350 Soundcore Rave 3S, for example, includes two wireless microphones and real-time vocal removal.
A dedicated karaoke setup puts singing rather than music playback first, and may offer more extensive microphone controls, song management, and accessories. WIRED’s Best Karaoke Gear guide covers those options in more detail.
How Do I Connect Multiple Phones to the Same Bluetooth Speaker?
Bluetooth multipoint lets two phones stay connected simultaneously, although switching between them varies by speaker. For larger groups, Spotify Jam and Apple Music SharePlay let guests choose music from their own phones while one device stays connected to the speaker. YouTube Music also supports collaborative playlists, enabling several people to add songs in advance or during the party.
Best Overall Party Speaker
LG xboom Stage 501 Specs
The Stage 501 turned the open workshop next to my testing studio into something close to a daytime rave (minus the crowd and superstar DJ). Bass was deep and clean, and carried easily across the room. Even when it was so loud I couldn’t hear myself think, there was volume to spare. And best of all, it sounded good, not just loud.
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, it has twin 5.25-inch woofers and two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. There’s 160 watts available on battery and 220 watts when plugged in. The battery is replaceable and lasts up to 25 hours. At full power, with the light show on, it’s less than that, but still more than enough for me.
There are louder and larger options here, but for me, the Stage 501 strikes the ideal balance between outright party power and decent sound quality. It even manages to impress at normal indoor listening volumes, which is often the downfall of party speakers.
LG has embraced the sillier side of the genre too. The app gives you EQ, AI karaoke, synchronized lighting, and DJ effects that are a bit cringe but hard to ignore. Two built-in phone/tablet stands are genuinely useful for karaoke, and there are twin mic inputs, though microphones are sold separately.
At 25.8 pounds, the cabinet remains manageable enough for me to move around on my own, but it is still a big unit to carry and find space for. If it’s too big, the smaller xboom Stage 301 keeps much of the same styling and app functionality, just in a much smaller package.
My Favorite Party Speaker
JBL PartyBox 130 Specs
At 24.8 pounds, the JBL PartyBox 130 isn’t exactly lightweight, but its modest size hits the sweet spot for me in my city home and garden. It’s solidly built, has impressive power for the size, and can be moved without risking my fragile L5 vertebrae.
Two 5.25-inch woofers and a pair of 1-inch tweeters produce 200 watts of output, with plenty of bass and enough volume to get a decent-sized party moving. JBL’s AI Sound Boost uses DSP (clever digital wizardry) to keep distortion under control as the volume rises, while an automatic EQ adjusts the balance depending on what’s playing. Both work well, although I got better results tweaking the EQ myself in the app, and for my ears, the LG xboom Stage 501 still outperforms this speaker.
The light show on this speaker is one of the best, and the app has a collection of lighting and DJ effects that range from fun to downright silly. Big, easy-to-use physical controls on the top of the speaker also make it easy to use without reaching for my phone.
The 15-hour replaceable battery feels a little short, but a 10-minute charge gives another 80 minutes of raving. The speaker is IPX4 splash-proof and has Auracast, optical, USB-C, and aux connections, plus dual mic and guitar inputs.
Best Premium Party Speaker
Marshall Bromley 450 Specs
Marshall has been bringing the party with its speakers since 1962, so its recent foray into Bluetooth party speakers isn’t much of a stretch. The brand's first release was the $1,300 Bromley 750, an enormous, hugely impressive party speaker that makes you look like a roadie.
But for most people and typical house parties, the smaller but still premium Bromley 450 is a much more manageable option. At 27.2 pounds, it’s still hefty, but it packs the punch of a small PA system.
It also looks the part, with Marshall’s signature black-and-brass finish and metal grille giving proper rock-and-roll vibes. Maybe I’m just old, but the classic design feels more authentic than the modern LED-loaded Bluetooth boxes. (The tiny reactive LEDs, however, feel a little limp compared to its rivals.)
Two 6.5-inch woofers powered by 90-watt Class D amps, plus four full-range drivers with 55 watts each and a pair of passive radiators (400 watts total power) provide plenty of volume. The 360-degree arrangement spreads sound impressively around a large room or garden, and bass is powerful without overpowering everything else. If you prefer your vocals front and center-, you may want to spend some time tweaking the EQ in the app regardless.
Connectivity is anything but retro, with Auracast, multipoint, RCA, USB-C, aux, and twin mic/instrument inputs. The physical controls are particularly nice and a joy to use. The replaceable battery lasts an impressive 40-plus hours, while IP55 protection makes this speaker genuinely usable outdoors without having to baby it.
Best Value Party Speaker
Soundcore Rave 3S Specs
With two wireless microphones and ingenious AI Vocal Removal that extracts the vocal track from almost any song you stream, the Rave 3S is already WIRED’s favorite karaoke speaker. But its 200-watt output, strong bass, and impressive beat-synced lighting also make it a solid party speaker.
The AI vocal removal tool is impressive, and much better than the party trick I thought it might be. It isn’t flawless— it occasionally leaves traces of vocals in a song, but it’s customizable via the Soundcore app, and more than capable of enabling enthusiastic duets with Olivia Rodrigo.
A 6.5-inch woofer and three 2.5-inch full-range drivers are loud and clear without sounding too bass-heavy, although if you’re looking for more boom with your bap, there is a BassUp mode that pushes the lower frequencies hard.
At 23.1 pounds, with a well-balanced handle, it’s fairly easy to move about, although being the size and weight of a full carry-on bag, it would benefit from wheels. My only other gripe is that the quoted 12-hour battery life doesn’t compete with the best, and it fell short of that figure in testing.
Best Party Speaker for Deejaying
Sony ULT Tower 7 Specs
Sony’s new ULT range of speakers stretches from the relatively manageable $450 ULT Tower 5 to the frankly ridiculous $1,200 ULT Tower Max. Sitting between them is the ULT Tower 7, with excellent sound, an ample selection of inputs, a combined 420 watts of output, and a 30-hour battery. Be warned, though, while it’s smaller than the Tower Max, it is still absolutely enormous and weighs 50.3 pounds.
Most party speakers will accept music from a DJ controller, but Sony goes further with RCA and balanced XLR inputs, plus an XLR output for expanding a wired setup. Auracast-based Party Chain can also connect up to 100 compatible speakers, so you can go head-to-head with Madison Square Garden on volume.
Inside is an 11-inch woofer, two 4.7-inch midrange drivers, and four tweeters, including a rear-facing pair that spread audio around the room. Bass is deep and effective, and at close quarters with the volume cranked, I could really feel it. It’s not quite bone-shaking at the club levels, but it’s still impressive.
The 360-degree driver configuration helps sound spread out and avoid sounding too boxed in, and while the bass is still quite directional, I really enjoyed the scale and ease with which this speaker filled the room.
If you have the budget and space, and you want to play loud all night, the Sony delivers, but I do wish it had a retractable handle. The built-in corner handles are OK-, but you need to angle it sharply at an odd angle to engage the wheels, and trust me, you don’t want to carry this speaker by hand very far.
Best Compact Party Speaker
Sony ULT Field 7 Specs
After testing the ULT Tower 7, JBL, and LG xboom models, Sony’s Field 7 felt positively pocket-sized. It sits at the junction between full party speaker and oversize Bluetooth speaker, and makes a great case for both. I think it’s ideal as a hi-fi replacement in a college dorm or apartment that can also escape outside.
The 13.9-pound cylindrical design is certainly different, but it’s well made, and can be used vertically or horizontally (though the vertical orientation does scream ashtray to me).
Sound is satisfyingly big for something you can easily pick up and carry. There’s plenty of depth and weight to the bass, and it kept a houseful of girls dancing in the garden without getting distorted. Just as importantly, at lower volumes, it remains controlled enough to work as an everyday speaker rather than something you only wheel out for parties.
The illuminated end rings are fun once the sun goes down, although plenty of rivals do the same trick better. More useful is the IP67 rating and excellent 30-hour battery life, which means this speaker really will survive soggy, grubby, festival style conditions.
There are also mic/guitar and aux inputs, and two levels of bass to choose from, plus a good smattering of inputs, as well as multipoint Bluetooth. It’s not designed to rattle windows, but it is a more practical size and weight without massively compromising on party volume.
Best Rugged Party Speaker
Soundboks Rider Specs
WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz tested the small but mighty Soundboks Rider and found a punchy, portable party speaker that swaps flashing lights and karaoke for serious volume and durability.
At 14.3 pounds it is much easier to move than most party speakers, but an 8-inch woofer and 1.2-inch tweeter still generate up to 118 dB of sound. Harry described the output as “astonishing,” especially as it stayed clear and detailed across the volume range, with bass that didn't overwhelm.
It’s also built for considerably rougher treatment than the average speaker, with a steel grille, thick plastic cabinet, and silicone ball corners. During his drop test, Rabinowitz was more worried about damaging his stairs than the speaker. IP66 dust and water resistance makes it well suited to outdoor use too.
The swappable battery lasts up to 35 hours at mid volume, or eight hours at full blast, which is up there with the best. It also charges over USB-C, which is very convenient for most people.
It's not without compromise, however. Especially given the price, Bluetooth 4.2 feels very old, and connectivity is limited to a 3.5-mm aux input. For $600, it is niche, but if your priorities are portability, durability, and huge, clean sound over party gimmicks, the Rider is difficult to ignore.

Over 5,000 prisoners of unintentional crimes released in six months

Over 5,000 prisoners of unintentional crimes released in six months
TEHRAN – A total of 5,059 prisoners convicted of unintentional crimes were released across Iran during the first half of the current Iranian calendar year, which started on March 21, with their combined debts amounting to 370 trillion rials (around $160 million).
Of those released, 261 were women, and 4,798 were men, IRNA reported on Sunday.
Some 1,034 prisoners were freed without any payment after their cases were settled through reconciliation, mediation and waivers by private complainants.
Since 1990, more than 198,000 prisoners convicted of unintentional crimes have been released and reunited with their families, the figures show.
During the previous Iranian calendar year, which ended on March 20, around 9,000 prisoners serving sentences for unintentional crimes were released.
Currently, 20,349 people, including 950 women and 19,399 men, are imprisoned for unintentional crimes, with their total debts estimated at 2.6 trillion rials, Mehr reported.
The provinces with the highest numbers of prisoners convicted of unintentional crimes are Tehran with 2,968, Fars with 1,898, Khorasan Razavi with 1,845, Isfahan with 1,582 and East Azarbaijan with 1,060.
During the Iranian calendar year 1403 (March 2024–March 2025), benefactors helped secure the release of 11,380 prisoners convicted of unintentional crimes across the country. In the same period, 2,441 prisoners were pardoned, ISNA reported.
The number of prisoners released in that year increased by 22 percent compared with 1402 (March 2023–March 2024). Of those released, 682 were women, and 10,698 were men, most of whom had been imprisoned because they were unable to pay financial debts.
Prisoners convicted of unintentional crimes can be released through several forms of assistance, including temporary leave, financial loans, and debt repayment. Reconciliation and waivers by complainants also play a significant role in resolving such cases.

Iran customs nears 3-day clearance target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:28:42 UTC
20:28:42 KST

Iran customs nears 3-day clearance target
TEHRAN- Iran’s customs clearance times have fallen sharply, with the average dropping from 143 hours to 73 hours—roughly a 50 percent reduction—bringing the country within about one hour of its three-day clearance target. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance is pursuing that goal as part of a broader foreign trade facilitation program.
According to Hassan Alidousti, acting deputy for planning and international affairs at Iran Customs, key factors include a larger share of low-risk goods on the “green path,” expanded use of risk profiles, smartization, and reformed customs procedures. Risk management allows goods to be classified by risk level, with controls matched to each consignment.
The ministry is also advancing coordinated border management and seamless transport. Officials note that more than 20 agencies are involved in border and trade processes, and not all delays originate with customs. Coordinated border management seeks better inter-agency cooperation and less duplication, while seamless transport aims to move goods from entry points to destinations with fewer unnecessary stops.
Essential goods are receiving priority. Grains, livestock inputs, edible oil, medicine, and medical equipment are on the green path and clear faster. About 4.5–4.6 million tons of essential goods are currently being cleared at customs, ports, and entry points, with livestock inputs, edible oil, and oilseeds making up much of the volume; Imam Khomeini Port holds a significant share.
Clearance time also depends on permits, transport, and foreign currency allocation. The minister has stressed coordination with the Central Bank and relevant agencies. By continuing risk management, smartization, coordinated border management, and seamless transport, Iran aims to complete the three-day clearance process and ease goods entry and clearance. Customs officials say the reforms are already reducing dwell time at entry points, and further gains are expected as more consignments qualify for the green path and digital procedures replace manual steps.

'We won't survive': Israeli hikers stranded in Himalayas plead for rescue as landslides worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:28:14 UTC
20:28:14 KST

As the hours pass, concern among the hikers is growing while severe weather continues to hamper rescue efforts. Dozens of Israelis are stranded in the village of Samagaun in Nepal’s Manaslu region of the Himalayas after harsh weather triggered rockslides, blocked roads and damaged bridges. The hikers fear conditions could deteriorate further and are calling for their evacuation to be accelerated.
“There are landslides here every few hours, right over our heads. There’s no need to wait for a disaster to happen,” one Israeli woman told ynet.
“There is no electricity and there have been rockslides near us," another Israeli said. "Our lives were saved by a miracle. We have no way to go back or move forward because bridges have collapsed and roads are blocked. There is a real danger to life here. Any additional landslide could cause flooding and destroy the village we are in. In this situation, our ability to escape or be rescued is almost nonexistent, and there is no real protection here if conditions deteriorate further.”
He said the hikers contacted their insurance company but were told that, at this stage, not everyone could be evacuated.
“Until now we have followed the instructions of the local agencies and acted accordingly, but we are very worried and afraid to stay here another night. We are pleading with everyone not to wait until there are casualties or missing people before the situation gets attention. We are not asking anyone to wait for a disaster before acting. We are asking for help now, while it is still possible to evacuate us safely.”
Dana Zarnitzky, 54, who is also awaiting evacuation, said: “We are two groups, one of four people and one of five. We arrived in Samagaun on Friday for an acclimatization day, and since then our route has come to a halt and we have been stuck because of insane weather.
“The situation worsened overnight, when rockslides began coming down from the mountains surrounding the valley. These landslides happen once every few hours and they are very dangerous because they can carry large amounts of snow and water with them and flood the valley.”
She added: “We are really asking them to speed up our rescue. We contacted the insurance companies in the middle of the night and they have all the required documents. Right now we are OK, but all it takes is one landslide and we will not survive.”
Yarin Tal, 23, who is also stranded in the area, described the fear among both travelers and local residents.
“The locals here are in a total panic. They are extremely worried because of everything that happened with the flood last month. It was like a horror movie here. I don’t think we are going to sleep tonight. Yesterday there were a lot of landslides and there was total hysteria here. We probably won’t sleep at night, we’ll all be on alert with our bags packed.
“We hope to be evacuated from here before dark. I’m afraid a terrible disaster will happen. There are landslides here every few hours, right over our heads. There’s no need to wait for a disaster to happen.”
PassportCard’s situation room said it is assisting dozens of Israeli travelers in several areas affected by the severe weather. According to the company, 17 of its policyholders are in the Annapurna region, 17 are in the Manaslu region, including Samagaun, four are in the Tsum Valley and two are in the Everest region.
Four policyholders require medical attention and are expected to be evacuated for treatment once weather conditions allow. As of now, the company said, none is considered to be in life-threatening condition. The company added that many roads are blocked and movement is severely restricted across large parts of Nepal.
Magnus Search and Rescue said in response: “The Magnus team is working to assist all Israelis stranded in villages in Nepal following landslides and flooding. We are working to evacuate all Israelis according to the urgency of their situation and condition. The weather conditions are certainly creating complications, but today a window of opportunity opened that allowed us to begin evacuations, and we will continue working until everyone reaches safety.”
Extreme weather has affected wide areas of Nepal in recent days. According to AFP, at least 10 climbers and guides, all Nepalese nationals, are missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of Mount Himlung before dawn. The peak, near the Tibetan border, rises to 7,126 meters.
Two helicopters and a rescue team were placed on standby, but weather conditions prevented them from taking off.
That incident is separate from the situation involving the Israelis, but heavy snow has also fallen in the Manaslu region in recent days and climbing expeditions there have been suspended. Expeditions on Mount Dhaulagiri have also been halted, while heavy rains across Nepal since Thursday have triggered landslides and blocked roads in various parts of the country.
Iris Lifshitz-Kliger contributed to this report.

Fatah sources say Cairo talks could delay Palestinian election

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Palestinian dialogue in Cairo could delay elections, Fatah sources say
A Palestinian national dialogue expected to be held in Cairo could include discussions on postponing the legislative elections scheduled for 28 November, senior Fatah figures have told The New Arab, although a Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) official insisted the talks are intended to help prepare for the vote.
The meeting, called for by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and expected to take place under Egyptian auspices, would bring together Palestinian factions for talks on elections and national unity, according to sources who spoke to The New Arab. They likened the proposed gathering to a 2023 meeting of faction leaders in Egypt’s New Alamein that failed to produce an agreement.
Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and factions within the PLO are expected to be invited, the sources said. One said that Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah figure who leads the Democratic Reform Current, and Nasser al-Qudwa, who heads the Palestinian National Democratic Forum, would not take part.
In a statement issued after a meeting chaired by Abbas’s deputy, Hussein al-Sheikh, the PLO Executive Committee backed the president’s call for an immediate, comprehensive dialogue to strengthen Palestinian unity. Abbas did not attend the committee meeting.
The committee also reaffirmed its commitment to holding legislative elections in occupied East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and the besieged and devastated Gaza Strip. Voting must take place simultaneously across all three, it said, for the electoral process to remain unified.
Questions over the election timetable
Senior Fatah figures told The New Arab they believed the timing of the dialogue could give Abbas a way to postpone the vote with the agreement of other Palestinian factions, rather than making the decision himself. They pointed to divisions within Fatah and the possibility of rival electoral lists led by figures opposed to his leadership.
Abbas postponed elections originally planned for 2021 indefinitely, citing Israel’s refusal to allow voting in East Jerusalem. His July decree setting a new legislative vote for 28 November 2026 marked the first official election timetable since then. Presidential elections are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.
"President Abbas has made a commitment to France and Saudi Arabia in particular, and to the world, to hold legislative elections. He therefore will not resort to postponing them by a decision of his own," the Fatah sources said.
However, a PLO Executive Committee source rejected the suggestion that the dialogue was a route to delaying the vote. "The national dialogue is not an alternative to elections, but part of the preparations for them," the source told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
"The aim of the dialogue is not to postpone the elections, but to reach a national understanding that sets out a strategy for confronting the challenges — foremost among them the separation of the Gaza Strip from the West Bank," the source said.
The official also criticised an emerging political alignment between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Dahlan’s Reform Current, arguing that it risked deepening the divide between Gaza and the West Bank.
The dispute comes amid wider doubts about whether an election can be organised across the Palestinian territories.
Israel’s position on voting in occupied East Jerusalem remains unresolved, while Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 people, has led to destruction and mass displacement, raising questions about voter registration, polling stations and access to the ballot.
Hamas and other factions have also objected to changes to the election law introduced by Abbas in June this year, including a requirement that candidates commit to the PLO’s political programme.

Swiss neutrality and food security initiatives suffer hefty defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:25:12 UTC
20:25:12 KST

Swiss neutrality and food security initiatives suffer hefty defeat
Swiss voters want no big overhaul of neutrality policy: a proposal for a stricter constitutional definition was roundly defeated on Sunday. An initiative to boost domestic food production was also heavily rejected.
Is Switzerland neutral enough? For most citizens, the answer is a clear yes: on Sunday, 70.2% rejected the “neutrality initiative”, which had proposed a stricter definition that would have reduced the government’s ability to sanction countries like Russia. Not one of the 26 cantons came out in favour. Turnout was 47%.
Lukas Golder, co-director of gfs.bern, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that voters had not rejected neutrality, but opted for a more “nuanced” version of it. A majority clearly believe parliament and government should be left “room for manoeuvre” when it comes to making neutrality policy, rather than pinning them permanently to a constitutional definition, Golder added.
The initiative, launched by the pro-sovereignty group Pro Schweiz, brought to a head various Swiss debates sparked by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine – and in particular, Bern’s subsequent mirroring of European Union (EU) sanctions on Moscow.
Claiming this watered down the country’s traditional stance, and served neither Swiss interests nor international peace, the proposal wanted no more such sanctions in future – unless approved by the UN Security Council. Its definition of a “perpetual and armed” neutrality would also have reduced cooperation with military alliances like NATO, except in case of imminent war.
>> Why was the initiative rejected on Sunday? And what’s next for Swiss neutrality? Read our post-vote analysis:
More
Six takeaways from the rejection of the neutrality initiative
How much cooperation is too much?
Centre Party Senator Marianne Binder-Keller told SRF on Sunday that the initiative would have led Switzerland into “total isolation” at a time of new security challenges. The result is a signal that the country is “part of the Western, rules-based security architecture, is a partner for cooperation, and participates in sanctions” in cases where international law is breached. Such a stance also serves Swiss security interests, she said.
But for Stephan Rietiker, president of the initiative’s backers at Pro Schweiz, the key question is how far such “cooperation” stretches. “Does it mean integration into the military structures of NATO, or does it mean preparations in case of a possible attack?” he told SRF. The initiative would still have allowed room for the latter scenario, he claimed – but it struggled to get this message across.
Uphill battle
Indeed, despite ample funding – including from billionaire and former government minister Christoph Blocher – polls early in the campaign made it clear the initiative was fighting an uphill battle. While it had some backers on the pacifist left, just one big political group, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, was in favour. All other parties and the government rallied around the status quo: a neutrality that respects the Hague ConventionsExternal link while allowing flexible responses to geopolitical changes. They also denied the country had shifted course in recent years. “Switzerland was neutral, is neutral, and will remain neutral”, Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said several times in the campaign.
The initiative also struggled to attract support with imagery based around a dove and the “give peace a chance” slogan – Switzerland, its argument claimed, could do more good through its diplomatic mediation than sanctions. Opponents claimed the initiative was “pro-Putin”, and that ultra-strict neutrality can end up helping aggressor states – an argument helped when the Kremlin itself spoke out in favour of the proposal.
Ultimately, if defeat for the initiative doesn’t mean an end to Swiss neutrality, it doesn’t mean an end to debates about it either. Bern will remain out of conflicts – and military alliances – but still faces questions about its place at the heart of a rearming Europe, and how much cooperation it wants with NATO and its neighbours. Swiss voters will soon tackle similar questions: in November, a referendum is scheduled on a proposed easing of the country’s weapons’ export rules.
More
Food security fares even worse
As predicted by the polls, the food security initiative – which aims to boost Switzerland’s self-sufficiency in food production – was also soundly defeated. A clear majority of 72.5% of voters voted against it on Sunday. Although the “no” vote was unanimous across the country, opposition was less strong in cities than in rural areas.
According to Golder of gfs.bern, the initiative had sought to achieve too much too quickly. For her part, Franziska Herren, who led the initiative, told SRF that “we did nothing wrong”. She added that it had been “surreal”, to say the least, to see how the entire political establishment had opposed the initiative. Herren warned that despite the result the problems relating to water resources and agriculture in the context of climate change still remain as before.
“The public did not want to be deprived of the freedom to choose for themselves what they ate,” said Petra Gössi, a representative of the opposing camp. According to Gössi, a centre-right politician from the Radical Liberal Party, Swiss agricultural policy still remained an issue, but the market also played a part in determining it and condemning meat was not a viable option.
Anne Challandes, vice-president of the powerful Swiss Farmers’ Union, was pleased with the clear result. “This is a show of support for farming families,” she said.
Largely overshadowed by the debates around the neutrality initiative, the proposal failed to gather any steam during the campaign. In theory, it should have received more support from farmers as it aimed to boost Swiss self-sufficiency in food production from 46% to 70% in a decade by promoting the domestic cultivation and consumption of plant-based food. Instead, the farming community perceived it as an existential threat due to fears that it would affect meat and dairy consumption.
With a campaign budget of CHF1.63 million ($1.96 million), the ‘no’ camp comprising associations representing the meat and dairy industries, as well as the Swiss Farmers’ Union, attempted to take the wind out of the sails of the food security initiative (budget CHF720,000) quite early in the campaign. They framed the issue as a “vegan diktat” telling people what they should eat, even though the initiative text does not prescribe a specific diet or call for any restrictions on meat production. To make matters worse, no political party besides the Young Greens backed the initiative and even environmental organisations like Greenpeace and WWF did not endorse it.
>> Switzerland may not be ready for more plant-based fare but other places are:
More
Dutch cities are banning meat advertising – will Switzerland follow?
The result proves that the farming lobby is still a formidable opponent in Swiss politics, especially without the support of the political left and Greens. Like previous attempts to make Swiss farming more sustainable, the food security initiative faced an uphill task to win over voters. Most of all, it had a fatal flaw that sank similar initiatives like the pesticide ban initiative and the drinking water initiative in 2021, as well as the biodiversity initiative of 2024: good intentions but too ambitious.

Voters in Geneva approve proposal for free contraception
The Social Democrat Party initiative on free contraception was approved on Sunday in Geneva. The proposal was approved by 58.46% of voters.
The initiative – backed by leftwing parties, the Centre Party and the Liberty and Social Justice Party – calls for the canton of Geneva to establish a framework to cover the costs associated with contraception. All recognised forms of contraception are covered: the pill, intrauterine devices (IUDs), implants, injections, patches, vaginal rings, the morning-after pill and condoms.
This free provision applies regardless of income or age. The proponents want a fairer sharing of a burden that currently falls mainly on women. Opponents, led by the Young Radical Liberals argued that contraception is a private matter. They did not want a “blanket” scheme, the cost of which is estimated at over CHF20 million a year.

Around 150 tents now occupy Madrid's Puerta del Sol after Saturday's protest over 87-year-old Maricarmen's eviction. Protesters, mobilised by the Tenants' Union, demand a housing decree on Tuesday: "Either rentierism falls or the government".
Puerta del Sol woke on Sunday to around 150 tents pitched across the square, as the encampment grew following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis that ended in the early hours of Saturday.
According to figures collected overnight, the camp began with around 100 tents and continued to grow, with further structures counted after 8am.
Those gathered spent the night on yoga mats, in sleeping bags and, in some cases, directly on the ground, while small groups stayed up talking into the early hours.
While the Civil Guard and National Police kept a constant watch over the square, although no incidents have been reported. The campers themselves have described a calm atmosphere, with stocks of food and water to sustain the protest over the coming days.
The initiative answers the call of the Madrid Tenants' Union, which urged people to camp out in Sol once Saturday's march was over. In its call, the organisation invited those unable to stay the night to bring sleeping bags, mats, food or water. One protester summed up the reason for the mobilisation in a line repeated in different groups: "all this is for Maricarmen".
The camp is strongly reminiscent of the one that began in Madrid on 15 March 2011 and led to the 15-M movement. Its slogan, “Sí se puede” — “Yes, we can” — became a symbol for people frustrated with Spain’s two main parties, the PSOE and PP.
The movement called for a political alternative that would put ordinary people first.
Maricarmen's eviction, the origin of the protest
The camp follows the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was forced to leave her rented flat in Madrid’s Retiro neighbourhood last Wednesday, after living there for 70 years. The case, now known as the "Maricarmen effect", has become the trigger for a day of protests called in 40 cities under the slogan "Not one more Maricarmen".
Saturday's demonstration, which started at 6.30 p.m. in Puerta del Sol and ended at the Congress of Deputies, brought together around 25,000 people according to the Government Delegation, although the Tenants' Union puts the figure at as many as 300,000 participants. Along the route there was a notable intergenerational presence, with families, young people and elderly groups chanting slogans such as "Where is the progressive Government?" and "We want to see Maricarmen come back".
The spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, Gonzalo Álvarez, who spent the night at the camp, explained in a live interview that the protest is seeking "structural changes" so that housing "is treated as a basic necessity and not as a financial asset". Álvarez also pointed out that Maricarmen's case has acted as a catalyst because of "the injustice, the harshness of what happened and the police response".
The core demand: Tuesday's housing decree
The main demand of the protest is for the Government to approve a decree on Tuesday that would include, among other measures, a freeze on rents. The union has called it the “Maricarmen decree”.
Álvarez warned that if the decree is not approved, the Government’s left-wing partners, including Sumar, should consider withdrawing their support and bringing down the Government.
Echoing this position, the Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Río described Maricarmen's case as a "point of no return" in Spain's housing struggle and warned that if the decree does not go through on Tuesday, the Executive "makes no sense at all" and should rethink whether it can continue.
Pablo Iglesias, founder of Podemos and one of the initiators of the 15-M movement in Spain, said that Maricarmen could become Spain's Rosa Parks and that he hopes this movement will spread across the country.
The debate is also complicated by divisions within the left-wing bloc. Podemos MEP Irene Montero has rejected the Government negotiating the decree with Junts, accusing the party of trying to force an agreement on the people who took to the streets on Saturday.
Montero called for the expropriation of 650,000 homes owned by vulture funds so they can be turned into social rental housing. Meanwhile, Podemos secretary-general Ione Belarra said her party would keep “piling on the pressure” to secure the strongest possible decree. But she warned that no single measure would solve the housing crisis without continued protests and pressure from the streets.

Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:20:53 UTC
20:20:53 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian P-18 Terek early-warning radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region and an ammunition depot in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region during a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on September 26, the strikes were carried out throughout September 25 and overnight into September 26. The P-18 radar was hit near Semenivske in the Donetsk region, while a separate strike targeted an ammunition depot in Sievierodonetsk.
The military did not specify which weapons were used in the attacks or provide an assessment of the damage to either target.
The P-18, also designated 1RL131 Terek and known by the NATO reporting name Spoon Rest D, is a Soviet-designed mobile two-dimensional early-warning radar operating in the VHF band. The system entered service in 1970 and remains in operation, with several modernization packages developed over the decades.
According to the General Staff, the radar can detect airborne targets at ranges of around 250 kilometers and at altitudes of up to 35 kilometers. It is used to detect and determine the coordinates of aircraft and other aerial targets before passing radar information to other elements of an air-defense network.
Unlike fire-control radars that directly guide surface-to-air missiles, the P-18 primarily serves as an early-warning and surveillance sensor. Its VHF operating band and long detection range allow it to contribute to the broader air picture available to air-defense units.
Czech defense electronics company RETIA, which offers modernization packages for the P-18, also identifies its long range and ability to detect low-observable targets as key characteristics of the system.
On September 21, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The mobile system, valued at an estimated $60 million, can detect low-flying aircraft, missiles, and drones at ranges of up to 150 kilometers.

Russia could approve Türkiye’s transfer of its S-400 missile defense systems to another friendly country, provided Moscow gives its explicit consent and receives guarantees that the systems will not be transferred again, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Sept. 26.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Lavrov was asked about reports that Türkiye could transfer the Russian-made systems to the United Arab Emirates and whether Moscow was involved in discussions between Ankara and Washington over the issue.

The United States has signaled greater openness in 2026 toward Türkiye’s potential return to the F-35 program, but a possible transfer of the S-400 systems to another country could be among the conditions involved in resolving the dispute.

Iran stood firm on Sept. 27 on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s rejection of the proposal that had created some optimism for breaking the Mideast war stalemate.
The waterway is key to the world’s energy supply and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was triggered nearly seven months ago with deadly strikes on Iran.
Iran’s plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and fulfilling conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago.
That agreement, which dissolved during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
“Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
“We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.”
But Trump said on Sept. 26 that he rejected the truce deal.
“They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” he told reporters. “They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine. I like making a deal too.”
Araghchi said on Sept. 27 that the Iranians “saw the first reaction from the U.S. president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators.”
“We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” the foreign minister added.
Meanwhile, parents across Riyadh received emails from schools on Sept. 27 announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week.
There was no official reason given but the move comes amid heightened tensions in the Gulf and near-daily attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.

US rejects conditions to reopen Hormuz, but Tehran stands firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:14:00 UTC
20:14:00 KST

Iran stood firm Sunday on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite President Donald Trump’s rejection of a proposal that had raised hopes of breaking the stalemate in the Mideast war.
The waterway is key to the world's energy supply and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was triggered nearly seven months ago with deadly strikes on Iran.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and fulfilling conditions in the cease-fire deal that fell apart months ago.
That agreement, which dissolved during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the U.S. naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
But Trump said Saturday that he rejected the truce deal.
"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he told reporters. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."
Araghchi said Sunday that the Iranians "saw the first reaction from the U.S. president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators."
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.
'Tool for pressure'
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, to reopen the strait and to launch talks on Iran's nuclear program.
But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.
At the U.N., Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan complained that the "international community has been absent" and is failing to live up to the responsibility to keep the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb open.
"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states," he said, stressing the waterways' importance to global energy security.
His Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, told member states that "Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
In New York, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, according to his office, and said: "Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table but, given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States."
Araghchi said at the U.N.: "Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days."
"The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he added.
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the U.S. until Iran's seven conditions are met."
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.

Hamas chief calls for talks with PA president Abbas, endorses Gaza roadmap
Hamas political chief Khalil al-Hayya has called for direct talks with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to establish a common national programme, while saying the group is ready to implement a proposed roadmap for Gaza as a "comprehensive package".
In his first interview since becoming head of Hamas's political bureau, Al-Hayya also revealed that the group's leadership had met US officials more than four times over the past two years and said Hamas had offered to mediate between the warring parties in Yemen.
Speaking to The New Arab's sister channel Al Araby TV, Al-Hayya urged Abbas to meet him to lay the foundations for what he described as "genuine national unity".
He said such talks should be followed by a meeting of Palestinian factions and their secretary-generals aimed at rebuilding national institutions and agreeing on a common political programme.
Al-Hayya said national reconciliation should provide the basis for rebuilding Palestinian institutions, beginning with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
Ending Israel's war on Gaza remained the immediate priority, he said, followed by national unity and humanitarian relief for the enclave.
Hamas has also agreed to participate in upcoming Palestinian elections, according to Al-Hayya, who said discussions with other factions and political figures had resulted in an electoral alliance whose lists were being prepared.
Al-Hayya said Hamas had initially proposed a single national electoral list bringing together Palestinian factions and political figures, although some groups opposed the proposal.
He said elections to the Palestinian Legislative Council and Palestinian National Council should affirm the political and geographical unity of Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem.
Gaza roadmap a 'comprehensive package'
Turning to the Gaza agreement, Al-Hayya said Hamas remained committed to a roadmap presented by former UN envoy Nikolay Mladenov and mediators following months of negotiations.
According to Al-Hayya, the roadmap begins with completing the first phase agreed in Sharm el-Sheikh last October and ultimately ends with Palestinian statehood and self-determination.
The stages between them address Hamas's weapons, a Palestinian government, international forces, Israeli withdrawal and internal security.
"The agreement is a comprehensive package," Al-Hayya said, arguing that no party should be allowed to implement one part while abandoning the remainder.
Hamas was ready to discuss the details and timetable for implementation, he added, but international pressure was needed to compel Israel to fulfil its commitments.
He accused the Israeli government of previously squandering opportunities for an agreement, saying its "intransigence" and targeting of negotiators had prolonged the war and contributed to the deaths of Israeli captives.
Hamas held repeated talks with US officials
Al-Hayya also revealed that Hamas officials had met US officials more than four times since last year, with the talks covering Gaza and the broader Palestinian issue.
He said Hamas had presented US officials with "facts and figures" about Israeli actions as well as the commitments the Palestinian group said it had made.
"We sensed understanding from the Americans," Al-Hayya said, adding that US officials had characterised the meetings positively.
But he said Hamas wanted this translated into action.
"We heard understanding and praise in private and in public, but we want real, practical action," he said.
Al-Hayya argued that regional stability would remain impossible without Palestinians securing their rights and establishing a state.
He also said Israeli settlement expansion and attacks in the occupied West Bank, alongside attacks on Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem, were "no less serious" than Israel's assault on Gaza.
Hamas offers Yemen mediation
Al-Hayya also revealed that Hamas had offered to mediate between the warring parties in Yemen and was working with several countries to advance the proposal.
"We have offered mediation between the disputing and warring parties in Yemen, and I hope this offer will be accepted," he said.
He called on Arab and Muslim states to overcome their differences and engage in dialogue, arguing that regional wars were draining their peoples' resources and benefiting their adversaries.
Al-Hayya said Hamas sought "balanced" relations across the region and wanted to broaden its diplomatic ties while maintaining a policy of non-interference in the domestic affairs of other states.
He also expressed hope for stability in Syria and said Hamas remained in contact with governments across the region.
Al-Hayya ended the interview by addressing Israel's upcoming elections, saying Palestinians had suffered under successive Israeli parties and that the identity of the next government was secondary to securing Palestinian rights.
"We absolutely refuse to allow the blood, suffering and cause of the Palestinian people to serve as fuel for Israeli elections," he said.
"What matters to us is that our people achieve their goals, aspirations and legitimate rights."
