Deputy chair of Turkey's AK Party resigns after trading allegation amid funds crisis
ANKARA, Sept 27 - A deputy chair of President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party stepped down after an opposition politician accused her of making a large profit on shares just before a funds crisis triggered a major selloff on the country's stock market.
Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, the AK Party's deputy chair responsible for social policies and who also served as family minister from 2016 to 2018, said late on Saturday she had asked Erdogan to relieve her of all her duties so the allegations could be investigated.
Main opposition Yeni Party spokesman Zeynel Emre alleged at a press conference on Saturday that Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, invested a combined 163 million lira ($3.3 million) in April this year mainly in shares of shipbuilder Ozata Denizcilik and later received about 2.17 billion lira ($44 million) from selling them.
Ozata Denizcilik shares traded at around 220 lira at the start of April and rose to 4,980 lira on September 15, before turmoil in Turkey's investment fund industry, as suspected share-price manipulation in thinly traded stocks triggered a liquidity crisis and sent share prices tumbling on September 16.
Emre alleged the timing of the transactions raised questions.
Kaya said on X that she considered it necessary to take political responsibility while the allegations were examined and asked Erdogan, to relieve her of all the posts she holds.
She did not comment further on the specifics of the allegation.
Turkish authorities took steps last week to support financial stability after some investment funds failed to meet withdrawals from almost half a million investors amid the selloff.
Ozata Denizcilik said in a regulatory filing on Friday that its chairman, Ozdemir Ataseven, and vice chairman, Gokhan Ataseven, had been jailed pending trial as part of an ongoing investigation into the funds crisis. REUTERS

Ukraine sanctions 44 people involved in Russia's sham parliamentary elections in occupied territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:06:36 UTC
20:06:36 KST

Ukraine sanctions 44 people involved in Russia's sham parliamentary elections in occupied territories
President Volodymyr Zelensky enacted sanctions against 44 people involved in Russia's illegal parliamentary elections held in occupied parts of Ukraine, according to a presidential decree issued on Sept. 26.
As Russia held its parliamentary elections from Sept. 18 to 20, it also organized, for the first time, the vote in the occupied territories.
Russia used sham elections in Ukrainian territories under occupation to project the image that residents accept Russian rule and are integrated into Russia's political system, according to Ukrainian officials and human rights organizations.
The sanctions target people who acted in Russia's interests and helped facilitate the occupation of parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, as well as Crimea, according to the decree.
Some of those sanctioned had previously been elected to Russian-installed local councils in occupied territories. The list also includes former Ukrainian lawmaker Yurii Onyshchuk, who began cooperating with Russian authorities after Russia occupied Melitopol, a city in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
Ukraine considers Russia's sham parliamentary elections in occupied territories illegal and says their results have no legal validity.
The elections were accompanied by "mass falsifications, forced voting, and predetermined turnout figures," Ukraine's presidential office said. Kyiv has accused Russia of using the voting process to consolidate its control over the occupied territories and seek to legitimize its attempted annexation.
"Occupation does not grant any sovereignty," Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelensky's commissioner for sanctions policy, said in the statement, citing international humanitarian law and UN resolutions affirming Ukraine's territorial integrity.
The information on the sanctioned individuals will be shared with international partners to coordinate sanctions in their jurisdictions, according to the statement.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 20 the vote was another attempt to impose Russia's political system on Ukrainians and create the appearance of legitimacy for the occupation. He stressed that a ballot cannot give Russia the right to represent Ukrainian citizens or change Ukraine's sovereignty over the territories.
Ukraine has urged the international community not to recognize any mandates resulting from the vote.
The European Union said Russia's organization of the elections in occupied Ukrainian territory violated international law and that it would not recognize either the vote or its results.
EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas said on Sept. 21 that she proposed measures against those facilitating sham elections in occupied Ukraine.
Russian authorities claimed exceptionally high turnout in the occupied territories — more than 81% in the occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, nearly 80% in Luhansk Oblast, more than 79% in the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and more than 74% in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast. By comparison, Russia's Central Election Commission reported nationwide turnout of around 56%.
The figures from the occupied territories cannot be independently verified. There were no independent observers with unrestricted access, while voting also took place through mobile ballot boxes and door-to-door procedures.
The number of "voters" in the Russian-occupied part of Donetsk Oblast — more than 1.5 million people — was double the number of people who actually lived in the region.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Popular tourist destinations in Pingtung County, including Xiaoliuqiu and Kenting, saw a surge in visitors during the four-day Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day holiday, with accommodation bookings in both areas exceeding 90% during the first two days.
Attractions including Flower Vase Rock on Xiaoliuqiu and Nanwan in Kenting were crowded with visitors as sunny weather encouraged people to travel south. Li Jiaqi (李佳旗), chair of the Liuqiu Township Tourism Development Association, said summer is normally the island's peak tourism season, but heavy rain and typhoons disrupted summer travel, making the long-weekend influx much needed by tourism operators, per UDN.
A guesthouse owner in Xiaoliuqiu, surnamed Lin (林), said Saturdays in October were already nearly fully booked. In addition to the National Day and Retrocession Day holidays, Lin expects some travelers who postponed summer trips because of bad weather to visit the island in the coming weeks.
Kenting also saw a strong rebound during the holiday. Tseng Chun-hui (曾春惠), chair of the Kenting Main Street Management Committee, said the area has about 250 vendors and that many businesses had struggled during the summer because of persistent rain.
“The good weather has finally brought people back,” Tseng said, adding that efforts to improve Kenting Main Street included clearer price displays and improvements to pedestrian space.
The pedestrian improvements are part of a broader project completed in August 2025 that redesigned about 1.41 kilometers of Kenting Main Street, adding pedestrian space and reorganizing road use. The project cost about NT$50 million (US$1.6 million) and also created 12 designated short-term parking areas, per CNA.
A restaurant owner surnamed Chang (張) in Hengchun said the weather had helped attract visitors. “The good weather is helping,” Chang said, noting that temperatures had been relatively comfortable and breezes had made conditions suitable for visitors seeking beaches and outdoor activities.
Long lines of vehicles were seen waiting to enter the Nanwan Recreation Area parking lot, while crowds also increased in Hengchun. Local businesses reported visitors from Hong Kong, which was observing its own Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, alongside domestic travelers.
The Kenting Bus Transfer Station project broke ground on Sept. 15 and is scheduled for completion in July 2027. Located near Kenting Main Street, the NT$117 million project will include eight bus bays, 60 automobile parking spaces, 25 motorcycle spaces, a 36-space YouBike station, and three taxi areas, per LTN.
The project is intended to connect bus routes serving the Hengchun Peninsula and improve public transportation access to Kenting, which is more than 9 kilometers from the existing Hengchun transfer station, according to the Kaohsiung Motor Vehicles Office.
Local tourism operators said they hoped the increase in visitors would continue through the upcoming holidays.

20:05:08 KST

Tony Blair can, apparently, sound slightly wistful when he describes how he once had a cloak-and-dagger meeting with Andy Burnham, who wanted to talk to him about standing for the party leadership. Before anyone gets too excited, however, this wasn’t in the past few months, during which Burnham succeeded in landing the job. The story dates back to 2010. That was when he was a callow member of Gordon Brown’s cabinet and understandably wary of his boss discovering not only his ambition to take over if Labour lost the looming general election, but also from whom he wanted advice.
Much has changed since then, not least Burnham himself. His journey out of Westminster and back again – which in his telling has become an almost spiritual pilgrimage of personal redemption – enabled him to shed the New Labour baggage that proved so cumbersome during his previous, and unsuccessful, runs for the leadership. In common with Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer – all of whom tried with varying degrees of success to distance themselves from Blair – Labour’s latest leader now also wants to keep Blair at arm’s length, and certainly far away from his party conference in Liverpool this week.
Their secret meeting long ago nonetheless underlines how often, since he left Downing Street in 2007, Blair has had a residual and sometimes illicit allure for those aspiring to fill his shoes. Part of that is because – with the exception of Starmer – those who came after him failed to win a single general election, let alone three. But it is also that this leader from the past still has a possibly unmatched ability to raise our sights, away from whatever the media tells us is most urgent, towards the colossal compound crisis now casting its shadow across the world and over Britain’s future.
Blair does not, of course, always make it easy to agree with him. There was an awful lot to dislike about his 5,700 word essay earlier this year, which said Britain had no power to stop either the AI revolution or Donald Trump. It led some to question once more the motives of a former PM whose proximity both to big tech firms and successive US presidents has so tainted his reputation. Burnham swiftly responded to the essay by saying Blair just didn’t get “what’s going on” with the impact of “40 years of neoliberalism” on working-class communities. He later promised that the interests of voters in Makerfield, where he was standing in a byelection, would be his test of what made good policy.
It was, however, a bit disingenuous for him to claim that Blair agreed “our relentless focus now should be on domestic issues, and fixing our own underlying problems, rather than on re-running divisive arguments about rejoining the European Union”. Indeed, the bulk of the former PM’s essay was about the inability of this country’s politics to navigate an international landscape being churned at terrifying speed by forces far beyond Britain’s control.
Conflicts in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have since put further pressure on government borrowing costs and household fuel bills. It is increasingly difficult to see how the inward-looking vision Burnham has painted so far, largely consisting of new powers for mayors and more regulation of privatised utilities, will deliver his promised “good growth in every postcode” any time soon. This week, his determinedly domestic focus relented and he acknowledged the government must also offer “resilience” in the face of global storms, before delivering a speech to the United Nations in New York on Tuesday night. The speech veered wildly from No 10 North in Manchester to Ukraine, Israel, Iran and China, briefly taking in the climate crisis, before setting out the need to create international safety standards on frontier AI and protect democracy from all kinds of Russian threats, including disinformation on social media.
It didn’t go nearly far enough for Blair. On Thursday, his policy institute published a paper calling for Britain to set a course for re-entry into a “reformed European Union” over the next decade. Rather than re-run old arguments about Brexit, he would prefer to start a new one, saying the need for the UK and the EU to build capability in defence and capacity on AI is more pressing than it ever was in the past.
Although Blair can point to polls showing a majority of the public and an even bigger slice of Labour voters would support rejoining, there is plenty of evidence to suggest relations with Europe have gone backwards under Burnham’s government. The prospect of Britain drifting alone on the tide of history felt closer to becoming reality last week when the annual state of the union speech from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, made repeated references to Canada, a country about 3,500 miles away to which she offered an associate EU membership, while barely mentioning the UK at all.
An EU-UK summit, originally scheduled to have taken place under Starmer’s premiership in May, was delayed until July and then to a yet-to-be confirmed date at the end of the year. What had been talked up as a “done deal” for a youth mobility scheme – by which young people from the EU and the UK could live, work and study in each other’s countries – risks being unstitched by new objections from some of Burnham’s newly appointed minsters that it fails his “Makerfield test”. There are similar claims that the EU’s “made in Europe” policy on supply chains will disadvantage British industry and be a further obstacle to an agreement, while progress that began in February to resolve the issue is said to have stalled.
There are a lot of mixed messages on all this just now. Recent comments that it must be possible to get a deal agreed with Europe in “an amicable way that will add percentage points to our growth” perhaps made him sound too much like a regional mayor who had missed the past decade of Brexit mayhem in Westminster. But others believe Burnham is considering a big leap beyond the “red line” election pledges that prevented Starmer from rejoining a customs union, the single market or allowing freedom of movement. Over recent days some of those around him have dangled out questions about how, “purely hypothetically”, a case for re-entry could be included in his speech to conference this Tuesday, the 10-year plan later this year or, as Burnham himself notably failed to rule out this week, Labour’s manifesto at the next election (whenever that might be).
Either way, the freshly minted new PM will not want to be seen taking inspiration from a sometimes toxic old one. There has been no contact between them since Burnham entered Downing Street and a meeting – clandestine or otherwise – is not scheduled. That seems a shame because, on the issue of Europe at least, Blair really isn’t the worst person from whom Burnham could take advice.

  Tom Baldwin is a former assistant editor of the Times and a former senior adviser to the Labour party. He is the author of Keir Starmer: The Biography

‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?

‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
Board of Peace excludes UNRWA from Gaza, aligning with repeated Israeli calls to sideline the refugee aid agency.
The United States-led Board of Peace (BoP) has said the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) will have no role in Gaza – echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation considered a lifeline for millions of Palestinians.
The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the “ceasefire” and Gaza’s reconstruction, said on Friday it would work only with partners it deems reliable and who it believes can meet the needs of Gaza’s population – a standard it says UNRWA does not meet.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Gaza watches Israel’s elections with fear and antipathy
- list 2 of 3Gaza’s recovery needs reach $71.5bn amid ‘most severe economic crisis’: UN
- list 3 of 3Israel’s policies threaten ‘very existence’ of Palestinians, Abbas tells UN
The move comes as the BoP unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan on Wednesday aimed at beginning Gaza’s reconstruction, nearly a year after a so-called “ceasefire” came into effect in the devastated Palestinian territory.
The plan, presented on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), comes as key elements of the “ceasefire” remain stalled, including the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas.
UNRWA was established in 1949 to cater to tens of thousands of Palestinians displaced from their homes by Jewish militias from areas that currently form part of Israel.
BoP’s stance on UNRWA comes as Israel’s genocide in the coastal enclave continues, with Palestinians facing nonstop attacks, severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and stalled reconstruction plans.
“Excluding UNRWA is not a neutral administrative decision; it is a deeply political one,” Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar told Al Jazeera.
“It aligns the Board of Peace with Israel’s longstanding campaign to marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future.”
So what has BoP said about UNRWA, and does it keep toeing the Israeli line on the future of Gaza?
What did the Board of Peace say?
The BoP unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint on the sidelines of the UNGA, with $2.4bn proposed for projects aimed at beginning Gaza’s recovery.
UNRWA was left off the list of UN agencies the board identified as partners.
“The Board of Peace’s policy as it relates to UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged,” the BoP said in a post on X on Friday.
“We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalised Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests.”
However, a BoP official, speaking to The Associated Press news agency on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.
The official said the agency’s programmes could continue if they served Gaza’s residents well, but maintained that “UNRWA’s days are over”.
The BoP, which US President Donald Trump launched earlier this year, was conceived to oversee the rebuilding of Gaza after nearly three years of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip.
What has UNRWA said?
In an indirect response, UNRWA acting Commissioner-General Christian Saunders said on Friday in Gaza, “UNRWA remains an institution of considerable humanitarian and strategic value, with capabilities and expertise that are difficult to replicate today.”
“To disregard these capabilities at a moment of such profound need is neither logical nor responsible,” Saunders said in a statement.
Former UNRWA chief Philippe Lazzarini on Thursday warned that removing the agency would have a “devastating” effect on Palestinians.
“They want to get rid of the agency, but on the other hand they know that if you get completely rid of the agency today, it might have a further … devastating impact on the population,” Lazzarini told AP on Friday.
In a separate statement on X, Lazzarini said, “grandiose plans are what the Board of Peace does best”, noting widespread suffering across Gaza amid Israel’s ongoing genocide.
The agency has about 11,000 Palestinian employees in Gaza and remains heavily involved in healthcare, education, water and sanitation services. Its exclusion is particularly significant given the scale of displacement and the continuing restrictions on aid entering Gaza.
UNRWA has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinians in Gaza, occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank as well as Jordan, Syria and Lebanon – the neighbouring countries where the Palestinian refugees have been living.
Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.
What has been Hamas’s response?
Hamas accused the BoP of adopting Israel’s position.
Spokesperson Hazem Qassem on Saturday called the decision to exclude UNRWA “a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position”, saying it was aimed at ending the agency’s operations, preventing it from delivering aid and undermining Palestinian refugees’ right of return.
Qassem said it was “strange for the peace council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip”.
Does the Board of Peace toe the Israeli line?
Experts say the workings and demands of the BoP align closely with Israel’s vision of the Gaza Strip and the Palestinians.
“The composition of the board reinforces this concern,” analyst Najar told Al Jazeera,” he said.
“Israel is a founding member, while Palestine is not. Not a single Palestinian sits on either the central executive board or the Gaza executive board. Yet these bodies include senior Trump officials, strongly pro-Israel figures, private-equity executives and Israeli businesspeople who will exercise influence over Gaza’s governance and reconstruction.”
Nevertheless, Najar said, while other members such as Turkiye may “provide some counterweight”, so the board does not present itself to be “entirely uniform”, the structure of power is “clear”.
“Palestinians are excluded from the bodies taking the strategic, financial and security decisions about their own land,” he added.
On UNRWA
Israel has for years sought to remove UNRWA from Gaza, accusing the agency of being infiltrated by Hamas.
The International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion in October, said allegations that “a significant part of UNRWA’s employees are ‘members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions'” had not been substantiated.
The BoP’s position strengthens the Israeli efforts to dismantle the UN agency.
Najar said Israel’s “hostility” towards the UN agency is also connected to what the agency represents: “the continuing existence of Palestinian refugees, their rights – including their right of return – and the international community’s unresolved responsibility towards them”.
“Removing UNRWA, therefore, serves a political purpose extending far beyond the delivery of aid,” he added.
Najar said Gaza could not be “credibly reconstructed” by excluding the UN agency. “Nor should reconstruction be used to erase Palestinian refugee rights or replace an internationally mandated institution with mechanisms that are more politically compliant. If the board is serious about rebuilding Gaza for its people, UNRWA must be part of that process, and Palestinians must be at its centre, not placed at the bottom of a foreign-controlled hierarchy,” he noted.
On Hamas disarmament
Hamas and other Palestinian factions agreed in July to a roadmap under which weapons would be surrendered in stages as Israeli forces gradually withdrew. The two processes were explicitly linked.
But following an August meeting between Nickolay Mladenov, the BoP’s director-general, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the board said Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the “Yellow Line” until Hamas’s decommissioning was complete, including “light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike”.
Hamas maintains that it will not implement its obligations unless Israel fulfils its own.
Israel currently occupies more than 60 percent of Gaza while most of the territory’s 2.3 million people remain displaced.
On reconstruction
Article 17 of the BoP plan calls for “temporary reconstruction” beginning in areas designated free of Hamas control, including humanitarian compounds for unarmed civilians.
The proposed system would direct reconstruction, aid and shelter towards areas outside Hamas’s control while Israeli forces remain behind the so-called “Yellow Line”.
However, Israel has refused to allow the Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza, open crossings or begin reconstruction until Hamas is completely disarmed.
After unveiling the reconstruction plan on the sidelines of the UNGA, BoP high representative Mladenov said once again the proposed plan depends on Hamas’s disarmament.
What is the situation in Gaza?
Almost a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin on any meaningful scale and Israeli forces continue to occupy large parts of the Strip.
At least 1,451 Palestinians have been killed and 4,953 wounded in Israeli attacks since the “ceasefire” began in October 2025, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
The healthcare system is on the verge of “total collapse”, the ministry said last week, while shortages of fuel, medical supplies and spare parts have disrupted hospitals, water and sanitation services.
The scale of destruction is also immense. More than half of Gaza’s hospitals and clinics remain nonfunctional, less than 1.5 percent of cropland is accessible and undamaged, and reconstruction needs have reached an estimated $71.5bn.
Nearly 84 percent of Gaza’s population – more than 1.76 million people – are living in displacement sites or damaged and inadequate shelters, the UN has said.

Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:03:59 UTC
20:03:59 KST

As Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham has promised to deliver “stability” in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable.
The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs.
We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time.
Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckons Ofgem could increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January.
At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer.
“We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday.
Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might have to turn the hose on it.”
Donald Trump made clear over the weekend that he has no intention of staunching the flames himself, by bringing the conflict to a close.
“I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.”
With UK inflation already above 3% and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.
Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget.
Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to be the most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years, which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs.
Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget, he announced this weekend.
But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year.
“I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund.
Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year.
Economists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta are calling for a gas price stabiliser, for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future.
Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act.
Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace.
It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts.
There are growing warnings, too, about the risks of market instability caused by the interaction of febrile bond markets and the AI mega-bubble.
Labour was already in a tricky fiscal bind, given demands for higher defence spending – not least from Healey himself, who now has the job of finding the resources.
The difficult decisions about how to do so – let alone fund Burnham’s wider priorities – look likely to be delayed until a spending review some time in 2027. It is very hard to see how that won’t necessitate a fresh round of tax rises.
The plan had been for a relatively modest budget, focusing on plans for devolution, and filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced in the summer.
This caution looked out of step with Burnham’s promise of a radical political reset and may be untenable if energy bills are going to soar. He and Healey face a tough autumn.

What’s the Best Pet DNA Test? We Tested the Most Popular Ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:02:00 UTC
20:02:00 KST

An at-home cat or dog DNA test kit promises to give pet owners clarity on a heap of important health data, like breed ancestry, blood type, and health risks. To access this info, owners just swab the inside of their pet’s mouth, seal the sample in a prepaid-postage envelope, and wait (for up to five weeks) for results to be sent to their inbox. Each company has a testing lab, and the results live in your online account, where they can be downloaded and even shared with your vet.
But because of several factors, such as sample size and comparison, these tests often give dramatically different results for things like genetic ancestry and breed traits (more on that below).
I tested several at-home DNA test kits, including two of the most popular kits—Basepaws ($104) and Wisdom Panel ($97)—on my two adult cats and talked to several animal experts to get insights into these tests—and whether they are worth your money, given the large disparity in results. Think of this as the WIRED guide to the increasingly popular at-home pet DNA test.
Table of Contents
Be sure to check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Cat Feeders, Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Automatic Cat Fountains, and Best Dog Accessories.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Easiest Interface
In my research, I've found that people widely consider Wisdom Panel the most trusted at-home pet DNA test kit (along with dog-only Embark, which former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes tested below).
Wisdom Panel offers several kits for dogs (listed below) but only one test for cats. It can identify more than 70 breeds, includes 45 health tests, determines blood type, and screens for more than 25 traits. It even provides a genetic consult for “at-risk” health findings and shows what the pet's family tree might look like based on DNA results. I especially liked that it tests for the most common conditions seen in cats or dogs with a similar breed makeup to your pet (based on the DNA sample), including important markers like drug sensitivity, immune deficiency, and bleeding disorders. It also identified the cat’s blood type (both of my cats were A) and transfusion risk (both were moderate).
The results arrived live online in my Wisdom Panel account within three weeks of mailing them. I really appreciated the interface, which was organized into clickable tabs that made the information easier to access and navigate. Plus, based on appearance alone, my cat Clover's DNA results seemed most accurate with this test (below). I also tested my run-of-the-mill gray tabby cat, Basil, but on all tests—including Wisdom Panel—he was almost entirely labeled as an “American domestic cat” and “polycat/domestic shorthair." That's basically the mutt final boss, a result of many generations of mixed breeding among different cat types, where ancestry and origin are almost impossible to determine.
Most In-Depth Results
WIRED reviewed Basepaws over half a decade ago, and a lot has changed since then. Basepaws offers a single breed and health test for cats that identifies up to 21 breeds, 64 genetic health markers, 50 genetic trait markers, blood type, and oral health. The wait time for results is five weeks, and when I first sent my cat Basil's test in, they couldn't extract enough DNA, so I had to send another sample and wait another five weeks. Rather than an easily digestible interactive screen with information like Wisdom Panel, Basepaws gives you essentially a mini book PDF to scroll through to find information. It feels more in-depth than Wisdom Panel, but it is also harder to disseminate the large pile of information.
Basepaws tests genes for markers associated with disorders in musculoskeletal and connective tissue; eyes; metabolic, autoimmune, and endocrine systems; blood; and more. Both of my cats, Clover and Basil, were cleared of any genes that would mark them as potential carriers of genetic diseases. It also identified blood type and transfusion risk, which were A and moderate (the same results I got with Wisdom Panel’s test).
Basepaws tests for oral health by comparing against an oral microbiome database. In this regard, Basepaws wins out. Dental health is a major concern for me, and I love that Basepaws screens for it and provides an oral health report (I have since started brushing my cats' teeth). My cat Basil was at high risk for all dental markers like halitosis, tooth resorption, and periodontal disease. Basepaws developed a health plan for him: “Adopt a daily oral health care routine, consider supplementing Basil’s routine with products accepted by the Veterinary Oral Health Council, and schedule an appointment with your veterinarian in the next month.” Although I was alarmed by the results, I appreciated that Basepaws provided recommended next steps so I could develop a plan of action for care. And it’s important to remember that these results don’t necessarily mean a pet is guaranteed to develop the disease.
"These can be a helpful flag for your veterinarian to keep an eye on [...] but do not necessarily mean aggressive testing is needed at that moment,” says Jamie Richardson, head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary. “DNA tests are tools to support—not replace—veterinary care.”
Some of the other Basepaws results, particularly the genetic and physical markers, seem off. Like Wisdom Panel, white calico Clover was marked as “likely” to be black in color, and none of the ancestral DNA breeds matched across tests for Clover.
Another Cat DNA Test Kit I Tested
Koko Genetics was a new name to me, but it offers a similar service to the two major brands above, with tests for both cats and dogs in “starter” basic and “advanced” kits. I tested the latter, which provides additional health insights by screening for genetic disorders or abnormalities. The process is exactly the same as with the other kits, where you swab your cat's mouth, register your kit online, and mail the results. The Koko Genetics interface wouldn't allow me to register two kits with different cats under the same login/username, so I had to create two separate accounts with two different emails, which was a slight pain. The results also took surprisingly long—it took over five weeks from mailing to being acknowledged as received, and an additional five weeks to get results.
This interface was the least user-friendly of all I tested, and many of the default options were in Spanish with no English options. The site where you access results is a little bare-bones, with additional information available if you click the tab. I found that much of the health trait info was scientific jargon, and I had to do further research to understand it. Clover was flagged as having a copy of the Acute Intermittent Porphyria (Variant 3) gene mutation, which can cause discolored teeth and urine and may lead to other health problems. Luckily, Clover has just one copy of the mutation and will not develop the disease, but she can transmit the mutation to her offspring. (She's spayed, so that is not a potential issue.) Wisdom Panel also tests for this, and she was not flagged as carrying it in that test.
Both cats were negative for all physical traits except black coat (which neither has), and I didn't find the info really helpful or interesting. There's also a family tree option, like Wisdom Panel's, where you can see what the previous generations' breed or coloring might've been.
Best Dog DNA Test Kit
One of my family’s favorite pastimes is placing low-stakes bets on the breeds that make up our beloved rescue dogs. Usually we’re wildly off with our estimates. For my dog Randy, all we knew was that he was a Chihuahua mix. The Embark DNA kit is the dog equivalent of Ancestry DNA for humans, given how detailed it is. The test kit uses a saliva sample, and you ship it off for processing. Within three weeks, we found out Randy had quite the cocker spaniel lineage, with show-dog cousins across the country (Princess Elysia of Eagle’s Wings’ parents, if you’re reading this, hello!).
The Embark app gives detailed breakdowns of behavioral, health, and longevity insights for the breeds that make up your pup. His personality analysis shows he’s closely aligned with his cocker spaniel roots, always on the lookout (check), sometimes high-energy (check), and rarely independent (spot on). —Julia Forbes
The kits below are also specifically for dogs from Basepaws and Wisdom Panel, two companies I've tested on my cats.
How Does a DNA Test Kit Work?
Pet DNA tests rely on pet owners collecting cells via a cheek swab, then placing the sample in a sealed stabilizing or preserving fluid for transit. You’ll mail the sample back to the lab in the prepaid envelope. It usually takes about five weeks to get results. (The first time I sent my cat Basil’s Basepaws sample, the company emailed that the results were inconclusive, and I had to wait for another kit to be sent, re-swab him, and wait another five weeks for results.)
At the lab, the sample is analyzed against the company’s breed and genetic health database. They use single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays—the standard technology for identifying breed ancestry—as well as data on inherited traits and the risk of common diseases. Essentially, different breeds have distinct patterns of SNPs in their genomes, which serve as genetic markers. These tests analyze the pet’s DNA sample for specific SNPs and then compare them to the company’s existing database to estimate the animal’s breed composition. This not only tells you about breed composition, but can also identify the specific DNA sequences that are markers for potential health risks, such as predispositions to diseases or hereditary cancers.
Don’t take the health or DNA test results as absolute truth, however. “This can lead to a false sense of security or false alarms," says veterinarian Amanda Chambers. Forward your results to your veterinarian and always follow up by scheduling a visit to the vet if your pet is marked as a carrier for any genetic disease.
What the Results Can—and Can’t—Tell You
After chatting with Richardson, I’ve found that these are the major areas of limitation with at-home DNA test kits:
- Results depend on the size/diversity of the genetic database
- Most kits test known markers only—not full genomes
- Feline data is less developed
- Misinterpretation of results can lead to unnecessary concern
Wisdom Panel claims its cat breed results are over 98 percent accurate and its dog tests are over 99 percent accurate. However, there's a huge disparity between the three kits I tested on my cats, particularly in breed ancestry. One problem with the vast disparity in results is that the three companies use different sample sizes and metrics to identify breeds.
But the biggest issue for cat owners taking these at-home DNA tests is that you can’t really identify most cats' breeds the way you can with dogs. Unless your cat is a purebred, about 95 percent of cats don’t belong to a recognized breed. Cats' genetic backgrounds are muddied—they're just similar mixes with different physical characteristics, so the tests only show the breed(s) they share the most markers with. Basically, these tests for cats aren’t able to reliably tell us about breed composition, just similarity to other breeds’ traits in the company’s data pool.
From my research, it seems the breed identification part of these tests is more accurate for dogs, as dog DNA is so much more diversified. Breeds have been clearly defined after centuries of diversification, and dog DNA mutates quickly, with genes changing after just a few generations. Cats are not much different from their Egyptian ancestors.
Interestingly, in a 2023 CBS report, the news organization sent dog and human DNA to different at-home test companies and received varying results, with the dog's DNA ranging from 65 to only 29 percent German Shepherd. The human DNA results were attributed to a bulldog, border collie, and cane corso mix.
In summation, unfortunately, there isn't a single catchall way to determine a pet's genetic makeup or ancestry. Humans like categories, and breeds are essentially human constructs based on how a dog or cat looks. The genetic part of the test is fun, but take it with a grain of salt—especially with cats.
A Note on At-Home Allergy Testing Kits
I recently tested both of my cats for allergies and intolerances using a similar at-home test kit, the 5Strands Pet Food & Environmental Intolerance Test, for $100. For this, you only need to send a fur sample in the mail to a lab; results were sent to my inbox within seven days. The report showed that both of my cats had strong intolerances to common ingredients in their diet, such as various types of fish and chicken meal. This sent me into a panic about my cats' health and (dis)comfort.
After further research, I learned that hair/fur samples are not an accurate way to measure allergies and intolerances. Studies show that kits claiming to provide these results perform no better than chance and often produce inconsistent or false results.
“There's no scientific evidence to support allergy testing through hair, fur, or saliva,” says Richardson. “Veterinarian-supervised elimination diets to test for food allergy and intradermal skin testing or blood tests to test for environmental allergies remain the gold standard.”
So, save your money and consult a vet instead if you suspect your pet is suffering from allergies or intolerances.
Meet the Experts
- Amanda Chambers is a full-time small animal general practitioner based in Kansas City, Missouri.
- Jamie Richardson is head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary.

A simple tactic can increase likability for socially anxious people, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

People with social anxiety often worry that others will judge them harshly, leading them to hold back from sharing personal details. A recent study shows that opening up about personal experiences increases how much others like a person and want to interact with them, regardless of the speaker’s own anxiety levels. The research, published in The Journal of Psychology, also highlights that the personal traits of the individual judging the interaction play a major role in these positive evaluations.
Social anxiety involves an intense fear of negative evaluation in social or performance situations. Individuals dealing with this condition often worry that they will fail to meet social expectations or that their peers will reject them. To protect themselves, they frequently adopt safety behaviors. These are defensive strategies, such as avoiding eye contact, staying quiet, or physically withdrawing from a group.
While these behaviors feel protective, they often create an unintended cycle. Peers might misinterpret the withdrawal as a lack of interest, unfriendliness, or aloofness. When peers react coolly in return, the anxious individual interprets this as a confirmation of their worst fears. The avoidance continues, preventing the person from experiencing positive social interactions that could challenge their anxious beliefs.
One specific behavior that anxious individuals tend to restrict is self-disclosure. Self-disclosure is the act of revealing personal thoughts, feelings, past events, and future plans to another person. In typical human relationships, people gradually shift from superficial small talk to deeper, more intimate exchanges.
Sharing personal information is a standard way people build trust and show warmth. When someone avoids doing this, they may struggle to form close bonds. Researchers Gabriela Lavinia Niță and Violeta Ștefania Rotărescu of the University of Bucharest wanted to see how varying levels of self-disclosure might change how socially anxious people are perceived.
They also wanted to shift focus away from just the person speaking to look at the person listening. Human perception is highly subjective. The researchers suspected that the listener’s own personality traits might shape how they grade someone else’s likability.
To test these ideas, the researchers designed a study involving 136 online evaluators. These participants acted as the “raters.” The researchers also selected four university students to act as the “speakers.” Two of these students had diagnosed social anxiety, and two did not. Each pair included one male and one female.
The evaluators rated each speaker at four distinct stages. First, they looked at a basic photograph of the speaker. Next, they watched a short video of the speaker sharing general personal information, such as their name, age, and hobbies. In the third stage, they viewed a video of the speaker detailing a happy memory from school. Finally, they watched a video where the speaker disclosed a sad or negative school experience.
After every stage, the evaluators filled out questionnaires rating the speaker’s likability. They also rated their desire for future interactions, which measures whether they would want to sit next to the speaker on a bus or ask them for advice.
The researchers found that sharing personal stories improved the speakers’ standing. Evaluators liked the speakers more after hearing them share positive personal stories compared to their initial impressions from just a photograph. This boost in likability applied to both the socially anxious and non-anxious speakers.
Sharing a negative experience also improved the evaluators’ desire to interact with the speakers in the future. As the speakers revealed more vulnerable aspects of themselves, the evaluators generally perceived them as more approachable. The simple act of opening up helped repair any initial hesitations the raters might have had.
Following the video ratings, the researchers conducted a second analysis focusing entirely on the 136 evaluators. These participants completed extensive surveys to measure their own personality dimensions. The surveys assessed traits like extraversion, agreeableness, and their own levels of social anxiety.
The researchers also measured the evaluators’ need for affiliation. This concept refers to a fundamental human desire to feel accepted, included, and connected within a social group. People with a high need for affiliation place a heavy priority on maintaining positive social ties.
The researchers anticipated that highly extraverted or agreeable evaluators would give out higher likability scores. Surprisingly, an evaluator’s extraversion and agreeableness did not alter their ratings. These broad personality traits did not make them any more or less generous in their judgments of the speakers.
Instead, an evaluator’s own social anxiety changed how they viewed the speakers. Evaluators who scored higher in social anxiety gave higher likability ratings to all the speakers, regardless of the speaker’s anxiety status. Anxious raters appeared to be a more lenient audience.
The same pattern emerged for evaluators with a high need for affiliation. People who strongly desired social connection provided more generous likability ratings across the board. The researchers suggest that individuals who crave acceptance are highly sensitive to any cues of social inclusion, prompting them to view others through a more positive lens.
When people want to belong, they might evaluate others leniently to avoid conflict and encourage a connection. This finding shifts the perspective on social rejection. If a socially anxious person feels disliked, it might not just be about their own behavior. The rejection could stem from the listener’s own lack of affiliative need.
While the results offer a new perspective on social dynamics, the study has several limitations. The researchers point to the halo effect, a psychological bias where a person’s physical attractiveness can inflate their perceived likability. Attractiveness could have influenced the ratings independently of the self-disclosure tasks.
The study also relied on self-reported questionnaires for the evaluators’ anxiety and personality traits. Questionnaires depend heavily on a participant’s self-awareness and honesty, which can sometimes skew the data. The length of the survey, which took nearly an hour to complete, may have caused participant fatigue, potentially leading to rushed answers.
Additionally, watching pre-recorded videos in an online format is quite different from real life. The videos lacked the immediate feedback and dynamic body language found in face-to-face interactions. In a real conversation, a socially anxious person might react poorly to unexpected pauses or the listener’s facial expressions.
Future research could use live, in-person interactions to capture the true back-and-forth of social exchanges. Observing how socially anxious individuals handle self-disclosure in real time would provide a more realistic picture of how likability forms. For now, the findings suggest that sharing a little bit about oneself is a reliable way to build a bridge with others.
The study, “Is Likeability in the Eye of the Beholder? A Quasi-Experimental Study on Personality, Social Anxiety and the Need for Affiliation in Assessing the Likability of Socially Anxious Adults,” was authored by Gabriela Lavinia Niță and Violeta Ștefania Rotărescu.

The hidden risks of using traditional Chinese medicine with Western prescriptions
Some plants and procedures common in Chinese medicine can affect Western medicines such as blood thinners and depression drugs
An elderly woman with a mechanical heart valve was taking warfarin, a blood thinner to prevent and treat blood clots, when she began using the Chinese herb danshen, often marketed for “blood circulation”. Her blood lost its ability to clot normally, resulting in severe bleeding complications.
For many Hongkongers, Chinese medicine is not an alternative so much as part of everyday life: a chrysanthemum tea, a bowl of tonic soup, a session of cupping, a proprietary pill bought from a pharmacy. The crucial distinction is not whether something is “natural”, but whether it is used as food, symptom relief or as a concentrated treatment alongside medicines that have their own powerful effects.

‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.
“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.
The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.
Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.
In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.
“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.
Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.
“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.
“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”
He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.
“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”
Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.
Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”
She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.
“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”
