The ‘elixir of long life’: how the elusive Chartreuse quietly became the trendiest drink around
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

It’s just after 9pm in drizzly Belleville, Paris. Too late for cocktails, too early for bedtime, but up the steep hill that straddles the 19th and 20th arrondissements, digestif hour is in sight.
In the past few years, more and more Parisians have been reaching for a glass of Chartreuse, an intensely green/yellow herbal liqueur with a folkloric backstory involving Carthusian monks, cholera and a recipe of omertà-like secrecy.
There are several types, of varying strengths, colours and prices, but none are that easy to find. At La Commune, a cultish leftwing hangout in Belleville, where tequila shots cost less than €4, they finished the Chartreuse the night before. A few doors down at Les Triplettes de Belleville, I spot a third-full bottle of the cheaper yellow stuff sandwiched between the gins. Hugo Césard, the 19-year-old bartender, pours me a €7 shot, my third of the night. On first taste, it behaves like ouzo: sweet, fennelly, cloyingly thick. Then you hit the more complex notes, which are closer to an Alpine meadow. This one is a navy-strength 40% ABV, while the green version is about 55%. In theAlps, you’re more likely to drink it in hot chocolate. To down it at room temperature is sacrilege, unless “you want to get very drunk”, says Césard. For me, alas, that ship has already sailed.
Round the corner at Combat, an edgy-cool bar run by women and frequented by thoughtful students and dressed-up boomers, they mostly serve it cold in a crystal-cut sipping glass or a cocktail called The Last Word, mixed with gin, lime and a maraschino cherry. I try both. Combat bartender Marie-Paule Corby, 30, loves its “complicated flavour”, though outside, a customer called Nour (also 30) is not a fan. “I only ever drank it in the Alps. Too sweet for me,” she says, and sticks out her tongue in disgust.
You’ll find Chartreuse in most ambitiously stocked bars, but interest among younger drinkers shot up mostly after the pandemic, says Theo, who works in La Cave Pigalle, a small chic wine shop in Pigalle in the 9th arrondissement. The same thing happened in the US, where it became a “sleeper” ingredient during the giddy era of the craft cocktail movement of the early 00s. Then came lockdown, and a taste for the weirder, top-shelf stuff grew further still, particularly here.
At the award-winning, taxidermy-filled bar Satan’s Whiskers in east London, it appears in various cocktails. The Pig on the Beach on Dorset’s Jurassic coast sells five different types, one of which – the Eau de Vie from 1941 – costs £50 a measure. It’s always been pricey, though disaster hit in 2021 when the Carthusian monks suddenly announced plans to cap production in order to “protect their monastic life and devote their time to solitude and prayer”. In a letter in 2021, they said: “Making millions of cases does not make sense in today’s environmental context and will have a negative impact on the planet in the very short term”, though rumour has it the decree came from the Vatican, which pointedly reminded the monks “that they were monks, not businessmen”. Today, according to a spokesperson for Chartreuse, the brand is shifting its focus back toward herbalism.
Back in Paris, at the beloved bottle shop La Cave de Belleville, Chartreuse is scarce. “We have an allocation – 24 bottles of green and 24 bottles of yellow, but that’s for a year”, says Remy Pousse-Vaillant, 46, a knowledgable liquor expert with a Kandinsky tattoo. There are currently five on the shelf, but that’s it until the next order. Under French consumer law, any item displayed with a visible price is considered sellable, which is partly why some caves stash the good stuff in the basement. The brand won’t divulge the numbers, only to say that they keep half and export half to the US, Japan, Australia, and “countries surrounding the Alpine arc”. They only make what they need to sustain the order, though Pousse-Vaillant thinks it’s not much over 1m bottles worldwide. Like most wine shop staff, he will neither confirm nor deny if he’s got Chartreuse in the basement.
Still, if we’ve learned anything from Birkin economics, it’s that few things sharpen our appetite like the prospect of scarcity. Is that why Chartreuse is back on the map? “Yes, partly,” he says. The stuff that creeps on to cocktail menus – espresso martinis, negronis, cosmos – “used to come from TV shows like Mad Men or Sex and the City”. Now it’s aggressive advertising campaigns meticulously engineered by savvy publicists. Take Campari, which turned Aperol into a global aesthetic, and M&S’s Clemencello, which, according to the supermarket, will be the most in-demand drink this Christmas, despite the fact that most of us have never heard of it. Chartreuse has a much lower profile. I only know about it because Jay Gatsby kept it in his secret cocktail cabinet – and from Bruce Springsteen’s memoir, in which he reveals he got hooked on the stuff when he first started drinking. Tom Waits is also a fan.
The story of Chartreuse began in earnest in 1605 when the Carthusian monks – herbalists, scholars and expert alcohol distillers – were entrusted with the recipe by Duke François Annibal d’Estrées. His manuscript outlined a 130-ingredient “elixir of long life”, which contained plants, barks, spices and roots and took the monks over a century to decipher. Finally they landed on what they call the “élixir végétal”, which is the base of today’s Chartreuse. The monks continued to develop the elixir while also trying to create a liqueur that was easier to drink. The first version was created in 1838 and was white, but variations in green and yellow followed in 1840, the green being more herbal in taste and the yellow sweeter. The green “health elixir” version of the recipe was even given to cholera patients – while it clearly wouldn’t have treated the disease, it may have provided some pain relief.
Today, just three people in the world know the recipe, and they’re all monks. It’s thought that the original two monks only shared the recipe with the third because one of the two was considering retiring. They are helped in the distillery by five lay people, who are also anonymous.
It’s a fine story and, as social media weasels its way into everything we eat or drink, perhaps it was only a matter of time before it landed on Chartreuse. The majestic labels, the photogenic shade of “grellow”, the mythological origins – and now the sheer dearth of the stuff. It all feels perfectly suited to the trend-fatigued in 2026, says Pousse-Vaillant. “In this era of AI, of Meta and of constantly [being online] I think people want something real, something authentic, something unchanged.” And the brand agrees. “As the monks say: ‘the cross stands firm while the world turns,’” a Chartreuse spokesperson said. “It is a good motto because the world is difficult right now. So what else can we do?”

====================================================================================================

Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.
When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”
The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.
Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.
Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.
Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries.
This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.
The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”
People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.
The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts.
The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”
Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.
And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.
This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.
But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead, has flushed workers without a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.
One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.
Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.
The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest rates free from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.
But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”
The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”
Peter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued that democracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altman salivates about an “awesome” future in which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”
The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about a superintelligent Golem.
Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to be answerable to no one and will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,” he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.
There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of the End of History in Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.
Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass: section 230 of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.
Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage. Reports of teen suicides and online bullying bred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed to hook users to their screens.
When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.
By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts to use antitrust law and other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace.
How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising to punish European countries who dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which is proving so lucrative for him and his family.
Still, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.
Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in a conversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”
Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”
Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

Dining across the divide: ‘Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

Robin, 68, Essex
Occupation Solicitor
Voting record As leader of the English Democrats – an anti-immigration party that wants an English parliament – Robin votes for himself. Never successfully
Amuse bouche Every year Robin and his wife do a cycle tour of the Netherlands. “There are separate cyclist lanes everywhere and it’s not hilly”
Aslak, 55, London
Occupation Software engineer and entrepreneur
Voting record He has lived in the UK since 2010 but, as a Norwegian national, hasn’t been able to vote here. He votes Labour in Norway
Amuse bouche Runs an art gallery that will shortly unveil a controversial work featuring a Norwegian royal
For starters
Robin I thought I’d be put with a full-on social justice warrior, but he wasn’t like that. I told him my father was in the army, I was born in Malaya, then sent off to boarding school when I was eight.
Aslak He was dressed nicely, shirt and blazer. Almost a stereotypically British chap. We talked a bit about the Vikings because everyone loves to talk about the Vikings when they meet a Scandinavian. He didn’t seem that interested in me or my opinions.
Robin I had a prawn starter, he had calamari, we shared a bottle of rioja. Apparently, they do karaoke there – not on this occasion, thankfully.
Aslak If there had been karaoke, I would have done Seven Nation Army. I’ve sung in several bands. For main we both had lamb chops, so that’s one thing we agreed on …
The big beef
Robin We shouldn’t be involved in Ukraine. We need to focus on our own interests and not get involved in foreign adventures.
Aslak Whether we like it or not, we live in a globalised world, with international trade, migration, alliances. You can’t isolate yourself. If there’s a war somewhere in Europe, it affects everybody. My worry is if Russia takes Ukraine, or a part of it, they won’t stop. Then there’ll be much more to pay – in money and lives – than from giving some support now.
Robin When the Soviet Union was dissolved there were promises that Nato wouldn’t expand to the east, promises that have been completely ignored. Most of Ukraine has been part of Russia since Catherine the Great. So from a historical point of view, you can see Putin’s argument.
Aslak Even if that was true, it isn’t today. A lot has happened in the meantime. Robin was happy for us to arm Ukraine, provided we charge for it. But he also said we should be willing to arm Russia at the same time, like a win-win situation. That sounds more like a business model than foreign policy.
Sharing plate
Robin We agreed people should be able to talk about things rationally. Once you think of another human being as an enemy, you’re not far off the next stage, which is that violence against them is acceptable.
Aslak We agreed a bit on surveillance. I’m against the government collecting information on citizens without any suspicions. It creates a scary power balance and causes people to self-censor, which is bad for democracy.
For afters
Robin The English Democrats campaigned for Brexit, and were obviously very pleased with the result. For a long time we have thought the British state, and its commitment to internationalist entities such as the EU, was against our interests. It hasn’t been a disaster economically; trade has continued to grow.
Aslak The biggest problem has been alienating your biggest trading partners. And students aren’t coming to Britain to study any more because they don’t know if they can stay. And it’s now no longer people from Europe coming, but from all over the world. I don’t see how this aligns with what a lot of Brexiters wanted.
Takeaways
Robin Aslak is a proper lefty, but he’s a proper lefty of the type I used to encounter years ago: rational about it, whereas one of the things we get with the culture wars is wild irrationality. We both said we’d enjoyed it.
Aslak We disagreed about most things, but it was friendly and respectful. Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa. Not that I’m woke … Well, maybe a bit.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake
Aslak and Robin ate at Zebrano in Brentwood, Essex.

‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.
Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.
As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.
“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.
Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.
“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”
Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”
The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.
In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.
Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.
However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.
Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.
Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.
“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.
“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Debt-hungry AI companies face increased risk as bond yields spike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

With Treasury yields climbing this week to their highest levels since 2007, companies reliant on debt are poised to see their borrowing costs rise. That means the AI infrastructure buildout, which has already reached historic levels, is about to get even more expensive.
JPMorgan Chase estimated in June that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued through 2030, as data center companies and others tied to the artificial intelligence boom race to build up capacity to meet what many industry experts view as insatiable demand for AI services.
As borrowers go back to the market, they're now looking at a 10-year Treasury yield that sits near 5.17%, up about 1 percentage point since the start of the year, meaning companies issuing debt are going to have to offer more attractive rates of return to lure investors.
The market isn't in panic mode, at least not yet. Shares of debt-heavy neocloud CoreWeave have held up fine, rising almost 8% this week, while Oracle, which has counted on the debt market for its AI expansion, has had a tougher time, falling 7% for the week and about 30% this year.
Meanwhile, Japan's SoftBank, a principal provider of capital for AI projects, raised $11.1 billion in a junk-bond sale this week, with yields as high as 9.75% for the 7-year tranche.
"They basically are price insensitive to that raise, which means they're price takers," said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, in an interview. "In my view, a lot of these companies need to be price insensitive. They need to get as much capital as possible to compete."
At the center of the AI craze are leading model developers OpenAI and Anthropic, which are each valued at close to $1 trillion in the private market. To provide the infrastructure needed for their advanced models, as well as models and services from a host of other companies, tech's hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft — have committed to hundreds of billions of dollars this year in capital expenditures, with an expected increase coming in 2027.
While a healthy dose of that investment is being funded through debt raises, those tech giants all have investment grade credit ratings, providing them with cheaper access to capital. But for the rest of the pack, bigger challenges lie ahead, according to some market participants.
Warning signs?
A senior private credit investor, who asked to remain unnamed in order to speak candidly on the matter, told CNBC that, moving forward, neocloud deals will be more difficult to finance, because the companies have less cushion to absorb the costs.
Riley Thompson, a vice president at Mitsubishi HC Capital America said in an interview that lenders are getting pickier about the projects they're willing to fund even if the borrower agrees to pay a higher rate.
"Instead of a roster of 50 neoclouds, there's probably 20 that the market's truly interested in," Thompson said.
CoreWeave, which went public last year, warns about rising rates in its SEC filings. In its latest quarterly filing, the company said that, as of June, every 100-basis point (1 percentage point) increase in rates could result in a $30 million jump in its interest expense, based on the balance of its outstanding floating rate debt.
An early warning sign may have landed this week, when Oracle's stock slid following a Bloomberg report that the company sent a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project to protect itself from higher expenses. The company is looking to delay payment on the campus, dubbed Project Jupiter, if it fails to come online as expected in 2028, the report said. Oracle said the project "remains on our planned schedule."
Rising interest rates aren't the only matter at hand. Prior to this week's spike in yields, the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI had started urging a slowdown in the pace of AI development after industry researchers went public with concerns that advanced models risk spinning out of human control.
At the same time, a nationwide backlash against AI data centers has emerged as a major issue heading into November's midterm elections, with 69% of respondents to a recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll, powered by SurveyMonkey, saying they oppose the construction of such facilities in their local area. On Monday, Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who's in the midst of a tight race for reelection, ordered a temporary halt to all data center-related environmental permits following a moratorium on grid approvals last month.
Still, demand for AI services is exploding. The latest example is Meta's Muse personal assistant app, which has rocketed in popularity since its launch earlier in September. Muse clocked more than 2.5 million global downloads in its first two weeks, passing ChatGPT at the top of Apple's App Store, and Evercore's Mark Mahaney told CNBC this week that it could reach 100 million users within six to 12 months.
Andrew Giudici, global head of corporate, project, and infrastructure finance at credit rating agency KBRA, said that even as rising rates may affect future deals, he doesn't see a major impact on borrower demand.
"In a normal environment, people might take a step back and pause a bit," Giudici said. "But I don't think that's going to happen here. I think you're going to continue to see relatively large issuance."
Haim Zaltzman, vice chair of Latham & Watkins' emerging companies and growth practice, said there's no doubt that as costs rise, "somebody will have to absorb it."
"But absorbing it in that kind of demand structure, where the demand is so great, is a lot easier," said Zaltzman, who works on AI infrastructure financing.
The equation is even simpler for Bernie Margulies, CEO of American Compute, which advises on risk management for GPU financing. He said borrowers are eager to secure financing even at higher costs, especially if they have commitments with OpenAI and Anthropic, which have been signing contracts to secure compute capacity years into the future.
"If you have a deal with Anthropic, will 50 basis points really stop you?" Margulies said.

Netanyahu’s 5 rivals pledge joint action ahead of key election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:59:26 UTC
19:59:26 KST

AA Photo
Five Israeli opposition leaders challenging Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have signed a document pledging to coordinate their efforts both ahead of next month’s election and in its aftermath, as the country heads toward a critical vote.
Yair Lapid, leader of the Yesh Atid party, announced on X that opposition leaders had gathered at his home after his party decided to run in the election alongside former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett under the “Together” slate.
Lapid shared a photo from his meeting with Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, Bennett, who is running under the Together slate, Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, and Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats.
He also posted an image of the document signed by the party leaders, pledging to work together toward a change of government.
“Even though there are ideological differences between us, we recognize that replacing the government is our common overriding goal, and we have a duty to work together to achieve it,” Lapid said.
Under the agreement, the parties will refrain from criticizing one another’s policies until the election.
Each party will seek to increase its own vote share in an effort to secure enough seats in the Knesset for the bloc to form a government capable of “preserving Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.”
The parties also agreed to begin working immediately after the election toward the formation of a joint government.
The document calls for the establishment of three working groups tasked with increasing the parties’ vote shares, outlining the main principles of the government to be formed after the election, and countering smear campaigns.
The leaders, however, did not agree on a candidate for prime minister.
In his first response to the agreement, Netanyahu claimed that the leaders would seek to form a government with and Arab parties.
Recent opinion polls in Israel indicate that the opposition bloc could win between 54 and 56 Knesset seats, while the governing bloc led by Netanyahu could secure between 50 and 52 seats.
Under Israel’s electoral system, a government requires the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset to be formed. Current polling suggests that neither bloc would secure enough seats on its own to reach the threshold required to form a governing coalition.
Netanyahu has also faced criticism within Israel over reports that countries in the region had warned his government in the weeks before Hamas’ October 2023 attack, but that those warnings were disregarded.

Poland and Lithuania preparing cross-border evacuation plan for Baltic states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:58:34 UTC
19:58:34 KST

The Suwałki gap, a strip of territory linking Poland and Lithuania - and therefore connecting the Baltic states with other NATO allies and the rest of the European Union - is of particular importance to the plan.
Poland and Lithuania are working on an international evacuation plan for civilians in the event of a major crisis or military threat.
If necessary, the plan would allow some residents of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to be moved across the Polish border.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, the head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, has announced that work on the proposal was already under way and that representatives of Lithuania and Poland were analysing procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capacity.
A detailed plan is to be drawn up once Poland and Lithuania reach an appropriate agreement.
The preparations are being carried out as part of Lithuania's "Vyčio Skliautas 2026" exercises, launched on 25 September to test its national mobilisation system and institutional cooperation in a crisis situation.
The drills will run until 3 October. One of their practical components is testing procedures for the evacuation of the population.
Around 3,000 officials, officers, and representatives of institutions, local authorities, companies, and non-governmental organisations are taking part in the exercises, along with about 1,000 volunteers. A delegation of around 20 people from various Polish institutions has also arrived in Lithuania.
During the drills, systems for warning residents, the organisation of assembly and registration points, transport, and the movement of evacuees through successive regions are being put to the test. Poland is also involved in work related to planning cross-border evacuation.
The Lithuanian authorities have stressed that the aim of the exercises is to develop and test procedures for dealing with crises. The exercises are training activities and do not mean authorities are expecting an imminent threat.
The Suwałki gap
The Suwałki gap, a strip of territory linking Poland and Lithuania - and therefore connecting the Baltic states with other NATO allies and the rest of the European Union - is of particular importance to the plan.
The area contains the main land routes between Lithuania and Poland. In the event of a serious crisis, the region could prove to be crucial for the movement of troops and supplies as well as for the evacuation of civilians.
"The Suwałki gap is of huge importance, both militarily and logistically," Vitkauskas said.
Poland prepares to receive evacuees
Poland is also preparing for the possibility of receiving evacuees from the Baltic states.
In September, representatives from Lithuania and Latvia visited Poland on a study trip focused, among other things, on mass evacuation, civil protection, and the organisation of reception and accommodation for evacuees.
Talks were attended by representatives of Polish services and institutions responsible for security and civil protection.
Lithuania has already drawn up its own evacuation plan for residents in the event of a military threat or crisis.
One of the main evacuation routes runs from Vilnius towards the Polish border. Authorities in Poland's Podlaskie Voivodeship are preparing the region for a potential role as a transit corridor for residents of the Baltic states.

Erdoğan: War criminals belong in court, not at UN

President Erdoğan spoke at the 21st MÜSİAD EXPO International Trade Fair. (AA Photo)
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said on Sept. 26 that war criminals “belong in courtrooms rather than at the U.N. rostrum,” referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“War criminals belong not at the U.N. rostrum, but in courtrooms where they will answer for the crimes they have committed and the blood they have shed,” Erdoğan said at business forum in Istanbul.
“We are determined to unmask the occupying Zionist mentality that considers itself chosen and superior to all other people and has no compassion, conscience, morality or principles,” he added.
“If those committing genocide are not held accountable before justice and history, the same atrocities will happen again.”
Erdoğan cited the death of 6-year-old Hind Rajab, who was killed in 2024 along with members of her family in Gaza, and said those responsible for the deaths of civilians in food queues, incubators, mosques, schools and hospitals will ultimately face justice.
“The Palestinian people are not alone or abandoned,” he said. “Our sisters and brothers in Gaza are not alone in their quest for rights and justice.
Erdoğan praised diplomatic delegations that walked out of the General Assembly hall during addresses by certain leaders, primarily Netanyahu, hailing their actions as a principled response to those he accuses of committing genocide.
“We will continue, to the best of our ability, to tell the truth and be the voice of the oppressed,” he added.
Erdoğan further said the region with Türkiye at its center is facing a “full-blown storm of crises,” while the global system is facing an impasse in terms of “legitimacy, representation and justice.”
He said the effects of regional crises are being felt across multiple sectors, including trade, energy supplies, food security and economic sanctions.
“Issues that were resolved in the recent past through exchanges of ideas are now being addressed through exchanges of missiles and drones,” he said, warning that the principle of “might makes right” is increasingly shaping international relations.
In his address this week to the 81st U.N. General Assembly, Erdoğan said Türkiye had stressed that no solution to crises from Palestine to Yemen, Sudan, Somalia or Iran could succeed without peace, justice and common sense.
Turning to technological developments, Erdoğan said artificial intelligence is reshaping both personal and professional life, with advances in AI models and robotics directly affecting production and consumption.
He highlighted the benefits of AI across sectors ranging from healthcare and education to agriculture and the economy, while warning that technological progress without sufficient regard for human values can produce harmful consequences.
The president also called for deeper discussions of the issue involving governments, the private sector, academia, businesses and civil society.

In fact, each of these countries has influence over Russia and can help make peace a reality. Building guaranteed, dignified security here in Ukraine means enhancing security and stability globally. I thank everyone who is not standing idly by and is helping Ukraine,” he added.
As reported by Ukrinform, a non-residential building in Kyiv’s Shevchenkivskyi district was damaged as a result of a Russian attack on September 27. The number of casualties has risen to four.

Gaza prepares for 1.25M voters amid destruction caused by Israeli attacks and security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:53:51 UTC
19:53:51 KST

Palestinian election authorities are preparing up to 110 polling centres in Gaza for about 1.25 million voters ahead of legislative elections on November 28, despite widespread destruction caused by Israeli attacks and continuing security concerns.
Jamil al-Khalidi, regional director of the Palestinian Central Elections Commission in Gaza, said that preparations were advancing on the technical and logistical fronts, with security remaining the main obstacle to holding the vote.
The commission has also prepared contingency plans in case ballot boxes, ballot papers or electoral ink cannot be brought into the enclave, he said.
Candidate registration opened on Saturday, with five party and independent lists filing applications within the first hour.
Security remains biggest challenge
Al-Khalidi said the commission was ready from a technical and logistical standpoint, but stressed a safe environment was essential for voters, candidates, political parties, election staff and observers.
“The main concern is security,” he said.
He urged the international community to help ensure conditions that would allow all sides involved in the process to operate freely and safely.
Al-Khalidi expressed hope that international observers would be allowed to monitor the election alongside local observers.
Up to 110 polling centres
The scale of destruction in Gaza has complicated efforts to identify suitable polling locations, according to al-Khalidi.
“The destruction is very extensive,” he said, adding that it has affected infrastructure needed for the electoral process.
The commission is coordinating with the Education Ministry to identify schools that remain accessible and can be converted into polling centres.
Current plans call for around 100 to 110 centres in the enclave to serve roughly 1.25 million eligible voters.
Al-Khalidi said the destruction had not diminished public interest in the election, pointing to what he described as a strong determination among Palestinians to participate despite the hardships of recent years.
In April, municipal elections were held in Deir al Balah in central Gaza, with tents used as polling centres in what marked the city’s first local vote in 22 years.
Backup plans for election materials
The commission has also drawn up alternatives in case key election supplies cannot be brought into Gaza.
“If the sensitive election materials cannot be brought in, we have acceptable and practical alternatives that would allow the vote to be held in line with international standards,” said al-Khalidi.
The alternatives cover ballot boxes, ballot papers and electoral ink.
He said the commission did not see technical obstacles that would prevent the election from going ahead, provided security conditions allow the process to proceed.
First legislative vote in nearly 20 years
The November 28 election would be the first Palestinian legislative vote since 2006 and only the third since the Palestinian Legislative Council was established.
Al-Khalidi described a return to the ballot box after nearly two decades as an important step toward rebuilding political stability.
“The experience of the past 20 years … has shown us that elections are the way out of our political crises and disagreements,” he said.
He cautioned, however, that elections alone would not resolve every political dispute.
“We do not claim that elections will solve all problems,” he said. “But we believe holding them is a first step that can be built upon.”
He said renewed elections could help expand political participation, strengthen unified Palestinian decision-making and address the consequences of years of political division.
Five lists apply in first hour
Candidate registration began on Saturday, with five party and independent lists submitting applications in the first hour, according to al-Khalidi.
He described the early turnout as a positive sign of public and political interest in the process.
Registration will remain open until October 7, while campaigning is scheduled to begin November 6.
Voting for security forces is set for November 26, two days before the general vote.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree in July setting November 28 for legislative elections in occupied East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
The Palestinian Legislative Council has been inactive since 2007 following a Palestinian political split and was formally dissolved by the Constitutional Court in 2018.
Legislative and presidential elections scheduled for 2021 were postponed by Abbas, who cited the absence of Israeli assurances allowing Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem to participate.

Estonia to hold regular National Defense Council meetings
Until now, the meetings of the National Defense Council have taken place ad hoc at the president's invitation, but the next Estonian president, Ülle Madise, wants to make the institution's work systematic, said future presidential adviser Taimar Peterkop.
Madise aims to organize regular meetings of the National Defense Council and, after taking office, will hire former Secretary of State Peterkop as the Council's adviser.
"I am very pleased that Taimar Peterkop agreed to take on the substantive preparation and organization of the National Defense Council's work. Taimar Peterkop knows broad‑based national defense both theoretically and practically, understands the importance of dignified human relations and of forward‑looking, determined and persistent joint action," Madise said in a press release.
According to the Constitution of Estonia, the President of the Republic is the highest leader of national defense, and the National Defense Council is an advisory body to the president.
The council provides an opportunity to bring together representatives of the president, parliament, government and defense forces to discuss national defense issues and helps shape a comprehensive view of the country's security.
"Times and circumstances require greater attention from those responsible for security so that confidence prevails in society. National defense means not only military defense but also the development of broad‑based national defense, and therefore I see the need to make the council's work more regular and consistent. Involving an adviser will help organize the council's work better and more substantively," Madise noted.
"I greatly appreciate the invitation from the future president to join her team. In this role I can apply my knowledge and experience in preparing for crises and resolving them, and thereby contribute to Estonia's ability to withstand crises in a tense geopolitical environment," Peterkop said in the press release.
Peterkop served as Secretary of State from 2018 to 2025 and before that, from 2015 to 2018, as Director General of the Information System Authority (RIA). Previously he worked at the Ministry of Defense as deputy permanent secretary and as a defense policy adviser at the Estonian Embassy in Washington. Peterkop currently works at the e‑Governance Academy as a senior expert in cybersecurity.
Peterkop graduated from the University of Tartu Faculty of Law and earned a master's degree in strategic leadership from the U.S. Army War College.
Estonia's next president Ülle Madise will take office on 12 October, giving the oath before the Riigikogu.

Why rheumatoid arthritis pain may persist even when inflammation is under control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:49:13 UTC
19:49:13 KST

Why rheumatoid arthritis pain may persist even when inflammation is under control
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- Semmelweis University
- Summary:
- Pain and fatigue in rheumatoid arthritis can persist even after inflammation improves, with depression, poor sleep, obesity, smoking, and chronic pain potentially helping sustain symptoms. Researchers say identifying these hidden drivers could prevent unnecessary medication changes and lead to more personalized treatment.
- Share:
Researchers at Semmelweis University say persistent rheumatic symptoms may be driven by more than inflammation alone. Sleep disorders, depression, obesity, smoking, and other health problems may also help keep symptoms going. In publications in Nature Reviews Rheumatology and The Lancet Rheumatology, the team also introduced a model designed to help doctors identify the underlying causes of symptoms earlier and tailor treatment more effectively.
The researchers examined how depression, smoking, obesity, sleep problems, and other health conditions are connected with difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the joints, leading to pain, swelling, and stiffness. In Hungary alone, it affects tens of thousands of people. Most patients respond well to treatment, but 6-28 percent fall into the so-called "difficult-to-treat" group because they do not achieve lasting remission despite therapy.
According to the studies in Nature Reviews Rheumatology and The Lancet Rheumatology, these additional health problems may do more than simply occur alongside rheumatoid arthritis. They may also contribute to keeping symptoms active.
A Vicious Cycle of Pain, Mood, and Sleep
Pain and depression, for example, can reduce physical activity, contribute to weight gain, and worsen both sleep and mood. Those changes can then intensify pain and make daily activities more difficult, creating a difficult-to-break "vicious cycle."
The researchers also developed a new model that could improve care for patients whose rheumatoid arthritis remains difficult to manage. Under the widely used "treat-to-target" approach, doctors regularly track measurable indicators of disease activity. If inflammation is not reduced enough, treatment is adjusted, such as by increasing the medication dose or switching to another drug.
The team argues that this same approach can also serve as a kind of "early warning system." If measurable signs of inflammation improve but symptoms remain, that may indicate the pain or fatigue is not being caused solely, or perhaps at all, by ongoing inflammation.
Looking Beyond Inflammation
"When target values improve but the patient still suffers from pain and fatigue, it is worth taking a step back. In such cases, instead of automatically prescribing more medication, doctors should look for what is maintaining the symptoms - whether it is chronic pain syndrome, depression, sleep disorders, or obesity," said Dr. György Nagy, head of the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology at Semmelweis University.
The researchers say they have seen this approach improve outcomes in difficult-to-treat patients. In many cases, it may also strengthen the doctor-patient relationship by focusing treatment more closely on what is actually driving the patient's symptoms.
A Model With Growing International Influence
The team's model has gained substantial international attention. Publications that introduced the concept of "difficult-to-treat" disease and the related treatment strategy have already been cited more than a thousand times by other researchers.
The definition is now used worldwide not only for rheumatoid arthritis, but also in discussions of other diseases.
AI Could Help Personalize Treatment
The researchers are now looking toward the next stage of the work. Alongside their own studies, they plan to participate in projects that use artificial intelligence to develop more effective treatments for people with rheumatoid arthritis.
"With AI-based pattern recognition, we could identify subgroups among patients, and with the help of these data we could create more effective, almost personalized treatment strategies for them," explained Dr. Lilla Gunkl-Tóth, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the publications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Lilla Gunkl-Tóth, Iain B. McInnes, György Nagy. Bridging the gap: combining treat-to-target and difficult-to-treat strategies in the management of rheumatoid arthritis. Nature Reviews Rheumatology, 2026; 22 (5): 319 DOI: 10.1038/s41584-026-01354-w
- Wenhui Xie, Tong Chen, Yuan Chen, Zhuoli Zhang, Shiyu Xiao. Associated lifestyle factors and comorbidities of difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Rheumatology, 2026; 8 (6): e425 DOI: 10.1016/S2665-9913(26)00041-X
- Lilla Gunkl-Tóth, György Nagy. Lifestyle factors in difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis. The Lancet Rheumatology, 2026; 8 (6): e408 DOI: 10.1016/S2665-9913(26)00108-6

Northern Ireland standoff puts peace and power-sharing at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:47:58 UTC
19:47:58 KST

Northern Ireland standoff puts peace and power-sharing at risk
A sudden revival of the 1990s confrontations between Orange Order marchers and Catholic demonstrators puts the police back in the middle — and leaders of Northern Ireland’s supposed unity government on opposite sides.
PORTADOWN, Northern Ireland — Hard-liners in Northern Ireland are reviving an age-old dispute rife with bitter symbolism that pits the rights of British Protestants against those of Irish Catholics — and risks the destruction of their supposed unity government.
Hundreds of residents of the Garvaghy Road, the main Catholic district in the otherwise staunchly Protestant town of Portadown, near Belfast, stood in the roadway in pouring rain overnight to block a Sunday morning parade by Northern Ireland’s main Protestant brotherhood, the Orange Order — a parade that had been banned since 1998 because of the widespread violence it triggered.
The Parades Commission, the British government-appointed group that for decades has adjudicated such zero-sum disputes, stunned Garvaghy Road residents by ruling Friday that a drastically pared-down Orange parade should be allowed to pass through the area Sunday morning. It had refused more than 1,300 previous requests from the group seeking to “finish” the parade it was blocked from completing in 1998.
Advertisement
A series of unprecedented late-night legal challenges followed Saturday, capped by a ruling from Northern Ireland’s senior judge after midnight stating that the courts had no power to overturn the commission’s independent judgment.
The scene is now set for a revival of a standoff with no obvious end point — and no apparent way to deliver a “win” for both sides.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland deployed several hundred officers to the site. Many of them sat Sunday morning in scores of armored Land Rovers parked on the narrow country lane that separates the would-be Orange marchers on a hilltop church from the Garvaghy Road demonstrators, out of sight beyond houses and hedgerows.
The two main parties in Northern Ireland’s cross-community government — revived only two years ago following a lengthy breakdown over Northern Ireland’s peculiar Brexit rules — are lining up on opposite sides of this renewed street battle of wills, raising the political stakes.
Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party that represents most Catholics and has grown to become the largest party in Northern Ireland, rallied in force alongside the Garvaghy Road protesters.
The Sinn Féin first minister of Northern Ireland’s government, Michelle O’Neill, won cheers as she told the partisan crowd: “The Garvaghy Road residents deserve to live free from sectarian harassment and intimidation.”
Advertisement
“Does anybody think this is a good idea? No right-minded person would make this decision,” said O’Neill, who expressed bewilderment over the Parades Commission’s U-turn. “Why, after 28 years of determinations to block a march down this road, did the Parades Commission think this is the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community?”
But Northern Ireland’s main pro-British party, the Democratic Unionists, stood alongside the blocked Orangemen as they waited in hope that the police would enforce the commission’s ruling by pushing the Catholics out of the road. The last time this happened, in 1997, it triggered three nights of Irish republican rioting across Northern Ireland.
“It’s a big day for Portadown. Obviously we have had a seismic win within the courts. The law is on our side,” declared the Democratic Unionist MP representing Portadown, Carla Lockhart.
She singled out O’Neill for criticism, branding the first minister as a law-breaker leading a mob.
“What does it say when you have an absolute rabble, thousands chanting, and our self-proclaimed ‘first minister for all’ leading the chants and standing unlawfully?” Lockhart said.
“But these men will continue to stand here,” she said, gesturing to a few dozen Orangemen standing outside the Anglican church, many of them under umbrellas. “They’ve the law on their side. We’ll ensure that the parade is put lawfully down the road.”
Advertisement
Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalist politicians appealed to the British government to intervene.
But U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would reverse the commission’s parade ruling only if Northern Ireland’s police commander, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, recommended another policy U-turn on security grounds. Such a decision would risk the growth of a Protestant counter-protest at the confrontation zone, as happened repeatedly in the 1990s, spurring widespread rioting and isolated killings across Northern Ireland.
“There have been big gains made in Northern Ireland and we don’t want to see things go backwards,” Burnham told the BBC. “Obviously (it’s) a challenging situation today. But it’s very important that we work to bring calm.”
Burnham’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, said what happens next depends on the judgment of the police chief, not his own. Underscoring the risk of a rapidly deteriorating security situation, he left the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool to fly back to Belfast.
“This is primarily a policing matter now,” Bryant told Sky News.
He noted that the demonstrators blocking the Garvaghy Road did not have approval from the Parades Commission. “The law states that if you want to mount a protest against a parade, you have to lodge an application with the Parades Commission,” he said. “It means the protest that is going on at the moment is unlawful.”
Advertisement
The Orange Order was founded near Portadown in 1795 to oppose the Catholic community and to celebrate their own side’s 1690 military triumph under the command of King William of Orange. The group mounts thousands of parades annually, concentrated on July 12, the anniversary of that 17th century victory. The Catholic side broadly loathes the parades as demonstrations of Protestant power, and since the 1990s has tried to block any Orange parades that pass near or through their communities.
Boutcher, the police commander, issued a carefully worded statement that underscored his desire to avoid physically confronting the Garvaghy Road protesters if possible. Instead, he said officers would collect video and photos to identify those breaking the law — potentially including, though he didn’t specify this, the Sinn Féin leaders — for eventual prosecution.
“The policing operation thus far has helped ensure there has been no violence or disorder,” Boutcher said. “We have an evidence gathering operation in place to detect any offenses and will continue to do this throughout today. I appeal to everyone to remain calm and peaceful.”

When ‘secret spot’ goes viral: The tourism trap of too many views, too many visitors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:47:34 UTC
19:47:34 KST

Digital demand can surge faster than physical infrastructure can adapt.
Tourism brings people, places, and cultures closer. It creates opportunities for communities, supports livelihoods, and contributes significantly to economic development. Globally, travel and tourism contributed $10.9 trillion, or 10% of global GDP, in 2024, supporting 357 million jobs and generating $1.9 trillion in international visitor spending.But the way people decide where to go is changing - and increasingly, the journey begins before the journey, inside a phone.On World Tourism Day 2026, observed on September 27, the global tourism sector is discussing how digital technology and Artificial Intelligence can redesign tourism. India arrives at that conversation amid extraordinary growth: Domestic Tourist Visits reached 428.55 crore in 2025, up from 67.7 crore in 2021, while Foreign Tourist Visits rose from 0.1 crore to 2.53 crore. Foreign Exchange Earnings from tourism increased from Rs 63,978 crore to Rs 2,76,831 crore over the same period, according to the Ministry of Tourism.The opportunity is enormous. So, is the question increasingly confronting destinations: what happens when a beautiful place becomes more famous online than it is capable of being on the ground?That is the emerging Instagram destination problem.
From travel guide to visual trigger
Instagram Reels have fundamentally changed travel discovery. A 20-second video can compress a mountain road, turquoise lake, café, waterfall or village into an irresistible sequence of drone shots, music, transitions and carefully selected frames.The Government of India has itself recognised social media's growing role in tourism. A Ministry of Tourism study titled “Social Media as an Influencer among Foreign Tourists Visiting India”, conducted through the Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management, examined social media's influence on foreign visitors.The ministry subsequently acknowledged the importance of Instagram, YouTube, influencers, vloggers and user-generated content in tourism promotion. Tourism policy expert Hemant Joshi, CEO of Atithi Foundation, says the challenge is that visitor demand can grow far faster than a destination’s infrastructure, carrying capacity and local ecosystem can handle. “We are increasingly seeing this in fragile mountain and rural destinations, where a viral post can almost instantly translate into traffic, waste, pressure on water and other local infrastructure, and disruption for communities. Recent experiences in places such as Manali, Ladakh and the Nilgiris are a reminder of this gap,” he said.
A viral viewpoint
Once someone interacts with travel content, similar destinations can flood their feed. Discovery therefore becomes less deliberate. A person who has never heard of a particular valley, café or viewpoint can encounter it repeatedly until an unfamiliar place starts feeling like a destination they need to experience.
The algorithm loves the photogenic
The problem is not that social media makes people travel. Travel inspiration has always existed.The difference is scale, speed and concentration. Algorithms reward content that attracts attention. Visually dramatic places are naturally suited to short-form video. That creates a feedback loop:beautiful destination → engaging Reel → high views → more creators → more travellers → more content → even more visibility.Travel enthusiast and hotel manager working in Gurgaon, Nitish Srivastava, who also creates travel content, says algorithms have a soft spot for what already grabs eyeballs. “So creators can end up repeatedly visiting the same popular places because they know the audience will respond,” he added.He said a creator can show the experience of a fragile place without necessarily turning its precise location into a mass-tourism instruction manual. “You can still share the experience without turning it into a ‘go here before everyone finds out’ trend. For me, protecting a place is more important than getting a few extra views,” Nitish said.Delhi-based traveller Harsh Shivam, who likes sharing travel-related content on social media, similarly argues that creators should exercise judgement when revealing particularly fragile or previously uncrowded locations. “Location is obviously an important part of travel content, but there is a difference between telling people roughly where a place is and giving them precise directions to a spot that may not be able to handle a sudden influx of visitors,” said Harsh.But he also highlights the other side: “Increased tourism can create opportunities for local businesses and communities.””That is the central paradox.Visibility can be economic development. The same visibility can become environmental pressure.
Can an algorithm create overtourism?
The reel doesn't show the queue
There is another problem: social media shows a destination, but rarely shows its carrying capacity. A reel might capture the waterfall. It probably won't show the road leading to it clogged with vehicles.It might show a pristine mountain lake. It probably won't show the plastic waste left behind.It might show an empty viewpoint. It won't necessarily tell you that the shot was taken at 6 am, during a brief window between crowds. “A place may only look the way it does in a particular season, or the experience may change significantly depending on the time of year. That context can be important in setting realistic expectations for people planning a visit,” said Harsh.Srivastava says his own experience has repeatedly demonstrated this gap: “Social media usually shows the best few seconds—the perfect light, empty viewpoint and cinematic angle.”
When the road becomes the bottleneck
India's tourism numbers make this increasingly important.Official Uttarakhand statistics show how dramatically visitor numbers can concentrate at individual destinations. Kedarnath recorded 243,012 visitors in 2021, rising to 1,564,248 in 2022 and 1,958,863 in 2023. Badrinath rose from 199,409 in 2021 to 1,780,429 in 2023. Tehri recorded more than 3.76 million tourist visits in 2023, according to Uttarakhand Tourism.The issue isn't simply how many people enter a state. It is where they go, when they arrive and whether local infrastructure can absorb the concentration. Roads, parking, public toilets, accommodation, drinking water, sewage systems, emergency services and waste collection all have finite capacity. And when tourism growth is faster than infrastructure, the first visible sign may not be a tourism statistic. It may be a traffic jam.
Too Viral to Handle
The environmental bill arrives later
Government research shows that the environmental consequences are not theoretical.A Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change report submitted before the National Green Tribunal documented significant waste pressures associated with tourism in Uttarakhand. Research cited in the report, in January 2025 found that 71% of the total solid waste generated in the Valley of Flowers was produced in only 37 days. Estimated waste generation was approximately 364 grams per visitor per day on the Gomukh trek and 580 grams per visitor per day on the Kedarkantha trek.These numbers reveal an important characteristic of tourism pollution: seasonality and concentration matter.A place can cope with relatively modest visitor numbers for much of the year and still experience severe pressure during a short viral or peak-tourism window.Ladakh offers another stark example. A carrying-capacity study by the GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment examined tourism pressure in the Leh Town Complex. The research recorded rapid growth in accommodation, air traffic and tourist influx, alongside concerns over waste generation and disposal. Ladakh's ecological vulnerability makes the equation particularly sensitive. Water, waste treatment, roads and energy are not infinitely expandable simply because Instagram demand rises.According to Kedarnath Nagar Panchayat data obtained through an RTI, Kedarnath generated 50.30 metric tonnes of waste between April and August 2026, more than 2.5 times the entire 2025 total.
Water is part of the tourism footprint too
Tourism's environmental footprint is also much bigger than litter.Niti Aayog's work on sustainable tourism in the Indian Himalayan Region highlights pressures involving water consumption, groundwater extraction, energy, accommodation, transportation and solid waste. That is why “hidden gem” is not necessarily synonymous with “sustainable destination.”A small community may have a beautiful landscape but limited sewage treatment, parking, waste collection, medical facilities or water supply.Goa shows that even beaches have a limitThe carrying-capacity question is not confined to the Himalayas. Goa recorded 10.8 million tourist arrivals in 2025, according to the state's tourism department.An assessment placed before the National Green Tribunal found that, using a criterion of 10 square metres per visitor, carrying capacity was exceeded at beaches including Palolem, Agonda, Siridao, Vainguinim and Coco Beach.The problem is therefore not “Instagram versus tourism.” It is tourism growth versus destination capacity.
The cost nobody sees on the reel
The local economy has something to gain—and lose
It would be simplistic to portray viral tourism as entirely destructive. A formerly overlooked destination gaining attention can mean more customers for homestays, restaurants, taxis, guides, artisans and small retailers.But benefits are not automatically distributed equally.If visitor numbers rise faster than local capacity, residents can face congestion, waste, water stress, rising costs and disruption to everyday life. Meanwhile, businesses may become increasingly dependent on a tourism boom they did not necessarily create or control.
India’s tourism challenge is therefore no longer simply about attracting visitors, but about distributing them intelligently. As Joshi puts it, “Digital platforms can be used to distribute demand by making credible, attractive alternatives discoverable rather than concentrating everyone on the same few locations.”Destinations, he argues, must plan for demand rather than chase it. “The objective should not be to make destinations less popular, but to make tourism growth more manageable, more geographically distributed and more valuable to the communities that host it.”
