'Marriage does not advance a child’s age': Delhi HC rejects Muslim personal law defence in POCSO case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:45:53 UTC
19:45:53 KST

'A person who is sixteen before the ceremony remains sixteen afterwards,' said Justice Narula
NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has refused to quash a POCSO case against a man who married a 16-year-old girl, holding that a marriage claimed to be valid under Muslim personal law cannot shield an adult from prosecution for sexual intercourse with a wife below 18.Justice Sanjeev Narula said the statutory age of 18 under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) cannot be replaced by the concept of puberty under personal law. “Put simply, marriage does not advance a child’s age. A person who is sixteen before the ceremony remains sixteen afterwards," he said, as quoted by ANI.The court was dealing with a petition filed by Bilal and another seeking quashing of FIR No. 189/2026 registered at Darya Ganj Police Station under Section 64(1) of the BNS and Section 6 of the POCSO Act. The petitioners had also sought disciplinary action against police officials and compensation for alleged false implication and harassment.According to the judgment, the girl was born on September 19, 2008, and married Bilal on December 20, 2024, when she was 16 years and three months old. Bilal was born on January 1, 1997 and was nearly 28 at the time. The couple subsequently lived together and the girl became pregnant. By May 2026, she was around eight months pregnant. Her age came to the notice of authorities when she visited a government hospital during her pregnancy.
The foetus later died in utero and the girl delivered a stillborn child on June 6, 2026. The judgment records that an order was subsequently obtained from the Sub-Divisional Magistrate for exhumation of the child for DNA profiling and collection of evidence.The FIR was not based on an allegation made by the girl herself. She maintained that the marriage had taken place with the consent of both families, that she had married of her own free will and that physical relations began after the marriage. She also supported Bilal during his bail proceedings and expressed a desire to have him by her side during her pregnancy.The petitioners argued that under Muslim personal law, a Muslim of sound mind who has attained puberty is competent to marry and that, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, puberty is presumed after the age of 15. They contended that since the girl had attained puberty before the nikah, the marriage was valid and the subsequent sexual relationship could not attract criminal liability.The High Court rejected the argument, observing, “Personal law may determine whether a marriage has been contracted and the civil consequences that follow. It cannot supply an exception to a criminal law where Parliament has provided none."The court clarified that it was not deciding whether the nikah was valid, void or voidable. Even if the marriage were assumed to be valid, it said, that would not take sexual intercourse with a person below 18 outside the scope of POCSO or the BNS. The court also rejected the argument that the girl's consent or the absence of force and coercion could take the case outside POCSO.“POCSO does not confer such a power upon the child, her parents, or the Court,” it observed.The court further said that the age difference between the couple did not by itself establish guilt, but was relevant while considering whether the court should exercise its exceptional jurisdiction to terminate a POCSO prosecution at the threshold.The HC also rejected the argument that the FIR was unsustainable because neither the girl nor her family had approached the police, adding in this case, once doctors learnt that the pregnant patient was below 18, the statutory reporting mechanism was triggered, the court said.The court also rejected the petitioners' reliance on constitutional freedoms under Articles 21, 25 and 26, holding that they could not create an exception to a generally applicable penal law enacted for the protection of children.“Constitutional liberty protects choice; it does not create an exception to POCSO or the BNS,” the judgment said.The court cautioned against an interpretation that would effectively introduce a marital exception into POCSO for children below 18.Justice Narula added that, “The statutory protection would then depend not upon the age of the child, but upon whether a marriage had been arranged before the sexual relationship was discovered. That would turn the legislation on its head."“The conclusion is narrower: a marriage claimed to be valid under Muslim personal law cannot, by reason of that status alone, confer immunity from POCSO or BNS for sexual intercourse with a wife who was below 18 at the relevant time. Any other view would create, through judicial decision, an exception which Parliament has expressly excluded,” he added.
The court acknowledged that individual cases may involve “affection rather than violence, and relationships rather than predation”, but said such circumstances could not permit courts to rewrite the statutory definition of an offence.Dismissing the petition, the High Court held that a marriage claimed to be valid under Muslim personal law cannot, merely because of that status, confer immunity from POCSO or the BNS for sexual intercourse with a wife who was below 18 at the relevant time.

Asian Games | DPRK sets world records in women's 69kg, China claims gold in wome's 77kg weightlifting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:45:28 CST
19:45:28 KST

Gold medalist He Renxiu (C) of China, silver medalist Ayanat Zhumagali (L) of Kazakhstan and bronze medalist Reihaneh Karimi of Iran pose during the awarding ceremony after the women's 77kg final of weightlifting at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Yu Yang)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Song Kuk Hyang of the DPR Korea smashed three world records en route to claiming the women's 69kg weightlifting title at the 20th Asian Games on Sunday, while China's He Renxiu took gold in the women's 77kg division.
Song set a new world mark in the snatch with 121kg, then broke records in the clean and jerk with 152kg and in the combined total with 273kg, finishing incredible 41 kilograms ahead of the silver medalist.
Chen Wen-huei from Chinese Taipei claimed silver with 232kg in total and Ingrid Grueso of Bahrain took bronze with a total of 229kg.
Being the youngest weightlifter in the category, 20-year-old Grueso, who was born in Colombia, said she was "super proud" of herself.
"This is the first competition of the year for me. I had two operations and I came here giving the best of myself," she said.
Later in the day in the women's 77kg, 22-year-old He lifted 118kg in the snatch with three successful attempts, trailing Kim Iseul of South Korea by eight kilograms. She then added 140kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 258kg.
Ayanat Zhumagali of Kazakhstan took silver with a total of 246kg, while Reihaneh Karimi from Iran claimed bronze at 243kg.
Making her debut at a major continental competition, He could barely contain her excitement. "This is my first time competing in an event of this calibre, and also the first time I've heard my national anthem played for me. I was overcome with emotion...I never thought I would shed tears," she said.
Speaking of her failed second clean and jerk attempt at 140kg, she said she regularly trains at that weight and quickly regained her composure. "I plan to go after the Asian and world records in this weight class in the future."
The weight class was only established in August this year, with just five athletes competing in the Asian Games.
The men's 85kg and 95kg divisions will take place on Monday. ■

KATHMANDU, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from landslides and floods triggered by continuous rainfall has risen to 10 in Nepal, while four people remain missing, the Armed Police Force (APF) said on Sunday.
Four members of a single family were killed in a landslide in Baglung district, while two others died in separate landslide incidents in Palpa district, where three people remain missing. A landslide killed one person and left another missing in Myagdi district.
Meanwhile, three more people were killed after floodwaters swept away their houses in other districts.
At least 66 houses have been washed away by floods in Parbat district and six in Rupandehi district, while 10 other houses have been destroyed by landslides in several districts, APF spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Xinhua.
"We are still collecting data on the losses. The loss figure is sure to rise," said Karki.
He said rescue and relief operations are continuing in the affected areas. ■

Tearful Johns praises fans for helping Knights end grand final drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:40:19 UTC
19:40:19 KST

Former Knights star Matty Johns has praised the Knights and their fans after Newcastle reached the NRL grand final for the first time in 25 years.
Johns became emotional as he hailed the supporters for sticking by the team.
What's next?
The Knights will face the Roosters in the NRL grand final on Sunday, October 4 from 7:30pm AEDT.
Former Knights star Matty Johns has broken down in tears as he heaped praise on the Newcastle team and its fans after a gripping and gritty NRL preliminary final win over Penrith.
The Knights played more than half the game with 12 men on the field after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip drop that graphically broke Nathan Cleary's leg.
Penrith scored shortly after to take a 14-6 lead into half-time, but Justin Holbrook's Knights defended resolutely against a scrappy Panthers side and managed to score three second-half tries to progress to the grand final against the Roosters.
The women's team won back-to-back NRLW premierships in 2022 and 2023, but Newcastle has not played in a men's grand final since Andrew Johns led the Knights to victory over the Eels in the 2001 grand final.
A quarter of a century and five wooden spoons later, the team will return to the final day of the season next week after a similarly remarkable upset win over the most dominant team in NRL history.
So it is hardly surprising that Hunter native and former Knights star Matty Johns was incredibly emotional straight after full-time.
"To be honest, I don't know what to say," he said on Fox Sports.
"It was unbelievable. Incredible effort in that second half. I just feel so happy for all the fans."
It became increasingly hard to find the words as tears started to flow and emotion took over.
"They've had to put up with a lot of shit for a lot of years to get back to where they are now," Johns said.
Even getting to the game on Sunday was tough as an issue with a freight train caused delays and cancellations on the Central Coast and Newcastle train line, forcing fans to find alternate routes and replacement services to get down to Sydney, which led to traffic jams on the M1 motorway on a sodden afternoon.
"But it just didn't stop them in the wet," Johns said of the crowd at Homebush, which was hugely in favour of the visiting Novocastrians.
"When you run onto a field like that and you look up and you see all those Newcastle fans, you don't leave the field defeated.
"If not for the fans they don't win today."
Holbrook sprinted around the field to pay tribute to the fans who turned up, and who have continued to turn up even when the team was struggling, including last year when they finished last for the fifth time in 21 seasons.
"We want to make our community proud, our Hunter region, and for the boys to deliver that performance, it was so good to see them all hang around," he said.
"We went down to 12 [when Crossland was sent off] and then 30,000 make you feel like you've got 14 out there."
Captain Kalyn Ponga agreed the supporters helped the team get over the line.
"They're a big reason why we won today," he said.
"They're loud, they're passionate, they're vocal and we're gonna need them next week."

Kapil Sibal alleges ‘unilateral’ EC decisions, seeks action against CEC Gyanesh Kumar

NEW DELHI: Rajya Sabha member Kapil Sibal on Sunday escalated the political row over the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR), accusing chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of taking "unilateral decisions" and demanding his removal from office.Sibal also urged the Supreme Court to examine the Election Commission's records, dissent notes and orders issued during the period under question, and consider nullifying elections conducted during the 10-month period he referred to.The former Union minister's remarks came amid a controversy over internal objections raised by election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi regarding decisions related to electoral rolls, the EC's IT systems and the SIR exercise.
Sibal alleges unilateral decision-making
According to Sibal, the Election Commission's own statement issued on Saturday acknowledged that decisions had not been taken unanimously over the past several months. He alleged that Kumar had taken decisions "unilaterally" rather than through the full three-member Commission.
Sibal claimed that Commission meetings were conducted without agendas being circulated or minutes being recorded, preventing the other commissioners from reviewing or commenting on decisions.
He said the alleged practices covered 10 months, including elections held in Bihar in June 2025 and West Bengal in April.The allegations follow a report by The Indian Express, which said Sandhu and Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders that they said were issued without their knowledge.Sibal also alleged that decisions concerning additions and deletions of voters were centralised in Delhi through ECI NET under Seema Khanna, who managed its operations, instead of being handled by statutory Electoral Registration Officers.He demanded that an FIR be registered against Khanna and that she be arrested, arguing that unlike the CEC, she does not have statutory immunity from criminal prosecution.Sibal also alleged that changes were made to Form 6, used for new voter registration, requiring details of parents or grandparents without the central government issuing the required notification.
EC responds to concerns over SIR and electoral rolls
The Election Commission on Saturday announced several decisions addressing issues that Sandhu and Joshi had raised in their internal communications.On Form 6, the EC said the additional declaration requiring new voters to provide details of their own or their parents' or grandparents' entries in the electoral roll from the previous SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court.It said the additional requirement was specific to the SIR exercise and that regular statutory forms would continue to be used outside an SIR.On access to electoral-roll databases, the EC said field officers have role-based access to ECINET according to their statutory powers. It also announced a review by a committee headed by a senior deputy election commissioner and including an independent IIT or IIIT expert to "double-check" the system's compliance with election laws and rules.The Commission further said agendas for all meetings would be circulated in advance and minutes issued, while directions issued by commissioners to EC officers would be complied with.
On the IT division, the EC said disputed changes in the distribution of work were never implemented after Sandhu and Joshi intervened, and that oversight of the division by the deputy election commissioner was never withdrawn.Sibal, however, claimed that the alleged irregularities meant elections conducted from Bihar through West Bengal during the period were "illegal". He called on the Supreme Court to take suo motu cognisance of the matter and consider whether recent elections should be annulled.The opposition has also demanded Kumar's removal and an independent review of decisions and electoral-roll changes made during his tenure.

Oleshky under siege: a city where people eat grass, hide bodies in a hospital basement and wait for an evacuation that never comes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:35:00 EEST
19:35:00 KST

Oleshky under siege: a city where people eat grass, hide bodies in a hospital basement and wait for an evacuation that never comes
Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city just nine kilometres from Kherson, is going through the hardest period in its modern history. Residents are trapped, with no safe way out, no food and no rescue in sight. Locals, their relatives and volunteers have shared messages with Ukrainska Pravda that show the scale of the catastrophe.
"I'll say it plainly: we're in absolute hell here. People are no longer boiling grass soup just for the animals, but for themselves too. And as for bread, I'm not even going to start talking about that."
"No food or medicine deliveries. No evacuation. No help of any kind. People are surviving however they can."
"Two men were carrying food from Radensk to Oleshky. On the way, they came under drone attack and both were killed. The food they were carrying stayed lying next to them. The sausage is untouched – the dogs won't eat it. They're eating the dead instead."
"The city is under blockade. People are dying of hunger. There's no food even in the hospital. The orcs have blocked and mined everything. And they are taking away the last of what people have."
"If the hospital closes, the city will die."
"If people stay, they're doomed."
The city has been on the brink of humanitarian catastrophe for nearly a year, since the end of 2025. Food supplies were last brought into Oleshky on 26 May. Since then, there have been no proper deliveries, leaving people close to starvation.
But food is not the only problem. Since the occupation began four years ago, and after the destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, the city has had no electricity, gas or drinking water. There is also a critical shortage of medicine. The hospital is the only thing still just about functioning, but even the staff there cannot always provide basic first aid.
All roads and approaches to Oleshky are mined. The city lies just a few kilometres from Ukrainian-controlled territory – close enough for drones from both sides to reach it freely. The skies above Oleshky are hunted daily, with drones targeting one another and anything moving on the ground below. Commercial hauliers who tried to reach the city by car with food in the summer came under heavy fire and had to turn back.
Evacuation is impossible. Oleshky is under complete blockade.
The Ukrainian side has appealed to both the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and its partners to help evacuate civilians. Six months of talks have produced no result. Russia, which has controlled the city since February 2022, has not agreed to a humanitarian corridor and is using local residents as a human shield against Ukraine's defence forces.
"I always say: it's the 21st century out here, but what is happening there feels like some kind of ghetto," says a volunteer who helps people escape the city.
Ukrainska Pravda has gathered testimony from Oleshky residents, their relatives, volunteers, officials and service members. We report on how how the city is surviving under occupation and whether there is any way out of a place where every road is closed.
Five hours on the road for food
Oleshky is an old Cossack town on the left bank of the Dnipro, near Kherson. Before the full-scale war, tourists and people from the oblast centre came here for the quiet and for the landscape: a place where the semi-desert of huge sand dunes meets pine forest, and forest gives way to the Dnipro floodplains. Residents of Oleshky, in turn, used to travel to Kherson, just nine kilometres away across the river. Since late February 2022, after Russia occupied the left bank and the bridges were destroyed, the connection between the two cities has been cut.
Oleshky is not the only place on the left bank facing humanitarian disaster. Food, medicine and transport links are also a problem in Hola Prystan, Stara Zburivka, Nova Zburivka and other settlements in the oblast.
But the situation is critical in Oleshky and the surrounding villages of the hromada (an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories). Volunteers estimate that up to 1,500 people remain in the city, including around 40 children. A further 4,000 people, including around 150 children, remain in the villages. Before the full-scale invasion, the hromada had a total population of almost 40,000.
With no electricity, people now rarely manage to contact their relatives. Some go months without getting in touch at all. Those who manage to charge their phones from a generator sometimes have only 20 or 30 seconds to call, or just enough time to send a text. Most often, they ask whether there is any way to leave and complain about the lack of food.
Food supplies were last brought into Oleshky at the end of May, when local businesspeople managed to get two commercial vehicles into the town.
Every attempt since then has failed. On 2 June, in one such attempt, four cars hit mines and two people were killed. By the end of summer, trying to enter the city had become pointless because of the constant attacks.
"The situation in our town is simply horrific. People have run out of food. They're cooking themselves a little soup from grass, throwing in purslane, goosefoot, amaranth. I won't even mention the animals – it's even worse for them. I just cry and cry. I don't know what to do," a local resident of Oleshky says.
Over the summer, people survived on whatever they had grown in their vegetable patches. Almost no one goes into the forest on either side of Oleshky, where they once gathered berries and mushrooms, or to the river, where they used to fish. They are afraid. If mines can be lying on streets near the centre of town, and loitering drones can hunt there, then places with tall grass and no one around are even more dangerous.
So locals ate their own vegetables and fruit. Some caught pigeons or pheasants. Others cooked borshch "the new way" – with eggs, courgettes, tomatoes and grass. People traded food among themselves. Some was bought and sold at a small makeshift market that sprang up near the hospital. But prices there are not just high. They are almost absurd: eggs sell for UAH 800 (US$18) a dozen, potatoes and onions for UAH 500 (US$11), courgettes for UAH 250 (US$5.60), tomatoes for UAH 200 (US$4.50) and peppers and carrots for UAH 75 (US$1.70) each.
"A neighbour brought courgettes to the hospital to give away for free," says a man whose acquaintances remain in Oleshky. "Someone he knew came up and asked: 'How much?' He said he was giving them away. The man burst into tears, thanked him and said that last time he had paid RUB 500, or US$6, for them. So even under blockade and hunger, there are people who profit from other people's misery." .
Some people take the risk and walk to the village of Radensk, 20 kilometres away, to get food. But such attempts are rare. The roads are mined, drones are hunting overhead, and a person on foot is easy to spot in open terrain. Even so, the walk takes around five hours, sometimes longer. One woman recently made the trip to Radensk for the first time. She told Ukrainska Pravda that prices there are lower and it is actually possible to buy some food. As well as shopping for herself, she bought supplies for loved ones she is helping to keep alive in Oleshky.
"I'm still coming to my senses after the trip to Radensk. I cycled there but walked back. I loaded myself up with almost 85 kilograms: a sack of grain, a carton of cigarettes for RUB 1,500 [US$18], 5kg of potatoes, onions, cabbage, peppers, pasta. I could barely carry it. I want to go again because it's not enough – and that was for three families.
That's how we survive. The main thing is not to get terrorised on the way," says an Olesky resident.
People who venture out to Radensk to look for food are stocking up for now or for late autumn. Selling anything is out of the question, because no one knows whether they will have another chance to leave. The Russians are also constantly hovering overhead with drones and can strike people at any moment.
All the roads leading out of Oleshky have turned into roads of death.
Volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova, who is originally from the city herself and still keeps in touch with people there, told UP that there have been many cases of Russian soldiers robbing people, attacking convoys carrying food to Oleshky and taking everything for themselves. Weapons are supplied to Russian forces, but food is not always available. So some local residents have even started writing on their gates or fences: "No food", "There is no food" or "Elderly people live here".
"If they [Russian soldiers] have to carry 20 kilograms of drones, ammunition or 20 kilograms of food, what are they going to carry? Obviously, the drones," she says. "Some soldiers spent 13 days getting to Oleshky during a rotation – travelling through fields and woods and along destroyed roads. So they may be sitting there hungry themselves, without food.
"People are robbed every day. An old woman I know had everything taken from her. She asked them: 'How am I supposed to survive the winter? What are you doing?' And they told her to shut up. They themselves admit that they do not care about people – they came to make money and that's it."
As winter approaches, the situation is only getting worse. Tetiana Hasanenko, Head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, told UP that it is not the case that some families have food while others do not. Everyone is going hungry.
"A few days ago, I heard for the first time that there are already cases of individual families eating dogs. A week ago, I was denying that such information was true, but now someone from there has confirmed it to me. There really is nothing to eat. The situation is not just getting worse by the day; it is getting worse by the hour.
And there is no chance of rescue. People have two options: either die of starvation or be caught by a drone or artillery strike and shot dead, because they will be killed. There is no third option. The chances of staying there without food and surviving are zero," Tetiana says.
Travelling to Radensk or other settlements to look for food will be impossible in winter. It is like playing Russian roulette: the ground will freeze and become covered with snow, while all the routes out of the city and the surrounding fields are littered with mines.
A hospital that no longer treats patients and a morgue overflowing with bodies
Until now, people in Oleshky who had run completely out of food and become too weak to carry on would go to the local hospital. The staff fed them whatever they could. However, volunteers say that even the hospital is running short of food. And even when food or fuel for the generator has somehow been delivered, there has been nothing left for other residents.
"The hospital has split into two camps," says the son of a man who has remained in Oleshky. Those who are loyal to the Russian regime have some food, and sometimes even meat and alcohol. But people who are called 'Ukraine supporters' have nothing. The hospital's senior supply manager has taken everything from the most recent deliveries that had been brought in as humanitarian aid and distributed it among his own people. He tells others that he has 200 people with disabilities and will give it to them first. But in reality, he sells everything: he gives petrol and food to whoever he wants. And people can see all of this."
However, even the hospital's continued operation is now in question. Civilian patients have already started being turned away. And, according to UP's sources, the hospital had been operating on a very limited basis even before this, so it would be simpler to say that it is effectively closed. There is nothing with which to provide even basic medical assistance – they can only stop bleeding. There are no medicines or antibiotics and no equipment. The generator is switched on once every few days because there is no petrol either.
"Things are really bad there," says Kseniia. It is running on its last legs. The hospital is asking local people to bring whatever porridge, grains or other food they have so they can at least give breakfast to bedridden patients, including those with amputations. It is the only place people can still go to spend the night because it is not being attacked. They can stay there and have some hot porridge if they manage to cook it while the generator is providing electricity. But the situation there is critical. And if the hospital stops working, it will be the end for Oleshky."
The hospital is the city's last stronghold. No other essential infrastructure – pharmacies or shops – is operating. Ambulances aren't operating either because some of Oleshky's streets are mined. If people are brought to the hospital at all, they are transported on a garden trolley. Many local residents have died of starvation or illness, been killed in military strikes or blown up by mines. Some were buried by relatives right in their yards or vegetable gardens, while others were simply left lying in the street.
"Usually, people who have suffered traumatic amputations or injuries are left lying there [in the street] until dogs eat them," says Tetiana. "Or they are simply covered with a piece of cloth. And they will lie there until worms eat the bodies."
The bodies of the dead were once kept in a morgue operating on the hospital grounds in Oleshky. Now, because the building has been damaged, the bodies have had to be moved to the basement of one of the hospital's other buildings, which is now overflowing with corpses. Some have been there for more than four months – since May.
"Everything is leaking and stinking in the hospital morgue," says Kseniia. The bodies in those black bags have decomposed. But why do they [Russian forces] say that no one is allowed to bury the bodies themselves? Because they want to take the bodies to Henichesk for forensic examination and produce a report saying that the Armed Forces of Ukraine are shooting people and attacking houses, and that people died from mine and blast injuries, artillery fire or drone strikes. Then they can pass all of this on to the UN. And of course, the forensic reports say whatever they need them to say. Although I am certain that they do not even open those bags containing the bodies."
A road of death, but also a road of life
There are no Ukrainian troops in Oleshky. They monitor the city from the right bank of the Dnipro River using drone cameras.
"The Russians are living in people's houses or trying to dig trenches on the outskirts and take up positions there," Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman from Ukraine's 34th Borysfen Separate Marine Brigade, told UP. "Their artillery is stationed a little further away. They have tried to move it closer, but the closer you move it to the riverbank, the further it can fire towards Kherson. And we are trying to keep the artillery away. We patrol constantly and try to cover the sky with drones so that we can monitor everything happening in Oleshky."
The Russians attack the city's main road with drones while simultaneously convincing people that it is Ukraine's defence forces who are preventing them from leaving and who have also mined the roads. Yevhen explains that remote mining does exist and that the Ukrainian Armed Forces do mine some routes to prevent Russian troops from receiving weapons supplies. However, they leave the main road clear so that people can get out. It is in the Russians' interests for civilians to remain in Oleshky because they use them as human shields.
"Their main objective is to prevent people from leaving the city. This allows the occupying forces to blend in with the local population. They change into civilian clothes, violating the Geneva Convention, and do not look like combatants. But we patrol the sky and have already worked out what each of them looks like," he adds.
There are times when Ukrainian defenders can hold back strikes on Oleshky to protect civilians, while Russian forces use the opportunity to launch active attacks towards Ukrainian positions.
Asked whether it is true that the Russians might have brought weapons in with some humanitarian aid during spring and summer 2026, the Ukrainian serviceman answered neither "yes" nor "no". He did, however, say that it would be "very logical". A vehicle supposedly carrying medicines, food or fuel into the city can disappear from Ukrainian drones' field of view for 10-15 minutes, and that is enough time to intimidate the driver and put "something" into the vehicle. Otherwise, it is difficult to explain where the Russians are getting ammunition and drones in a city that is completely cut off.
The Ukrainian serviceman says that the defence forces help local residents leave the city via the main road and sometimes use drones to guide people along a route that is safer, relatively speaking.
"There are not that many ways out of Oleshky," explains Voronetskyi. "And the central road can at least be monitored to some extent. So it is a road of death, but also a road of life. Of course, there are often aerial battles too, when the Russians try to shoot down our drone with theirs, and we use ours to shoot down theirs. And all of this happens at a height of 1.5 - 2 metres above the ground when you are using a drone to guide people. We want as many people as possible to leave the city. If there were no civilians there, it would be much easier for us to operate."
Is there a way out of occupied Oleshky?
The only way out for people in occupied Oleshky and the surrounding villages is evacuation to territory controlled by Ukraine. But as of now, there are no signs that Russia is prepared to give up using civilians as a human shield against the Ukrainian Armed Forces and allow people to leave through a humanitarian corridor. Of course, Russian propaganda doesn't miss the opportunity to claim that Kyiv is to blame for people starving in the Russian-occupied town and that "provocations" by the defence forces would be possible during any evacuation.
Russian sources cover the humanitarian catastrophe in Oleshky selectively and through a political lens. They reduce everything to two claims: that local residents are suffering because of Ukraine's actions, while the occupation administration (which in fact has not been there since 2023, having fled after the flooding caused by the destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant) is providing aid, medical care and basic governance. Meanwhile, attention is directed away from the fact of the occupation and its consequences, and towards the image of Russia as the country which is "saving" people.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukraine had reached agreements with the Russian side, while the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was supposed to assist with the evacuation of people from the grey zone. The list of local residents, as well as arrangements for the defence forces to maintain a ceasefire, had been agreed. However, as of 22 September, Russia has still not confirmed its readiness to allow the evacuation.
Lubinets said he is preparing renewed letters to the ICRC, the UN and Ukraine's partners, as the situation in Oleshky is critical.
"I do not want to create false expectations among people or give specific timeframes [for when the evacuation might take place] until Russia confirms its readiness for a humanitarian mission," the commissioner said. "But we are using every available mechanism to secure the evacuation of civilians who have effectively found themselves trapped."
He added that his office, together with the defence forces, is currently trying to provide local residents with food and humanitarian aid.
The ICRC confirmed to Ukrainska Pravda that it is maintaining contact with the Ukrainian and Russian authorities regarding Oleshky. The Committee is ready to provide support for an evacuation as soon as it is safe for people to do so.
Locals do not believe a humanitarian corridor will be established. In more than four years, there has not been a single official evacuation of civilians from Oleshky. Not after the destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, when homes remained flooded, nor now, when the city has found itself on the brink of starvation.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer with the NGO Humanity, told UP that the most practical and safest option could be an agreed evacuation across the Dnipro towards Kherson. This would make the process quicker, while avoiding the need to travel through occupied territories and Russia. The Red Cross could provide security for the humanitarian corridor.
"The fact that the evacuation is not being carried out across the Dnipro is a very big mistake. I see that this is not even being communicated [by the Ukrainian authorities]. We actually have people from Oleshky who are afraid of filtration and of travelling through Russia for several days. Buses would be able to evacuate a maximum of 300 people. And this is a good initiative. But there are many more people than that," Vorontsov says.
No one crosses the Dnipro independently as the front line runs along the river, with sabotage and reconnaissance groups and military personnel operating there, making it extremely dangerous in general. Fighting for the river islands between Kherson and Oleshky is still ongoing.
But the fact remains that some people did manage to escape the city through mined fields. They were driven by the thought: "I would rather die on the road than die of hunger," and would make their way on foot, one or two at a time, from Oleshky towards Radensk or Hola Prystan. From there, they could take a taxi to Nova Kakhovka or Skadovsk. After that, everyone went their own way.
For those who are only now hearing about the situation in Oleshky, one question naturally arises: why did the locals not leave earlier? The answer is that escaping the occupation is not easy, and people are facing several problems at once.
The first is that some locals do not have their documents because they were burned or destroyed by the flooding after the destruction of the Kakhovka hydroelectric power plant. To leave the occupied territory, a Russian ID is generally required, and not everyone has one. To obtain one, people need proof of identity or Ukrainian documents. But people in the occupied territory cannot obtain these from the state or Ukrainian authorities. Relatives or acquaintances have approached government institutions asking for copies or electronic versions of Oleshky residents' Ukrainian IDs but have never received them.
The second problem is the local people, particularly older residents, who do not want to leave their homes.
"'I built this house and I am not going anywhere' is the statement of a person who genuinely has nowhere to go," says a volunteer who helps people from the occupied territories. "Ukraine has nothing to offer them. It is not as though an elderly woman arrives, volunteers take her by the hand, give her an address and tell her to go to such-and-such a village where there is a house. They arrange her pension and provide her with assistance as an internally displaced person. Nothing like that exists – there is no help, no houses. People leave and think: 'What do we do next? Where are we going to go?'"
The third problem is that some men of conscription age are afraid that the Russians will pull them out of their cars at checkpoints and either take them to a basement or send them to fight for Russia in the so-called "special military operation".
Many locals also hoped that after the successful counteroffensive and the liberation of Kherson from Russian occupation in November 2022, the Ukrainian Armed Forces would enter Oleshky in the same triumphant fashion. The same mood persisted at the beginning of 2023, as people believed that the military would cross the Dnipro.
A year or two later, some had already begun to feel guilty for waiting and remaining under occupation. Then the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant's floodwaters washed away some of the locals' hopes and plans, along with all their documents and belongings. Without documents, they became hostages of their own city.
Ester Vratarova, a volunteer with the NGO Humanity, explained to Ukrainska Pravda why people had not left Oleshky, saying that it was extremely difficult to do so, while Russian propaganda was spreading the idea that people simply did not want to leave.
"Leaving an occupied territory is difficult – it is not an easy walk in the park. And not everyone has access to information as it is spread mostly by word of mouth. There have been no organised state evacuations, and there still are none. So blaming people who were literally taken hostage, turned into a human shield and had their territory turned into a ghetto is completely immoral. And we must do everything we can to prevent this idea from spreading," Vratarova stresses.
A winter that people in Oleshky may not survive
There are still surviving houses in Oleshky, as well as parts of apartment blocks where some floors and basements remain intact. It is possible to find a roof over your head, but living under it is not always safe.
Last winter, three elderly women and a man froze to death in their flats, volunteers say. And these are only the cases they know about. It is impossible to count how many quiet deaths occur in Oleshky.
Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, responsibility for the population of an occupied territory lies with the occupying power. It is required to provide people with food, medical care and proper sanitary conditions. But the Russians have no regard for any international requirements. It is pointless to expect them to provide people in Oleshky with food.
"Russia is responsible for this territory," says Kseniia Arkhipova. "And if people remain there, they are doomed. Truly doomed to die. So while there is still an opportunity, they need to leave Oleshky on foot in one direction."
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha raised the humanitarian catastrophe in Oleshky as a separate issue at the 21-26 September UN General Assembly session. Meanwhile, as world leaders listen and discuss the issue from the rostrum, people in the small town on the bank of the Dnipro are facing one of the most difficult choices of their lives – try to get out or stay. And in either case, deadly danger hangs over them.
Natalia Bodnar, Anastasiia Zazuliak, Ukrainska Pravda

Lufthansa flight diverted after powerbank explosion
A Lufthansa passenger airplane flying was diverted after a passenger's powerbank caught fire on board, the airline said.
The aircraft was flying from Frankfurt to Lisbon and was ultimately diverted to the French city of Lyon, where it landed safely at around 10 p.m. (20:00 UTC) on Saturday evening, the German flag carrier said.
The 198 passengers and six crew members on board the flight were put up in hotels for the night and rebooked onto alternative connections to Lisbon the following day.
Travelers often carry powerbanks to charge their smartphones, in the event that no power outlet is available. But using powerbanks has been banned on Lufthansa Group flights since the beginning of 2026. The airline made an exception for the use of approved medical devices.
Lufthansa does not allow the powerbanks to be stored in overhead compartments, only in the front seat pocket, on the passenger's person or in hand luggage stored under the seat.
The crew on the Lisbon-bound flight were able to secure the powerbank in a designated lithium safe bag until landing.

Merz's conservatives no longer a big tent 'people's party'?
Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, continues its soul-searching after its terrible results in recent regional elections.
While the party is generally considered to be more pro-business, it does have a workers' and employees’ wing and that part of the party is now warning the wider CDU that it is no longer a true Volkspartei, literally a "people’s party" or a big tent party.
Germany has two parties that traditionally have been considered a Volkspartei: CDU on the center-right and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) on the center-left.
One of the two parties used to reliably get the biggest share of the vote, but that was not the case in elections in three German states this month.
The SPD has fallen further from its heyday, often coming only third or fourth in the polls. The poor showing of the CDU in recent elections in Saxony-Anhalt and especially Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania suggests the CDU is on a similar trajectory. Instead, it’s the far right and the far left that are gaining voters.
In a new appeal, the CDU's employees' wing argues that too many people no longer feel represented by the party — and that the party risks becoming a political bubble talking mainly to itself.
The group says it wants the CDU to become more representative, not just in its rhetoric but in who actually gets involved and ends up in parliament. That means more people from different backgrounds and professions — from industry and skilled trades to healthcare, education and small businesses.
The group’s leadership also took aim at Chancellor Merz directly, saying that he had promised years ago to broaden the party’s appeal, but failed to do so.
How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy
Would you think that espionage could significantly boost a country's economy? In the case of communist East Germany, that seems to have been the case — and to a significant degree.
According to Reuters news agency, a study by the Rockwool Foundation suggests that espionage boosted East Germany's GDP by a whopping 7.4% in the 1970s and 80s.
How, you ask? Well, the notorious Stasi stole scientific and technical information from companies in the West, handed it to companies in the East and helped them increase productivity and growth.
"Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany's position within the socialist bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in Western markets."
The authors stressed that the East Germany case offers crucial insights for today, as countries again seek to protect strategic technologies, tighten export controls and screen foreign investment in sensitive industries.

Germans grow more conscious about (not) eating meat
Germany is famous for its variety of sausages and meats. But things seem to be changing somewhat and more people are eating less of some forms of meat — even if they're far from giving it up entirely.
A study in connection with World Vegetarian Day (on October 1) found 93% of households purchase meat. And the overall amount of meat bought hasn't actually gone down. That's only the case for sausages: Fewer people buy them and their overall sales have dropped.
According to the authors of the study, the data suggest that people are not necessarily moving toward vegetarianism or veganism. Instead, many are becoming more conscious about their diet and are trying to reduce their meat consumption without giving it up completely.
Around 43% of meat-eaters do concede that it would be better for them to eat less meat, and 27% say they do hope to buy less in the future. The favorite meat is chicken, followed by pork.
Meat substitutes are also becoming more popular with around 35% of households buying them.

Polish MP calls for immigration crackdown after Ukrainian kills priest
Poland should tighten its border controls following a deadly knife attack by a Ukrainian national, former Polish Deputy Prime Minister and current Law and Justice (PiS) MP Henryk Kowalczyk has said, warning that the killing could fuel another wave of anti-Ukrainian sentiment.
A 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen attacked five people at a Catholic abbey in the southeastern city of Jaroslaw on Thursday, killing a priest and injuring four others, according to Polish officials. The suspect, who according to investigators had entered Poland from Germany overnight and was apparently heading toward the Ukrainian border, was detained at the scene. “This will certainly trigger another wave of hostility toward Ukrainians,” Henryk Kowalczyk, an MP with the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, told Polish Radio’s Jedynka on Friday.

“We do not control the German-Polish border at all,” he said, contrasting Warsaw’s approach with Berlin’s selective checks. Poland “cannot accept all migrants who ended up in Germany and then enter our country,” he argued.
The MP also said that punishing the attacker was not enough, urging the Polish authorities to draw broader conclusions from the deadly incident.
“This is a signal that we should check people in advance, rather than just say that we will punish them severely,” he said.

Relations between Warsaw and Kiev have also been strained by historical grievances. Tensions escalated after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky named a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which Poland holds responsible for massacres of Polish civilians during World War II.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor, citing the decision to honor the UPA.

Türkiye launches national AI platform EVREN to bolster defence industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:29:55 UTC
19:29:55 KST

Türkiye has launched its national artificial intelligence platform EVREN, aimed at strengthening the country's defence industry.
EVREN serves a broad range of users, from defence industry firms and technology companies to academics, entrepreneurs and students, bringing data, AI models and high-performance computing power together on a single platform, according to a statement from the Presidency of Defence Industries on Sunday.
Prompt, response and usage data on the platform are processed on high-performance GPU infrastructure located in Türkiye, preventing sensitive data from being transferred to cloud services abroad.
It can be accessed at evren.ssyz.org.tr using e-Government authentication.
Contribute, earn credits, use GPU power
EVREN operates through a contribution-based credit model rather than direct paid access.
Users can earn credits by uploading datasets, labeling data or sharing their trained models.
The credits can be used for model training and large language model (LLM) inference operations through the platform's high-performance GPU pool.
The system aims to make users active participants who contribute to the development of the EVREN ecosystem rather than merely receiving services.
Access to 11 open-weight large language models
EVREN offers end-to-end data labeling and model training capabilities for computer vision tasks such as object detection, segmentation and classification.
An inference layer covering 11 open-weight large language models has also been activated on the platform.
Existing applications can connect to EVREN's infrastructure through its API architecture, real-time response support and automatic model routing features.
To encourage broader use of the infrastructure, API calls made through Nov. 1, 2026, will be offered without limits and without deductions from users' credit balances.
Platform reaches 7,500 active users 
EVREN has reached 7,500 active users in a short period and is intended to contribute to the development of Türkiye's AI ecosystem and efforts under the Artificial Intelligence Action Plan.
The platform will be further developed with domestically developed large language, image and audio models, while its computing infrastructure will be strengthened through a distributed GPU management approach.

'A theft from citizens': Spain hits 1,000 days without a new budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:29:02 UTC
19:29:02 KST

The Spanish Ministry of Finance insists that a budget will soon be put forward for 2027. "We are confident it will be approved and we are not contemplating any other scenario," sources told Euronews.
Spain has today reached the symbolic milestone of 1,000 days without a new national budget, the main tool for steering the country’s economic policy and setting priorities for public spending.
The left-wing coalition government led by Pedro Sánchez, made up of PSOE and Sumar, has gone the entire legislative term without passing a single budget. Instead, it has been governing with the budget approved in 2022 for the 2023 financial year.
That year, after Sánchez returned as prime minister - without a parliamentary majority - the government argued that the 2023 election results had made it difficult to bring a new budget bill before the Congress of Deputies.
Despite repeated promises from both the prime minister and the former finance minister, María Jesús Montero, no budget was presented in 2024 or 2025. In June this year, Sánchez also ruled out Spain having a new budget in 2026.
While in opposition, Sánchez himself told then-prime minister Mariano Rajoy of the centre-right party Partido Popular that "to govern without a budget is not to govern at all."
Article 134.3 of the Spanish Constitution stipulates that the government must submit the national budget to Congress at least three months before the previous year’s version expires. It also allows the previous budget to be extended if a new one is not approved - a provision the government has relied on due to the difficulty of securing enough parliamentary support to pass a new one.
César García Novoa, professor of financial and tax law at the University of Santiago de Compostela, argued that this was a distortion of the rule.
"The regulation, without spelling it out, is designed for an extension of one year at most; it is an emergency mechanism," he said.
García Novoa added that budget extensions exist in other European countries, "but they are always tied to short-term, exceptional situations, such as Belgium’s government crisis."
Fernando Navarrete, a Popular Party MEP and member of the European Parliament’s budget committee, shares García Novoa’s view: "Until Sánchez, the understanding was that the extension lasts for one year. If after that there is still no majority to approve a budget, you have to call elections."
Navarrete described the 1,000 days without a new budget as a democratic anomaly. He added that if his party governed after the elections due next year, it would change the law to prevent such an issue from happening again.
Navarrete also argued that going so long without a new budged amounted to "a theft from citizens, who have not been able to decide through their representatives how much public money is spent and on what."
Government hits back
Spain’s Ministry of Finance disagrees, however.
In comments to Euronews, officials insisted that the government has "approved measures to protect citizens from the crisis stemming from the conflict in Ukraine or in the Middle East due to the rise in energy prices."
On access to housing - currently the main concern for Spaniards, according to Spain's Centre for Sociological Research - ministry sources point to the €7 billion earmarked in the State Housing Plan for the period 2026-2030.
Without a new budget, and as the housing plan was not included in the 2023 budget, the government has to resort to extraordinary channels to finance it.
This is what Navarrete means when he criticises the government for using emergency mechanisms "designed for other situations," adding that not having a new budget prevented Spain from "responding to global disruptions."
Brussels
García Novoa argued that just continuing with the extended 2023 budget "limits Spain’s ability to set out the reforms required by the European Union" and weakens the country’s credibility in Brussels.
Under its fiscal rules, the European Union has required member states since 2024 to present a medium-term plan that guarantees sustainable public finances and promotes investment and reforms.
Spain has such a plan, but without a new budget "we cannot show how we are going to fulfil it", Navarrete said. "The European Commission relies on its own economic forecasts to supervise us."
He added that although Brussels was concerned about Spain not having approved budgets for 2024, 2025, and 2026, there has been no particularly strong reaction as it is seen as an internal political problem.
"It is a mistake and I do not understand their stance, because Spain is breaching its European commitments, overspending on public money and passing the hot potato to the next government," Navarrete told Euronews.
Elections on the horizon?
The Spanish Ministry of Finance insists that a budget will soon be put forward for 2027.
"We are confident it will be approved and we are not contemplating any other scenario," sources told Euronews.
Although it is unlikely that the government will submit a 2027 budget before 30 September, the latest date on which it should do so under the Constitution, it has already opened talks with several political parties to negotiate its approval.
"The extension of the current budget has not prevented Spain from growing above the EU average or from achieving record employment. The new budget must consolidate this trend and strengthen the welfare state," the ministry's sources told Euronews.
However, some, including Navarrete, view the move as a possible pretext for calling a general election if parliament rejects the new budget.
"I do not believe they will present it because they do not have a majority, but if they do, it will be to use it as electoral propaganda with the help of the ministries. Yet another abusive use of Spanish taxpayers’ money," Navarrete said.

Impoverished, Hakim’s family is in disarray. With its debts mounting and its members facing another eviction, he said he has considered taking his life several times over the past year and a half.
Mar’i cannot afford treatment for his debilitating leg injury, which has developed severe infections. He said he sustained it while working as a labourer inside Israel in 2019. The wound worsened after Israeli soldiers severely beat him when they forced his family from the Tulkarem camp. Diabetes and other untreated conditions have piled on, but he is unable to pay for the needed medical care.
“This joint here is completely gone,” he said, gesturing at the swollen, blackened lower leg that prevents him from working.
“The medicine – by God, the medicine, I haven’t been able to get. My wife and kids tell me: get out travel. Go to America, Turkey – so I can the medical treatment I need… I’m a sick man.”
His mother, Salwa, sat beside him, less than a kilometre (0.6 miles) from their former four-storey home. She wept when asked about the family home that was built floor by floor after they were first displaced in 1948 from al-Khudayra, the Arabic name for Hadera, a city in Israel. “We really put a lot into that house,” she said.
After their removal, the Israeli military razed the Mar’i home so a road traversing the now-emptied camp could be built. “Seeing it destroyed was really painful for us – all of us,” she said.
It has been more than 20 months since Israeli forces emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps in a sweeping military operation in the northern West Bank, displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians whose families had already been refugees for three generations. Constantly renewed orders for a closed military zone now prevent their return.
Since January 2025, Hakim’s family has been forced to move four times. First, they fled to a converted youth centre before landing in a cramped apartment with their four children, all under 15.
Unable to pay rent, the family could see the landlord’s generosity run its course as this once-temporary housing arrangement now has no end in sight. Hakim owes money at the local shops for food he bought on credit. Some nights, the children eat at neighbours’ houses.
“I have children. I have food. I have drink,” he said. “My hands are empty. Nobody is with me. Nobody is standing beside me.”
‘We’re already at the brink’
The Mar’i family is among more than 33,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem camps by Israeli forces in early 2025. This is the largest single episode of forced displacement in the West Bank since Israel’s occupation began in 1967, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).
UN satellite imagery shows that 20 percent of all buildings across the three camps have been destroyed and another 28 percent are damaged.
“The level of destruction we are seeing is severe and unprecedented,” said Roland Friedrich, director of West Bank affairs for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
According to Friedrich, 85 percent of those displaced have no regular income after many lost jobs when the camps were emptied. More than 80 percent of residents are renting, an unfamiliar expense for families who never paid for housing or utilities inside the camps.
The closed military zone covering the camps is renewed every two months, Friedrich said, with no indication of when – or whether – residents will be allowed to return. “What we saw there is forced displacement,” Friedrich said. “The UN’s position is very clear: People have to be allowed to return. The camps must be rebuilt.”
Unlike after the 2000-2005 second Intifada when the Jenin camp was rebuilt, displaced families and UNRWA staff fear there is no return plan this time.
The Israeli military stated the camps were emptied for “operational security” in its effort to root out fighters from the camps. Friedrich worried the aim of the military operations is to “change the geographical expression of the Palestinian refugee issue”.
Now more than 20 months into what was meant to be an emergency response, funding shortages have left UNRWA unable to cover the vast needs of the displaced population. It has moved some operations to keep schools and basic health clinics functioning. With funds dwindling, the agency has shifted to a “targeted approach”, leaving thousands without support.
Friedrich pointed to a rise in gender-based violence linked to the economic strain on families and to growing depression and anxiety among displaced children observed by UNRWA’s psychosocial teams. “We’re already at the brink now,” he declared.
‘Everyone went their own way’
While Hakim’s displacement plays out in the shadow of the camp, the family of Khadija Zbeidat face their own imminent eviction on the outskirts of Tulkarem. They live in the neighbourhood of Dhinnaba, where sparse houses are interspersed with greenhouses. They are unable to afford a residence closer to the city centre.
As Khadija sat on a couch in the middle of the yard, her many children and grandchildren ran past a small patch of plants she has planted – one of her few remaining joys. “I love plants,” she said. “We had many flowers in our home in the camp. Having the plants here is all I have to feel like myself,” she told Al Jazeera.
Khadija, a widow, shares a tiny spartan room with nine family members, nearly all children, along with a small bathroom and a kitchen barely big enough for one person to cook in. A worn couch takes up one corner. The ceiling is peeling above it.
The room was given to them rent free by a relative of Khadija’s brother-in-law after they spent four months crammed into her daughter’s house with nine other people. “It got really cramped, the pressure on each other,” Zbeidat said. “And we became a burden too.”
Khadija’s family was displaced in January 2025 from the Tulkarem camp’s Haret al-Nadi section, a significant part of which has been destroyed, she said.
“The camp was excellent,” she said of their life before. “I swear, I wish they’d take us back. Everything was close to us, dear – … the closeness, that sense of belonging and the warmth, the company and the neighbours.”
The memories that she cherishes most dearly and that bring her to tears are of food: the stuffed grape leaves and the maamoul cookies made as a neighbourhood together for Eid. This year, there was none of it.
“Nothing. No cookies,” she said. “Nobody even had it in them to do anything any more. Everyone went their own way – scattered.”
Like the Mar’i family and others, they were not allowed to bring their belongings during their abrupt displacement. Some residents have since been allowed to retrieve belongings once or twice from their homes in the camps, but much of what they own remains left behind. Khadija’s daughter-in-law at one point returned to the ruins of the camp – at the risk of being shot – to retrieve a doll left behind that Khadija’s granddaughter Sandy would not stop crying about.
In Tulkarem, displaced families live either in the poorest areas closest to the camp, like the Mar’is, or on the cheaper outskirts, like the Zbeidats, remaining close enough to the health and schooling services that UNRWA still provides. But even a simple trip to buy groceries requires Khadija, who has no car, to travel 2km (1.2 miles).
At night, the family sits outside rather than in the stifling heat of the poorly ventilated room, watching Israeli military drones pass low overhead. “What to do? We’re used to seeing them, to having them around, to them raiding houses,” Khadija said. “It doesn’t matter any more.”
The military raids that always haunted life in the refugee camps have now come to wherever the displaced refugees have fled to. “We don’t feel safe,” Khadija said. “Nor the kids. It’s dangerous. When they want to go out somewhere, my heart stays busy until they come back.”
Waiting to be kicked out again
For months after the displacement, landlords, relatives and shopkeepers absorbed much of the shock, allowing families to stay for free or buy food on credit. But as the emergency stretches to almost two years now, that informal safety net is fraying. The pressure is felt particularly in economically moribund Tulkarem, where many families had relied on jobs inside Israel before Palestinian work permits were revoked after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023.
The owner of the property where Khadija’s family is staying recently sent his sister to tell Khadija’s family to leave. “They think it’s been too long,” Khadija explained. “They want the land, to benefit from the land and the room. … But where can we get money, where to pay from? The rent is very high, and we can’t afford it. We don’t know what to do if she comes again and kicks us out.”
Hakim’s family is on the brink of eviction too. Like others, he received from UNRWA a one-time rental subsidy of 3,000 shekels ($985) and a separate 1,700-shekel ($560) multipurpose cash payment for short-term assistance. “Every minute, I am waiting for the landlord to kick us out,” he said.
Khadija’s family survives on credit from shopkeepers who know their situation and, for now, still extend it – but patience is wearing thin.
Hakim said this goodwill is collapsing: “You tell them: ‘Give me a day, two days. Be patient with me.’ They won’t bear it.”
As distant as a return to her family’s lands in 1948 feels now, Khadija still hopes to return to the camp one day. But she worries that her children may inherit an even more precarious existence than the one that preceded this latest dispossession – refugees for generations displaced yet again. “Only God knows what tomorrow will bring us,” Khadija said.
If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, these organisations may be able to help.

Lithuania warns of evacuation challenges in event of Russian attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:26:00 EEST
19:26:00 KST

Lithuania warns of evacuation challenges in event of Russian attack
Civil defence officials from Lithuanian municipalities bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast have warned of potential problems with evacuating residents in the event of a Russian attack.
Source: Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT
Details: Evacuation could be particularly difficult in the Dieveniškės Loop area on the border with Belarus. Pavel Goj, an emergency readiness official in Šalčininkai District Municipality, said the municipality had an approved evacuation plan and that the routes had been coordinated with the Armed Forces' military commandant's office.
Goj said the main road would likely be blocked, so alternative routes rather than main roads would be used where possible.
He added that the municipality's ability to evacuate residents would also depend on how much time was available. If everyone had to be evacuated within 24 hours, the transport currently available would not be sufficient.
Goj said that if the evacuation had to be completed within a single day, the available resources would not be enough, but he believed residents could be evacuated if the municipality had two or three days.
In his view, traffic management and transport could pose the greatest challenges during a mass evacuation.
Meanwhile, Valdas Tamulevičius, the official responsible for emergency readiness in Varėna District, which borders Belarus, said the evacuation of residents with special needs was the greatest concern.
He said those able to leave independently would do so using their own vehicles, while the municipal administration would arrange transport for everyone else.
Tamulevičius said the biggest challenge would be evacuating residents with special needs, such as bedridden patients, as they would require ambulances. He noted that there would not be enough ambulances to evacuate all such residents within the planned three-day period.
Municipalities bordering Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast have also highlighted problems involving transport and communications.
The Jurbarkas District Municipality administration said that a mass evacuation could require around a quarter of the district's population – approximately 5,000-5,700 people – to be evacuated, while the administration's existing resources would allow it to evacuate only around 5,000 citizens.
The municipal administration said the main challenges would be mobilising specialised transport for bedridden patients and keeping residents informed amid possible communications disruptions.
Pagėgiai Municipality has also identified transport capacity, maintaining communications and managing large flows of people as the main challenges. Exercises are currently being used to test arrangements for evacuating its residents to Telšiai District.
Vilkaviškis District Municipality described a somewhat different situation. Robertas Fišeris, its emergency readiness official, said the railway running through the district could also be used to evacuate residents.
Fišeris said the municipality was in a favourable position because it had a railway, which helped address the transport issue. He added that funding issues had been resolved through various projects and that the main task now was to continue training and preparing.
Background:
- As reported, Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international population evacuation plan that would be used if some residents of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia needed to be evacuated across the border.
- This week, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Lithuania had prepared evacuation plans in response to the growing threat from Russia. He clarified that he was referring to plans for evacuating cities, including Vilnius.
- On 25 September, Lithuania launched its largest annual national mobilisation exercise, Vyčio Skliautas 2026 (Vytis Vault 2026), aimed at testing how the country would respond to a deteriorating security situation and transition to a wartime mobilisation regime.

Discount store sparks revolution on Sylt, reshaping the island of the rich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:22:12 UTC
19:22:12 KST

The German island Sylt has long battled acute housing shortages and locals being pushed out. Now, of all things, a discount chain offers a remedy: Lidl is building a completely new housing complex in Tinnum.
Living above a discount supermarket on the otherwise exclusive North Sea island beloved of high earners: how this new Lidl is set to completely transform the world-famous luxury holiday destination of Sylt, with its dunes and thatched-roof houses.
On Sylt, the traditional shopping experience is being completely reimagined. On a 16,000-square-metre site, Lidl is combining a state-of-the-art store on the ground floor with 15 new flats directly above. The homes, between 44 and 78 square metres in size, are explicitly designed for permanent residence. For the island this is a genuine breakthrough, intended above all to provide commuters with affordable housing close to their workplace. Mayor Tina Haltermann is full of praise, describing it as a pioneering step that shows how modern retail and residential space can be combined while using as little land as possible.
The old building becomes a new XXL hub for everyday needs
Anyone who assumes that the old structure has simply been torn down to make way for the new build is wrong. The existing Lidl building is being retained and recycled. It will be merged with the new complex to create a vibrant local services centre. The plans are already on the table: a pharmacy, a health and beauty store and regional businesses will move into the existing areas. This will establish a new, central point of contact for the people of Sylt and their visitors.
Eco milestone: a supermarket made entirely of wood
Lidl is using a resource-efficient hybrid timber construction method, partial greening of the façade and roof, and radical material recycling. Outside, processed concrete is reused as paving; inside, secondary plastics and recycled glass and aluminium are employed.
In energy terms, the complex is designed to be completely self-sufficient. A large photovoltaic installation on the roof provides green electricity, while waste heat from product refrigeration is captured via cutting-edge ventilation systems and heat pumps to heat and cool the building.
XXL shopping comfort and high-speed charging stations
For customers, the new development means an upgrade in every respect. The 1,600-square-metre sales floor offers extra-wide aisles and a completely new style of product presentation. With 184 parking spaces, shopping remains as relaxed as possible. A particular highlight for electric car owners: three ultra-modern charging columns with six charging points are being installed on site, delivering ultra-fast DC power between 60 and 180 kilowatts to charge vehicles.

Energy, shipping, and ending the war — Budanov spoke about preparations for the trilateral talks in October
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is planning a meeting with the United States and Russia in October. They will discuss ending the war, strikes on energy infrastructure, and shipping security.
Ukraine plans to hold a trilateral meeting with the United States and Russia next month. The issues expected to be discussed include a possible end to the war, reducing strikes on energy infrastructure, and the safety of shipping, Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov said in a comment to Novyny.LIVE, as reported by UNN.
According to Budanov, the Ukrainian side is preparing for a meeting at which a number of security and technical issues are to be considered.
"First, we are planning such a meeting. Second, reducing strikes on the energy sector. Well, terrorism is abnormal in principle. Security, shipping, and so on. We have many technical issues," the Head of the Office of the President said.
He named next month—October—as the tentative timeframe for the talks. At the same time, Budanov did not specify the exact date, location of the meeting, or composition of the delegations.
The Head of the Office of the President had previously also spoken about preparations for the October round of talks. In particular, on September 12, on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum in Kyiv, he confirmed to the media that Ukraine was preparing for talks in October in a trilateral format. At the time, he did not comment on a potential location for the meeting.
The United States proposed a technical meeting in the UAE
On September 25, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the American side had proposed preparing a meeting of representatives of Ukraine, the United States, and Russia at the technical level. Washington proposed the United Arab Emirates as a possible venue. At the time of the statement, Kyiv was awaiting proposals from the United States regarding the date. According to the president, the Ukrainian and American negotiating groups had also agreed to hold consultations with the European side. After that, the United States was to establish contacts with Russia, and approximately ten days later the parties planned to return to discussing the results. This timeframe concerned the consultations, not an announced date for trilateral talks.
That same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the possibility of such a meeting had been discussed during a phone call between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. He allowed for it to take place in the near future, but did not provide any specific parameters.
What is being discussed regarding energy and shipping
The issue of a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure had already been raised during diplomatic contacts in September.
On September 14, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to support de-escalation if its American partners could ensure Russia's genuine and long-term readiness to stop the strikes. This position was voiced after Trump's statement that the parties had allegedly reached an agreement not to attack energy facilities. At the same time, as Reuters reported, neither Ukraine nor Russia confirmed that such an agreement had been concluded at the time.
A separate area is the safety of maritime transport. On September 23, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to do its part to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea, provided that Russia took genuine steps toward de-escalation.
According to the president, Egypt, India, and Turkey proposed their own options for ensuring maritime security. Ukraine supported measures capable of ensuring safe shipping and was awaiting a response from the Russian side.
Context
On September 6, American representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in Kyiv after visiting Moscow. Following the meeting, the president confirmed Ukraine's readiness for trilateral talks. The parties also discussed the supply of air defense systems and support for Ukraine's energy sector ahead of winter.
We remind you
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was looking for excuses not to meet and not to end the war.
