News
Researchers have found that evening temperatures have risen by 9.5 degrees Celsius
Night-time temperatures in Bulgaria rise sharply over the past 20 years
The cities Sofia, Pleven and Blagoevgrad are experiencing the most pronounced warming
Sunday 27 September 2026 10:45
Sunday, 27 September 2026, 10:45
PHOTO BTA
Font size
A climate change study by the GATE Institute for Big Data and Artificial Intelligence at Sofia University has attracted considerable public attention in Bulgaria. Examining temperature ranges in eight Bulgarian cities over the past two decades, researchers found that evening temperatures have risen by 9.5 degrees Celsius during this period.
The three cities experiencing the most pronounced warming are Pleven, Sofia and Blagoevgrad. The smallest temperature increase over the past 20 years has been recorded in Sliven, Varna and Burgas.
According to GATE researchers, Bulgaria’s transition from a temperate to a tropical climate has now begun irreversibly. The four factors that contribute to heat stress in humans - temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation -  have reached extreme levels in recent years.
Prolonged periods of warming are also affecting patterns of illness and human immunity. Respiratory infections, for example, are becoming more frequent, while the psychological burden on people is also increasing.
PHOTO BGNES
The question of how to tackle extreme heat has already been placed on the agenda by a number of municipalities. In Sofia, a strategy to mitigate heat stress is being prepared, focusing on additional greenery, light-coloured surfaces and the creation of heat shelters.
The Association of Southwestern Municipalities in Bulgaria has mapped heat islands in the municipality of Blagoevgrad and is currently developing a heatwave action plan that could also be adopted by other municipalities.

Syrian Fly Dar Airlines becomes first to receive air operator certification since fall of Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:32:28 UTC
18:32:28 KST

DAMASCUS Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport has granted Fly Dar Airlines an Air Operator Certificate, making it the first Syrian private airline to receive the certification since the fall of Bashar Assad’s government in December 2024.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The move is part of Damascus’ efforts to rebuild its aviation sector and open the industry to greater private investment.
The certificate was presented on Thursday, September 24, during a ceremony at the authority’s headquarters in Damascus. The event was attended by Omar al-Hosari, head of the Civil Aviation Authority, and Abdul Hamid al-Awak, speaker of the Syrian People’s Assembly.
Capt. Mohsen al-Sallal, Fly Dar’s general manager and chairman, received the certificate on behalf of the company, which will establish its main operating base at Damascus International Airport.
Al-Hosari said the certificate was issued after the airline completed the required regulatory, technical, and operational procedures, allowing it to move toward commercial operations in accordance with Syria’s civil aviation regulations and applicable standards.
He described the certification as more than just licensing a new airline, saying it is part of a broader effort to reorganize Syria’s aviation market, expand private-sector participation, encourage domestic investment, and promote competition among carriers.
Fly-Dar completed certification process, Civil Aviation Authority says
According to al-Hosari, Fly Dar completed a five-stage certification process that took approximately six months.
With its certification, Fly Dar becomes Syria’s third national air operator, joining the state-owned Syrian Airlines and the privately owned Fly Cham.
The company plans to operate flights beyond Damascus International Airport. Al-Sallal said its proposed network includes connections between several Syrian cities and airports, including Aleppo, Latakia, Deir ez-Zor, and Qamishli.
Fly Dar has yet to announce a specific date for the launch of scheduled commercial flights or provide details about its fleet and initial destinations. Its next challenge will be turning regulatory approval into actual operations.
The certification comes as Syrian authorities work to rehabilitate airports, modernize air navigation systems, and expand international flight connections following years of war and isolation that severely affected the country’s aviation infrastructure.
Syrian Civil Aviation Authority announces expansion to Syrian Airlines
Earlier in September, the Civil Aviation Authority announced an expansion of Syrian Airlines’ international network to include direct flights from Damascus to Copenhagen and Vienna. The initiative is part of efforts to reconnect Syria with European cities and reduce travelers’ reliance on connecting flights through other countries.
Damascus is also holding discussions with international aircraft leasing and financing companies as it seeks to support the aviation industry's recovery.
Meanwhile, Flynas Syria, a Syrian-Saudi joint venture announced in February, is preparing to begin operations during the final quarter of 2026, according to the timetable announced when the partnership agreement was signed.

'Israel stopped caring': Irish columnist contrasts teams ahead of contentious soccer match
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:31:46 UTC
18:31:46 KST

Ireland's discomfort ahead of its match against Israel stems from the knowledge that it has compromised its position, while Israel "stopped caring about that a long time ago," Irish Times columnist Ken Early wrote on Saturday.
In a sharply worded column, Early argued that Ireland simply wants to get through its matches against Israel without creating unnecessary problems, while Israel approaches the confrontation far more confidently. Ireland, he wrote, is caught between competing interests and fears it could harm itself.
Early began by noting that the word "uncomfortable" had repeatedly appeared in comments by senior Football Association of Ireland officials and national team coach Heimir Hallgrímsson.
Association CEO David Courell called it an "uncomfortable and unwanted" situation; Hallgrímsson acknowledged that some of his players "felt very uncomfortable playing the game," and technical director John Martin described it as a "very uncomfortable situation."
From there, Early reached his central conclusion: "Why do we feel uncomfortable? Because our position is a compromise. We feel that maybe we should not have played against Israel, but we are playing. We are aware of the noise and prefer to keep our heads down. We don't want trouble."
According to Early, that contradiction is also apparent in the association's conduct. Last November, its representatives voted by a 93% majority to call on UEFA to suspend Israel from European competitions, but in July, 68% voted to play the matches.
Early argued that the association does not want to alienate its supporters but at the same time "fears losing money and points from UEFA." He extended his criticism to the Irish government, which he said "does not want to risk its relations with the United States."
The columnist also addressed the controversy sparked by Hallgrímsson when he said last week, "We are not playing with genocide, we are playing against genocide."
The Israel Football Association responded sharply, accusing him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy," while the Irish coach later acknowledged, "From a leadership perspective, maybe it wasn't wise of me to draw attention to myself like that."
According to the column, the Irish association even complained privately to UEFA about the Israeli response but refrained from another public confrontation.
Comparing Israel, Ireland
At this point, Early drew his central comparison between the two sides.
"Ireland wants to get through these games without creating unnecessary trouble. Israel stopped caring about that a long time ago," he wrote. "While the Irish association officials and players hesitate and try to find the right words, the Israelis speak with the confidence of believers."
As an example, Early cited Manor Solomon, who was asked by an Austrian journalist this week about comments made by Austria's president concerning the war in Gaza. Solomon questioned why he, as a soccer player, was expected to weigh in on the issue and made no attempt to hide his displeasure with the question.
Early noted that, unlike the Irish, the Israeli "did not look uncomfortable for even a moment," arguing that Solomon felt free to respond directly and forcefully to the journalist.
Early also linked this attitude to the Israeli decision not to exchange shirts after the match and to the fact that Israel's coach is not expected to shake Hallgrímsson's hand.
Column levels direct criticism at Ireland
According to Early, those steps reverse the picture: "The implication is that they, Israel, are the ones who have been offended, and that we, Ireland, are the ones who have made ourselves unworthy of respect."
The column, which also levels particularly harsh criticism at Israel, concludes with its most direct criticism of the Irish approach.
Ireland's players discussed the possibility of staging some form of protest before the match, but Early questioned what such a gesture would mean if they were going to take the field regardless.
"This is the fundamental contradiction Ireland has been struggling with all week," he wrote. "The only meaningful protest they could have made would have been to refuse to play. If the decision has been made that the game is going ahead, it is time to just play it."

Dozens of Israeli travelers in Nepal were receiving assistance on Sunday after heavy rain, flooding concerns, and severe weather disrupted major trekking regions across the country.
Clal Insurance & Finance said its rescue teams, operating through its partner firm, "Magen Search and Rescue," are on the ground rescuing Israeli travelers insured by the company who were caught in extreme weather in Nepal and needed help.
"Clal Insurance & Finance is working alongside all its rescue teams in Nepal to assist every policyholder in need of rescue. We are in contact with all relevant parties to ensure a safe outcome and to guarantee that all our policyholders are rescued and brought to safety," said Dror Zessler, deputy CEO and head of the Claims Division at Clal.
PassportCard said it was assisting 40 insured travelers in areas affected by the weather, including 17 in the Annapurna region, 17 in the Manaslu region, including Samagaon, four in the Tsum Valley near Chumling, and two in the Everest region.
Four of the travelers require medical attention and are expected to be evacuated for treatment once weather conditions permit, the company said. None of the insured travelers is currently believed to be in life-threatening danger, and their families are in regular contact with the situation room.
Israelis trapped in Nepal say there is 'no way to go back'
Israelis talked to Israeli media about the situation on ground, with many trapped in certain areas that were closed down due to security risks. "There are landslides here every few hours on our heads. We don't have to wait for a disaster to happen," one Israeli woman told Ynet.
Yarin, an Israeli hiker who spoke with N12, said that there are "dozens of Israelis" trapped in the village of Samagaun, and there is no clear way to either go back or continue their trek due to the rains.
"Since last night, the weather conditions have been very difficult. There is no electricity, and there were rockfalls near us, and our lives were miraculously saved," Yarin added.
Local authorities issued warnings overnight due to the risk of flooding, and travelers staying at major tourist sites and along trekking routes were instructed to move to safer areas. Nepalese authorities had already warned trekkers to avoid high-altitude routes as heavy rain and snowfall threatened flooding, landslides, rockfalls, and damage to trails and bridges.
PassportCard teams were operating simultaneously in several locations and conducting ongoing assessments based on the weather and the ability to travel through affected areas. In the Annapurna region, insured travelers were staying in several villages while the situation room worked to help them continue their journeys when conditions allowed.
Nepal travel severely restricted as flood danger persists
Travel across large parts of Nepal remained severely restricted, with numerous roads blocked and trekking activities suspended in affected areas. Nepal's weather authorities had warned ahead of the storm that heavy rainfall could increase the danger of floods and landslides and urged travelers to suspend Himalayan treks.
According to PassportCard's current forecasts, the weather is expected to gradually weaken, although restoring normal travel in affected areas could take several days.
PassportCard said its situation room would remain available around the clock and continue assisting the travelers and their families until the emergency ends and normal travel can resume.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Nicotine Is Mounting a Comeback in the Wellness Movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.
An ironic development emerging alongside the “Make America Healthy Again” movement is the portrayal of nicotine as a wellness and performance-enhancing product. Across social media, podcasts, natural medicine communities and tech startups, prominent wellness personalities and other influencers are portraying nicotine as a misunderstood compound whose potential benefits have been overshadowed by its negative association with cigarettes.
In these circles, nicotine is now being hailed as a natural product that can be used for everything from improving focus to protecting against cognitive decline. As a pulmonary physician-scientist who studies nicotine addiction and the health consequences of tobacco and nicotine products, I am concerned about these claims.
Some of this rebranding stems from the observation that nicotine is a naturally occurring plant compound found primarily in tobacco and in nightshade vegetables such as tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant in trace amounts. Proponents of nicotine use also draw on studies suggesting that nicotine can affect certain aspects of cognition and brain function. However, extending these findings to broad claims about productivity, brain health, longevity or wellness goes well beyond what has been shown in human studies.
The greatest health risks arise when tobacco is burned, which generates thousands of toxic substances, including carcinogens, carbon monoxide, and fine particulate matter. Repeated exposure to these combustion products can cause cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, and numerous other smoking-related illnesses.
Nicotine’s comeback as a wellness product is more about non-smoking options, such as nicotine pouches, or some combine nicotine with other substances marketed as cognition enhancers, like caffeine and nootropics. While many smoking-related diseases result from the chemical products of combustion, nicotine itself has well-known negative effects on the brain and body.
Nicotine activates the sympathetic nervous system—the body’s “fight or flight” response—which increases heart rate and blood pressure and disrupts sleep. Repeatedly kick-starting this system can place additional strain on the heart. Exposure is also of particular concern during critical phases of development.
Not to mention the extremely well-known risk that nicotine is addictive. It activates reward pathways in the brain, acting on receptors for acetylcholine, a key neurotransmitter involved in attention, learning, and memory. Though it may temporarily increase alertness and attention, nicotine does not reproduce normal acetylcholine signaling. The effects last much longer and alter activity throughout the brain.
With repeated exposure, the brain adapts to nicotine’s presence. Receptors become less responsive, and so the brain compensates by increasing the number of nicotine receptors, contributing to dependence. Activation of these receptors also influences the release of other neurotransmitters, including dopamine, which plays an important role in reward and reinforcement.
A common claim within wellness communities is that nicotine is a cognitive enhancer that improves focus and productivity. While there are some studies indicating that nicotine may temporarily enhance attention, vigilance, reaction time, and some types of memory, the results are mixed.
If any benefit does exist, the research suggests that this may only be the case for people with mild cognitive impairment. For healthy individuals, it doesn’t appear to offer any boost and may even worsen cognitive operation among higher-performing people.
In addition, many of these studies include people already dependent on nicotine. When these regular users stop consuming nicotine, they’re likely to experience irritability, anxiety, restlessness, and impaired attention. Reintroducing nicotine often relieves these symptoms, making it difficult to determine whether any improvements reflect true cognitive enhancement or are simply the reversal of withdrawal symptoms.
Wellness influencers also promote nicotine as a tool for managing stress and improving mood. Nicotine does activate reward pathways in the brain, which can create a sense of pleasure and wellbeing—temporarily.
Long-term users of nicotine often find that the substance makes stress and anxiety harder to manage. Research consistently shows that people who quit smoking experience reductions in anxiety, depression, and stress, along with improvements in mood and overall quality of life over time. In fact, long-term discontinuation of nicotine use is associated with better mental health.
But the most ambitious claims emerging from the pro-nicotine wellness movement suggest that nicotine protects against Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s, and other forms age-related cognitive decline. Or further, that nicotine slows biological aging and promotes longevity.
There’s some kernels of research underneath these claims, such as laboratory studies showing that nicotine can affect cellular pathways related to oxidative stress and animal studies suggesting effects on inflammation and other mechanisms linked to aging and disease. However, such findings have not translated into anything that indicates nicotine promotes healthy aging, extends lifespan or prevents age-related disease in humans.

Marko Mihkelson: Defeatism is not deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Marko Mihkelson: Defeatism is not deterrence
The snowball of speculation about an imminent Russian attack on Europe is gathering pace. Isolated facts are being mixed with wishful thinking, worst-case scenarios and, at times, little more than the need to grab attention, writes Marko Mihkelson.
We should be careful not to confuse speculation with strategy. The reality is straightforward: a major war is raging in Europe, yet the Allies continue either to ignore it or to treat it as merely a regional conflict over territory. Russia has not changed its strategic objectives. Its aim is to destroy Ukraine's sovereignty and reshape the existing European security architecture - in other words, to weaken and ultimately dismantle NATO.
The uncomfortable truth is that we have done far too little to force the Kremlin to abandon these objectives or to make clear that pursuing them would come at an unbearably high price. Instead, we are creating, almost as a self-fulfilling prophecy, the impression that a Russian attack on NATO is inevitable.
Russia understands that it can confuse and paralyse us through information operations alone. Constant speculation about the Baltic states and Poland risks creating the impression that this is primarily a problem for two or three countries on Russia's doorstep, while the rest of Europe can somehow remain untouched.
We have seen this delusion before with Ukraine: if only the issue in Donbas could somehow be settled, peace would return. The same logic is now being applied to NATO's eastern flank. If Russia gets what it wants there, perhaps everyone else will be safe.
But this is not how Russian strategy works. We should not forget Moscow's December 2021 ultimatum, which demanded that NATO roll back its military infrastructure to the 1997 lines. Russia was not merely asking for a settlement over Ukraine. It was demanding a fundamental revision of Europe's security order.
And if Russia sees that even members of the Coalition of the Willing are unwilling to articulate a clear strategic objective — namely, helping Ukraine achieve victory and pushing back Russian aggression — why should the Kremlin believe that we will have the resolve to defend NATO itself?
Russia's campaign against the West would not necessarily begin with a conventional attack. It can start by undermining NATO from within: interfering in elections, amplifying polarising narratives, exploiting political divisions and spreading fear. It can seek to isolate Ukraine by limiting Western support and then test our willingness to stand together.
This is already a war in which Russia is using terror against the West, and we need to recognise that reality if we are serious about bringing it to an end.
The first step is strategic clarity: Russia will not stop simply because we ask it to. It will stop when the costs of continuing its aggression become greater than the benefits it expects to gain.
That means the Coalition of the Willing should, at a minimum, pursue three concrete objectives.
- First, we need a substantial increase in military support for Ukraine — for example, a minimum of 0.25% of GDP annually — alongside continued support for Ukraine's financial system to help cover the costs of the war.
- Second, we should prepare for a military humanitarian mission to protect Ukrainian cities and critical strategic infrastructure from Russia's massive aerial terror campaign.
- Third, we need to apply decisive economic pressure on Russia so that its war machine can no longer operate at its current scale.
If we fail to do this, we should expect more acts of Russian terror across Europe. Defense companies and their executives may become targets. We must also be prepared for false-flag operations in which Russia could attempt to blame Ukraine for an attack causing casualties in a NATO country.
And we must recognise another vulnerability: our own political divisions. Russia is actively seeking to deepen them through interference and information operations. Developments in the France and Germany, as well as in Poland, show how important it is that our political disagreements do not become a strategic gift to the Kremlin.
Above all, we need to stop the submissive avalanche of speculation along the lines of: "Help, the Russians are coming!"
This kind of defeatism does not strengthen deterrence. It weakens it. Instead of endlessly speculating about where Russia might attack next, we should be talking - and acting - to ensure that Russia loses the war of aggression it started. And we should make clear that such aggression will have serious consequences for the dictatorship ruling Russia.
The fear that decisive action might somehow undermine strategic stability is itself becoming a tool of Russian escalation. If every step that could strengthen Ukraine or Europe is rejected because it might provoke Moscow, Russia learns precisely the wrong lesson: that fear works.
That is not deterrence. A new strategic stability in Europe cannot be built on permanent Russian threats, Western hesitation and Ukrainian sacrifice. It can emerge only when the security architecture of Europe is defended and strengthened — and when Russia has been defeated in the war of aggression it launched against it.
Our task is not to predict the next Russian attack. Our task is to make sure Russia understands that aggression will fail.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

British PM Burnham refuses to back Heathrow’s third runway project

British PM Burnham refuses to back Heathrow’s third runway project
LONDON – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham declined to give his backing on Sept 27 to plans to build a third runway at Heathrow, saying it was a matter for people who live near London’s main airport.
The government led by his predecessor, former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, announced in 2025 it supported Heathrow’s expansion proposal, which must undergo a lengthy planning process before construction can begin.
“I think, principally, it’s a matter for London,” Burnham told the BBC in an interview at the start of the governing Labour Party’s annual conference.
“I think you’ve got to hear the voice of people there first. It’s not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation.”
Burnham’s refusal to immediately back the plan is the latest development in a long-running debate over a project that has divided politicians for two decades.
Heathrow said at the weekend that plans to open the third runway could be delayed by four years, meaning it would not be operational until 2039.
The airport operates at 99 per cent capacity and risks being overtaken in Europe by other airports. Its two runways compare with four each in Paris’ Charles de Gaulle and Frankfurt Airport, and six at Amsterdam’s Schiphol.
Heathrow is just 24km west of London. Residents have for decades complained about noise pollution, safety risks from flights over the densely populated city, and more recently, about the impact of soaring carbon emissions.
But businesses and workers’ unions have raised concern about delays to Heathrow’s expansion and the impact on Britain’s growth prospects and jobs.
GMB, a union which represents workers across Heathrow, said while local voices should be heard, many were workers who supported expansion and that “this isn’t just a matter for London”.
“Heathrow is Britain’s front door, and businesses in every region trade through it,” said Warren Kenny, GMB London Regional Secretary. “I urge the prime minister to unleash our potential and build.” REUTERS

18:21:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery said military interoperability between Taiwan and the United States is essential to deterring a Chinese invasion.
The two militaries should conduct joint exercises, including air, maritime, and combined drills, Montgomery said in Taipei on Friday, per CNA. The US should station combat-training teams in Taiwan to train Taiwanese forces, while the two sides should jointly develop operational plans.
Senior military officers from both countries should make reciprocal visits, and the US defense secretary should meet with their Taiwanese counterpart, he said. “It’s very hard to cooperate and fight together in wartime if you don’t work together in peacetime.”
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) should also be able to visit Washington and meet with US President Donald Trump, as Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and Chinese leader Xi Jinping have done, Montgomery said.
He added that the US refusal to engage in meaningful military cooperation with Taiwan over the past 45 years has prevented the two militaries from achieving the necessary level of interoperability, CNA reported.
Montgomery said the factors driving Xi’s approach to Taiwan depend on his internal beliefs rather than the strength of his political position. This means Taiwan and the US must remain prepared, he said.
Taiwan must strengthen societal resilience, while the US should provide arms, conduct exercises, and prepare crisis-response plans in the Indo-Pacific, he said.
Regarding regional security, Montgomery said he was unsure whether the risk of military conflict with China had increased but that the previously discussed 2027 window was no longer applicable. A conflict could occur in 2029 or 2030, he said.
However, Montgomery said China was more likely to employ economic coercion combined with cyber operations. Beijing could use diplomatic, economic, and legal measures alongside cyberattacks, disinformation, and even military action to undermine Taiwan’s societal resilience, he said.
Montgomery therefore stressed that the Lai administration should continue strengthening societal resilience. More work is needed to ensure that communications networks and energy and financial systems are adequately protected and have sufficient redundancy to withstand pressure from China, he said.

Parliament to meet all electricity needs with solar power from Konya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:20:20 UTC
18:20:20 KST

This file photo shows an aerial view of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye (TBMM) complex in the capital Ankara.
The Turkish parliament is moving to cover all of its electricity consumption with renewable energy through a large-scale solar power project in Konya, the country’s agricultural heartland.
The Turkish Grand National Assembly plans to build a 20-megawatt peak-capacity photovoltaic solar power plant on a 300-decare site in Konya. The facility is expected to generate around 36 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to meet the Parliament complex’s current electricity consumption.
A second solar installation is also being built on the complex’s multi-story parking facility. The 472-kilowatt peak-capacity rooftop system is expected to produce approximately 750,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity each year.
The projects are part of a broader “green transformation” program at the Parliament, which operates on a 450-decare campus in the capital Ankara. The institution has received a Green Certificate for its sustainability efforts.
Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş said the institution had saved 2.5 million kilowatt-hours of electricity, 300,000 cubic meters of natural gas and 20,000 tons of water since June 2023 through conservation measures. He said renewable energy investments were expected to provide an additional economic contribution of 115 million Turkish Liras ($2.3 million) at current values.
The Parliament has also introduced systems to reduce water consumption and reuse resources. Rainwater collected from a large greenhouse and the main building’s roof is filtered and reused for irrigation, while a greywater recycling system supplies water for landscaping and ornamental pools.
Smart irrigation systems equipped with rain sensors have been installed across the complex, at the official residence and at social facilities. The systems automatically stop irrigation when rainfall is detected.
Two composting machines have also been introduced. The machines can turn leftover food into cat and dog food and landscaping waste into fertilizer.
The Parliament plans to complete two additional environmental projects in the coming months.

American warship sunk by missiles off Scotland in live fire
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:15:58 BST
18:15:58 KST

The decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring has been sunk off the Hebrides during the joint US-UK live-fire exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026, in an engagement that drew in warships and aircraft from both navies, according to US Naval Forces Europe and Africa, which has released footage of the strike.
The video shows the American destroyer USS Paul Ignatius launching a missile and the frigate being hit. Other attackers took part alongside her, among them aircraft and further surface vessels, and the full order of battle has yet to be set out.
We will be bringing you an in-depth look tomorrow at what happened off the Hebrides, how the engagement was put together and which units and weapons were involved.
Paul Ignatius is an Arleigh Burke-class Flight IIA destroyer, hull number DDG-117, commissioned in July 2019 and named for the former Secretary of the Navy who held the post under Lyndon Johnson. She has been forward-deployed to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain since June 2022, one of the American destroyers held in Europe for ballistic missile defence and wider tasking across the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
Klakring was an Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigate, decommissioned in 2013 and laid up at the Philadelphia Naval Inactive Ship Maintenance Facility until she was towed down the Delaware River on 12 August ahead of the Atlantic crossing, making first for Campbeltown. The exercise itself was originally planned for a window in May before moving to the second half of September at the QinetiQ Hebrides range in north-west Scotland.
A Request for Information issued by the Ministry of Defence in August 2025, inviting industry to take part, described Atlantic Thunder 26 as “a US-UK multi-domain exercise designed to validate SUW kill chains, build resilient kill webs and deliver strategic messaging through kinetic demonstration.”
The strike was only one part of the exercise though, Klakring is expected to now settle at a depth of around 6,000 feet, where uncrewed underwater vehicles are to carry out battle damage assessment and seabed survey work, a phase the Ministry of Defence treated as central when it approached industry last year.
The precedent is Atlantic Thunder 22, held off the same range in September 2022, which ended with the sinking of the former USS Boone by HMS Diamond, USS Arleigh Burke, RAF Typhoons and US Navy P-8 Poseidons, and was billed at the time as the most complex multinational sinking exercise staged in UK waters.

UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
September 27, 2026
British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.
London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act" and explosive-related offenses.
The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines. The authorities said they believed the incident to be "contained."
Counter-terrorism police were leading the probe.
"We are in the early stages of an investigation," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in an online statement, adding that the authorities were "working closely with our partners" to understand the circumstances of the incident.
The statement urged the public to share any information they may have related to the issue.
Praise from Trump and Burnham
US President Donald Trump praised those involved in the arrests. “It was an amazing job," he told reporters in the US.
"We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," Trump said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understood that the incident would be "deeply concerning" for many people.
In a social media post, Burnham thanked the police and armed forces for their response and expressed his gratitude to residents who had been evacuated from their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."
Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'
Local police said they had received a call overnight on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.
"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.
He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."
"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.
He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.
The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.
Officials stay tight-lipped
A spokesperson for the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."
The background for the incident was not immediately clear.
The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

Israel to impose weeklong closure on West Bank during Sukkot
Essential workers will still be allowed into industrial zones, subject to the security guidelines of the IDF’s Central Command
Defense Minister Israel Katz has instructed the IDF to impose a general closure on the West Bank starting Sunday, following a military recommendation. The closure is expected to remain in place throughout the coming week, including the Sukkot holiday and its intermediate days.
The decision follows recent attacks and comes ahead of the holiday period. During the closure, Palestinian workers will be barred from entering Israeli communities in the West Bank for work.
Essential workers will still be allowed into industrial zones, subject to the security guidelines of the IDF’s Central Command. Other exceptional permits will not be approved, apart from those required under the state’s commitments to the High Court of Justice.
The head of an association representing nursing institutions has appealed to Katz and Health Minister Haim Katz to exempt caregivers from the closure. In a letter, he warned that barring them could disrupt care at dozens of geriatric institutions in Israel.
According to the letter, about 940 caregivers from the West Bank work in institutional nursing care. The association says they have passed security checks and are usually exempt from closures through permits tied to the institutions where they work.
They help elderly patients with daily tasks such as getting out of bed, bathing, dressing and changing diapers. The association warned that suspending their entry could leave thousands of patients without the care they need.

Turkish anti-drone guns put on show for 12 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:08:23 UTC
18:08:23 KST

- ASELSAN demonstrated its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down several types of drones before delegations from 12 countries.
- Mounted on an 8×8 wheeled vehicle, the system also hit a moving ground target while both were in motion.
Turkish defense company ASELSAN has shown its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down drones and hitting a moving target while driving, in a live-fire demonstration watched by military delegations from 12 countries.
The company released video of the firing.
The demonstration focused on drones, and KORKUT 35 engaged fixed-wing, delta-wing and small mini and micro drones, with particular attention to kamikaze drones built to dive into their targets, ASELSAN said. In a separate scenario, the system, mounted on an 8×8 wheeled armored vehicle, fired at a moving ground target while both were in motion, to show its accuracy and how tightly its rounds grouped.
ASELSAN says the system can also engage fighter jets, helicopters, cruise missiles and air-to-ground missiles, and describes it as a cheaper way to defend troops and key sites against low-cost aerial threats.
KORKUT carries twin 35 mm cannons that together fire about 1,100 rounds a minute, with an effective range of roughly 4 km (2.5 miles). It uses ASELSAN’s ATOM programmable ammunition, which bursts in the air near a target and scatters tungsten fragments, raising the chance of hitting small drones that are hard to strike directly. A typical battery pairs a command vehicle that searches for and tracks targets with gun vehicles that each follow and fire at an assigned target.
The system entered Turkish service in a tracked configuration and has been exported. ASELSAN unveiled the 8×8 wheeled version at the Eurosatory defense show in Paris in 2024, giving it higher road speed to keep up with moving units. In January 2026, the company released footage of the wheeled KORKUT 140/35 shooting down a first-person-view drone while on the move.
The system is also heading to Europe. In February, ASELSAN and Czech defense group CSG formed a joint venture to produce KORKUT in the Czech Republic for European and global customers, and unveiled a version mounted on a Tatra 6×6 truck. In September, KORKUT was identified among air defense systems in a public reveal by the Pakistan Air Force, though the variant supplied has not been disclosed.

Andriy Rizol on How Cultural Diplomacy Advances Ukraine’s Interests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

The Watch Ukrainian Association has organized more than 800 cultural events in 268 cities across 55 countries since March 2022, according to the organization. Its activities range from film screenings and photo exhibitions to concerts, lectures and international tours by Ukrainian artists.
The association says its projects, organized with partners and without state funding, have raised about Hr. 16 million for Ukraine’s armed forces, military intelligence and the rehabilitation of service members. It has held events at the Council of Europe, European Parliament, European External Action Service, UNESCO, US Congress, UN, UK Parliament and OSCE headquarters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Its key initiatives include the CinemAid Film Marathon, Culture vs War, The Will to Win and Empowered. In 2024, Culture vs War became the umbrella brand for its cultural diplomacy projects.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Andriy Rizol, a producer and chairman of the association’s board, spoke to Kyiv Post about how culture can communicate Ukraine’s experience of war and build support abroad. Rizol is also CEO of Babylon and an honorary ambassador of Ukraine for cultural diplomacy.
What Germany’s Wingcopter 262 Means for Ukraine’s Drone War
“Be free to create”
Kyiv Post: How did Watch Ukrainian begin focusing on international cultural diplomacy?
Andriy Rizol: When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, we realized immediately that we had to act. On the fifth day of the war, we launched the CinemAid Charity Film Marathon. It brought together more than 70 events in 15 countries and helped us build a network of coordinators around the world while raising funds for the Armed Forces.
In April 2022, we launched the Culture vs War multimedia project. It combined documentaries, photo exhibitions and art books, with Ukrainian artists as protagonists.
We believed that international trust in artists was often higher than trust in politicians or the military — especially when artists were directly involved in the war. We wanted to tell the world about Russia’s war through their personal stories of resistance and their experiences.
What is the main message you want international audiences to take away?
Our slogan is “Be Free to Create.”
Ukrainians want victory, but we also need to explain why. We are fighting to preserve our freedom to create and to shape our own future.
The stories of our protagonists demonstrate this in different ways: members of the band Antytila through their service in a medical unit; Taras Kompanichenko through his moral support for the Armed Forces; Serhii Zhadan through his ability to inspire; and the first artists who volunteered to defend Ukraine, including Akhtem Seitablaiev, Serhii Mykhalchuk, Yaroslav Pilunskyi and Dmytro Linartovych.
How do you choose the protagonists?
The first criterion is a shared worldview. We look for prominent people who are known in Ukraine and internationally and who can serve as moral reference points.
But they cannot simply be made to speak from a script. Their stories have to reflect their genuine personal experience of the war.
This approach resulted in four feature-length documentaries, “Culture vs War,” “Palyanytsia,” “Empowered” and “Veterans’ Theater,” as well as seven short films focusing on individual artists.
Working with the government
How do you cooperate with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?
We began our dialogue with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs early in the full-scale war. It has always been based on equal partnership, and in some cases representatives of our organization also assist the MFA.
I have known Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha since his time as ambassador to Turkey, when we organized Ukrainian Film Days there. We have warm professional relations, and he understands the role culture can play in diplomacy.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Tetiana Sybiha has revitalized and brought together the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, supporting humanitarian, cultural and charitable projects involving diplomatic and civic communities.
We also cooperate with the Diplomatic Academy of Ukraine and its head, Ihor Ostash, who has extensive diplomatic experience and a strong interest in culture and art. Together, we work with young diplomats on public and cultural diplomacy.
In August, we launched the School of Cultural Diplomacy together with the Institute for National Resilience and Security and the Diplomatic Academy. Its purpose is to strengthen joint efforts by increasing the expertise of professional diplomats.
We are gradually building an ecosystem that includes the MFA, diplomatic missions, the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, the Diplomatic Academy and independent cultural institutions. The goal is to move from parallel efforts toward a coordinated system.
At the same time, Ukraine needs broader consolidation of cultural figures, specialized institutions, government and business to develop a comprehensive global cultural diplomacy strategy.
In 2024, the MFA granted me the status of Honorary Ambassador of Ukraine for Cultural Diplomacy. This has led to invitations to conferences, working meetings and panels where I can share our experience and develop joint initiatives.
Our goal is to make cultural diplomacy a priority and culture a national security priority.
For us, cultural diplomacy is not soft power. It is an effective tool for advancing Ukraine’s national interests and strengthening Ukraine’s ability to act internationally. In principle, it is an effective weapon.
That is why we focus on major political platforms and authoritative institutions capable of influencing decisions on support for Ukraine.
Why has the Veterans’ Theater resonated so strongly?
                                                                                                                                                                         
The idea emerged during a creative session of the Watch Ukrainian Association in April 2024. It was proposed by director, actor and civic activist Akhtem Seitablaiev.
We saw the project as a possible form of therapy through culture. At the same time, communicating the reality of the war to international audiences was becoming increasingly difficult as war fatigue grew.
We therefore created an art project that combined a stage production with a documentary featuring veterans as protagonists. It speaks about the war and its real consequences without necessarily putting the war itself “in the frame.”
The flagship production is “Eneida,” directed by Olha Semyoshkina, with Akhtem Seitablaiev as artistic director. It has attracted significant interest both in Ukraine and abroad.
The documentary “Veterans’ Theater” was screened in 19 countries as part of the Empowered UA film marathon.
For us, however, the motivation goes beyond the success of a particular project. We want to create trends, influence public discussion and help address real challenges.
Cultural diplomacy is essential to Ukraine’s future
What should Ukraine’s cultural presence in the world look like by 2030?
There are still remnants of an inferiority complex in Ukrainian society, but the situation has changed fundamentally.
Ukraine now has unique experience and significant achievements in military technologies, unmanned systems, IT, medicine, banking, logistics, e-document management, public services and volunteer practices, as well as in creative industries, documentary filmmaking, contemporary music and art. No other country has exactly the same experience.
Our next film is titled “Novators,” or “Innovators.”
By 2030, I want Ukraine to be respected and understood as a reliable and desirable partner of the democratic world. Cultural diplomacy can contribute to this.
We also need to change our perspective. We should not only learn from the world; we should also show what the world can learn from Ukraine.
That is the idea behind Empowered. We should no longer portray Ukrainians only as people who are poor, deprived or exhausted. We should show Ukrainians creating solutions, products, technologies, ideas and cultural phenomena that can be useful and interesting to the world.
The Empowered project was initiated by Watch Ukrainian with the support of the European Union and the MHP-Hromadi Foundation. It continues and develops the Culture vs War approach, seeking to strengthen the image of modern Ukraine as a strong country of talented people capable of enriching civilization across different areas of life.
We communicate this message through the personal stories of our protagonists.
I believe in large, ambitious, systemic and consolidated projects that produce concrete results. We simply do not have time for hesitation or delay.

'Left' in existential crisis: From CPI-CPM rift in Kerala to Delhi rout, old fault lines deepen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:06:39 UTC
18:06:39 KST

The Left faces a deeper political challenge as electoral setbacks, internal tensions and shrinking influence converge
There was a time when the Left’s political footprint stretched from West Bengal to Tripura and Kerala. Its influence travelled further still, through trade unions, university campuses, farmers’ movements and a cadre network that kept the red flag visible even where Communist parties were not in power. That map has steadily grown smaller.For India’s Left, the question is no longer only about shrinking electoral numbers. It is increasingly about where the Communist movement still has the political space, organisational confidence and social influence to assert itself. In Delhi, the SFI-AISA alliance has struggled to translate visible participation in student mobilisations into votes. In Kerala, the two principal constituents of the Left Democratic Front, the CPM and CPI, have found themselves publicly at odds over even the distribution of positions within the opposition, and that too after a heavy defeat in the assembly elections.
These may appear to be separate battles, but they have come at a particularly difficult moment for the Left. The Kerala defeat has left it without a state government, the CPM and CPI are publicly disagreeing over the way forward, former chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan is facing a probe, and the Delhi university results have again exposed the gap between the Left’s visibility in student movements and its electoral reach.
The timing makes these developments particularly significant. The Left’s retreat has been a long process. The fall of the Left Front in West Bengal in 2011, the loss of Tripura in 2018 and the steady decline in its parliamentary strength had already reduced the Communist parties’ national footprint. Kerala had remained the exception, a state where the Left retained a durable organisational network and, in 2021, even broke the state’s established cycle of alternating between the LDF and UDF governments. Its defeat in 2026 means that India currently has no state government led by a Communist party.But the more revealing question may be what is happening beneath the election results. Is the Left merely going through another electoral trough, particularly after a decade in power in Kerala, or are the latest developments exposing older fault lines, from leadership and alliance tensions to the difficulty of converting traditional political mobilisation into electoral support?
Pinarayi probe: Another challenge after Kerala defeat
On September 22, the UDF government ordered a police inquiry based on an Enforcement Directorate report concerning allegations involving former chief minister and current leader of opposition Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and son-in-law PA Mohammed Riyas in the CMRL-Exalogic case. The state government said the inquiry would be entrusted to the state police; reports said it would initially be conducted by the Crime Branch without registration of an FIR.The underlying allegations are already part of an ED investigation. The agency has alleged financial irregularities involving payments made by Cochin Minerals and Rutile Ltd to Veena's now-defunct company Exalogic Solutions, and has sought action against Vijayan and others. The Kerala government's decision followed legal advice on whether the information and material supplied by the ED warranted a preliminary inquiry.For the CPM, however, the political dimension is inseparable from the legal one. Party general secretary MA Baby has said the party will fight the matter “legally and politically”, while accusing central agencies of having been used against opposition leaders.That places the Left in an unfamiliar position in Kerala. For a decade, Vijayan and the CPM were operating from government. Now the former chief minister is leading the opposition while facing a probe ordered by the government that replaced him.The probe comes only months after the LDF lost power following a decade in government, at a time when the CPM is already examining what went wrong and trying to regroup in opposition. The question is therefore not simply whether the allegations withstand investigation. The episode also puts Vijayan and the record of the previous government back under scrutiny at a particularly difficult moment for the party.
DUSU polls: Why isn't Left mobilisation becoming votes?
The Delhi University Students' Union election offers a different window into the Left's problem, particularly its ability to convert activism and issue-based mobilisation into electoral support.The SFI-AISA alliance had been visible in campaigns around issues including student housing, examinations and accountability, and had participated prominently in the CJP mobilisation. Yet its electoral numbers declined in three of the four central-panel contests compared with 2025. Its presidential candidate Ananya Raturi received 5,377 votes, almost identical to the 5,385 polled by the alliance's candidate last year. But its vice-presidential tally fell from 4,163 to 2,383, the secretary vote from 9,535 to 8,734 and the joint-secretary vote from 8,425 to 5,837.The results also showed that student politics cannot simply be read as a binary contest between the major national parties and the Left. ABVP won three of the four central-panel positions, while Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen won the vice-president's post with 30,615 votes. He had previously been associated with Congress-affiliated NSUI but contested independently after not receiving its ticket.For the Left, the striking element is the gap between mobilisation and electoral conversion. A political organisation can be prominent in protests, articulate grievances on campuses and participate in wider movements, but that visibility does not automatically translate into votes.The presidential contest is particularly revealing. The Left candidate finished with 5,377 votes, while ABVP's Yash Dabas won with 24,576 and NSUI's Vijay Shankar Meena polled 22,523. The result does not erase the Left's presence on campus, but it does expose the difficulty of turning that presence into control of student institutions.And that is why the DUSU result matters beyond one university election. Student politics has historically been an important space for the Left to recruit, organise and build its next generation of political workers. Sitaram Yechury, for instance, rose through student politics at JNU before eventually becoming CPI(M) general secretary.The question for the Left now is simpler: if it can still bring young people to protests and movements, why is it struggling to bring them to the ballot box?
CPI vs CPM: When opposition itself becomes a battlefield
The strain is also visible inside Kerala's Left alliance. After the LDF's assembly defeat, the CPI demanded the post of deputy leader of the opposition in the assembly, arguing for a larger role within the alliance. The CPM, however, rejected the demand, with Vijayan publicly opposing it.On the surface, the disagreement is about a post. But underneath it is a larger debate about how the LDF should function after its election defeat. The CPI has argued for greater sharing of responsibilities and “collective leadership”, while the CPM has maintained that the alliance should follow its established conventions.The disagreement soon spilled into public. CPI state secretary Binoy Viswam criticised Vijayan's stand, while senior CPI leader C Divakaran went further and questioned Vijayan's authority to dismiss the demand. Divakaran also argued that Vijayan should have taken responsibility for the election defeat rather than becoming leader of the opposition.The CPM pushed back too. CPM state secretariat member C N Mohanan questioned the CPI's electoral strength and accused it of using pressure tactics against the larger ally.The dispute may appear procedural because the deputy leader's post is largely an organisational and parliamentary position. But its political significance lies elsewhere. The CPI has sought greater recognition after the LDF's defeat, while the CPM, as the dominant force in the alliance, remains the principal party responsible for its direction.The two parties have since tried to prevent the dispute from escalating further. But the episode illustrates a problem that often becomes sharper after an electoral defeat: who takes responsibility for the loss, and who gets to decide the course correction?
From Bengal to Kerala: How did the Left reach here?
Kerala's 2026 verdict completed a long retreat. West Bengal's Left Front had ruled continuously from 1977 until 2011, while Tripura remained under Left Front rule for 25 years before the BJP ended that run in 2018. Kerala subsequently became the Left's last major governing base.But the story of the Left's decline has not been the same everywhere. In West Bengal, the 2011 defeat ended 34 years of uninterrupted Left Front rule and the Communist parties have since struggled to recover their old electoral space. In Tripura, the BJP displaced the Left after 25 years in power and emerged as its principal rival. Kerala followed a different trajectory, with power traditionally alternating between the LDF and Congress-led UDF.That is what made the LDF's 2021 victory particularly significant. The Vijayan government returned for a second consecutive term, breaking Kerala's four-decade pattern of alternating governments and giving the Left something it no longer had elsewhere: a state where it could demonstrate that it remained capable not only of surviving, but of retaining power.The 2026 defeat is therefore different from Bengal and Tripura and cannot automatically be equated with the organisational collapse witnessed elsewhere. Yet the scale of the setback raises questions beyond normal anti-incumbency. The LDF was reduced from 94 seats to 35, while the UDF won 102. The CPI(M) also suffered defeats in areas traditionally associated with its organisation, including parts of Kannur. BJP candidates won three seats, Chathannoor, Nemom and Kazhakoottam, including constituencies that had been held by LDF leaders.The larger national trajectory has been just as stark. At its parliamentary peak in 2004, the Left parties together had 59 Lok Sabha MPs and provided crucial outside support to the first UPA government. Twenty-two years later, their presence in Parliament and across state governments is a fraction of what it was.The decline cannot be traced to a single election or a single cause. The Left has had to contend with the loss of old strongholds, changes in the nature of work and organised labour, the rise of powerful regional parties, the BJP's expansion into states where the Left once had substantial space, and the challenge of reaching a generation of voters with little memory of the Communist parties at the height of their political influence.
Kerala had, for years, stood apart from that national decline. The 2026 result does not mean the Left's organisational base in the state has disappeared, but it has removed its last seat of state power and made the problems elsewhere much harder to ignore.
With no Communist-led state government left, a diminished parliamentary presence, weaker conversion of student mobilisation into votes and visible friction among its own principal parties, the Left finds itself at one of its most difficult political moments.The challenge is no longer simply how to win the next election. It is whether the political space that once made the Communist movement a national force can still be reconstructed, and whether the Left can address its old fault lines while finding its place in a changing political landscape.

Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Istanbul Culture Route Festival kicks off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:05:50 UTC
18:05:50 KST

AA Photo
The Istanbul leg of the Türkiye Culture Route Festival, organized by the Culture and Tourism Ministry, kicked off with a range of cultural and artistic events.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy officially opened the festival at the Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM).
More than 400 events will take place at 23 venues and over 50 locations across the city. The program includes 40 concerts and 15 exhibitions and installations, as well as talks, recitals, modern dance performances, musicals, theater productions and workshops for children and adults.
The main stage will host concerts by Özcan Deniz, Oğuzhan Koç, Murat Boz, Kıraç, Simge, Poizi, Bengü, Ceza and Bayhan.
During the opening, Ersoy visited exhibitions at AKM, including “Three Painters,” featuring works by Alaeddin Aksoy, Mehmet Güleryüz and Komet from Mustafa Taviloğlu’s collection.
He also highlighted “The Faces of Colors,” which explores emotions, thoughts and experiences through colors and human faces.
The “A Vision for an Advancing Future” exhibition by ASELSAN, previously presented in Eskişehir, Bursa and Ankara, has also moved to Istanbul. It features works in which international artists reinterpret discarded electronic and industrial waste.
The festival’s gastronomy program features more than 200 selected food venues and five culinary routes. Ersoy noted that Istanbul has 86 restaurants included in the Michelin Guide’s selection and cited a 2025 Travel Trends report by the Mastercard Economics Institute, which identified Istanbul as the world’s top gastronomic city based on international dining expenditure.
The five routes are “Beyoğlu-Galata-Karaköy,” “Historic Peninsula-Fatih,” “Beşiktaş-Istinye Bosphorus line,” “Kanlıca-Beykoz-Şile” and “Kadıköy-Moda.”
This year’s festival is being held in 26 cities. Ersoy said Balıkesir, Denizli, Hatay, Kocaeli, Muğla and Tekirdağ would join in 2027, bringing the total number of host cities to 32.
The international program includes concerts by the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and the National Arab Orchestra. The Stanislavsky and Nemirovich-Danchenko Ballet, one of the longstanding representatives of Russian ballet, will also perform in Türkiye for the first time.
The festival program also features pianist and composer Büşra Kayıkçı’s new project “Beyond Wall” and “Legacy of a Gaze,” an exhibition showcasing more than five decades of work by Yann Arthus-Bertrand.

British police said on Sunday they had arrested five men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and the army was examining a number of vehicles after security was stepped up at a British air base used by US air forces in southwest England.

Armed officers arrested five men, who are being held on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police said a 400-metre cordon was in place around the base as the bomb disposal unit investigated the vans. Local residents in 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated and armed officers were patrolling the site.

Trump and the chain of setbacks in Iran, China and Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:02:13 UTC
18:02:13 KST

Contrary to the image Donald Trump has tried to project of American power and influence in the world, recent days have been marked, for him, by a series of setbacks—setbacks that this time appear not in a single file, but simultaneously across several important arenas of US foreign policy. Reuters, in a report, addressed this very issue, citing Trump's speech at the United Nations, his meeting with China's president, the war against Iran, and the unsuccessful efforts to end the war in Ukraine as signs of the limits of his ability to advance Washington's demands.
In his speech at the UN General Assembly, Trump tried once again to present an image of American power. While defending his administration's conduct in the war with Iran, he threatened Tehran that if an agreement was not reached, it might face harsher military measures. Trump even spoke of the possibility of Iran's annihilation and emphasized that Washington remains ready to use its military power to achieve its objectives.
But raising the level of threats does not necessarily mean an increase in America's ability to achieve its political goals. The war with Iran—which Trump has from the outset tried to frame within the context of American military power—continues, and has become one of the most complicated files of his administration's foreign policy. Iran's resistance to American military and economic pressures has meant that Washington has been unable to convert these pressures into a clear and lasting political outcome.
Developments in recent days also show that the path to an agreement remains difficult. On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Iran put forward proposals to end the conflicts and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but Trump did not accept these proposals. Under these circumstances, the continuation of the conflict shows that American pressures have still not been able to force Tehran to accept Washington's core demands.
On the other hand, many of America's European and Asian allies have not gone along with Washington's requests for greater participation in confronting Iran. This matters from another angle as well; because American power does not depend solely on this country's military strength—the ability to build coalitions and bring allies along is also an important part of Washington's global power.
The China file shows a similar picture. In his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump tried to use the summit as a sign of his ability to manage one of the world's most important geopolitical rivalries. However, according to Reuters, the tangible result of this meeting remained largely confined to maintaining the trade truce and preventing an escalation of economic tensions between the two countries.
While important files such as Taiwan, trade, artificial intelligence, and China's role in international developments remain points of disagreement between Washington and Beijing, no concrete achievement was reached that could be said to resolve these disputes. This shows that even when Trump enters direct negotiations with China's leader, the gap between a display of power and the achievement of a real agreement remains considerable.
Of course, this does not mean America is empty-handed against China, or that Trump lacks tools of pressure. Washington still possesses considerable economic, technological, military, and diplomatic leverage. But the main issue is the extent to which these tools can be converted into a political outcome. Indeed, the ability to exert pressure is different from the ability to impose a final result.
On the Ukraine file as well, Trump faces a similar challenge. He had repeatedly promised that he could end the war between Russia and Ukraine, and in recent months has made efforts to bring Moscow and Kyiv closer to an agreement. However, Washington's efforts to reach a ceasefire—including in the energy sector—have so far not led to a stable and significant outcome.
The continuation of the fighting between Russia and Ukraine shows that American influence, even in a file where Washington plays an important role, is not sufficient to impose a final solution. Russia and Ukraine both have their own particular interests and calculations, and Trump cannot simply force them to accept a demand merely by announcing it.
These three files reveal an important point about the Trump administration's foreign policy. America remains one of the most powerful actors in the world, and its president has extensive economic, military, and diplomatic tools at his disposal; but there is a gap between the "ability to create pressure" and the "ability to convert pressure into a political outcome."
In the Iran file, the war continues; regarding China, fundamental disagreements remain unresolved; and in Ukraine, Trump's efforts to end the war have not yet led to a final agreement. For this reason, this set of developments can be seen as a sign of the difficulty of converting American power into political outcomes.
Trump can still threaten, exert pressure, and make decisions that affect global equations; but developments in recent weeks show that in international politics, a display of power is not the same as achieving the desired result. The important question now facing the American president is to what extent Washington can convert its power into results—not just in a single file, but simultaneously across several major global crises.

Swimming in Dangerous Waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:02:13 UTC
18:02:13 KST

While debates rumble on regarding a national pantheon and Poland’s threats to block Ukraine’s EU accession should the monument include the graves of the 20th-century Ukrainian nationalist leaders Stepan Bandera and Roman Shukhevych, plans are underway, in the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district of Odesa region, for a different kind of memorial burial site.
It will be a pantheon for Black Sea dolphins and it is slated for construction within the Tuzlivski Lagoon National Reserve – a unique area comprising forests, steppe, and 13 lagoons, connected to the sea, which attract a vast array of wildlife, including dolphins.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The idea for this pantheon was suggested by Ivan Rusev, a prominent ecologist who works at the reserve. Since 2022, Russian drones have frequently sparked fires inside the protected area. However, the most severe impact of Russian aggression in the area has been on the Black Sea dolphin population, which has plummeted catastrophically.
Rusev estimates that over 50,000 dolphins have fallen victim to the war over the past four and a half years. In just the last couple of months, 89 dead dolphins have washed up on the shore.
Apart from falling victim to the hundreds of Russian drones that explode into the sea before reaching the Ukrainian coast, vast numbers of dolphins have succumbed to marine pollution caused by fuel oil, gasoline, sunflower oil, and other liquid commodities. These substances spill into the sea whenever Russian missiles and drones destroy storage facilities at Ukrainian sea and river ports.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
Furthermore, intensive underwater radio surveillance by Russian warships and submarines – and specifically the use of powerful sonar systems – disrupts the dolphins’ ability to navigate underwater. This, too, leads to the deaths of these Black Sea cetaceans.
The remains and skeletons of dead dolphins found along the shore have already formed mounds at several locations within the protected coastal area. Once the planned pantheon is built, some of these remains will be interred there in a mass grave dedicated to the animal victims of the Russo-Ukrainian War. It will be the first monument constructed within the vast nature reserve.
Murky political waters
Yet the war has made it difficult for many Ukrainians to dwell on environmental damage, however grave. Survival under constant shelling and developments at the front naturally come first. At the same time, another threat to the country’s resilience is drawing growing—and increasingly sarcastic—attention: corruption, and the struggle to contain it.
Recent events have served as a reminder that Ukrainian politics often bears a closer resemblance to unsophisticated TV entertainment than to a platform for ideological confrontation and debate over how best to organize the economy and public services.
The process of exposing corruption and dealing with suspected perpetrators also displays a show-business dynamic which overshadows the legal procedure. However, theatrical as the scandals may appear, their effect on the political environment is real and they stir up the waters of government, making them almost impossible to navigate safely.
The saga of Operation Carthage, which led to the arrest, on corruption charges, of a deputy prosecutor general, is being followed like a soap opera popular for its most obvious plot twists.
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – who had denied involvement in his subordinates’ corrupt activities – promised to resign following a conversation with President Volodymyr Zelensky, but then he vanished from the media spotlight for a week, during which time no official charges were brought against him.
Kravchenko remained in his post and was not called in for official questioning. Then, having authorized, for himself, a business trip to Paris, as prosecutor general, he left the country using a VIP taxi service. That same night, his wife also departed Ukraine via the Shehyni border crossing.
Kravchenko did not arrive in Paris, and having spent four days in lively speculation as to whether Kravchenko would return home from his “business trip,” Ukrainians began asking themselves who would be the next top civil servant allowed to flee abroad before his/her actions were investigated by the proper authorities.
It is hard to imagine the now ex-prosecutor general turning up in Kyiv, but were he to do so, he would almost certainly stand trial. However, Ukraine’s judicial system is not accustomed to being harsh on corrupt former officials, and Kravchenko would be unlikely to face imprisonment. What is more, if he were tried by judges from Odesa or Odesa region, he would have absolutely nothing to worry about.
That judicial leniency has an especially Odesan variation. Since 2021, for minor, non-violent offences, judges in the region have regularly handed down suspended sentences that include a requirement to read a list of fiction books selected by the judge—usually classics. Two teenage thieves received such a sentence in 2021.
During their trial, the judge at the Malinovskyi District Court noted that the defendants were barely able to articulate their actions coherently and displayed a remarkably limited vocabulary. In view of this, the judge ordered them to read works by Mark Twain, Jack London, and the Ukrainian national poet Taras Shevchenko. Since then, the reading requirement has been expanded to include writing a 500-word essay on each assigned book.
The most recent sentence of this type was handed down just a few days ago at the Dobroslav District Court in Odesa. A Russian-speaking resident, who had used the internet to justify Russian aggression and to promote the idea of Russia occupying Odesa region, received a suspended sentence.
The ruling required her to read two adventure novels by the Ukrainian writer Ivan Bahrianyi (1906–1963) and to read and provide written commentary on the Budapest Memorandum – a document signed by the US, the UK, and Russia, under which Ukraine surrendered its nuclear arsenal to Russia in exchange for guarantees regarding its security and territorial integrity.
One wonders which titles the Odesa courts might include in the reading list for a wayward prosecutor general. But beyond these darkly comic courtroom remedies, the region remains exposed to the far more immediate dangers of war.
As the shipping industry mourns the death of the Ukrainian captain of a cargo vessel recently hit by a Russian missile off the Odesa coast, we can only hope that the dolphin community migrates away from these dangerous waters a little earlier than usual this autumn.

Chinese choreographer blends street dance with traditional Chinese cultural elements
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:01:07 CST
18:01:07 KST

Fang Zhenghua (R) instructs Homies dancers at Dancehome studio in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, June 13, 2026.
Fang Zhenghua, a post-90s choreographer, has participated in the production of a series of eye-catching dancing performances, including a show featuring dancers and humanoid robots at the opening ceremony of the 48th WorldSkills Competition. For Fang, street dance has never been merely a passing trend.
Fang's love for street dance began at the age of 13, when he first learned popular dance moves from television. That early fascination soon grew into a lifelong pursuit, driving him to explore new possibilities on stage. A big fan of Chinese martial arts novels since childhood, Fang has integrated Sichuan Opera face-changing techniques, traditional Kung Fu movements and other distinct Chinese cultural elements into his choreography.
In March 2025, Fang and Homies, a street dance team of his studio Dancehome, won third place at the VIBE Dance Competition with their work "Sword and Qi in Sichuan." This was the first time a Chinese team had claimed an award in the competition's 30-year history. His team has also collaborated with domestic humanoid robot developers, staging performances that showcase China's technological advances.
Nearly 20 years of dedication has brought Fang to stages around the world. "When we compete abroad, our goal is not just to show the world how Chinese dancers move," he said. "We want them to see a rich, diverse China through every step we take." (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie)
