Column: Learn from history: beware of resurgence of Japanese militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:01:06 CST
18:01:06 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
"My home is by the Songhua River, in northeast China. Forests and coal mines lie there. And soybeans and sorghum stretch across hills and plains."
The ballad On the Songhua River captures the deep grief of people from northeast China, a fertile homeland reduced to a ravaged wasteland during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression.
As one of the cultural emblems of that painful chapter, the ballad has etched the trauma of the September 18 Incident into the collective memory of the Chinese nation.
This Sept. 18 marked the 95th anniversary of the incident. Ninety-five years ago, the incident marked the beginning of the 14-year Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and set the stage for the World Anti-Fascist War.
Ninety-five years on, the roar of artillery may have long faded into history, but the lessons of that era still echo today.
WHITEWASHING CAN'T CONCEAL AGGRESSIVE NATURE
On the night of Sept. 18, 1931, a loud explosion near Liutiaohu on the northern outskirts of Shenyang shattered the peace of northeast China. The Japanese Kwantung Army blew up a section of the South Manchuria Railway, and blamed it on Chinese troops. Under this pretext, it immediately attacked Chinese military barracks and shelled the city of Shenyang.
This was no hasty military provocation, but a meticulously planned operation long in the making.
On the very day of the incident, the Japanese military quickly staged the scene, planted false evidence, and released fact-distorting statements to the international community at the earliest opportunity. Major Japanese newspapers uniformly adopted the narrative that "Chinese troops bombed the railway, forcing the Japanese military to act in self-defense" to shape domestic public opinion.
Simultaneously, the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs provided fabricated photos and testimonies to international news agencies. When the League of Nations discussed the issue of the northeast China, Japan, the aggressor, was the first to portray itself as the victim, putting forward a motion to "punish China severely," and using its status as a permanent council member to steer the direction of the investigation.
To drum up support for the puppet state of Manchukuo in northeast China, various Japanese media and publications dressed up the deliberate aggression through absurd narratives such as "establishing a paradise of the kingly way," "protecting residents in Manchuria," and "maintaining local order."
This bandit logic of portraying aggression as "self-defense" and premeditation as "response" may deceive people for a while, but not forever.
In 1932, the Lytton Commission dispatched by the League of Nations released an investigation report, recognizing China's sovereignty over its northeastern provinces and ruling that Japan's military actions constituted aggression. In 1933, the League of Nations formally demanded Japan withdraw its troops from northeast China.
The verdict of the Tokyo Trials explicitly stated that the war which Japan waged against China began on the night of Sept. 18, 1931. There is no way for Japan to talk its way out of this historical verdict.
APPEASEMENT NEVER DELIVERS GENUINE PEACE
As early as 1927, at its Eastern Conference, the Japanese government established the "national policy" of seizing northeast China. In carrying it out, however, the Japanese military, wary of international backlash, adopted an incremental approach to test the reaction and bottom line of the international community.
In the early days of the September 18 Incident, Japan's top decision-making body internally worried that tough intervention from European and American powers would derail its plans. Hence, it rolled out the so-called "no expansion" policy, claiming that "Japan has no intention of occupying Manchuria."
Unfortunately, the Council of the League of Nations adopted a resolution issuing a "warning" to both Japan and China, failing to distinguish the aggressor from the victim. Such tacit approval and appeasement by European and American powers toward Japan's expansion completely dispelled Japan's concerns and in effect condoned Japanese militarists' act of aggression.
Facts have proved that appeasing Japanese militarism cannot bring genuine peace. On the contrary, it only emboldened Japan to expand its aggression even more recklessly.
Barely four months after the September 18 Incident, over one million square kilometers of land across the three northeastern provinces of China fell entirely under Japanese occupation.
Japan imposed 14 years of oppressive rule over northeast China, plundering resources, perpetrating massacres, subjecting people to forced labor, carrying out germ warfare and human experiments through Unit 731, and imposing education aimed at erasing Chinese national consciousness -- the list goes on and on.
Countless people in northeast China were displaced and forced to be homeless, just as described in the ballad On the Songhua River.
More egregiously still, using northeast China as a springboard, Japanese militarists later launched a full-scale invasion of China.
ENDURING WARNING OF SEPTEMBER 18 INCIDENT
Even to this day, Japan's right-wing forces still refuse to acknowledge the historical facts of aggression such as the September 18 Incident. They keep whitewashing and glorifying the history of aggression, and even fabricate a "victim" narrative.
While denying their crimes of aggression against China, they repeatedly play up the national trauma of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. They dress up aggression against China as "the Manchurian Incident and the rise of the military," while describing the establishment of the puppet state of Manchukuo as "declaring the founding of a state," attempting to use seemingly neutral terms to obscure their guilt of aggression and mislead the international community.
Poisoned by such a distorted narrative, young people in Japan have little awareness of the historical crimes of militarism. In recent years, militarist symbols such as samurai swords and the rising sun flag have become increasingly common in Japanese idol groups, e-sports, and film and television productions.
Recently, the Japanese fashion brand WEGO was found to be planning a collaboration with My Hero Academia, a Chinese-insulting anime that sparked massive controversy for naming a character in a way seen as alluding to Unit 731's human experiments. The collaboration was launched on Sept. 18, triggering strong concern among Chinese consumers.
This is just the latest example of the spread of Japan's right-wing views of history.
To remember the September 18 Incident is to debunk the false narrative peddled by Japan's right-wing forces. The incident was the first link in the chain of Japanese militarist expansion, making clear that Japan was the outright perpetrator and aggressor, anything but a "victim" of war.
It is completely a double standard to focus only on one's own suffering while ignoring the disasters one has inflicted on others. Such a one-sided narrative is a grave distortion of history, and just hurts countries and peoples that suffered from aggression all over again.
To remember the September 18 Incident is not to fuel hatred, but to set the record straight, cherish peace more, and build a better future.
It is a mirror that reflects the heinous acts of Japanese militarists: systematic manipulation of public opinion, acts of aggression, self-exoneration and distortion of history. It is a line of defense that constantly reminds the world of the importance of upholding historical justice and the post-war international order, and preventing militarism from making a comeback.
Remembering the September 18 Incident and delivering justice to history, to the people and to the international community should be the shared responsibility of all peace-loving people.
Editor's note: The author is an international affairs observer.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Police officers examine the crime scene of a shooting in Lwandle, Cape Town Metro, Western Cape province, South Africa, Sept. 27, 2026. Ten people were killed and 11 injured in a shooting early Sunday in a township in the Cape Town Metro, South Africa, local police said.(South African Police Service in the Western Cape/Handout via Xinhua)
CAPE TOWN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Ten people were killed and 11 injured in a shooting early Sunday in a township in the Cape Town Metro, South Africa, local police said.
According to a statement issued by the South African Police Service (SAPS) in the Western Cape, police reports indicated that gunmen entered an entertainment venue in Lwandle, which also sells braaied meat, at around 1:46 a.m. local time (2346 GMT Saturday) and opened fire on patrons.
Lwandle is a township about 40 km east of central Cape Town.
"Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities," police said. "Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained."
Local police have opened cases of murder and attempted murder. A multi-disciplinary team led by serious violent crime detectives has been established to investigate the shooting, according to the statement.
"Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet," the statement said.
Police said the identities of the deceased would be released once their next of kin had been informed.
"SAPS management has increased deployments to the area while the search for the gunmen continues," police said.
Police also appealed for information from witnesses or anyone who could assist with the investigation, saying all information would be treated confidentially. ■

"Lancang-Mekong Melodies: Lao People Singing Chinese Songs" grand final held in Vientiane
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
17:00:30 CST
18:00:30 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- The grand final of the fifth "Lancang-Mekong Melodies: Lao People Singing Chinese Songs" competition has been held here, bringing together more than 700 people to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival and promote people-to-people exchanges.
The event, held on Friday night, was attended by officials from China and Laos, representatives of cultural institutions, and members of local communities.
In his remarks, Deng Liqiang, a counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Laos, said music is a universal language that transcends national borders.
Noting that over the past five years, the competition has become a symbol of cultural exchanges between China and Laos, he expressed the hope that the event would continue to attract more Lao young people to learn about China and develop an interest in Chinese culture.
Vansy Soukchaleurn, deputy director of the Department of Culture and Arts under the Lao Ministry of Culture and Tourism, said that the competition has helped implement the action plan for building a China-Laos community with a shared future in the new era.
Through music, the event has strengthened the bond between the two peoples and showcased the longstanding friendship between China and Laos, Vansy added.
The competition attracted hundreds of Chinese-language music enthusiasts from across Laos, with contestants ranging in age from 8 to 53. Following a series of qualifying rounds, 12 contestants advanced to the grand final.
After a closely contested final, Viengsavanh Yayongsue won the championship with the song "We Are Different."
Luo Weijian, director of the Chinese Cultural Center in Laos, said this year's competition reached a wider audience than previous editions, attracting participants from across Laos, from Vientiane to mountainous towns in the north, and from the banks of the Mekong River to the southern highlands.
Singers from diverse ethnic backgrounds and regions came together, united by their shared connection to the Mekong River. Luo said the event's growing popularity reflects the Lao people's interest in the Chinese language and culture.
The competition was hosted by the Chinese Cultural Center in Laos and supported by the China General Chamber of Commerce in Laos.
A photo exhibition marking the 65th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Laos was also held at the venue, along with a display of traditional Chinese culture. ■

Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”
Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.
“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.
Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.
“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”
Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.
His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.
Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.
Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.
Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.
The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.
Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.
An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.
Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.
In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”
Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’
“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area
September 27, 2026
Northern Ireland's Protestant, pro-British Orange Order was set to parade through a mainly Catholic and nationalist area on Sunday.
It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.
Thirty-five members of the Orange Order are to march silently through Garvaghy Road in the town of Portadown, without any bands or other Order supporters participating.
About 2,000 people gathered on the street Sunday morning in a counterprotest to prevent the march.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for "calm on all sides." In a BBC interview, he said "big gains" had been made in Northern Ireland "and we don't want to see things go backwards."
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, a member of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, spoke against the decision to allow the march to take place.
"Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever," she said, also voicing her support for the local residents to protest against the march, which she labeled "unwanted" and "sectarian."
Carla Lockhart, an MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said local residents have nothing to fear from "thirty five men walking down a road silently and with no bands and in an orderly fashion."
History of conflict
Garvaghy Road was one of the epicenters of the conflict between the Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and the Protestant, pro-British unionists in the late 1990s.
Back then, clashes between residents and the marchers repeatedly triggered disorder, also known as the Drumcree dispute.
As part of the Good Friday Agreement, a deal signed in 1998 that largely ended three decades of conflict between the two sides known as the Troubles, an entity was established to regulate contentious processions named The Parades Commission.
The Commission repeatedly rejected the Orange Order's requests to march through the area, with a High Court ruling quashing the rejection this year due to a procedural error. The Order then issued a fresh application, which was approved.

Some Pancreatic Cells Are Just One Genetic Tweak Away From Treating Diabetes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

A human pancreas typically contains about a billion beta cells, the primary producers of insulin. Among people with diabetes, these cells are either missing or dysfunctional, and thus scientists have been looking for ways to replenish their numbers as a possible long-term treatment or even cure for the condition. A team of researchers recently took a step closer to that reality, genetically altering another type of pancreatic cell to produce and release insulin in response to high blood sugar.
The researchers engineered ductal cells, which—as some previous studies had found—occasionally transform into beta cells all on their own. This is an unusual phenomenon among cells in adult bodies, which tend to be firmly fixed in their identities, and it hinted to the scientists that these ductal cells would be a good place to start.
Scientists previously had no clue what genes were driving this metamorphosis, said Jian Li, a postdoctoral researcher at Harvard Medical School who led the recent study in Science Translational Medicine. The researchers therefore took an approach called a genetic screen, which involves breaking little bits of DNA all across the genome to see which are important for a certain biological process. It’s a bit like individually removing pieces of a car engine without a schematic and seeing what breaks to learn which components are involved in delivering fuel or are essential for steering.
Through this process, the researchers found that taking out a gene called ALDH3B2 turned ductal cells into beta-like cells at a higher rate. Without the genetic alteration, fewer than 1 percent of ductal cells spontaneously took on a beta-cell-like state, but when ALDH3B2 was silenced, that proportion increased to about 8.5 percent.
Those initial experiments were performed on human cells in a dish, which the researchers then transplanted into mice with diabetes. Human insulin began circulating in the mice, and the animals’ glucose levels dropped to near-normal levels. These effects persisted for six weeks.
Science has previously explored some gene therapies for diabetes with the hopes of offering long-term relief. For example, a clinical trial launched earlier this year is taking the creative approach of equipping muscle cells with the genetic instructions to make insulin. Other emerging treatments aim to generate new insulin-producing cells in the laboratory and then transplant them into the patient.
This comes with a few risks, namely activation of the immune system. This new study points to another possibility: harnessing the cells that already exist in the pancreas and causing them to change function by turning off some of the genetic switches that maintain their identity.
That method also has its own hurdles, one of the most important of which is ensuring that only the target cells are edited. ALDH3B2 is used by many cells in the body, not just in the pancreas, so precision is important to prevent unforeseen complications.
There’s also a major lingering question: How is this gene involved in turning ductal cells into beta cells? “That's the part we need to verify first,” Li said. Then, “the next step is either gene therapy or to find specific small molecules to inhibit this gene to see if we can achieve a similar—or even better—effect.”
Even partial improvement could make a massive impact in the lives of the estimated 830 million people who have diabetes worldwide, including many who die each year due to related complications.

‘I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

It would be unwise to overstate things, the world being as it is, but what happened in the UK with stuffed peppers is a tragedy. You know the ones I mean: traffic light bell peppers stuffed with a cupboard raid of rice, breadcrumbs, lentils, nuts and veg – 70s stuffed peppers. The kind you might find in a wholefoods cookbook, cheerfully distended and jaunty of cap, with the physiognomy of PC Plod. I used to make them at university sometimes, my sensibilities being, as ever, several decades out of touch. I think I was trying to channel the vegetarian cookbooks my parents once had – in the years before discovering pesto, these peppers were the vegetarian’s lot. The recipes I concocted bore things like buckwheat groats, curly leaf parsley and yeast extract. To this day, I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks to such peppers and their generous cargo of junk.
It’s a shame, because stuffed vegetables so obviously do not have to be this way. Take chiles rellenos: think about what it takes not just to stuff a poblano, but to blacken it over flame, then to peel off its skin, fill with cheese, secure the seam with a toothpick, coat in flour, dip in fluffy whisked egg, and fry until the batter is crisp and puffed.
I recently decided it was time for me, too, to get on the stuffed vegetable beat. (It only took a couple of decades of recovery post my vegetarian spell.) It was late summer, and I was running out of ways to cook squash. Any allotment tender will know the feeling: the delight of the first little speckled courgette, the beauty of the flowers, the wonder that the earth could provide such riches. Then, the second wave of courgettes, then the third, then the panic of stewing, souping, roasting, baking, and pickling through the glut. You end up grating courgette into dishes it has no business being in; smuggling it into cakes, or, as I found myself thinking: “stuff these courgettes”.
So, partly because I wanted to learn how to honour nature’s bounty, and partly because aubergines were yellow-stickered in the shop, I applied myself to the stuffed vegetable arts. For help, I went cap in hand to the cookbooks of the dolma belt – an area of stuffed-vegetable excellence, which maps nicely on to the contours of the Ottoman empire, from the Balkans across Turkiye and Palestine, through West Asia and to Iran. Calling this a region doesn’t exactly make sense – it spans time zones, languages and continents. But across this swath, there has been a Cambrian explosion of stuffed peppers, aubergines, summer squash, courgettes, cabbage and vine leaves. It makes the British stuffed pepper seem like a half-formed thought.
So, I learned a little about texture, construction and contrast. I fried onions and minced beef, and mixed them with spiced maftoul, then spooned this into halved, hollowed-out peppers. I repurposed a few little globe squash, the size of closed fists, and filled them with lamb, bulgur and handfuls of soft herbs. I learned from Palestinian cookbooks (nowhere does stuffed vegetables quite like Palestine) that a special manakra – a long, curved blade, great for coring things and much easier to use than a knife – provides a first line of defence against mid-cook meltdowns. And crucially, I learned that no matter the fateful and seemingly inherent vegetarian-ness of stuffed vegetables over here, meat is probably the best stuffing you can use. So much pain could have been avoided, I think, if the ancestry of British stuffed veg came through the dolma belt, and not through macrobiotic cookbooks.
The downside of all this, of course, is that such dishes take for ever. But now that the evenings are longer and summer FOMO is thankfully done, it’s a good time for such kitchen projects. In previous years, it’s been starting on the Christmas cake or ill-advisedly trying to reverse engineer a Mr Kipling fondant fancy. This year, it’s the seemingly modest – and actually momentous – challenge of stuffed veg dishes which, under ideal circumstances, require an entire production line of volunteer peelers, corers, rollers, folders, idlers, pot watchers and gossipers to produce.
Top of the list: Kurdish yapraxi silq – the Noah’s ark of stuffed vegetables: an elaborate layering of simmered, translucent, onion layer sheaths; tiger-striped and hollowed out courgettes; aubergines and tomatoes, their bellies gouged; and rolled up swiss chard leaves. I found the recipe in Pary Baban’s delightful Nandên. I’ve already made one of her other yaprax (stuffed vegetable) recipes: aubergine and cucumber filled with rice and minced lamb, then – gorgeously, surgically – sewn shut with needle and thread. This is the level we’re at. I will report back when I have finished constructing this yapraxi silq, in this lifetime or the next.

====================================================================================================

My Instagram reels addiction has ruined my ability to have a conversation. But can I get it back? | Hannah Ewens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

It’s never pleasant to confront something unflattering about yourself, particularly when you catch yourself in the act. Recently I was mid-conversation with a stranger at a party, when I suddenly became conscious of my internal monologue: yes, hurry up, get to the point, you’re going to say this, then that, and what is the takeaway here?
This wasn’t the first time I had noticed a shift in my real-life interactions. Over the preceding months, I had felt tired, even irritated, when loved ones so much as veered close to an anecdote or detail about their lives that I thought I had already heard. During interviews I conducted as a journalist, it sometimes took a heroic effort to concentrate on conversations once they failed to be truly stimulating. Ordinarily I am endlessly curious about people, but I couldn’t ignore a creeping feeling that my attention was waning.
The source of the problem was clear to me. At the beginning of the year, I became freelance and started working from home full-time, and I found myself constantly scrolling social media. I hadn’t noticed before how much Instagram aggressively forces short-form video into our feeds in the form of “reels”, but now they were the majority of what I was seeing. Hours of my “working day” were spent watching them. It seemed obvious that this content, algorithmically fed to cater to my interests and concerns, had started competing with real-life interactions. Subconsciously, I had begun to expect conversations to provide speed, relevance and the ability for me to skip through at will.
It would be highly unusual if this was only happening to me. TikTok and Instagram have boomed in popularity since the pandemic. My very offline boyfriend, who doesn’t use social media, thought what I was saying was horrific – as disgusting as me watching videos on 2x speed, as I am wont to do.
It has long been argued that “digital dualism” is a false construct – there is no real separation between offline and online spheres. So of course an increase in digesting short-form content could affect how we relate to people in real life. It was a relief when a friend told me she got addicted to reels and now can’t bear irrelevant information in conversation. And it was even better when another said it would be nice to be able to skip through and speed up interactions in the way you do reel to reel.
Short-form video weakens our ability to hold an intention after an interruption, according to one 2023 study, which is troubling when you consider that to have a conversation you must remember information and hold your intentions to reply. One of its authors, user experience researcher Francesco Chiossi, said that my experience is a perfect example of the impatience that watching too much short-form content engenders. “The deeper we try to go, the more information we have to retain and the more impatient we become,” he says. To compensate, he adds, we switch topics, interrupt, drift off or pick up the pace because we (perhaps falsely) believe we’ve already processed what is being said.
With the threat of losing my real-life friends in mind, I emailed Marissa Fond, sociolinguistics professor at Georgetown University, for advice on what someone should do if they find their attention waning during everyday conversations. “They could take a deep breath, notice that they’re participating in a practice they don’t like, slow down and try to engage their curiosity about the content or person involved,” she replied. In other words, retrain yourself for the friction and pace of life, dummy.
I’ve tried mentally berating myself when I clock I’m getting irritated or distracted. I remind myself that this is exactly (probably) why some tech overlords don’t let their own kids have social media. My next step will be deleting the apps on days off. After all, it’s true that the best conversations are nothing like content. They aren’t all sparky like electricity but take on the form of water. They allow me and another person to meander, to seep into places we have no business being, to become emotional. We push and pull and create a unique tide between us. There is no “hook”. No frenetic pace. Any clear takeaway is often submerged by more questions. Sometimes it’s boring but often it can be quite beautiful – if you have the patience for it.
Hannah Ewens is a freelance editor and writer, and the author of Fangirls: Scenes From Modern Music Culture

Police received a call at around 12:45am GMT on Sunday about “three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the [RAF Fairford] air base” in the west of England.

“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said in a statement. “A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles while the Army’s Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit conduct examinations”, she added.
“As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place.”

“We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our port and working with the British worked out great… We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” the US President said.
The US mission to the UK issued a security alert on Sunday encouraging Americans “to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security. Local authorities are evacuating certain residents in the area out of an abundance of caution.”
“We remind US citizens that UK authorities rate the threat of terrorism in the UK as severe”, the security alert noted.
In March, three US B-1B Lancer bombers touched down at RAF Fairford after what is believed to be the first US strike mission against Iran launched from a British base, during the war on Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful military force that operates alongside the country’s regular armed forces, warned in July that bases used to launch attacks on Iran could be treated as legitimate targets.
Authorities have not linked Sunday’s arrests to Iran or said RAF Fairford was a target.

- The U.S. Army's Emerging Threat Replication Program flight-tested a PDW C100X drone at Fort Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania, on Sept. 25.
- Testing covered inert training munitions, thermal systems and possible use in future training scenarios.
A U.S. Army program that builds realistic enemy threats for training flew Performance Drone Works’ C100X drone at Fort Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania, on Sept. 25, testing its thermal camera, its ability to drop inert practice munitions and whether it could be used in future training scenarios.
The flights were carried out by members of the Emerging Threat Replication Program, the U.S. Army said in a photo release from the Pennsylvania National Guard’s training center. The Army did not say what results the testing produced, how many aircraft were flown or when the drone might be added to training events. It also did not describe how the C100X differs from the company’s C100.
PDW builds the C100 as a multi-role quadcopter that can scout, drop munitions, carry cargo or launch smaller first-person-view drones. The U.S. Army has bought C100s for units under a company-level small drone requirement, and soldiers have flown them at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California. A PDW official said in January that this effort was laying the groundwork for the Army’s planned Medium Range Reconnaissance drone program, expected to start at the end of fiscal 2026 and into 2027.
In July, during the Army’s Project Convergence Capstone 6 experiment at Fort Irwin, soldiers fitted a C100 with a standardized weapon attachment kit and a conversion kit that lets it drop mortar rounds.
Fort Indiantown Gap, the Pennsylvania National Guard’s 17,000-acre headquarters, has become one of the Army’s main drone training sites. Its Unmanned Aircraft System Training and Innovation Facility was chosen as the primary site for training soldiers on drones bought under the U.S. Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, and the post has restricted airspace up to 26,000 feet (7,900 m).
The installation has also rebuilt several ranges for drone and counter-drone training this year, adding a mock village made from shipping containers for first-person-view drone pilots and ranges where troops shoot at clay targets and drones with shotguns and machine guns to simulate incoming one-way attack drones. Range staff said they are working to make training match the drones soldiers now face in combat.

“The psychological barrier of 2,500–3,000 kilometers has already been overcome. Moreover, everything depends on the pace of technological development,” noted “Madyar.”

At the same time, according to Brovdi, despite technological advancements, people remain the most important asset.
“Our people are our most important asset, our number one priority. First, we have far fewer people than the Russian Federation. Second, our tactics are different: the enemy attacks, we defend ourselves. We defend ourselves with drones; they attack with manpower,” he added.
The commander of the Unmanned Aerial Systems Command stated that Ukraine currently produces about 10 million drones per year, and “we are constantly increasing the scale of their deployment.”
“My unit alone—which makes up 2.5% of the Ukrainian army—carries out over 250,000 combat sorties per month. A quarter of a million per month, and that number is growing,” added “Madyar.”

ISLAMABAD Pakistan’s cybercrime authorities have arrested a 17-year-old boy who allegedly turned to an artificial intelligence platform for guidance on poisoning his father, officials said.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) said information received from the FBI indicated that the teenager was allegedly planning to kill his father and had sought information from the AI platform Claude about carrying out the plan.
The NCCIA said in a statement that the suspect was influenced by the popular US television series Breaking Bad and had asked various AI chatbots for information on how to produce methanol.
An NCCIA investigating officer told the BBC that the suspect was still being questioned and that the case remained under investigation. The officer said the arrest was made on the basis of the suspect’s digital footprints.
According to the First Information Report (FIR) registered in the case, the FBI information was conveyed to the NCCIA by Pakistan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry through an official communication on September 22.
Suspect allegedly used Claude AI to research toxins
The information alleged that a user of Claude AI had been conducting detailed research into lethal toxic substances, their use, and potential effects.
The FIR said digital evidence shared with Pakistani authorities indicated that the user had allegedly made an initial attempt to poison his father by mixing laboratory-grade methanol into his food. After the attempt failed, he allegedly sought further information from the AI about abrin, a toxic substance derived from rosary peas.
Investigators also seized an iPhone 15 Pro Max during a search of the suspect’s home, along with several chemicals, including methanol, ethylene glycol, hydrochloric acid, potassium hydroxide, and sodium hydroxide. The FIR identified the substances as potential chemicals that could be used in preparing poison.
According to the preliminary report, the FBI also shared the email address linked to the account and information on multiple IP addresses with Pakistani authorities. Using these details, NCCIA Lahore began tracing the suspect digitally and verifying his identity through the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) system.
Suspect received chemicals from Australia, Islamabad
The suspect allegedly sourced chemicals from Australia and Islamabad before preparing a poisonous mixture at his home. The NCCIA spokesperson said the teenager reportedly administered the substance to his father on one occasion, but the alleged poisoning attempt was unsuccessful.
According to NCCIA director Hassam Bin Iqbal, the suspect had an interest in chemistry. His aim was to experiment with producing biodiesel from methanol by using sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide in the process. “After that, the suspect turned to AI and asked what reaction methanol would cause in the human body if ingested, and what effects it would have on the liver,” he said.
The case highlights a growing concern over the misuse of artificial intelligence, particularly by young users who may turn to AI tools for information that can have serious real-world consequences.

'I hate the word coexistence': Yoseph Haddad’s plan to bring Arab-Israeli partnership to Knesset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:57:11 UTC
17:57:11 KST

Arab-Israeli partnership has emerged as a key issue ahead of Israel’s first elections since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks.
Yoseph Haddad, a leading Arab-Israeli activist, is running for the Knesset in the second slot on the new People of Israel party list, behind chairman Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter. The right-wing party has endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In a recent interview with The Jerusalem Post, Haddad spoke about the importance of Arab-Israeli partnership, his political redlines, and his vision for bringing new faces into the Knesset following October 7.
“We’re going to be the surprise of this election,” Haddad told the Post.
He said he firmly believes the party will pass well over the threshold, securing its spot in the next Knesset.
Recent polling has shown the People of Israel party hovering just above the electoral threshold, at around five seats.
Haddad is a vocal supporter of Israel, advocating consistently for the country on news outlets and social media. He has also gone on numerous international speaking tours.
Especially after the October 7 attacks, Haddad’s online platform grew rapidly, and he became a prominent voice on social networks, often appearing as a guest on TV programs across the country.
Haddad was seriously wounded in the Second Lebanon War in 2006, while serving in the IDF.
He established a nonprofit foundation, Together Vouch for Each Other. It calls for connecting Arab society with Israeli society at large and for finding solutions to the issues of Arab society.
“As an Arab, as a Christian, as an Israeli, with all those identities that strengthen each other, I’m entering politics and bringing everything I’ve been doing over the last 10 years into Israeli politics,” Haddad said of his decision to run on the People of Israel Knesset slate.
Jewish-Arab partnership over coexistence
When asked about coexistence between Arabs and Jews in Israel, Haddad immediately rejected the term, saying he prefers to speak of “partnership.”
“I hate this word, ‘coexistence,’” Haddad said. “You’re not going anywhere. I’m not going anywhere. You don’t like me, I don’t like you – but since we’re not going anywhere, let’s live in coexistence.”
He said that the term “coexistence” may be more appropriate for describing Israel’s relationship with neighboring countries such as Jordan and Egypt, but that when it comes to Arab citizens of Israel, he prefers the concept of partnership.
“Partnership is something that exists in Israel,” he said, before giving an example of what he described as Jewish-Arab partnership during the October 7 attacks.
Haddad pointed to an Arab Israeli from Rahat who was working as a bus driver at the Supernova music festival on October 7. Haddad said he helped save more than 30 Israelis, all of them Jewish.
“When he was asked why he didn’t run away, he said, ‘I’m an Israeli, and there were Israelis there. Why would I run away?’” Haddad explained. “That’s partnership, not coexistence.”
Combating Arab sector crime rates
On the rise in crime in Arab society during the government’s term, Haddad said that while he largely disagrees with the approach of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police, he believes responsibility for the situation also lies with leaders in Arab society.
“We have shared responsibility,” Haddad said. “I know that my country has responsibility. I also know that the leaders of Arab society and Arab society have responsibility as well.
“Bottom line, you have hundreds of Arab Israelis who were killed because of crime. The office that’s supposed to make sure that those numbers do not spike and arrive at that place didn’t do the job.”
Haddad also said Arab community leaders have a responsibility to cooperate with authorities and work to improve conditions in Arab society.
“They’re not doing it. They’re responsible, too,” he said. “Hopefully, when I reach the goal, and we will be as close as possible to where the decisions are being made, we’re going to affect them [the decisions], and we’re going to change them – including the situation with Arab-Israeli society in terms of protection and violence. That I promise you.”
New faces in the Knesset
The party has sought to bring together people who were never in the Knesset or part of the political or security failures surrounding the October 7 attacks.
“We’re the only party in Israel today that has only new faces, new spirit, new people,” Haddad said.
Despite the party’s emphasis on bringing new faces into politics, it has backed Netanyahu for prime minister rather than rival candidate Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the Yashar party.
When asked whether this support for Netanyahu was contradictory, Haddad said there is an “ideological gap” between him and Eisenkot.
He said that, ideally, he would want entirely new candidates for prime minister, to replace Netanyahu, but he argued that such a scenario is not realistic.
“What I’m saying is, look at the map. If it was up to me, all 120 [members of Knesset would go home. Let’s bring a full new 120. We’re saying that realistically it’s not possible,” Haddad said.
“So I’m acting only based on what’s going on and based on the fact that we are a right-wing Zionist patriotic party.”
Arab party redlines
Regarding the two main Arab-led lists running in the election – the Joint List and Ra’am – Haddad drew a firm redline against partnering with either party and sharply criticized their positions.
The Joint List includes Hadash, Ta’al and Balad, which agreed to run together.
“All those three different parties do not even agree with each other. They’re running together only because it’s the only way that they can pass the threshold and actually have something. But between them, there is even hatred,” Haddad said.
“All of them are terror supporters,” he added, saying he believes the parties should be barred from running in the election.
Haddad also criticized Ra’am chairman Mansour Abbas, claiming he presents different positions to the Israeli public in Hebrew than in Arabic.
“Because what Mansour Abbas is telling you in Hebrew is not what he’s telling me in Arabic [through the media],” Haddad said.
He also criticized Abbas’s decision to place former Yesh Atid MK and former senior police official Yoav Segalovitz second on Ra’am’s slate.
Segalovitz was the first Jewish candidate to run on the party’s list, and the decision to add him to the slate has been widely seen as a way for Ra’am to be viewed as a more viable coalition partner in a post-October 7 reality.
Haddad argued that Segalovitz was brought onto the list to “shield” Abbas from criticism over his positions on Hamas.
“He was brought as a shield to Mansour Abbas because Mansour Abbas can’t say that Hamas is a terrorist organization. Pathetic. Sad,” Haddad said.
“Segalovitz is the useful idiot of Ra’am,” he added.
Haddad said he believed the People of Israel party could win support from Arab-Israeli voters.
“I still have a goal of taking two seats from the Arab votes,” Haddad said about his plans to pass the threshold.
Plans to improve Israel’s public diplomacy
Haddad also said he plans to become public diplomacy minister in the next government.
The current government agreed to shut down the ministry in 2023, shortly after the October 7 attacks.
“It’s going to be a big office, not because I want a big office,” Haddad said regarding the necessity of reviving the ministry.
“Because of anti-Israeli propaganda, terror supporters, pro-Palestinians, the IDF shut down multiple operations – operations that could have helped our security, Israeli citizens’ security, and could have probably avoided casualties on our side.”
Haddad said that he wants to be the “shield” for the IDF and Defense Ministry.
“Every week I will have a press conference in Hebrew for Israelis, to explain to them what’s happening; [a press conference] in Arabic for the Arab world, to also attack every lie they write about us. And [a press conference for] the Western world in English.”
“Because I want to show the hypocritical world how they are acting when it comes to us, and how they’re acting when it comes to the rest of the world.
“And how they’re talking about only one side of the story, with no facts, [while] the other side, with the facts, is completely ignored,” Haddad continued.
Haddad said he also has a plan for his first 100 days in office, which he said he would unveil soon.
“I’m proud of my country, and I’m proud of Israeli society,” Haddad said.
“And I’m proud to tell you that there are so many great people here who support me, support my way.”

Private schools in Riyadh moved to remote learning from Sunday through Thursday, October 1, without publicly explaining the decision, amid renewed Houthi threats against the Saudi capital.
Notices sent directly to parents said in-person classes would be suspended and replaced by remote learning. One notice distributed by Al-Rowad schools said classes would be held through the Classera platform from 16 to 20 Rabi' al-Thani 1448, corresponding to September 27 through October 1.
As of Sunday morning, the official website of the Riyadh education administration had not announced a blanket suspension of in-person classes at all schools in the city. It therefore remained unclear whether several private institutions had coordinated the move, had received instructions directly from authorities, or had made the decisions independently.
The academic calendar shows that the current week was scheduled to be a regular school week following the Saudi National Day holiday on September 23 and 24.
The notices have drawn particular attention amid an escalation in tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. On Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition announced that air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed two drones launched by the Houthis toward the Riyadh area. Two ballistic missiles launched toward Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia were also intercepted.
Not first time Riyadh targeted by Houthis
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said the forces were "tracking and monitoring missile and unmanned aerial vehicle threats toward the kingdom."
This is not the first time Riyadh itself has been targeted during the current escalation. On September 19, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones toward "sensitive targets" in the Saudi capital.
Saudi Arabia later announced that it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh and accused the Houthis of attempting to target civilians and civilian sites in the city, which is home to more than eight million people.
No confirmation as to why change happened
The timing is particularly unusual because the threat to the capital renewed over the weekend. According to the Saudi-led coalition, the two drones headed toward the Riyadh area were intercepted before reaching their targets.
At the same time, civil defense authorities issued alerts in Khamis Mushait and Abha. No similar alert was reported in Riyadh, and there were no reports of casualties or damage resulting from the latest interceptions.
Saudi schools routinely shift to remote learning during emergencies, and similar decisions have been made in recent months because of severe weather conditions. In previous cases, however, Riyadh's education administration issued an official announcement explaining the reason for the move.
As of Sunday morning, no public explanation had been issued. Therefore, no official confirmation linked the switch to remote learning directly to the Houthi threat.

Former Ukrainian defense minister unveils 'Army of Robots' to accelerate autonomous warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:56:31 UTC
17:56:31 KST

Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on Sunday announced that he was launching a new defense tech initiative called “Army of Robots,” modeled on the success of his Army of Drones project that was launched in 2022.
Fedorov was controversially dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July and has since turned his attention to defense tech, launching a fund and his own company.
According to Fedorov, the concept would see humanoid robots operating autonomously alongside unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), and other unmanned weapons systems.
"There will be humanoid robots that will perform simple tasks: reloading a machine gun, replacing a battery, or installing a sensor. These are things a robot can be taught quickly and carry out after a rapid deployment to the battlefield,” he said at the launch.
The broader concepts would see humanoid robots playing active combat roles on the battlefield, including engaging hostile forces, reducing the need to expose human troops to danger.
While still an early-stage initiative, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Fedorov aims to have a humanoid robot kill a Russian soldier within the first six months of the program’s launch.
“Russia is quickly copying technologies and putting them into production. The answer is not more people on the front lines, but full autonomy: robots that fight, scout, evacuate, and supply. Ukraine needs its own Manhattan Project for Physical AI,” it reads on the initiative’s website.
Defense innovation hub
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have dramatically expanded their use of unmanned systems in 2026, placing more than 590,000 drone orders through the government’s Brave1 Market since January, according to new figures released by the country’s Defense Ministry.
Interceptor drones, designed to hunt Russian reconnaissance UAVs and counter Shahed-type one-way attack drones, have become the most frequently ordered category.
Copter-type FPV kamikaze drones remain the second-most requested, while fixed-wing kamikaze UAVs have shown the fastest growth, with peak monthly orders reaching six times the January level.
Bomber drones account for the largest share of spending, and “mothership” drones that are used to deploy smaller UAVs rank among the most expensive technologies.
Brave1, launched in 2023 by the Ukrainian government, fast-tracks military innovation by funding developers, testing and certifying new platforms, and connecting them directly with front-line units. The wartime pipeline has moved ideas to prototypes to deployment in weeks rather than months or years.
Last week, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said that 650 additional types of drones had been accepted in the army with strike copters accounting for the largest number (238) of newly codified models. Another 231 fiber optic platforms were accepted, followed by 42 new interceptor drones, 32 mid-strikes UAVs that strike Russian logistic targets, and nine deep-strike drones that strike far into Russian territory.
Completed combat missions increase ePoints, driving procurement
Brave1 uses a digital marketplace and ePoints system to let combat units acquire drones, unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), and electronic-‑warfare tools based on completed combat missions including confirmed reconnaissance, strike operations, and robotic logistics or evacuation tasks. These points can be exchanged for drones, unmanned ground vehicles, and electronic warfare equipment.
Manufacturers can also track how their equipment is used on the battlefield, providing quick combat feedback.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, June marked the highest monthly procurement volume to date, exceeding UAH 5 billion (about $111 million), and average delivery time for stocked items fell to eight days.
Like drones, Ukraine has rapidly expanded its use of UGVs, with dozens of companies producing systems for logistics, reconnaissance, and strike missions. UGVs now appear across multiple brigades and are used daily in trench and urban operations to reduce the risk to soldiers.
Ukrainian media have reported that the number of units using UGVs has increased from 67 in late 2025 to 167 by the spring of 2026.
International partnerships expand
Ukraine launched Brave International in June, establishing a framework for international initiatives, including UNITE Brave NATO, Brave Norway, Brave France, Brave Germany, and Brave Lithuania. The budget for the first programs under Brave International exceeded €100 million already in June, and all competitions are open to Ukrainian and foreign companies.
The initiative is a central aspect of Ukraine’s broader strategy to become a hub for defense innovation. Brave1 supports thousands of tech solutions for the front lines and has attracted interest from global investors and partners as small start-ups have become instrumental in holding off Russian forces.
In July, Airbus Defence and Space became the first Western industrial partner to join Brave1. Canada has also announced plans to build its own defense-drone marketplace using the Brave1 model as a foundation.

Russian Attacks on Kyiv Kill 1, Injure at Least 10 Since Saturday
Putin made similar claims on Friday, Sept. 25, telling journalists that Russia was “not preparing for any military action against Europe,” while, in the same remarks, he accused the Baltic states of violating the rights of Russian speakers.
“We already know how to respond, and we have developed a certain approach to this,” Putin said according to EU Perspectives. “We respond on humanitarian grounds and within the framework of international law.”
However, Putin gave no examples of the alleged violations and did not say what that response would look like.
But, the Kremlin has long used claims of protecting Russian-speaking populations to lay the groundwork for hostile actions against its neighbors. The same thing happened in Ukraine.
Although frequently used to minimize its aggression, Russia’s rhetoric consistently reflects its long-standing hostility toward the West.
Putin also mocked security concerns in Estonia as “political clowning.”
Two weeks earlier, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened to wipe Lithuania “off the map” if nuclear weapons were deployed there, claiming NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defense.
Hybrid ‘incidents’ or direct attacks?
Europe’s defense build-up comes as a response to Russian hybrid attacks, which have, over the past few months, nearly doubled and visibly intensified.
Russia’s campaign of drone incursions, sabotage and cyberattacks against EU infrastructure has increased to the point that several EU member states now describe it as direct attacks.
Lithuania has recently strengthened defenses around critical infrastructure, while the US confirmed a new troop rotation to the country this week.
After weeks of escalation between Moscow and Berlin, the German and Russian foreign ministers met for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Late August, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow unexpectedly – for the first time during his post as a chief – to allegedly deter the Kremlin from attacking a NATO country.
During the same summit in New York, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia might target another European country with drones, missiles or even a ground operation in an effort to fracture Western unity and distract from its heavy losses on the battlefield.
Diplomacy stalls
Lavrov’s comments came as Kyiv and Washington stepped up efforts to end the war, urging the Kremlin to join the table for trilateral talks.
On Wednesday, 51 countries signed a joint statement, urging Moscow to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
On Friday, Putin again pinned the blame on Kyiv for stalled diplomacy.
Zelensky rejected the framing just a day after, saying that Putin always finds an excuse not to meet or attend a trilateral discussion.
Ukrainian authorities consistently push for a direct meeting with and negotiations with Russian diplomats.
So far, the Kremlin has rebuffed every proposal – even Zelensky’s public letter to Putin in June, in which he proposed a face-to-face meeting and said he was ready for a full ceasefire.

87 companies join U.S. Space Command’s third wargame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:51:28 UTC
17:51:28 KST

- U.S. Space Command held its third APOLLO INSIGHT wargame with commercial companies on Sept. 23, focusing on very low Earth orbit and cislunar space.
- The command said 217 participants from 87 companies registered, and a fourth exercise is scheduled for Dec. 16.
U.S. Space Command held the third of four wargames with commercial space companies on Sept. 23, this time focused on spacecraft that operate outside the orbits most satellites use today, including very low Earth orbit and the space between Earth and the Moon.
The tabletop exercise, part of a series called APOLLO INSIGHT, brought military planners and industry together to work through several scenarios. Before the event, the command said 217 people from 87 companies had registered, including 24 companies that had not taken part in the first two rounds. The command did not say which companies attended or describe the scenarios in detail.
“For this upcoming exercise we currently have 217 participants registered representing 87 different companies, including 24 new additions since our first and second events,” said Cmdr. Heather Thomas, chief of the command’s commercial integration branch, before the exercise.
The exercise was moderated by retired Brig. Gen. Bruce McClintock, a senior policy researcher at RAND. He said the discussion centered on companies developing what he called non-Keplerian space capabilities. That term describes spacecraft whose paths do not follow the simple, predictable orbits set by gravity alone, for example because they keep firing engines to hold a position or because they move under the pull of both Earth and the Moon.
McClintock said several companies are making progress in very low Earth orbit, which sits below the altitudes where most satellites fly, and in cislunar space, the region between Earth and the Moon.
“The problem sets examined during APOLLO INSIGHT could be tested through combined maneuvers to further develop TTPs across the space enterprise,” said retired Brig. Gen. Bruce McClintock, referring to tactics, techniques and procedures.
U.S. Space Command, which plans and runs U.S. military operations in space, launched the series this year to bring commercial companies into its planning. The first exercise, held March 23 in Colorado Springs, Colorado, focused on the threat of weapons of mass destruction in space. The second, on June 24, also in Colorado Springs, dealt with maneuver warfare in space.
Gen. Stephen Whiting, the command’s commander, said in an Aug. 30 interview with Fed Gov Today that the military cannot handle space operations on its own.
“The U.S. commercial space industry is a massive advantage for our nation, and we’ve got to be able to leverage their cost curves and their innovation points,” said Gen. Stephen Whiting.
Whiting also said the command needs to work more closely with allies and commercial firms on tracking objects in space, and to use artificial intelligence and machine learning to close gaps in surveillance.
The fourth and final exercise of the year is scheduled for Dec. 16 at the Aerospace Corporation, which hosted each of the earlier events. Thomas said the command plans to keep running commercial integration exercises into 2027.

RAF Fairford is home to the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. According to the unit’s website, the base serves as the “preferred forward operating location for bombers in Europe” for U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.
During the latest U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, several American aircraft took off from the base for strike missions against the Islamic Republic, although those operations were very limited. Security at RAF Fairford has been significantly tightened in recent days, with roadblocks and armed police preventing access to the base and emergency vehicles stationed nearby. “Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces,” the IRGC said in July.
That same month, according to a report in The Telegraph, Iran launched an unprecedented cyberattack against Britain that knocked a power station offline for four days.
Witnesses and British media reports said security measures at RAF Fairford had been significantly increased in recent days. Roadblocks were set up near the base, armed police staffed them and prevented access, while emergency vehicles were stationed nearby. Around 30 emergency vehicles were also seen around the base Sunday morning, including ambulances and fire engines.
Britain’s Daily Mail reported that a “Delta” alert had been declared at RAF Fairford, the highest threat level the U.S. Department of Defense can impose, although there has so far been no confirmation of that report.
The newspaper also reported that security had simultaneously been increased at other U.S. bases in Britain, while RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk was placed on “Charlie” alert, the second-highest threat level.

Tattoo culture researcher: Women have always been the main source of inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:50:00 UTC
17:50:00 KST

Tattoo culture researcher: Women have always been the main source of inspiration
Tattoo artist and researcher of Estonian tattoo culture Oskar Poll told ETV that while tattoos during the Soviet era often featured maritime motifs and women, the range of subjects has since expanded considerably.
Oskar Poll has been tattooing for about 10 years. "A solid eight years," he said with a smile. "The first two were a trial period."
His studies are also closely tied to tattooing: he wrote both his bachelor's and master's theses on the history of tattooing in Estonia and is now pursuing the same subject for his doctoral dissertation. Poll earned his bachelor's degree in graphic art from the Estonian Academy of Arts. While there, he began photographing Soviet-era tattoos, a project that later developed into his master's thesis. Poll approached people on the street to find tattoos to photograph.
"Sometimes I felt like a stalker," he said. "I'd spot someone with a tattoo from a distance, follow them, explain what I was doing and ask how, when and where they got it and whether I could take a picture. Eventually, I got to the point where I could tell what kind of tattoo a certain type of person would have."
For his master's thesis, Poll examined, among other things, which tattoos were most popular during the Soviet era and what they meant. According to Poll, maritime imagery was the most common at the time, including anchors, ships, seagulls and similar motifs. Images of women were also popular.
"Women have always been the main source of inspiration in tattooing. In the West, tattooing was very male-dominated for a long time because it was associated with male-dominated subcultures and men would have images of women tattooed on themselves," he explained.
For his doctoral dissertation, Poll has moved on to the transition period. He is studying how Estonia's first professional tattoo artists began working in the country starting in the 1990s.
"I'm focusing on how the first studios and tattoo artists emerged here, where the machines and other equipment came from and where the idea of becoming a tattoo artist came from because for a long time, that kind of job simply didn't exist," Poll said.
The history of tattooing in Estonia has not previously been studied in this way. According to Poll, that is both interesting and daunting. "Everything you say and do is what people will later either accept as the truth or argue with you about."
Comparing Soviet-era tattoos with those of today, Poll said the main difference is the sheer range of choices available.
"Back then, there were certain set images: you'd see skulls, roses, cats, military symbols and anchors. Now the range of places to draw motifs from is so broad, especially thanks to the internet. And the tools used are certainly different as well. Today we have machines. During the Soviet era, there were homemade machines in prisons at one point, but before that, it was a needle and ordinary ink," he said.
Tattoos have also become popular among women. "During the Soviet era and before that, it was more of an exception," Poll said.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Marcus Turovski
Source: "OP"

Can Iran shift trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:49:32 UTC
17:49:32 KST

Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
Iran is looking for alternatives to export its oil as the US blockades its southern ports.
Tehran, Iran – With Iran’s southern ports subject to a United States naval blockade, Tehran is looking for alternatives to export oil and import goods. The Caspian Sea on Iran’s northern coast is seen as one portal for Iran to the outside world.
Recent efforts at the United Nations to end the deadlock between Iran and the US appear to have failed as US President Donald Trump said Tehran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was unacceptable.
With no breakthrough in sight on ending the war launched by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28, Tehran is making adjustments to export oil and import essential goods. But maritime trade via the Caspian Sea has its own logistical challenges, experts said.
Caspian challenges
The Caspian Sea, the world’s largest landlocked body of water, is shared by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. Shipping on the sea has been increasingly challenged by declining water levels in recent years.
In April, UN Environment Programme Executive Director Inger Andersen said Caspian water levels had dropped by about 2 metres (6.6ft) since the 1990s. Sea levels are projected to recede by an additional 8 to 21 metres (26ft to 69ft) by the end of the century.
Shahram Fadakar, director general of the Iranian Department of Environment’s Office for Coastal and Marine Ecosystem Protection, told local media last week that water levels have been dropping by more than 20cm (7.9 inches) annually over the past two to three years. This could affect trade between all Caspian countries, including Iran.
This month, Masoud Polmeh, secretary-general of the Shipping Association of Iran, told state-linked media that Iran’s northern ports could once handle berth vessels weighing up to 6,000 tonnes. Due to reduced water levels, they can now handle only 4,000-tonne vessels.
Iranian ships entering the Caspian Sea via Russia’s Volga River have become stuck due to low water levels, sometimes remaining stationary for days and weeks at a time before their crews are rescued.
“Fortunately, that hasn’t happened in our ports,” Polmeh added.
Northern bound
The vast majority of Iran’s maritime trade has been conducted via its southern ports, but the US naval embargo and air strikes on infrastructure are forcing Tehran to shift trade to the Caspian Sea and its land borders.
While there are currently no active military attacks against interests in the north, Vali Kaleji, an independent writer and researcher in Iran on Russia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, said changes in logistical operations have put huge strains on Iran’s land borders.
At the Norduz border crossing with Armenia, as many as 1,800 trucks queue for several days at a time to enter Iran. At other terminals, wait times range from 10 to 15 days to enter Iran although Kaleji said this is not due solely to freight shifting to Iran’s roads.
“Limited terminal capacity, customs procedures, road infrastructure and ongoing construction projects have also contributed to the congestion. Meanwhile, sanctions on Iranian airlines and the resulting influx of passengers towards Iran’s land borders with Armenia and Turkey have further exacerbated problems at the border terminals,” Kaleji told Al Jazeera.
The eastern Caspian rail route provides a connection for transporting Iranian cargo to Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and China. But Iran’s rail freight connections with the South Caucasus region, which were severed during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War from 1988 to 1994, remain closed.
“The revival of the Julfa-Nakhchivan railway route, part of the Soviet-era railway network in the South Caucasus, also depends on the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, particularly the implementation of the TRIPP project,” Kaleji said, referring to a US-supported transit corridor in the region.
“Since a major share of transit and trade along the western route of the North-South Transport Corridor takes place through this route, the absence of a railway connection between Iran and the South Caucasus remains a major obstacle to accelerating and increasing the volume of trade and transit, particularly under conditions of intensified maritime blockade in the south.”
Trade obstacles
Iranian authorities have not provided details on which commodities and at what volume trade has been directed northwards, including to the Caspian ports of Anzali, Amirabad and Nowshahr. But there have been indications of such a shift, particularly with the import of essential goods, such as food.
Last month, Ports and Maritime Organization chief Mohammad Shakibi-Nasab told state-linked media that Iran’s total nominal port capacity was 300 million tonnes, only 30 million tonnes of which is linked to its northern ports.
The northern ports’ share of essential goods transport has gone up from 18 percent in the years before the US-Israel war on Iran to 30 percent today.
There are stark differences between maximum loads carried by vessels using Iran’s northern and southern ports, he said. One vessel in the south could potentially carry the cargo of 20 ships travelling on the Caspian Sea.
In early September, Hadi Haghshenas, the governor of the northern province of Gilan, said container arrivals at Caspian ports had increased by 50 percent year-on-year during the five Iranian calendar months that ended on August 22.
He also said, unlike the Port of Shahid Rajaei in southern Iran, the northern ports were closer to major cities in central Iran, such as Tehran, Isfahan and Arak. That proximity could help bring down land transport costs for imports reaching end users.
The China-Aktau-northern Iran route, which takes cargo by rail from China across Kazakhstan to Aktau, then by ship to Caspian ports and into Iran by road, could expand regional trade, Haghshenas added.
The Iranian government is trying to complete the missing sections of the Rasht-Astara railway, a strategically important project with Russia.
This would complete the western rail branch of the International North-South Transport Corridor, which passes through Iran, Azerbaijan and Russia.
Russian reliance
Tehran’s northwards shift risks an overreliance on Russia as a trading partner and exposure to the vulnerabilities of sanctions that have come with Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There have also been claims that some transferred Russian technology may be aimed at helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.
Iranian and Russian authorities have said they want to expand their military cooperation but did not comment on the latest media reports.
While Iran’s Caspian region has been less heavily targeted in US-Israeli attacks, Ukraine did attack what Tehran said was an Iranian fishing vessel in July, killing one civilian. Ukraine said it was a Russian military ship carrying military cargo to Iran.
The fact that both Russia and Iran are sanctioned and at war could complicate trade between the two countries via the Caspian route.
“Integration with Russian infrastructure adds disruption problems because it is being targeted by Ukraine, and that includes civilian retailers,” Ezana Tedla, an analyst at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, told Al Jazeera.
“Beyond the existing infrastructure, there’s also the well-established diaspora and personal networks throughout southern routes, especially in the UAE, that help Iran’s trade take place.”
With imports essentially blocked via Iran’s southern ports, authorities said barley, maize, wheat and oilseeds are priorities for northern ports.
Tedla said most of Iran’s northern-bound exports are light goods like processed food and packaging materials. Iran does not possess the port infrastructure and vessels to significantly step up imports via the Caspian.
While there was a small increase in the share of northern-bound exports in past years, this trend has plateaued since 2023.
“Iran’s valuable exports are directed towards the south and are in heavy, bulk commodities like mineral fuels and oils and iron ore, which are the easiest to convert to hard currency,” Tedla said.
“Finally, it is not clear that even if the port infrastructure was expanded, the market would be there as Iran’s northern neighbours have their own hydrocarbon and metal industries that will overlap.”

Russia Blocks Aid to Oleshky, UN Says
