The President of Kazakhstan dismissed the defense minister after 14 servicemen were killed during exercises in the Caspian Sea
Kyiv • UNN
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dismissed Dauren Kosanov and appointed Aidos Myrzakhmetov as defense minister. The decision was made after the deaths of 14 servicemen during the exercises.
President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dismissed Dauren Kossanov as defense minister on September 27. Aidos Myrzakhmetov was appointed as the new head of the ministry. This was reported by UNN, citing the official website of the president of Kazakhstan.
The personnel decisions were made against the backdrop of the deaths of 14 servicemen during exercises in the Caspian Sea.
"By decree of the Head of State, Dauren Zhumatayevich Kossanov was dismissed from the post of Minister of Defense of the Republic of Kazakhstan," the statement on the head of state's website said.
The statement did not specify the reason for the dismissal.
In a separate decree, Tokayev appointed Aidos Myrzakhmetov as defense minister, dismissing him from his previous post. Before that, Myrzakhmetov commanded the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan.
It should be noted that Kossanov's resignation was preceded by a tragedy in the Mangystau Region. On September 24, during the Khazar Korgany — 2026 naval exercises, servicemen were swept out to sea while personnel were being disembarked from the Kaysar boat. According to reports on the circumstances of the incident, the weather deteriorated sharply and the wind intensified. A total of 17 military personnel ended up in the sea. Three were rescued, while 14 died. The search operation ended on September 25 after the bodies of the last two victims were found. Kazakhstan declared this day a day of national mourning.
As part of the investigation, five officials from the Defense Ministry system were detained: the chief of staff — first deputy commander-in-chief of the Naval Forces, two commanders of military units, the commander of a marine infantry company, and the boat commander. They are suspected of negligence in the performance of their duties and violating navigation rules, which resulted in grave consequences. A government commission headed by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev was established to investigate the causes of the tragedy.
Separately, on September 26, Tokayev ordered a comprehensive inspection of the Defense Ministry, including the financial and logistical support of military units. The initial results are to be presented to the president within seven days.
On September 27, Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber announced the start of a state audit of the defense agency. The audit concerns the effectiveness of the use of budget funds and the provision of support to military units.
For reference
Dauren Kossanov headed Kazakhstan's Defense Ministry from June 8, 2025, replacing Ruslan Zhaksylykov. Previously, he served as deputy defense minister and commander-in-chief of the Air Defense Forces.

SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus
Students of the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata said on Sunday they were violently attacked after objecting to a meeting held on campus by an allegedly rightwing group, a student representative told DW.
A scuffle broke out between the students and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat (ABGP) after the student union confronted the group saying it had not been informed about the meeting and questioned the participants before the confrontation turned violent.
The students allege that members of the group attacked them with knives.
Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus.
She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion.
The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives."
Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity.
The campus remains tense, with students inside and members of the ABGP gathered outside, according to the student representative.
Modi says India follows 'zero tolerance' policy against terrorism
Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Sunday that India follows a "zero tolerance" policy against terrorism, ahead of the 10th anniversary of the 2016 strikes against targets in Pakistan.
Speaking on his "Mann Ki Baat" radio program, Modi linked the 2016 strikes, carried out after an attack that killed 19 Indian soldiers, with the 2019 Balakot airstrikes and 2025's Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message to Pakistan over the past decade.
Meanwhile, Defense Minister Rajnath Singh separately said India was prepared to carry out any strike against terrorism if anu neighboring country continued what he described as a "state policy of terrorism," the Hindustan Times reported.
Singh said India sought peace and dialogue but would not compromise on national security, according to the report.
"India wants peace, but India will not compromise on its security under any circumstances," Singh was quoted as saying by the newspaper. "India believes in dialogue. India believes in dialogue, but if any country gives shelter to terrorism against India, then the scope of dialogue ends right there."
Jaishankar meets Canadian foreign minister, says ties ready for 'higher level'
Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met with Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as the two countries attempt to rebuild frayed ties,
Jaishankar referred to the meeting as a "productive discussion" as New Delhi and Ottawa "prepare to take the relationship to a higher level."
Ties between the two countries were tested following the killing of Sikh separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in 2023, which triggered a major diplomatic dispute between India and Canada.
More than 56 killed, 1,000 houses destroyed as heavy rains lash Uttar Pradesh
At least 56 people died due to heavy rain and storms in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh over the past three days, authorities said on Sunday.
The deaths were reported across India's most populous state, where 63 districts were affected.
According to a statement by the state disaster management department, "exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh."
More than 1,000 houses were damaged, while several people were also left injured, authorities said.
The Relief Commissioner's office's statement said the state recorded 66.5 millimeters (2.62 inches) of rain between Friday and Sunday, compared to the season average of 7.6 millimeters.
Last month, heavy rainfall and thunderstorms claimed dozens of lives across India, as the country grapples with extreme weather.
Cricket: Kohli says 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last
Indian cricketer and one of the game's biggest global stars, Virat Kohli announced on Saturday that the 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last for India, as the veteran batter looks for another title.
"For me, it's the last World Cup I'm going to play for India," Kohli told broadcaster JioStar on Saturday.
The 37-year-old, who now plays only One Day International (ODI) cricket, said he was motivated to "leave everything out there" and help India win the tournament.
"And, of course, the goal is absolutely to win the World Cup and whatever it takes, I'm absolutely ready."
Kohli has scored 14,941 ODI runs and a record 54 centuries, and was part of India's 2011 World Cup-winning team. He retired from T20 internationals after India's 2024 World Cup victory and from Test cricket last year.
The 2027 ODI Cricket World Cup will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
At least 19 dead in Nagaland due to spurious liquor
At least 19 people have died in the northeastern state of Nagaland after allegedly consuming suspected spurious liquor, prompting a police probe and crackdown on illegal alcohol, local media reports said on Sunday.
Eight deaths were reported in Mokokchung district and 11 in Tuensang, while police have arrested 19 people and seized nearly 3,000 bottles of liquor.
A Special Investigation Team has been formed to trace the source and supply chain, with liquor samples sent for forensic examination, authorities said.
CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka detained by Assam Police, Dipke says
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, posted on X on Sunday that CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka has been detained by the police in the northeastern state of Assam while on a visit to the state.
Earlier, Ranka talked to reporters in Assam, where he targeted the chief minister.
"Himanta Biswa Sarma is scared that if we expose the reality of Assam's schools, the country will find out what the condition of the schools here is really like," Ranka said.
The CJP leader said the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader is "scared that people will find out how the rights of the people are being taken away in Kaziranga, and how their water, forests and land are being taken away and handed over to their corporate allies."
He accused Sarma of being scared that "people will find out how manmade floods were created in Assam, and how hundreds of people lost their lives."
Ranka also brought up the delimitation in Assam in 2023, which critics say altered demographic weights.
"We know how you redraw the boundaries of the constituencies during the assembly elections," Ranka said. "In one village, people ended up voting in three different constituencies, simply so that you could rig the election and win. But we are not people who are going to be afraid."
Protests, vandalism at Punjab's university over rape allegations
Large student protests erupted overnight on Saturday at Lovely Professional University in Punjab's Phagwara, after claims circulated on social media that a female student had allegedly been raped and subsequently died by suicide, according to reports.
Videos showed students smashing windows and flower pots, while some objects and parts of the private university building were set on fire.
However, some students posted on social media that the vandals were not university students but outsiders.
Reports also said students blocked the Jalandhar–Phagwara National Highway. Ppolice later cleared the highway.
Kapurthala Superintendent of Police Gaurav Toora said police had received no complaint or information about any rape and learned of the allegations only after reaching the campus.
Police said a report has been registered based on a students' statement, while investigators are examining the allegation and CCTV footage.
The university urged students to ignore the "rumors" and said they were safe, media reports said.

ECI frames new rules for voter roll revisions amid furor
India's Election Commission (ECI) on Saturday said all decisions concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously, amid reports of differences within the poll panel, media reports said.
At a meeting, chaired by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, held on Saturday, the commission also eased the process for voters who receive notices over discrepancies, the reports said.
According to the reports, the new mandates for those who receive notices:
- local electoral officials will visit homes to collect documents and upload them into the Election Commission's system
- hearings only in exceptional cases, preferably online
- an authorized adult family member can appear on behalf of a voter
- help desks and special enrollment drives for people who were left off electoral rolls, including first-time voters
- an independent expert would review the ECI's system for compliance with electoral laws
The ECI, while extending the deadline for claims and objections in Delhi to October 30 and in Maharashtra to October 12, said SIR had been completed in 20 states and Union territories, including Bihar and West Bengal, the reports said.

India opposition INDIA bloc to meet over voter roll revision
The opposition INDIA bloc parties are likely to meet in New Delhi on September 30 to discuss concerns over the Election Commission of India (ECI) and its Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rollsand a coordinated joint response, the Times of India newspaper reported on Saturday.
The proposed meeting comes amid growing calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after an Indian Express investigation found that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registration and electoral data.
The three commissioners are overseeing the SIR, a voter-roll revision that the ECI says aims to remove the names of deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Critics, however, say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and resulted in the removal of millions of eligible voters, potentially benefiting the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
On Friday, Congress workers staged protests across several states demanding Kumar's resignation. Police used water cannons and detained protesters in several locations as they attempted to march towards election offices.
Congress has called for an independent audit of the revision process and greater transparency over deleted and restored voters.

India news: SRFTI students violently attacked in Kolkata

SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus
Students of the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata said on Sunday they were violently attacked after objecting to a meeting held on campus by an allegedly rightwing group, a student representative told DW.
A scuffle broke out between the students and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat (ABGP) after the student union confronted the group saying it had not been informed about the meeting and questioned the participants before the confrontation turned violent.
The students allege that members of the group attacked them with knives.
Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus.
She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion.
The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives."
Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity.
The campus remains tense, with students inside and members of the ABGP gathered outside, according to the student representative.

IDF eliminates man who drove motorcycle in Noa Argamani abduction on October 7th
Israeli forces used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to reduce the risk to civilians during the airstrike on central Gaza
Israeli forces killed Saher Nidal Latfi Sakr in an airstrike Saturday in the Nuseirat area of central Gaza, according to a statement from the IDF.
Sakr drove the motorcycle seen carrying Noa Argamani away from the Nova music festival during the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
The IDF and ISA said the strike was carried out with Gideonim Unit 33 of Israel’s Lahav 433 police division. They described Sakr as affiliated with global jihadist organizations in Gaza and said he had supplied weapons to Hamas during the war.
The agencies also alleged that Sakr had recently worked with Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad operatives to plan attacks on Israeli troops and civilians, in violation of the ceasefire agreement. They said they used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to reduce the risk to civilians.
Video of Argamani being taken from the Nova music festival near Kibbutz Re’im became one of the most widely seen images of the Oct. 7 attack. Her then-partner, Avinatan Or, was abducted separately.

Israeli forces rescued Argamani from Nuseirat on June 8, 2024, along with Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov and Shlomi Ziv. The operation was named for Arnon Zmora, an Israeli counterterrorism officer who died of wounds sustained during the rescue.
Or remained in captivity until October 13, 2025, when he was released after 738 days.

US immigration officers instructed to halt arrests of non-criminal immigrants: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:15:23 UTC
17:15:23 KST

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have been instructed to stop arresting immigrants who do not have criminal convictions or pending criminal charges, according to agency sources.
Under the reported directive, federal immigration agents may arrest immigrants with criminal convictions or pending criminal charges, while those with final deportation orders but no criminal convictions or charges would not be arrested, The Daily Wire reported.
The reported change would also end so-called “collateral arrests”, under which officers may detain others without legal status encountered while pursuing a criminal target, according to sources.
The reported directive comes amid increased scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies and ICE operations.
Several ICE officers expressed frustration about the reported change, with one source suggesting it could be linked to the upcoming midterm elections.
“We believe it has something to do with the midterms coming up,” said one source. “They’re trying to calm things down before the elections.”
“We’ll see the arrest numbers go down,” said another source.
The reported change comes about a week after an ICE officer shot and wounded a Venezuelan man in the state of Texas during an attempted traffic stop.
The officer, who was reportedly hired by ICE last year after previously working for another federal law enforcement agency, had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the incident, according to US media reports citing federal officials.
ICE subsequently reminded officers that they “must activate” their body cameras during enforcement activities, according to an internal notice cited by The Washington Post.
A federal judge ordered Wilber Rafael Garces Perez from Venezuela to appear at a 30 September hearing, temporarily preventing his deportation.

NPF gets most, BJP second as 111 MPs, MLAs switch parties since 2022: ADR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:14:14 UTC
17:14:14 KST

At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026
NEW DELHI: At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026, according to an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) and National Election Watch (NEW). The report, released on September 24, covers elections and by-elections held during the period and includes 26 Lok Sabha MPs, seven Rajya Sabha MPs and 78 MLAs.The cases span 17 states and Union Territories, with Nagaland recording the highest number at 32, followed by West Bengal with 20, Telangana with nine, and Goa and Punjab with eight each. Maharashtra and Meghalaya recorded six cases each, Manipur five, Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat four each, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan two each, while Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi recorded one each.
NPF received most lawmakers, BJP second
Of the 111 lawmakers, 32 joined the Naga People's Front (NPF), accounting for 29 per cent of the total. The BJP received 29, or 26 per cent, followed by the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) with 20, or 18 per cent.The Congress received nine lawmakers, or 8 per cent, while Shiv Sena received eight, or 7 per cent. NPP received six, or 5 per cent, and the People's Party of Arunachal (PPA) received four, or 4 per cent.
Together, NPF, BJP and NCPI accounted for 81 of the 111 lawmakers, or 73 per cent.The NPF's figure was largely linked to the political realignment involving the Nationalist Democratic Progressive Party (NDPP) and NPF in Nagaland. ADR classifies party mergers separately from individual defections, making the distinction important when reading the overall figures.
Who were the 29 lawmakers who joined BJP?
Of the 29 lawmakers listed as having joined the BJP, seven were Rajya Sabha MPs and 22 were MLAs. No Lok Sabha MP in the ADR dataset moved to the BJP.The seven Rajya Sabha MPs were originally elected from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP): Swati Maliwal, Ashok Mittal, Harbhajan Singh, Raghav Chadha, Sandeep Kumar Pathak, Vikramjit Singh Sahney and Rajinder Gupta. The seven AAP MPs subsequently joined the BJP in April 2026.Among the MLAs were eight Congress legislators from Goa, four Congress legislators from Gujarat and two from Himachal Pradesh. The report also lists five JD(U) MLAs from Manipur as having moved to the BJP.Other BJP entrants included Samajwadi Party MLA Manoj Kumar Pandey from Uttar Pradesh, Congress MLA Nirmala Sapre from Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka MLA G Janardhan Reddy, whose Kalyana Rajya Pragathi Paksha (KRPP) merged with the BJP, according to the ADR analysis.Four Gujarat Congress MLAs, CJ Chavda, Arjun Modhwadia, Arvind Ladani and Chirag Patel, resigned, joined the BJP and subsequently contested by-elections.
Nagaland, West Bengal account for major share of cases
Nagaland recorded 32 cases, all involving MLAs. The cases were largely linked to the NDPP-NPF realignment, with 25 representatives originally elected from the NDPP among those who changed parties and 32 lawmakers joining the NPF.West Bengal recorded 20 cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs. All 20 were originally elected on AITC tickets and subsequently moved to the NCPI, according to the analysis. The MPs have claimed a merger with the NCPI, with the matter pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.Telangana recorded nine cases, all involving MLAs originally elected from the BRS, while Congress emerged as the principal recipient. Goa recorded eight cases involving Congress MLAs who moved to the BJP. Punjab also recorded eight cases, including six Rajya Sabha members and two MLAs.Maharashtra recorded six cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs elected from Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) who subsequently moved to Shiv Sena led by Eknath Shinde. Meghalaya recorded six MLA cases, while Manipur recorded five.
NDPP, AITC and Congress recorded most exits
Among the parties from which lawmakers moved, NDPP recorded the highest number of exits, with 25, or 23 per cent of the total. AITC followed with 20, or 18 per cent, while Congress accounted for 19, or 17 per cent.BRS recorded nine exits, or 8 per cent. AAP and NCP each accounted for seven, or 6 per cent, while Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) accounted for six, or 5 per cent. JD(U) recorded five, or 5 per cent, and NPP four, or 4 per cent.Together, NDPP, AITC and Congress accounted for 64 of the 111 lawmakers who changed parties, or 58 per cent.
Not all 111 cases were individual defections
ADR's analysis divides the 111 cases into four categories based on how the change took place.The first covers individual switches or defections, where a legislator voluntarily leaves one party and joins another without resigning from the House.The second covers party mergers, where the original party or a substantial section of its legislative wing formally merges with another party, such as the NDPP-NPF case in Nagaland.The third covers resignation followed by a by-election, where a legislator resigns from the Assembly or Parliament, joins another party and subsequently contests and wins a by-election.The fourth covers disqualification followed by a by-election, where a member is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, later joins another party and wins the seat again through a by-election.
ADR also noted that recent defections had been associated with the fall of governments in some State Assemblies.
ADR cautions that list may not be exhaustive
ADR and NEW said they made every effort to identify and include all relevant cases but cautioned that the list may not be exhaustive because of the lack of systematically maintained and readily accessible official data on lawmakers changing political parties. Other relevant cases may therefore not have been included.

Major incident declared near RAF Fairford as men held on suspicion of explosives offences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:10:19 UTC
17:10:19 KST

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation in which five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences near an RAF base used in US attacks against Iran.
After the declaration of a major incident at RAF Fairford, a bomb squad was sent to the village of Whelford and extra security measures were put in place, including the fortification of entrances to the base. Roadblocks and armed police have been seen in the area over the weekend.
After their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday morning were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act, the Metropolitan police said.
Eighty-five households were evacuated and taken to a leisure centre in the early hours of Sunday morning, while the army’s bomb squad examined three suspicious vehicles. Police said they were working to get local people back into their homes as soon as possible.
Materials were seized after the arrests by armed officers under the Explosives Act and were being examined to see how dangerous they were and whether they were technically capable of being used in an attack, the Guardian understands.
The operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting that investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.
The Gloucestershire constabulary assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said: “Around 12.45am today police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles travelling towards RAF Fairford. Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. The men were taken into custody where they remain.”
The broad circumstances of the arrests and proximity to RAF Fairford have led investigators to consider whether any plot was sponsored by Iran or another state. In July, a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”. Security sources said they were keeping an open mind on state involvement.
Julian Tudsbery, a resident of Whelford, said three “suspicious vans” had been spotted in the village and reported to police in the early hours of Sunday morning.
“Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said of the person who reported the sighting. “It just rang out so she dialled 999.”
On Sunday afternoon, overhead pictures showed a remote-operated bomb disposal robot inspecting the three vans. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around.
Tudsbery said he was evacuated at about 7am. “[The police] were then banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident.
A government spokesperson said: “The prime minister is being kept updated on the incident in Gloucestershire. We are grateful to the emergency services, who have acted quickly to detain several suspects and put measures in place to keep the community safe. It would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing.”
There have been protests in recent months over the British government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.
At the time of Iran’s warning in July, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.”
Gloucestershire police said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.
“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place.”
A police spokesperson said the situation was contained and local people need not be alarmed.
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said: “I would like to thank all those emergency and specialist teams who have acted so swiftly regarding the incident in Gloucestershire. We can be reassured that this is being dealt with, and it is exactly why our emergency response teams and armed forces are on standby 24/7.”
Armed police have been seen blocking access to the main gate of the base, and many emergency vehicles including police cars, ambulances and fire engines were visible on Sunday morning in Fairford, the town near the base.
A spokesperson for the US air force said they would not discuss specific force protection measures.
“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors and their families,” the spokesperson said.
“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”
The MP for South Cotswolds, Roz Savage, described the situation as “worrying” but said it was believed to be “contained”. She said: “I have contacted the police for further updates and I’ve been told that it is believed the incident is contained. I would like to thank them for the work they are currently doing.”
In May, the Royal International Air Tattoo, which is usually held at the base, was cancelled due to the escalating geopolitical situation in the Middle East.

Mikk Kasesalk: Estonian culture has no other refuge anywhere in the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

Mikk Kasesalk: Estonian culture has no other refuge anywhere in the world
Estonia's competitiveness must largely rely on capable, educated people, but that idea is under pressure as the education system's capacity fails to keep pace with demand, writes Mikk Kasesalk.
Societies are held together not only by laws and institutions, but also by shared beliefs. When those beliefs are strong, we take many of the common obligations stemming from them for granted. When they weaken, we increasingly have to ask why we should take on those obligations at all and bear the costs associated with them.
I would highlight three convictions that have played a key role in Estonia's development:
- We must defend our country.
- Everyone is responsible and individual effort matters.
- Culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state.
The annual drafting of the state budget provides the clearest indication of how important these convictions are to the government of the day and how it weighs them against one another.
We must defend our country
The story of a small nation that, against all odds, built a state of its own, lost it and then regained it through song is one of the deepest layers of our shared beliefs. That story has shaped Estonia's self-image and also strongly influences our thinking on security and foreign policy.
There is currently a very broad political consensus in Estonia on the need to rapidly increase defense spending. NATO and relations with allies are at the heart of our security policy, while the security threat posed by Russia gives defense spending an exceptionally strong position in state budget discussions.
The broader the political consensus on the necessity of a particular expenditure, the more important it is to maintain critical oversight of how the money is used. The need for defense spending does not mean that every defense expenditure is automatically justified. Even before the recent scandals in the defense sector, experts warned that money may have been allocated to defense faster than it could be put to effective use.
Every euro spent without justification undermines trust in government decisions and strengthens the hand of those who argue that public money is being spent carelessly. When it comes to national defense, there is no question whether the state is willing to pay for it — its importance is clearly reflected in the state budget. But the greater the spending, the greater the accountability must be for ensuring that it is justified.
Everyone is responsible and individual effort matters
After the restoration of independence, Estonia was built on the belief that a free market and individual effort lead to success. Estonia's competitiveness must largely rely on capable, educated people because we have neither vast natural resources nor historically accumulated wealth on which to build our success. That idea is now coming under pressure because the education system's capacity is not growing in line with demand. This is particularly evident in higher education where funding stumbles from one crisis to the next.
The promise of a society built on effort is credible only if people have a reasonable opportunity to develop their abilities and advance through their own efforts. The education system is one of the institutions that creates that opportunity. If capable people who are willing to work hard are denied educational opportunities for reasons beyond their control, the moral promise that "work hard and you will succeed" becomes less credible.
This spring, negotiations on administrative agreements between the education and research minister and the Council of Rectors raised the question of what will happen to young people graduating from high school in the coming years. Their numbers are higher than in previous years and there are not enough places for them in higher education. The problem did not emerge overnight. A few years ago, the same parties sought to resolve the long-term funding crisis in higher education, but the Ministry of Education and Research ultimately failed to fully pay the amount promised to universities under the agreement reached at the time.
During negotiations on the administrative agreements signed in May, it was agreed that universities would gradually add up to 1,000 study places a year over the next four years, while the education and research minister pledged to find €146 million to fund them and included that commitment in the state's next budget strategy.
If the additional funding is not found, increasing admissions will mean either dividing existing funding among more students or abandoning plans to create the additional study places. In either case, pressure on the capacity and quality of Estonian-language higher education will increase as demand grows.
This is where the principles of individual effort and state responsibility come together. The state cannot promise people that effort matters while failing to create the opportunities through which that effort can bear fruit. If we consider individual effort to be a foundation of Estonia's success, the importance of the education that makes it possible must also be reflected in the state's budget choices.
Culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state
Estonian culture has no refuge anywhere else in the world, no place where it will survive if we ourselves do not value it. It is therefore difficult to understand why culture has been one of the areas expected to make additional savings year after year. Why is culture repeatedly among the first areas to come under pressure for cuts whenever the state's finances deteriorate?
Lennart Meri is credited with saying: "Culture is as important to society as vitamins are to the human body." The effects of a deficiency may not be immediately visible. The consequence of prolonged underfunding of culture may not be the immediate closure of an institution or the cancellation of an event. The shortfall may also manifest itself in existing activities being kept going at the cost of lower pay and heavier workloads for those working in the field.
Culture should not be seen as an expense that can be afforded only when there is money left over. Its value does not lie solely in what can be measured in ticket revenue, visitor numbers or economic impact. Culture also creates new meanings and connections through which society makes sense of itself.
That value cannot be totaled up in a spreadsheet. But the meanings that are never created and the bridges between people that are never built make the Estonia we collectively experience increasingly duller, poorer and easier to abandon. If culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state, its place in the state budget must reflect that as well.
Inevitability or political will
How much can the Estonian state weaken the institutions through which the Estonian language and culture are passed on to the next generation before it begins to undermine the very rationale for its own existence?
The scale of the sums involved helps illustrate the choices we are actually talking about. Estonia's 2027 state budget amounts to about €20 billion. Defense spending will reach approximately €2.4 billion in 2026 and will account for at least 5 percent of GDP in the following years as well.
Covering the agreed increase in higher education funding will require €146 million over four years. There is no comparable overall figure for the needs of the cultural sector, but the entire budget of the Ministry of Culture's area of government is around €350 million a year. Purely to illustrate the scale, even if we were to use one-tenth of that amount as a point of comparison, we would be talking about roughly €35 million.
These figures do not mean that defense spending, higher education and culture are directly interchangeable items in the budget. They do show, however, that the sums involved are on very different scales. Scarce resources place limits on the choices available, but they do not predetermine how we choose among the options we have.
The budget is where abstract values become concrete choices. Every line in the budget is the result of someone's decision and many of those decisions could be made differently.
This brings us back to the three convictions mentioned at the outset. National defense protects the possibility of the Estonian state's continued existence. Education gives people the opportunity to develop their abilities and advance through their own efforts. Culture creates and carries forward the meanings through which society makes sense of itself. None of these can replace the others.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:07:00 UTC
17:07:00 KST

Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it
September 27, 2026
Iran on Sunday insisted on its conditions for reopeningthe Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's public rejection of the proposal that had birthed some hope for reopening the key waterway.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights," he said.
Iran proposed a seven-day plan aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within days.
Tehran said it had transmitted the proposal to Washington via Qatari mediators.
Iran's plan, Araghchi said, called for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including Lebanon, and fulfilling the conditions of the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump rejects plan, but no communication to Iran
Trump publicly rejected Iran's proposal on Saturday while speaking to reporters at the White House.
"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly."
Responding to Trump's comments, Araghchi said Iranians "saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators."
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.
The strait stalemate
Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely shut to international shipping despite Trump's claims that the US controls it.
Early Sunday, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) — set up by Iran to manage the Strait of Hormuz — warned ships of consequences if they use "illegal routes" in the region.
"This risks financial and life losses for the vessel, owner, master and crew, and seriously restricts its future Strait of Hormuz passage," it said in a post on X.
The authority said if ships breach its rules, all vessels belonging to the company could face restrictions in the future.
Around a fifth of global oil demand passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war began. The waterway is also a crucial route for liquefied natural gas and fertilizer.

Feature: Confucius Institute emerges as engine of opportunity for Afghan students
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
16:05:04 CST
17:05:04 KST

Students take a Chinese language lesson at the Confucius Institute at Kabul University in Kabul, Afghanistan, Sept. 26, 2026. Founded in 2008, the Confucius Institute in Kabul has equipped hundreds of Afghan students with Chinese language skills over nearly two decades. (Photo by Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua)
KABUL, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Inside a modern, well-equipped classroom at Kabul University, Jawid Ahmadi sits upright, intently absorbing every inflection of his Chinese instructor's carefully enunciated tones.
For Ahmadi, the intricate characters on the whiteboard represent far more than linguistic skill. They form a calculated pathway to personal advancement and stronger ties between Afghanistan and its neighboring China
"My primary goal is to continue my education in China, pursuing a master's degree and eventually a doctorate," Ahmadi explained with quiet determination. His family regards his linguistic progress as a potential catalyst for upward mobility.
"Learning Chinese can contribute to my personal economic growth and, at the same time, to the economic development of my country," Ahmadi told Xinhua inside his class. Beyond individual ambition, Ahmadi envisions himself as an intermediary.
"I want to be a bridge of communication and understanding between Afghanistan and China," he added. Ahmadi belongs to an expanding generation of young Afghans who perceive mastery of Chinese as a strategic asset capable of unlocking scholarships, professional opportunities and broader horizons.
The Confucius Institute at Kabul University admits only a limited number of high-school graduates each year through public entrance exam, even as demand for Chinese-language instruction significantly exceeds its capacity.
Abbas, who completed his studies at the institute approximately one month ago and now holds a position with a private firm, attributes tangible career advantages to his language skills.
"Learning Chinese can be particularly valuable in the economic sphere, as it creates greater opportunities for employment as well as broader avenues for business and trade," he observed.
"Interest in learning Chinese is growing with each passing day."
For a growing number of young Afghans, proficiency in Chinese has unlocked pathways to higher education, employment and commercial enterprise, motivating an expanding cohort to master the language and seize emerging opportunities.
Heela Wardak, another alumna, describes a transformative trajectory. Following her graduation, she secured various positions in Afghanistan before relocating to Beijing, where she currently teaches Pashto language at Beijing Foreign Studies University.
She regards the institute as an essential conduit for mutual comprehension. "The Confucius Institute serves as a bridge connecting Afghans with the Chinese people," Wardak Xinhua. "It provides Afghans with an opportunity to learn about Chinese culture, the way people live, the country's economic progress and other important aspects of Chinese society."
Through her fluency, Wardak believes she has contributed meaningfully to fostering dialogue and reinforcing ties between the two neighboring nations.
Founded in 2008, the Confucius Institute in Kabul has equipped hundreds of Afghan students with Chinese language skills over nearly two decades. At present, more than 100 students are enrolled across all academic levels, according to Wahidullah Halimy, the institute's executive director.
The surge in demand, he noted, stems from the availability of scholarships in China, expanding employment prospects and the growing footprint of Chinese enterprises, particularly those engaged in Afghanistan's mining sector.
"Graduates of the Confucius Institute find employment in Chinese companies," Halimy told Xinhua. "All of our graduates secure employment, and they are also satisfied with their professional careers."
Interest has risen consistently year after year. To accommodate the expanding cohort of aspiring learners, Halimy has urged Afghan authorities and the Confucius Institute to facilitate the placement of additional Chinese instructors.
Complementary courses are also offered at Nangarhar University in eastern Afghanistan and at a private institution in Kabul.
For a rising number of young Afghans, Chinese has evolved beyond a mere academic subject into a pragmatic instrument of economic mobility, cross-cultural exchanges and enhanced bilateral engagement at a pivotal moment in Afghanistan's pursuit of broader international partnerships. ■

No public mentions of Taiwan at official Xi and Trump meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

Taiwan not openly discussed at Xi and Trump meeting
September 27, 2026
US President Donald Trump picked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping up directly from the airport and in his welcoming remarks he praised the strong friendship between their two nations, as well as recalling how China and the US fought together as allies during World War II.
"Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said. "Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country," he said at the White House, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that fought alongside China against the Japanese between 1941 and 1942.
However, these pilots did not actually volunteer to fight with the People's Republic of China, whose leader was visiting Washington and which was not founded until 1949. The Americans were risking their lives for the former Republic of China, whose government relocated to Taiwan after communist victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949.
"China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen," Trump said at a state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening. Sun Yat-sen was the founder of the Republic of China in 1912 and the Kuomintang, or KMT, which remains a major political party in Taiwan today.
Taiwan a major problem between US and China
Ever since the end of World War II, Taiwan has been a point of contention between Beijing and Washington. For decades, the US government ignored the communist regime in the People's Republic of China. But since 1972, Washington has acknowledged the "one China principle," according to which there is only one China, whose legal government is in Beijing and Taiwan belongs to it. Diplomatic relations between the US and China were only established in 1979.
The Taiwan Relations Act came into effect in 1979 too. The US law legalized arms exports to Taiwan. It also allowed the US government to take military action to prevent changes to the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.
A potential war between China and Taiwan would not only jeopardize stability in the Asia-Pacific region but also plunge the global economy into a prolonged recession, as supply chains would be severely disrupted.
During their high-profile meeting, Xi did not openly urge the US to respect the "one China" principle as he has done in the past, and Trump did not mention Taiwan in public either. In May, he put on hold a $14-billion arms deal that the US had concluded with the Taiwanese government late last year. The arms sales deal remains under review.
"Given the US' production capacity and its own military needs, it will take some time before approved arms can be delivered," said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and professor at the National University of Singapore. "It remains unclear what else the US can currently offer Taiwan."
Ahead of crucial midterm elections in November, Trump urgently needs some positive headlines. He and his Republican party rely on farmers for support so they need China to import US agricultural goods. In 2023, before their current trade war, China imported $43 billion worth of soy, beef, wood and other goods from the US. However Beijing has drastically reduced its imports since.
Taiwan mentioned behind closed doors
China used the meeting "to make clear to Trump its opposition to any US military support for Taiwan," said William Yang, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. "Xi wants to convey this message personally and behind closed doors, thereby influencing Trump's decision on arms sales to Taiwan."
China's Xinhua news agency said that Xi had addressed the issue behind closed doors. It reported that Xi had expressed hope that the US would take strong action against Taiwanese independence and said that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was clear. He reportedly added that "building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight."
It will not have pleased Taiwanese politicians that the US president openly considered treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip in its negotiations with China, German sinologist Eberhard Sandschneider of the consultancy Berlin Global Advisers suggested during a political chatshow on German public television. "People living on the island of Taiwan do not take this lightly. This is an existential issue for Taiwan."
He added that he did not think China would take military action against Taiwan. That would be a move just as illogical as the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US attack on Iran, he argued.
Nobody is playing poker in China, Sandschneider continued. "Clear strategic interests are pursued there. National sovereignty and winning back Taiwan are key concerns. At the same time, it is well known that any military attack on Taiwan would not only lead to a military disaster but also to an economic collapse. The resulting setback for the global economy would call into question the Communist Party's legitimacy," the expert said.
De Zheng contributed to this article, which has been translated from German.

TOKYO, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- China swept both synchronized diving golds on Sunday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, as Chen Yiwen and Chen Jia won the women's 3m springboard synchro and Yang Hao and Lian Junjie took the men's 10m platform synchro crown.
Chen Yiwen and Chen Jia scored 328.56 points, well ahead of South Korea's Kim Su-ji and Kim Na-hyun, who took silver on 254.70. Malaysia's Ong Ker Ying and Lee Yiat Qing claimed bronze with 243.72.

Chen Jia, making her Asian Games debut, called the experience "very new" and noted the different atmosphere compared with domestic competitions.
China then added the men's 10m platform synchro title as Yang and Lian scored 465.54. Malaysia finished second on 377.52, with South Korea taking bronze on 375.90.
Olympic champions Yang and Lian, who have continued their partnership since Paris 2024, said they have adjusted some dives this season.
"Because the difficulty has been lowered, we need to pay more attention to the quality of the execution," Yang said. He added that their daily training and competition focus remains on another Olympic gold at LA28.
Malaysia also had a strong day, taking silver in the men's 10m platform synchro and bronze in the women's 3m springboard synchro.

Air bombs, drones and artillery: Russian attacks on five regions claim eight lives
Kyiv • UNN
As a result of the strikes on September 26–27, eight people were killed and 42 injured in five regions. The casualties included children, including an 11-month-old girl.
As a result of Russian attacks on September 26–27 in Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Donetsk, Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk regions, a total of eight people were killed, while another 42 suffered injuries and trauma. This was reported by UNN, citing statements from the State Emergency Service, the National Police and regional authorities.
Children are among those affected, including an 11-month-old girl. Residential buildings, businesses, medical facilities and educational institutions were damaged.
Zaporizhzhia: one killed, four affected, and a repeat strike in the morning
At night, as a result of Russian attacks on one of the frontline communities in Zaporizhzhia district, a man was killed and four other people were affected. Ten residential buildings were damaged, and another was completely destroyed. A fire broke out at the scene.
On the morning of September 27, Russian forces struck the settlement again, causing a new fire. While surveying the area, rescuers found and saved a woman trapped in one of the apartments.
All emergency services were working at the sites of the attacks.
Odesa region: strike on a business and a massive fire
As a result of a massive Russian attack on Odesa region, one person was killed and two others were injured. A production workshop, warehouse facilities and cargo vehicles were damaged. A massive fire broke out. According to the State Emergency Service, most of the employees managed to avoid danger because they were in a shelter during the air raid alert. This helped prevent a greater number of casualties. Due to the threat of repeated strikes, rescuers had to temporarily withdraw to safe locations. Psychologists from the State Emergency Service provided assistance to those affected.
In another district of the region, a drone attack damaged the facade and windows of a hotel, a medical facility building, a non-food goods store and a two-story residential building.
More than 140 rescuers, as well as five members of a firefighting unit of the National Guard of Ukraine, were involved in eliminating the consequences.
Donetsk region: three killed, Kramatorsk hit 16 times
On September 26, police recorded 1,309 Russian strikes on the frontline and residential areas of Donetsk region. Three people were killed and five others were injured.
Russian forces launched 16 strikes on Kramatorsk, eight of them with guided aerial bombs. Two civilians were killed and four others were injured. Two apartment buildings and 13 private houses, an administrative building, an outbuilding and four civilian vehicles were damaged. The occupiers dropped four KAB-250 bombs on Shabelkivka. One person was killed and 16 private houses were damaged. Another person was injured in Sukhanivka as a result of an FPV drone strike.
Russian forces attacked Sloviansk with drones and Smerch multiple rocket launchers. An apartment building and six private houses, a hospital and a gas station were damaged.
In Bylbasivka, seven private homes were damaged as a result of shelling with Tornado-S multiple rocket launchers. In Oleksandrivka, a non-residential building and vehicles were damaged; in Novyi Kavkaz, a private house and an outbuilding were damaged.
Sumy region: among the 30 injured are an infant and teenagers
In Sumy region, three people were killed and another 30 suffered injuries and trauma as a result of Russian shelling.
In the Sumy community, two people were killed and another 28 were affected by guided aerial bomb strikes. They include 11-month-old and eight-year-old girls, as well as two teenagers. Residential buildings, educational and administrative institutions were damaged. In the Znob-Novhorodske community, a 19-year-old man was killed and two other people were injured in a drone attack. In the Seredyna-Buda community, an apartment building and an administrative building were damaged. Police are documenting the aftermath of the attacks and collecting evidence of war crimes.
Dnipropetrovsk region: more than 20 attacks, injured man in serious condition
According to the regional authorities, as of 07:30 on September 27, Russian forces attacked two districts of Dnipropetrovsk region more than 20 times with drones and artillery. One person was injured.
In Nikopol district, Nikopol, Marhanets, Pokrovsk and Myrove communities came under attack. An enterprise and a market were damaged, and fires broke out. In Synelnykove district, the Russians attacked the Mykolaivka community. The injured man was taken to hospital in serious condition.

‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
08:03:21 UTC
17:03:21 KST

‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
The prospect of an AfD-led government in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt has exacerbated long-standing fears that the far-right Russia-friendly party may gain access to sensitive information of interest to the Kremlin, fuelling debate as to whether and how it can be barred from classified intelligence.
What happens when Germany’s domestic intelligence service is monitored by the very people it is meant to spy on?
The once speculative question has acquired sudden urgency – for both Germany and its allies – in the wake of a regional election that has put the German far right on the cusp of power for the first time since 1945.
The Alternative for Democracy (AfD) party scored a resounding election win in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and is trying to form a coalition government in the small eastern state, one of 16 that enjoy broad powers under Germany’s federal system.
If it succeeds, the Moscow-friendly party could notably gain access to intelligence gathered by agencies tracking both domestic and external threats, a prospect that has spooked officials amid escalating tensions over the war in Ukraine and a surge in hybrid attacks attributed to Russia.
Watch moreOnly the beginning? German far right's breakthrough shakes Europe to its core
According to French investigative and satirical weekly Canard Enchaîné, such concerns were enough for France’s domestic intelligence agency to notify its German counterpart last week of its plans to withhold sensitive information about far-right extremists and Russia should the AfD govern in Saxony-Anhalt.
Unmasking spy cops
Germany’s domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has consistently ranked right-wing extremists as the greatest threat to German democracy. Its latest annual report, published in June, said their number had increased significantly to 58,700 last year, fuelled by a surge in support for the AfD.
The BfV stirred controversy last year when it designated the AfD as a right-wing “extremist group”, though the classification was suspended in February after a legal challenge from the party.
While the national party is now designated as “suspected extremist”, pending a court ruling, its local chapter in Saxony-Anhalt has a “confirmed extremist” label that means it is under surveillance by federal intelligence, including undercover agents.
German officials fear that an AfD government in the eastern state could use routine intelligence sharing to find those agents and scupper efforts to monitor it, said Jacob Ross, a Senior Research Fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
“If the AfD gets hold of the interior minister job in charge of police forces and intelligence, they would potentially have access to files about their own surveillance,” Ross explained. “One of the big fears in the intelligence community, and more widely in German politics, is that they would then very rapidly try to find out who within their own ranks is spying on them.”
An asset for Russia
A greater concern for Germany and its allies is the possibility that sensitive information regarding German, European and NATO security arrangements might end up in Russian hands.
Before the election in Saxony-Anhalt, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius told German newspaper Bild that he opposed sharing classified information with AfD officials should they enter regional governments, stressing that their “close ties to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin are undeniable”.
The far-right party has repeatedly sparked alarm in Berlin by requesting information on vulnerabilities in German and NATO defences that would be of interest to Russia. In a heated debate at the Bundestag last November, a lawyer for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling conservatives accused the AfD of harbouring a Russian “sleeper cell” intent on investigating Germany’s critical infrastructure.
Fears of sensitive information falling in Russian hands are well founded, according to Anton Shekhovtsov, director of the Austria-based Centre for Democratic Integrity and an expert on the European far right and its links to Russia.
With Hungary’s Viktor Orban out of power, “The AfD is now the largest and strongest pro-Russian party in the entire European Union,” Shekhovtsov argued, citing “extensive links with Russia that have been built over many years”. He added: “Obviously this is a weak spot for Germany and for the EU when it comes to dealing with Moscow and the political warfare that it is waging in Europe.”
Read moreFive takeaways from Germany's regional elections after far-right gains
According to a New York Times report published on Tuesday, the German federal government has moved swiftly to allay concerns among EU allies, drafting plans to block an AfD-led state government from reviewing sensitive intelligence.
One notable measure involves denying AfD officials access to a secret war plan drafted in 2024, a 1,000-page blueprint detailing how Germany and its allies would respond to a Russian attack similar to the invasion of Ukraine. Other possible steps include withholding intelligence concerning Russian subterfuge and investigations into far-right extremists.
The Austrian precedent
There are precedents for European countries restricting access to intelligence when dealing with far-right parties that are seen as cozying up to Russia. One notable example is Orban’s Hungary, which France accused of “betraying” the EU by leaking information to Moscow, just weeks before the longtime nationalist leader was voted out of power.
Austria also came under intense scrutiny after the far-right Freedom Party joined a coalition government in 2017 and secured the interior ministry portfolio, leading some European partners to place limits on intelligence sharing.
“The perception at the time was that Austrian security and intelligence services were deeply penetrated by Russia,” said Ross. “Those in Germany who argue in favour of excluding AfD from information flows often point to the Austrian case, warning that Germany could also lose its reputation as a trustworthy ally when it comes to intelligence-sharing mechanisms.”
Placing caveats on intelligence sharing is relatively commonplace, including between close allies, said Dan Lomas, an assistant professor in International Relations at the University of Nottingham specialising in intelligence and security-related issues.
“Intelligence services that cooperate on, say, counterterrorism might seek to limit the flow of other intel when they think it could be leaked,” he explained. “They might also seek to bypass specific figures in government, sharing information with other domestic services but with the caveat that it mustn’t be passed on to certain officials.”
Such limitations could pose logistical challenges should AfD continue its ascent at the regional level, warned Ross, pointing to the specificities of Germany’s federal system. Just days after triumphing in Saxony-Anhalt, the party also topped elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, underscoring its dominance in swaths of the country.
In the event of a major crisis, “keeping AfD-run states in the dark could create holes in operational plans”, he said. “Because while the army and the defence of German territory are within the purview of the federal government, the police forces needed to secure roads, convoys and power stations are the responsibility of individual states.”
Breach of trust
Another long-term problem, added Lomas, is that such limitations breed mistrust between security services, elected officials and the broader public, while also posing problems of democracy.
“Even if you find a practical way to work around the AfD, doing this is corrosive at a time when public trust in liberal Western democracies is already under threat,” he said.
Read moreHow far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
Efforts to restrict far-right access to state secrets could lead to legal challenges from AfD, which argues that the country’s mainstream parties are undermining democracy by thwarting the will of voters.
Jork Herrmann, an AfD spokesman, told the New York Times, “It would be utterly undemocratic and impossible to justify to voters to withhold intelligence information from the party based on unsubstantiated and unprovable allegations.”
If the courts agree with Germany’s domestic intelligence agency and confirm AfD as an “extremist” organisation that poses a danger to the constitution, that would give the federal government “legitimate grounds not to share sensitive information”, said Shekhovtsov. But if they don’t, he added, “it’s hard to see on what grounds they could be kept in the dark.”
The conundrum facing German officials underscores the limitations of the “firewall” strategy aimed at keeping the far right out of power, argued Ross. He contrasted that approach with French President Emmanuel Macron’s decision last week to convene all major parties – including Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party, which is polling well ahead of rivals ahead of elections next year – for an intelligence briefing on the threat of hybrid attacks from Russia.
“Macron seems to think it’s best to brief the National Rally rather than have pro-Russian experts do so,” he said. “In Germany, we’re counting on the firewall to hold firm. But if it doesn’t, then we have a huge problem.”

At least 27 people killed in 2 mass shootings in South Africa's Johannesburg, Capetown
At least 27 people were killed in two mass shootings in South Africa's two main cities, police said on Sunday.
The first incident occurred Saturday evening when eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed a bar west of Johannesburg and shot 17 people and wounded 15 others.
The suspects opened fire on customers drinking outside and then moved inside to continue shooting, police said, where they killed 13 males and four females.
The motive for the shooting was still unknown, police said, adding that the suspects torched two vehicles before fleeing.
In a separate shooting at an entertainment venue in a township outside Cape Town early on Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more.
Five of the victims were declared dead at the scene while the others succumbed to their injuries while being taken to hospital.
No suspect has been arrested in either case, police said.
The attacks come as South Africa, awash with legal and illegal firearms, grapples with persistent gun violence often linked to gang rivalries and competition among informal businesses.
The country of about 62 million people records roughly 60 murders a day, among the highest rates globally.
In March, soldiers moved into violence hotspots in Johannesburg to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime, described by President Cyril Ramaphosa as one of the biggest threats facing the country.
South Africa has repeatedly turned to the army in times of crisis, from enforcing strict Covid-19 lockdowns in 2020 to deploying troops during the deadly riots sparked by the jailing of ex-president Jacob Zuma in 2021.
Soldiers were also sent into the streets in 2023 after a wave of truck burnings raised fears of wider unrest.

Almost one of us: is Sydney Sweeney on her way to converting?

Hong Kong delays AI copyright law to focus on guidelines first
Government puts legal amendment on hold to draft guidelines balancing creative rights with tech development
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Hong Kong authorities will delay a proposed legal amendment to protect copyrighted works from being used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models and will issue operational guidelines first, the South China Morning Post has learned.
The Copyright (Amendment) Bill 2025, which aimed to introduce an “opt-out” mechanism for text and data mining to support AI technology development, was originally scheduled to be submitted to the Legislative Council in the first half of last year. The item was removed from Legco’s legislative agenda last August.
The legislative proposal, which was mentioned in last year’s policy address, did not appear in the 2026 blueprint or the city’s first five-year plan, delivered together earlier this month.
The “opt-out” mechanism had raised concerns after it was proposed in 2024, with critics saying it would “involve a lot of effort” for copyright holders to approach AI companies to check whether their work had been used for AI-generated content. They counter-proposed an “opt-in” mechanism.

NHS trust removes 10 staff from duty over Noah Woods data breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:51:16 UTC
16:51:16 KST

An NHS trust has apologised after the medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods were accessed by unauthorised people after his disappearance.
Noah was found dead in a pond in Brantham, Suffolk, after going missing from a playground. More than 1,300 members of the public joined a search for the boy before police discovered his body.
A spokesperson for East Suffolk and North Essex NHS foundation trust said 10 employees had been “removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded”. The trust said in a statement that disciplinary action was being explored as a result.
Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at the trust, said: “We have apologised unreservedly to Noah Woods’ family for the extra anguish this breach of trust has caused them at an already devastating time.”
He added that unauthorised access of patient data was “completely unacceptable” and said the matter had been reported to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO).
Mansfield added: “As soon as we became aware of concerns that Noah’s medical records may have been viewed inappropriately, we launched an urgent internal investigation. Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason.”
The chief executive of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, said on Friday that NHS staff would be suspended immediately if found snooping on patients’ records for unauthorised reasons. He said: “We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough.”
There have been previous cases of NHS staff looking at patient records in high-profile cases, including the 2023 Nottingham attacks and the 2024 Southport dance class knife attack.
An inquest heard this week that Woods escaped from the park “through a gap in the fence”. He became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk constabulary said.
Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk constabulary said his death was not being treated as suspicious.
After the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday, Noah’s family said they would like him to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”.
In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.”
Noah’s father, Rhys Woods, paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.”

The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been asked to appear before an Australian Senate inquiry into AI after revelations that an OpenAI agent hacked the country’s Medicare database.
Written requests have been sent to OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei ahead of public hearings in Canberra on Thursday, a spokesperson for inquiry chair Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said on Sunday.
“There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites,” Hanson-Young, a senator from the Australian Greens, said in a statement.
Altman and Amodei “must front up, face the Senate’s questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like”, she added.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside business hours.

OpenAI said it learned of the breach in August and that the incident was unintentional and did not compromise any private information. The Medicare breach was one of at least four involving Australian government websites, according to the company.
The incident is one of the highest-profile cases of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States.
Pressure for tighter regulation
The breach could push Albanese’s Labor government to toughen AI-specific laws it is preparing for next year, technology policy experts say.
It could also add pressure to Australia-US relations, already tested by Canberra’s ban on social media for teenagers, they added.
The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on Australian communities, industries, water and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.

In Germany, intelligence services are searching for Russian “weapons caches”; there is a threat of sabotage at a defense company — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
German intelligence services suspect that weapons for sabotage against a defense company have already been hidden in Bavaria. The investigation is classified.
According to German intelligence, Russian intelligence has created weapons caches in Germany. As BILD has learned, a search for these caches is currently under way, reports UNN.
Details
On the evening of June 11, 2026, Serbian police stopped two cars near Subotica that were heading toward the Hungarian border. In the Peugeot belonging to Danilo Bogdanović, a Serb with a Russian passport, they found drone components, while in the black Volvo belonging to Slobodan Dučić, they discovered a concealed compartment containing two tin cans packed with explosives. Investigators assessed that a flying bomb could have been assembled from these materials. Bogdanović and Dučić were arrested.
The next day, a friendly intelligence service passed information to its German counterparts about a suspicious truck traveling to Germany from Serbia. According to the Serbian authorities, the truck contained a compartment for smuggling weapons. However, Serbian police failed to intercept the vehicle.
On June 27, Bavarian border police detained the truck as it entered from Austria. The Serbian driver was detained, banned from entering Germany, and sent back to Austria. The truck was confiscated. Investigators did indeed find concealed compartments—but they were empty. The security authorities concluded that the delivery of the weapons about which the Serbs had warned may have reached its destination in Germany earlier. According to BILD, the weapons may have been intended for an attack on a defense company in Bavaria that is of major importance for military aid to Ukraine.
The search for the weapons is in full swing. According to the German government, several networks of saboteurs controlled by Russia are currently operating in Europe. They are believed to be coordinated by the GRU, which is apparently conducting covert operations in Europe with the help of a special-operations unit. German investigators suspect that the weapons from the truck are already in a cache in Germany and ready to be used for acts of sabotage.
In response to BILD's inquiry, all authorities involved in the case unanimously cited the need for secrecy. The pages of documents that BILD was able to see in connection with the investigation bear the words "officially classified" printed in red at the top.
