- list 3 of 3How an OpenAI ‘agent’ hacked Australia’s Medicare and what that means
The inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on safety, data transparency, Australian communities, industries, water and energy. It is one of several state and federal inquiries into AI.
“There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites,” Hanson-Young’s spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday.
The statement said Altman and Amodei “must front up, face the Senate’s questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like”.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside business hours.
The Medicare incursion, condemned by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States.
Addressing reporters in New York on Wednesday, Albanese said the agent, developed by OpenAI, accessed public and nonpublic data on the government’s Medicare portal in June.
OpenAI responded after the news conference, stating that while it was still investigating, there was no evidence patient records were accessed and that it learned of the breach in August only.
The company’s review had identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as its “models attempted to look up answers”, it said.
Australia’s Labor government is tightening tech regulations with new online safety laws, age bans and proposed digital duty of care frameworks.

Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:05:31 UTC
16:05:31 KST

Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
In early September, Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia’s largest cultural center abroad. The center had operated in the heart of the German capital for more than 40 years. It remained open after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, even as similar institutions across Europe shut down. What finally brought it to an end was a drone attack on Leipzig Airport that German authorities described as Russian sabotage. Meduza tells the center’s story.
In early August, a DHL cargo plane approaching Leipzig Airport had to climb sharply when the airport unexpectedly closed. After the plane landed in Hanover, inspectors found minor damage caused by a collision with an unidentified flying object.
At Leipzig Airport, bomb disposal experts found and defused a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator near a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane. Ten days later, another drone bearing traces of explosives was found near the airport.
German authorities investigated for nearly a month before blaming Russia for the attempted sabotage. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced Germany’s response: the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova criticized the decision. Speaking about the Russian House, she said:
The Russian House was obviously a thorn in their side. Why?.. Its first and foremost purpose is to teach Russian. Demand was enormous. […] That’s the Russian House’s main offense — the reason the German establishment disliked it so much.
There are more than 70 Russian Houses worldwide. The full-scale war has disrupted their work.
The worldwide network of Russian Houses took its present form in 2008, when President Dmitry Medvedev signed a decree creating Rossotrudnichestvo, a Russian federal agency for cultural outreach abroad. Officially overseen by the Foreign Ministry, the agency runs Russian language courses and promotes Russian culture, science, and education.
Before the war, Russian Houses operated in at least 77 countries. Their work became more difficult after the EU imposed sanctions on Rossotrudnichestvo following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In July 2022, the EU added the agency to its sanctions list, accusing it of promoting the ideas of the “Russian World,” funding propaganda projects, and spreading “Kremlin narratives” and historical revisionism.
After the EU’s decision, Russian Houses suspended operations in six European countries: Slovenia, Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Romania. The Russian House in Baku also suspended operations in 2025 after a passenger plane crashed near Aktau. In July 2026, the Russian House in Chișinău closed indefinitely. Moldovan authorities called it a “tool of the Kremlin’s hybrid influence.”
In Berlin, however, the Russian House kept operating after the sanctions against Rossotrudnichestvo. Its seven-story modernist building on Friedrichstraße, within walking distance of the Russian embassy, opened in 1984 as the House of Soviet Culture and Science. It was the Soviet Union’s largest cultural center abroad. Russia later took ownership of the building, and the center became the Russian House of Culture and Science.
The Russian House’s activities changed little over more than 40 years. At its 20th anniversary celebration in 2004, then-director Anatoly Bogushevsky said the center drew about 300,000 visitors a year. Its main aim, he said, was to give people in Germany “as comprehensive a picture as possible of a new, reformed Russia seeking to strengthen democracy.” Its activities centered on a Russian language center, a Russian college, a Pushkin Library with more than 40,000 books, small clubs and workshops, concerts, and film screenings.
Decades later, the 29,000-square-meter building, which occupies an entire Berlin block, still housed children’s clubs and workshops — some free, others paid — as well as a movie theater, concert halls, and exhibition spaces. Rossotrudnichestvo says more than three million people attended events there over the past 15 years. Some events, however, were difficult to describe as purely cultural. After 2022, the theater sometimes screened RT material that called Ukrainians Nazis, and the center held photo exhibitions on similar themes.
Two agreements signed in 2011 and 2013 governed the Russian House’s operations. The first established its status as a cultural and information center; the second gave Russia the right to lease the building for 99 years. Throughout that period, Germany paid about 70,000 euros a year in property tax on the land beneath it. In return, Germany received the right to lease the Goethe-Institut building on Baumanskaya Street in Moscow on the same terms.
Berlin long resisted politicians’ calls to close the Russian House because terminating those agreements could put the Goethe-Institut in Russia at risk.
Even so, sanctions severely hampered the Russian House’s work. All its assets in the EU were frozen, and it could use its bank account only under Bundesbank supervision. Its ability to receive money was tightly restricted: EU legal entities were barred from providing it with funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly, while it could accept only enough from third parties to maintain the building.
The Russian House nevertheless continued collecting rent on apartments and offices in the building. Tagesschau.de found that 115 people lived there in June 2023. In 2018, for example, the Russian House earned about $2 million from rent. Meduza asked Rossotrudnichestvo what would happen to the apartment residents after the closure but had received no response by publication.
The Russian House has drawn espionage allegations
Once the invasion of Ukraine began, German authorities increasingly suspected that the building could be used for spying and to skirt sanctions. In January 2023, Berlin prosecutors launched a probe into possible violations of the country’s foreign trade law. It led nowhere. Prosecutors closed the investigation after Germany froze the Russian House’s accounts, and Moscow hit back by freezing the Goethe-Institut’s accounts there.
The allegations gained renewed attention in the summer of 2026, when German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung and WDR reported on a French Interior Ministry document. According to the document, Russian intelligence services use the Russian House as a front, and the center’s mission is to influence the diaspora to support Moscow’s policies.
Green Party Bundestag member Robin Wagener called the allegations plausible, saying, “The center’s activities are not limited to harmless language courses.” Christian Democratic Union lawmaker Roderich Kiesewetter called it a “disinformation center” and an extension of the Kremlin. An investigation by CORRECTIV also found that the organization running the Russian House maintains a branch in Dresden called the German-Russian Cultural Institute.
In August 2026, Green Party Bundestag member Sara Nanni, who works on defense issues, pointed to unusual mobile phone and GPS “signal activity” near the building. She said it could indicate that powerful equipment for intercepting signals or communicating covertly was operating inside. Kiesewetter also said that although 100 people lived in the complex, the building used a disproportionate amount of electricity. He and Free Democratic Party member of the European Parliament Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann said the building might serve as a hub for technical intelligence gathering and the coordination of cyberattacks.
Many of the building’s business tenants, however, had no connection to Rossotrudnichestvo. They included the Samowar Hof restaurant and Mnogo Knig, one of Berlin’s few Russian-language bookstores. Businesses there may also have faced pressure from Russian authorities. Journalist Ilya Barabanov said that in 2024, a complaint from Rossotrudnichestvo led the bookstore to remove his book “Nash biznes — smert” (“Our Business Is Death”), about the Wagner private military company, from sale. Meduza published the book.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
The closure led to deportations and cost dozens of people their jobs
Staff assigned from Russia to the Russian House and Rossotrudnichestvo were ordered to leave Germany within seven days. On September 10, they arrived in Belarus along with diplomats from the closed consulate in Bonn. According to Ekho, only about seven Russian House employees were specialists assigned from Russia; they were the ones who had to leave Germany. The rest had been hired locally, and some were German citizens.
Sabine Gimaeva, who owns the Samowar Hof café that opened in the Russian House more than a decade ago, told Meduza that many cultural and educational projects stopped almost immediately after Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure. Commercial tenants were given until December to leave. Gimaeva said the closure would affect more than Russians:
People of all different nationalities come here, with all kinds of passports — including a lot of Ukrainians. […] So to me, this is about much more than just our café closing. A whole network of services that very different people have used for years is disappearing from one building all at once.
In Gimaeva’s view, the German authorities’ decision hurts “ordinary workers and private businesses” rather than Russian state institutions. Businesses may struggle to relocate on short notice, she said, and some may close, costing people their jobs:
People who have worked and supported themselves for years may now end up relying on German welfare. I feel like very few people are talking about those consequences right now.
The Russian House closed just before the September 20 election to Berlin’s state parliament, and the decision quickly became a campaign issue. Even before the closure was announced, Social Democratic mayoral candidate Steffen Krach stood outside the building with a sign reading, “Here’s something we can expropriate, friends in the Left Party! Are you with us?” He did not clearly state his position on the Russian House’s status; his gesture appeared to invoke the Left Party’s plans to nationalize housing. Krach did not respond to Meduza’s request for comment.
On September 4, after the foreign minister’s official announcement, two protests took place outside the Russian House — one supporting the closure and one opposing it. Reforum Space Berlin, a space for antiwar Russians created by the Free Russia Foundation, helped organize the protest in favor. Its coordinator, Yulia Abdullaeva, who has lived in Berlin since 2011, told Meduza that alternatives to the Russian House already exist in the city:
The question isn’t whether individual classes held there were good or bad. It’s whether the Russian state should still have a venue of its own in central Berlin today, using culture as a tool of its foreign policy and propaganda. […] All the community activities people genuinely need — Russian lessons for children, cultural events, a library, films, educational programs — can exist (and already do!) in independent organizations, without Russian state control.
Supporters of keeping the Russian House open held their own protest that day. One organizer was the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, a party that advocates better relations with Russia. Alexander King, co-chair of its Berlin branch, told Meduza that closing the Russian House and the Bonn consulate amounted to “far-reaching measures that could bring us closer to a possible military conflict.” In the September 20 election, the party failed to clear the 5% threshold for seats in parliament.
Samowar Hof owner Sabine Gimaeva also attended the protest in support of the Russian House. “To me, that’s a perfectly normal way to stand up for what matters to me — if a decision directly affects my family, our business, the people who work here, and cultural projects that have been here for years, of course I’m not going to pretend it doesn’t concern me,” she said.
Die Welt estimated that several hundred people attended the protest against the closure. Deutsche Welle gave more precise figures: about 250 people attended the rally supporting the closure, and about 500 opposed it. Reforum Space Berlin coordinator Olga Galkina, however, told Ekho that the two sides were roughly equal in number. In her view, those who wanted to keep the center included ethnic German immigrants known as “late resettlers” and Putinverstehers, or Putin sympathizers. Abdullaeva made a similar distinction:
I wouldn’t apply the label ‘Putinverstehers’ to everyone who went to the Russian House. It was mainly about the politics of defending the Russian House. For many people, it really was, above all, a place where they could hear Russian, go to a concert, or take their child to a class. I used to go there fairly often myself, but since the full-scale war began, I haven’t gone back — because the war changed what this institution means to me.
The Left Party, which won the Berlin election, had not publicly commented on the Russian House’s closure during the campaign. Earlier, however, the party’s deputy federal chair, Maximilian Schirmer, had called the center “a propaganda institution.”
The parties that finished second and third — the Christian Democratic Union and Alternative for Germany, respectively — differed in their positions. The Christian Democrats, Berlin’s current governing party, had consistently called for the Russian House to close. Alternative for Germany had not stated a position directly, though its Bundestag member Karsten Hilse attended the protest in support of the center.
As the Russian House closed, Rossotrudnichestvo announced plans to expand the network. On September 8, agency head Igor Chaika signed agreements to open 11 new Russian Houses in Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Senegal, Mali, Sierra Leone, São Tomé and Príncipe, Togo, Madagascar, Armenia, and Thailand. The agency’s deputy head also said a new Russian House in Germany “will definitely open” and that the search for new partners was already underway.

The deputy chair of the ruling party resigns amid allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:03:00 UTC
16:03:00 KST

Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya, AA Photo
Ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) Deputy Chair Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya resigned from her posts early on Sept. 27 to allow an independent investigation into allegations linking her to a public fund controversy in Türkiye.
Kaya, who previously served as family and social policies minister, stepped down as deputy chair in charge of social policies to prevent her office from becoming a subject of debate. She took political and conscientious responsibility to ensure a healthy inquiry, she said.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan showed a clear will for a meticulous investigation into the matter regardless of the individuals involved, Kaya said on social media.
"The duty we undertake toward our nation requires taking political and conscientious responsibility when necessary," she said, noting she asked Erdoğan to relieve her of her duties so authorities could clarify the claims.
Following Kaya’s resignation, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik stated the authorized bodies are closely monitoring the fund crisis. He noted the party’s guiding principle aligns with Erdoğan’s directive that "whoever is responsible will be held accountable."
“We are proceeding with the necessary steps regarding political responsibility. All officials are working meticulously,” Çelik said in a subsequent statement. “There are actions to be taken for the integrity of the investigation, and we are carrying them out. We will make a decision when legal measures need to be taken.”
Kaya's resignation follows reports implicating her in a high-profile financial inquiry dominating the public agenda in recent weeks. Authorities have detained scores of suspects and seized assets linked to the alleged illicit funding scheme across multiple provinces.
The veteran politician entered Parliament in 2015 and led the Family and Social Policies Ministry between 2016 and 2018.

Kiew shoppers feel the pinch from Russian strikes on supply networks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

AFP Photo
With one eye on the shelves and the other on his phone, Maksym Tarasenko has gotten used to keeping an eye out for Russian drones above Kiev as he shops.
But Tarasenko, 26, is unable to feed his caffeine habit, as his favorite fizzy drink is no longer in stock at his local supermarket. "There's absolutely no Coca-Cola left, not even the equivalent," he said.
Last month, he said the Silpo store where he shops had no potatoes, cereals or many vegetables
In the last nine months, there have been three times as many airstrikes on civilian warehouses in the Kiev region than in the first four years of Russia's invasion in February 2022.
Two-thirds of them have happened since the start of August, according to an AFP analysis of data from the ACLED conflict monitor up to Sept. 18.
Ukraine's food minister, Taras Vysotskyi, has said the wave of attacks has "seriously disrupted, even rendered inoperative" the supply chains used by major retailers, which are based on centralized logistics platforms.
He called on brands to decentralize their logistics, focus on short-term supply chains and use smaller warehouses or ones located in neighboring countries.
The Fozzy group, which owns Silpo, announced in early August that it was reorganizing its supply chains, allowing shelves to be restocked, albeit without some brands.
With fruit carefully stacked, a slew of special offers and light music, everything might appear normal.
But clients are glued to their devices: Above the capital, thick black smoke rises after a Russian strike on a market near the city's central station.
For Tarasenko, Moscow is trying to create "widespread panic" among citizens.
The first shortages prompted a rush on certain products as residents sought to stock up before winter, he said, but he is remaining calm.
"A little market has been set up near where I live. I sometimes buy basics there, it's a little bit cheaper," he said.
And if the situation gets even worse, he has already found a grower in the provinces where he can get his potatoes.
In the Kiev suburbs, about 10 kilometers from the supermarket, firefighters busy themselves around a huge skeleton of charred metal.
Bottles of oil, packets of salt and a few tin cans lie among the debris. Just the day before, the building was being used as a warehouse for the ECO Market chain.
According to Oleg Pendzyn, an economist, these types of Russian attacks have caused an estimated deficit of 1.3 billion euros ($1.5 billion) for the Ukrainian state.
Vysotskyi, the food minister, has warned that the reorganisation of logistics could increase the cost of foodstuffs by up to 2.5 percent, while Ukraine's central bank said annual inflation stood at 8.1 percent in August.
"It's hitting my wallet hard!" said Anya Dmyterko, a 35-year-old vendor at the market in Boryspil, outside Kyiv.
"With 1,000 hryvnias ($22.20), I could buy food, meat, treats for the kids," she said. "Now, you can hardly buy anything."
As the sirens screamed again at the central market in Boryspil, Dmyterko pushed her own shopping trolley without looking up.
Since August, the smell of burning has filled the air around the small town surrounded by warehouses, making it a prime target for Moscow.
In the evening, when the drones approach, Dmyterko said she quickly grabs her three children and they head to the basement.
Despite the threat from above, life continues at the Boryspil market. In Dmyterko's shop, new customers arrive as her shelves have not been as badly hit by shortages and inflation as bigger supermarkets.
Most Ukrainian families buy 45 percent of their products at markets every month, said Pendzyn. Thirty percent is spent in local grocery stores.
Such stores source their supplies directly from domestic producers, a set-up that, for now, eliminates any risk of food shortages, he added.
Supermarkets are mostly used by "the young urban population with comfortable incomes", the economist added.
Pendzyn said he was particularly worried by Russian strikes on the Black Sea ports, because Ukraine depends on them for 90 percent of its exports and no land route can absorb such a volume.
The sound of anti-aircraft guns pierces the sky as conversations at the market revolve around rising prices and the coming winter.
Dmyterko lines up jars of gherkins and tomatoes.
"The main thing is that there's food and water," she said. "No Coca-Cola is not a disaster."

‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:59 UTC
16:00:59 KST

When Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.
“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in a lengthy post. “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.
“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”
For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.
St Andrews, ranked second in the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.
But the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.
“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”
Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”
Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.
“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.
“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”
One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews had turned into the Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”
Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”
St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.
“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.
“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”
The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, Edinburgh University offered guidance on how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.
“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”
Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.
“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.

‘Viscerally dedicated to social issues’: behind Lula’s drive to win final term in Brazil’s crunch election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:59 UTC
16:00:59 KST

On 1 January 2023, a few hours after being sworn in for his third stint as Brazil’s president, a ravenous Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sneaked away from a celebratory cocktail party packed with politicians and diplomats to grab a snack with one of his oldest friends.
“This is your penultimate term,” that friend, the Dominican theologian and writer Frei Betto, recalls telling Lula as the pair chewed the fat in a back room of the foreign ministry in Brasília.
Betto says Lula laughed off his provocation, insisting: “No, Betto! It’s the last one. I’m done!”
But the theologian was unconvinced. “I’m certain that in four years’ time you’ll stand for a fourth,” he assured the leftwing veteran during their 40-minute tête-à-tête.
“And sure enough, he did,” Betto added last month, as his forecast came true.
On 4 October, just a few weeks shy of his 81st birthday, Lula will indeed seek to extend his legendary five-decade career in what will be the former union leader’s seventh presidential election since his first in 1989.
Lula ran three unsuccessful campaigns before finally making history as Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and winning re-election in 2006.
In 2022 he staged a sensational comeback, defeating the far-right incumbent, Jair Bolsonaro, before thwarting a coup attempt masterminded by his rival a week into his third term.
Four years later, Lula will face Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator, in October’s election, with the pair neck and neck in the polls.
“I honestly don’t see how we can lose this election. I really don’t,” Lula told a podcast recently, although analysts say the vote is too close to call.
During a recent rally in the country’s north-east, a region traditionally associated with Lula, who was born into rural poverty there in 1945, Bolsonaro claimed: “You’re looking at the next president of Brazil.”
Betto, whose full name is Carlos Alberto Libânio Christo, remains confident his comrade of more than four decades will prevail and narrowly win one last term as president. “Politics is his calling,” he says of Lula. “He’s a political animal – he breathes it 25 hours a day.”
But the social activist fears that if his latest prediction is wrong, the consequences for Brazil’s 214 million citizens will be dire. “What’s at stake is the return of a neo-fascist government that washed its hands during the pandemic and dismissed as insignificant the deaths of 700,000 people in Brazil from Covid-19,” Betto says of Jair Bolsonaro’s administration, when the president’s anti-scientific response and sabotage of vaccination efforts was widely blamed for the high death toll.
Betto’s greatest fear is that a second Bolsonaro presidency would help Donald Trump to tighten his grip on Latin America, where he is trying to reassert Washington’s dominance as part of the so-called “Donroe doctrine”.
The most dramatic episode of that campaign came in January, when US special forces invaded Venezuela, abducting President Nicolás Maduro and in effect capturing the government he left behind.
Cuba, which Betto has visited regularly since becoming friends with Fidel Castro after they met in 1980, is also in Trump’s crosshairs. The US has been trying to topple its communist government by suffocating the economy and cutting off the country’s fuel supply.
Betto, 82, believes another Bolsonaro presidency would bring “complete alignment with the US”.
“We would become what Venezuela is today: an American protectorate,” he says. “There would be a devastating wave of privatisations, and social issues would get much worse. Rightwing governments are focused on the elites, focused on the financial markets, and aren’t concerned with the people.”
This week Lula’s campaign accused Trump of seeking to “colonise” Brazil and trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour to capture its natural resources.
The theologian also fears a Bolsonaro win would deal a body blow to the democracy he and Lula were trying to rescue when they became friends in São Paulo’s industrial heartlands in the early 1980s.
While Bolsonaro’s 2023 putsch flopped, Betto believes Brazil’s failure to punish those responsible for abuses during the 1964-85 military regime has left the door open to future power grabs.
“The problem is that we didn’t investigate the crimes of the dictatorship the way Chile, Argentina and Uruguay did,” he says. “So there’s a very strong dictatorial residue in the Brazilian armed forces … that could resurface at any moment.”
The civilians and soldiers responsible for the failed 2023 coup were arrested, tried and jailed during Lula’s third presidency. The ringleader, Jair Bolsonaro, received a 27-year sentence – hence his oldest son seeking the presidency in his place. “All of this could be overturned with Flávio Bolsonaro’s election, because he would have the power to pardon them,” Betto says.
Before the 2022 election there was a powerful outpouring of concern – in Brazil and around the world – over Bolsonaro’s overtly authoritarian plans. But Betto, who has personal experience of the dangers of authoritarian rule, does not detect the same level of alarm now at the prospect of Bolsonaro’s son winning power.
Betto was jailed twice during Brazil’s dictatorship: first suffering 15 days of beatings at the navy’s secret service base in Rio, then spending nearly four years behind bars in São Paulo for helping political dissidents to flee abroad.
“Honestly, the possibility of living under a dictatorship again is truly terrifying,” he says. “The only people who could possibly think a dictatorship is a good thing are those who haven’t experienced it first-hand, like I have.”
Betto says part of the blame for the far-right’s advance lies with the left, which has lost ground to evangelical churches and conservative forces in poor communities, where leftwing Catholic activists such as him were once deeply embedded. “We have to go back to the favelas,” he says. “We have to go back to rural areas. We have to go back to all the places where there are marginalised or excluded people.”
The bestselling writer also worries that Lula – who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term, if he wins – has failed to groom an heir. “I don’t see anyone in the Workers’ party today who has his charisma or political potential,” he says, calling possible successors too inexperienced or lacking in popular appeal.
Speaking during a recent visit to Rio, Betto described his euphoria at his friend’s historic victory nearly 25 years ago. “It was a moment of immense joy for all of us – and of immense hope for Brazil,” says the activist, who recalls reading Lula a passage from Psalm 72 at his home a few hours before his election was confirmed. The psalm says: “He shall have pity on the weak and poor. He shall preserve the lives of the needy.”
Betto believes Lula’s decision to seek re-election stems from his obsession with social justice – even if the theologian sometimes thinks his friend is insufficiently leftwing and missed a historic opportunity to implement agrarian reform when he first came to power.
“Lula is someone who is completely, viscerally dedicated to social issues, because of his personal experience with childhood hunger and abandonment,” he says, noting how four of the 12 children Lula’s mother, Dona Lindu, had died of starvation and extreme poverty.
“I hope Lula wins and I will do everything I can to make that happen,” he adds of next week’s crunch election, before admitting: “But things aren’t easy.”

‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:58 UTC
16:00:58 KST

The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape.
Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness.
Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages.
The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS.
About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre.
Such is the anger locally that the new campaign against the AI datacentre has drawn in tens of thousands of people, uncovered what campaigners say is evidence of secret deals and adopted tactics being used by activists in the US such as Erin Brockovich.
A recent public meeting in Great Torrington was hosted by Elizabeth Humphreys of the US campaign group Not in My Valley. She was one of the forces behind achieving a permanent datacentre ban in Coachella, California, over concerns about air pollution, water and energy use.
“We’re fighting the largest companies that have ever existed in the world, and that is scary but we are all fighting this together,” Humphreys said.
“This is a global issue; we are all connected. People across the world are standing up and fighting back.”
Today within the halls and pubs of Great Torrington and the villages of Huntshaw and Weare Giffard, the AI project is the main talking point. And the question being asked is: why here, in a protected UN biosphere, on productive farmland?
The proposal was first announced to the public this summer with a call by Xlinks for a collaborative approach. But adopting the tactics of veteran campaigners like Brockovich, people from the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group took to their keyboards – researching, rallying and requesting more information in a series of freedom of information (FoI) applications.
What they uncovered fuelled the rising tensions. Documents released under FoI revealed the company had been in closed discussions with council officials since March 2025.
In April, the council issued a letter of “in-principle support” before any environmental statement or public consultation – and more than a year before the proposal was made public.
Torridge district council told the Guardian the pre-application process was standard practice and was confidential. A spokesperson said it was not confirmation of any proposal and intended to offer guidance on whether a proposal was acceptable in principle in planning terms.
In an email dated 18 December 2025, council officials and the developers discussed creating links with a sixth form college in Exeter and a stakeholder engagement plan. “Who do we all feel it is critical to get onboard and when both locally and further afield?” the email asked.
Emily Clark, of the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group, said: “Email exchanges and private meetings spanning the past 18 months reveal some officers treating the project as a foregone conclusion. Community frustration is understandably at boiling point.
“How can the largest and most costly infrastructure proposal in the nation be conducted almost exclusively in secret?”
FoI requests also uncovered a detailed site plan not released to the public. It revealed the two largest buildings would measure 335 metres by 267 metres and cover approximately nine hectares (22 acres) of ground footprint each – both big enough to house Exeter Cathedral 18 times over, campaigners say. Xlinks said its proposals cover about 344 hectares (850 acres) but only a third would be developed; the majority of land would be open to the public or used for new habitat creation to support wildlife, they said.
The campus would also house a 1.8GW battery energy storage system (BESS) involving 1,720 containerised units, dwarfing the largest operational BESS currently in Britain, such as the 100MW Bramley facility in Hampshire.
The UK urgently needs vast BESS facilities to balance electricity supply and demand as wind and solar power generation increase. The government estimates the country requires 23-27GW of battery capacity by 2030 to meet its clean power goals, which it describes as a “very significant level of increase”. But according to research by the House of Commons Library, the government does not hold data on the projected land use required for the expansion, has no specific policies for their location, and has no definitive estimate of the number of operational BESS facilities or their current total capacity. Campaigners in Devon say this creates a “regulatory wild west”.
Clark said: “We’re facing the biggest construction proposal of its kind in the UK, and for that matter, in Europe. It would not only annihilate 850 acres of prime north Devon farmland and breathtaking countryside – an ecological gem – but have massive repercussions for the entire region.
“At their sole public town hall meeting in June, Xlinks assured residents they intended to work collaboratively with our community. Regrettably, genuine dialogue has been nonexistent.”
Those rallying against the proposal cite its proposed location in a globally protected environment, water consumption, wastewater runoff potentially containing toxic Pfas, known as “forever chemicals”, air pollution, high background noise, safety and fire risks associated with the BESS and the industrialisation of open countryside.
In the last few weeks 30,000 people nationally have signed a petition launched by Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, the cabinet member for rural affairs for Devon county council, calling on the government to pause all datacentre and BESS plans outside designated AI growth zones.
“Proposals like this outside AI growth zones are highly problematic, because they may seek to evade regulation and government scrutiny,” said Cottle-Hunkin. “We need an urgent national conversation on AI and associated infrastructure to make sure it’s on the right scale and in the right place.”
After the hottest summer on record, north Devon remains under a hosepipe ban and the potential water usage of such a vast site is a significant concern.
Xlinks says the data campus will be self-sufficient in water terms, recirculating it to absorb heat and topping up mainly from rainwater. But an FoI answer revealed that under extreme conditions, such as severe heatwaves and serious droughts, annual water consumption could reach approximately 2.9bn litres.
Xlinks told the Guardian that the design on which that water consumption estimate was based had been superseded by a new design that would be released during public consultation and in the planning application.
Community tensions erupted this week when protesters rallied and demanded answers about secrecy and due diligence outside a Torridge district council meeting. Doug Bushby, the chair of the council, responded by threatening to call the police over “unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations, abuse, harassment and intimidation”.
When planning applications were received, he said, “they will be dealt with within the same legislative, professional and operational boundaries that exist for all planning applications”.
Meanwhile, PR agents for Xlinks are contacting parish councils for private conversations.
On 18 September, Monkleigh parish council said the PR company Coast Communications had sought a closed meeting. Councillors said the minutes should be made public, and a recording released, but this was refused.
“As a result … Monkleigh parish council will not be accepting the invitation from Coast Communications on behalf of Xlinks to a closed meeting with them and therefore no meeting will be taking place,” the council said.
Xlinks is no stranger to Great Torrington. The company was behind a plan in 2024 to bring wind and solar energy to the UK from Morocco through subsea cables that would come ashore on the north Devon coast, including the building of a new electricity substation. But the government said it would not support the project because it was not in the UK’s national interest and did not clearly align strategically with the government’s mission to build homegrown power.
Xlinks said in a statement its £13.8bn AI and BESS project would bring significant economic investment, between 600 and 1,200 jobs and clean energy infrastructure to the region.
“We will ensure that the Devon data campus is designed sensitively for local people and the environment,” the company said.
“We are carrying out nature and wildlife surveys on site. We must legally improve biodiversity by at least 10%, and plan to exceed this by some margin. Buildings will be sited to minimise visibility, through topography, landscaping and the existing treeline.”
An environmental impact assessment was under way and any mitigation required would be built into the design and secured through planning conditions, Xlinks said.
A spokesperson for Torridge district council said Xlinks had planned to undertake a public consultation in July, but this was postponed until later in the year: “When any proposals are received these will be validated and details will be published on the council’s planning portal … We appreciate that this proposal will understandably continue to generate a lot of local interest.”
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Every battery storage facility we build helps protect families from future energy shocks.
“We have commissioned the national energy system operator to develop the first ever strategic spatial energy plan, which will support a more actively planned approach to energy projects, to bring good jobs to communities and help to lower bills.”

61m tonnes of rubble: Gaza aid workers face delicate task of clearing ruins concealing up to 10,000 bodies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:58 UTC
16:00:58 KST

It took all day to clear a section of road in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood in Gaza City. At the end of it, Ahmed Alyan, a UN engineer, was exhausted, surrounded by mountains of rubble despite the day’s work.
“I feel as if we are holding a spoon and trying to empty the sea,” Alyan said, beads of sweat trickling down his forehead after a long, hot summer day.
Alyan is part of a World Food Programme (WFP) team who have been working on Beirut Street, once a busy main thoroughfare lined with shops, offices and homes and filled with traffic and people. But now it is virtually deserted.
The road was blocked by piles of rubble, stones and the wreckage of destroyed shops. Nearby, a tower stood tilted after some of its concrete foundations were damaged, while displaced families continued to live inside. In some parts of the road, sewage flowed from the ground after the drainage system was damaged and blocked by Israeli bombardment.
The UN estimates that removing the bulk of the rubble in the Gaza Strip could take at least seven to 10 years and cost billions of dollars. That would make the removal of war debris in Gaza one of the largest rubble-clearance operations in modern history.
“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” said Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine.
The task is being carried out in extremely difficult and hazardous conditions. The clearance teams are working in ruins containing countless dead bodies and unexploded bombs. So far, 580km of roads have been cleared, which has in turn made possible the movement of aid trucks, relief teams and residents.
However, the reconstruction of Gaza is a huge challenge facing international and local organisations. After more than two years of work, about 907,000 tonnes of rubble have been removed and more than 300,000 tonnes recycled and reused. But this represents only about 1.5% of the total rubble.
To make things more difficult, the Israeli authorities have banned the necessary equipment from entering Gaza on the grounds that almost any aid that is not food or medicine could be “dual-use” and could somehow benefit Hamas.
Initially, the WFP work was limited to removing debris from the roads and pushing it to the sides to create a passage for trucks. But the sheer quantity was overwhelming, and continuing Israeli bombardment during the nearly year-old ceasefire kept adding to the gargantuan task. Some roads had to be reopened several times.
Meanwhile, the so-called yellow line, a demarcation established at the start of the ceasefire last October, keeps creeping forward as Israeli troops seize more of the territory. The area still accessible to people and aid workers is barely 30% of the whole Gaza Strip, making the problem of what to do with the rubble even more acute.
“One of the ways we have tried to address this problem is by recycling and reusing the rubble in different ways,” Cilliers said.
The UNDP has begun managing five rubble-crushing sites across Gaza, where debris collected from roads and damaged critical infrastructure is processed for reuse. The rubble is first sorted to remove non-concrete materials, including metal and steel rods. The concrete is then crushed into smaller pieces, eventually down to roughly the size of a marble or a very small rock.
UNDP relies on seven crushers across Gaza, all of which were already in the territory before the war. Two of the seven were reconstructed by local engineers in Gaza over the past year, based on models they had available, as they were unable to bring new machinery into the strip.
At one of the crushing sites, a large space that had previously housed UN warehouses, piles of rubble are stacked across the yard. Trucks arriving with large amounts of debris stop on a weighbridge before tipping their cargo on to the piles.
There is a constant roar in the area as the mechanism breaks the concrete into smaller pieces, and the air is thick with dust.
The condition of the machinery poses a big challenge for the teams carrying out the work. Most of the equipment available in Gaza has become severely worn out. The machinery frequently breaks down during operations, partly because of the acute shortage of spare parts, engine oil and other resources needed to maintain and operate it.
With major restrictions on the entry of construction materials still in place, engineers are reusing the crushed rubble for a number of essential purposes. Much of it is used to repair roads and fill potholes, while some is placed beneath tents and shelters to raise them above rainwater and sewage.
Nehal Abu Hassan, a member of the WFP team, said: “These materials cannot be compared with the natural materials normally used to build roads. Their quality is lower, and they are difficult to work with. But there is no alternative. These solutions have been imposed on us by the reality we are living in.”
Removing some of the rubble has already had a big impact. “The road has become wider, the problem of rodents and insects has decreased and cars can pass through more easily,” said Ibrahim Daradona, a displaced man from Jabaliya who is living in the Tel al-Hawa area of Gaza City. “The rubble was even a danger to children playing here.”
More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters, as dire humanitarian conditions persist after nearly three years. Rubble has become part of the environment in which they live every day.
The removal of rubble has also helped revive Gaza’s local economy by creating space for people to start new activities and reopen shops and small businesses. “One of the things we have seen is that when we clear rubble in front of damaged shops and businesses, many of them reopen within around 20 days,” Cilliers said.
Despite all the efforts to remove rubble and restore access to residential areas, the remains of homes carry a particular sensitivity. Every metre of rubble may conceal things that cannot be seen from the outside.
“Rubble in some areas does not represent just debris to people; it represents their entire life and memories. In some cases, there may be bodies still under the rubble. That is why removing it is a very sensitive issue for families and communities,” said Abu Hassan.
The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian issues in Gaza. According to estimates cited by the UNDP, between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies may still be buried.
UNDP has said it is working with organisations including the International Committee of the Red Cross to identify locations where human remains may be buried and prioritise them during rubble-removal and recovery operations.
“We are also working on a forensic process to identify remains, [to] ensure that they are handled properly and that religious burial rights are respected, and [to] provide the necessary documentation and certificates for families. This is extremely important for families in Gaza,” Cilliers said.
Unexploded ordnance in rubble and on roads is a serious challenge for teams clearing the debris. UNDP and WFP teams coordinate with the UN mine-clearing arm, Unmas, the British charity the Halo Trust and other organisations before beginning clearance work, to identify unexploded ordnance and protect workers and returning families.
Given the limited capacity to remove explosive ordnance in Gaza, these organisations cannot disarm or remove all unexploded items. But they can identify hazardous areas and mark them.
Alongside the danger from explosives, rubble may contain other hazardous materials, including asbestos, which can pose a serious health risk when its fibres are inhaled.
Partly standing damaged buildings pose another risk. Some families return to their homes believing they are safe, only for the structures to collapse suddenly. Assessing the safety of damaged buildings before residents return is therefore an important part of the recovery process.
“The progress in early recovery is slow, we are trying to do what we can despite the limitations on bringing in the equipment and services we need,” Cilliers said.

The best thing I ever ate? Mum’s boeuf à la mode on my 21st birthday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:58 UTC
16:00:58 KST

Though we were nurtured by Mum’s cooking daily, my parents’ brood thought little of the effort required, though we devoured the efforts made. It wasn’t until later in life, having donned the mantle of cook as a career, did I begin to appreciate quite what was required to feed a large, boisterous family well. For the most part, we ate simple Scots fare – lentil soup, mince and tatties, suet puddings – but, on occasion, Mum would sit at the counter, trawling through her favourite books, cigarette in hand, and, indicating a find, would duly pen a shopping list.
One such instance was for a birthday feast – Mum’s and mine, for I was born on Mum’s birthday – and the date was the 21st. And this particular birthday was my 21st. Birthdays for the most part were celebrated by just the family around the table at home, and, usually in both Mum and Dad’s hands: the triumphant entrance of a splendid cake, made in whichever child’s favourite flavour (chocolate for my sister, while I adored a spiced fruit cake, thickly iced). I always felt that mum’s birthday was overshadowed by mine, which seemed somewhat unfair. So, for this celebration, I volunteered to bake a cake – an offer she kindly accepted. And so Mum graciously relinquished her kitchen – in itself quite something, for the kitchen was her domain – but more of that anon.
Giving her offspring free rein, Mum set dealing with all else that was to grace the table. Now, Mum was a gifted cook and all too often dazzled friends and family with dishes that quite simply wowed. Ah, what I would give for a last cigarette with her to ask how it was that a pot of boeuf à la mode would take centre stage. This was not by any means the norm for a gathering in the 1980s, particularly on the east coast of Scotland, when the realm of food so familiar today was still in its infancy. But any excuse to cook from Elizabeth David and for Mum to flex a considerable talent.
The dish is a classic of French provincial cooking and the chosen recipe was indeed David’s, from her book of the same name – a masterpiece that is now a constant companion of mine, too. A secondary cut of beef is barded, rolled and tied, then simmered in wine and herbs. There is much freshly milled pepper, sea salt, a few gratings of nutmeg, some pork rinds, and cognac or whisky. To the pot is added a calf’s foot or, more likely in Blighty, pig’s trotters, to ensure the resulting beef, when served cold, is set in a limpid jelly. A cold beef dish? In Scotland? In the very home of Angus beef? The very thought of it still makes me smile. It is a wonderful dish, with a flavour of great depth; rich but surprisingly light, the jelly – dark, shiny and limpid – is nigh-on miraculous. Set in the jelly around the beef are carrots cooked until tender, and though there is a temptation to add other vegetables, such thoughts are best left in the shadows.
Recipes abound for this dish, served hot or cold in cuisine bourgeoise, or dishes referred to quite simply as regional or provincial cookery, and is one of the many dishes grounded in the tradition of the slow cooking of lesser cuts, elevated by wine, herbs and a plethora of vegetables. Such dishes eschew the current vogue or zeitgeist: such cooking has a timeless quality; at once ancient and modern – and utterly delicious.
Mum, quietly going about the business of spooning away all that could cloud the jelly, peeling carrots in between, and on occasion testing the beef for doneness, made a lasting impression. The chosen vessel for serving the finished dish was a deep ashet (Scots for a serving dish), on which the beef, when cooled, could be sliced, the carrots dotted around and the whole thing then placed in the consomm, which, when refrigerated, would set into the aforementioned clear jelly. For all its appearance, it is no simple dish, but nothing hones knowledge like practise. And, as is the magic of such dishes, all the effort is returned manifold because serving the dish requires nowt but carrying to the table.
And alongside? A salad of green or bitter leaves and a pot of mustard – and, being British, a pot of horseradish cream, too. C’est tout. Though a pan of mashed potatoes is hard to resist, serving warm vegetables alongside would garner the wrath of David, for the jelly would dissolve and the cook has already had to deal with the incensed Presbyterian spirit of John Knox at the use of wine and herbs. And, lest we forget, there is pudding to come: the birthday cake.
And so it was my turn to honour the efforts made by Mum on her own birthday, and, having offered to make a cake, I felt it should be of equal measure. Of course, I had one in mind. While trawling a favourite secondhand bookshop, I chanced upon a book dedicated to chocolate by Judith Olney. On the cover was a cake I coveted, and now had the perfect reason to make. A chocolate cake, but not layered: no, this was a wild confection made entirely of chocolate, in the form of a cabbage.
I will spare the details, but suffice to say no one was allowed within a considerable radius as I melted bar after bar of dark chocolate, and painted leaf after leaf of cabbage, each carefully cleaned, dried and wiped clean. I covered every surface I could find with these oddments, and when a chocolate cake had been baked, cooled, scooped out and the centre folded through with chocolate mousse and cream, and shaped into a round, I began the task of peeling each painted cabbage leaf from the chocolate. If I had skimped, the chocolate broke. Anyone coming close hot-footed it in the other direction as a Pig-Pen cloud of intent hovered above my bowed head. Then, after some considerable time, the cloud departed. I sat up straight, because, by some miracle, I had enough leaves to enclose the cake. Though I say it myself, as I recall – or maybe it’s through rose-tinted glasses – the result was not too shabby.
What I do recall, though, was a beautifully laid table agleam with glass, brightly polished silver and perfectly pressed white napkins, wine decanted – and in the middle, pride of place, a great boeuf à la mode.

Between three countries, a young Lithuanian finds her way home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

When people ask 20-year-old Sofija Kaniauskaitė where she is from, the question rarely has a simple answer.
The short version is Lithuania. The longer story begins when she moved to Northern Ireland at age 5, where she spent most of her childhood and teenage years, before moving to Croatia to study at university.
This story is based on a press release from Kaunas University of Technology
This summer, however, Kaniauskaitė returned to Lithuania for several months, taking an internship at Kaunas University of Technology while experiencing something she had never done before: living independently in the country she has always considered home.
“I have always considered myself Lithuanian and, although I have spent most of my life in Northern Ireland, I still feel closer to Lithuania,” she said.
Growing up between cultures
At home in Northern Ireland, Lithuanian culture remained a constant. Her family spoke Lithuanian, listened to Lithuanian music and lived near other Lithuanian families.
Lithuanian food was served at home, while Christmas and Easter were celebrated with traditional dishes. Outside the home, Kaniauskaitė became part of Northern Irish life, celebrating Halloween, Valentine’s Day and local holidays with friends.
“There was quite a clear divide between the culture at home and the culture outside it, and I was part of both,” she said.
Balancing the two cultures was not always easy. As a child, she was eager to fit into Northern Irish society, while her mother worked to ensure that Lithuanian traditions remained part of her life.
“I’m grateful to her for that now,” Kaniauskaitė said.
She also found herself sometimes feeling like an outsider, although friendships with local people and people from other backgrounds helped her navigate those differences.
“Northern Ireland is very diverse, so living there taught me to be more open-minded,” she said. “Growing up among people from different backgrounds taught me to understand and accept others, and that has become an important part of how I see the world.”
A move to Croatia
When it came time for university, Kaniauskaitė chose Croatia, where she is studying digital marketing in Zagreb.
Her decision had a personal side, too: Her boyfriend, Filip, lives there. The couple have been together for almost six years, including four years in a long-distance relationship before she began university. They have spent the past two years living together in Croatia.
Living in Zagreb has given her another culture against which to compare Lithuania and Northern Ireland.
She says Lithuanians can sometimes appear reserved and distant, while Croatians tend to be warmer and more openly sociable. Neither approach, she emphasises, is necessarily better.
“As someone who values personal space, I feel comfortable with Lithuanian culture,” she said. “Lithuanians can sometimes come across as cold, but you generally know where you stand with them.”
Croatia, meanwhile, has taught her to slow down.
Growing up in a small town in Northern Ireland, she was accustomed to a quieter environment. Zagreb, with a population of about 800,000, initially surprised her with its noise and fast pace.
When she returns to Lithuania, she appreciates the quiet streets, orderly traffic and greenery.
“Lithuania, to me, is first and foremost about family and nature – enjoying what surrounds you and appreciating what you have,” she said.
Returning to Lithuania
Her decision to spend the summer in Lithuania was about more than gaining professional experience.
Kaniauskaitė wanted to spend more time with relatives and immerse herself more deeply in a culture she had maintained from abroad but had never experienced as an independent adult.
“There is a lot of uncertainty about my future, and I realise that the time I can spend with my family in Lithuania is limited,” she said.
She also wanted to test her own ability to live in Lithuania.
Although she speaks Lithuanian fluently, she said she is not always confident in her language skills. Living and working in the country gave her an opportunity to challenge herself.
She chose an internship in the International Relations Department at Kaunas University of Technology because her own experience of moving between countries gave her an understanding of the challenges international students can face.
“I wanted to help other students facing difficulties similar to those I have experienced myself,” she said.
During the internship, she has worked mainly with international students, managing an email inbox, answering questions about applications and helping resolve problems.
She also interviewed students online and helped welcome and coordinate new arrivals during Welcome Week.
Having moved countries twice herself, Kaniauskaitė says she can easily relate to students adjusting to a new environment.
Her own social circle reflects that international experience. In both Lithuania and Croatia, many of her friends are international students rather than locals.
“Meeting and communicating with different people helps me become more open to new connections,” she said.
Feeling Lithuanian
Perhaps the most important part of her time in Kaunas has been something much simpler: speaking Lithuanian every day.
For years, her visits to Lithuania had been limited largely to summer holidays with relatives. This time, she experienced ordinary life in the country – working, living independently and constantly surrounded by the Lithuanian language.
“Being able to speak my native language every day helped me feel more Lithuanian,” she said. “When I’m here, I have absolutely no doubt that I am Lithuanian.”
She has also noticed qualities in Lithuanians that remind her of herself.
She describes Lithuanians as logical and direct, with a strong preference for clarity and doing things properly. Growing up, she was often told she was the same way.
“It feels special to recognise these similarities between myself and other Lithuanians, even though I haven’t lived in Lithuania for a long time,” she said.
Finding her place in Kaunas
Before arriving in Kaunas, Kaniauskaitė knew little about the city. She had heard Lithuanians say there was not much to do there and arrived without particularly high expectations.
Several months later, her view has changed.
“What I appreciate most about Kaunas is its calm atmosphere and nature, but calm certainly does not mean boring,” she said. “The city is lively and there is plenty to do – you just have to look for it.”
For her, the appeal lies in the balance between city life and nature.
“You can feel the rhythm of the city while still being able to escape into nature, relax and slow down for a while,” she said.
Kaunas has gradually become more than a temporary home for an internship. The experience has strengthened her desire to return to Lithuania someday, whether to study, work or live.
That decision, however, can wait.
Kaniauskaitė has one more year of her bachelor’s degree in Croatia before she plans to pursue a master’s degree. She has not yet decided where.
“I enjoy living in both Croatia and Lithuania, so ideally I would like both countries to be part of my life,” she said.
For now, she does not feel pressure to choose one country over the other. Living in different places, she says, is a privilege – and she remains open to adding more countries to the story.
“I would like to continue having experiences like these in the future – perhaps not only in Lithuania or Croatia, but in other countries too,” she said. “My future is still very uncertain, so time will tell where this journey eventually takes me.”

Northern Ireland protesters block Orange Order march in Portadown
Crowd gathered on Garvaghy Road on Sunday to protest against a court ruling allowing the march.
Thousands of protesters have blocked a route into the Catholic area of a Northern Irish town that a Protestant organisation was due to march down.
Northern Ireland’s High Court permitted the Protestant Orange Order organisation to march through a mainly Catholic area in the town of Portadown on Sunday for the first time in 28 years, reviving one of the region’s most contentious marching disputes.

The court rejected a final attempt by residents to stop the parade from passing through the Garvaghy Road, after Northern Ireland’s Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction granted on Saturday.
Thousands of people, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein and the party’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the road to protest against the decision.
“This is madness,” McDonald told reporters shortly after 8am (07:00 GMT) when the march was due to begin. “This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.
“This is a dignified and united community, and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”
McDonald and O’Neill urged the British government and police to intervene to stop the parade. O’Neill said she had spoken to Britain’s minister for the region and the Irish government.
Police vans parked nearby had earlier played out a warning that anyone taking part in the protest was committing a criminal offence.
A small group of Orange Order members wearing traditional silk orange sashes and black bowler hats gathered in another part of the town, a picture posted on X by Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) lawmaker Carla Lockhart showed.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm, saying there have been “big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards”.
Jon Boutcher, the head of Northern Ireland police, called for “those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law”, referring to the protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there have been no signs of violence or disorder.
“Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland.”
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, from the DUP, which supports Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, said on Sunday that threats of violence were unacceptable. “No one in Northern Ireland wants violence or disorder,” she added.
The Irish government said it was “very concerned” about the situation and that its priority was to avoid “a return to the divisions of the past”.
The Orange Order is a Protestant organisation closely associated with unionism, the political tradition that favours Northern Ireland remaining in the UK.
The Parades Commission, the independent body that rules on disputed marches in Northern Ireland, approved Sunday’s procession with a 35-person limit, barred bands and accompanying supporters, and required the march to finish by 9:30am (08:30 GMT).
The dispute over the Drumcree parade and Garvaghy Road became one of the most bitter marching confrontations of the “Troubles”, the decades-long conflict over Northern Ireland’s political status that largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
Repeated attempts by the Orange Order to return from Drumcree Parish Church along Garvaghy Road triggered protests, violence and major security operations during the 1990s.

The Takeaway: UN General Assembly debate Day 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:52:08 UTC
15:52:08 KST

The Takeaway: UN General Assembly debate Day 5
From artificial intelligence to migration, some of the forces reshaping the twenty-first century took centre stage at the UN General Assembly on Saturday. Leaders wrestled with a common dilemma: how to harness profound technological and social change without allowing it to deepen the divisions already separating countries and communities. This edition of The Takeaway distils key points from Day 5 of the annual high-level debate.
AI: Great promise, serious peril
Why it matters: Artificial intelligence emerged as one of the day’s defining themes, with speakers describing a technology capable of transforming economies and improving lives, but also potentially widening inequality, undermining trust and threatening security.
- China’s Vice President Han Zheng said AI should be developed “for the positive and for good”, while calling for efforts to narrow the digital divide.
- Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan described AI as “the most urgent frontier”, arguing that governments need to invest in infrastructure and skills alongside safeguards and rigorous rules. His bottom line was distinctly human: “Human beings must remain in control and accountable.”
Who gets to shape the AI future?
The big picture: Several speakers warned that the AI revolution risks reproducing a familiar global divide, with technological power and decision-making concentrated in a few countries.
- Jamaica’s Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith cautioned against allowing AI to “deepen old inequalities and create an entirely new global divide”, calling for investment in infrastructure, skills and capacity in developing countries.
- Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Haji Hasan put the question even more pointedly: “The Global South cannot simply become a destination for data centres while decisions about AI are made elsewhere.”
- Belize’s Prime Minister John Briceño noted that well-governed AI could expand access to knowledge and improve public services. Poorly governed, however, it could deepen inequality, displace workers and leave developing countries dependent on technologies and rules created elsewhere.
The rules are struggling to keep up
Reality check: Technology is evolving across borders faster than many governments can regulate it.
- Moldova’s Prime Minister Vasile Tofan warned that “technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere”, with AI widening that gap.
- Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul captured both sides of the argument, imagining AI helping humanity prevent famine and cure cancer, while warning that in the wrong hands it could disrupt economies and influence global peace and security. “Whenever power becomes global, responsibility must become global, too,” he said.
Migration puts solidarity to the test
Beyond technology: The movement of people across borders brought the debate back to immediate human realities.
- Djibouti appealed for international assistance as thousands fleeing violence in Yemen place pressure on the country’s capacity to receive refugees.
- The Holy See called for an end to the suffering of hundreds of thousands of stateless Rohingya, while Tunisia urged countries to move beyond treating irregular migration primarily as a security issue and address underlying causes such as conflict, poverty and unemployment.
- The Philippines stressed that migrant workers are entitled to human rights and protection from trafficking and exploitation, regardless of status.
Youth as an opportunity, not a crisis
Looking ahead: Zambia offered a different perspective on demographic change, describing Africa’s youthful population as one of the continent’s greatest assets.
- Foreign Minister Mulambo Hamakuni Haimbe noted that by 2050, one in every four young people worldwide will be African, arguing that education, skills, technology, entrepreneurship and decent jobs will determine whether that demographic shift becomes an engine of global prosperity.
And up next: The General Assembly returns on Monday for the final day of the 2026 general debate, bringing this year’s week of speeches, warnings and prescriptions for a changing world to a close. Follow Meetings Coverage here, and a special site dedicated to the debate here.

There was a shooting at the same tavern about a month ago, and Saturday's shooting could be retaliation for that, he added.

"Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet," the statement said.
