In Chuhuiv district, an apartment building and 15 private vehicles were damaged in Lebiazhe, while power lines were hit in the village of Zarichne.
In Bohodukhiv district, strikes damaged four private houses in Zolochiv, private homes in Riasne and Kalynove, and private vehicles in Skovorodynivka and Sinne.
In Lozova district, a private house and a civilian enterprise were damaged in Lozova, an administrative building and four cars in Zlatopil, and a private house in Dobropillia.
A residential building and a hangar were hit in the city of Izium.
In Kharkiv district, the attacks damaged cars in Pytomnyk and Ruska Lozova, a private house in Tsyrkuny and a shop in Derhachi.
Evacuations continue as Russian strikes persist
The transit evacuation center in Lozova received 185 people over the past day, Syniehubov said, adding that it has registered a total of 62,012 people since it opened.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify the figures.
Citing the General Staff of the AFU, Synehubov said Ukrainian units repelled four Russian attacks near the settlements of Ternova, Kozacha Lopan and Lyman in the Southern Slobozhanskyi axis.
In the Kupiansk axis, Russian forces made three attempts to improve their positions, launching assaults toward Kupiansk, Radkivka and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi.

Libya's national oil firm has announced that an oil pipeline blocked for several days by an armed group had reopened, ending a disruption it said had cost $95 million.
The pipeline links the Al-Sharara oilfield in southwest Libya to the Zawiya export terminal on the Mediterranean coast.

Blockades of oil and gas facilities have been common in Libya in recent years, driven by social grievances, security threats or political disputes.

Martin Mölder: Politicians' battle over attention and memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Martin Mölder: Politicians' battle over attention and memory
The opposition wants voters under no circumstances to forget what happened in the previous elections — namely broken promises and the hiding of their real political intentions, notes Martin Mölder.
Since the moment the current government became a minority government, the question of why the opposition still does not distrust the government and replace it in one way or another with some other government has noticeably increased. The possibility would exist mathematically, and there is much talk, but it is not visible or not likely that it would happen.
Elections are rarely won in the way some of the more common understandings of democracy prescribe to us. Decisions are not made in such a way that parties present their political programs and then the public discusses them and voters finally decide in favor of the party politically closest to them. Reality is much more multifaceted.
Before elections, a complicated battle takes place over voters' attention and memory. The object of that attention or memory is often not political positions, but rather various events and situations that have the potential to push voters in one direction or another. Not only with reason, but also with emotions. What is said out loud does not have to match what the battle is actually about. Perhaps we do not want democracy to function this way, but reality is often exactly like that.
The stakes are high, because voters' memory and attention can change quickly, and with that also what is important and what is unimportant. Larger changes in recent history have come rather from factors that are not under anyone's control, but there is always an attempt to shape events and context accordingly.
Let us recall even the coronavirus crisis, under the cover of which measures restricting people's freedoms became possible overnight — measures that in any other situation would have provoked much stronger public outrage. People's attention was elsewhere. Or let us recall the beginning of the war in Ukraine, which quickly made voters forget how dissatisfied they had been at that moment with then‑Prime Minister Kaja Kallas's government and the Reform Party's energy and coronavirus policies.
Even now, a battle is underway over whether to keep or change voters' memory and attention. The opposition wants voters under no circumstances to forget what happened in the previous elections — broken promises and the hiding of their real political intentions. That voters would not forget Kaja Kallas's Russia‑transit scandal or the current artillery‑shell procurement scandal. That they would not forget how disappointed they have been in the governing parties over the past three years.
The government itself wants to divert attention from all of this as much and as quickly as possible. This has not yet succeeded, but one can be sure that they will try at any cost. Experience shows that fear often works very well. The previous elections were largely decided by fear — fear of war and fear of a different kind of government, which was very effectively instilled in part of the voters. If it worked once, then certainly the thought arises that maybe it will work again.
Let us now return to distrust of the government and changing the government. All parties behave self‑interestedly; this is natural and normal, and it must be so. Democracy is born from what and how happens between parties. It is an emergent phenomenon at the system level, not a property of the system's components. What matters is that the system is designed so that self‑interest cannot be entrenched at the system level.
From the perspective of directing and maintaining attention, no opposition party should want to be in government right now, because it is not in their interest. It would free the Reform Party from the heavy burden of governing and allow them to recover before the elections in the position of an opposition party. It would allow voters to forget why they do not like the current government.
By entering the government, the opposition would put itself in a significantly more difficult position before the elections. One cannot simply gift support to anyone. Except for the exceptional background of the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Reform Party has recently been rather weak in the eyes of voters while governing, and has enjoyed high support rather as an opposition party.
Emphasizing the question of distrust directs attention to the fact that we must, until the elections — even if we do not like it — accept this unpopular government. That there is currently no possibility of forming some other government, because the distribution of power in the Riigikogu is exactly as it is. That in Estonia's political system, alongside regular elections, there is no mechanism that would help bring a seriously derailed system back on track. This directs voters' attention to possible shortcomings of the system.
Nor is it in the interest of any opposition party right now to create some cross‑party or apolitical interim government that would govern us until the elections. For the same reason. Such an interim government would potentially be something that saves the Reform Party and frees them from their current difficult role.
Half‑jokingly, one could say that the Reform Party itself — not the opposition — should be the one thinking about the idea of an interim government, but in doing so they would have to briefly admit that they cannot manage governing, and naturally this would have its own negative effect.
In short, over the next five months it is not worth taking some of the more prominent contours of Estonian politics too literally. What is said directly is of course important, but often the talk is simultaneously about something else entirely. Words can also be used to direct attention, to make one forget or remember.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Mass deployment of interceptor drones in Ukraine expected within a few months — Budanov
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
09:40:00 EEST
15:40:00 KST

Mass deployment of interceptor drones in Ukraine expected within a few months — Budanov
Kyiv • UNN
Prototypes of interceptor drones are already destroying jet-powered "Shaheds" in combat. Ukraine is scaling up their production, currently intercepting 55% of such UAVs.
The mass deployment of interceptor drones could begin within several months. Prototypes are already being tested in combat conditions, where they are destroying enemy drones, and the next task is to scale up the production and use of such systems, said Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, in a comment to Novyny.LIVE, reports UNN.
According to Budanov, the new developments are being tested directly while countering enemy attacks.
We are now testing prototypes not as before in laboratories, but in real-world conditions, and they are doing their job, said the Head of the Office of the President.
Budanov suggested that the mass deployment of such systems could begin within several months. At the same time, he did not name a specific date, production volumes, or the names of the interceptors.
Ukraine is scaling up measures against jet-powered drones
The previous evening, in his address on September 26, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced several effective prototypes of interceptors for Russian jet-powered drones. According to him, individual teams are already using these developments in combat conditions. The president noted that interceptors had been identified that could become the primary means of protection against this threat. Ukraine is currently increasing their production and securing the necessary components.
The issue was also considered at a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief on September 25. Participants heard reports on test results, interception figures, and the experience of teams engaged in intercepting jet-powered "Shaheds."
Following the meeting, Zelenskyy announced the acceleration of production of the designated countermeasure systems. New decisions were also made on deploying production of various types of jet engines in Ukraine.
What is known about the test results
The president had already announced the creation of prototypes of high-speed interceptors against jet-powered "Shaheds" on September 3. At the time, he noted that the developments needed to be brought to the required level of effectiveness. Ensuring a sufficient number of high-speed interceptor drones and low-cost missiles to counter the new threats was identified as a comprehensive task for Ukraine's defense industry and cooperation with partners.
On September 15, Zelenskyy announced the successful engagement of a "Shahed" during the testing of another Ukrainian development against jet-powered drones. At the same time, according to him, certain technical issues still required further work. On September 17, the president announced another positive test result—the downing of a jet-powered "Shahed"—and announced the scaling up of the relevant solutions.
What proportion of jet-powered "Shaheds" are being neutralized
According to data cited by Zelenskyy on September 26, since the beginning of the month Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet-powered "Shaheds." More than 1,500 of these drones were shot down or suppressed. The president estimated the current interception rate for jet-powered "Shaheds" at 55%. At the same time, according to him, the interception rate for conventional "Shaheds" exceeds 90%.
Recall
Interceptor drones against conventional "Shaheds" are already being used by the Defense Forces. In parallel, Ukraine is developing new means of combating jet-powered drones.

Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:36:44 UTC
15:36:44 KST

Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
Passengers board their train after being evacuated due to an air raid alert near the border with Poland in Ukraine on Sept. 18, 2026. (Ania Tsoukanova / AFP via Getty Images)
On Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers from the Polish border. The attack near Yahodyn caused no casualties, but it drew attention to one of Ukraine's most important links to the outside world amid the pressures of Russia's war — the railway.
Ukrainian state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said its monitoring team detected the threat early enough to evacuate the crew before the strike on the locomotive.
Russia has targeted Ukraine's railway throughout the full-scale invasion, but the intensity of attacks has risen sharply over 2026. At the same time, Ukraine increasingly depends on the railway for passengers, trade, diplomacy, and wartime logistics.
"The first goal is to disrupt logistics, both passenger traffic and the movement of goods," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told the Kyiv Independent.
"The second follows from that — weakening the economy, disrupting transport links with neighboring countries. Intimidating our partners may also be one of their goals."
While Moscow is unlikely to erode international support for Ukraine, he said, the immediate impact on transportation and trade is more serious.
read also
A lifeline
Ukraine historically developed around an extensive railway network, making it far more heavily dependent on rail than most European countries. Its road infrastructure, meanwhile, remains less developed.
Around 60% of the country's freight is transported by rail, and trains account for about 37% of domestic and international passenger transportation, according to Serhiy Vovk, director of the Centre for Transport Strategies.
In many European countries, he said, rail typically accounts for around 10% to 20% of passenger and freight transport.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen."
The dependence is even greater in foreign trade. About half of Ukrainian exports move by rail, Vovk estimates. For products such as iron ore, metals, and some agricultural goods, moving comparable volumes by road would be prohibitively expensive and place enormous pressure on highways.
Pressure on the railway could grow further if stable operations at Ukraine's Black Sea ports are not restored after another sustained Russian bombing campaign.
"If the issue of stable port operations is not resolved by November or December, domestic storage facilities may remain filled with grain and processed agricultural products that need to be exported," Vovk said.
The railway also became the backbone of Ukraine's "iron diplomacy," carrying foreign leaders and officials between the western border and Kyiv after the airspace closed in 2022.
Passengers increasingly feel the growing pressure on the railway. An attack hundreds of kilometers away can disrupt schedules for hours, and Russia's growing use of drones against trains and railway infrastructure means evacuations or emergency stops can become necessary along the route at any time.
But these visible delays are only one part of a wider disruption that can ripple through the network. Passenger trains operate on fixed schedules and are generally prioritized, while freight trains only move when capacity becomes available.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen. So the passenger sees the delay. But the larger hidden impact is felt by businesses and the economy," Vovk said.
read also
Real bottlenecks
Vovk does not see attacks on border crossings alone as a strategy capable of cutting Ukraine off from Europe. Western Ukraine has a relatively extensive railway network, so traffic can be rerouted when a route or junction is damaged.
But since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. More than half were hit this year alone.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt."
Replacing the locomotives is difficult. Ukraine uses a 1,520-millimeter rail gauge, meaning most European locomotives cannot simply be transferred into service, and available compatible stocks abroad are limited.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt," Vovk said.
Amid migration, mobilization, and losses among railway workers, Ukraine is also short of about 10% of the locomotive crews it needs, he said. Unlike a damaged track, that shortage cannot be fixed quickly.
"You cannot train a qualified driver in a year," Vovk said.
read also
A winter stress test
New rules allowing trains to continue operating under lower-level air threats rather than automatically stopping came into effect on Sept. 18. Under the highest threat level, boarding and disembarkation are suspended while passengers and staff move to shelters.
Decisions on trains already in motion are made on a case by case basis, using information from Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring teams.
The company is also dispersing rolling stock and passenger flows, developing protected facilities for workers and passengers at major junctions, and exploring greater use of electronic warfare systems.
With winter approaching, preparedness becomes more urgent.
"A train that stops for hours in an open area in summer is an inconvenience. In freezing temperatures, particularly with children or elderly passengers on board, it can become a safety problem," Vovk said.
Protocols may increasingly need to ensure that trains stop near stations or populated areas where passengers can access shelter, electricity, and heat, he said.
Besides protecting tracks and stations under constant Russian threat across the country, Ukraine also needs to restore and procure locomotives, train new personnel, and build reserves.
"Otherwise, when passenger and freight volumes increase, the problem may no longer be whether the tracks are available, but whether there are enough locomotives — and enough people — to keep trains moving," Vovk said.

According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,384 tanks, 25,442 armored combat vehicles, 154,245 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,428 artillery systems, 2,163 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,677 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,762 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

'You could be the next Maricarmen': Madrid protest camp grows after eviction outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:31:12 UTC
15:31:12 KST

A protest camp in Madrid grew to include dozens of tents on Sunday after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home sparked outrage over gaps in tenant protections.
Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher after police broke down her door on Wednesday have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due in 2027.
Thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday, rattling keys and blowing whistles as they called for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult.
“You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner at the rally.
Authorities put the turnout at around 25,000, while the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organised the protest, said more than 300,000 people took part.
After the march, activists set up camp in Puerta del Sol square in the city centre. The union urged more people to join them.
“It’s time to change the rules of the game,” said Maria Juarez, a 47-year-old psychologist. “People aren’t going to leave until something changes once and for all.”
Police looked on as about a dozen tents were pitched outside the Madrid regional government headquarters, surrounded by thousands of protesters, an AFP reporter at the scene said.
By the early hours of Sunday, El Pais reported that the camp had grown to around 150 tents, with hundreds of people planning to spend the night. News agency EFE put the number of tents at around 100.
‘Live in fear’
Abascal was forced to leave the flat where she had lived for 70 years after a property firm acquired it and raised the rent by 275 percent to $3,000 (€2,650), according to the tenants’ union.
Her eviction has become a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis. In a video posted online hours before the march, she urged Spaniards to join the protest.
“I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction.
“I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added.
Enrique Ortega de Miguel, a 38-year-old graphic designer who lives with his mother, said Spain’s housing market was “impossible”.
“It is a struggle to find a place you can afford, then you live in fear of being forced out,” he told AFP at Saturday’s march.
Maricarmen Arnedo, a 76-year-old pensioner, said that while older people were being forced out of their homes, “young people can’t move out of their parents’ homes”.
“We want house prices and rents to come down, because I’m fed up with washing the underpants of my 53-year-old son,” she added.
Pressure to act
The government is expected to approve a package of measures dubbed the “Maricarmen decree” at its next cabinet meeting. The proposals would include the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions.
A similar bill was defeated earlier this year, but Abascal’s case has increased pressure on political parties to act.
The Bank of Spain estimates that the country, home to around 50 million people, is short of 700,000 homes based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Spain has little public housing, while increased demand, including from tourism and population growth linked to immigration, has pushed up rents, analysts say.

Tensions between Germany and Russia hit a flashpoint in early September after Berlin accused Russia of being behind a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport earlier this year.

Morality Beyond the Head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:21:39 UTC
15:21:39 KST

Introduction
Consider a common occurrence. An ordinary person is going about their business when there is a sudden emergency which endangers someone’s life. That person despite their fear, or often multiple people, unthinkingly spring into action. This may be running into a burning building and dragging out its unconscious occupants. Or jumping into treacherous waters to save a drowning child. We call these people heroes. When asked about why they did it afterwards, however, it is just as common for that person to say that they weren’t a hero at all, they just did what needed to be done. In such situations reflective thought and egoistic self-interest take a back seat and we just respond to a moral need. These examples challenge standard Western theories of ethics that hold that ethical responses are (or should be) grounded in reflective moral deliberation and the following of moral rules. Or more plainly that ethics requires a separate thinking self. The cases of everyday heroes on the other hand point to their extraordinary actions arising from an immersion in the situation rather than being stuck in their heads.
Such examples point to the possibility of a non-ego-based ethics. They suggest that moral action does not require deliberation or even a sense of being a separate self. In fact, these may be what often gets in the way of responding to a moral need. The idea that selflessness leads to compassion is familiar from Buddhism and other Eastern traditions. But you don’t need to accept any of that to follow the argument here. Rather it emerges from a surprising Western phenomenological source — Jean-Paul Sartre. The phenomenological basis of the insight means that it can be tested right now, in your chair, with nothing more than your own direct attention.
In The Transcendence of the Ego (TE),1 Jean-Paul Sartre developed an account of selflessness. He argued that consciousness is fundamentally non-egological, and that meaning, including ethical significance, is given in the world prior to reflective thought. The moral phenomenology developed in this short book is profound and yet remains under-explored. According to Sartre, we do not first encounter neutral facts and then impose a moral interpretation. The ethical salience of a situation and the demand that it makes of us is already present in how it appears to us. We just need to get out of the way so that the ethical response can naturally flow.
While Sartre describes in detail how non-reflective consciousness grounds ethical responsiveness, he doesn’t provide a method for reliably accessing this moral openness in our everyday lives. Most moral demands made of us do not occur in emergencies. As such egoistic and self-interested thought all too often get in the way of a compassionate response. A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:21:26 UTC
15:21:26 KST

A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian) is a city on the left bank of the Dnipro River, across from Kherson on the right bank. Only nine kilometers (about six miles) separate them in a straight line. People once crossed between them by bridge, but the bridge is now closed. The two cities are on opposite sides of the front: Ukraine controls Kherson, while Russia has controlled Oleshky since 2022. As in other cities near the front, life in Oleshky is difficult and dangerous. By September 2026, conditions had deteriorated so badly that people in both Ukraine and Russia were calling the situation critical. Those who remain are trying to survive without food, electricity, and adequate medical care. They cannot leave safely and often cannot even bury their loved ones. Here is what Meduza has been able to learn about conditions in the city.
The situation in Oleshky was already being called critical in Ukraine in the spring. By September, even the Kremlin agreed
“It’s a humanitarian catastrophe, people are driven to despair,” Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Oleshky’s evacuated Ukrainian administration, told The Kyiv Independent in April 2026. She tries to keep in touch with residents and tells Ukrainian media what is happening there.
“If the situation doesn’t improve, people will just die there from hunger. Because there’s no way out, no food supplies coming in,” Anna, an Oleshky resident who recently escaped to a Ukrainian-controlled area, told the outlet.
In the summer, the U.N. mission in Ukraine said Oleshky’s last store had closed in January 2026, and all food deliveries had stopped by late May. Medical care was available only for the most urgent cases. Ambulances no longer responded to calls, and patients with serious conditions could not be transferred to other hospitals. Anyone trying to enter or leave the city faced two dangers: drones overhead and mines on the ground.
In July, Human Rights Watch said shortages of food and medical care in Oleshky were compounded by the collapse of basic utilities. The city had no electricity or gas, and people had switched to wood-burning stoves. People who had managed to leave Oleshky said they were afraid even to go out for water because drones circled overhead and mines lay scattered along the streets. Human Rights Watch said it was impossible to say for certain whose weapons they were. Both Russian and Ukrainian forces had used drones and mines in the area during the war.
At the time, the Russian occupation authorities in the Kherson region still denied that there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, communications were unreliable, and utility crews could not make repairs because of shelling. On September 21, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the situation in the city critical. “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to obstruct deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops are continuing to work to resolve the situation,” he said.
Oleshky is in its fifth year under occupation. Why is there talk of a humanitarian catastrophe now?
Continued fighting and the gradual deterioration of infrastructure appear to have made conditions worse.
In the fall of 2022, when Russian troops retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson, Oleshky became a frontline city. The destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam flooded Oleshky in the summer of 2023, badly damaging its infrastructure. The occupation administration says Ukrainian attacks have hampered repairs and deliveries of food and medicine.
As the use of FPV drones increased along the front, Oleshky — like Kherson across the Dnipro — became increasingly dangerous. Drone attacks killed civilians as well as soldiers. Mines added to the danger. The area around the city was so heavily mined that, by early 2026, getting in or out had become very difficult. That was when conditions in Oleshky began to deteriorate rapidly, Hasanenko said.
Gardens fed Oleshky’s residents through the summer. No one knows what winter will bring. Some are reportedly already eating dogs.
It is difficult to reach Oleshky’s residents now, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Some go months without making contact. Those who can charge a phone with a generator and occasionally call or send a message say food is scarce. “People have run out of food. They’re making soup with weeds, throwing in purslane, lamb’s quarters, and amaranth. I can’t even talk about the animals anymore — they have it worst of all. I just cry and don’t know what to do,” one Oleshky resident told Ukrainska Pravda.
Through the summer, residents survived mainly on what they grew in their gardens. Bartering is widespread in the city. “Anything you can still buy costs, say, a thousand rubles. A kilogram of sugar or salt is a thousand rubles; so is a pack of Citramon [painkillers]. But money is actually worth nothing, because no matter how much you have, no one is selling anything,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
Some people risk traveling to Radensk for food. The village is 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) from Oleshky, farther from the front, and better supplied. But the trips are dangerous because of mines and drones. An Oleshky resident who recently returned from Radensk told Ukrainska Pravda that she brought back 85 kilograms (about 190 pounds) of food for three families. She rode a bicycle to Radensk but returned to Oleshky on foot.
Hasanenko told Ukrainska Pravda that people in the city had begun eating dogs: “A week ago, I was still denying the reports, but now someone there has confirmed it to me. There’s really nothing to eat. The situation isn’t just getting worse every day — it’s getting worse every hour.”
According to Ukrainian officials, Russian troops in Oleshky are also short of food, so they have been taking it from civilians. Some residents have begun putting signs on their fences saying things like “No food here” or “Elderly people live here.”
Oleshky’s hospital has been called the city’s last refuge. It stayed open after pharmacies and stores closed. But conditions there are dire, too.
Residents weakened by malnutrition used to be taken to the local hospital, where staff fed them as best they could. Recently, the hospital, already operating at limited capacity, has all but stopped functioning. Staff can still stop bleeding, but there are no medicines or equipment, and there is not enough fuel for the generator. According to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources, the hospital has begun turning away civilian patients.
“The hospital is asking local people to bring whatever grains or anything else they have, so it can at least give bedridden amputees breakfast. It’s the only place people can still come to spend the night, because it doesn’t get shelled, and get a hot meal if someone cooks it off the generator. But things are critical there,” said volunteer Kseniia Arkhypova, who is from Oleshky and remains in contact with people there.
According to Arkhypova, Russian troops do not allow residents to bury the dead themselves because they “want to take the bodies to Henichesk for examination and produce a report saying the Ukrainian Armed Forces shot them.” Bodies awaiting burial used to be taken to the morgue, but it has since been destroyed, so they are kept in the hospital basement. “Everything’s leaking, and it stinks,” Arkhypova said, and bodies have been piling up since May. Some people quietly bury loved ones in their yards or gardens.
“The occupiers won’t allow the bodies of people killed [in shelling] to be released. There are about 100 bodies in the hospital basements. […] We know of cases where bodies are simply left lying under the scorching sun and no one removes them. At best, if someone knew the person who died, they might cover the body with branches or a piece of cloth,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
More than a thousand people remain in Oleshky, including dozens of children. Few manage to leave.
Ukrainian volunteers estimate that about 1,500 people, including 40 children, still live in Oleshky. Another 4,000 people, including 150 children, live in nearby villages. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, these communities had a combined population of 40,000.
People remain in the city for different reasons. Some are elderly or have limited mobility. Others feel they have nowhere to go. Some have no documents. To leave through occupied territory, they need a Russian passport, but getting one in Oleshky is impossible because the city is cut off by land and air. Russia refuses to open a humanitarian corridor to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Some men of draft age fear they will be sent into the Russian army if stopped at checkpoints. Some people cannot leave relatives behind in Oleshky. Others have no money or are simply afraid of being killed on the way out.
There is no organized evacuation from the city. Ukrainian officials say the Russian army does not want civilians to leave because their presence deters Ukrainian strikes. Meduza found no comments from the occupation authorities explaining why they have not arranged an evacuation.
In any case, under the Geneva Conventions, the occupying power is responsible for civilians in occupied territory. It is obliged to provide the population with food and medicine “to the fullest extent of the means available to it.”

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, on Saturday – the first such meeting between the two countries’ top diplomats since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The meeting took place behind closed doors on Saturday, Sept. 26, on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Deutsche Welle reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the meeting, which reportedly lasted 22 minutes, Wadephul called on Moscow to “reject the dangerous path of escalation” against Germany, Europe and NATO, a German Foreign Ministry spokesperson told AFP.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said the talks were held at Germany’s request, with the German side asking for restricted media access.
Hybrid attacks won’t shake support for Ukraine, Wadephul says
According to the German spokesperson, Wadephul told Lavrov that incidents such as the recent attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which Berlin has accused Russia of doing, and other hybrid attacks would not weaken Germany’s resolve to support Ukraine.
The German side also condemned Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
The unnamed German diplomat also condemned Russian attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine.
“This attempt to increase pressure does not change anything in Russia’s hopelessness: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers are dying in a hopeless positional war, while the Russian economy continues to collapse.”
Russian Attacks on Kyiv Kill 1, Injure at Least 10 Since Saturday
Relations deteriorate amid retaliatory closures
The talks come after weeks of rising tensions between Berlin and Moscow.
On Aug. 4, an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport – a major hub for military deliveries to Ukraine.
After a nearly monthlong investigation, the German government concluded on Sept. 1 that Russia was responsible.
In response, Wadephul ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and ended the agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
Moscow rejected the accusations as “entirely fabricated,” and retaliated the closures on Sept. 7, ordering the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg to close by Sept. 18 and shutting the remaining branches of the Goethe-Institut, Germany’s cultural institute, across the country.
According to TVP World citing the Russian embassy in Berlin on Sept. 11, Germany then ordered more than 150 employees of Russian missions and their family members to leave the country.
“A broken drone of unclear origin that caused no harm – is this a ‘reasonable’ reason to deprive hundreds of thousands of German citizens and Russian citizens residing in Germany of access to consular services?” the embassy said in a statement.
The tensions have remained sour since.
On Tuesday, Sept. 22, a crashed drone and suspected explosive material were found near the Bundeswehr’s Wunstorf Air Base in Lower Saxony.
The German investigators are examining them for possible links to the Leipzig case.
Sybiha briefed on the talks
“I am grateful to Minister Wadephul for conveying our firm shared positions to the Russian side: insisting that Moscow end its war, reaffirming unwavering support for Ukraine, and warning against further hostile actions against Europe,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a statement on X.
The two ministers discussed next steps to advance peace efforts and achieve a ceasefire, as well as ways to increase pressure on Russia and strengthen Ukraine’s resilience ahead of winter.
This winter is particularly important, as Russia is widely expected to target additional critical infrastructure. Instead of targeting just the power grid, the campaign is believed to also include the water supplies.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues working on securing the Patriot interceptors it urgently needs to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
First meeting since Baerbock
The previous meeting between German and Russian foreign ministers took place in January 2022, when the former Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock met Lavrov less than a month before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
According to Deutsche Welle, Wadephul is representing Germany at this year’s UNGA in place of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who stayed home amid domestic political pressure after his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) performed poorly in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
Lavrov, meanwhile, is leading Russia’s delegation under a decree signed by Russian President Vladimir Putin in August.
Putin has not attended the UNGA in person since 2015, and his travel abroad has been limited since the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for his arrest in 2023 over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.
On Sept. 18, ahead of the UNGA high-level debate week, US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Besides allowing Trump to impose up to 100% of tariffs on Russia’s energy buyers, the bill also creates enforceable financial and travel penalties against individuals, state bodies, and commercial intermediaries involved in the illegal removal of Ukrainian minors.

Cambodian FM warns UN of strains on global peace, calls for rebuilding trust in multilateralism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:14:54 CST
15:14:54 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn alerted the United Nations that a mix of political rivalries, climate issues, widening inequalities, and rapid technological transformation is threatening global peace, stability and cooperation.
In a statement delivered to the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Saturday, Sokhonn, who also serves as a deputy prime minister, noted that while the world has thus far been spared another global conflict, armed struggles continue to inflict immense human suffering across many regions.
"Concurrently, geopolitical rivalries, climate change, widening inequalities, rapid technological transformation and transnational threats are placing growing strains on international peace, stability and cooperation," he said.
He added that at a time when international cooperation is more necessary than ever, trust among nations is being tested. Furthermore, confidence in multilateral institutions and their capacity to respond effectively to common challenges is under increasing pressure.
"The world needs the United Nations not less, but more," Sokhonn said. "But it also needs a United Nations that commands trust because it is principled, representative, effective and capable of delivering on the purposes and principles of its Charter."
He stressed that sovereign equality must remain a fundamental pillar of international relations, asserting that international law must apply universally.
"The Charter does not prescribe one standard for the powerful and another for the less powerful," he said. "All member states, large or small, are equal before the Charter and are bound by the obligations it establishes."
Sokhonn also highlighted that rapid technological advancements illustrate both great promise and significant risk.
"Artificial intelligence and digital innovation can accelerate development and expand opportunities, but their misuse can also deepen inequality, insecurity, and transnational crime," he said. ■

MEXICO CITY, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Music and the glow of a full moon brought China's Mid-Autumn Festival to life on Friday, giving local audiences a taste of one of China's most cherished traditional celebrations.
Held at Mexico City's Palace of Fine Arts, the concert, titled "Under the Same Moon," brought together Chinese and Mexican musicians for an evening of cultural exchange.
Renowned Chinese erhu player Li Cangxiao performed with young Chinese pianist Luan Jingxu, joined by Mexico's Humboldt Quartet and percussionist Javier Perez.
The program featured a mix of Chinese and Mexican works, including Li's "Kangding Capriccio," Mexican composer Jose Pablo Moncayo's "Huapango" and the Chinese classic "The Butterfly Lovers," composed by He Zhanhao.
For Rogelio Rivero Chong, director of the Teotihuacan Archaeological Zone, the event offered an opportunity for Mexicans to learn more about Chinese culture.
"It is very important to have these events and to learn about China's traditions," he told Xinhua.
Rivero Chong said the festival's emphasis on family reunion also strikes a familiar chord in Mexico, where family holds an important place in society.
He was particularly impressed by the erhu's performance in "Huapango," saying he had not expected the Chinese instrument to blend so well with the Mexican composition.
"I really didn't expect it to sound so good. The instrument is impressive, as was the pianist's performance," he said.
The Mid-Autumn Festival, one of China's major traditional holidays, is associated with family reunions, the full moon and the sharing of mooncakes.
The event was organized by Mexico's Culture Ministry and the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature, in collaboration with the Chinese Embassy in Mexico and the China Cultural Center in Mexico. ■

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Slovak biotechnologists have developed a new bioplastic made from algae and other biological materials, offering a potential alternative to conventional plastics derived from fossil fuels.
The material was developed by Slovak company BioX Technologies to address environmental concerns linked to the production and disposal of conventional plastics, the News Agency of the Slovak Republic reported Saturday.
"Plastics have many great properties -- they are lightweight, durable and practically indispensable in many industries. The problem arises with single-use plastics and also because we can't recycle them forever," said Ema Ondrejkova of BioX Technologies.
"That's why we're looking for materials with similar properties that are not made from crude oil but from renewable resources and are also biodegradable," she added.
A key feature of the new material is its end-of-life treatment. Unlike conventional plastics, which generally need to be collected, sorted and processed for recycling, the new material is designed to biodegrade under appropriate conditions. Some formulations can also be made edible, according to the researchers. ■

Who are the inspiring figures of today’s Bulgaria?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:12:06 UTC
15:12:06 KST

Article
Who are the inspiring figures of today’s Bulgaria?
Bulgarians around the world can also nominate candidates for “Awakener of the Year”
Sunday 27 September 2026 08:15
Sunday, 27 September 2026, 08:15
PHOTO BNR
Font size
Who today inspires people to become more active, preserve their heritage and culture, help others or make a difference in the world around them? This is the question at the heart of the “Awakener of the Year” initiative, which for more than a decade has recognised individuals, organisations and projects for their contribution to Bulgarian society.
The term "buditel" (“awakener”, "enlightener") has deep roots in Bulgarian history. Traditionally, it refers to the writers, educators and revolutionaries of the Bulgarian National Revival period who devoted their lives to preserving the Bulgarian language and culture and nurturing national consciousness in the years of the Ottoman domination. Today, the initiative uses the term in a broader sense, referring to people and causes that inspire and unite us as a community and contribute to the development of society.
Iva Doichinova
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The campaign was launched in 2014 by journalist and public figure Iva Doichinova and is supported by the Bulgarian National Radio. Until September 30, anyone can nominate an individual, organisation or project they believe deserves recognition for its work or needs support to continue advancing its cause.
Nominations should be sent to buditel@bnr.bg, accompanied by a brief text outlining the nominee’s mission and work over the years. Journalists and politicians are not eligible for nomination.
A special jury will select ten finalists from all the entries. It comprises last year’s recipient of the award Martin Atanasov, journalists Dobrina Cheshmedzhieva, Daniel Nenchev and Svetoslav Ivanov, entrepreneur Nikola Rahnev, historian Dr Rumen Manov, and the initiative’s founder, Iva Doichinova.
PHOTO Ani Petrova
Following the announcement of the finalists, the winner will be chosen through a public vote on a dedicated online platform.
The organisers are calling for nominations of people and causes that deserve to be brought into the spotlight, regardless of whether they are active in Bulgaria or abroad.

‘Our house was under water’: Bangkok floods force thousands into shelters as disaster declared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:09:30 UTC
15:09:30 KST

Thousands of Bangkok residents awoke in shelters on Sunday after flooding triggered by days of heavy rain in the Thai capital inundated homes and roads, with some starting to dry out their homes and belongings.
Nearly 4,900 people have been evacuated to shelters, with about 52,000 households affected by the floods, which prompted a disaster declaration across the capital, according to the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA).
More than 330mm of rain fell in some areas of the city between Thursday and Sunday, the weather agency said.
Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but several Bangkok residents said this year was worse.
“Our house was under water for about 30 hours,” office worker Kosin Nilset, who lives along the Premprachakorn canal on the outskirts of the capital, said on Sunday morning.
“This time, the water level is higher than the 2011 flood,” the 44-year-old said.
Widespread deluges across the south-east Asian country in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.
Kosin and his family lifted their belongings once they saw the water level was higher than the canal retaining wall, but their ground floor was still left soaked.
“At least tap water and electricity are working,” Kosin said, as he used a broom to sweep out water.
Pedestrians in plastic rain ponchos trudged through murky flood waters in Bangkok’s east – knee-deep in some areas of a grocery store parking lot – floating their belongings in plastic tubs alongside them, AFP journalists saw.
Water levels in Bangkok’s network of canals remained high on Sunday morning, with authorities working to speed up drainage, the BMA said.
More rain was forecast throughout Sunday for Bangkok and its surrounding provinces, but would begin to taper off on Monday, it said.
Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to heat up because of fossil fuel emissions.
Bangkok governor Chadchart Sittipunt said several roads were still flooded and warned Bangkok residents in a Facebook post to avoid unnecessary travel.
Chadchart visited a temporary shelter on Saturday night in a school in the Kheha Romklao area, where he said about 1,000 people were evacuated.
Some rested on cots and benches with their dogs in hallways, while others lay with blankets on the floors of classrooms where desks and chairs were pushed to the side.
Hundreds of city schools will be closed on Monday, according to the BMA.
Some convenience stores had empty shelves over the weekend as residents raced to buy essentials.
The prime minister’s office asked the public to avoid panic-buying and warned that price gouging was a criminal offence.
Thidarat Silsuwan, 56, lives alone in her partially submerged house along the Premprachakorn canal.
“I have been sleeping on the table for two days now,” she said.
She did not want to go to a shelter as she worked to clean up and salvage her belongings.
“I tried to lift everything up, but I gave up on large electric appliances like the refrigerator and washing machine. I guess they are broken.”

South Africa: Pair of mass shootings leave dozens dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

South Africa: Pair of mass shootings leave dozens dead
September 27, 2026
At least 27 people have been killed in separate mass shooting incidents in South Africa's Gauteng and Western Cape provinces overnight.
In the first incident, gunmen armed with assault rifles killed 17 people and wounded 15 others at a bar in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg, police said on Sunday.
Manhunt underway for 8 suspects in Wedela shooting
Gauteng police said they have launched a manhunt for eight unidentified armed men following the deadly shooting.
"They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the South African Police Service (SAPS) said.
Emergency services declared all 17 victims, 13 men and four women, dead at the scene. Authorities said the shooting occurred Saturday at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 UTC).
A motive for the shooting was not known, the SAPS said, adding that "suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols."
10 killed in Lwandle tavern shooting, Cape Town
In a separate shooting in the Western Cape, police said gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township at 1:46 a.m. (2346 Saturday GMT).
Authorities said five of the victims died at the scene while another five succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital.
Police said no arrests have been made and that a "multi-disciplinary team" led by serious and violent crime detectives had been established to track down those responsible.
More police resources have been sent to the area as the search for the perpetrators continues.
The latest incidents came just days after at least 11 people were gunned down at a home in KwaZulu-Natal Province.
That shooting occurred in KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.
Sense of 'shock' following Wedela shooting, says DW correspondent
DW correspondent Thuso Khumalo was at the scene in Wedela and said there was a definite of "shock" following the shooting.
"People are very worried here," Khumalo said, pointing to the number of community members who were standing near the police cordon.
On the question of whether the victims had been specifically targeted, Khumalo said police suspected it was a retaliatory attack involving gangs.
"They are saying, one of the victims was already on their list, on their radar, the intelligence radar," Khumalo said, adding that he was being investigated for a previous incident.
Wedela is situated in an area where there has been a security crackdown on illegal mining involving the deployment of police and soldiers.
"The criminals think it's a fashion. They want to make it something which we need to get used to, but that cannot be allowed and tolerated," said deputy provincial police commissioner Major General Fred Kekana.
South Africa's high rate of violent crime
South Africa is grappling with violent crime and has one of the world's highest murder rates, with around 60 people dying violently in the country each day.
In one of the stories that has made international headlines in recent days, Johannesburg police are still trying to track down those responsible for a spate of killings in which the bodies of 10 women have been found in close proximity to one another.
Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found concrete evidence to suggest the same person or people were responsible.
In March, South Africa's leadership deployed troops to hotspots to support police dealing with rampant criminality that President Cyril Ramaphosa has described as one of the biggest challenges facing the country at present.

The cold drink stirring up a viral debate about professionalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:07:26 UTC
15:07:26 KST

In brief
- A recruiter in the US said Gen Z candidates are showing up to interviews with iced drinks and she perceives it as "too casual".
- The take has proven divisive, with some agreeing and others viewing it as a dated idea of professionalism.
It's yet another debate dividing generations and the internet. At the heart of this one? Iced coffee in a job interview.
A recruiter's TikTok video has set off a viral online debate about whether it's appropriate to bring an iced coffee to an interview.
"My Gen Z candidates are showing up to their interviews with iced coffee, iced latte in hand," US-based recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen said in the video.
"It is perceived, from my opinion, my hiring standpoint, that when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just like a stop on your list of errands on the day."
"It looks a little too casual to me," she added, advising candidates to finish their drinks before or after meeting with prospective employers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
While some commenters agreed that bringing an iced drink into a job interview was unprofessional and too informal, others argued it was an outdated and arbitrary way to judge a candidate.
"Are you expecting my whole day to revolve around a 30 min meeting?" one commenter wrote.
"As a millennial, can we please let go of the weird rules boomers and Gen X imposed on us? Interviews are stressful enough," said another.
"It's not about coffee it's about professionalism," another commented. "Surprised people aren't getting that."
Wehniainen later joked on LinkedIn that she had accidentally started a national debate and her comment section had become a battlefield.
She said she was "never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate".
"My point was simply about avoiding distractions."
An industry insider's take
Amy Slade-Symons has been a career coach for around 10 years and worked in talent recruitment and HR for more than a decade before that.
She told SBS News she personally wouldn't bring a coffee into a job interview, but it also shouldn't be a big deal if you do — as long as you're on time.
"It's just always is bad form if you turn up late, no matter what, and you're holding some form of drink in your hand," she said.
She noted, though, that she can't speak for everyone, and different hiring professionals have different biases.
But "if the candidate makes a great impression — skills, experience, motivation for the role, what they can bring — I think that eclipses most things", she added.
Government analysis suggests young people face an increasingly difficult path into the workforce, with the transition from education to employment becoming more complex and many entry-level roles ultimately going to more experienced candidates.
Australia's workforce is more generationally diverse than ever, with four generations working alongside one another.
With Generation Alpha beginning to enter the workforce in the coming years, that could soon become five.
That brings different communication and leadership styles, expectations around formality and workplace attire, and approaches to learning together in one place, Slade-Symons said.
She has seen those expectations change significantly over her own career.
"I've gone from wearing a suit, stockings, full face of makeup, through to going into the office wearing trainers and a nice frock and maybe a business jacket over the top if I'm having a formal meeting," she said.
"You interview people now, and I might be online wearing a hoodie because that's the environment that they work in, or wearing a T-shirt."
As workplace norms evolve, she said it's easy to look at younger generations and think: "In my day that was different."
When it comes to iced coffee, her advice is that it's probably not worth risking it, even if it feels silly.
"Get their focus on the conversation about your skills and experience and how wonderful you are."

Swiss vote on tightening neutrality rules, ending peacetime cooperation with NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:07:24 UTC
15:07:24 KST

Swiss vote on tightening neutrality rules, ending peacetime cooperation with NATO
ZURICH – Swiss voters will decide on Sept 27 whether to approve a more restrictive form of neutrality that would block their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
The country is holding a referendum on whether a strictly defined version of neutrality should be written into its Constitution.
While Swiss neutrality has been internationally recognised since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815, how the government implements it is not spelt out.
The right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP) has said that Switzerland’s traditional position has been eroded after Bern imposed sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
The campaign has funded posters across the country featuring white peace doves and urging people to vote “No war, yes to neutrality”, ahead of the vote.
Still, opinion polls suggest voters will reject the proposal, with one of the latest surveys showing 68 per cent against, with 31 per cent in favour.
Fabio Wasserfallen, a professor of European politics at the University of Bern, said: “Swiss voters like neutrality, but they approve of how the government is implementing it at present.
“They are also generally in favour of the sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine and don’t want that to change.”
The campaign wants the Constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defence alliance unless attacked, and that it refrains from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
It says Swiss neutrality has served the country well in the past, keeping it out of both world wars, and also helps Bern offer its “good offices” to help negotiate peace between warring parties.
“Switzerland has not had a war for 200 years because it is permanently armed and neutral,” said Christoph Blocher, a billionaire businessman and backer of the SVP. “But neutrality has been followed less and less in recent years,” he said, with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions.
Apart from the SVP, most parties and the Swiss government oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national security and prevent Switzerland from training with NATO. REUTERS

Youth today have more chances to experiment, says Pärnu street artist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:05:00 UTC
15:05:00 KST

Youth today have more chances to experiment, says Pärnu street artist
Pärnu street artist Kristjan Tamm, known as Kryptik, says young artists today have more legal chances to learn street art than when he first started more than 20 years ago.
Tamm discovered graffiti back when the internet was still uncommon in Estonian homes, searching for U.S. graffiti websites during school computer classes and trying to recreate what he saw. His first pieces appeared on abandoned buildings and ruins.
"But, as you'd expect, you can't really get anything right at first," he admitted.
Tamm never ran into trouble with police, saying he chose where he'd work carefully. Nowadays, he noted, young folks have more authorized opportunities to experiment, including workshops like the ones he runs at youth centers.
"They don't have to go out on the streets at night to find somewhere to practice," Tamm said.
The Pärnu artist's roots are still firmly rooted in graffiti — particularly its lettering tradition, which artists use to develop their names and personal styles — but street art has expanded beyond classic graffiti, with paints and other tools more readily available now as well.
He carries a large suitcase packed with spray paint for his murals, which can take anywhere from one to three days to complete, depending on size.
Weather, however, is a practical challenge. Rain can cancel an outdoor workday, so Tamm checks the forecast each morning when planning his schedule. Outdoor projects also go on hiatus in winter, although he continues to work indoors during the colder months.
Commissions and awards
Today, Tamm mainly creates commissioned murals, with the location and client's wishes shaping the work. Animals and birds feature frequently in his pieces, and one of his more unusual canvases, a wastewater pumping station, he transformed into an aquarium.
"The location itself tends to dictate what will work there," he explained.
Several years ago, Tamm was awarded the Pärnu City Cultural Award for his creative work. He said the recognition was unexpected, but also showed how much street art's place in Estonia has changed.
"The change we've seen in Estonia has been huge," he said.

Giving voice to a lost history: retracing the steps of the Black lives that shaped Manchester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

They are the stories that have survived decades, despite being largely ignored by official acts of commemoration, obscured, or erased from the landscape. Now, chapters from Manchester’s Black history are being brought to life by a series of walking tours in the city, led by local historians, including Linford Sweeney, the Moss Side-raised genealogist, and the urbanist Hayley Flynn.
The Heritage in Action trail – guided walks exploring the lives of people whose labour made the city what it is and the city’s direct relationship with transatlantic slavery – will run in the city on 7 October, World Cotton Day. The events have been produced by the Guardian’s Legacies of Enslavement programme and the charity Greater Manchester Moving, which works to improve the region’s wellbeing through physical activity.
From the “great crowd” of Black Georgians who gathered at the city’s collegiate church to campaign for abolition in 1787, to the Pan-Africanist politicians, writers and economists who led postwar independence struggles after meeting in Manchester, or artists including Nina Simone and Miriam Makeba, whose Manchester concerts galvanised and inspired, the city has a rich history of Black activism.
But despite being home to one of the UK’s largest postwar Black communities, and the city’s evolution depending on the cotton produced by enslaved Africans, there are few commemorations of Black history in Manchester’s public realm. The Len Johnson Memorial Campaign is hoping to rectify that by bringing a bronze statue of the British boxer, civil rights activist and trade unionist to the city.
While there are sculptures of the Black peace campaigner Erinma Bell and Yomi Mambu, the city’s first Black lord mayor, in Manchester town hall, a statue of Johnson would mark the first outdoor statue of a Black person in Manchester.
Meanwhile, Black and working-class historians are taking to the streets. In May, the Guardian’s Legacies of Enslavement programme funded a series of trial walks for October’s forthcoming heritage trails, which explore the histories behind landmark locations.
They include the Peace Garden, where there is a plaque commemorating enslaved Africans and a quote from the abolitionist Olaudah Equiano. Both are dwarfed by a huge, nearby statue of Abraham Lincoln, raising questions about whose remembrance is privileged by society.
The great African American abolitionist Frederick Douglass was believed to be staying at an address in St Ann’s Square when he learned his freedom from enslavement had been secured. There is no plaque there.
The branch of Holland & Barrett that now occupies the address was a stop on the Decolonial Dogs heritage trail, led earlier this year by Bilal Zafar Ranjha and Elmi Ali, as part of the partnership between the Guardian and GM Moving.
The trail began at Manchester Cathedral, telling the story of the 1787 antislavery meeting, led by the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson, that led to one in five Mancunian adults – 10,500 people – signing a petition against the trafficking of enslaved Africans.
Ali said he believed such moments in history showed how “people are more progressive than institutions”. He added: “Do people know one in five of the population in that period signed up to support what would be the equivalent to Black Lives Matter now?”
Chetham’s Library was another landmark building on the tour. There, Ali said: “This building knows who traded cotton in Manchester … What it does not contain, what Manchester never recorded, are the names of the people who picked that cotton.”
Drawing on research from Dr Cassandra Gooptar, of the University of Hull’s Wilberforce Institute, Ali told the stories of enslaved Africans including Archy Gordon, 50 years old and blind, and Sam Kerr, 19, who lived on the Success plantation in Hanover, Jamaica, which was owned by one of the Manchester Guardian’s founding investors, George Philips.
“Historical amnesia and whitewashing history” is how Ranjha described the situation, which has left these stories untold.
Reflecting on this “amnesia”, Prof Anandi Ramamurthy, an academic specialising in post-colonial histories, culture and mental health who took part in the Decolonial Dogs trail, said: “To me, if you want people to talk about community cohesion, that cannot be done without transparency and without accountability – all the institutions of Manchester need to come forward and look at their past, so we’re able to come together and to envision a different future.”
Ali added: “Global majority citizens of the country are framed constantly as new arrivals, which is how erasure works – but Africans have been here for centuries.”
Sweeney’s 7 October tour looks at the impact changes to the built environment have on local identity and memory in Black communities.
The streets of Moss Side and Hulme in Manchester have been remodelled substantially twice in the past 60 years – first by the slum clearance programmes of the 1960s, in which Edwardian terraces were condemned, and again when 1970s buildings such as the Moss Side Precinct shopping centre and Hulme Crescents council estates were pulled down in the 1990s.
Sweeney’s tour links lost and surviving landmarks from the area with the legacy of the Windrush generation, weaving the stories of the workers, activist spaces, venues, shops, and vanished streets of the area with personal recollections.
Stops on the tour include Hulme’s Nia Centre – “a beacon of cultural expression and community empowerment” – where Simone performed in 1991, Sweeney says.
A May trial event for Sweeney’s tour brought memories flooding back for Pauline Weir, a lifelong community organiser. Weir recalls how Black homeowners such as her father got “next to nothing” for their homes when they were subject to compulsory purchase orders under the postwar “slum clearance” scheme.
“I think the lack of recognition of our history is purposeful,” Weir said. “And I think when they had the compulsory purchase orders, it was purposeful. Every time they’ve demolished physical buildings, they demolish community.”
Flynn’s “myth-busting” city centre tour raises deep questions about the city’s approach to memorialisation over centuries.
Starting at the River Irwell, where Manchester city centre meets Salford, it moves to the Northern Quarter, via stops including the Peace Garden, Chinatown and the gay village, drawing on Flynn’s knowledge of urban histories and countercultures.
Flynn explores the present-day politics of space, gentrification and community, while looking back at the past that shaped Manchester’s urban landscape.
Reflecting on abolition and the solidarity shown by some Lancashire cotton workers with enslaved Africans, Flynn said: “When we celebrate the city’s support for abolition we symbolise that through the iconography of Abraham Lincoln, not of the enslaved people themselves, nor, on a local level, the labourers who went on strike.”
Against this backdrop, the Grass Routes Movement CIC x Rooted Liberation walk, featuring Sajida Ismail and Anisa Saleh, is an act of healing, exploring the violence that underpinned the relationship between the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and Manchester’s waterways, and commemorating the human toll with moving acts of remembrance.
Their interactive, immersive, poetic walk travels along Manchester city’s canals to Manchester Science and Industry Museum, taking in sights of lost industry, goslings and graffiti.
Saleh said: “It’s not about pointing the finger, or apportioning blame. It’s about how we can be together and give voice to this history.
“A walking activity is a vessel for that difficult task, and the care that underlies the process is part of the ongoing legacy, the corrections, the acknowledgments. Let’s all be a part of that, in ways that are helpful and healing.”

London’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

London’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a frenzy of takeover deals this year, sparking anger over high City pay during the cost of living crisis.
The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK stock market listed companies has surged 175% in 2026 to $132.9bn (£100bn), according to the London Stock Exchange, as overseas buyers snap up British companies at record pace.
Fees paid to investment bankers, lawyers and accountants working on these deals topped £1.2bn, official filings suggest, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets.
The bumper fees were fuelled by a string of corporate takeovers driven by a flood of private equity cash and acquisitive American buyers targeting undervalued British businesses. The spree of acquisitions of listed companies has led to concerns over the future of the London stock market.
The takeover frenzy has fed advisory business at the biggest banks and law firms in the City. Bankers at JP Morgan have been the busiest, advising on more takeovers involving UK companies than any other bank this year – a total of 14 deals worth a combined $89.4bn (£67.6bn), according to the LSE. The leading law firm was Slaughter and May, it found.
UK bankers have also benefited from soaring bonuses, after the government scrapped a rule capping bonuses at two-times annual salaries in late 2023. Each bank now sets its own upward limit. Big investment banks such as Goldman Sachs now allow performers to be paid up to 25 times their annual salary.
The surge in business comes while the banking sector lobbies against paying higher taxes in the UK.
Jamie Dimon, the billionaire boss of JP Morgan, has issued several warnings to Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget on 28 October. The industry body UK Finance echoed the view this week.
Lenders in the UK currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.
The most lucrative deal in the City this year was the £10.6bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by the private equity firm EQT, which is expected to generate more than £370m in fees. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Deutsche Bank are working on the deal for EQT, while Intertek paid Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Cazenove and PJT Partners.
Lawyers at top City firms have started to out-earn some bankers. Partners at the “magic circle” firms Linklaters and Clifford Chance were paid an average of £2.5m and £2.3m respectively in the year to April, their highest ever. A&O Shearman partners were paid £2.2m.
At the boutique bank Evercore, which the LSE said had advised on five deals in the UK stock market this year, the firm’s “members” – senior managing directors who are dealmakers – were paid an average of about £2m. Its best-paid member collected £16.2m this year.
Overall, dealmaker fees are likely to be even higher this year as the figures do not include deals which did not complete, were rejected or for which documents have not been published – including the £5.7bn takeover of the FTSE 100 airline easyJet by the private equity firm Apollo Global Management, agreed last month.
While pay continues to climb in the City, millions of UK households are struggling with the cost of living.
Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the national secretary at the GMB union, said financial brokers were paid huge sums “while the people who keep this country moving struggle to make ends meet”.
“The UK needs to seriously re-examine what we value and hold dear – is it the people who build, who create, who look after us and our loved ones in their hour of need? Or is it a bloated financial sector?” she asked.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, repeated his call for a windfall tax on lenders’ profits as interest rates have risen, saying that “if banks can afford bonanza payouts for their top brass, they can clearly afford to pay more tax”.
“People up and down the country are struggling, and things could get a lot worse with energy prices set to shoot up,” he said.
Earlier this month figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, slowed to 3.9% in the three months ended in July, down from 4.1% in the three months ended in June.
There are fears that, while dealmakers’ pay is rising on the takeover boom, investment banks could lose out on revenue from their sell-side research and work on flotations as more companies leave London’s stock market and fewer line up to join.
Despite hopes that 2026 could spark a revival on the UK stock market, there were just seven listings in the first half of the year, raising £577m in total, according to data from the professional services company EY. However, this week, Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, said it was planning one of the biggest UK listings in years.
