China's Sun Sibei overcomes warmup crash to claim historic Asian Games BMX freestyle park gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
13:24:53 CST
14:24:53 KST

Sun Sibei of China competes during the women's park final of cycling BMX freestyle at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's Sun Sibei recovered from a warmup crash and a disappointing first run to win with 93.80 points on her second attempt on Sunday as the women's BMX freestyle park event made its Asian Games debut.
Japan's Miharu Ozawa took silver with 91.20 points, while China's Sun Jiaqi claimed bronze with 90.20.
Six riders from China, Japan, South Korea and Malaysia contested the final at Aichi Sky Expo. BMX freestyle park, which made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo Games in 2021, was contested at the Asian Games for the first time at Aichi-Nagoya 2026.
The danger of the discipline was evident from the opening run. Malaysia's Mohd Nor Aszeril Nur Airen Sofea crashed before completing her routine, and Ozawa also ran into trouble on her first attempt, scoring just 25.60.
Sun Sibei, the first Chinese rider to compete, posted 85.60. Sun Jiaqi then thrilled the crowd with a series of aerial tricks, scoring 86.80 to lead after the first round.
Ozawa transformed the contest on her second run, landing a sequence of difficult tricks to post 91.20 and move into first. Sun Sibei answered with a flowing, high-difficulty routine worth 93.80, reclaiming the lead with one rider still to come.
Sun Jiaqi improved to 90.20 on her final run and celebrated on completion, but the score left her one point shy of silver. She appeared disappointed when the result was displayed, drawing sympathetic applause from spectators.
"I did everything I had planned," Sun Jiaqi said afterward, adding that she was pleased with her performance. Asked about her longer-term goal, she replied: "To surpass myself."
Sun Sibei said her warmup crash had made her question whether she could perform at her best. Her first run, though enough to place her second at the halfway point, had fallen short of her expectations.
She added that Ozawa's second-round score added to the pressure, but dwelling on it would have disrupted her own rhythm. "I had to focus on every move in my run," she said.
Sun Sibei said winning the inaugural Asian Games title had strengthened her determination to pursue another goal: "I hope I can make it to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics." ■

Katsuki Hayato of Japan celebrates after the men's marathon race walk final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Hayato Katsuki won the men's marathon race walk on home soil at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday, while Kazakhstan's Yasmina Toxanbayeva took the women's title.
China claimed two silver medals and a bronze across the two races.
Katsuki completed the 42.195-kilometer course in 3:03:36, finishing more than three minutes ahead of China's Zhou Yingcheng, who clocked 3:06:40. Japan's Motofumi Suwa took bronze in 3:08:57, with China's Tang Yushuai finishing fourth.
The 35-year-old Katsuki, who won the 50km race walk at the 2018 Asian Games, said this year marked the first time the Games had staged the marathon distance, adding that he was "definitely stronger over the marathon distance than over 35 kilometers" and he hoped to see a long-distance race walk return to the Olympic program.
Zhou, making his Asian Games debut, said he was pleased with silver. "Just being able to compete on this stage already feels like a victory," he said. "There's still a gap between me and the gold medal, but that gap is also a source of motivation."
Toxanbayeva won the women's race in 3:22:20. China's Danzengquzong took silver in a personal best of 3:26:09, while compatriot Ma Li fought back from a three-minute penalty to claim bronze in 3:32:26.
Ma, who received three red cards after covering more than 10 kilometers and served time in the penalty zone, said she had little hope of a medal at that point. Encouraged by her coach to keep pushing, she clawed back positions late in the race.
"I was unlucky, but perhaps lucky too," Ma said. "I kept chasing the walkers ahead of me."
Both races were held on a looped course near Nagoya Castle, passing the Aichi Prefectural Government Office and Nagoya City Hall. ■

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attacked five opposition leaders on Sept. 26 following their agreement to coordinate an election campaign to unseat his coalition government.
The five leaders met at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid to organize their strategy ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The meeting brought together Lapid of Yesh Atid, Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar, Naftali Bennett of Together, Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan of the Democrats.
In a joint document released after the talks, the five leaders declared replacing the current government their shared highest objective despite ideological differences.

Netanyahu responded to the agreement on social media platform X, claiming only his right-wing Likud party could prevent the bloc from taking office.
"Only a strong Likud will stop them," Netanyahu said.
The prime minister posted an artificial intelligence-altered version of the opposition group photo, inserting United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas and Hadash-Ta'al leader Ahmad Tibi into the frame.

Netanyahu has headed the current right-wing administration since December 2022, facing mounting domestic criticism over prolonged regional military campaigns and pending corruption trials.

Ancient Egyptian fortress uncovers soldiers’ homes, royal inscriptions, and horse burial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:15:35 UTC
14:15:35 KST

Excavations at Tell el-Abqain, an ancient Egyptian fortress in the Beheira Governorate, have uncovered New Kingdom soldiers’ homes, food stores, royal inscriptions and a horse burial.
Announced last week by Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry, the finds confirm the site’s strategic importance in protecting the the country from Libyan tribal attacks during the New Kingdom period.
In the northern sector of a large mudbrick residential complex, archaeologists found a four-meter wide main road running east to west, intersected by aanother street running south to north.
The main road reaches the southern entrance of the Tell el-Abqain fortress, connecting the residential area to the military site.
Several different rooms were discovered throughout the residential complex. Some, archaeologists found, contained silos for storing grain and cylindrical pottery ovens used for preparing food. A collection of rooms was also uncovered near the southeastern corner of the fortress, where three stone wells bearing the titles of King Ramesses II had previously been found.
Mohamed Abdel-Badie, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector, noted that some of the discovered rooms, particularly those north of the main street, were used to store wheat.
Within those rooms, the excavation team located large pottery jars containing carbonized wheat grains, serving as direct evidence of ancient food storage and resource management.
One of the most notable finds at the site was that of the complete burial of a young male horse.
Preliminary studies showed the remains belonged to a medium-sized breed known for agility and speed, suggesting that it had likely been used for training, military activities, or pulling war chariots during the New Kingdom period.
The complete positioning of the horse's body, the direction of its head, and the orderly nature of the burial suggest it was buried deliberately, likely ceremonially.
A few meters from where the burial was found, archaeologists discovered cylindrical pieces of alabaster and limestone, believed to have been part of the decorative fittings of a chariot horse’s harness.
Numerous royal inscriptions found at Tell el-Abqain
Additionally, a fragment of a limestone stele bearing the remains of a hieratic inscription for the 19th Dynasty pharoah, Merneptah. It describes his strength and comparing it to the power of the deity Set, alongside a reference to the ancient Egyptian creator god Ptah.
Set, a powerful god in the ancient Egyptian pantheon, is often associated with chaos, the desert, and foreigners.
Khaled Abdel-Ghany Farahat, Beheira Antiquities director-general and excavation supervisor, explained that this is the first timein the history of excavations in the Beheira region that such a thing has been discovered.
The remains of a second limestone stele was also found at the site,with the birth name, coronation name, and Horus name of King Ramesses II, inscribed in hieroglyphics. A third stele depicting a bound Libyan captive in a bent posture of submission, was also found.
Role of religion in soldiers’ lives
Also found at the site were a number of scarabs, some bearing the names of Kings Ramesses II and Seti I, while others carry the names of several deities, including Amun, Sekhmet, Ptah, and Set.
A collection of religious amulets related to concepts of protection, fertility, renewal, and strength was also found, including amulets in the shape of a fish, a lotus flower, a cobra, the "nefer" sign, and a baboon.
Both the discovery of the scarabs and the amulet reflect the role of religion in the lives of the soldiers and residents living at the fortress.
Several pottery vessels and shards used for storage and cooking were also found at the site, alongside a a pilgrim flask associated with pilgrimage to Abydos and assorted stone tools. Various pieces of jewelry and similar accessories were also found.
Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy stated that the discovery adds a new dimension to understanding ancient Egypt’s border security systems, as well as shines new light on the day-to-day activities at the fortress.

Ismail Haniyeh's ex-bodyguard arrested for planning terror attack against European Jews - report
Unknown

2026-09-27

A former bodyguard of assassinated Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was granted asylum and British citizenship, was arrested on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack against Jewish communities and Israelis in Europe around the second anniversary of the October 7 massacre, the Sunday Times reported on Saturday.
According to the British newspaper's investigation, the suspect, whose identity cannot be published for legal reasons and who is referred to as "Mr. X," served on Haniyeh's personal security detail in Gaza before moving to Britain more than a decade ago.
Although it was known when he received refugee status that he had worked for the leader of the terrorist organization and that he had previously been arrested in Egypt for operating a weapons-smuggling tunnel into Gaza, he was granted asylum in the UK.
Mr. X lived in England under the cover of working as an IT consultant, changed his legal name several times, and ostensibly led an ordinary life.
He now faces extradition to Germany, where he is accused of being a central figure in a plot to attack Jewish community centers, Israeli diplomats, and pro-Israel demonstrations in Germany or neighboring Austria. Officers from Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA) arrested him in central London last November after Israel's Mossad and German intelligence services uncovered the plot.
The indictment, first revealed by the German newspaper Bild, describes how Mr. X transported handguns, ammunition, and camouflage equipment from Berlin to Vienna.
He also recorded a video in advance in which he appeared masked and armed in front of a Hamas flag, describing the planned attack as an act of retaliation on behalf of the Izzadin al-Qassam Brigades. A law enforcement official described him as a "vital figure" in the plot.
Mr. X given permanent residency, citizenship by UK
Mr. X arrived in Britain in 2012, when he apparently left the Gaza Strip for the last time. In 2015, he applied for asylum, and the British Home Office granted him permanent residency while Theresa May served as UK Home Secretary. He was later granted British citizenship.
In an unusual move, a judge at a London magistrate's court granted Mr. X an order barring publication of his name for 100 years. The decision was amended only last Thursday after an application by the Sunday Times, with the court ruling that his name could be published only after the conclusion of the criminal proceedings against him being conducted concurrently in Britain.
German security officials have warned that the involvement of Mr. X, who was able to travel freely across Europe using his British passport, reflects a dangerous shift in Hamas's tactics as the terrorist organization seeks to expand the reach of its terrorist activity beyond the Middle East and into Europe.

What the West misses when it judges China’s dogged AI pursuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:10:00 UTC
14:10:00 KST

What the West misses when it judges China’s dogged AI pursuit
- China pursues AI to avoid repeating past strategic mistakes and demands a level playing field, emphasising human talent and shared global technological foundations.
- China's AI success stems from both state subsidies and fierce domestic competition, creating cheap, efficient models despite Western criticism.
- US-China AI rivalry reshapes the global economy with differing strengths, risks of social unrest in China, and America's potential to innovate rapidly remain significant.
AI generated
PHILADELPHIA – China’s artificial intelligence success story, often criticised in the West for being unfairly underwritten by the Chinese government, reflects the country’s resolve not to repeat a strategic mistake made 150 years ago, said Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan during a discussion on US-China rivalry.
China missed the industrial revolution, but it will not make the same mistake twice, said Balakrishnan during a Sept 25 conversation with former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd, who is now the global president and chief executive of the Asia Society in New York.
“Because China missed it. China underwent a century-plus of humiliation and unequal treaties. This time, China has absolutely no intention of missing it again,” the minister said in an hour-long exchange, during which he challenged how the US seizes competition from China.
“You need to understand, it is not just a matter of competition with America, being No. 1 or No. 2, and I am projecting into China’s motivations, but China says: ‘This is my turn, my time in the sunshine. Why should anyone get in the way, especially when I have the human talent, the brain power?’” he said.
“So from China’s perspective, ‘I am not going to make the strategic mistake made a century and a half ago. This is a strategic opportunity, and I do not want anyone to get in my way. And all I am asking for is a level playing field, access to technology and to get ahead as quickly as I can.’”
Their intense competition is sharply different from the Sputnik-era contest between the US and the Soviet Union, he said, because today’s superpowers rely on a shared global technological stack and brainpower rather than isolated ecosystems.
“What is interesting is that the mathematical and computational basis for AI, the foundations that both America, China and the rest of us are operating on, is essentially the same stack. The mathematicians, the techniques, the machines are the same,” Balakrishnan said.
“And because it is the common stack and it has been open and competitive, the rate of acceleration has been dramatic.”
Rudd pointed out that China was building its success on an “unlevel playing field”.
“What is working in China is… state-driven investment in its techno-industrial strategy, plus net exports, and this becomes unsustainable,” he said, pointing to China’s weak domestic consumption and its reliance on exports for growth that have flooded other economies.
Balakrishnan said the use of subsidies did not fully explain the country’s AI prowess, and that what also drives Chinese AI companies is the cut-throat domestic competition, which results in the creation of cheap and efficient Chinese AI models.
“Let us assume all subsidies, direct or implicit, are removed. Do you think that would automatically remove the academic, scientific, technological edge of China? I do not believe so.
“Do you think that the hyper competition domestically is going to disappear? It is not.
“The easy answer is (to) just blame it on subsidy, but I am saying there is something more going on than that, and we had better understand what that source of competitive advantage is, and that it is real,” he said.
Rudd accepted the pushback, but said both forces were at work – China’s scientific brilliance as well as its subsidies, which have led to global overcapacity and set off a political backlash in the US and Europe.
“They are applying through conscious industrial strategy, subsidies, which underpin their model, which is producing political blowback here, hence the tariff war from the US and the reduction in the trade surplus of America, and on the cusp of bringing about a similar reaction in Europe,” Rudd said.
A fundamental imbalance existed in the global economy before AI, Balakrishnan also pointed out, as the two discussed how the two economies evolved.
China became the world’s manufacturing hub, while the US benefited from cheap consumer goods and low interest rates funded by Chinese trade surpluses that were invested in US Treasury bills.
In the West, higher productivity historically led to higher wages that created a massive middle class, which consumed products and fuelled more economic growth.
But the coming AI economy may not follow this same trajectory, since a company can reap huge productivity gains without hiring thousands of workers or raising wages.
The bind is worse for China, where the pressure of an ageing and shrinking population creates an incentive for Beijing to deploy AI rapidly to remain competitive. However, going too fast could lead to social unrest by worsening youth unemployment.
America has its own problems, Balakrishnan said, including deficits of trillions of dollars that are a result of its industrial and trade policies.
But it is capable of surprises when it leans into its longstanding strength: turning new science into profitable products faster than anyone else.
“That is why, at least from Singapore’s perspective, we do not count America out. It is still capable of pulling a rabbit out of the hat,” he said.
In an interview with the Singapore media on Sept 26 as he concluded his trip to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly, Balakrishnan said the exchange with Rudd was an effort to understand a world being reshaped by the US-China relationship and their intense rivalry over AI.
“He pushes, I push back, and the to-and-fro occurs. The objective is not to convince each other. The objective is to sharpen our perspectives and to explore the issues in greater depth and breadth than we would otherwise,” Balakrishnan said.
“The people who watch that conversation don’t have to agree with Kevin or me, but if Kevin and I have succeeded in making you think about the issues, then we have succeeded,” he said.

What is the Form 6 row?
The controversy centres on the requirement for new voters to provide details linking themselves or their parents or grandparents to electoral rolls from the previous SIR.According to Indian Express reports, Election Commissioners Joshi and Sandhu had objected to incorporating the requirement into Form 6, arguing that the statutory form could not be altered without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.

Can solar power work underwater? Scientists test solar panels 10 metres beneath the sea

2026-09-27

14:02:04 KST

According to the researchers, perovskite-based solar panels could operate for five and a half years underwater.
Ten metres beneath the South China Sea, scientists have found an unlikely place to generate power from the sun.
Last week, researchers announced that they had successfully tested solar panels at underwater depths previously considered impractical for the technology.
Designed to capture the wavelengths of sunlight that can pass through seawater, the panels could eventually keep underwater equipment running for longer without relying just on batteries, they argue.
During a two-hour trial near the Weizhou Islands, off the southern coast of mainland China, the panels generated power from sunlight at a depth of 10 metres. Lab tests suggest that they could operate continuously for years, too.
The research, published in the science journal Joule, takes underwater solar well beyond previous studies, which have focused on depths of just two metres or less.
How can solar panels work 10 metres underwater?
One of the biggest obstacles to generating solar power underwater is that sunlight fades below the surface – and fast.
By a depth of 10 metres, much of the sun’s energy has already been absorbed or scattered by the water. But some types of light can reach deeper than others.
According to the researchers, enough blue and green light reaches these depths to generate electricity, so the team developed solar cells designed to make the most of it.
They used what are known as perovskites, an alternative to the silicon found in most solar panels, which can be adjusted to absorb different wavelengths of light.
In laboratory tests recreating conditions 10 metres underwater, the cells turned around 35 per cent of the sunlight that reached them into electricity.
The researchers then put bigger versions to the test in the South China Sea. At two metres deep, their 115 square centimetres of solar panels generated 1,416 milliwatt-hours over two hours, or about half the capacity of a rechargeable AA battery.
At 10 metres, they generated 324 milliwatt-hours over two hours – a small amount but still far beyond what the researchers expected.
Their panels also showed almost no loss in performance after 1,160 hours under simulated underwater conditions. Based on their tests, the researchers estimate they could operate continuously at 10 metres below the sea for around five and a half years.
“This work presents the first functional validation of submerged solar cells practically operating at a water depth of up to about 10 meters, greatly broadening their application scope,” says study author Wen-Hua Zhang, from China’s Yunnan University and Southwest United Graduate School in Kunming.
How solar is going off-grid
Once the sole domain of rooftops and wide open spaces, solar power continues to appear in places where electricity and fuel can be difficult to access.
Earlier this year, Dutch researchers unveiled the world’s first solar-powered ambulancein rural Kenya, designed to bring healthcare and medical equipment to hard-to-reach communities that lack reliable access to electricity or fuel.
In Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, solar has also begun to help power a remote former radio station, a site accessible only by boat or helicopter that previously relied on diesel-fuelled generators.
Other projects have found space for solar in existing infrastructure. In Switzerland, solar panels installed between railway tracks are generating electricity without taking up more land. The panels can also be removed for track maintenance, allowing railways to double as solar farms without disrupting services.
Underwater solar power could solve a different problem.
Ocean sensors, cameras and communication equipment can operate far from power supplies, but they must eventually be retrieved when their batteries run out.
The researchers believe the technology they studied could provide a lasting source of power for this kind of equipment.
First, however, they need to find out how well their solar panels work deeper undersea. They say their next step is to do just that and establish how far beneath the waves solar power can go.

Sebb’s, Glasgow G1: ‘A delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Sebb’s is a basement restaurant on Miller Street in Glasgow with a door that’s perilously easy to miss, even though it’s bright red. The first time I tried to find it, I waltzed past and almost ended up in the pants department of TK Maxx. I was luckier the second time around, and soon found myself descending a set of stairs into a room with the distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley: there’s no natural light, there are booths that are perfect for conspiring in, a DJ playing psychedelic rock and food served in brown paper bags. The 13th Floor Elevators at noon on a Thursday?! Absolutely – as well as the globally ranging delights of sobrassada and ancho honey pitta, tandoori pork belly with tamarind chutney, barbecued squid with zhoug and preserved lemon aïoli, and trout ceviche with habanero, mango and tequila. It’s as if the Big Lebowski took up cooking.
Sebb’s opened in late 2024, and just over a year later, head chef Danny Carruthers’ food had already snagged the place a Michelin bib gourmand – to my mind by far the most interesting part of the whole tyre company’s advertising hoopla. Bibs are designed to reward places just like Sebb’s: odd, informal, intriguing – the type of place where you can pop out to for lunch without needing four spare hours, a booking months in advance and a decorative Patek Philippe watch on your wrist.
Instead, I’m a solo lunchtime walk-in on a summer’s day. And they treat me beautifully, settling me at my table with an alcohol-free Crossip cooler cocktail – bitter, long and with an olive in it, this is the kind of no-alcohol build that makes you forget to miss the gin – and a round of pakoras with cheese and piccalilli. I order coronation cauliflower, aware it sounds like the sort of thing with which Mrs Dooms-Patterson might torment Jerry on The Good Life. And it turns out this cauliflower is an absolute stonking triumph: tiny, nutty florets, blackened but still sweet and crunchy, in a slick of silky, cashew-based sauce that’s fragrant with coconut and scattered with plump sultanas. As it happens, directly above Sebb’s, at street level, is Margo, a smarter, more composed restaurant that, like Sebb’s, is run by Scoop, the team also behind the city’s Ox & Finch and Ka Pao. Which basically means that Margo Leadbetter is upstairs, while downstairs is where the people who actually enjoy themselves are.
Sebb’s menu is a delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns, and the dishes are a testament to a chef who has learned little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, and who wants to deliver maximum joy. Atom dip arrives first: sweet, smoky, mashed aubergine, red pepper, earthy hazelnut dukkah and strained yoghurt, with a warm pitta served unceremoniously in a brown paper bag. The humble aubergine, elevated.
Then those pakoras: will I make friends by declaring that the best pakora in Britain is in a Glasgow basement, even though the place reminds me of nothing so much as turning up mid-soundcheck for some sort of music event? These pakoras are thoroughly crisp outside with a gloriously squidgy interior, paper-thin onion that’s properly fried through, and all dotted with creamed piccalilli and blanketed in grated sheep’s cheese.
Rump fillet comes seared yet blushing pink, sliced thinly, beautifully arranged and served with cowboy butter – a Glasgow spin on beurre maître d’hôtel that features shedloads of garlic, herbs, mustard and chilli – sweetness, sharpness and umami. For me, this dish pretty much sums up Sebb’s, because it’s a riot of unbridled tastiness with a huge nod to French gastronomical technique. You can have spiced fries with garlic and herb aïoli alongside, or Isle of Wight tomatoes with urfa pepper, capers and pine nuts, which, on a menu this far-ranging, lands like a postcard from somewhere unexpectedly close.
Mimicking just about every Maccy D’s from Land’s End upwards, Sebb’s soft-serve machine is broken the day I go, so instead they offer me chocolate sorbet, which remains one of the best things I’ve eaten all year: a culinary sleight of hand, and so without the bad stuff that it’s practically a health tonic.
I ate lunch with one of my favourite people (me, on a day off) and enjoyed myself so much that I found myself recommending Sebb’s to random people at Glasgow Central Station, and again later on my travels in Leeds, Birmingham and London. Now that is the sign of a properly good little spot.
- 
  Sebb’s 68 Miller Street, Glasgow G1, 0141-739 9381. Open all week, noon-9.45pm (last orders). From about £30 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

Undercover police officer lied to spycops inquiry about sexual relationship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

An undercover police officer who infiltrated leftwing and animal rights campaign groups appears to have lied to the spycops inquiry when he claimed he did not have a sexual relationship as part of his deployment.
The officer who used the fake name Dave Evans had originally testified that he did not have any relationships while using his fake identity.
But this week, he was forced to admit to the inquiry that he did have a relationship with a woman that lasted at least six months. Under questioning, he said it was “possible” that it could have continued for two years, but could not recall how long.
Evans made the admission after campaigners drew evidence of the relationship to the attention of the spycops inquiry.
A central issue of the inquiry is how the undercover officers frequently had sexual relations with women, but did not disclose to them their true identities. Four of the spies fathered, or are alleged to have fathered, children with women they met while working undercover.
Evans was one of about 139 undercover officers who were sent by their police superiors to spy on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over more than four decades. He infiltrated the Socialist Workers party and animal rights groups including London Animal Action between 1998 and 2005.
In his first statement to the inquiry signed four years ago, he wrote: “I did not engage in any sexual activity whilst in my undercover identity.”
But in a second statement that he signed this year, he admitted that “with the benefit of hindsight”, he should have disclosed that he had a relationship with a woman known as Olivia.
He made the admission after the inquiry had been told about his relationship with Olivia by campaigners. This evidence was mainly supplied by Helen Steel, a social justice campaigner who was a defendant in the celebrated McLibel case.
Steel was herself deceived into a two-year relationship by another undercover officer, John Dines. She spent 18 years searching for Dines; at one point senior police officers spent £2.5m of public funds to relocate him to ensure that she did not find him.
Evans was asked by Don Ramble, a barrister at the inquiry, if he had lied in his first statement. He replied:”I accept that it was not completely truthful with hindsight.”
He said he had not originally disclosed the relationship to the inquiry “because she was not an activist nor part of any target group, I did not feel this was relevant”.
During his covert deployment, Evans pretended to be a landscape gardener as part of his false persona. He met Olivia in 1998 when he attended a college course in his fake identity. At no point did he reveal to her that he was actually a police officer.
The inquiry heard evidence that Evans and Olivia together attended social events with animal rights campaigners and at least one demonstration. Olivia is not giving evidence to the inquiry.
The spycops inquiry has been scrutinising wide-ranging wrongdoing committed by undercover officers. The government is considering whether the remaining stages of the inquiry, which has been running for more than a decade, should continue in a different format.
Victims of the surveillance however say that any move to cut short the inquiry would result in a cover-up.

Poland is racing ahead with military spending – but will it help or damage its economic growth story?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów.
As recently as two years ago, their destination – a hi-tech weapons facility opened this month – had been a cornfield. Now, as Poland drives up defence investment at one of the fastest rates in the developed world, this rural spot has been transformed amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“Everyone has had to move twice as fast to meet the Polish needs,” says Jim Price, the managing director of MBDA Polska, the local subsidiary of the European multinational arms group. Based in the UK, the former Royal Marine says Poland is shifting from importing its weapons to manufacturing them at home.
“When it became clear there is a need to defend Nato’s eastern flank, in the event of a war itself, they needed to be able to do things in the blink of an eye. So we decided to invest in-the country to create a facility. We had to build up our Polish subsidiary – and that means Polish jobs.”
Poland’s defence budget has grown at a blistering pace. Since Vladimir Putin ordered Russian troops into Ukraine almost five years ago, spending as a share of Polish gross domestic product (GDP) has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. In cash terms, this equates to $53bn (£39.8bn), the fourth-highest in the EU after Germany, France and Italy.
Attention in Warsaw is clearly focused on the risk of an imminent Russian test of Nato resolve. However, there is also another motive: growing the economy.
Inside the soundproofed, airlock-style doors enclosing his office in Warsaw, Marcin Bosacki, Poland’s deputy foreign minister, says Russian aggression is heavily influencing the Polish government’s plans for economic development and cooperation with EU and Nato allies.
“[It] is clearly benefiting Polish security; Polish defence, and the Polish economy as well,” he says.
Strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Putin (“a traditional Russian imperialist”) from attacking Nato, Bosacki adds.
“The only thing which Putin understands is solidarity and power. And so the more we are united and strong, the less likely the outcome of more aggressive Russian provocations against Nato member states is.”
Hope remains for a diplomatic solution. This month, Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Next month, further negotiations are scheduled in Abu Dhabi.
However, diplomatic sources believe Russia is unlikely to cede ground – rendering Nato’s demonstrations of military readiness critical.
History shows defence and economics are closely intertwined. Statisticians first devised GDP as a metric in response to the 1930s Great Depression and needs of wartime planning to gauge the capacity of an economy.
Poland has been through an economic miracle since the Solidarność (solidarity) movement that arose from the Gdańsk shipyard strikes paved the way for its transition from communism almost four decades ago. Living standards have shot up from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
Joining the EU in 2004 and securing catch-up funds from Brussels – which was spent on new roads, railways, and other productivity-enhancing infrastructure – also helped. Annual output surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, with Poland among the fastest-growing EU countries at an annualised rate of 3.9% in the second quarter despite the global headwinds caused by the Iran war.
However, Poland’s defence boom is not cost-free. Nor has economic development helped it avoid political polarisation.
The rising military budget is among the reasons why Poland is predicted to run the biggest fiscal deficit in the EU next year, at 7.1% of GDP. Last week, Moody’s downgraded the country’s long-term sovereign credit rating to the lowest level since 2002, amid an apparent lack of willingness to rebuild fiscal buffers.
Leszek Kąsek, a Warsaw-based economist at ING Bank, said: “This path is not sustainable. You should ask people if Poland can maintain its growth story and whether politicians will be ready to adjust?”
Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. But despite its economic turnaround under EU membership, and as it secures billions of euros in defence funds from Brussels, support for Eurosceptic politics remains.
In the run-up to the general election next year, the defence of the country, support for Ukraine and EU relations will be highly politically charged.
Outside the foreign ministry in Warsaw, protesters wave placards in a “Poles for peace” nationalist rally, organised by rightwing politicians opposed to the EU and its support for Ukraine.
Inside the building’s marble halls, where the Polish flag appears to be positioned next to those of Nato and the EU at almost every opportunity, Bosacki says divisions over the benefits to Poland of membership to both institutions has emerged for the first time.
This year, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has backing from the rightwing Law and Justice party, attempted to block the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk’s liberal, pro-EU government from accessing €44bn (£38bn) of defence investment loans approved under the bloc’s security action for Europe (Safe) programme.
“I think our right is so eager to regain power they will use anything,” Bosacki says. “Here for the first time, the opposition was [against doing] something which, in my opinion – and the opinion of the majority of Poles – is clearly benefiting Polish security, Polish defence and the Polish economy as well.”
Through Safe, Warsaw secured the largest single disbursement in the loan programme. The government has pledged to channel almost 90% of it to domestic industry – led by Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ), the state-owned defence conglomerate.
However, in the race to build up capacity, the tills are ringing for US-arms manufacturers supplying Patriot missiles, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets.
In March, the International Monetary Fund cautioned that the positive economic spillovers from EU defence investment would not necessarily flow for the governments taking out their chequebooks.
However, Warsaw is doing defence deals with international partners, including the UK, to help develop its domestic manufacturing base at the same time as building military readiness.
The British defence group Babcock is working with PGZ to help build a fleet of new frigates. Known as the Miecznik, or swordfish, programme, the company has a shipyard at Gdynia on the Baltic coast. The first ship was launched this summer by Tusk.
“It’s a must for Poland, basically, to invest more. But they want to do it in a smart way,” says Andrzej Maciejewski, Babcock’s country director for Poland, who is based in Warsaw.
“We’re addressing this ambition – that these great investments in defence will bring greater value for money and, in the longer run, these capabilities.”
BAE Systems is partnering with the PGZ subsidiary Mesko, which makes ammunition and rockets, to build an artillery plant in Poland’s old southern industrial heartlands near Katowice.
By 2028, Poland plans three new munition factories. During a visit to the Mesko facility in August, Tusk said figures for 2023 showed Poland was capable of producing only 5,000 rounds of 155mm ammunition – a Nato-standard artillery shells. “More is used in one day on the Russian-Ukrainian front,” he said. This year, Poland will have increased production to 30,000 rounds, with a goal of 200,000 a year in the next two years.
This month, Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, visited Czosnów for the opening of the MBDA facility. Pollard said it would help support jobs in both countries, including in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton.
Despite this, Britain is increasing defence investment at a slower pace. The government has committed to increase spending from 2.3% of GDP last year to 3%, but has not spelled out precisely how or when this will be achieved.
In Poland, there are signs its investment spree is beginning to pay off for local contractors.
Maciej Klemm, the co-founder of Advanced Protection Systems (APS), which builds counter-drone systems in Gdynia, has increased its headcount from about 150 staff to 200 this year.
Amid growing Russian drone incursions into Polish airspace, APS is playing a role in the Warsaw’s $4bn San programme to build an “anti-drone wall” to protect the country’s eastern flank.
“We are spending a lot of money as a nation, and we are almost a poster child for it,” Klemm says. Splitting his time between Poland and the UK, where he still lives with his family after graduating from the University of Bristol in the 2000s, Klemm also sums up Poland’s recent economic history.
“I was moving to Britain at the time there was a big wave of Poles coming over here. Now after Brexit, that wave partly receded and went the other way. Now, companies like ourselves and others are showing we have technical talent; we can build on this, and grow companies in Poland.”

I have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversed | David Harewood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:55 UTC
14:00:55 KST

As Labour party conference approaches, politicians will debate spending priorities, fiscal pressures and the UK’s place in the world. Before those discussions begin, I want ministers to picture a hospital ward I visited in Sierra Leone with Unicef (United Nations Children’s Fund).
Inside the special-care baby unit at Makeni regional hospital were rows of tiny premature babies, some no bigger than my hand. Around them stood dedicated nurses and anxious parents, all willing these newborns to survive.
Then I saw something that stopped me in my tracks. It was 2019, and I noticed a UK aid sticker fixed above a tiny incubator. Inside was a premature baby fighting for breath. Nearby stood oxygen equipment that staff explained had been funded through UK support. I learned that when power outages struck the hospital, as they often did, that equipment helped keep vulnerable newborns alive.
Being in the presence of these sometimes inconceivably small children, seeing the UK aid sticker labelled across the incubators that were keeping them alive, emotion completely overcame me. It was not only sadness. It was pride. Pride that people in Britain, most of whom would never meet that baby or their family, had helped make survival possible. Seven years later, that moment remains one of the most impactful of my life.
When you are standing beside a newborn fighting for every breath, politics feels very far away. But the truth is that babies live or die because of political choices.
Since 2017, Unicef has supported Sierra Leone’s government to establish special-care baby units, providing sick and premature newborns with specialised treatment that was previously unavailable to many in the country.
I met doctors and nurses doing extraordinary work despite limited resources. I saw community health workers connecting families with health facilities, and mothers receiving advice and support.
One of them was Josephine, whose one-month-old daughter, also called Josephine, had been born dangerously premature at seven months. She told me she believed that without the special-care baby unit, both she and her daughter might have died during or after labour.
That is what aid means. It is not charity, and it is not an abstract number on a government spreadsheet.
The results in Sierra Leone show what that investment can achieve. Since the expansion of the special-care baby units began, annual admissions have risen from around 1,000 to 14,000, while survival rates had improved from 78% to 90% by the end of 2025.
But those gains are now under threat. Since the start of 2025, global aid funding has fallen sharply as major donors have scaled back support. The UK has already reduced spending on overseas development from 0.7% of national income to 0.3%. Around the world, programmes that help keep children healthy, safe and in school are facing growing uncertainty. In Sierra Leone, those cuts are no longer a future concern. They are already being felt.
I learned last week that the UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end this December, two years earlier than planned.
I’m already hearing about the consequences. International paediatric support and specialist neonatal nurse training has ended. Reductions affecting the free healthcare programmes have also damaged the availability of lifesaving medicines for newborns, children and pregnant women.
The danger is not just that units such as Makeni might suddenly close. It is that the foundations supporting them are gradually eroded. Medical equipment needs spare parts and trained technicians. Oxygen must remain available. Nurses need continuing training and clinical mentorship. Medicines must reach hospitals. Infection prevention, referrals, outreach and follow-up for small and sick babies all require sustained investment.
Without that support, the progress I witnessed will be lost.
Sierra Leone is building national capacity. But transferring skills and building resilient health systems takes time. Ending support prematurely risks pulling away the scaffolding before the structure is strong enough to stand alone.
The scale of the unmet need makes that risk even more alarming. About 45,000 newborns in Sierra Leone require specialised care each year, but existing services reach only about 31%. Approximately 31,000 small and sick babies are still left without access to the essential care they need.
This is not a programme that has finished its job. It is a programme that is working, but still reaches only a fraction of the children who need it. That is why I support Unicef UK’s No Choice But Childhood campaign.
The Guardian’s recent report suggests that ministers are looking for ways to make a smaller aid budget work harder. That is an important discussion. But the question should not only be how aid is spent: it should also be who it is spent for. If children bear the greatest consequences of poverty, conflict and climate shocks, they should be a clear priority in how aid is allocated.
The UK government should ringfence at least 25% of its overseas development spending for programmes that directly support children. The government must also set out a credible route back to spending 0.7% of national income on overseas development. Restoring that commitment will not happen overnight, but without a clear path, temporary reductions risk becoming a permanent retreat, with tragic consequences.
I understand the pressures on public finances: governments must make difficult choices. But we should be honest about what those choices mean.
In Makeni, they can mean whether oxygen is available when a premature baby cannot breathe. Whether a nurse has the training and equipment to act. Whether a mother goes home carrying her child.
The special-care baby unit I visited remains open, for now, but declining support is making it harder to sustain its quality, while extending the same care to thousands of newborns who are still not being reached.
No child chooses where they are born, and as Labour conference gets under way, I hope ministers think of children – like the tiny baby I saw in the incubator. That is what our choices can do.
- 
  David Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassador

Food prices vs minimum wages: Where in Europe has pay kept up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

Euronews Business compares five years of food price rises and minimum wage changes in 26 European countries to see where workers on the lowest pay can afford more food than they could in 2021.
Food prices have risen sharply across Europe over the past five years, but minimum wages have risen even faster in most of the 26 countries examined by Euronews Business.
Malta is one exception. A worker on the minimum wage there can buy about 6% less food with their gross pay than they could five years ago, despite a rise in wages. Minimum-wage workers in Spain and France have also lost ground.
Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 34% across the EU between August 2021 and August 2026, according to Eurostat. Hungary recorded the highest rise in the bloc, at 57%, followed by Bulgaria (54%) and Romania (53%). Cyprus had the lowest increase, at 21%.
Among the wider group of 35 European countries, Switzerland recorded the lowest increase, at 5%.
Turkey was an outlier: food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 752% over the same period.
Turkey’s exceptional rise reflects years of high inflation, fuelled in part by a sharp fall in the lira, which pushed up the cost of imported goods and inputs. The lira’s decline was partly driven by a series of interest rate cuts that began in 2021, even as inflation rose. Lower rates made the currency less attractive to hold, adding to pressure on its value. Turkey reversed that policy in 2023 and raised rates sharply, but prices continued to rise.
Across the EU, food prices were already rising before Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The war added to the pressure by driving up energy, fertiliser and transport costs, as well as disrupting agricultural markets. Those costs fed through to supermarket prices.
Among the EU’s largest economies, food prices rose by 25% in France, 30% in Italy, 34% in Germany and 35% in Spain between August 2021 and August 2026.
How minimum wages compare
Monthly gross minimum wages also rose over the same period in many European countries with a statutory minimum wage.
Hungary recorded the largest increase in the EU, at 93%, while the minimum wage rose by 46% in Germany, 29% in Spain and 20% in France. These changes are measured in local currencies.
Turkey recorded the largest increase among the countries compared, at 823% over five years. Minimum wages also more than doubled in Serbia (103%) and Montenegro (102%).
But higher wages do not necessarily mean workers can afford more food. The comparison measures how much food a monthly gross minimum wage could buy in August 2021 and August 2026. It does not show how much money workers had left for groceries after tax, rent and other expenses.
Simply subtracting the food price increase from the minimum wage increase can be misleading, especially when inflation is high, as in Turkey. Comparing what the wage could buy at each point gives a clearer picture.
In three of the 26 countries compared, minimum-wage earners lost purchasing power when measured against food prices.
Malta recorded the biggest fall, at 6%. A minimum-wage earner who could buy 100 baskets of food in August 2021 could buy only 94 in August 2026. Spain and France followed, with falls of 5% and 4%, respectively.
Serbia and Montenegro recorded the largest increases in the amount of food a minimum wage could buy, at 37%. A minimum-wage earner who could buy 100 baskets of food in August 2021 could buy 137 in August 2026.
Croatia, Albania, Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Lithuania also saw increases of more than 20%.
Food purchasing power rose by 10% in Ireland, 9% in Germany, 7% in Greece, 6% in Belgium and the Netherlands, and 3% in Portugal.
The chart above, indexed at 100 in August 2021, shows how the amount of food a minimum-wage earner can buy changed over the five years.
In Turkey, the minimum wage rose by 823% and food prices by 752%. The difference is 71 percentage points, but the increase in food purchasing power was only 8%. Both wages and food prices rose steeply in lira, with wages rising slightly faster.
The chart above tracks Turkey’s minimum wage and food prices, both indexed at 100 in August 2021. It shows that minimum-wage earners lost ground at times in 2021 and 2022, when food prices rose faster than their wages. Since January 2024, the minimum wage has remained ahead of food prices, leaving workers able to buy more food than they could at the starting point.

Travelling with friends? These are the most popular cities for group holidays in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:02 UTC
14:00:02 KST

Where are groups travelling to for the rest of 2026? London, Paris and Marseille top Kayak’s most searched destinations for group holidays.
Revive the group chat, dust the cobwebs off the travel spreadsheet and get the posse to turn “let’s plan the trip” into “all flight tickets and stays are booked!”... Sometimes, this is easier said than done.
In Opodo’s “Solo Travel Trends 2026: The Year of Travelling Alone with Purpose” report released in August, as many as 30% of the 9,000 travellers surveyed said they opted to go the journey alone because their friends or family weren't available.
But when the group chat does finally deliver, travelling with friends can have its perks.
Dividing costs among friends for accommodation, rental cars, petrol and even food can “unlock significant savings”, according to Kayak, which added that renting a large villa overlooking an ocean view is a lot less expensive once the nightly rate is shared between five or more people. “The trick? Knowing where to go.”
Top searched destinations for groups
Kayak surveyed hotel and holiday rental searches for bookings made by parties of five or more between March and September for stays between July and December 2026.
In both cases, Europe took centre stage, with London ranking as the most searched hotel destination for groups. According to Kayak, the average price per night was €181 – 6% less than the previous year.
Second on the list is Paris, where the average hotel stay per night was found to be €144, a 3% decrease from last year. Meanwhile, the French capital was also the most searched for holiday rental destination for groups, with rental rates averaging €151 a night.
Other French destinations proved popular on the holiday rentals ranking, including Marseille and Nice, which took the second and eighth spots on Kayak’s list.
Steeped in more than 26 centuries of history, the port city of Marseille is typically less crowded from during October and November and the climate becomes cooler, too – making it ideal for exploring its oldest neighbourhood: the Panier District, dating back to 600BC.

Lithuania’s interior minister wants to restore warning shots for police and border guards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania’s Interior Ministry is proposing to restore police and other law enforcement officers’ ability to fire warning shots and ease some restrictions on when they can use their firearms, saying the changes would strengthen officers’ protection.
The proposals have drawn scepticism from police unions, which say they were not consulted during their preparation and question whether warning shots should be brought back.
Under current rules, an officer may use a firearm when there is an unavoidable danger and an unavoidable necessity. The Interior Ministry wants to remove those specific requirements.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the current wording relies too heavily on subjective assessments, which can be difficult for an officer to make in a rapidly developing situation.
“These are statements of an evaluative nature. If the state asks an officer to do their job and the officer has 1 to 10 seconds to make a decision, can they assess whether there is an unavoidable danger?” Katelynas said.
He stressed that firearms would remain a last resort under the proposed rules.
“The firearm is used in a way that causes as little harm as possible, while the safeguards are being further strengthened,” said Darius Domarkas, head of the ministry’s Public Security Group.
The ministry also wants to restore the option of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional means of de-escalating a situation.
“There was no possibility of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional warning when a situation is escalating and needs to be de-escalated,” Domarkas said. “There was only a verbal warning.”
Warning shots were abolished in Lithuania about a decade ago. Former police officer and instructor Dalius Mackela said there were good reasons for removing them.
“If we fire those 9 grams into the air, they don't just disappear,” Mackela said, referring to the approximate weight of a bullet. “If, God forbid, that 9-gram bullet comes back down and finds an object, someone will be hurt. Who will stand up for the officers then?”
Mackela also questioned whether the proposed changes were necessary, saying existing legislation already clearly establishes when police may use firearms.
The debate over firearms use intensified this summer after a group of irregular migrants attacked border guards. Under the ministry’s proposals, border guards would have more flexibility to use firearms against equipment used to cross the border.
“They could act against equipment used for illegal border crossings, such as ladders or tunnels,” Katelynas said.
The minister also said officers who fire at a suspect would be guaranteed legal and psychological assistance.
Police unions, however, say changes to firearms rules alone would not address their concerns.
“The whole complicated situation is being turned into a show, with the emphasis being placed where it shouldn’t be,” said Ineta Kursevičienė, head of the Federation of Police Trade Unions.
Roma Katinienė, chairwoman of the Police Trade Union, said law enforcement agencies needed an agreement on procedures following the use of firearms or special measures.
“What is needed is a common agreement among law enforcement institutions on simplified procedures when a firearm or special measures are used, so that officers do not become hostages to three or five years of litigation,” Katinienė said.
The unions pointed to several lengthy cases involving officers.
In May, a court acquitted police officer Darius Šerpytis, who had been charged with causing a death by exceeding his powers. The investigation and court proceedings lasted three years.
A separate case involving border guard Karolis Ilgevičius has been ongoing for two years. He is accused of shooting at the tire of a fleeing suspected smuggler’s vehicle and killing the driver.
The unions also criticised the Interior Ministry for failing to consult them before preparing the proposed changes.
“Unfortunately, with the current interior minister, as a trade union, we have not had a single meeting,” the Police Trade Union chairwoman said.
Katelynas said the unions would now have an opportunity to give their views on the proposals.
He said Lithuania’s security environment had changed and that law enforcement officers therefore needed rules adapted to the new circumstances.

Ethiopia’s federal military has said it is handling rising tensions in the country’s north with restraint, as fears grow that Ethiopia could be heading towards another civil war.
In his first comments on the recent military developments, Army Chief of Staff Field Marshal Berhanu Jula said the army was responding to what he called provocations from the Tigray front with “wisdom and restraint”.

He accused Eritrea of funding and supporting armed groups to weaken Ethiopia, describing the “Tsimdo” alliance as an extension of a longstanding pattern of hostile alliances, which he said cannot confront the state without outside backing.
Eritrea, wary that landlocked Ethiopia may be seeking to invade it to gain access to the Red Sea, denied the accusations.
The fighting has spread from Tigray into neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions after seven armed groups announced an alliance, the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, committed to removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
In Afar, the latest battles have taken place around Abala, where the military has been trying to prevent rebels from seizing control.

Internet access was reportedly cut across northern Ethiopia on Friday, a day after the UN said it was alarmed by reports of drones being used against civilians there.
The renewed fighting has put the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray, under severe strain. It comes weeks after Washington lifted sanctions on Ethiopia and Eritrea tied to atrocities from the last war, saying the “national emergency … has expired”.
It marks the most serious challenge yet to that agreement, raising fears of a wider regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across Ethiopia.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ethiopia’s president sought to portray the country as a force for regional stability, accusing unnamed external actors of meddling in Ethiopia’s affairs while highlighting Addis Ababa’s role in supporting peace efforts in neighbouring Sudan.
Alemayehu Weldemariam, a professor of law at Indiana University, told Al Jazeera that the federal government bears much of the blame for the collapse of the Pretoria Agreement.
“This war has been in the making for a while now. Much of the provisions in the cessation of hostilities [in the 2022 agreement] were primarily sabotaged by the federal government itself,” he said, citing fuel, service and cash restrictions imposed on Tigray, and the government’s failure to set up the interim administration the deal had promised.
“What was supposed to be an interim arrangement turned out to be permanent,” with Tigray excluded from national elections since, he added.

Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
04:56:41 UTC
13:56:41 KST

Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after U.S. President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump said on Saturday he rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Despite Trump's public statements, mediators facilitating Iran's talks with the United States have not officially relayed a U.S. rejection of the plan, according to Araghchi.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi posted.
The U.S. has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to stop Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, which have drastically reduced shipping through the area even as Trump repeatedly asserts that the U.S. controls the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
It said Trump was privately skeptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November U.S. midterm elections.
A U.S. official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were "positive and constructive."
Conflict has disrupted oil flows, harmed global economy
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.
Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
"If there is seriousness on the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araghchi said. If the U.S. were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks "on mutually agreed subjects."
That could potentially include discussions of Iran's nuclear program. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the U.S. accepted its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons."
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with U.S. and Israeli attacks.
Since then, the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading the conventional forces of Iran and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck U.S. allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests.
Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom.

The Ukrainian MAUL evacuation robot managed to evacuate a wounded soldier after triggering a mine and being hit by a drone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:52:07 EEST
13:52:07 KST

The Ukrainian MAUL evacuation robot managed to evacuate a wounded soldier after triggering a mine and being hit by a drone
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian MAUL robot evacuated a wounded soldier after triggering a mine and being hit by a drone. Sweden plans to produce up to 500 vehicles annually.
The Ukrainian MAUL unmanned ground vehicle, designed to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield, continues to be improved based on the real-world experience of military personnel. It was the soldiers’ feedback, rather than artificial intelligence, that formed the basis for most of the vehicle’s improvements, Defence Blog reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to AIDronesUA head Kostiantyn Hushcha, after combat missions, military personnel pass their observations on to engineers, who can quickly turn them into technical changes and new tests.
This primarily concerns the reliability of the running gear, the protection and securing of the wounded person, the interaction between onboard systems, and the ability to quickly repair the vehicle and return it to the front.
MAUL has already survived a mine blast and a drone strike
MAUL is an all-wheel-drive unmanned vehicle with an internal combustion engine, created specifically for evacuation missions. The wounded person is transported in an armored capsule, while the operator can monitor their condition through an internal camera. The vehicle can carry up to 200 kg and reach speeds of up to 70 km/h.
MAUL attracted widespread attention after an operation in November 2025, when it was used to evacuate a Ukrainian soldier who had remained wounded behind Russian positions for 33 days. During the six-hour operation, the robot struck an anti-personnel mine and lost a wheel, and later withstood a direct hit from a Russian drone while still managing to deliver the soldier to medics.
MAUL production is planned to expand beyond Ukraine. AIDronesUA and Sweden’s NJORD Technology plan to manufacture 400–500 such vehicles annually in Sweden for the needs of the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine.

Local governments set for major funding overhaul next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
04:50:00 UTC
13:50:00 KST

Local governments set for major funding overhaul next year
Local governments will, beginning next year with the planned change, gain greater freedom to decide over their finances. This is something municipalities have awaited, though in the first year it may punch a hole in the budget of some rural municipalities.
Currently, local governments receive money from two main sources – a share of their residents' income tax and about €122 million from the state support fund.
The problem is that the state money comes with a label, meaning it is intended for a very specific purpose, and the size of the support has not changed for 10 years.
With the reform, this same sum will be taken out of fixed envelopes and placed into a kind of common pool, which is the revenue base of the local government. Local hovernments will begin deciding themselves what the money is most needed for, and the amount of money would also change in the future along with income tax receipts.
The ministry hopes the change will take effect on 1 January.
"The draft has been coordinated and is awaiting the minister's approval to move forward to the government and from there to the Riigikogu, so that the changes could enter into force at the beginning of 2027," said Hardi Alliksaar, head of the local governments department at the Ministry of Regional Affairs.
Since in the first year some local governments would end up in deficit compared with the current system, the Association of Estonian Cities and Municipalities wants €3.4 million to offset the differences that arise.
"This 3.4 million is a one‑time sum. It is not annual or some ongoing support, but a one‑time amount to smooth out the transition deficits. After that it proceeds routinely, as circumstances and the economic situation dictate," said Saue municipal mayor Andres Laisk, who also leads the finance and tax policy working group of the Association of Estonian Cities and Municipalities.
Signatures for the state budget will be placed on Monday. No cash injection is foreseen for the equalisation fund.
"There is no decision regarding the 3.4 million, but it has also not been a precondition for moving forward with the processing of this draft, and therefore we still wish to proceed with it," Alliksaar noted.
One of the local governments that may lose money during the transition is Jõelähtme municipality. Even if the state does not find money for the transition period, the reform is, in the long term, correct and necessary.
According to Jõelähtme municipal mayor Andrus Umboja, the municipality will manage anyway.
"We must complete our activities, we cannot leave anything undone. We must still repair those roads and ensure money for textbooks for schools or salaries for principals. We will surely ensure these. But the question is one of principle, whether local governments are treated equally or not," Umboja said.

by William M. Reilly
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Most of the 194 scheduled speakers at the UN General Assembly's General Debate on Saturday touched on shared global challenges, with many calling for greater cooperation to address issues affecting their regions.
The global topics ranged from multilateral diplomacy, one of the reasons for the world body's creation, to Security Council reform and the development and possible regulation of artificial intelligence. While regional concerns were widely represented, much attention focused on water.
Vice President Aren Palik of Micronesia said his people were seeing a rise in illnesses linked to marine life and vector-borne diseases. The country is therefore strengthening its health capacity.
"The ocean is the heart of Micronesian identity," he said, urging UN member states to fortify ocean governance, sustainable fisheries management and effective marine biodiversity conservation.
Palik said plastic pollution threatens to degrade Pacific ecosystems and communities, calling on the international community to respond with renewed political resolve, scaled-up financing and accelerated implementation.
"Let us choose cooperation over division," the vice president said.
Cabo Verde Prime Minister Francisco Carvalho said that for his country and other small island states, "the climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is a present reality," referring to droughts, desertification, water scarcity, ocean acidification and rising sea levels.
"Just look at what is happening on the island of Sal, where, only two days ago, rising sea waters flooded the avenue in front of the hotels," he said. That is also a question of justice, he added, because those who have contributed the least to this crisis cannot continue to bear some of its most serious consequences.
Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin was another speaker whose country had a keen interest in water.
As a mountainous country, home to thousands of glaciers, Tajikistan knows the "value of water" and its vulnerability, he said, adding that "water has remained at the heart of Tajikistan's international engagement."
He said a UN Water Conference will take place in Abu Dhabi later this year, followed by a high-level preparatory meeting in New York in 2027, a UN Water Conference and a final comprehensive review of the Water Action Decade in the Tajik capital Dushanbe in 2028.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla said Cuba is facing multidimensional aggression from the United States, describing it as a continuation of hostility spanning almost seven decades of an economic blockade.
He said the situation has worsened since January due to Washington's fuel blockade of the island, which he characterized as an act of war under international law, and further alleged that the United States has blocked aid from reaching Cuba and intimidated foreign entrepreneurs into abandoning their investments in the country.
Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister Prak Sokhonn, who also serves as minister for foreign affairs and international cooperation, said his country is now combating online fraud, which has become "one of our highest national priorities," highlighting efforts to strengthen its legal and institutional framework and intensify law enforcement operations against scam centers and the criminal networks behind them.
No country can succeed alone in tackling the problem, since criminal networks operate across borders, said Prak, calling for collective and coordinated action at the national, regional and global levels to disrupt and eradicate online scam operations.
Lao Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Thongsavanh Phomvihane pointed to his country's heavy contamination by wartime unexploded ordnance (UXO) from more than five decades of hostilities. Clearance is central to its development agenda.
Removing UXO is not merely a technical task, but is also about restoring safety, securing agricultural land and reclaiming development opportunities for communities, he said. ■
