'Open your eyes': Why China's sixth Antarctic base is raising concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
04:20:20 UTC
13:20:20 KST

China's plan to build sixth Antarctic base raises concerns
China is preparing to build its sixth research station in Antarctica, expanding into Marie Byrd Land — a remote, little-studied stretch of the continent's west.
It has some experts and politicians worried.
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie is among those concerned about Australia's defence priorities.
"Five bases have already been built, and China claims there is no geopolitical motive," she said.
"Open your eyes, [Department of] Defence."
Whether that alarm is warranted depends on who you ask.
China says the new base, which it plans to build next year, will support research into climate change, ice sheets and marine systems.
And it is far from the only country with a significant presence.
The US operates three permanent year-round bases. So does Australia, which claims 42 per cent of the continent, while Russia has five year-round stations.
But experts warn what matters most is not the station itself.
It is what the project might signal about China's deepening influence inside the institutions that govern Antarctica.
Military use or just science?
Jiliang Chen, a lecturer in Antarctic law and governance at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania, sees the new station mainly as a matter of prestige.
"Building a station is China capitalising on its strength in this strategic game," Mr Chen said.
China's new station is being developed as per the Antarctic Treaty System's environmental assessment procedures.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, member states cannot veto a proposed new station.
The treaty was originally signed by 12 countries in 1959 and designed to ensure the use of the area for peaceful purposes only and the protection of the environment.
Mr Chen said a stronger physical presence helped consolidate China's role in future decisions on the continent.
"It gives people one more thing to be proud of, scientists more facilities to do research, and more projects to plan," he said.
One complication is that equipment such as satellite systems, communications hardware, aircraft and drones serve civilian research and can easily be adapted for military use.
That dual-use capability is why Mr Chen believes inspection and transparency matter most.
Other experts are more suspicious.
Elizabeth Buchanan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), points to China's existing satellite ground stations and its Military-Civil Fusion policy, which enables civilian companies to develop or supply technologies for military use.
Her deeper worry is that China's spread of stations could eventually let it operate across Antarctica without depending on other countries.
"Polar power with serious polar independence means we have very little leverage left,"
Some say that framing is overblown.
The Antarctic Treaty prohibits military bases, weapons and new territorial claims, while permitting military personnel and equipment for peaceful purposes.
China's embassy in Canberra told the ABC it was "fully committed to ensuring its activities in the region strictly align with the Antarctic Treaty System".
Tony Press, the former head of the Australian Antarctic Division, said he believed mining and military fears were exaggerated, citing the cost and difficulty of moving people and equipment across such a hostile environment.
"Antarctica is a terrible place to fight a war from,"
Unlike China's year-round Quinling station, the new base would run only in summer, hardly the profile of a strategic outpost, Mr Press said.
Instead, he said China was making a geopolitical statement.
"China is obviously doing the old strategic thing of making sure they've got stations around Antarctica that demonstrate quite clearly that they are a big player in, and have an interest in, all parts of Antarctica," he said.
Working the system, not breaking it
Analysts say China is finding ways to become increasingly influential without breaking the rules.
China joined the treaty later than other countries, in 1983.
"China has always been nervous about natural resources and probably more hungry for economic growth," Mr Chen said.
Fishing is where this showed most clearly, he said.
China joined the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), largely because of its interest in Antarctic fishing, Mr Chen said.
Ms Buchanan pointed to the broader growth of China's fishing fleet and domestically built fleet of icebreakers as part of its "Polar Silk Road" strategy.
She said China was also preparing to unveil a nuclear-powered icebreaker, which she said would reduce its reliance on gateway ports such as Hobart.
China is limiting the size of its high sea fishing fleet, except for the polar regions, Mr Chen said.
Antarctic krill fishing is an exception in China's plan for high sea fishing.
Emperor penguins caught in the middle of geopolitics
China has generally opposed new marine protected areas in Antarctica.
Nearly half of Antarctica's 60 emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure since 2016 as sea ice they depend on has retreated, according to researchers from the British Antarctic Survey.
Efforts to list them as a Special Protected Species have stalled at CCAMLR, blocked by China and Russia.
The stated objections cite insufficient scientific evidence, or argue that such a listing would address a symptom (habitat loss) rather than its underlying cause of climate change, which sits outside the treaty's scope.
Lyn Goldsworthy, an adjunct researcher at the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies, said China was operating from a strategic perspective, and wanted to avoid restricting access to certain areas in case it had "certain aspirations" in the future.
Ms Goldsworthy added China appeared to join the conservation body CCAMLR for the purpose of fishing first, not marine biology or conservation.
Krill is another source of tension.
The tiny crustaceans are a primary food source for penguins and whales.
Next month's CCAMLR meeting, known as the "Krill Convention", will debate fishing limits.
China has a particular interest in Antarctic krill, which is increasingly valuable as an ingredient in aquaculture feed and nutritional supplements.
Krill products were pulled from shelves in Australian supermarkets after environmental campaigns, but China and Norway are pushing to raise the current catch limit much higher.
Ms Goldsworthy described years of stalemate.
"You have China saying, 'We don't believe in marine protected areas, you should give us our krill fishery'. Other countries are saying, 'No, we won't discuss krill fishery expansion until we've progressed marine protected areas,'" she said.
"There is now a deep distrust."
The underlying ecological concern that over-concentration of fishing in certain areas damages predator populations and habitats has become inseparable from the geopolitics around it, Ms Goldsworthy said.
One flashpoint was an area where heavy Chinese fishing activity overlapped with an Argentine-Chilean proposal for a marine protected area, she said.
Experts say Russia has also played a "disruptive" role, objecting alongside China to new marine protection sites.
'Treaty not about to topple over'
Indi Hodgson-Johnston, a senior lecturer in marine and Antarctic law and policy, describes a pattern of "quiet disruption" by China, but technically no broken rules.
"The treaty is not about to topple over. I can't see that happening," said Ms Hodgson-Johnston, who works at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania.
"There's disruption everywhere at the moment. I would say Antarctica is just not a special case,"
However, ASPI's Ms Buchanan warned consensus-based governance could just as easily mask a "holding pattern" while one party's capacity and presence grows.
"We can't continue to assume, blindly, it's all happening in good faith," she said.
"We need a dual-track approach that has some optimism in continued adherence to the treaty while crafting a mighty stick or plan B to balance China's expansive ambition in Antarctica."
The ABC has approached the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for comment.

In Switzerland, voters are voting for stricter neutrality: the result could force the country to lift sanctions against the Russian Federation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
07:17:07 EEST
13:17:07 KST

In Switzerland, voters are voting for stricter neutrality: the result could force the country to lift sanctions against the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
The Swiss are voting for stricter neutrality, which could lead to the lifting of sanctions against states participating in the war. The initiative would also limit cooperation with NATO.
In Switzerland, a referendum is being held on Sunday, September 27, on enshrining a significantly stricter principle of neutrality in the Constitution. If the initiative is supported, the country will no longer be able to join sanctions against states involved in wars, with the exception of UN sanctions, BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
One of the immediate consequences could be a review of the current sanctions against Russia. The Swiss government officially states that, if the initiative is approved, the existing restrictions against states at war would likely have to be lifted. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Bern largely joined the EU sanctions.
The initiative also provides that Switzerland should not join or cooperate with military or defense alliances. An exception would be possible if the country itself were subjected to a military attack or such an attack were being directly prepared.
Cooperation with NATO also called into question
Switzerland is not currently a member of NATO either, but it cooperates with other states in the security sphere. The country’s government warns that the new rules would significantly limit such interaction and Bern’s ability to respond to international crises.
The Swiss Federal Council and Parliament opposed the initiative. Its supporters, by contrast, believe that stricter rules would prevent the authorities from interpreting neutrality arbitrarily and help preserve the country’s role as an international mediator.
Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the Constitution since 1848. The current referendum concerns not abandoning it, but how strict the rules governing its application should be in the future.

Eviction of 87-year-old puts Spain’s deepening housing crisis in the spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
04:00:54 UTC
13:00:54 KST

Images of an octogenarian being evicted from the home she had lived in for seven decades on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police officers, have sparked indignation across Spain.
At the weekend, days after the first protests began, Madrid’s central Sol plaza was still full of anger at the treatment of Maricarmen Abascal. Tens of thousands of people marched through Spain’s capital on Saturday, rattling keys as they called for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult. Some brought tents and sleeping bags, announcing plans to set up a protest camp. Come Sunday, many were still there: their demand, a nationwide reckoning over access to housing.
The catalyst was the eviction of Abascal, now known across the country by her first name. The 87-year-old woman with a disability said she had been forced to leave her home after she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
“This eviction is the canary in the coalmine,” said political scientist Cristina Monge. “It’s become a symbol, seen as the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the issue of housing.”
It was, as newspaper El País said in an editorial, a glimpse of a housing market that had become completely unmoored from the average income in Spain, as rents rose 80% in a decade, while the cost of homes had climbed by 63%. “The law was upheld, and the market worked. But it is the law of the jungle in a broken market, and it is a failure.”
The investment fund linked to the eviction of Maricarmen did not reply to a request for comment from the Guardian.
The eviction had left many in Spain grappling with a sense of “powerlessness”, said Monge, given that the issue of housing had also been at the forefront of the Spanish Indignados movement, or 15-M, the years-long anti-austerity and anti-corruption protest movement that involved millions of Spaniards and reshaped the country’s politics.
“Now, 15 years later, housing is still the number one concern of Spaniards. And there are still evictions every day, to the order of about 25,000 per year,” she said. “But the paradox is that the country’s government includes some of the same people who led the 15-M protests. And still, housing remains an enormous challenge.”
As anger mounted last week, politicians laid the blame on each other for the eviction. Rights campaigners and researchers weighed in with potential solutions, citing the more than 3m homes believed to be sitting empty across the country or government figures that suggest social housing makes up just 2.5% of the total stock in Spain, compared to 14% in France and 34% in the Netherlands.
The head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions called for investment funds to be “kicked out” of the housing market. “Homes are for living in, not for large corporations to do business,” said Unai Sordo of the Workers’ Commissions (CCOO) as he called for a tax system that would make “the business of hoarding homes unprofitable”.
The UN’s special rapporteur on the right to housing, Koldo Casla, called on Spain to amend the laws governing its legal system, describing it as “impossible to understand” how the profitability of a real estate company had been prioritised over Maricarmen’s right to housing.
The leftwing coalition Sumar, the junior partner in the government, said it would push the socialist-led government to greenlight the expropriation of Maricarmen’s former home as well as put forward a package of rent freezes.
The widespread demand for change has cast a spotlight on the deep divisions that exist among Spain’s political parties when it comes to the issue of housing. These divisions were laid bare earlier this year when the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the hardline Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted to end a moratorium on evictions that for six years had managed to shield some vulnerable tenants from eviction.
On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who is under fire for not doing more to ensure his government had carried through on its promises of making housing a priority, promised to swiftly introduce a raft of measures. “Maricarmen’s eviction is a social tragedy that we cannot accept,” he said.
While his government had in 2023 managed to pass legislation that strengthened tenant protection and widened access to rent control, regions led by the People’s party had wielded their powers over housing to avoid implementing parts of the legislation.
Among those who had ignored parts of the legislation was the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who in recent weeks has faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office.
The striking contrast between the allegations against Ayuso and the eviction of Maricarmen repeatedly cropped up last week, from the decision to hold Wednesday’s protest in Madrid on a boulevard next to the penthouse, to the chants urging “Ayuso’s penthouse for Maricarmen”.
The regional leader has so far sought to downplay the significance of Maricarmen’s eviction, describing it as “one out of the 25,500 that take place every year in Spain” and noting that it had been authorised by the country’s courts.
While the story of Maricarmen had dominated headlines, turning the octogenarian into the poster woman for those bearing the brunt of Spain’s soaring real estate market, many pointed to her plight as a glimpse of a wider reality.
“Maricarmen’s case is not an isolated incident; it is just one more example of the suffering endured by thousands of households in Spain,” Amnesty International Spain said in a statement. “Bold measures must be taken immediately. Institutions must go beyond simply expressing regret in the press, they must take action.”

12:51:46 KST

Detained Tunisian flotilla activists: Worsening health amid family anguish
As activists’ health deteriorates, families describe the toll of separation, hunger strikes and uncertainty.
Tunis, Tunisia – For nine-year-old Yassar Naouar, visiting his father in prison has become an exercise in staying strong. He tries not to cry in front of Wael, fearing that seeing his son in tears would make an already painful situation harder for him. After leaving the prison, Yassar finds a corner where he can finally let the tears fall.
Hichem Naouar, Yassar’s grandfather, says the boy has changed since his father was detained. He now sleeps beside his mother after waking up screaming at night and his results at school have worsened. When Yassar told his mother that other children kept asking whether his father was a thief, she asked him what he thought.
“Never,” the nine-year-old replied.
Wael’s youngest child, four-year-old Sumud, is too young to understand why her father is in prison. Hichem says he took her to visit him. When she saw her father behind the glass, she leaned forward to embrace him, only to hit her head against the barrier.
Hichem spoke to Al Jazeera on Wednesday outside the Tunis Court of Appeal, where he had gone to follow the latest challenge to Wael’s detention. He repeatedly choked up as he described what he had seen during his most recent visit.
Wael was sitting with his hand against his cheek, his father said, his elbow trembling and his gaze fixed in the distance. He was struggling to see clearly and to keep water down without vomiting. He was dizzy and had difficulty controlling his left leg. Wael later told Hichem that other prisoners had said he sometimes wakes during the night calling out his youngest daughter’s name.
For his father, however, Wael’s story is also about the kind of person he has been. He recalled an incident during the Sumud land convoy in Libya in May, when armed men tried to kidnap another participant. Wael intervened, pulled the man away and helped him escape before returning to the men and telling them they could take him instead.
During the first Sumud flotilla, a woman fell into the sea and was close to drowning. Wael immediately jumped in and rescued her.
“Wael’s strength is in the strength of his ideas and in his commitment to his people. Whenever he heard about any injustice against workers or employees, you would always find him at the forefront,” Hichem said.
The case and its wider fallout
Wael, 41, began a hunger strike on August 16 to protest his continued detention and was transferred to hospital as his condition deteriorated. He suspended his strike after 38 days following appeals from his lawyers and supporters, saying the decision did not mean abandoning his demands.
Four activists, Ghassan Henchiri, Ghassan Boughdiri and Nabil Channoufi, have been held since March following an investigation by Tunisia’s Economic and Financial Judicial Pole, a specialised body that handles financial and economic crimes. The investigation concerns alleged financial irregularities linked to fundraising for the Global Sumud Flotilla, an international campaign seeking to deliver aid to Gaza and challenge Israel’s blockade of the Palestinian territory.
The state-owned TAP news agency, citing judicial sources, reported that investigators are examining the origin and use of funds collected for the flotilla and whether any were diverted for other purposes. The activists and their defence team have repeatedly denied wrongdoing and maintain their innocence. None of the four has been convicted.
For their lawyers, the issue is also why the men should remain in prison while the investigation continues.
Ghassan Ghribi, a member of the defence committee, described the latest extension of their pretrial detention as an “exception to the exception”, arguing that freedom should be the rule and detention the exception. The four-month extension was ordered on September 11 and the defence challenged the decision before the Court of Appeal in Tunis.
“The investigating judge spent six months on the case without carrying out any investigative work, other than questioning the activists,” Ghribi told Al Jazeera. He said the extension should be based on clear reasons and that the four men were being made to pay the price for what he described as a lack of investigative work.
The Court of Appeal rejected the challenge on Wednesday, leaving the quartet in pretrial detention for another four months while the investigation continues. Henchiri, Boughdiri and Channoufi remain on hunger strike.
Authorities have presented the case as a financial investigation into the handling of funds raised for the flotilla, rather than a prosecution linked to the men’s political or pro-Palestinian activities. The government has rejected accusations that the judiciary is being used to silence opponents, saying the judiciary is independent and that legal proceedings are conducted according to the law.
The fallout has also widened beyond the four men. Fourteen people detained after the September 19 protest calling for their release have since been placed in pretrial detention, lawyer Rafed Rabbeh confirmed to Al Jazeera on Friday. Among them is a 17-year-old who was brought before a juvenile judge. Tunisia’s Child Protection Code says priority should be given to preventive and educational measures and that pretrial detention should be avoided as much as possible for children.
Rabbeh said the detainees face several charges, including participating in a gathering allegedly intended to disturb public order and commit an offence, publicly attributing unlawful acts to a public official without proof, and making public statements deemed to damage the reputation of a person or official body. The charges are based on several provisions of Tunisia’s Penal Code.
The toll on those left behind
Speaking by phone from Gafsa, Ghassan Henchiri’s father, Sebti, said his son remains conscious but is visibly exhausted after being on hunger strike since September 9.
“According to what his sister told me after visiting him, he is still holding up. The fatigue is visible. He is exhausted, but he is still conscious,” Sebti said.
Ghassan has not been taken outside the prison for further medical examination of a head injury sustained during his detention in Israel, Sebti told Al Jazeera. Ghassan and his family have raised the issue with both the prison administration and investigating judge. They were promised that he would receive the necessary medical examinations, but that has not happened, Sebti said.
“It could be a superficial injury, but with the conditions in prison and the high temperatures, it has exhausted him,” he said.
Ghassan also has other health problems, including living with one kidney and suffering from back problems, Sebti said. He has developed a skin rash that keeps him from sleeping, but his request to see a dermatologist was rejected because the prison doctor did not consider it serious, Sebti said.
“I will remain steadfast, I will not give up my right and these malicious accusations are false,” Ghassan told his father.
“He is my son, my brother, my companion, my whole life,” Sebti said. “Ghassan is a man of integrity. I am not saying that because I am his father. Everyone knows that about him.”
Ghassan’s detention has also reshaped family life. He had been working at a high school and was recently engaged, Sebti said.
He described Ghassan’s political commitment as something rooted in the family. He has been involved in student activism and later trade unions since 1978, campaigning for freedom, the right to organise and a better, more dignified life for Tunisians. Ghassan grew up with those principles and was influenced by his father’s activism.
“This is what Ghassan was raised on and what influenced him,” Sebti said.
Human Rights Watch has also raised concerns over the use of financial and money-laundering investigations against civil society actors in Tunisia.
For the Naouar and Henchiri families, the impact of the detentions is being felt at home, in prison visits, anxious phone calls and children asking when their fathers will return.
Yassar still asks about his father and has told his grandfather he is ready to go on hunger strike too.
Asked where her father is, four-year-old Sumud answers: “Palestine. Prison”.

He said the UN Security Council, given its responsibility for international peace and security, should examine the matter urgently.
The letter reiterated Iran's position that US and Israeli military actions against it violate its sovereignty and territorial integrity and breach Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, including through an illegal blockade. It said these actions have included strikes on civilians and civilian targets, resulting in the deaths of more than 3,600 people, including at least 254 children and 251 women, with many more wounded.
Darzi said Iran believes certain European countries facilitated the attacks by providing territory, airspace, military facilities and other logistical and operational capacities, and that such conduct could breach obligations under the UN Charter. He said the matter may also fall under the concept of participation or assistance in an act of aggression as defined in UN General Assembly Resolution 3314 (XXIX).

Israeli, Jewish protesters rally against NYC 'NAZA' screening, display October 7 massacre footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:47:49 UTC
12:47:49 KST

Dozens of Israelis and Jewish Americans from the New York area held a rally in the city overnight on Sunday in front of the Lincoln Center, where a screening of the controversial film NAZA took place.
During the rally, organized by the Israeli-American Council (IAC), LED screens mounted on small trucks displayed excerpts from October 7: Bearing Witness to the Massacre - a graphic, raw documentation of the October 7 attack in Israel, which includes footage filmed by Hamas terrorists during the massacre.
Alongside this footage, the screens displayed documented material contradicting claims made in the film, as well as questions regarding its sources, methodology, and production.
Organizers stated that their goal was to counter the narrative presented by NAZA with documentation of the events of October 7, ensuring that the massacre that sparked the war is not forgotten.
"Films have editors. History does not," the IAC stated. "Our presence here is the message: We will not allow October 7 to be erased from the story."
Members of American-Israeli diaspora attend rally, protest film
Members of the Israeli-American and Jewish communities from New York and New Jersey attended the rally carrying protest signs and wearing promotional shirts. Among the participants were Nova festival survivors Rom El-Hai and Shelev Biton, alongside Younes Al-Garnaoui, an Israeli-Bedouin who saved dozens of people on October 7, including Nova survivors.
The Consul General of Israel in New York, Ofir Akunis, said regarding the campaign led by the Israeli Consulate in cooperation with the Foreign Ministry: "We will not let lies and blood libels prevail. The filmmakers are shameful individuals. We will not stand by and pass over their incitement against our heroic soldiers and the State of Israel in silence!"
The film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Basel Adra (with co-directors Rachel Szor and Hamdan Ballal), was screened as part of the New York Film Festival and presents testimonies from 24 soldiers and intelligence personnel about the mechanics of combat in Gaza.
Organizers say film ignores contradictory information, context of war
Protest organizers argue that the film presents the war while ignoring information that contradicts some of its claims, and without giving sufficient weight to the Hamas attack on October 7 that led to the war.
The IDF has already responded to the claims raised in the film.
"This is a complete lie," the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit stated. "The IDF has never planned, approved, or carried out a strike in Gaza where 500 civilians were expected to be killed, or anything close to that number. Furthermore, no credible claim has been raised throughout the war indicating that an IDF strike caused anything close to that number of fatalities. The filmmakers could not verify this claim; there is no real supporting evidence, yet they published it anyway."
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir also held a consultation on the matter. In a statement, the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit noted that he insists this is a deliberate attempt to directly harm the legitimacy of the IDF and the State of Israel.
He added that the IDF operates in accordance with international law, the spirit of the IDF, and its core values, leading efforts to minimize civilian casualties with a significantly lower ratio of civilian-to-combatant harm compared to other militaries around the world.

In addition the governors of New York and New Jersey on Friday declared states of emergency in counties expected to see the worst of the storm, including New York City. Connecticut's governor activated the state's Emergency Operations Center.

Israel’s election should be decided by Israelis, not American politicians - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:47:22 UTC
12:47:22 KST

A short while ago, in these pages, I asked why an Israeli institution was polling American Jews about whom they wanted to win Israel’s upcoming election.
My argument was simple: American Jews have every right to care deeply about Israel and every right to have political opinions about it. But they should not become a surrogate Israeli electorate.
Then Hillary Clinton came along and demonstrated why the distinction matters.
Appearing on Morning Joe, the former secretary of state made no secret of her feelings about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“I love Israel, and I hate Netanyahu’s government and his policies,” she said. She is entitled to that view. Netanyahu has plenty of critics in Israel, and Americans certainly do not surrender their freedom of opinion when the subject turns to Israeli politics.
But Clinton did not stop there.
“If the Israelis want to vote for that again,” she said, “then I think the United States has to take a very tough position.” She added that the United States “could work with a new government.”
That is a very different proposition.
Clinton was not saying that Washington should respond firmly to a particular future Israeli policy. She was linking America’s posture toward Israel to the choice Israeli voters make at the ballot box.
Vote one way, and Washington could work constructively with your new government.
Vote the other way, and the US should get “very tough.” That sounds uncomfortably close to a warning.
To be clear, Clinton does not make American foreign policy today. She is a former secretary of state and former presidential candidate expressing her own view. But she remains one of the most prominent figures in American public life, particularly in the Democratic Party, and her formulation deserves scrutiny.
The issue is not whether Netanyahu deserves reelection – that is for Israelis to decide on October 27. They may return him to office. They may send him home. I would make the same argument regardless of which Israeli candidate an American political figure was attempting to help or hinder.
The issue is whether a friendly democratic country should be told that the quality of its relationship with Washington may depend upon its voters producing an acceptable result.
Israel is an American ally. It is not an American protectorate.
There is, of course, nothing unusual about governments preferring one foreign leader to another. Presidents and prime ministers are human beings. Some work well together. Others can barely tolerate being in the same room.
Nor is there anything improper about the US opposing an Israeli policy. Allies disagree. Washington has every right to pursue American interests, just as Jerusalem has every right to pursue Israeli ones.
But there is an important line between disagreeing with the government a democracy elects and suggesting that voters themselves should contemplate foreign-policy consequences before choosing it.
Interestingly, US President Donald Trump recently came close to stating the correct principle.
Asked about endorsing someone in Israel’s election, Trump said, “I think it’s most appropriate for me to stay out of the Israeli elections.”
'I may endorse somebody'
He then immediately weakened his own argument by adding, “I may endorse somebody.”
Still, his first instinct was right: stay out.
That principle should apply whether the American politician involved is Trump, Clinton, or anyone else.
Unfortunately, American political involvement in Israeli electoral politics has precedent.
In March 2024, then-Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer used a major Senate speech to call for new Israeli elections, arguing that Netanyahu had “lost his way.” Schumer went further: he said that if Netanyahu’s coalition remained in power after the war, the US should take a more active role in trying to change Israel’s course.
Imagine reversing the countries.
Suppose a senior Israeli politician announced shortly before an American election that Americans ought to replace their president, and warned that if they failed to do so, Israel should reconsider its approach to the United States.
Americans would quite properly tell him to mind his own business. Israelis are entitled to the same respect.
Clinton’s comments were made more troubling by another part of the interview. Referring to reporting that Netanyahu had received a warning before the October 7 massacre, she speculated that perhaps he “wanted to see what they could plan so that he could then come down hard and it would enhance his position.”
She also conceded: “I don’t know what his thinking was.”
There are grave questions about the failures preceding October 7. Israelis have every right to demand answers, accountability, and a full accounting of what went wrong.
But suggesting, without evidence, that an Israeli prime minister might knowingly have allowed Hamas to proceed in order to enhance his political position is an extraordinary thing for a former American secretary of state to say.
Israeli voters can evaluate Netanyahu’s record for themselves.
That brings me back to the question I raised in my previous column.
We seem increasingly comfortable treating American opinion as another participant in Israel’s electoral process. First, an Israeli think tank asks American Jews whom they want to govern Israel. Now a former American secretary of state suggests that if Israelis return the current government to power, America should become “very tough.”
There is an escalation there.
American Jews expressing an opinion is one thing. American politicians expressing a preference is another.
Hinting that Israelis should expect consequences if they vote the wrong way crosses still another line.
None of this requires Americans to remain silent about Israel. The US-Israel relationship is too important for that. Friends should speak honestly, particularly when they disagree.
But friendship also requires respecting democratic decisions one might dislike.
When Israelis enter the voting booth on October 27, they will have plenty to consider: security, the economy, religion and state, the judicial system, the conduct of the war, the failures of October 7, and competing visions of the country’s future.
Whether Hillary Clinton will approve of their choice should not be one of them.
Last week, I argued that American Jews should not become a surrogate Israeli electorate.
Neither should American politicians.
The writer is an attorney and the father of Alisa Flatow, who was murdered in an Iranian-sponsored Palestinian terrorist attack in 1995. He is the author of A Father’s Story: My Fight for Justice Against Iranian Terror (now available in an expanded paperback edition on Amazon.com) and is the chair of the Religious Zionists of America-Mizrachi. A new oleh, he divides his time between Jerusalem and New Jersey.

India seeks fair access to vaccines, drugs made from shared pathogens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:42:49 UTC
12:42:49 KST

NEW DELHI: India has called for a global system that ensures countries sharing pathogens and biological resources during a health emergency also get timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, medicines and technologies developed from them.The demand was made at the UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in New York, where India stressed that the credibility of the WHO Pandemic Agreement would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.Union health secretary Punya Salila Srivastava said countries contributing pathogens should receive the benefits arising from their use, while respecting national sovereignty. She also said ongoing negotiations on the PABS system should not be prejudged and that implementation should take into account national circumstances and capacities.Drawing on its experience during Covid-19, India also called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good, citing its role in disease surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.
India highlighted its contribution during Covid, saying it supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, besides providing medical assistance to more than 150 countries.At the meeting, India also outlined measures to strengthen pandemic preparedness, including expanding laboratory networks, emergency coordination, the health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity.
The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, is aimed at strengthening global preparedness for future pandemics. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for urgent completion of negotiations on the PABS system, saying delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.India stressed that pandemic preparedness must remain rooted in national health systems and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national efforts. It also called for equity and global solidarity to remain central to preparations for future outbreaks.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

A crime scene was established and an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash has commenced, NSW police said. ■

German, Russian foreign ministers hold rare talks amid rising tensions
Russia’s top diplomat Lavrov dismisses German Foreign Minister Wadephul’s call to abandon ‘dangerous path of escalation’ with Europe.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has called on Russia to abandon its “dangerous path of escalation” with Germany, Europe and NATO during talks with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, in New York.
The meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday — the first such talks since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was requested by the German side, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. It was held before Lavrov’s address to world leaders.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US seeks to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks as seven killed in Kyiv
- list 2 of 3Lavrov: Russia’s war in Ukraine will continue ‘through to the end’
- list 3 of 3Russia scales up strikes on Ukraine as largest steelmaker halts operations
In his speech on Saturday, Lavrov told the UNGA that Germany is not only Kyiv’s “main sponsor” but also seeks to be a leading military power in Europe.
“Does Berlin understand what this could lead to? Didn’t they … learn the lessons of World War II?” he asked.
Diplomatic relations between Berlin and Moscow have been frozen since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
They deteriorated further after a drone incident at Leipzig airport in eastern Germany last month, which Berlin blamed on Russia. Moscow has firmly denied involvement and accused Germany of fabricating evidence.
European countries have linked Russia to drone incursions near airports, military bases and critical infrastructure across the continent in the past year.
After his UN speech, Lavrov told a news conference that he had learned nothing new from his German counterpart in talks that Berlin had not already said publicly in its official statements.
“I told him that frankly … you could just have called me and said: ‘Read my statement,'” Lavrov said.
Still, the ministers discussed bilateral ties and the war in Ukraine, officials from both sides said.
Wadephul urged Lavrov to do “everything possible to reach an agreement on grain exports via the Black Sea”, a German delegation source said, as reported by the Reuters news agency.
The meeting comes amid diplomatic efforts to revive Russia and Ukraine’s Black Sea grain and energy exports that have been restricted by attacks on vessels and port infrastructure.
Lavrov told the news conference that Russia had been in talks with India, Egypt and Turkiye about proposals to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
“There is a need for separate discussions with the Ukrainians, and not in the language of requests, but rather demands,” he said, blaming Ukraine for the attacks on vessels.
Kyiv has said it is open to agreements and blames all the fallout from the war on Russia and its invasion.
Wadephul notified his European allies of the meeting afterwards in a message seen by Reuters.
“I used this opportunity to reiterate our position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and to call for an immediate and complete ceasefire, most pressingly with a focus on grain exports, and the energy infrastructure,” he wrote.

Powerful storm batters northeast US, hundreds of flights canceled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:33:00 UTC
12:33:00 KST

US: Powerful storm batters northeast, flights canceled
September 27, 2026
Heavy rain and strong winds pounded the northeastern United States on Saturday, forcing authorities to cancel hundreds of flights and leaving thousands without electricity.
New York, Boston and Philadelphia were in the firing line of the 'Nor'easter,' named after the northeasterly winds.
What is a nor'easter storm?
Nor'easters are large cyclones in the western North Atlantic Ocean, which typically form off the east coast of the US.
They can occur throughout the year but are more frequent between fall and early spring.
Nor'easters are almost always accompanied by heavy rainfall or snow, as well as strong winds.
What have authorities said about the nor'easter?
Residents in low-lying and coastal areas were warned of potential flooding and road closures, as the storm coincides with high tide.
"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the National Weather Service said in its latest forecast.
"Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses," it said.
Some 95,000 people in the states of New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Pennsylvania were facing a power outage as of 3 p.m. on Saturday (1900 GMT), as per poweroutage.com.
Local leaders urge caution
New York Governor Kathy Kochul said the storm was particularly impacting the coastal areas of New York City and Long Island.
"Conditions are extremely dangerous. Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life," she said in a press briefing.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned residents of the strong winds, saying "Don't travel if you don't have to."
Flights, events canceled
Hundreds of flights were cancelled due to the storm, with 253 at Boston's Logan airport alone, according to tracker FlightAware.
Airlines including JetBlue, United and American have issued travel alerts, allowing passengers to change their flights without a fee.
As of 6:13 p.m. local time (2213 GMT), FlightAware said 439 flights involving US airports had been canceled and 2,459 flights were delayed.
Major cultural events have also been called off.
The Global Citizen and All Things Go Festivals in New York, and the Oceans Calling Festival in Maryland were canceled.
"Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we've had to cancel," said organizers of the Global Citizen event in Central Park, which was meant to feature Lenny Kravitz, Lauryn Hill, Alicia Keys and country stars Lainey Wilson and Shaboozey.
British Pop star Ed Sheeran's Weekend concerts near Boston were also canceled due to the storm.
About five inches (13 centimeters) of rain was forecast in areas of Massachusetts, including Boston. That's equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain.

Iran's senior armed forces spokesman, General Abolfazl Shekarchi, said the Strait of Hormuz remains under Iranian control despite American provocations, warning that no vessel can guarantee safe passage without Tehran's approval.
Speaking in a televised interview, Shekarchi reviewed the history of the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, which he said was imposed on Iran under US leadership. He said the war, despite heavy losses, helped build the capabilities of Iran's armed forces from its early days, citing popular mobilization through the Basij as a key achievement.
Shekarchi said Iran's post-revolution military shifted its doctrine from conventional to asymmetric warfare, which he described as relying on lower-cost, simpler but effective equipment to counter the enemy's expensive heavy weaponry.
He said Iran had once been unable to buy basic medical supplies for wounded troops during the Iran-Iraq war, but has since become self-sufficient in producing modern defense equipment.
Shekarchi said Iran's armed forces are now significantly stronger than at the start of previous wars, adding that Iran's missiles and drones have become more advanced and that the country holds surprises for any future act of aggression using new military technology. He said Iran has not attacked the sovereignty of neighboring Muslim countries and that its responses have targeted American interests and facilities within those countries.
He warned neighboring Muslim states to reconsider their positions, saying reliance on the United States would not serve them, and said Iran would not make the slightest retreat in the face of the enemy.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Shekarchi said any vessel attempting passage outside Iran's designated routes would not be secure, and warned Washington against any interference in the strait, saying such a move would be met with force. He said Iran, as a global power, would never allow the United States to regain its former position in the international order, adding that American forces have no path to safety other than withdrawing from West Asia, and that the sooner they leave, the smaller their losses would be.
Referring to US President Donald Trump and Israeli regime’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Shekarchi said Iran would continue to pursue the killers of the country's martyred Leader and the Iranian people even after the end of the war, adding that they would be punished for their actions.

Foreign ministry says UN Resolution 2758 does not define Taiwan as part of China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:29:05 UTC
12:29:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The foreign ministry reiterated Saturday that UN Resolution 2758 neither affirms that Taiwan is part of China nor authorizes Beijing to represent Taiwan within the UN system.
No party should therefore use the resolution to exclude Taiwan from participating in the UN system, the ministry said in a statement. It added that Taiwan and China are not subordinate to each other and that only Taiwan’s democratically elected government can represent its 23 million people in the UN system and other multilateral mechanisms.
The foreign ministry said China has intensified efforts in recent years to distort the resolution, erase Taiwan’s existence, promote the narrative that the “Taiwan issue” is an internal matter, and construct a legal basis for potential aggression intended to alter the regional status quo.
Beijing has also used coercion and inducements to pressure countries in the Global South to align with its position, the ministry said.
It pointed out that the San Francisco Peace Treaty did not transfer Taiwan to China after World War II and that Beijing has never governed Taiwan.
The foreign ministry called on the international community to counter China’s distortion of Resolution 2758 and uphold the rules-based international order. It also urged the UN to remain neutral and refrain from assisting China in suppressing Taiwan’s legitimate right to participate in international affairs.

China sends two pandas to the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:28:53 UTC
12:28:53 KST

Two giant pandas have arrived in the United States from China after a Washington summit between the two countries.
A chartered FedEx cargo plane carrying Ping Ping and Fu Shuang landed in Atlanta on Sunday after leaving Sichuan earlier in the day.
The pandas' transfer had been already agreed but the departure was announced on Thursday during President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.
The black and white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a "panda diplomacy" programme to foster foreign ties.
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will spend the next 10 years at Zoo Atlanta, according to an agreement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association.
They departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on the chartered plane at around 3am, Xinhua News Agency reported.
A farewell ceremony was held for the pair before their journey by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Ping Ping, born in March 2020, was described by Xinhua as a "sturdy yet agile male panda", whereas Fu Shuang, "a chubby, vivacious female", was born in October 2020.
Senior veterinarians and keepers from the United States were accompanying the pandas, monitoring their health in real time and attending to their dietary and other needs during the journey. 
The Chinese side has also arranged for two teams of veterinarians and keepers to travel to Zoo Atlanta in advance to make the necessary preparations.
Upon arrival in Atlanta, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will undergo quarantine and health checks. 
Chinese veterinarians and keepers will stay at the zoo throughout the quarantine period to care for the pandas and help them adapt to their new surroundings through acclimation and behavioural training. (AFP/Xinhua)

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu's UNGA speech pushed Israel's military prowess over its desire for peace - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:55:17 UTC
11:55:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu channeled his inner Golda Meir in his Thursday speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.
He began with a story about visiting his brother Yonatan shortly before the Six-Day War. Netanyahu asked whether Israel would win. His older brother replied that it would because it had no choice.
That theme – Israel fighting because it has no choice – ran throughout Netanyahu’s 40-minute speech.
And what does that have to do with Golda?
One of the stock stories that former United States president Joe Biden recounted innumerable times was about meeting an unfazed Golda shortly before the Yom Kippur War. After hearing her describe the threats facing Israel, Biden asked why she seemed so unconcerned.
Israel, she told him, had a secret weapon: “We have nowhere else to go.”
Both Yonatan and Golda’s statements remain true, and it is worth reminding the world that on occasion, Israel will fight because it must – because it has no other choice and no place else to go.
But that was only one part of Golda. There was another part as well, one Netanyahu did not channel in his speech, but would have done well to.
The Golda of Sparta vs the Golda that humanizes Israel
There is another Golda, the one who famously said: Israel can forgive the Arabs for killing its sons but can never forgive them for forcing it to kill theirs.
Whether one agrees is immaterial. This line presents an empathetic Israel, one that regrets the destruction it must inflict on those seeking its elimination. It humanizes Israel.
Yet the Golda that Netanyahu opted to channel was the Golda of Sparta.
The Golda that he left out was the Golda of Athens, the one who expended extensive effort in diplomacy.
Right now, it is the Spartan image of Israel that is losing support around the world. The UN provided Netanyahu with a tremendous opportunity to highlight the country’s Athenian side as well.
That doesn’t mean downplaying Israel’s need to fight and win or ignoring the world’s blind hatred and staggering hypocrisy – two elements that dominated Netanyahu’s speech.
It means complementing that message with some vision of the better future Israel wants.
That future may not arrive tomorrow, next year, or even in the next generation. But Israel must offer some horizon – explaining not only what it is fighting against but what it is fighting for.
It is clear why Netanyahu showcased the Israel of Sparta. His primary audience was an Israeli public tired of being the world’s punching bag and of being libeled as child killers and perpetrators of genocide.
Netanyahu pushed back, calling out some of the most egregious offenders by name: Qatar, French President Emmanuel Macron, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
He took them on with characteristic confidence and rhetorical force. For many Israelis, that was satisfying.
But Israelis were not the only audience listening.
Israel losing American public support
Israel has precipitously lost public support in the US. Powerful cultural, demographic, and political forces in America are at work that Israel cannot change.
What it can change, however, is the perception that it is merely a modern-day Sparta.
Israel can demonstrate that its softer side exists and has always longed for peace – the Israel not jubilant over its constant need to fight and defend itself but genuinely anguished by it.
Like previous Netanyahu UN speeches, this one, too, had props. He held up a Starlink satellite internet dish to illustrate Iran’s repression, as well as a beeper similar to those that exploded in the possession of Hezbollah terrorists in 2024.
The beeper plays well in Israel. It elicits pride in the country’s ingenuity, daring, and ability to strike its enemies in ways they never anticipated.
But is that the only image Israel wants the American public to carry away?
Might Netanyahu not have found room for another prop, image, or passage that could begin rebranding Israel not only as a formidable war machine – which it must be to survive – but also as a country dedicated to peace?
Israel must be capable of being Sparta. The world it lives in has given it little choice. But Israel is not only Sparta, and it does itself no favors by presenting itself solely that way.
Netanyahu’s speech explained forcefully why Israel must fight. What it failed to convey – and what Israel must begin conveying – was the future it hopes that this fighting will ultimately make possible.

Asian Games | Swimming review: Six days of records, breakthroughs and a new generation at Aichi-Nagoya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:50:05 CST
11:50:05 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Six days of racing, a world record, a historic seven-gold haul and a wave of teenage talents made swimming one of the defining stories of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
China topped the swimming medal table with a record 30 gold medals and 54 medals overall, surpassing the 28 golds it won in Hangzhou three years ago. Japan finished with seven golds and 37 medals.
The headline achievement came from 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo, who completed a remarkable campaign by winning the men's 400m freestyle on Friday in an Asian Games record time of three minutes 41.28 seconds.
Zhang became the first swimmer in Asian Games history to win seven titles at a single edition, surpassing the previous mark of six shared by Japan's Rikako Ikee and China's Zhang Yufei. His haul included four individual freestyle titles, from the 200m to the 1,500m, as well as three relay golds.
He also helped China set Asian records in the men's 4x100m and 4x200m freestyle relays.
"I feel much calmer than I had imagined," Zhang said after his seventh title. "Of course, I'm very happy to win these seven gold medals, and I will turn them into greater motivation going forward."
His performance was part of a broader change of the guard in Chinese swimming.
The most striking example was 13-year-old Yu Zidi, who made a spectacular Asian Games debut with three gold medals. She set an Asian record of 2:06.10 in the women's 200m individual medley, the second-fastest time in history behind only Summer McIntosh's world record of 2:05.70. Yu also set Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley.
"I don't see myself as a genius. What I've achieved has come from putting in the work, day after day," Yu said.
Meanwhile, established names including Qin Haiyang, Xu Jiayu, Pan Zhanle, Li Bingjie and Zhang Yufei continued to deliver gold medals.
Li, who won five golds at the Games, including the women's 400m and 800m freestyle, described the campaign as a valuable test after a difficult period.
"I think my potential lies in my ability to finish strongly," she said, adding that she had gradually found a better training approach and mindset after a period of trial and error.
Zhang Yufei, meanwhile, successfully defended her women's 50m butterfly title in 25.41 seconds. The victory prompted an emotional reaction from the veteran, who wiped away tears on the podium.
"Winning has become quite common for me, so now I'm more focused on the times and on pushing myself to achieve better results," Zhang said.
The six-day competition also produced one of the most spectacular swims in recent Asian Games history.
On Thursday, 17-year-old Japanese swimmer Shin Ohashi clocked 2:04.83 to win the men's 200m breaststroke, becoming the first man to break the 2:05 barrier and lowering the world record previously held by China's Qin Haiyang.
He said he had initially targeted a time in the 2:03.00 range, but after producing 2:04.83, he was already looking further ahead. His next target is the 2027 World Championships, where he hopes to win gold before turning his attention to the Olympics.
"I hope I can swim 2:02.00, or even 2:01.00 in the future," he said, who also shared gold with China's Dong Zhihao in the 100m breaststroke and collected silver in two medley relays.
Qin, who had set the previous world record at the 2023 World Aquatics Championships in Fukuoka, said Ohashi's breakthrough reflected the growing competitiveness of the event.
"The event is becoming increasingly competitive, with a growing diversity of techniques and styles among the world's top swimmers," Qin said.
Ohashi's world record and Zhang's seven-gold feat highlighted a meet in which established records repeatedly came under threat. Chinese swimmers produced Asian or Games records across individual and relay events, while Japan's Yumeki Kojima, also 17, set two world junior records and won the men's 400m individual medley.
Beyond the major swimming powers, Aichi-Nagoya also brought historic firsts for several teams.
Bahrain's Mikhail Arkhangelskiy won the men's 50m butterfly in 22.91 seconds, tying the Asian record and giving Bahrain its first-ever Asian Games swimming medal.
"I'm really proud and happy that Bahrain gave me the chance," Arkhangelskiy said. He added that he will now turn his attention to the World Championships in Budapest, hoping to continue improving.
Chinese Taipei secured its first men's swimming gold at the Asian Games when Wang Kuan-hung won the men's 200m butterfly in 1:55.05. The result improved on his silver at the Hangzhou Games.
Kyrgyzstan also celebrated a first, with Denis Petrashov taking silver in the men's 200m breaststroke, marking the country's first-ever swimming medal at an Asian Games.
For China, the six-day campaign was about both achievement and transition. As Zhang Zhanshuo put it after his historic week, the Asian Games is not his ultimate goal. "I still need to settle down and face the gaps between myself and the world's best."
The world record is already in his sights. "Everything is possible. I will stay humble and keep pushing forward," he said. "I'm still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best. I will turn these gold medals into greater motivation." ■

These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:49:07 UTC
11:49:07 KST

These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
- Date:
- September 26, 2026
- Source:
- Stockholm University
- Summary:
- Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.
- Share:
When archaeologists uncover adults and children buried together in medieval graves, a natural assumption is that they belonged to the same family. New research from Stockholm University, published in Science Advances, suggests that was often not the case.
Scientists analyzed DNA from 142 people who lived during the late Viking Age and Middle Ages. The group included more than 60 children and adolescents recovered from multiple graves at Sigtuna, near Stockholm, Västerhus in Jämtland, and Fjälkinge in Skåne.
Shared Graves Were Often Not Family Graves
The genetic evidence revealed that close biological relatives were surprisingly uncommon among people placed in the same grave. This was true even in cemeteries where researchers found many biological family connections among the wider population.
"We often assume that adults and children sharing a grave were parents and children or other close family members. In most cases, that was not what we found," says Maja Krzewińska, Centre for Palaeogenetics, Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University, lead author of the study.
The findings indicate that decisions about who was buried together were often shaped by more than close biological relationships. Social, religious, or other community factors may also have played an important role.
"Archaeologists have debated the relationships between people buried together in this type of grave for a long time. Ancient DNA has finally given us the tool we have been waiting for to test these interpretations directly," says Anna Kjellström, researcher at the Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University.
Children Followed Adult Burial Customs
The DNA analysis also provided new clues about childhood in early Christian Scandinavia. Ancient DNA allowed researchers to determine the biological sex of children whose remains were too young for sex to be identified reliably from their bones.
The burial patterns showed that boys and girls often followed the same cemetery customs as adult men and women. At Västerhus, for instance, men and women were generally buried on different sides of the churchyard. Boys and girls were placed according to that same pattern.
The researchers say this suggests that gender identity was recognized from an early stage of life and was reflected in burial practices.
"The children were not treated as a separate category. In death, they appear to have been treated according to the same social and religious principles as adult men and women," says Anders Götherström, Professor of Molecular Archaeology, Centre for Palaeogenetics, Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University.
DNA Reconstructs One Medieval Family
Among the people buried at Västerhus, researchers also reconstructed the story of an especially notable family.
A woman identified as Lady 56 was genetically connected to several other people buried in the churchyard. DNA linked her to her parents, her brother, and two daughters. But evidence from her grave suggests that her life may have stretched far beyond the local community in Jämtland.
Lady 56 was buried with a scallop shell, an unusual object to find in a medieval Scandinavian grave. The shell was also a widely recognized symbol associated with pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain.
Its presence suggests that Lady 56 may have completed one of medieval Europe's most famous pilgrimages, traveling thousands of kilometers across the continent to the western edge of Christian Europe before eventually returning home.
Lady 56 died before the age of 30. Her parents, brother, and daughters were also buried in different parts of the same cemetery in Jämtland.
Ancient DNA Opens a Window Into Medieval Society
Together, the findings show how archaeogenetics can reveal far more than biological family relationships. By combining ancient DNA with archaeological evidence, researchers can begin to reconstruct how medieval communities were organized, how children were treated, how religious customs shaped burial practices, and how people related to one another in both life and death.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Stockholm University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maja Krzewińska, Anna Kjellström, Reyhan Yaka, Ricardo Rodríguez-Varela, Zoé Pochon, Vendela Kempe Lagerholm, Charlotte Hedenstierna-Jonson, Torun Zachrisson, Natalija Kashuba, Verónica Sobrado, Thijessen Naidoo, Kıvılcım Başak Vural, Mattias Jakobsson, Gülşah Merve Kılınç, Jan Storå, Anders Götherström. Equal in death: Ancient genomic analysis of children’s early Christian burials. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (28) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb8588

German foreign minister sees no readiness for peace during first meeting with Russian counterpart since 2022
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said that during a meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov, he saw no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to refrain from further escalation.
Source: Deutsche Welle, citing Wadephul speaking on German TV channel ZDF; Tagesschau
Details: The officials met on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. Wadephul said he had used the conversation to urge Russia to abandon its path of escalation.
He said he had made it clear to the Russian delegation that actions such as the attempted sabotage involving drones at Leipzig/Halle Airport were unacceptable.
Wadephul said he had made it clear to Lavrov that "a line had been crossed, we expect this not to happen again, and we are ready to respond at any time".
Meanwhile, Wadephul stressed that he had not conducted any negotiations with Lavrov concerning Ukraine's future. The minister emphasised that such negotiations were a matter solely for the Ukrainians themselves.
Quote from Wadephul: "There are indeed fundamental differences between the positions of our governments, and these also need to be discussed. During the Cold War, exchanges of views and contacts between the two sides never ceased. And I thought it was right, particularly now, to try to find an initial opportunity for such dialogue."
Details: The German foreign minister warned the Russian representative that Berlin would continue its comprehensive support for Ukraine and maintain economic pressure on Russia.
"This support is absolutely unwavering, and Russia must now come to the negotiating table. There is no justification whatsoever for this war, which is claiming countless lives, including Russian lives, but above all those of Ukrainian civilians," Wadephul said.
However, the minister acknowledged that he had seen no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to heed his call to begin negotiations on ending the war.
"To all those who keep saying that Germany needs to negotiate, that Germany needs to talk to Russia, I say now: we are doing so. And unfortunately, Russia is currently showing no willingness to adopt a constructive negotiating position," the foreign minister said.
According to Russian state propaganda agency TASS, the meeting lasted "just over 20 minutes" and covered "bilateral relations and the situation surrounding Ukraine". Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting had taken place at the request of the German side.
The foreign ministers of Germany and Russia last met in Moscow on 18 January 2022. At the time, Annalena Baerbock travelled to the Russian capital amid Russia's rapid military build-up near Ukraine's borders and warnings from Western intelligence agencies that Moscow was preparing for a full-scale invasion.
Background:
- The resumption of diplomatic contacts at this level was preceded by a series of Russian nuclear threats against European countries.
- On 10 September, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened to wipe Lithuania "off the map" if nuclear weapons were deployed on its territory, and claimed that its NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defence.
- On 11 September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius, saying that if nuclear weapons were deployed in Lithuania, the country would come under the sights of Russian nuclear weapons.
- On 21 September, it was reported that intelligence officials from three EU countries believed Moscow was planning to step up provocations against NATO in the coming months.
- On 25 September, Russian state news agency RIA Novosti published a column headlined "Russia is in for another SVO. It will be very short", which threatened Lithuania with a nuclear strike. The article was subsequently deleted.
- On the same day, political scientist Sergei Karaganov, an adviser to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, called on television for preparations to use weapons of mass destruction.
- "Europe is the source of humanity's greatest troubles and Russia's greatest troubles. A nuclear war in Europe can easily be won... We would rather it did not come to that. But we must be prepared for it, and they must know that," Karaganov said.

Northern Ireland court allows Protestant march in Catholic area
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:42:17 UTC
11:42:17 KST

Protesters block Orange Order from marching through Catholic area in Northern Ireland
PORTADOWN, Northern Ireland, Sept 27 - Around 2,000 protesters blocked a Protestant parade from marching through the Catholic area of a Northern Irish town on Sunday, creating a standoff with both sides declining to disperse and police in between them keeping their distance.
The attempt to hold the parade through the town of Portadown followed the lifting of an almost 30-year ban on the contentious route, but the marchers were halted by crowds including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill of Irish nationalists Sinn Fein.
The protesters, also including Sinn Fein leader, Mary Lou McDonald, gathered in the rain on the Garvaghy Road overnight after Belfast's High Court in a late-night sitting dismissed an application by residents to stop the parade.
CALLS FOR CALM
Annual attempts by the Protestant Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region before the route was banned in 1998, the same year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended the three decades of violence known as the "Troubles".
"This is madness," McDonald told reporters on the road, a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant town of Portadown. "This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable."
The leaders of Ireland and Britain, who are co-guarantors of the peace accord, called for calm. "There have been big gains made in Northern Ireland and we don't want to see things go backwards," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC.
Irish premier Micheal Martin shared Burnham's concern but also called the ruling by Northern Ireland's Parades Commission to allow the parade "incomprehensible" and "wrong."
The commission, which regulates marches in the British-run region, on Friday permitted a smaller-than-usual 35 people to take part in the march between 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) and 9:30 a.m.
It had initially continued the ban for this year's parade, but that decision was quashed by the High Court in August over a procedural error.
ORANGE SASHES AND BOWLER HATS
A small group of Orange Order members wearing traditional silk orange sashes and black bowler hats gathered at another part of the town but the march did not start.
A senior member told the BBC they would wait for police to tell them the route was ready.
Police vans parked near the Garvaghy Road and flanked by officers in riot gear played out warnings that anyone taking part in the protest was committing a criminal offence.
The Drumcree dispute exploded in the mid-1990s when, in the wake of ceasefires by Northern Ireland's main guerrilla groups, it became a symbol of the wider dispute between mainly Catholic nationalists, who consider themselves Irish, and Protestants loyal to Britain.
The Orangemen, who take their name from Protestant King William of Orange who defeated deposed Catholic King James II at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, say their parades are part of their Protestant cultural tradition.
Whilst most of the parades that take place across Northern Ireland each year are uncontroversial, nationalists say parades passing through Catholic areas are an offensive display of triumphalism designed to intimidate them.
PEACE PROCESS BROUGHT 'INTO QUESTION'
McDonald and O'Neill called on the British government and police to intervene. Britain's minister for the region, Chris Bryant, has the power to revoke the Parades Commission's ruling at the request of Northern Ireland's police.
Bryant, who was returning to Belfast from his Labour party's conference in Liverpool to meet political leaders, told the BBC he had not received any request from police following several conversations with its chief constable.
O'Neill, whose party shares power with the largest pro-British party in a devolved administration established as a key part of the 1998 peace deal, warned that the dispute brought into question how the peace process works.
Gavin Robinson, leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, told a news conference: "It is shameful ... that we see a first minister, a collection of ministers who are participating in an unlawful protest, who are blocking the road and who are giving two fingers to the police, the courts and the rule of law." US official gives ultimatum to nations in Middle East: Stop trade with Iran, or US will cut ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:36:59 UTC
11:36:59 KST

A top US Treasury Department official, Jonathan Burke, visited countries across the Middle East, warning them that continuing trade with Iran would completely shut them out of trading with the US, according to a Friday Wall Street Journal report.
"You either trade with Washington, or with Iran," he told Iran's trade partners across the Middle East and Europe, according to the WSJ report.
Since the introduction of Operation Economic Outcast in August, the US has imposed significant sanctions on Iran. Regional partners, including Iraq, stopped Iranian flights to and from their countries in response to the US threatening to sanction any airport that services Iranian carriers.
The US campaign against Iran is especially effective due to the growing distrust between the Islamic Republic and the Gulf Arab states.
“We’re seeing a new urgency from our partners,” Burke told the WSJ. “They’re taking it very seriously.”
Burke visited Oman first, as it had often served as an intermediary between Tehran and the West. His visit showed officials that the US was serious about enforcing sanctions against Iran, and that refusing to cooperate could have economic consequences, Middle Eastern officials told the WSJ.
In total, Burke visited over 50 countries across the Middle East and Europe, warning them to cease relationships with Iran.
Flights from Iran to China and Russia remain open; however, within those countries, Iran-affiliated businesses and agents still face sanctions from the US.
Pezeshkian acknowledges impact of US sanctions
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, Iranian President Mahsoud Pezeshkian acknowledged the significant impact that US sanctions were having on Iran; however, he refused to accept defeat and turned the conflict around on US President Donald Trump, insisting that Iran was a victim of US terrorism.
“The US president described us as terrorists,” he said. “We have been the victims of terrorism.”
He went on to describe Trump as a "bully." In an interview with Qatari state-funded broadcaster Al Jazeera on Saturday night, Pezeshkian added, "We will die, but we will not bow our heads."
"America and Israel think they can overthrow us with these pressures, but we will overcome all problems with strength," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera.
Iran's regional relations collapse under US threats
Over the last 50 years, Iran has faced increasing sanctions from the US; however, vital regional banking and trade relations have persevered.
The war this year has weakened Gulf ties as Iran targeted energy infrastructure in other countries in the region, attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which is the gateway for approximately one-fifth of the world's oil, and allowed the Iran-linked Houthi militia to do the same to the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea's Hormuz equivalent.
Faced with the risk of the US sanctioning them for maintaining connections with Tehran, many of Iran's trade partners have cut ties.
“Iran has been a problem for 50 years, and we’ve kind of reached our peak at tolerating this problem,” Burke told the WSJ.
