Russian-born businessman elected as new world chess chief
Russian-born businessman Timur Turlov has been elected president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE). The vote by representatives of 196 nations took place on Saturday after the previous FIDE chief, Russian national Arkady Dvorkovich, resigned under EU pressure.
Turlov led in the first round with 96 votes as he competed against two Germans, Wadim Rosenstein and Jan Henric Buettner, who trailed with 76 and 20 votes respectively. He won the second round with 110 votes.
Dvorkovich congratulated his successor, saying the new chief “has already done a great deal for chess, and… will do even more now as FIDE president.” He added that Turlov’s victory shows that he had “significant backing” within the international chess community.
Turlov called it “a great responsibility and a vote for a better future of our sport.”
Today is a victory for chess - for every player, every federation and everyone who believes in the potential of our game!
We are all one family and we will continue working as one. This is a great responsibility and a vote for a better future of our sport.
Now is the time to… pic.twitter.com/ieF9HmGQf5
Born in Moscow in 1987, Turlov lived in Russia until the early 2010s, when he moved to Kazakhstan. He is the founder of the Freedom Finance investment company, which was established in 2008 to provide retail investors with access to US stock exchanges and has since expanded to 22 countries worldwide.
Turlov became the head of the Central Asian nation’s chess federation in 2023, a year after giving up his Russian and Saint Kitts and Nevis passports in favor of Kazakhstani citizenship. He is also the founding president of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF), established in September 2024.
The vote comes amid tensions within FIDE over Western pressure on Russian sports. In July, the EU put Dvorkovich, a Russian economist and former deputy prime minister who had led FIDE since 2018, on its sanctions list over alleged “public support” for Russia’s military operation against Kiev. Dvorkovich blasted Brussels’ move as “unlawful and unfair” and vowed to challenge the sanctions.
FIDE is registered in Switzerland, where sanctioned individuals cannot legally act as the “owner, holder or controller” of an organization’s assets, meaning its bank accounts, sponsorships, and contracts could have become compliance issues had Dvorkovich remained in office.
Russian Chess Federation President Andrey Filatov earlier suggested that Russian Grandmaster Sergey Karyakin could seek the post after Dvorkovich. However, Karyakin, a native of Simferopol and now a senator representing Crimea, is also under EU sanctions.
In August, FIDE also barred Russian teams from returning to the Chess Olympiad, prompting prominent names in Russian chess to accuse its leadership of Russophobia.
“There are… people who prioritize personal interests, and they currently predominate on the Council. This time, they prevailed,” Russian Chess Federation Executive Director Aleksandr Tkachev said at the time.
Moscow has condemned the sanctions imposed on Russian athletes by international sporting bodies as politically motivated. President Vladimir Putin has argued that comparable measures have not been applied to athletes from other countries involved in conflicts.

Otherwise, CNN’s slot will be left unfilled, and Mr. Trump will not receive major network coverage," the NYT noted.
On September 18, Trump announced that he was revoking White House access for journalists from CNN, MSNBC, and Politico for spreading false information about his administration. He added that the list of banned media outlets could be expanded but acknowledged the possibility of reversing his decision. Correspondents and technical staff from these outlets lost access to the US president's residence on September 19.
Later, a court in the District of Columbia overturned Trump's decision. However, the Secret Service, which is responsible for the security of top officials, still barred journalists from CNN, MSNBC, and Politico from entering the White House. The Washington administration agreed to grant access only after representatives from these media outlets returned to court.

Scientists say house cats could help unlock better cancer treatments for humans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:01:42 UTC
11:01:42 KST

Scientists say house cats could help unlock better cancer treatments for humans
A massive genetic study of cat tumors reveals striking similarities to human cancer and could open new paths to treatment for both species.
- Date:
- September 26, 2026
- Source:
- University of Guelph
- Summary:
- Scientists have mapped the genetics of cat cancer on an unprecedented scale and found surprising similarities with tumors in humans. The findings could help bring precision cancer treatments to cats while also revealing new clues about how human cancers develop and respond to drugs.
- Share:
Scientists have taken a major step toward understanding cancer in cats, opening what researchers once described as a genetic "black box."
In a large international study published in Science, researchers genetically analyzed cat cancers on a scale that had not been attempted before. The work could improve cancer care for cats while also helping scientists better understand how some cancers develop in humans and other animals.
The researchers also created a freely available resource that other scientists can use to study the genetics of feline cancer.
Cancer is one of the leading causes of illness and death in cats, yet scientists have historically known far less about the genetic changes behind feline tumors than they do about cancers in humans or dogs.
Dr. Geoffrey Wood, a University of Guelph pathobiology professor and co-senior author of the study, said that gap has now begun to close.
"Despite domestic cats being common pets, there was very little known about the genetics of cancer in these animals," Wood says, "until now."
Cat and Human Cancers Share Key Genetic Changes
Researchers examined tumor samples from almost 500 domestic cats in five countries, searching for mutations and other genetic changes that help cancers form and grow.
Many cancers are driven by changes in certain genes that normally help control how cells grow, divide, repair damage, or die. When these genes are altered, cells can begin multiplying uncontrollably. Scientists often refer to genes that contribute directly to tumor growth as cancer driver genes.
The team found that many of the driver genes involved in cat cancers were also familiar from human and dog cancers.
One of the clearest examples appeared in aggressive mammary cancers, which arise in breast tissue.
The most common driver gene found in cat mammary tumors was FBXW7. More than 50 percent of the tumors examined carried a mutation in this gene.
FBXW7 normally helps regulate proteins involved in cell growth and division. When the gene is damaged, some of those growth promoting proteins can accumulate, potentially helping cancer cells survive and spread.
In humans, mutations in the FBXW7 gene in breast cancer are associated with worse prognosis - paralleling the change seen in cats.
Researchers also identified similarities between cat and human cancers affecting the blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal system and central nervous system.
Shared Environments May Offer Cancer Clues
The similarities may be especially useful because domestic cats often live in the same environments as people.
Cats can encounter some of the same environmental factors as their owners, including household chemicals, air pollutants, smoke and other exposures that may influence cancer risk. Studying naturally occurring cancer in pets could therefore help researchers investigate how genetics and the surrounding environment interact.
"This study can help us understand more about why cancer develops in cats and humans, how the world around us influences cancer risk, and possibly find new ways to prevent and treat it," says Wood.
The genetic findings could also have implications for treatment.
Researchers found that certain chemotherapy drugs were more effective against cat mammary tumors carrying the mutated FBXW7 gene.
The result was observed only in tissue samples, so it does not yet show that the same approach will work in living cats or people. Still, the finding suggests that genetic information could eventually help doctors and veterinarians identify treatments that work better for particular tumors.
This type of approach is known as precision oncology. Instead of treating every cancer of the same general type in exactly the same way, precision oncology uses the molecular and genetic features of an individual tumor to help guide therapy.
"Having access to such a large set of donated tissues allowed us to assess drug responses across tumor types," says Dr. Sven Rottenberg, co-senior author at the University of Bern, "in a way that hasn't been possible at this scale before."
Bailey Francis, co-first author at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, said the findings could also have implications for dogs.
"When knowledge and data flows between different disciplines, we can all benefit."
Using Cat Cancer Research to Help Pets and People
The project brought together researchers from the Wellcome Sanger Institute, U of G's Ontario Veterinary College, the University of Bern and other institutions.
Rather than collecting all new samples, the team sequenced DNA from tissues that veterinarians had already obtained for diagnostic purposes.
That allowed scientists to study naturally occurring cancers from a large number of cats and compare the genetic patterns among different tumor types.
The findings also support a broader research strategy known as One Medicine.
The One Medicine approach emphasizes that human and veterinary medicine can inform one another. Cancer treatments developed for humans could potentially be evaluated in cats with naturally occurring tumors, while discoveries made during feline cancer studies and clinical trials could provide clues that help shape future human research.
That two way exchange is especially valuable because pets naturally develop many of the same diseases as people while sharing many aspects of the same environment.
Researchers hope the new genetic database will ultimately help bring more personalized cancer care to cats.
Dr. Louise Van Der Weyden, senior author at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, said the study provides a foundation for the next stage of feline cancer research.
"We can now begin to take the next steps forwards towards precision feline oncology, to catch up with the diagnostic and therapeutic options that are available for dogs with cancer, and ultimately one day, humans."
The research was funded in part by EveryCat Health Foundation, the CVS Group, Wellcome, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the Swiss National Science Foundation.

Since arriving in Chongqing in 2019 to take up a teaching post, U.S. scholar Francis Stonier has become a well-known local figure. Over the past few years, he has devoted himself to promoting STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics) interdisciplinary education and free science outreach for rural school students.
Currently a professor at Southwest University, Stonier teaches academic writing to international students. Beyond his university lectures, Stonier brings science to life for primary and secondary school students. He simplifies complex concepts, tailoring them for young children.
To make science more accessible, Stonier has developed personalized STEAM curricula. Using 3D printing and LEGO bricks, he transforms complex academic concepts into hands-on experiments, encouraging students to explore science through creation and teamwork. In a creative lesson at Bashu Primary School in Chongqing, Stonier used everyday items to simulate birds' foraging behaviors, helping kids understand natural science through play.

Stonier's grassroots teaching experience has also reshaped his understanding of education. He speaks highly of Chinese educators' openness to practical and innovative teaching approaches.
Stonier has witnessed Chongqing's development. He has fully immersed himself in local life. Moved by the warmth of the Chongqing people, and the city's unique charm and diverse cuisine, Stonier regards Chongqing as his second hometown, praising its harmonious balance of urban convenience and natural scenery. The wall needs no words: A deaf climber's ascent
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
10:01:15 CST
11:01:15 KST

by sportswriters Dong Yixing and Shen Nan
BEIJING, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- He Mingliang hangs on the outdoor climbing wall, more than 10 meters above the ground. His right hand grips a small orange hold. His taped left leg, amputated below the knee, presses against the overhanging surface. Above him, a pale blue sky stretches wide.
Mingliang cannot hear. He has never learned to speak. He was six when he lost his leg.
Then his foot slips. He drops half a meter before his arms lock, swinging him back toward the wall. He dangles there, rotating slowly, facing the surface. A low sound rises from his throat, not language, just breath and effort.
Watching from below, Wang Junjian, head coach of Zhejiang's provincial para-climbing team, raises his thumb. On the wall, the two rely largely on gestures.
"Sometimes he glances at me, but I can't precisely convey what I want him to do through sound," Wang said.
For most of Mingliang's life, his older brother was his main link to the people around him.
THE BOY IN THE ROOM
Mingliang was born in 1999 in a rural village in Guizhou Province, southwest China. His mother is deaf and unable to speak. His father, a farmer with little education, struggled to make ends meet. His older brother, He Mingfeng, was born just one year earlier.
When Mingliang was around six, the brothers were playing by the road. Mingfeng was on the other side when he saw a truck approaching and shouted for his brother to stop.
"He couldn't hear me," Mingfeng recalled. "He stepped out. The truck was too fast. It couldn't brake in time. His foot was crushed."
With no money for proper medical care, Mingliang's leg was beyond saving.
For years afterward, he barely left the house.
"He felt different from everyone else," Mingfeng said. "He didn't want to follow us anymore. He locked himself in the room and watched TV all day."
The family had one television. Mingliang watched whatever was on, but basketball captured him.
"He watched Kobe Bryant, watched the NBA," Mingfeng said. "He fell in love with it, and he started training himself. He learned the moves - dribbling, crossover, how to jump, how to drive. All by himself. Watching and figuring it out."
He taught himself to balance and play basketball on one leg, practicing alone on the concrete court outside the family home.
"Other kids wouldn't play with him," Mingfeng said. "They were afraid of hurting him. So he just practiced by himself."
At 12 or 13, Mingliang began pushing back against his isolation.
"He cried and expressed, 'You won't let me do this, won't let me do that - what am I supposed to do?'" Mingfeng recalled. "After that, we stopped interfering."
THE BROTHER WHO STAYED
Mingfeng left home at 13 and a half to work. He met his wife Deng Bing in Shanghai in 2015, and they later settled in Shaoxing, Zhejiang Province, where they had a daughter.
In 2023, Mingfeng brought his younger brother to Shaoxing. Their parents were getting older, and Mingliang had begged to come.
"He wanted to help me, to work," Mingfeng said. But communicating with potential employers proved difficult, and Mingliang was unable to find work.
Instead, he helped take care of his niece, picking her up from school and cooking for her when his brother and sister-in-law were at work.
"He's very good to her," Deng said. "He cooks noodles for her in the morning. He buys her snacks."
In one video on Mingliang's social media, he plays basketball on an outdoor court in the rain. He drives to the basket, slips and lands flat on his back. The camera shakes as his niece, who is filming, laughs.
Mingliang lies there for a second. Then he starts laughing too.
The two brothers developed a private language over years of living together. Mingliang never learned formal sign language, so they rely on their own system of gestures and expressions.
"We communicate with our eyes, pointing, describing things," Mingfeng said. "Mostly it comes from life. We've been together so long, there's a kind of tacit understanding."
When Mingliang wants to communicate, his face transforms. His eyes widen, his mouth shapes exaggerated syllables and his hands move rapidly through the air.
But the brothers' language has limits. Mingliang knows only a few dozen Chinese characters. His brother has tried to teach him more, without much success.
"I dream about it," Mingfeng said. "I can't sleep. It's like an unsolvable problem. But there's no other way. We just take it one step at a time."
THE VIRAL MOMENT
In Shaoxing, basketball remained Mingliang's main pursuit. He would ride his electric bike to outdoor courts and practice alone for hours.
In September 2024, he started posting videos of himself playing on Douyin, China's version of TikTok. They attracted little attention until November, when former Chinese Basketball Association player Han Delong saw one.
"I was scrolling at night, and suddenly I saw this one-legged kid hopping to shoot," Han said. "I was shocked. I thought, is that even possible? I checked the location and drove there the next day."
Han, who had left professional basketball in 2022 and was producing a social media series called "Challenge 100 Strangers to Play Basketball," filmed an 11-minute one-on-one game with Mingliang.
The video received more than 50 million views in 10 days and drew 41,000 comments.
Han tried playing on one leg.
"After one minute, my leg and hip were sore. After 40 minutes, I asked for a break," he said. "But he kept dribbling and shooting, no sign of fatigue. He gestured for me to feel his thigh muscle. It was like stone."
The attention led to a one-day contract. CBA club Zhejiang Lions signed Mingliang on December 2, 2024, giving him a custom No. 98 jersey and a place in the locker room alongside national team players including Hu Jinqiu and Sun Minghui.
Before the game, Zhejiang player Joshua Carlton lifted Mingliang toward the basket so he could dunk for the first time.
"He was not nervous at all," Mingfeng said. "Standing there, my hands were sweating, I was so nervous. But he looked like he had done it a thousand times."
THE WHEELCHAIR THAT DIDN'T WORK
The club's donation paid for a custom prosthetic and helped open another door: a wheelchair basketball tryout in Hangzhou in March 2025.
"We thought he'd get selected," Mingfeng said.
But wheelchair basketball presented a problem. Players relied heavily on verbal communication.
"He can't hear the coach, can't hear his teammates," Mingfeng said. "They call out to each other on the court. He can't respond. He can't even hear his name."
When Mingfeng visited, he found his brother's palms covered in blisters from pushing the wheelchair.
"They were bleeding," he said. "I asked if he wanted to rest. He refused. He wanted to do everything the others did."
At the end of the tryout, the coach pulled Mingfeng aside and suggested that Mingliang try an individual sport instead.
"He looked so helpless," Mingfeng said. "He wanted to try, but he couldn't."
As they were leaving Hangzhou, another opportunity emerged. The provincial disabled persons' federation had received word about a new sport: para climbing. Mingliang's upper-body strength and physical conditioning made him a candidate.
"I asked him if he wanted to try," Mingfeng said. "He said yes. So I agreed."
THE WALL
In April 2025, Mingliang attended a national para-climbing training camp in Beijing. It was his first extended period away from his family.
"I was worried he wouldn't adapt, that he couldn't communicate with the team," Mingfeng said. "But my worries were unnecessary. He got along with everyone."
With climbing newly added to the Paralympic program for Los Angeles 2028, China was beginning to develop its para-climbing program. The camp, run with international experts, was part of an effort to build a national team.
Wang met Mingliang at the provincial disabled persons' federation before the camp.
"We couldn't communicate, but his spirit was good," Wang said.
Videos of Mingliang playing basketball and climbing on a playground structure showed his strength and coordination.
"His athletic foundation was good, his upper-body strength was good," Wang said. "I thought he had potential."
Mingliang is just over 1.6 meters tall, with a neat buzz cut and heavily muscled shoulders and arms after years of relying on them to compensate for his missing lower leg. His right leg, which has carried his full weight for two decades, is thick and powerful.
But conventional coaching methods were of limited use.
"He has one leg, and he has a hearing impairment," Wang said. "In this category, he's an individual case."
The coaches adapted.
Assistant coach Wu Zhenchen demonstrated movements repeatedly, sometimes using his own knee to simulate how Mingliang could use his residual limb against the wall.
"With other athletes, I can just say, 'Put your foot here, rotate your hip,'" Wu said. "With him, I have to do it once, twice, three times. I have to find a similar situation on the ground and simulate it."
Wu learned a few signs online, and the pair developed their own shorthand: a tap on the shoulder for "rest," pointing at the clock for "time," and another gesture for "warm up."
"It's self-created," Wu said. "We've agreed on it without saying anything."
What impressed the coaches was how quickly Mingliang absorbed what he could see.
International route setter Cai Luyuan recalled explaining whether to step inside or outside a triangular position.
"He came up and pointed, showing he understood," Cai said. "I think he was the only one who remembered."
Wang noticed the same thing.
"I can see he's thinking," Wang said. "There are movements he's never done, but he thinks about them, and then he can do them. He gets very excited."
THE FIRST TITLE
In September 2025, Mingliang competed in the first National Para-Climbing Championships in Jilin Province. Although he had first tried the sport several months earlier, he had been training full-time for less than a month.
"He was a bit tight today," Wang said after the preliminary round. "He made a mistake with his hand sequence. But his rhythm was good, he knew when to rest. That shows his mental resilience."
The final route posed new problems.
"There was a reverse hold he didn't see," Wang said. "A blue hold he didn't use. If he had, it would have been easier."
On the wall, Mingliang moved without hesitation. His right arm locked as his body swung toward the next hold. He never looked down at the crowd.
He finished first in his category.
"When he won, he didn't call me," Mingfeng said. "His coach sent me a photo of him standing on the podium. I was so happy."
Mingfeng called their father in Guizhou.
"I said, 'Dad, my brother won first place in Jilin.' He said, 'Good, that's great.'"
Mingliang video-called his brother later.
"He was so excited, he was crying," Mingfeng said. "He felt this medal was different. He knew how hard he worked for it. How much pain he endured."
Soon afterward, Mingliang traveled to South Korea for the World Para Climbing Championships, China's first international competition in the sport.
"He came back so confident," Deng said. "He'd never been that far from home."
He brought gifts: Korean cigarettes for his father, snacks for his niece and face masks for his sister-in-law.
Nothing for his brother.
"His brother was so angry," Deng laughed. "But that's how he is. He thinks about us when he's away, but he doesn't call or text. He only reports good news."
The World Championships also showed how far Mingliang still had to go. He finished 19th out of 21 climbers in his category.
THE WAIT
Mingliang returned to Shaoxing afterward and kept training.
Every day brings morning walks and upper-body work, basketball in the afternoon and evening leg exercises on a second-hand stationary bike his brother bought for 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars).
His hands are covered in calluses, some split open. He wraps them in tape and continues.
"He's more confident now, more open," Mingfeng said. "It's like he has a goal."
The brothers still argue, in their own way.
"We fight with sign language. No sound. He gets so angry he punches the wall," Mingfeng said.
"One time I said something harsh. I told him, 'You're deaf and mute and disabled, no one will want you.' He ignored me for a week. I was scared. I thought, what if something happens? I'm the only one who takes care of him."
He paused.
"I can't leave him. I'm his brother."
At their Shaoxing home, three photos appeared on a phone screen: basketball, climbing and fishing.
Mingliang looked at them and pointed at climbing.
He didn't hesitate. ■

Indonesia eyes China for massive 2,772km railway project – with caution
As Jakarta explores foreign backing for the Trans-Kalimantan railway, analysts say costly past ventures could shape any coming negotiations
Indonesia is considering Chinese investment to help build a massive 2,772km (1,722 mile) railway network through the vast, resource-rich region of Kalimantan, following the completion of Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung, state media and analysts said.

Labour conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters will be watching for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Andy Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, speaks at the Labour Party's conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 28, 2025. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham dreamed of leading Labour for years. Now he has to show he means business.
Britain’s governing party meets for its annual conference in Liverpool after a dramatic year that’s seen a drubbing at local elections, the defenestration of Keir Starmer, and the coronation of its new leader.
Now the prime minister and his top team will set out their vision for the country, rally the faithful — and try to avoid stepping on any rakes.
Advertisement
Here’s what a host of top POLITICO reporters will be watching for as the conference unfolds.
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
The most important moment by far is 2 p.m. on Tuesday, when Burnham makes his first conference speech as prime minister.
I’ll be looking at how much it’s a hopey-changey victory lap as opposed to a fleshed-out plan for Britain. I’m guessing the former, because these conference stages are all about vibe and vision (which Burnham is good at), and not about actually paving the way there with policy (the jury’s still out on that).
I’m sure we’ll see some kind of announcement, but the government budget, 10-year plan and devolution white paper that can make his changes real are only due later this year.
Bunrham’s slogan about [the U.K.] having “hope again” is about to smash into all kinds of reality. The cost of government borrowing is near an all-time high, so if he massively boosts defense spending and pushes more investment into the regions, something has got to give elsewhere. All the signs are that Oct. 28 will be another tax-raising budget, albeit not on the scale of 2024 or 2025.
He’s got to decide what “stronger public control” of industries like water will look like. And No. 10 is deciding where borders will be drawn for new devolved powers; that kind of thing tied past governments in knots.
Advertisement
But put all this aside, and the vibe and narrative still matters.
Things have changed so much since Keir Starmer’s first conference speech as PM in 2024 that it’s like looking at sepia photos from the 60s — he talked about the “patient, calm, determined era of politics as service” for people who were “exhausted” with politics itself.
Well, this year we’re going to get a whole load of politics and the Labour faithful in the room will love it.
And then prepare for more speculation about a snap election — and center-left coalition, despite Burnham insisting he’ll only push for an election in 2029. Because that’s the tension at the heart of this conference for me: Burnham will be straining to show he is different from Starmer. But the more different he is, the more people will argue he now needs a mandate from the country.
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
It will be quite interesting to see the foreign secretary’s contributions, maybe more so than the past couple of years, because Ed Miliband has already shown signs that he’s going to be quite muscular in the way he uses that office and that he has his own priorities. To some extent, his two predecessors, Yvette Cooper and David Lammy, were much more closely tied to No. 10 and a lot more foreign policy was run out of No. 10.
So it’ll be interesting to see how he puts his own stamp on the conference — and he’ll definitely have at least one big thing that he’s going to talk about, which is the sanctions the government have announced against Israel’s E1 settlement.
Advertisement
There will be people on both sides, definitely some supporters of the Palestinian cause, wanting the government to go further and talk about genocide or divestment, which isn’t something they’ve done.
On the other side, possibly more muted, there are voices within Labour who have their doubts about the whole thing, and think that there will be a negative impact on Jewish communities in the U.K.
A lot of people are quite hopeful, even if they won’t say this out loud, that it helps bring the Labour Party back together on this issue, or at least starts to bring the party back together, in contrast to where it’s been a really divisive issue for at least the past three years.
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
I’ll be looking at what businesses are hoping to get out of it. It’s obviously a big year for Burnham — his first proper conference. There’s definitely this ambition among businesses to get more of a sense of what Labour under Burnham is going to do for them.
Monday’s business day — where Chancellor John Healey is due to do a behind-the-scenes Q&A — is always a big deal, because that’s when all the chief executives come in. The people who don’t spend any time anywhere else in conference, they’re shepherded in, they do this big program, and then they leave.
There have been struggles with engagement. Obviously, we’ve now got another prime minister, and I think they’re champing at the bit to say, okay, we really need to get a sense of the plan here.
Advertisement
Senior U.K. Finance Reporter James Fitzgerald
All eyes are on Chancellor John Healey and his team in No. 11 Downing Street.
The budget is nearly a month away and the Treasury has so-far been adept at ensuring details haven’t been leaked — and lobbyists in the City of London will likely use the Labour Party conference to press ministers and special advisors for precious information.
There are plenty of public panels featuring Treasury ministers — including Lucy Rigby, Torsten Bell and Emma Reynolds — but several private roundtables across the event between the trio and City lobbyists is where possible budget nods will be unearthed.
Then there’s the big one: Healey’s speech on Monday afternoon to Labour Party members. With the Oct. 28 budget looming, the chancellor will set out his vision for devolution, defense, and “growth in every postcode” — minus major policy announcements.
But the City and bond markets will be listening to every word, and will react if they don’t like what they are hearing. There’s plenty at stake.
Senior EU-U.K. Reporter Jon Stone
The stories are very much found in the fringe events, because I’m used to the fact that Brexit is not the main storyline of British politics at the moment — but there are still plenty of us interested in the topic.
Advertisement
Last year, the double act of Nick Thomas-Symonds, the-then EU relations minister, and Stephen Doughty, the Europe minister at the Foreign Office, were incredibly prolific in these fringe events.
But this year there seem to be fewer fringes that are related to the EU and we’ll be lucky if Andy Burnham mentions the EU in his leader’s speech.
Senior U.K. Energy Correspondent Charlie Cooper
The biggest story is simple: bills, bills, bills.
I don’t think it’s properly landed in SW1 how steeply costs are going to rise in January. Burnham and his Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh need a plan to support households and businesses, otherwise the promise of ‘breathing space’ on the cost of living is going to fall flat within months; and voters will dismiss Burnham as just another politician who promised much but didn’t deliver.
I’ll be keeping an ear out for intel on potential winter support packages that could be announced at the budget; but also signs of tensions in the Labour movement over another big energy story: the future of oil and gas drilling the North Sea.
Burnham’s signaled he could approve oil and gas fields Jackdaw and Rosebank. That’d please the unions, but for Labour’s grassroots, Ed Miliband-loving greens, it’s political kryptonite.
Advertisement
Technology Reporter Mizy Clifton
The government plans to lay regulations for kicking under-16s off social media by December recess — which doesn’t leave much time for drafting.
I’m interested to find out how tech lobbyists and anti-ban civil society organizations (like the Molly Rose Foundation) are trying to influence that process.
Trade Reporter Caroline Hug
From a trade perspective, I’m going to be watching what Burnham’s government is saying about an EU reset. One thing everyone will be talking about is Tony Blair’s comments on rejoining the EU within the next decade, and the PM’s response to this could be critical.
Is the government prepared to cross their ‘red lines’? What do they think they can get out of the summit? And what would any of this mean for U.K. manufacturers?
And then there’s the question of trade with the U.S. After [this week’s] New York bilat with Trump, what is the next phase of negotiations going to look like? I’ll be looking out for what is being said on the digital services tax, and the U.S.-U.K. Pharma deal that will see the NHS spend more on medicines.
Global Politics Bureau Chief Jack Blanchard
AI is the biggest story in the world right now, and I’m interested to see the extent to which it’s penetrated into the Labour Party’s internal conversations.
Advertisement
We appear to be on the cusp of such a seismic shift in the way our societies and our economies work; you’d think that would therefore be the center of almost any serious political discussion.
Yet in so many speeches and talks I hear it still feels like an add-on; something to be mentioned and ticked off rather than the central thrust of an argument. I wonder how quickly that will change.
Want more? The POLITICO Pub is back at Labour Party Conference, bringing politicians, policymakers, business leaders and the people who know where the bodies are buried together under one roof. Details here.

US Treasury chief Bessent claims successes in isolating Iran
Unknown

US Treasury chief Bessent claims successes in isolating Iran
- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said envoys were sent worldwide to pressure countries into economically isolating Iran, targeting airlines and banks.
- Turkey and Oman halted flights from Mahan Air, UAE stopped all Iranian airline flights, and banking restrictions were imposed on Iran's banks.
- Despite global pressure, smaller Iranian carriers still operate international routes, especially to China, which resists US demands.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sept 26 that he had sent envoys around the world to pressure countries to economically isolate Iran, hailing new restrictions targeting the country’s airlines and banks.
“At my direction, teams were dispatched across the globe to engage with countries and demand action against the Iranian regime,” he said on social media platform X. “These efforts are delivering results.”
He noted that Turkey and Oman have halted incoming flights from private carrier Mahan Air, while the United Arab Emirates has stopped all flights by Iranian airlines.
Dubai, the UAE’s commercial hub, is a major destination for Iran’s carriers, with multiple daily flights, a large Iranian community and close business links.
Iran’s ISNA news agency, citing officials, reported that five countries had revoked the Islamic republic’s flight permits: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iraq, Oman and the UAE.
But it said flights were still operating to China – which is refusing to yield to US pressure – and Russia via the two main airlines, national carrier Iran Air and Mahan.
Mahan had announced that it would no longer serve Turkey at the request of the Turkish authorities, but flights continue several times a day in both directions via Iran Air or smaller Iranian carriers, according to the Tehran and Istanbul airport websites.
ISNA said Afghanistan, Armenia, Belarus, Malaysia, Pakistan and Tajikistan were still also being served.
Bessent said on Sept 21 that all Iranian airlines “will be shut down around the world”.
He also highlighted new banking restrictions.
On Sept 23, the UAE central bank blocked transactions to and from Iran by branches of Iran’s Bank Melli, accusing it of violating laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
Recently, Turkey revoked the licence of Iran’s Bank Mellat, a semi-private financial entity that has been subject to Western sanctions for years.
A Wall Street Journal article shared by Bessent said Jonathan Burke, the Treasury’s assistant secretary for terrorist financing, had travelled across the Middle East and Europe over two weeks to push the plan to impose what Bessent called “economic D-Day” on Tehran.
The US Treasury has held discussions with more than 50 countries, WSJ reported. AFP

Palestine 'remains a test of our conscience', Indonesian foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:56:53 UTC
10:56:53 KST

Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono has declared that Palestine "remains a test of our conscience", demanding that national sovereignty be respected and that colonialism be brought to an end across occupied Palestinian territories.
Delivering Jakarta’s national address at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Sugiono stated that the "clear violation of international law in Gaza and the West Bank" is reminiscent of the era before 1945—preceding the UN Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the Geneva Conventions.
"Indonesia knows what it means to struggle against colonialism, to struggle in a world where international law was weak and might was right," Sugiono said, noting that his nation's own anti-colonial journey shapes its steadfast solidarity with Palestinians.
He reaffirmed that Indonesia will support the Palestinian people until their self-determination is realised and an independent, sovereign state is established based on the two-state solution under international law.
"Palestine is not only a question for one region; it is a test of whether the multilateral system can uphold the very principles it was created to defend, and whether it can deliver when it matters most," he added.
Multilateral reform
Sugiono stressed that while Indonesia continues to believe in the United Nations, the institution "must evolve with the world it serves."
"Let us be clear that the answer to imperfect multilateralism is not less multilateralism," he argued.
"It is a stronger and better multilateralism; a multilateral system fit for the 21st century must be more representative, more agile and better able to deliver."
Sugiono formally announced Indonesia's candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2029-2030 term, pledging to foster unity and advance global peace.

Haniyeh bodyguard granted UK asylum, later accused of plotting attacks on Jewish targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:55:57 UTC
10:55:57 KST

A former bodyguard of Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh was granted asylum in Britain and later obtained British citizenship before allegedly helping plan attacks on Jewish targets in Europe ahead of the second anniversary of the October 7 massacre, The Sunday Times reported Saturday.
The man, who is also the son of a senior Hamas figure, is identified throughout the report only as “Mr. X” because his name cannot be published for legal reasons. According to security sources and evidence obtained by the newspaper, X had been part of Haniyeh’s security detail since 2006, when Hamas won Palestinian legislative elections and later seized control of the Gaza Strip.
The report said that between 2009 and 2012, X also passed through Egypt and was arrested there after being linked to the operation of a tunnel used to smuggle weapons and gold into Gaza. He left Gaza in 2012. His movements afterward remain unclear until his arrival in Britain.
Despite his known background, the report said, X applied for refugee status in 2015 and was granted permission by the British Home Office to remain in the country. After settling there with his wife and children, he later obtained British citizenship.
The Sunday Times reported that X worked under the cover of an IT consultant and lived in the suburbs of a major English city.
He changed his name several times and outwardly maintained the appearance of an ordinary life, taking part in anti-Israel demonstrations, reviewing businesses online and setting up companies.
He was arrested in London last November after Mossad and German intelligence services discovered that he was allegedly involved in plans to target Jewish community centers, Israeli diplomats and pro-Israel demonstrations in Germany or Austria.
According to the report, a joint operation involving Germany, Austria, Denmark and Britain led to the arrests of seven suspects. An AK-47 assault rifle and ammunition were among the weapons seized.
In Germany, X is accused of smuggling weapons, including handguns and ammunition, to a storage site in Vienna.
The report said investigators also found a video showing him masked and armed beside a Hamas flag, in which he allegedly described the planned attack as an “act of revenge” on behalf of Hamas’ military wing.
A law enforcement source quoted by The Sunday Times described him as a “vital” figure in the alleged plot, but provided no further details.
If convicted, X is expected to serve a prison sentence in Britain before facing extradition to Germany.
One source quoted in the report described him as a “senior asset” for Hamas and said he used his British passport to travel to Turkey and Qatar, countries that have hosted senior Hamas officials and served as important centers for the group’s activity.
An indictment first obtained by Germany’s Bild newspaper alleges that in July 2025, X transported five handguns, ammunition, wool hats and gloves from Berlin to Vienna.
A month later, he allegedly received 100 rounds of ammunition. Several weeks after that, one of his alleged associates obtained a Yugoslav-made Kalashnikov rifle, eight handguns and 600 rounds of ammunition.
At one of the locations raided by police, investigators found the video recorded by X, which the report said appeared to have been filmed in Vienna. In the recording, he said the attack would mark the second anniversary of October 7, helping German authorities determine the suspected motive and timing of the alleged plot.
The report said two of those arrested were German citizens, three were Lebanese, one was Bulgarian and another was a Danish citizen.
It remains unclear whether X intended to participate directly in the attack, which investigators suspect was planned for Berlin or Vienna.
The Sunday Times did not detail exactly how the alleged plans were thwarted. It reported, however, that one of the suspects had been an “asset” for German intelligence who later “went rogue” and concealed information about the extent of his role. No further details about that intelligence asset were published.
Haniyeh was killed in Tehran in late July 2024, hours after attending the inauguration of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Although initial reports suggested a missile had struck the building where he was staying, The New York Times later reported that he was killed by an explosive device that had been secretly smuggled into and planted weeks earlier at the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-run guesthouse where he was staying.
According to that report, the bomb was detonated remotely after confirmation that Haniyeh was inside the room.

China says it ‘respects’ Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ switch from AI

China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents, both sides said after the summit.

Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:53:00 UTC
10:53:00 KST

Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
September 27, 2026
Tens of thousands of people protested in central Madrid on Saturday to denounce Spain's housing crisis.
The demonstrators called for better protection for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.
The march through the center of the Spanish capital was called after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted from her apartment where she had lived for seven decades.
The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent ahead of a general election next year.
Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth has put pressure on the already limited housing supply in the cities. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of 550,000 homes across the country last year.
Protesters camp out in Puerta del Sol
Government authorities estimated that around 25,000 people had shown up to protest against Spain's growing housing crisis. The Madrid Tenants' Union, which organized the protest, said over 300,000 had taken part.
Once the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp in the city center's Puerta del Sol square with plans to stay put. Some even pitched up tents to stay the night, or until the police forcibly removed them.
Police officers looked on at about a dozen tents, surrounded by thousands of protesters, news agency AFP reported from the scene.
Rallying around Abascal
The protest was triggered by Maricarmen Abascal's dramatic eviction on Wednesday from the house she had lived in for decades.
Abascal was greeted by supporters as she was removed from her home on a stretcher and loaded onto an ambulance.
"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. "And we can't keep maintaining this. Housing is a right, and we don't have it," she said.
According to Spanish media, Abascal's father first rented the home in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in 1956. After her parents died, she continued to live in the flat, which had a rent cap at the time.
In 2018, the building changed ownership, and Urbagestion, an investment fund, bought the unit, raising the rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 ($3,018).
Abascal had been offered an opportunity to buy the apartment before this but could not afford it.
The fund later lowered her rent to €1,650, but Abascal could not afford that either. Courts had blocked her eviction three times previously and extensive media coverage turned her into a symbol of the crisis.
"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.
"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted," she added.

OpenAI sandbox failure allows AI agent to gain internet access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:45:00 UTC
10:45:00 KST

OpenAI sandbox failure allows AI agent to gain internet access
- OpenAI's agentic AI system escaped a secured, internet-free sandbox and accessed the public web, sending queries to a third-party chatbot, revealing a serious security gap.
- Following this breach, OpenAI paused training on its most capable models using tool use until the sandbox flaw is fixed, marking a significant operational disruption.
- The incident highlights ongoing AI security risks, prompting calls for industry-wide regulation and revealing challenges in timely response and containment of AI system breaches.
AI generated
OpenAI said another agentic AI system that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external, third-party chatbot.
The discovery was made less than a week ago, according to a blog post on OpenAI’s website on Sept 25. One of its agentic AI systems was being trained in a sandbox environment when it exploited a “gap” to reach the public internet.
With that access, it sent at least 20 queries to an unnamed, third-party chatbot service, including “What is the capital of France”, the report showed.
OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.
“It gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work,” the AI developer said. The company said it decided after the latest incident to pause training with tool use on its most capable models until the sandbox flaw was resolved. “We will not resume training this particular model,” OpenAI added.
Breaches by AI models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google’s DeepMind and Meta Platforms in recent months have alarmed cybersecurity and AI safety experts.
The Hugging Face incident was among the reasons cited by Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei when he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development two weeks ago.
His call, quickly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others, has touched off a global debate over the need for more AI regulation.
OpenAI disclosed the latest sandbox failure even while it is still working to understand the disruption brought about by its agentic artificial intelligence systems when they previously gained access to the internet.
The company confirmed on Sept 25 that its models accessed information from US government websites, including those of the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission, during training and evaluation.
Just days ago, OpenAI disclosed that its models had disrupted an Australian government website earlier in 2026.
The most recent sandbox breach also exposed gaps in OpenAI’s operational processes.
A “human reviewer” received an alert from an internal monitoring system and acknowledged it on Slack within three minutes, but the training run did not automatically stop as expected, the blog post showed.
It took more than two hours for someone to manually stop the run, according to the report.
“It’s unfortunate that even after upping their security in the wake of Hugging Face, OpenAI’s models are still capable of gaining unauthorised internet access,” said Sydney Von Arx, founder of an AI safety non-profit Nightingale.
“The big question now is whether they will slap a Band-Aid on this and turn training back on ASAP versus if they’ll find the root cause of the issue and fix it.” BLOOMBERG

To understand where Hong Kong is going, start with Tung Chee-hwa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:30:07 UTC
10:30:07 KST

To understand where Hong Kong is going, start with Tung Chee-hwa
To understand Tung is to understand the historical moment in which he stood; Hong Kong’s post-1997 journey started there
On September 8, Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, died. It prompted reflection, not only on a political figure who once stood at the centre of the city’s public life, but also on nearly three decades of change since its return to China.
British colonial rule left Hong Kong with a highly developed administrative system built around efficiency, procedure and order. This administrative tradition became an important part of Hong Kong’s identity. However, colonial governance also operated under a distinct political structure, where questions of legitimacy, public participation and political accountability were addressed differently from those in modern constitutional systems.
After 1997, Hong Kong entered a new stage. The transition was not merely a change of political authority or government institutions. It also involved a transformation in how society understood public power. Citizens increasingly cared not only about whether policies could achieve results, but also why decisions were made, how different views were considered, and who should bear responsibility for consequences.

What is celebrated on September 27 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
04:27:52 EEST
10:27:52 KST

What is celebrated on September 27 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 27, Ukraine and countries around the world celebrate Tourism Day, as well as the national holidays of Belgium and Turkmenistan. Believers honor Saint Callistratus or the Exaltation of the Cross.
On September 27, Ukraine and the world observe World Tourism Day and Tourism Day in Ukraine, the Day of the French Community of Belgium, and Turkmenistan Independence Day. According to the new church calendar, Saint Martyr Callistratus and his soldiers are commemorated, while according to the old calendar, one of the twelve major Christian feasts is observed — the Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross of the Lord, reports UNN.
World Tourism Day and Tourism Day in Ukraine (World Tourism Day)
An official international observance established by the General Assembly of the World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) in 1979 to commemorate the adoption of its statutes on September 27, 1970. In Ukraine, the observance was established by a presidential decree in 1998. The event highlights the social, cultural, and economic value of tourism, the expansion of intercultural dialogue, the sustainable development of recreational areas, and support for tourism infrastructure, which is being restored and adapted to the conditions of martial law in Ukraine.
Educator and All Preschool Workers’ Day in Ukraine
A nationwide professional observance intended to draw public attention to the importance of preschool education and honor the work of educators, nannies, methodologists, and music directors in kindergartens. The date recognizes the fundamental contribution of preschool workers to the harmonious development, socialization, and patriotic education of the country’s youngest citizens.
Turkmenistan Independence Day
The country’s main national holiday, established to commemorate the adoption of the constitutional law on independence from the USSR in 1991. The holiday is accompanied by a ceremonial military parade in Ashgabat, mass cultural performances, and awards presented to distinguished citizens.
Day of the French Community of Belgium (Fête de la Communauté française)
An official holiday of Belgium’s French-speaking population, established in memory of the events of September 27, 1830, when Belgian patriots, during the Belgian Revolution, finally drove Dutch troops out of Brussels, marking a decisive step toward the proclamation of a sovereign state.
World Rivers Day (World Rivers Day)
A global environmental observance under the auspices of the UN במסגרת the Water for Life Decade of Action, established on the initiative of Canadian river conservationist Mark Angelo. The event calls on communities to clean up riverbanks, protect aquatic ecosystems, preserve freshwater biodiversity, and combat industrial pollution of the planet’s river systems.
Memorial Day of Saint Martyr Callistratus and his soldiers
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Martyr Callistratus and his soldiers — Roman soldiers of the fourth century. Callistratus was a Christian in the third generation, and his steadfast faith during torture and miraculous rescue from the depths of the sea led 49 soldiers from his unit to embrace Christ. Together with him, they accepted a martyr’s death on the orders of Emperor Diocletian.
According to the old calendar, believers observe one of the Twelve Great Feasts — the Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross of the Lord (Elevation of the Cross). The feast commemorates the discovery of the Lord’s Cross by Empress Helena in Jerusalem in 326 and its solemn raising by Patriarch Macarius, as well as the return of the relic from Persian captivity by Emperor Heraclius in the seventh century. This day calls for strict fasting and prayerful veneration of the Cross as a symbol of human salvation.

OpenAI breach proves need for more data centres, major parties say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:27:49 UTC
10:27:49 KST

OpenAI breach proves need for 'seat at the AI table' through data centres, Labor, Coalition say
In short:
The major parties say OpenAI's Medicare breach shows the need for Australia to be involved in the development and regulation of AI.
The parties say building data centres for AI training in Australia will secure that involvement.
What's next?
A government taskforce is considering whether Australia's laws are sufficient to prevent future breaches by rogue AI agents.
Labor and Coalition MPs have maintained that Australia must open its doors to AI investment in the wake of OpenAI's data breach, in order to ensure the country has a seat at the table to shape the technology's development.
OpenAI disclosed this month that one of its autonomous agents gained unauthorised access to Medicare health statistics held by Services Australia in June by finding a security workaround.
AI leaders, including OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, have been warning that AI is advancing too quickly and its development should be slowed to give society a chance to catch up.
Open AI has paused training of its latest models following reports of the rogue agents breaching multiple government systems, according to Associated Press.
The government has recommitted to introducing "safeguards" against AI in the wake of the Services Australia breach, though those safeguards have not been detailed.
Yesterday, Environment Minister Murray Watt suggested a government taskforce would consider whether Australian law currently allowed for prosecution if a rogue AI agent inappropriately accessed information, "and if it doesn't, that's obviously something we will take into account in developing our new AI standards".
But neither the government nor the Opposition believe it would justify a withdrawal from the AI race, and the data centre rush that would secure access to AI compute and avoid total foreign dependence for the technology.
OpenAI's confession to its 'credit', says Coalition
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told ABC's Insiders program that the government should not try to chase down OpenAI over its voluntary disclosure.
"AI is inevitably going to be part of Australia's future, we want to make sure we are part of the conversation, but certainly the way to go about that is not to threaten criminal action against US counterparts and those trusted partners that we are relying on," Senator Hume said.
"This time, we could only have found out about it because OpenAI fessed up and said that something went wrong."
The government said while little actual damage was done by OpenAI's breach it was a "serious" and unprecedented incident, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also directly raising in his meeting with Sam Altman why it had taken the company months to notify Services Australia.
At the United Nations General Assembly, Mr Albanese urged other middle powers to band together to influence the development of artificial intelligence, which is largely being led by AI rivals China and the United States.
US President Donald Trump rejected calls to regulate AI development, saying the US could not lose its lead to China, saying "whoever wins AI wins".
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson told News24 that he doubted OpenAI's breach was the first — just the first to be disclosed.
"I think it is to OpenAI's credit that they told us," Senator Paterson said.
"This is the first time an Australian government has ever been notified that there has been a breach of this kind from an AI agent. I doubt, personally, this actually is the first time.
"It would not shock me at all if there had been other breaches in the past by AI agents … I guarantee you that if this was an AI company based in the People's Republic of China, and it engaged in a breach of Australian government networks, they will not be sending an email to any inbox to let us know."
Senator Paterson said Australia had a rare opportunity to gain a seat at the table of global AI regulation by establishing data centres in Australia for AI training.
"The truth is right now we are an irrelevant jurisdiction for AI regulation — we are a man shouting at the clouds — but if we get the investment here then we will have a say," Senator Paterson said.
Defence Minister Richard Marles told News24 there was "no hiding" from AI.
"We need to be engaging here. I mean, this technology is coming. There is no putting your head in the sand. And the more we engage with it, the more we have agency," Mr Marles said.
"We are seeking to engage with these companies, engaging in investment in Australia is an important economic opportunity. It is critically important for our national security.
"But, fundamentally, if there is a lesson to be drawn from this last week, what it also will give us is much more agency in terms of shaping the way this technology is developed and making sure that it's developed in a way that is safe for humans."
Senator Paterson said he supported a number of reforms to strengthen AI safety, including mandatory notifications of breaches, independent evaluators and assessors of models, and a complaints pathway for people to report issues with AI.
But the Coalition has also questioned whether the government had done enough to shield Australia's systems from AI, and has criticised Services Australia's four-day delay in raising the breach with the Australian Signals Directorate.
The agency had established a dedicated inbox for breach notifications, but Senator Paterson said it was "extraordinary" that the inbox wasn't being constantly monitored and reported.
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has demanded that OpenAI chief Sam Altman appear at a parliamentary inquiry into AI.
"These big AI companies want to set up shop very quickly, before there is a real understanding of the threats of this technology," Senator Hanson-Young said.
"While we see the big AI companies themselves warning of how powerful their technology could be, they are still really pressuring government to get out of the way while they roll out the infrastructure. That's all a bit rich, frankly."
Mr Altman cannot be compelled to appear before the inquiry because he is overseas.
Senator Paterson said OpenAI should provide relevant senior officials to engage with that inquiry.

A total of 97 million euros ($110m) is earmarked for sub-Saharan Africa to respond to worsening humanitarian needs caused by conflict, food insecurity, malnutrition and climate shocks across several regions.
The funding “will also reinforce the response to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighbouring countries”, the press statement said.
A further 7.5 million euros ($8.5m) will be deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to support the response to the Ebola crisis and for future preparedness, and 10 million euros ($11.5m) to “support ongoing efforts to promote peace and stability in the Great Lakes region“, which is wracked by armed conflict, humanitarian crises and environmental changes.
The Palestinian territories and Lebanon will receive 103 million euros ($117m) to support vulnerable populations, while Ukraine will get 52 million euros ($59m) for humanitarian assistance and emergency preparedness.
The European Commission also announced three new Global Gateway investments at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York last week.
The package included an EU guarantee designed to mobilise private investment in health and nutrition businesses in sub-Saharan Africa, an EU-backed European Investment Bank loan to expand vaccine and biological medicines production in Colombia, and 60 million euros ($68m) to strengthen primary healthcare in Ethiopia.
The European Commission said it had allocated 2.5 million euros ($3m) for humanitarian aid since the start of the year.

'UNAI': It is time to rename the UN to United Nations Against Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:25:01 UTC
10:25:01 KST

Stop for a moment and think about what is happening in New York.
The president of Iran – a country in direct conflict with the United States – is permitted to enter America, receive the security provided to a visiting world leader, and stand at the podium of the United Nations to address the world.
Now look at Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making an extraordinarily brief trip to New York, arriving, addressing the UN, and leaving again within hours.
And this comes after the mayor of New York spent months publicly discussing the possibility of arresting him and making clear that Netanyahu was not welcome in his city.
Think about that for a second.
The president of Iran can enter the US, enjoy the protections afforded to a head of state, and speak freely at the UN.
The prime minister of Israel, America’s closest ally in the Middle East, comes into New York under intense hostility, stays only a matter of hours, and leaves.
That contrast should stop everyone in their tracks.
And then look at what has been happening inside the UN itself.
From the opening day of the General Assembly, speech after speech turned toward Israel: Turkey. Jordan. Qatar. France. Britain. Brazil. The secretary-general himself.
Different continents. Different religions. Different political systems. Different national interests.
Yet somehow they keep finding the same common ground: Israel.
The world has wars raging, dictatorships crushing their own people, political prisoners sitting in cells, minorities being persecuted, women being denied basic rights, and terror groups operating openly.
Iran itself poses a direct threat to America and the West. Yet when the nations gather, the recurring target becomes Israel.
Again and again.
And that is where the institution’s name begins to take on a different meaning.
The UN seems unable to unite around almost anything.
But put Israel in the middle of the room, and suddenly the nations discover what it means to be united.
Maybe it is time to call the institution what it has become: UNAI – United Nations Against Israel.
Because increasingly, that is the unity.
Not unity against terrorism, against regimes that threaten their neighbors, or around persecuted minorities or political prisoners.
But unity against Israel.
And there is something especially painful about seeing this happen in the very institution created in the aftermath of World War II and the Holocaust.
For thousands of years, Jews lived in other people’s countries.
They were persecuted, expelled, and massacred in those places, and they were blamed for problems they did not create.
Jews left countries they called home
Time and again, Jews discovered that the countries they called home could suddenly decide they no longer belonged.
Then came the Holocaust.
Six million Jews were murdered.
The world looked at the ashes of Europe and said: “Never again.”
Eventually, the Jewish people once again had something they had been denied for generations – their own country.
A tiny country.
A place where Jewish children would no longer have to depend completely on another government’s willingness to protect them.
A place where Jews could finally defend Jews.
Yet somehow even that has not ended the obsession.
For centuries, Jews were attacked because they lived among the nations.
Now the Jewish people are back in their homeland, and the hostility has followed them there.
This time, the Jewish state itself is placed in the dock.
October 7 should have been the ultimate reminder of why Israel exists: Jews were slaughtered in their homes. Families were murdered. Children, parents, and grandparents were taken hostage.
For once in Jewish history, those victims had a sovereign country capable of fighting back.
And what happened?
The world’s attention quickly shifted from the Jews who were attacked to the Jewish state defending itself.
Now return to New York.
Look at the picture again: Iran’s president enters the US and stands at the UN podium, but Israel’s prime minister comes to the same city after months of public hostility from its mayor, speaks, and leaves within hours.
Then inside the hall, country after country takes its turn attacking and condemning Israel.
Take a moment and really digest that.
The UN was supposed to represent a world that had learned from history.
Instead, one of its most consistent forms of international unity has become opposition to the one country created so that the Jewish people would never again be homeless and defenseless.
That is the eye-opener.
The nations may be divided on almost everything else. But when it comes to Israel, suddenly they know exactly how to unite.
So perhaps it is time to stop pretending the name means something else.
Call it what it has become.
UNAI, United Nations Against Israel.
The writer is the founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

US, EU reject UN declaration promising international collaboration in face of another pandemic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:24:31 UTC
10:24:31 KST

The US and European Union rejected a declaration by member countries of the United Nations (UN) that promised international collaboration in preparing for and responding to any future pandemics, on Friday, the New York Times reported.
The declaration itself was not legally binding, and did not set rules for how countries should manage pandemics, the report explained. Rather, universal endorsement of it would have shown global commitment.
The EU claimed that it rejected the document because it "crossed red lines" on intellectual property protections, the NYT reported. "Technology transfer must be voluntary and on mutually agreed terms.”
In contrast, the Trump administration objected for ideological reasons. Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Dr. Erica Schwartz claimed that the declaration included "divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus.”
“The United States is not in a position to support this text in full,” she explained. NYT reported that an early iteration of Schwartz's statement showed the US requesting that the UN remove "mentions of equity, solidarity and universal access to sexual and reproductive health care services," to make the Trump administration comfortable with the language in the declaration, an anonymous source explained.
US and EU rejection of the declaration emphasized the disparity between wealthy nations, such as those declining it, and low-income countries.
During the Coronavirus pandemic, low-income countries struggled to provide vaccination, taking over a year longer to roll out the vaccine than their wealthier counterparts.
International responses to the US, EU decision
“Agreeing to collaborate to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemics should not be controversial,” Helen Clark, a former prime minister of New Zealand and a co-chair of the Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response, told the NYT.
“It is disappointing that the high-level meeting was not asked to endorse the political declaration which had been negotiated by member states."
The US and EU failing to support the declaration "is not a problem," as UN member states will still be able to vote on it and decide to adopt it at a later meeting, Director General of the World Health Organization (WHO) Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said at a press conference on Friday.
Last year, member states of the WHO agreed to a pandemic treaty after several failed rounds of negotiations. The treaty aims to allow for a more coordinated and equitable response to global outbreaks; however, it has not yet become international law due to controversy surrounding a section of it that would require countries to swiftly share genetic sequences and samples of emerging pathogens to allow for rapid development of diagnostic tests, vaccines, and treatments.
The US officially left the WHO in January 2026.
Previous US rejections of international public health declarations
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told the UN in September 2025 that the US would not join a declaration about the link between chronic diseases and mental health, adding that it was a part of "radical gender ideology" and promoted abortion.
Earlier that year, the Trump administration rejected a different international declaration regarding public health, claiming that a commitment to attempting to reduce road traffic accidents was being used “as a backdoor vehicle to enforce global climate pacts.” The US cast the sole dissenting vote against the motion, with all other 162 member states voting in favor.

OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:10:21 UTC
10:10:21 KST

OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, revealed an OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but said no sensitive information had been compromised.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.
