Singapore proposes a UN framework convention on AI safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
01:03:00 UTC
10:03:00 KST

Singapore proposes a UN framework convention on AI safety
- Singapore proposes a UN Framework Convention on AI Safety to create international rules and institutions for AI safeguards, emphasising the need for global cooperation and shared standards amid rapid AI advances.
- Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan highlights risks from AI such as loss of control, misuse by rogue actors, and socio-economic disruption, stressing human oversight and universal safety mechanisms.
- Balakrishnan calls for revitalised multilateralism to address geopolitical challenges, including maintaining open sea lanes, and explains China’s AI drive as a strategic effort to secure a level playing field.
AI generated
PHILADELPHIA – As the US and China accelerate their artificial intelligence push, it is too late to ask for a safety pause, but what would help is the creation of institutions that can set safeguards and standards, Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan told the United Nations in a speech on Sept 26.
“We must collectively formulate new rules and be prepared to create new institutions, if necessary, for new technologies,” Balakrishnan said while delivering Singapore’s national statement at the General Debate of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.
“We must explore all options, including the idea of a UN Framework Convention on AI Safeguards,” he said in a 20-minute speech that advocated revitalising multilateralism to tackle acute geopolitical challenges.
A framework convention, like the one adopted by the UN on climate change, could be in the form of a broad international treaty that establishes foundational principles and cooperative institutions and provides the architecture for international action.
A similar call was made by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who used his address at the UN to stress the need for a common international legal framework for AI.
Balakrishnan said new institutions would also be necessary amid loud calls for AI safety from top AI tech leaders, safety researchers and lawmakers, who warn that AI capabilities are advancing faster than the human ability to safely manage them.
“We may also need an international institution that can perform for AI some of the functions that currently exist for setting common technical standards in other domains,” the minister said, citing the examples of the International Telecommunications Union, which manages global telecommunications and digital networks, and the International Atomic Energy Agency, which oversees the peaceful and safe use of nuclear technology.
Balakrishnan said the risks arose from three possibilities – the loss of control over autonomous systems; the misuse by rogue actors to create bioweapons or other weapons of mass destruction, and pervasive political and socio-economic disruption.
“But the genie is already out of the bottle,” he added, in a reference to the clamour for safety as well as the nascent efforts between the US and China to set up a dialogue on the issue.
“It is too late to call for a halt, especially given the superpower rivalry and the huge financial incentives for companies that already have frontier models,” he said.
He used the analogy of a car and traffic lights to bring the point home. “To drive a high-performance car quickly and safely, you need a powerful engine, but equally, you need good brakes,” he said.
“And especially if you are going to go beyond your neighbourhood or cross boundaries, you need effective shared rules, traffic lights, insurance, norms of behaviour, and seat belts.”
“Our safeguards must keep pace,” he said, calling for rigorous testing and evaluation before deployment. “We need clear limits on what autonomous systems can do, and mechanisms to intervene when they behave in ways we do not intend.”
He also said these mechanisms had to be universally recognisable.
“Since the risks from AI do not remain confined behind borders, it means we also need rules of the road that will form a shared global understanding of how we will collectively confront this challenge, just as all of us instinctively understand traffic lights the same way, whether we’re here in New York, or in Beijing, Moscow, or Singapore,” the minister said.
Above all, human beings must ultimately remain in charge.
“Do you want the nuclear button to be in the hands of a human being or an AI?” he asked.
Any durable international approach must also give all states a meaningful stake, not only those with the “most advanced models, the deepest pockets or the largest set of armaments”.
Singapore is contributing to ongoing efforts too.
“This week, we joined the call for greater safety and security of frontier AI models,” he said.
More than 20 countries and the European Union signed a declaration led by Finland and Norway on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York. It calls for binding international government oversight over frontier AI models, rather than corporate self-regulation
Global cooperation over AI must begin now, Balakrishnan said.
“Rules do not stop us or slow us down. They give us the assurance and the confidence so that we can move faster and more effectively for the benefit of all our peoples.”
Why China is dogged in pursuit of AI
During a Sept 25 conversation with former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd, who is now global president and chief executive of the Asia Society in New York, Balakrishnan zeroed in on the US-China battle over AI.
China sees the AI race through a deeply historical lens, he said. Having missed the 20th-century industrial revolution, it is especially keen not to miss the boat a second time.
“Because China missed it, China underwent a century-plus of humiliation and unequal treaties. This time, China has absolutely no intention of missing it again,” Balakrishnan said, in a wide-ranging, hour-long discussion that challenged the ways in which the US seizes the competition from China.
“You need to understand it is not just a matter of competition with America, being No. 1 or No. 2, and I am projecting into China’s motivations, but China says: ‘This is my turn, my time in the sunshine. Why should anyone get in the way, especially when I have the human talent, the brain power?’,” he said.
“So can you understand (that) from China’s perspective, ‘I am not going to make the strategic mistake made a century and a half ago. This is a strategic opportunity and I do not want anyone to get in my way. And all I am asking for is a level playing field, and access to technology, and to get ahead as quickly as I can’,” he said.
Rudd pointed out that China was heavily using state subsidies to win the AI race, a part of the frequent Western criticism of the Chinese economy, where domestic consumption remains weak and growth comes from exports.
Balakrishnan agreed on the pervasive use of subsidies, but said they did not fully explain the country’s successes with AI. China also has a scientific and technological backbone, he pointed out, that has beaten the US and Western European nations in manufacturing and adoption of robotics, electric vehicles and renewable energy.
What also drives the Chinese AI companies is the cut-throat domestic competition, which results in the creation of cheap and efficient Chinese AI models, he added.
The US, he said, had a longstanding ecosystem edge that “quickly converts technology into products and services and companies and a profit-generating machine”.
‘Even big powers need partners’
In his UN speech, Balakrishnan also renewed a call for multilateralism in the face of rising trade barriers, supply chain disruptions, worsening climate change and massive tech disruptions.
“Our interstate relations are increasingly dictated by raw power, where the outcomes are determined on the basis of size, leverage and coercion, and this poses obviously a clear and present danger for smaller states like Singapore,” he said.
“But the point I wanted to make is that even the more powerful states would ultimately pay a price, because hard power, on its own, cannot secure supply chains, protect populations from pandemics, or stabilise a warming planet. Even big powers need partners to secure their long-term national interests.”
The question was not whether we need multilateralism but how to make it fit for purpose, said Balakrishnan, suggesting that international law must be consistently complied with while existing international institutions are reformed.
In particular, he dwelt on the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation and overflight to protect global supply chains in the wake of the Iran war, which has halted crucial oil, gas and fertiliser shipments across the Strait of Hormuz.
“Transit passage through straits used for international navigation is a right for all of us,” he said.
“It’s not a privilege subject to fees and tolls, and this is customary international law, which means it is binding on all states, whether or not they consider themselves parties to UNCLOS,” he said.
UNCLOS, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, an international treaty adopted in 1982, establishes a legal framework governing all activities in the world’s oceans and seas. It was concluded under the presidency of former Singaporean diplomat Tommy Koh.
“The largest economies depend on the open sea lanes as much as the smallest, and we in Singapore hold ourselves to the same standard,” said Balakrishnan.
“The Strait of Singapore is less than two nautical miles at its narrowest, and yet nearly a quarter of the world’s seaborne trade passes through the Strait of Singapore,” he said.
Singapore, along with Indonesia and Malaysia, the other two littoral states of the straits of Malacca and Singapore, have worked with other users of these waterways to keep them open, secure and accessible to everyone, he said.
From Singapore’s perspective, the problem in the Persian Gulf goes beyond energy and economics, Balakrishnan told Singapore media in a press conference hours after his speech.
“It is a stress test of UNCLOS, the freedom of navigation and the right for overflight by planes in straits used for international navigation,” he said.
“That’s why we have to watch closely... and stake out our position, not gratuitously and not provocatively, but carefully and firmly.”
The minister also said that he had met “several” of the seven candidates in the running to succeed Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, whose second five-year term ends on Dec 31, describing them as experienced and committed to UN reform.
On the sidelines of the UN assembly, Balakrishnan hosted the ministerial meeting of the Global Governance Group, which consists of 30 medium and small economies that want to engage the major Group of 20 economies.
He also held a reception for 108 nations that are part of the Forum of Small States, which was co-founded by Singapore in 1992. He also co-chaired the ASEAN-Gulf Cooperation Council Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.
Concluding the week-long trip, Balakrishnan said he is returning home to Singapore “slightly encouraged” despite the UN’s failure to stop ongoing conflicts.
“The fact that the conversations have begun… and people are assessing each other’s bottom lines, red lines, concerns and ambitions is a very useful step.”
For a small and trade-dependent Singapore, the engagement at the UN – the only apex international organisation with universal participation – was vital, he said.
“We need a world that is stable, predictable, where rules apply, sanctity of contract is recognised, and states behave accordingly.”

Remittances have become a talking point in Australia's migration debate.
Some anti-immigration activists argue remittances drain money from the Australian economy, while others say that view ignores migrants' economic contribution and the support these payments provide to families overseas.
So what's the real impact — both for the economy and for migrants and their families?
Mrinaal Datt, who moved to Australia from India four years ago and is the founder of Indian Women Abroad, regularly sends money back to India — often a few hundred dollars at a time.
She told SBS Examines that the remittances went towards her partner's parents' medical expenses.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"In Indian and a lot of South Asian cultures in general, they have a saying that you don't just marry a person, you marry the whole family," she said.
"It's not just you and your partner. It's your siblings, your parents, their parents. You can't think of not supporting your family. It's just not comprehensible to an average person who comes from India.
"It just feels like it's your duty as a child to support them through all their medical procedures."
A Money Transfer Australia report said $35 billion was sent from Australia as remittances in 2024, including nearly $7 billion to India.
"When someone earns that money in Australia, but remits part of that portion overseas, that portion is not being spent here," political commentator Jaimie Johnstone said in a recent social media post about the report.
"That money is not going to an Australian cafe or restaurant. It's not being spent with an Australian tradie, it's not being used to purchase Australian products, not in an Australian shop, not circulating within an Australian household.
"And if we're going to have a serious national conversation about immigration, surely capital flowing out of our domestic economy should be part of that conversation too."
But Ryan Edwards, an associate economics professor at the Australian National University, says we should be sceptical of these numbers.
"We don’t really measure money going out very well ... those numbers are actually much softer," he said.
Even if those estimates were correct, "that would still be under 1 per cent of our economy" and tax had already been paid on the income.
He noted the argument against remittances didn't account for the benefits migrants bring.
"The real counterfactual here is one of a migrant versus no migrant," he said.
"You take away that person, yes, you've stopped the money from flowing out, but you've also stopped all the jobs, the wages that they spend here, often on things that Australians are producing, and the tax that they've paid.
"We know that most migrants tend to be net positive fiscal contributors."
Muhammad Omair Ziaee is a technology and healthcare entrepreneur of Pakistani heritage. He sends money to his family and employees back home in Pakistan, but he says most of the money his businesses make is spent in Australia.
"If we compare to the money which we're sending over ... that's under 20 per cent of what we actually earn and what we spend over here," he said.
Remittances part of culture
Supriya Singh, an adjunct sociology professor at La Trobe University, said money is "one of the foremost ways" to show care in many cultures.
"If you come from China, you come from Vietnam, you come from any part of the Middle East, you come from the Pacific; sending money home is a way you tell your family that you belong, that you're thinking of them, that you care for them."
She said care was expressed differently across cultures.
"Across the world, it's the people who do not send money home that are in the minority," she said.
However, Singh said remittances can be used as a tool for financial abuse, noting the issue came up during Victoria's Royal Commission into Family Violence.
"When a person is using them not for care but for appropriation. If the parents demand too much of the child and the child does not have enough money for his or her own settlement expenses, then remittances can become a medium of abuse," she said.
Strain on already tight budget
Datt from Indian Women Abroad said remittances are a cultural practice but can strain already tight budgets.
"I think parents have to realise is that your child is not your retirement plan," she said.
"Everyone who comes abroad knows that it is really really hard when you're paying for the university fee. So many people are living paycheque to paycheque. It really is like a cultural thing. I actually hope things will change for the next generation."
She added her contributions to Australia outweighed the remittances back home.
"If you think about all the money that we spent, the flights that we paid, the income tax that we pay, our rentals, our mortgage now, I think we've spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in Australia," she said.
"The $200 or $400 is sent back home. That's nothing in comparison."
According to a World Bank estimate, global remittances to low and middle-income countries reached $924 billion in 2023, and continued to be "essential drivers of economic and human development".

These include name or gender mismatch; less than a 15-year gap with a parent; less than a 40-year gap with a grandparent; being one of six progeny mapped to the same parent; and less than a nine-month gap between siblings.Until now, notice recipients had to appear before the ERO at the specified time and place with documents proving eligibility to remain on the rolls. With large numbers of notices in states like Delhi, including to prominent persons, many said citizens were forced to run around to retain voting rights.
EC has also denied reports that field officers were locked out of ECINET, saying role-based access exists, but agreed to an independent audit. A senior DEC-led panel will review ECINET to double-check that it complies with the provisions of the Acts and rules and submit a report to EC.

IDF expands Personal Security Branch to protect troops, officials from global threats - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
00:32:40 UTC
09:32:40 KST

Over the past year, the Operations Directorate underwent a significant restructuring to update personal security policies for service members of all ranks, both domestically and abroad.
In recent months, the specialized branch's mandate expanded, taking responsibility for the security of IDF personnel both in Israel and abroad against a wide array of threats - ranging from active-duty soldiers to high-profile officials, major generals, and the Chief of Staff.
In an interview with Walla, the head of the expanding branch discussed the growing risks, active intelligence alerts, and the joint operational response across Israel's defense establishment.
"We are responsible for the entire spectrum of terrorist threats. This has hit home even more acutely since Operation Roaring Lion in Iran, driven by what the Iranians call 'settling scores' abroad, as well as the spike in antisemitic incidents we’ve been seeing," the branch head explained.
He added, "About a year and a half ago, it was published that we extracted a soldier from Thailand following public calls to harm him, along with various other antisemitic incidents in places like Amsterdam, as well as legal challenges."
An international incident mobilized the security establishment, changing it forever
On November 2, 2022, details were cleared for publication regarding a 19-year-old lone soldier serving on active duty. Flying on a commercial flight to visit family in Uzbekistan, she departed the capital, Tashkent, heading toward Dubai in the United Arab Emirates as a layover on her way back to Israel.
Due to a severe medical emergency involving one of the passengers that required immediate attention, the plane made an emergency landing at around 5:00 a.m. in Shiraz - one of Iran’s major cities.
The soldier immediately alerted her family, who quickly notified her commanders. The information reached the Mossad, senior IDF officials, and the prime minister quickly. The minutes that followed were tense and felt like an eternity, as everyone understood she could be detained by local authorities the moment her identity was discovered.
A few hours later, under a total blackout in Israel and with the Mossad guiding and monitoring the entire situation, the plane took off for the UAE and then returned to Israel. It was a high-stakes crisis, with every development reported directly to the prime minister, the Defense Minister, and the IDF Chief of Staff.
The incident marked a turning point in how the IDF views the safety of its service members worldwide. In its aftermath, the Personal Security Branch was established under the command of Lt.-Col. "A" within the Security Division of the General Staff’s Operations Directorate.
Once it became clear that this sensitive issue required multi-agency coordination beyond the military alone, the decision was made to establish the Security Division within the Operations Directorate under the command of Brig.-Gen. "T."
This created a single, centralized authority responsible for issuing policies and technical directives across all service branches, directorates, arms, and regional commands. "Another step was appointing a dedicated intelligence officer for this domain, alongside a specialized reorganization within the Intelligence Directorate that I cannot elaborate on," Lt.Col. A. explained.
Route analysis, location tracking at the press of a button
One of the branch's initial tasks was a comprehensive risk analysis of global flight paths and routes that could pose a hazard to IDF personnel (similar to the emergency landing in Iran). In collaboration with the National Security Council (NSC), clear rules were established detailing which flights are off-limits due to the risk of emergency landings or layovers in enemy or hostile nations.
"All of this painstakingly gathered data was made accessible to every soldier via a dedicated app, allowing them to easily check what is permitted and what is off-limits," Lt.-Col. A. said. "Service members enter their full itinerary, including transit flights, and receive real-time threat advisories - including operational security guidelines and cybersecurity protocols. That's why we call it 'personal security.'"
The attack on Maccabi Tel Aviv soccer fans in Amsterdam in November 2024 served as another major red flag. Pro-Palestinian groups carried out coordinated attacks against Israelis across several locations in the city against the backdrop of the "Swords of Iron" war, sharing real-time information and documenting the violence on social media. Parts of the media described the events as a pogrom, while Dutch authorities characterized them as an antisemitic attack.
"When it started, we got a call saying the Chief of Staff wanted to know if any active IDF personnel were there. We checked and discovered a significant number of soldiers we had no prior record of - either because they had landed in another country and traveled to Holland by land, or because they were moving between cities. That event proved we had to expand our tracking and oversight capabilities for all IDF soldiers worldwide.
"Today, if an earthquake strikes Venezuela, for instance, I can generate a report at the press of a button showing whether any soldiers are there or just passing through. We handle everything directly from the branch and no longer have to scramble for information after the fact."
One ongoing challenge involves instances where a soldier flies abroad, and civil-military systems fail to automatically flag them as active-duty or career personnel, though a solution has been developed to retrieve this data that remains classified.
"Another major concern is dual citizenship, especially given the rise in antisemitism - whether it's protests outside the homes of soldiers living abroad or service members facing mandatory draft requirements in foreign countries that they need to resolve legally," noted the head of the Personal Security Branch.
"Because of this, all soldiers are required to report dual citizenship so we can vet their situation and issue appropriate instructions. We want to avoid a scenario where a soldier flies overseas and is arrested by local authorities for unresolved paperwork. This happened to us at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, and we later discovered that mandatory draft laws exist in several European countries as well."
Doxxing, legal warfare, and the exposure dilemma
An equally complex threat involves the public exposure of soldiers' personal details, doxxing campaigns, and global efforts to issue arrest warrants.
"I sign off on all exposure protocols for commanders and officials regarding whether their name and rank can be published," said Lt.-Col. A. "There is a clear military order that we enforce to protect the identities of IDF personnel. On one hand, we want to allow public visibility - and we work closely within the intelligence community alongside the Shin Bet and Mossad. But unlike them, while they are covert organizations, the IDF is a public-facing entity."
"I recently explained this at Shin Bet headquarters: 'The IDF is the people's army; it comes from the people and returns to the people.' That makes it difficult to enforce a total gag order on the identity of a brigade training base commander or a brigade commander. On the other hand, we have a vital interest in protecting them from arrest abroad or from being targeted.
"We manage this tension on a daily - almost hourly - basis in close coordination with the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit. We constantly balance the desire for public engagement with the necessity of keeping service members safe. Ultimately, we set the policy on who can be named publicly, and it escalates up to the Head of the Operations Directorate (Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen). That provides a major advantage, as he has a macro-level view of the entire IDF and access to intelligence that gives us the full picture. I can conduct a proper risk assessment and damage control evaluation even if information happens to leak."
However, the Security Division's responsibilities extend beyond mandatory and career soldiers. An equally complex issue involves reservists who have completed their service and travel the world as private citizens. The Personal Security Branch has limited authority and oversight over them, as civilians are not required to report their locations to the military.
Despite this, the Operations Directorate’s Security Division works in tight coordination with the Foreign Affairs Ministry and the Justice Ministry.
"If a complaint is filed against a reservist, or if there is an intent to file one, we bring in the Military Advocate General’s International Law Department, working alongside the Justice Ministry and handling operational coordination with the Foreign Ministry. We manage these cases jointly through a streamlined framework we established to tackle the issue," Lt.-Col. A. said.
"Most of these reports stem from content posted online during 2023–2024. We aren't seeing new cases emerge. However, it's crucial to highlight the risk posed by hostile groups using data-scraping techniques: the moment a service member lands in a country and posts about it online, these groups sometimes manage to track them down."
Recently, a specific fund published allegations targeting naval reservists who allegedly took part in intercepting a protest flotilla. Following an investigation by the Personal Security Branch, it turned out the claims were made solely because the individuals listed details about their naval service on LinkedIn.
"We are formulating policies for these scenarios to define what is permissible online, even for reservists who are civilians and not fully subject to IDF regulations. At this stage, our focus is primarily on public awareness so everyone understands the threat," Lt.-Col. A. emphasized, clarifying that the individuals in question had not actually participated in intercepting the flotilla, but were targeted simply for having served in the Navy. "
We also recently saw a social media campaign involving career officers. We called them in, presented the risks, and explained our recommendations."
Psychological warfare, espionage, and physical threats
Beyond direct threats abroad, the Personal Security Branch also navigates the evolving online landscape of public diplomacy and legal warfare, particularly surrounding public controversies.
For instance, regarding the film NAZA - which sparked intense public debate in Israel and within the military, raising concerns about a potential wave of media and legal attacks against IDF soldiers - the branch head noted that it is too early to gauge the long-term impact.
The Security Division is currently awaiting a formal legal assessment from international law experts in the Military Advocate General's Corps.
"It's important to emphasize that none of these threats have materialized into actual legal complaints or immediate physical danger so far. It concerns us primarily because the line between legal proceedings and someone attempting to cause physical harm is very thin, which is why I treat this as a personal security issue."
Beyond the media arena, the IDF is bracing for immediate physical threats: revenge efforts by Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas surrounding the sensitive High Holy Days, alongside warnings from the defense establishment regarding a fresh wave of espionage targeting IDF personnel and security officials - aimed in part at uncovering classified operational methods utilized during the war.
"This is the core purpose of the Security Division," Lt.-Col. A. explained. "Where we used to look strictly at VIP protection, today - when we sit down with partner agencies like the Shin Bet, Mossad, the Israel Police, and the Defense Ministry - we evaluate threats holistically with a completely different level of access.
"Take espionage cases, for example: I can immediately assess whether a threat impacts the Chief of Staff's immediate surroundings or affects someone traveling anywhere in the world. That is the Security Division's key advantage; previously, every security agency handled these matters in isolation."
According to the branch head, there are cases where the unit handles real-time threat mitigation regarding cyberattacks and mobile device security:
"We have significantly expanded our capabilities in executive protection. What has changed most is our capacity for intelligence monitoring - detecting a threat early and issuing an immediate alert and operational response. I cannot comment on specific operations, but we address these risks both through broad contingency plans and targeted interventions. We have encountered incidents - certainly involving senior officials, but also lower ranks - where we had to intervene, and we successfully protected our people. We have faced these threats continuously."
Asked whether there have been actual physical attempts on the lives of senior officials, Lt.-Col. A. replied, "Abroad, almost none - that falls largely under the Mossad's domain. But domestically, there were clear intentions that we identified early enough to prevent them from escalating into an attack. In other words, we never let it reach a 'near-miss' physical attempt."
He continued, saying, "We focus on identifying when something is brewing and deploying a response, supported by the Shin Bet and, for overseas matters, the Mossad. I am glad to say that our adversaries have had zero success so far, and I hope it stays that way. We work hand-in-hand with everyone - the Shin Bet, Mossad, and Police - because this is a challenge that affects us all."
Reflecting on the current threat environment and the enemy's motivation to target IDF soldiers and commanders at home and abroad, Lt.-Col. A. concluded: "There is far more focus on this now, and clear intent. Yes, their motivation is very high."

From Zurich to Rehovot: Harry Langbeheim’s paintings reveal the visual world of S.Y. Agnon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
00:32:29 UTC
09:32:29 KST

Following his retirement 10 years ago after a long and successful career in the biotech sector, research scientist and business executive Harry Langbeheim has captured a niche in the art world for his colorful illustrations of S.Y. Agnon’s stories.
“I found that there are hundreds of books and articles interpreting Agnon’s stories in writing, but almost no visual interpretations,” said Langbeheim, a polyglot native of Zurich who studied under the renowned illustrator and graphic artist Alex Diggelmann.
“Diggelmann was a great person; I learned so much from him. He told me never to stop painting, even if I chose another profession for a living.” And that’s exactly what Langbeheim did.
He arrived in Israel in 1973 to earn a doctorate in immunology at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot. A year before finishing his degree, he married Rosie, a young immigrant from Germany. Their first child was born when they were living in Silver Spring, Maryland, for two and a half years while he did postdoctoral research at the National Cancer Institute in nearby Bethesda.
Even though Langbeheim was offered a job there, he and Rosie knew from the start that they would go back to Israel. “We’ve lived in Rehovot for 53 years. It’s a very positive place for everything connected with science,” said Langbeheim. Rosie’s mother, now 105, lives nearby.
Upon their return, he began working as a research scientist with start-ups spun out of Weizmann, moving on to COO and CEO positions at various biotech companies in the Rehovot area at the dawn of the Start-Up Nation era. The list of companies he had a hand in establishing includes, among others, Sigma Aldrich (acquired by Merck in 2015), LSRI, Matis Medical, Ethrog Biotechnologies (now Invitrogen), and Savyon Diagnostics.
In 1999, he started dividing his time between industry and academia, becoming a senior lecturer in biotechnology and entrepreneurship at ORT Braude College (now Braude College) in Karmiel, and later teaching similar courses at Ben-Gurion University in Beersheba.
“It gave me the possibility to spend 50% of my time teaching, which I enjoyed very much. And it was also good for business,” he said, noting that he took on several former students as interns or employees.
Langbeheim never stopped drawing and painting
THROUGHOUT his professional career, Langbeheim never stopped drawing and painting.
For 25 years, he produced a parasha-of-the-week cartoon for “Shabbat Shalom,” a weekly newsletter distributed by Oz VeShalom–Netivot Shalom from 1997 to 2025. Chillingly, the last issue in which his cartoon appeared was Simchat Torah 2023.
“I had decided before that this was to be my last issue. You always have to know when it’s time to stop. But after October 7, I don’t think I could have continued anyway,” he said.
Over the years, he illustrated scenes from Bible stories. After he retired at age 67, he turned his attention to Agnon. “You can show Gan Eden however you want – nobody knows what it looked like – but I wanted to illustrate something that could actually be seen,” he explained.
“When I first came here and was learning Hebrew, I discovered the stories of S.Y. Agnon. One of my grandfathers, who was from Poland but knew Hebrew fluently, read Agnon’s stories in the original from a volume printed in 1933. When I read the story, I see it, so why not put it on paper?”
In 2017, he went on a European trip sponsored by Beit Agnon – the Agnon heritage center based in the Nobel laureate’s former Jerusalem house – led by Rabbi Benny Lau and literary scholar Prof. Ruhama Albag. Among the sites they visited was Buczacz, the author’s Galician hometown mentioned in his writings.
“Buczacz is an actual place you can visit. There, I found everything I was looking for, and since then I’ve painted almost 40 paintings just from the stories of Agnon,” said Langbeheim. Using India ink pen and watercolors, he strives to provide an authentic and precise visual expression of the narrative events.
“I paint only what Agnon writes. I’m a scientist. So I put the story in Excel and find a sentence I can illustrate. In one story, an Indian chief takes a concubine, and she is described as having tattoos. This is what I illustrated. Of course, what I draw is not necessarily what other people might imagine when reading the same scene.”
The first exhibition of this collection took place in August 2023 at Rehovot’s Yad Labanim, attracting many visitors, though the events of October 7 truncated the show’s expected run.
Later, his works were displayed in the gallery of the Jerusalem Theatre, and piqued the interest of Galia Duchin Ariel, founder of the Global Art Gallery in Tel Aviv. She booked Langbeheim for a solo exhibition at the gallery, at 13 Merkaz Ba’alei Melaha Street, scheduled for October 6 to November 6. The grand opening will be on October 9 at noon.
Langbeheim creates his paintings in his home studio, which doubles as a safe room. “In the last three years, since we have 11 grandchildren, there have always been people sleeping there,” he said with a chuckle.
The Langbeheims’ three children all live in Israel. The oldest, Avi, resides in Hannaton, a kibbutz in northern Israel, and is working on the rehabilitation of the Gaza border communities. Their daughter, Tanya, is a rabbanit kehilatit (community religious leader) in Kibbutz Tirat Zvi and other northern communities. “And the youngest, Hagai, lives two houses from us, in Rehovot. He works with a medical diagnostics company.”
In January and February 2027, a new series of Langbeheim’s works will be exhibited at the Jerusalem Theatre. These are the fruit of his new project – paintings illustrating the stories of Rabbi Nahman of Breslov.

UN's Albanese claims Jews in Nazi camps were called ‘Muslims,’ distorts history of 'antisemitism'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
00:32:16 UTC
09:32:16 KST

During the Holocaust, Jews being taken to the gas chambers in Nazi concentration camps were referred to as “the Muslims,” UN Special Rapporteur on the Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese claimed in an interview with the Latin American and Caribbean Confederation of State Workers (CLATE) published earlier this month.
“In fact, when they were being taken to the gas chambers, there are some accounts of life in the concentration camps saying that Jews were called ‘the Muslims,’” Albanese said.
The term Muselmann, German for “Muslim,” was used at Auschwitz and other Nazi concentration camps to refer to prisoners in a state of extreme exhaustion or suffering severe symptoms of starvation, according to the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial. The term, whose etymology “has not been definitively explained,” referred to prisoners in this physical state and was not a Nazi racial classification identifying Jews as Muslims.
According to the Memorial, prisoners categorized as Muselmänner often died soon afterward or were chosen to be executed.
Albanese made the assertion that “Jews were called ‘the Muslims’” as part of a broader argument that antisemitism originally encompassed discrimination against the broader category of “Semitic peoples,” rather than Jews specifically.
Albanese overrides history of antisemitism
“When the word ‘antisemitism’ was coined, it referred to anyone who was not European and who came from the Middle East,” Albanese said.
While stating that “Jews were Semites,” she went on to assert that, because they were the “largest such group present in Europe,” the word evolved to “overlap with the concept of anti-Judaism” before later coming to refer specifically to prejudice against Jews.
“So there was a racist hatred of the non-white, of the non-pure, of the non-Christian, which then crystallized into antisemitism as hatred of Jews,” she said.
Albanese subsequently acknowledged that hatred of Jews “as Jews” exists and is “extremely serious,” but added that "it must not be confused with criticism of the State of Israel."
History of the term ‘antisemitism’
Contrary to Albanese’s claim, however, the term “antisemitism” was originally created specifically to refer to hostility toward Jews.
According to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, the term was coined in 1879 by German journalist Wilhelm Marr “to designate anti-Jewish campaigns [and] was spread through use by anti-Jewish political movements and the general public.” The IHRA notes that the term has “since its inception referred to prejudice against Jews alone.”
While the term “Semitic” refers to a group of languages, including Hebrew and Arabic, “antisemitism” has historically referred specifically to hostility toward Jews. Merriam-Webster defines the term as “hostility toward or discrimination against Jews as a religious, ethnic, or racial group.”
Albanese's history of antisemitism
Albanese has come under scrutiny over allegations of antisemitism and anti-Israel bias numerous times in the past, particularly by the United Nations watchdog UN Watch.
Slamming the rapporteur's comments in the interview, the NGO wrote, "Even in Nazi death camps: She cannot name Jew-hatred without replacing the Jews."
In another instance, Albanese called the State of Israel the "common enemy of humanity" when delivering remarks at the Al Jazeera Forum in Doha earlier this year.
Referring to the Jewish state with “the language of collective demonization... echoes some of the darkest chapters in modern history,” responded Combat Antisemitism Movement's Director of European Affairs Shannon Seban.
In 2024, Albanese posted on X/Twitter, in response to French President Emmanuel Macron, who called the October 7 Hamas massacre "the largest antisemitic massacre of our century," saying: "The greatest antisemitic massacre of our century? No, @EmmanuelMacron. The victims of 7/10 were not killed because of their Judaism but in response to Israel's oppression."
Albanese has repeatedly drawn parallels between Israeli policies and fascist or Nazi regimes, while denying Jewish people's right to self-determination and self-defense under the UN Charter.

The United States and Russia have relaxed rules for combat AI: machines may be given more freedom to decide whom to attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
03:28:06 EEST
09:28:06 KST

The United States and Russia have relaxed rules for combat AI: machines may be given more freedom to decide whom to attack
Kyiv • UNN
The draft UN rules removed the mandatory human verification of a target before a strike. This could increase the risk of mistaken attacks and civilian casualties.
The United States and Russia succeeded in weakening a number of proposed restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence in lethal autonomous weapons. In particular, the requirement that a human verify an AI-selected military target before a strike was removed from the document, The Washington Post reports, writes UNN.
Details
The issue concerns UN negotiations on future international rules governing the use of autonomous weapons. According to the publication, they represented the biggest progress in recent years toward a potential global agreement in this area.
However, during the final stage of the negotiations, the U.S. and Russian delegations secured the removal of several safeguards at once. In particular, the requirements that systems operate "predictably" and "reliably" were removed from the text, as was a provision on taking into account the ethical aspects of using AI in combat.
What threat could this pose to people
The greatest concern was caused by the removal of a provision requiring a human to verify a military target identified by artificial intelligence before a strike was carried out.
In simple terms, this concerns the risk of the emergence of combat systems in which an algorithm could independently find and select a target, while human control over the final decision would be weaker or not guaranteed at all by international rules.
This could mean that machines would be able to make life-and-death decisions without human control
According to her, the consequences could include a greater number of civilian casualties, difficulties in determining who is responsible for an erroneous strike, and a faster transition to automated warfare.
The particular danger lies in the speed of such systems. If states deploy autonomous weapons on a mass scale, algorithms could potentially detect targets and respond much faster than humans. In the event of an error, misidentification, or incorrect data, there may be significantly less time for human intervention.

EC says SIR decisions taken unanimously by full commission
NEW DELHI: Election Commission asserted Saturday that the decisions regarding special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were taken unanimously by chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.The statement came following the first meeting of the "full" Commission after a report in The Indian Express suggested the CEC disregarded the views of the two ECs on SIR-related calls, which sparked a political row, with the opposition targeting the govt and the CEC.
"The order for SIR issued on 24.6.2025 for all States/UTs, starting with Bihar, followed by West Bengal and 30 other States/UTs was issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission," the EC said.It also denied the claim that Sandhu and Joshi wrote to the Cabinet secretary to flag concerns over policy matters or IT processes.SIR has been implemented in 20 states and UTs and is under way in 12 others. The poll panel also refuted the claim that Sandhu and Joshi wrote separate letters to the cabinet secretary to flag their concerns about policy matters or processes adopted by EC's IT division over which they no longer had control.
The letter was "related to the work of an officer on deputation to EC. The work re-distribution orders issued by the officer concerned were not actually implemented after the orders of the two commissioners and the oversight over the IT division by the DEC was never actually withdrawn," EC said.The report said Sandhu and Joshi had called the move "a clear violation" of the law that governs EC and sought action against senior DEC Maneesh Garg, and linked the commissioners' objections to field officers allegedly being locked out of ECINET making it a "centralised" software directly controlled by EC.The allegations linking the commissioners' objections to SIR and alleged lack of access to field officers to ECINET were seized upon by opposition to point their guns at the CEC. LoP Rahul Gandhi demanded he be imprisoned while opposition appeared set to seek his removal afresh.
Saturday's full commission meeting and the statement issued later sought to fix this; it cleared the air point by point, besides conveying the message that the three members had resolved their internal issues.EC decided to concede on a slew of matters raised by the commissioners through internal notes, deciding that the agenda for all meetings shall henceforth be circulated in advance and the minutes issued. Also, annual performance appraisal reports of all officers would be completed by Dec 31 every year. The statement said all directions issued by the commissioners to the officers of the commission will be complied with and foreign trips for officers approved by the full commission.On opposition's claim of disenfranchisement of 13 crore voters in SIR, EC said the final figure of electors will be known only after final publication of the roll in the remaining 12 states of Phase 3.

Lavrov jokingly evades question on Russia’s alleged targeting of Romanian base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 27. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, speaking at a press conference following the high-level week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, has jokingly evaded a question on whether Russia still views the Romanian base in Deveselu as a target due to the American weaponry stationed there.
"Well, that’s a secret," the Russian foreign minister responded with a laugh.
His comment came after a journalist representing a Romanian media outlet reminded the minister of remarks by Russian President Vladimir Putin, who once stated that the Romanian base was among Russia's targets because of the US weapons located there, and asked Lavrov whether Russia was "still targeting Romania."
The situation the journalist referred to occurred about a decade ago. On May 12, 2016, then-NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg, speaking at the Romanian military base in Deveselu (Olt County in the country's south, 180 kilometers from Bucharest), officially announced the operational readiness of the US Aegis missile defense system deployed there. Shortly thereafter, speaking at a press conference following talks with the Greek Prime Minister, the Russian leader stated that under these circumstances, Russia would be compelled to take countermeasures to minimize the threat posed by the deployment of US missile defense elements in Romania. Putin noted at the time that while missiles with a range of 500 km were being deployed there, their range would increase to 1,000 km within a few years.
The Romanian Foreign Ministry subsequently issued a statement asserting that the missile defense agreement with the US governs the defensive nature of the Deveselu system, emphasizing that it is not directed against Russia.

It has long been known that, in addition to supplying weapons and materials to Russia, North Korea is sending its own troops directly to fight against Ukraine. At the same time, North Korea itself is upgrading its weapons based on combat experience in Ukraine. It is also adopting new types of weapons, some of which are Russian-made,” he noted.
According to Budanov, North Korea has already established mass production of single-use attack drones. In the opinion of the head of the Presidential Office, this in no way contributes to stability in the Korean region.
“And when you see how rapidly the North Korean regime is militarizing, the question naturally arises: why? First and foremost—to be prepared for active combat operations in its region. Incidentally, just recently there was another incident on the demarcation line between the Republic of Korea and North Korea. The situation is escalating by the day. And it’s only a matter of time before a trigger event occurs that could lead to uncontrollable consequences,” he added.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 22, North Korea tested a guided projectile from an upgraded 240-mm multiple launch rocket system (MLRS) with an improved guidance system and increased range.
